He tried it again, slower, listening for the click. Still nothing, which meant the problem was not in his house at all. It was somewhere up the line, out on the street, invisible.

"Power's out for the whole block," his dad called from the porch. "Might as well come outside while it lasts."

The street was strange without its orange porch lamps and glowing windows. Arthur and his sister Maya stood on the grass, and Maya was the first to notice. "Look up," she said. "There are way more stars than usual." Arthur looked. The sky was crowded with them, a pale smudged river of light running across the dark. They argued about whether that river of stars was real or a cloud, and their dad mediated by suggesting they figure it out instead of shouting.

Maya still had battery on her phone. She searched and read out loud: "A 2016 world atlas of light pollution estimated that about 80 percent of North Americans can't see the Milky Way from where they live." She frowned. "It's called the Milky Way. That smudge."

"So that's it," Arthur said, working it through. "The streetlights and everything, all that artificial light, they wash it out. But tonight everything's dark." He thought of it like a simple equation: less ground light, more stars visible. He wanted proof. He clicked his flashlight on and held it near his face, staring upward. The faint stars closest to the horizon seemed to fade. He clicked it off, and they crept back.

"Try it again," Maya said, holding out her phone with its bright screen.

He did, twice more, and each time the stars near the light dimmed. Overhead a skein of migratory geese crossed the Milky Way, stitching a dark line through the pale river, and Arthur kept watching until the last of them passed.

Mason laced his cleats in the locker room, but his eyes kept drifting to the girl sitting two benches down, pulling on a helmet just like his. Her name was Priya, and she was trying out for the boys' baseball team with everybody else. A boy named Derek stomped over and said, "This is the boys' team. You can't be in here."

"The gym is open tryouts for baseball," Priya said calmly. "It says so on the sheet."

"There's a girls' softball team," Derek insisted. "So why would they let you..."

Mason wondered about that too. Why would the school run open tryouts if there was a whole separate team for girls? There had to be a reason, some rule working behind the scenes that nobody could see, like a current under the ice. He thought about how you might deduce it. If the school offered softball, that might be one factor, but maybe it wasn't the only one. Maybe the school had to let her try out no matter what.

"Come on," Mason said to Derek, "let's just go. Tryouts start in two minutes."

Out on the field, Coach Ramos set up a hitting rotation. Priya stepped into the cage fourth and smashed a line drive into the gap in left field. Derek stared. Mason noticed that Coach didn't even blink, as if a girl trying out were the most ordinary thing in the world. That was a clue. Coaches follow rules, Mason thought, even rules that aren't posted on the gym door.

After tryouts, he checked the athletic handbook on the bulletin board outside the locker room, running his finger down the pages. There it was, plain as a box score: Title IX, a U.S. law signed in 1972, bans discrimination based on sex in schools that receive federal money. And it had been applied to their sports programs. So that was the hidden rule. It covered the whole school, which meant Priya's tryout wasn't a favor or an accident. It was the law doing its quiet work.

The next day Mason found Derek by the lockers. "I figured out the Priya thing," he said. "It's Title IX, a U.S. law signed in 1972, banning discrimination based on sex in schools that receive federal money. It got applied to sports programs too. She has the same right to try out as us."

Derek frowned. "So my hypothetical girls-only baseball world isn't happening?"

"Not at this school," Mason said. He slung his bag over his shoulder. "Rosters get posted at three. Want to walk down and see who made it?"

Derek snapped his locker shut and followed him down the hall.

Alexa sat cross-legged on her bed with her notebook open and her door shut, which meant her brother had to knock before barging in. She wrote three words across the top of the page: stomache, sleep, school. For two weeks her stomach had knotted up like a wrung-out towel every morning, and last night she had lain awake until the ceiling turned gray with dawn. Was it the math test? The test was over now, but the knot was still there. That was the pattern she couldn't figure out. If the anxious feeling were only about the test, it should have vanished when the test did. Maybe she was missing the real cause, the way you miss a leak because the water shows up on a faraway ceiling.

She had budgeted her worry time like her dad budgeted money, giving herself ten minutes after dinner to feel anxious and then closing the drawer. It hadn't worked. The feeling leaked out anyway, into her intestine, her chest, her dreams about showing up to class with no shoes on. Her friend Priya knocked then, two soft raps, and Alexa waved her in.

"You look like you're doing a science experiment," Priya said, plopping onto the rug.

"Kind of. I'm trying to find the cause of my stomach knots. I ruled out the math test." Alexa turned the notebook so Priya could see.

Priya tilted her head. "Can I tell you something? Last year mine got so bad I couldn't eat lunch at school. It lasted months and it was messing up everything, so I told my mom, and she took me to a doctor. The doctor said feeling anxious sometimes is normal, but when it's really intense, lasts a long time and gets in the way of daily life, it can be an anxiety disorder. And that it's treatable." She shrugged. "It got better. Not like a trivial little thing you shake off, but actually better, because I got help."

Alexa stared at her list. So the problem might have a name, and a name might have a fix. She flipped to a clean page and wrote, "Tell Mom. Ask about doctor." Then she underlined it twice and slid the notebook across the rug.

"Can you come with me when I show her?"

Scarlett raced through the library doors with her sketchbook under her arm and exactly forty minutes before the poster contest entries were due. The task was to draw your favorite place, and she had chosen the reading corner right here, with its worn green chair and the tall window behind it. She plopped down, grabbed a pencil from the shared box on the craft shelf, and started sketching fast.

The poster had to be bold. Judges walking past a wall of entries would give each one about two seconds. But when she held up her sketch of the chair, her lines looked pale and tired, as if the drawing itself wanted a nap. She scrutinized the paper, then the pencil, and noticed tiny letters stamped on the barrel: 4H. Last week, in Mrs. Okafor's art bin, she had grabbed a pencil stamped 6B and it had made rich, velvety darks. She turned the box over and found a jumble of Hs and Bs, all mixed together like camouflage, hiding the one she needed.

"I bet it's the letters," she whispered. She lined up four pencils on the table: 4H, H, 2B, 6B. One by one she drew a short stroke with each, pressing the same way each time. The 4H stroke was faint. The 6B stroke came out dark and soft as charcoal dust, darker than the 4H by a mile. She grinned so wide a boy at the next table looked over. "What are you doing, science?"

"Sort of," Scarlett said. "H is hardness and B is blackness. So this 6B is my new best friend."

She remembered the library's "shelf of eloquent posters," the fancy ones the librarians made for book month, and how their dark lettering had jumped out from down the hall. That was the look she wanted. With the 6B she redrew the chair, layered the window shadow until the paper seemed to glow, and added a cat curled on the cushion that had not been in her plan at all.

At the front desk she slid her entry across the counter with two minutes to spare. The librarian held it up to the light.

"Now that," the librarian said, "you can read from across the parking lot."

Scarlett said, "6B. Blackness."

Luca had watched the district swim finals on his cousin's phone four times already, and by the time the school bus rattled past the bakery on Miller Street, he was watching it a fifth. On the tiny screen, Rafael Deng touched the wall and threw his fists up. The silver medalist, a kid from Hollow Creek named Osei, had lost by four hundredths of a second. "Four hundredths," Luca muttered. "That's less than a blink."

Marcus slid into the seat across the aisle, crunching the brittle shell of a candy he'd smuggled out of last period. "You know who won, right? Rafael's ranked first in the whole league." He held up the sports app on his own phone. "Osei's ranked third. So Rafael's way better."

"Maybe," Luca said slowly. He didn't actually think maybe. He thought no, and it bothered him that he couldn't say why yet. Rankings were everywhere, on the app, on the news, even on the laminated list of cafeteria milk prices, and they all looked like they were telling you everything. First meant best. Third meant not as good. Case closed.

But the numbers on the race results page gave times, not just places, so Luca tried something. He wrote the top eight times on the back of his history worksheet, one under another, and subtracted each one from the next. First to second: four hundredths. Second to third: three hundredths. Then seventh to eighth, and his pencil stopped. The gap there was eleven whole seconds. He did it again in case he'd borrowed wrong. Eleven seconds. "Marcus," he said, "look at this. The ranking says they're all one step apart, but the steps aren't the same size. Rafael's first and Osei's second, and it's four hundredths. Seventh and eighth are a whole swim apart."

Marcus peered at the worksheet, chewing. "So the ranking is a lie?"

"It's not a lie, it's just..." Luca hunted for the word. "It shows who beat who. It doesn't show by how much. First and second could be four hundredths apart, or a whole minute apart, and the list looks exactly the same."

Marcus grinned and pulled out a crumpled paper from his backpack, the class ballot for team captain, still folded from lunch. "Okay, smart guy, then figure this out. The vote was me versus Dana, and I lost." He smoothed the ballot flat on his knee. "Does that mean Dana crushed me?"

Luca took the paper and counted the tallies under each name, his lips moving, the bus swaying around the corner by the gym. Then he started to laugh, and it took him a second to get the words out. "Marcus. It was fourteen to thirteen."

Marcus stared at the tally marks, then out the window, then back at the paper. "So technically," he said, "I lost by less than a blink." He held up his hand, and Luca high-fived it so hard the brittle candy crumbs jumped right off his worksheet.

Gavin raised his hand so fast his chair scraped the floor. Mr. Okafor had just asked whether anyone could settle the argument Gavin and Priya had been having since Tuesday, and Gavin was not going to let the moment slip away. "Priya says most students at our school walk to school," he announced. "I think that's wrong. Almost everybody gets dropped off. The car line every morning goes all the way past the gym."

"That's your opinion," Priya said, arms folded. "You can't prove a thing by looking at one line of cars."

Mr. Okafor didn't jump in, which annoyed Gavin, because usually teachers jumped in constantly. Instead the class sat there with the question hanging in the air like the smell of disinfectant from the hallway. Gavin stared at the sparse corkboard by the window, where only two faded posters hung, and tried to think. He remembered last fall, when he'd claimed the cafeteria ran out of pizza by Wednesday, and Maya had counted for a whole week and shown it lasted until Thursday. He'd been wrong then, too, and it had stung, but not as much as being wrong without knowing would have.

"Wait," he said slowly. "It's not just an opinion. It's a claim. Like, it could be checked. Nobody has checked it yet, but we could." Priya tilted her head. "How?" she asked. "Follow everybody home?" Someone laughed. "A survey," Gavin said. "We ask every student how they get to school and count it up. Then we'd know if most of them walk or not." The word felt good in his mouth, solid, like a handle on a door he could actually open.

Mr. Okafor suggested they postpone the debate until they had data, and the class agreed to run the survey at lunch on Thursday. On Thursday, Gavin stood at the cafeteria door with a clipboard, pencil shaking slightly from too much excitement and not enough breakfast. The first twenty kids mostly said "bus," which surprised him. By the time the third lunch period started, his tally sheet was a mess of slashes and smudged graphite, but a pattern was climbing out of it anyway, one he hadn't predicted and Priya hadn't either.

They counted the sheets in Mr. Okafor's room after school, the radiator ticking, the hallway outside gone quiet. Priya totaled the walkers; Gavin totaled everyone else. He looked at her total, then at his own, then out the window at the empty car line loop, still painted yellow. "So I was wrong," he said, "but I was right that we could find out." Priya grinned and spun the clipboard toward him. "Count them again," she said. "I want to see your face when you get to the end."

The zit had appeared overnight, dead center on Emmett's chin, and school pictures were tomorrow morning at 8:40. He discovered it in the car's side mirror while his mom drove to Halsted's Pharmacy for toothpaste and laundry detergent. He leaned toward the glass, tilting his jaw. The bump was small but determined, like it had been appointed to its post specifically to ruin the photo.

"You've been staring at that mirror for three blocks," his mom said.

"I'm not staring." He turned forward. His little sister Ivy, mercifully absorbed in her tablet, didn't look up.

At the pharmacy, his mom headed for the detergent aisle, so Emmett drifted to the wall of face washes near the pharmacy counter. He had never once in his life looked at this shelf. There were at least thirty bottles, blue and orange and green, promising things like "oil control" and "deep clean." He picked one up, then another, comparing. The labels used the word "oil" over and over, but he didn't know why oil mattered. His face wasn't oily. It was just... broken out.

"Which one works?" said a voice. A girl from his grade, Priya, stood beside him holding two bottles, turning them over to read the backs.

"I have no idea," Emmett admitted. "I got a huge one on my chin and pictures are tomorrow."

"Same. Except mine are on my forehead." Priya held up a bottle. "Listen to this. It says it fights oil, so I looked up why. Puberty hormones make the oil glands in your skin produce more oil, and that oil is called sebum, and it clogs your pores and that's how you get acne. The whole thing is just plumbing."

Emmitt turned his own bottle over. "So the wash is trying to get the sebum out before it clogs anything."

"That's what I figured." Priya compared her two bottles again, squinting at the fine print. "This one says 'for oily skin' but doesn't actually say it removes oil. This one is explicit about it, right here: 'removes excess oil.' So this one."

He grabbed a matching bottle. Then he hesitated, because a thought had been building. "Wait. If hormones cause it, washing won't stop new oil from coming."

"Right, but it clears out what's there tonight." Priya shrugged. "It's the best we've got before 8:40 tomorrow."

His mom rounded the aisle with the detergent and gave the bottles a curious look. "New skincare routine?"

"Emergency," Emmett said.

At home, he washed his face exactly as the label directed, twice because he was nervous, and studied the chin in the bathroom mirror. The zit remained, slightly less angry, a small wave in what he suspected might turn out to be a tsunami. He set an alarm for 6:45 so he could wash again in the morning, and put the bottle on the sink where he couldn't miss it.

At breakfast, Ivy pointed at his chin. "What's that?"

"Sebum," Emmett said, and grabbed his backpack.

The lights went out at 7:40, right in the middle of Alexandra's homework, and the whole house sank into a black so complete she couldn't even find her own elbow. "The power's out," her little brother Marcus announced from the hallway, as if she might not have noticed.

Alexandra fished the flashlight from the kitchen drawer and did some thinking while Marcus bumped into the coffee table behind her. The streetlights outside were dark too, which meant it wasn't just their house. And on the walk home from school, after the storm, she had seen a wire lying across the sidewalk two blocks over. It had looked harmless, dull and quiet, not sparking or humming like wires in movies. But her science teacher had once said something Alexandra had never forgotten: a fallen power line can still carry deadly electricity even when it is not sparking, so it should be treated as live, kept well away from, and reported. Mr. Okafor had made them all repeat it twice, which had seemed ridiculous at the time and now seemed like the smartest thing anyone had ever done.

"Marcus, do not eat that cheese," she said, shining the flashlight on him. He froze with the block halfway to his mouth. "That's for dinner. It's the most nutritious thing we have until the fridge situation stabilizes." The situation, as far as she could tell, was that the temperature inside would fluctuate every time he opened the door to graze, and the cheese would not survive his snacking until morning.

Her phone was at nine percent, so she typed fast: "Mom. Power out on our street. I think it's the downed wire on Elm, two blocks from school. I saw it on the way home. I did NOT touch it, I stayed way back. Please call it in to the power company, my battery is almost dead." Send. The battery dropped to eight percent, then seven, as if to add commentary.

Twenty minutes later the porch lit up, the refrigerator hummed like a released prisoner, and headlights swept the window. Marcus cheered. Alexandra's phone buzzed once before it died: "Reported. Proud of you. Also I'm bringing pizza, keep your paws off the cheese." Alexandra laughed and hid the cheese behind the milk anyway.

Michael had exactly four dollars and seventy-five cents, and the gumball machine at Nguyen's Corner Store held a red gumball that he wanted more than anything. The machine took only quarters, and the change machine by the register was broken, so he dumped his crumpled bills and random pennies onto the counter and started counting. Mr. Nguyen watched him sort, then slid a piece of graph paper across the counter.

"Your sister was in here yesterday," Mr. Nguyen said. "She left this." The paper had a coordinate grid on it, with a line drawn through some points, and at the top, in his sister Amy's handwriting: 2x + 3 = 9, and then (3, 5) circled twice.

Michael frowned. "That's my math homework," he said. "And her battleship game." Last night Amy had called (3, 5) on him, and he had insisted his ship was safe because he moved up five first and then across three. Amy had laughed so hard her milk almost came out her nose, and then she had refused to tell him why. She only said the answer was in the equation.

He counted his money again. Two quarters short. Mr. Nguyen was already ringing up a customer, so Michael sat on the crate by the ice cream freezer and stared at the paper. He tried the equation the way his teacher had started it in class. Something times two, plus three, makes nine. He thought about six, because six plus three was nine. Then the something had to be three, because three times two was six. So the line crossed x at three.

"So x is three," he muttered, and looked at the circled pair. Three had to be the first number. But which way did it go? He remembered Amy's battleship call, and her laughing. Maybe the first number was the across one, not the up one. He borrowed Mr. Nguyen's pencil and found 3 on the horizontal line at the bottom, moved across to it, then counted up five and marked a dot. Then he checked two more points from the grid, moving across by the first number and up by the second, and every single dot landed right on Amy's line. He tested it once more, carefully, in case the first try was just luck. The dots still landed on the line.

Michael grinned. He turned the paper over and wrote Amy a battleship challenge of his own, with coordinates all along the line. If she called (2, 7), she'd better mean across two first. Then he pushed the coins and bills across the counter. "Three dollars and seventy-five cents," he said, "and I'll sweep the floor for a dollar." Mr. Nguyen handed him a broom and, when the floor was done, two quarters.

At home, Michael held the gumballs in one hand and the paper in the other. He called out, "Amy! (1, 9)!" He heard a groan from behind the couch, then the sound of her battleship sinking.

Grandma Wei arrived on Thursday, and by Friday night Isla had a problem: what to wear to her cousin Marisol's wedding shower on Saturday. Grandma had barely unpacked before she started pulling clothes out of Isla's closet and sorting them into two piles, one for yes and one for no.

"Not the white dress," Grandma said, holding up Isla's favorite one like it was a wet sock.

"It's a wedding thing," Isla said. "Marisol's whole theme is white. The invitations are white. The cake is white. The bride even wears white."

Grandma set the dress on the no pile and smoothed it flat, as if to preserve its feelings. "White is for mourning at funerals," she said. "In traditional Chinese culture, that is what we wear. For the dead." Then she pointed at Isla's rust-colored skirt. "Wear this."

Isla stared at her. She had never heard anything like this. Her brain started running its usual algorithm for arguments with Grandma: state facts, provide evidence, lose anyway.

Dad came through with the lasagna, and Isla got her chance. "Dad, tell Grandma white is a wedding color."

Dad put down the dish and rubbed his neck. "Both are true," he said. "Lots of Western brides wear white. And in Grandma's tradition, white is worn for mourning. Different people, same color, opposite meanings." He gave the no pile a guilty glance. "At your Aunt Po's funeral, everyone wore white. Marisol's wedding, the bride will too. Nobody's wrong."

Isla chewed on that through half a plate of lasagna. Same color. Two meanings. That meant the shower was going to be a room full of people doing opposite things at the same time, and only some of them would know it. She imagined Marisol's grandmother from Mexico, her neighbors, her own grandma, all handing gifts and thinking completely different thoughts about identical white napkins.

So she tested it. "Grandma, what if everyone at the party wears white except me? Won't I look like I'm at the wrong event?"

"Then you will look like the only person there with respect," Grandma said.

"That's a rebellious plan," Isla said. "Wearing not-white to a white party."

"Rebellious," Grandma agreed, spearing a meatball.

Isla tried one more angle. "Grandma, Marisol asked me to hand out the favors. White boxes with white ribbons. If I wear the rust skirt, the pictures will look strange."

Grandma put down her fork. For a moment Isla thought the algorithm had finally found a winning input. Then Grandma said, "The boxes are white?"

"Every single one."

Grandma looked at the window for a while. "Then the boxes are for mourning," she said, "and Marisol must pick new boxes, or I must pick new eyes." She picked up her fork again and went back to the lasagna. "Hand me the bread, and on Saturday you wear the rust."

Jaxson sat at the kitchen table with a box of tissues, a trash can between his feet, and a nose that refused to cooperate. He blew for the ninth time that hour. Nothing came out, yet his nose still felt packed tight, like someone had stuffed a sock in each nostril.

"That's it," he said to his little sister, Priya, who was drawing a monarchy at the counter, a queen with a very tall crown and about forty pet hamsters. "I'm nominating chicken soup as the cure. Mom said it's in the freezer." He microwaved a bowl, ate it slowly, and waited. His throat felt better. His nose did not. He blew again, hard, and got almost nothing. "That doesn't make sense," he said. "If my nose is full of mucus, where is it? Why can't I blow it out?"

Priya looked up from her hamster palace. "Maybe it's not mucus." She had been home from school with the same cold last week, and she'd spent an entire afternoon on the couch with Mom's phone reading about it. "Mom read me that a stuffy nose during a cold is caused mainly by swollen blood vessels and inflamed tissue in the lining of the nose, not only by a buildup of mucus. Your nose is puffy inside. It's swollen shut."

Jaxson touched the side of his nose gently, thinking. If the blockage was swelling and not snot, then blowing harder was useless. Maybe even a bad idea. What helped swelling? He ran a towel under hot water, wrung it out, and held the warm cloth over his nose and cheeks like a bandit mask. Priya giggled. "You look like an impoverished robber." He breathed through the warmth, in and out, and slowly, the tightness loosened. Not gone, but looser.

"Okay," he said, setting down the tissues for good. "I'm done fighting a swamp that isn't even there." He slid the box across the table to Priya. "Keep these. Your turn is coming." Priya pointed her crayon at him and said, "Then you'll owe me a hot towel, bandit."

Alexis laced his skates in the bench area of Riverside Ice Arena and watched his best friend Dante glide past the tryout line with his usual speed. That was the strange part. Dante was the fastest skater in sixth grade, but this morning he had wobbled twice during warm-ups, and when Coach Reyes blew the whistle, Dante's stop was so abrupt that he nearly fell over backward. Alexis filed that away and took his own turn around the cones.

The tryouts were for the school hockey team, and thirty kids had shown up to participate. Alexis wanted a forward spot, but so did Marcus Tran, who had been talking all week about how he was going to take it. Marcus was fast, too. During the second drill, Alexis noticed something. Marcus kept yawning on the bench. When the puck came to him, he reacted late, half a second behind, like a video with bad lag.

Between drills, Alexis sat next to him. "You look like you're skating through glue," Alexis said.

"I was up till two playing Starfall Six," Marcus admitted. "I only slept six hours. I figured I'd be fine."

Alexis had spent a week researching sleep for a science project, mostly so he could win arguments about bedtime. "Kids our age are supposed to get nine to twelve hours a night," he said. "Even teenagers only get to drop down to eight to ten. Six isn't on the chart for anybody."

"Whatever," Marcus said, and skated off, wobbling on the first turn.

Alexis thought about it while he waited for the scrimmage. He had a theory, one he couldn't see directly: the problem wasn't skating skill, it was an invisible cause, missing sleep, slowing everyone who had it. He could test it. His own plan had been to stay up nervous and wake at six, but instead he had gone to bed at nine thirty, and his legs felt springy on every crossover. When the scrimmage started, he cut left, took the pass, and scored on a rebound while Marcus watched the play arrive a beat too late.

At the end, Coach Reyes posted the list on the rink door. Alexis made forwards. Dante, who had crashed into the boards twice, made alternates. Marcus's name was not on the paper at all.

On the walk out, Dante pulled his hood up. "My cousin said there's a supplement for this. He's basically an entrepreneur, he sells protein powder to eighth graders out of his locker."

"Forget the powder," Alexis said. "Try nine hours."

Dante groaned. "That's so much sleeping."

Alexis pointed at the scoreboard clock, which still glowed above the empty ice. "You've got tryouts again in March. That's like ninety nights. You could test it properly."

Dante squinted at the clock, did some visible math, and said, "Fine. But if I turn into a grandpa who goes to bed at eight thirty, you're carrying my bag."

Alexis swung his own bag over his shoulder and said, "Deal," and the doors hissed shut behind them.

The story Kayla had written was called "The Race," and it was one hundred percent terrible, though she hadn't known that until her brother Dex read it aloud at the kitchen table while she ate her cereal.

"The morning was cool. The track was quiet. Maya was nervous. The other runners were fast. The race was about to begin." Dex paused. He read the next line. Then the next. By the fifth sentence his voice had gone flat as a pancake left out overnight, and by the tenth he was yawning into the page. "Sorry," he said. "It's just... nothing about it moves."

"You're the one who's not moving," Kayla said, but she took the draft back and stared at it. The dilemma was real. Ms. Reyes wanted a final copy tomorrow, and Kayla's problem wasn't that she had nothing to say. She had lots to say. It all just sat there.

She counted the words in each sentence. Four. Five. Four. Five. Six. Four. Every sentence was about the same length, like fence posts in a row. She wondered if that could be the trouble, though she couldn't see how sentence length would change anything on paper. It seemed logical, at least, to test it. She grabbed a pen.

First she cut the weak adjectives. "Cool morning" became "morning." "Fast runners" became just "the runners," because Maya could show they were fast by losing to them. Then she rebuilt the opening. She made one sentence long and winding, following Maya all the way from the parking lot to the starting line with her shoelaces double-knotted and her heart going like a drum. Then she made the next one very short.

"Nobody looked at her."

Dex glanced over from his toast. "Better," he said, which from Dex was practically a parade.

She kept going. Some sentences she stretched until they nearly snapped; others she chopped down to two or three words, and those little ones landed hard after the long ones, the way a single drop of water sounds loud after rain. She read a paragraph aloud to calibrate the effect, quietly at first, then in a full voice, because quiet wasn't telling her much. The rhythm was there. When every sentence had been about the same length, the story had sounded monotonous; mixed lengths gave it something like a pulse.

At the kitchen table the next morning, she slid the new draft across to Dex. He picked it up with the expression of a boy expecting to be bored.

"The gun went off. Maya ran."

He looked up. "Keep going," he said.

Emily had been assigned to sort carrots at the food bank for two hours, and so far the carrots were winning. They came in boxes from a farm stand, and in every box, strange as it seemed, some carrots were wrapped separately in paper with a rubber band. Not the pretty ones. The crooked, split, ordinary ones.

At the third box she stopped and looked down the sorting table at Mr. Alvarez, whose granddaughter had dragged him along to volunteer. "Why would anyone wrap the ugly carrots?" she asked.

Mr. Alvarez squinted at one. "My grandmother used to do this. She called it gleaning."

"Gleaning?"

"From an old story. The Book of Leviticus, in the Hebrew Bible, tells farmers to leave the edges of their fields unharvested, for the poor and for strangers." He turned the carrot over like evidence. "No modern farm does that. But somebody here might."

So the wrapped carrots were not bizarre at all, Emily decided. They were the edges of the field. The question was who was leaving them, and why they never said so. She formed a verdict by the end of the hour: nobody at the food bank knew, because nobody at the food bank had ever asked.

She found her answer taped inside the fourth box, a folded note in pencil:

To whoever opens this. My father farmed forty acres and never once took the whole harvest. He said a field belongs partly to people you will never meet. I cannot farm, so I do this instead. Please do not tell anyone, it embarrasses my wife. Signed, a friend.

Emily read it twice, then went looking for Mr. Alvarez. He was in the back, excavating a pallet of dented cans that had slid half behind the shelving. She held out the note. He dried his hands on his jeans and read it, and then he laughed, quietly, the way you laugh at something that is not actually funny.

"That man," he said, "is doing a five-thousand-year-old thing with a rubber band."

Emily put the note back in the box, exactly where she had found it, and kept sorting. The next wrapped carrot she set down gently, like it was somebody's.

Samantha taped the folded program to her bedroom mirror so she would see it while she practiced. The order of songs ran down the page, and at the bottom, in her music teacher's handwriting, was the note she kept rereading: "After the last song, exit stage left, row by row." She hummed the second verse of "Oh, Shenandoah," stopped, and looked at the note again.

The problem was the word "left." In the mirror behind her, her bedroom door appeared on the right, but Samantha knew it was really on the left, because a mirror flips things. The audience, she thought, would be like a mirror. They would face her. So when they looked at her, her left side would be on their right. If stage left meant the left side as the audience saw it, she would walk toward the piano. If it meant her own left, she would walk toward the drums. Two options, and no way to check the answer from her bedroom.

She needed a test. At school the next day, she found Marcus, who had been in last year's concert. "When Mr. Okafor said exit stage left, which way did you actually go?" Marcus pointed toward the gym's far side, the side away from the piano. Samantha stood where a singer would stand, faced the empty bleachers, and checked which hand was on that side. Her left. She worked it out on the spot: stage left and stage right are the performers' left and right as they stand facing the audience.

The night of the concert, the gym lights radiated heat down onto the rows of singers, and Samantha felt the last song approaching, imminent and unstoppable. When the final note ended, Mr. Okafor raised his hand toward the far wing. Row by row, the singers filed off. Priya, beside Samantha, started to turn toward the piano. Samantha caught her sleeve. "Stage left is our left," she whispered, "not the audience's." Priya turned, and they stepped off together into the dark wing, where Marcus was waiting with two bottles of water.

Asher sat in the back row of his new classroom while the teacher talked about the election posters on the wall. "Some of these are propaganda," she said, "posters made to persuade you, not to inform you." Asher copied the word into his notebook, though his mind kept drifting to the moving truck parked outside his old house three states away. His whole life was in those boxes, and tomorrow he would have to face them.

He remembered the last night in the old house, when his sister Priya had dug through a mountain of boxes hunting for her bedsheets. "Nobody labeled anything," she had groaned, pulling out a frying pan, a lamp, and a box of comic books. Asher had stood in the doorway watching her work by flashlight, and an idea had started to digest slowly in his head. The boxes had no writing on them, just brown opaque flaps, all looking the same, so every single one had to be opened and searched. There had to be a better way.

Now, after his first day at the new school, he walked through the empty rooms of the new house. His parents wouldn't arrive with the truck until morning, but the first boxes, the ones they had shipped ahead, were stacked in the garage. Asher found a marker in his backpack and got to work. On each box he wrote two things: the room it belonged in, and what was inside. "Kitchen, pots and pans." "Priya's room, bedsheets." When the truck came, his uncle would only have to read a box once and carry it straight to the right place, instead of dropping everything in the living room like last time.

The next morning, the truck rumbled into the driveway. Asher handed boxes off the lift one by one, pointing with the marker. "Bathroom, up the stairs." "My room, second door." Priya grabbed a box, read the label, and grinned. "Bedsheets," she said. "You're a genius." By lunch, most of the boxes had already found their rooms, and Asher carried the last one, marked "My room, comic books," up the stairs two at a time.

Benjamin's laptop was so dilapidated that it made a sound like a dying kazoo whenever he opened more than three tabs, but it still ran a spreadsheet, which was all he needed. The problem was this: his cousin Marcus had sworn, in the family group chat, that TJ Ruiz was a better hitter than Sam Okafor, and Benjamin had exactly one weekend to prove him wrong. Batting average said Marcus was right, and Benjamin did not enjoy that.

He started copying numbers into the spreadsheet, row after row, while eating chips over the keyboard. His mother paused at the doorway and remarked that the hygiene of a desk used as a cafeteria was not something she wanted to quantify, then left him to it. He was still sulking over the averages when he remembered Saturday at his uncle Ray's sports bar, the TV turned to a baseball classic, his uncle swirling his drink.

"Some smarty-pants wrote a book called Moneyball," Uncle Ray had said. "Michael Lewis, 2003. It was about how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players." Then he had gone back to his wings, as if he hadn't just handed over a weapon.

Benjamin sat up so fast the chair squeaked. On-base percentage. Not hits. Times a player reached base, walks included. He found the columns for walks, typed the formula, and dragged it down the whole sheet, watching new numbers appear like something rising to the surface of a lake.

When he re-sorted the players by the new column, Sam Okafor climbed from eleventh to third, and TJ Ruiz sank like a stone with a family. Sam walked constantly; it didn't look exciting, so nobody talked about it, but there he was on base, inning after inning, being quietly useful. Marcus was ranking players with half the picture. Benjamin spent another hour checking, re-checking, and making the chart prettier than it needed to be, because charts that looked official won arguments.

He pasted the chart into the group chat and waited, hands folded behind his head. Three dots appeared. Then Marcus replied: "ok but I was still right about the nachos." Benjamin typed back, "Send me the nacho data and we'll see," and hit send before he could reconsider his life choices.

Colton's phone buzzed at 6:47 on Tuesday, right as he sat down to spaghetti. The skate park group chat had gone from three messages a day to forty, because someone had pasted a letter from the local paper.

The letter said the town should never have agreed to install the skate park behind the elementary school, and it ended with a sentence Colton read four times: "The new park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste." His dad leaned over his shoulder, fork in hand. "Half of that sentence you could check," Dad said, and went back to his pasta.

Colton scrolled. Ravi had written "SO TRUE what a waste of money!!" and Marisol had written "no way, the park is awesome," and then the two of them had started typing in all caps about whose fault it was. Nobody had typed anything about the two million dollars.

He put his fork down. He could not see the town's bank account from the dinner table, but a cost was the kind of thing somebody had to have written down. The Parks Department had a website. He found a page about the skate park, and there it was, a citation at the bottom pointing to the town budget, and the budget said two million dollars. So that half of the sentence was true, or at least checkable, which was not the same as agreeing with it.

But "a waste" was different. He stared at the two words. Ravi thought the money should have gone to a pool. Marisol thought the park was the best thing in town. There was no budget page for awesome. His little sister wandered through the kitchen and he asked her, out of pure curiosity, whether she thought the park was a waste. "It's where I learned to drop in," she said, and took a garlic bread stick with her.

Back in the chat, Colton typed slowly, then faster: "Two different things got mixed in one sentence. The two million dollars part checks out, I found it in the town budget. The waste part is just what the guy thinks. You can't look that one up." Ravi replied with a thinking face. Marisol replied, "wait, so we were fighting about which part?" and then, a minute later, "because I only care about the park part."

Colton looked at the two distinct arguments, one about money that could be counted and one about fun that could not, sitting there in the same sentence like they belonged together. He picked his phone back up and typed: "new rule. If you can check it, link it." Ravi sent a thumbs up. Then a link appeared, from Ravi, to a petition for the pool. "This one you can check," Ravi wrote. "It has zero signatures."

Hazel had forty dollars and a plan: new basketball shoes, the ones with the springy sole, if they went on sale before Saturday's tryouts. The mall food court smelled like pretzels, and above it all a video wall played the shoe ad on loop. "Everybody's switching," a deep voice said, while a hundred blurry feet stamped past the camera. A famous point guard Hazel kind of admired looked straight at her and said, "I don't lace up anything else." Then the screen flashed the words REVOLUTIONARY and UNSTOPPABLE in gold.

She stopped walking. Something about that ad was like the wartime posters she'd been digging through for her library project. She'd started with posters from the 1940s, stern faces and pointing fingers, and then found something better. In a dusty reference book she read that the Institute for Propaganda Analysis was founded in the United States in 1937 to teach the public how to recognize propaganda. She'd written the sentence on an index card, but she hadn't really believed people needed lessons in spotting tricks. Now, standing under a thirty-foot shoe ad, she thought maybe they did.

She tested it like a game. First ad: "Everyone's switching." Her social studies teacher would say that was a bandwagon appeal, the same move as a poster showing a whole town buying war bonds. Second: REVOLUTIONARY and UNSTOPPABLE, words so vague they meant nothing, just loaded words, the book's term for language built to push feelings instead of facts. Third: the point guard. Would he really wear those shoes if the company didn't pay him? Celebrity testimonial, she scribbled on her hand with a pen from her pocket. Three tricks in one minute. She despised feeling handled, like her forty dollars had a target painted on it.

Inside the shoe store she picked up the box. The springy sole felt the same as the plain pair on the next shelf, which cost eighteen dollars less. An ambiguous sign said SALE, but the tiny print said "selected styles," and none of the selected styles were her size. "Can I try both?" she asked the clerk, a teenager named Priya who was balancing a stack of boxes one-handed while helping an older man find wide sizes.

Priya set the boxes down. "Smart question. Half the spring is the price tag, honestly." The older man chuckled. Hazel ran the length of the aisle in each pair. The cheaper ones gripped better on the slick floor; she could feel her cuts quicker. It wasn't proof, exactly, one run down one aisle, but it was evidence.

She bought the cheaper shoes, and with the leftover money she bought a pretzel and slid half of it across the table to a boy from her school, a refugee named Amir who'd arrived in the fall and usually sat alone with nothing from the food court. "For tryouts?" he asked, pointing at the box. "For tryouts," she said, and laced them up right there, double-knotted.

"Everybody's switching," she muttered at the video wall on her way out, and walked past it in her new shoes.

Ellie had been on the couch for three days, and she was tired of soup. She propped herself up on the armrest and watched the vapor rise from her mug of lemon tea, curling and vanishing near the ceiling. Her throat still felt scratchy, and her nose was red from tissue after tissue. The math competition at school was on Friday, and she wanted more than anything to be back for it.

When Mom came home from the pharmacy, Ellie sat up with an abrupt bounce. "Did you get the medicine? The kind that kills germs?"

"Everything the doctor said to get," Mom said, holding up a bag of cough syrup, tissues, and popsicles.

"Not that. Antibiotics," Ellie said. "Lily's little brother had a sore throat, and he took antibiotics and got better fast. If I take them, I could be back at school by Friday."

Mom set down the bag. "That's for the doctor to decide. We have a video call with her in ten minutes."

When the call started, Ellie asked right away. "Can you prescribe antibiotics? I need to get better fast. I have a competition."

The doctor shook her head, not unkindly. "Antibiotics kill bacteria, but they have no effect on viruses, so they wouldn't help you. A cold or the flu is a virus. Antibiotics just don't work on it."

Ellie frowned at the screen. "Then how do I get better?"

"Rest, fluids, time. Your body does the work."

So Ellie made a plan to conserve her energy. She spent Thursday on the couch doing practice problems in her head, drinking tea, and sleeping whenever her eyes got heavy. She noticed that the more she rested, the less her throat hurt, and by Friday morning her fever was gone and her nose had almost stopped running.

At school, she slid into her seat just as the competition papers were handed out. Lily leaned over. "You made it."

"Rest and fluids," Ellie whispered, "and a lot of nothing." She picked up her pencil and read the first problem.

The gym smelled like popcorn and rubber soles, and Alexandre had a problem: his cousin Theo, the best shooter on the Ravens, had gone cold for three games, and today Coach Ramirez was watching from the bleachers, deciding who would start in the tournament. Alexandre kept a small notebook with every shot Theo took, home and away, because the local paper only printed one number and he wanted to know how it was built.

By halftime Theo had made 4 of 10, and the scoreboard screen flashed his season average: 40 percent. In the third quarter he got hot, swishing five straight, and the average ticked up to 50. The announcer's voice boomed over the squeak of sneakers. "Theo Cardoso, up ten percentage points today, folks." Two rows down, a radio reporter said into her microphone, "That same jump is a 25 percent increase for the young guard."

Alexandre stopped chewing his popcorn. Ten and twenty-five, about the same shot? He wrote both numbers and stared at them, then leaned toward the reporter. "How can it be ten and also twenty-five?" She smiled but kept talking into her recorder, so he turned to his notebook instead. He counted the season totals again, slow and careful, the way he counted everything. Both phrases pointed the same direction, from 40 to 50. Maybe they were two doors into the same room. He wanted to disclose the trick to somebody before the buzzer.

Next to him, Marcus was scribbling a sign that said MARCUS SAW IT FIRST, because his older brother worked the scoreboard clock and Marcus wanted the whole gym to know. "Check this," Alexandre said, showing him the notebook. "Ten percentage points, or a 25 percent increase. Same change, different words." Marcus squinted, then grinned. "So when the paper says Theo improved 25 percent, he only made one more shot out of ten?"

"Exactly," Alexandre said. Coach Ramirez wrote something in a small book and underlined it twice, his face neutral as a locked door, though his prescription for winning was famous: defense first, always. Theo caught a pass at the top of the key, rose, and released.

The net snapped clean, and Marcus held his sign over his head.

Marcus had been at Dev's house for exactly eleven minutes when Maya stormed through the kitchen and slammed her mug down so hard that coffee slopped across the counter. "Some people have no respect," she snapped, without looking at either of them, and then she was gone, her bedroom door booming shut behind her. Dev winced and kept arranging the ant farm on the table. "That's my sister," he said. "She's like that."

Marcus wasn't so sure. Maya had driven them to the pool last weekend and had been funny the whole way there, joking about the geese that seemed determined to colonize the whole parking lot. A person didn't just turn into a slamming-doors person overnight, did it? But maybe she did. Maybe the pool trip had been a one-time fluke and the real Maya was the mug-slamming Maya. He wanted to know, because if Maya was truly mean, he'd rather know before he asked her the big favor: she owned the only real microscope in the neighborhood, and Dev had promised they could look at the ants up close.

While Dev searched the garage for tweezers, Marcus noticed things. Maya's phone lay on the counter, screen lit up, buzzing again and again. There were missed calls, a dozen of them, all from somebody labeled Nonna. Her chair was pushed back from the table at an odd angle, like she'd jumped up mid-meal. And her coffee wasn't even coffee; it was cocoa, half untouched, which was strange for a girl who bragged about drinking three espressos a day. Maybe the slam wasn't about personality. Maybe it was about whatever was on that phone.

Then he heard her voice through the wall, thin and wobbly, the way his own voice had gone when their dog ran off last spring. "Is she okay? Tell me she's okay." Marcus stood very still. He couldn't see her, and he couldn't see what the calls were about, but he could see the shape of it now, the way you can guess at a rule after watching enough examples.

On the counter, Dev's little speaker was still playing the podcast his dad had left on. The voice was saying, "In 1977, psychologist Lee Ross named it the fundamental attribution error: we blame other people's actions on their personality while underestimating their situation." Marcus nudged Dev. "The fundamental attribution error," he whispered. "That's what I just did to your sister." Dev nodded slowly, then pointed at the hallway, where Maya was coming out with red eyes and her car keys. "Hospital bag's in the trunk," she said. "Nonna fell. You two okay here?" Marcus held up the ant farm. "Can we look at them under your microscope when you get back?" Maya managed half a smile. "If you wash my mug."

Juliette lined up at the free throw line for the third drill in a row, and her knee sent up a small, hot signal, like a match struck under her kneecap. She made the shot anyway. Coach Ruiz blew the whistle and called for layups, twenty of them, and Juliette started to run.

By layup fourteen the match had become a torch. She stopped on the baseline, hands on her knees, and pretended to be catching her breath. Across the gym, Danny from the baseball team sat on the bleachers with his arm wrapped in ice, sulking. "Pitch count," he said when he caught her looking. "Coach says I hit my limit for today." He rolled his eyes. "My arm feels fine."

Juliette had heard Danny's older brother talking last week, something about growth plates, areas of growing cartilage near the ends of kids' bones. The weird part was what he'd said next: the cartilage is weaker than the bone around it. That was why young athletes had limits on repetitive stress, limits that felt pointless because nothing hurt yet. She had tuned most of it out, thinking it was baseball stuff. Now she stood in a gym doing her twentieth layup on a knee that only complained sometimes, and wondered whether the pain was the whole warning or just the part she could see. Maybe the real damage was quiet. The thought seemed to magnify every ache she had ignored since September, including the day she'd jumped rope for an hour on a sore ankle because quitting felt like despair.

She jogged to the sideline. "Coach, my knee's been aching after practice, and it's not going away. Can I sub out of the jumping drills?"

"Smart," Coach Ruiz said. "Ice it."

Danny raised his ice pack toward her like a toast. "Look at us. Bench buddies."

She hadn't solved anything. She still didn't know if she'd been reckless or just tired, and the doctor appointment on Saturday loomed like a full-court press. But when the team ran suicides, she sat, watching, and pressed the ice against her knee until it burned cold.

Nolan got to Desh's house first, so he had the best view of the disaster. The science club's robot, built over three weekends for the county fair, sat dead in the middle of the garage, and the four members who arrived after him were already shouting.

"It's the battery," Marcus insisted. "I tested it Friday. It drains way too fast, like something is consuming all the power in ten minutes."

"You're wrong," Amelia said. "I watched the wheels on Saturday. The left one jerks. It's a motor problem."

Desh shook his head. "The wiring is the problem. I checked the circuits, and the backup sensor cable is pinched."

Nolan had been out of town and had seen nothing but a group chat full of arguing. Then Priya, the fifth member, was absent, sick with the flu. At her mother's suggestion, Nolan called her, and she asked him to read her text out loud to the group. He held up his phone.

"I only ever worked on the sensor that detects toxic gas," Nolan read. "I know that part works. I tested it with vinegar fumes Sunday. But I never saw the whole robot running. Someone else has to tell me about the rest."

Everyone went quiet. Nolan looked around the garage at four people who had each seen exactly one piece of the machine, and the shape of the argument suddenly made sense to him. He remembered a story his grandfather told him, from ancient India, about blind men who each touch a different part of an elephant and then describe the animal completely differently. The one holding the trunk imagines a snake; the one at the leg insists it is a tree.

"It's the parable of the blind men and the elephant," he said. "That's us. We've each only touched one part."

Desh grinned slowly. "So nobody's wrong. Everybody's just holding a different piece." They ran the robot whole, with all systems on, and watched together. It lurched left because of the motor, and the motor strained because the pinched cable made the sensor draw too much power, which drained the battery and set off the toxic-gas alarm by the vinegar residue Priya had left inside.

"So Marcus's battery, Desh's cable, Amelia's wheel, and Priya's sensor were all real," Nolan said, unscrewing the pinched cable cover. "Just one at a time."

Twenty minutes later the robot rolled straight across the driveway, and Amelia whooped so loud that Desh's neighbor looked over the fence. Marcus filmed it on his phone to send to Priya, and at the end he added, "Your nose works. The whole elephant works."

Mackenzie had read The Lighthouse of Hallow Bay three times, but for her book club report she needed something more than a summary. She carried the novel, a stack of yellow sticky notes, and a pencil to the reading nook by the window, where the afternoon light fell in a warm stripe across the cushion. She had decided on a small ritual: every time the blue door of the old boathouse appeared in the story, she would mark the page and write one sentence about what was happening there.

The first blue door showed up in chapter two, when the main character, Ivy, pressed her ear against it and dreamed of the father who had disappeared at sea. Mackenzie wrote "hope of his return" on the note and pressed it onto the page. In chapter five, Ivy hid behind the same door while her cousin searched for her, and in chapter nine, the door stood open, letting in the wind while the family argued inside. Mackenzie sat back and looked at her row of notes like a string of flags.

At the kitchen table that evening, her older brother Dev leaned over her shoulder. "What's with all the yellow paper?"

"Every time the blue door shows up, I mark it," Mackenzie said. "I'm trying to see if it means something different each time."

Dev nodded. "Recurring image like that is called a motif," he said, and went back to his sandwich.

In the nook the next morning, Mackenzie formulated a test. If the door really changed meaning, then the last time it appeared should be almost the opposite of the first. She found the final mention in chapter twenty: Ivy painting the door gray herself, the day she finally stopped waiting for news of her father. Mackenzie read the page twice, then peeled off her first sticky note and laid it beside the last one. Hope of his return, one said. Letting him go, said the other. Same door, same hinges, same blue paint, but by the end it meant something entirely different. She checked the middle notes and saw the pattern in order, hiding place, shelter, then farewell.

That afternoon Dev found her taping the sticky notes in a long line down the hallway, chapter by chapter, like train cars.

"You know that's going to leave marks on the wall," he said.

Mackenzie stood at the far end and looked down the row. "Look at it from here," she said. "It goes from blue to gray."

Eleanor set her fork down beside her meatloaf and stared at the newspaper folded next to her plate, because the draft for her current events report was due by email at eight o'clock tonight, and it was already six forty-five. The article she had chosen ranked quarterbacks by something called passer rating, and the numbers made no sense to her at all. One quarterback had 104.2. Another had 158.3, and the caption under his photo called it perfect.

"Why would a perfect score be a weird number like that?" she asked her brother Marcus, who was stacking green beans on his knife like he was building a wall.

Marcus shrugged. "It's just what it is. Football stuff." He wanted to finish dinner fast so he could colonize the whole living room couch before their cousin arrived, spreading his blanket and controller across every cushion like territory he claimed by sitting on it first.

"A hundred would be perfect," Eleanor insisted. "Like on a test. If the scale starts at zero and ends somewhere, perfect should end at one hundred." She flipped the paper over and ran her finger down the ranking column again, counting the quarterbacks listed there. Twelve names, twelve different numbers, all squeezed down from games she had never watched. Somewhere behind each number were completions and yards and touchdowns and interceptions, and all of it had been crushed together into a single figure, the way her school averaged test scores into one grade. But the top number still bothered her, hanging there like a picture she couldn't get to hang perpendicular to the floor.

"Maybe it's not out of a hundred," Marcus said through a mouthful of beans. "Maybe the whole scale is different."

Eleanor grabbed her mother's phone from the counter and typed "passer rating maximum" into the search box. She read, scrolled, and read again. "It says the passer rating combines several passing statistics into one number," she announced, "on a scale from zero to a maximum of 158.3." She set the phone down. "So a perfect rating isn't a hundred. It's a strange number, and it's the top of the whole scale."

Marcus had stopped stacking beans. "So that guy with 158.3 is literally the best you can be?"

"By the rating, yeah." Eleanor was already rewriting the first line of her report in her head. She had planned to argue that the rankings were unfair because her favorite team's quarterback sat seventh, but now she understood that his number was built from everything he had done all season, folded together. Seventh wasn't a judgment of him as a person. It was arithmetic. She picked her fork back up and speared a green bean off Marcus's abandoned wall.

At 7:58 she hit send, then carried her plate to the sink. Marcus had claimed the couch, blanket and all, and was waving the remote at her.

"Want to watch the highlights?" he asked. "That perfect guy plays tonight."

Eleanor dried her hands on the towel. "Show me the numbers at the end," she said, and sat down on the last free cushion.

The bus jolted over the pothole by the gym, and Peyton grabbed the seat in front of her before she slid into the aisle. In her backpack was the sign-up sheet for Saturday's three-on-three basketball tournament, and one blank line left: her third teammate. She had until the last stop to decide.

"I still say Dez," said Marcus, leaning over from the next seat. "He's got the same average as Priya. Ten points a game. I did the math twice."

Peyton pulled out her notebook, where she'd copied the numbers from the rec center's weekly sheets. "Same average, but look." She turned the page so he could see. "Priya scored ten, ten, nine, ten, eleven. Every single week. Dez scored twenty-two, then two, then eighteen, then zero, then eight."

Marcus squinted at the columns. Rain had begun to saturate the windows, blurring the parking lots and mailboxes into gray streaks, and he had to tilt the notebook toward the light. "So? They both average ten."

Down the aisle, Dez was holding court near the back, retelling last week's game in a loud voice. "Twenty-two points! It was a siege out there, they double-teamed me all night, and I still dropped twenty-two." A couple of kids laughed and pounded his shoulder. Priya sat quietly by the window, retying her shoelace the way she did before every game, careful and slow.

Peyton frowned at her numbers. The average treated Priya's week and Dez's week the same, but the weeks underneath weren't the same at all. She thought about Saturday. Three games guaranteed, maybe five if they kept winning. She needed somebody she could count on every game, not one brilliant game and then a collapse. She tested the idea on Marcus.

"Okay, forget averages. If I tell you our first game, Priya gives us ten points. Can you promise me Dez does?"

Marcus rubbed the back of his neck. "No. He might give us two. He might give us twenty."

"Right. An average hides how the games are spread out." She tapped the two columns. "Priya's all bunched together. Dez swings between great and terrible."

Marcus was quiet for a second. The bus hissed to a stop and two fifth graders clattered down the steps. "I wanted Dez because he's fun," he admitted. "But you're right, we need steady. Put Priya down."

Peyton wrote the name, then got up and walked back through the swaying aisle. She sat down across from Priya, who looked up, surprised.

"Want to be on our tournament team Saturday?" Peyton asked. "Three games minimum."

Priya's slow smile spread. "I'll be there. Every game."

"I know," said Peyton. "That's why I asked."

Marcus turned around in his seat and held out his fist, and Priya bumped it just as the bus lurched forward into the rain.

Grandpa's creek had yielded exactly zero fossils in three days of searching, which Victoria considered a personal insult. She had a shoebox of rocks on the porch rail, and she spread them out now: speckled ones, banded ones, one gray lump with shiny flecks that looked like someone had spilled glitter into wet concrete.

Grandpa came out with two glasses of lemonade and peered over her shoulder. "Grandma wants to retire that shoebox, by the way. She says it's full of dirt and mystery."

"It's full of specimens," Victoria said. She picked up the glittery one. "This one's igneous, I think. It was melted once, like lava, and then it cooled." The banded one went in a second pile. "Metamorphic. Squished and cooked underground until it got stripes." The third pile was softer rock, layered like a stack of pressed sandwiches. "Sedimentary. Made from mud and sand piling up."

"That's a lot of science for a shoebox," Grandpa said.

She held up her favorite find, a black stone from the creek bend. "I checked this one four times for fossils. Nothing." She had checked the banded one too, and the glittery one, dragging her thumb over every surface like a detective looking for fingerprints. Nothing, nothing, nothing.

Then she turned over a piece of the layered sandwich rock, and there it was: a curl pressed into the stone, small and perfect, like a snail that had signed its name a very long time ago.

"Fossil!" She nearly knocked over the lemonade.

Grandpa leaned in. "How come it's in that one and not the fancy ones you kept checking?"

Victoria lined up the three piles side by side. "The melted kind was too hot, I bet. The squished kind too. Anything living in there would've burned up." She tapped the soft layered pile. "Only these. Fossils are almost only ever in sedimentary rock."

"So the glitter rock is controversial."

"It's a paperweight," Victoria said. She wrapped the fossil in her bandana like it was a visiting ambassador, and carried it inside to show her grandmother.

Samuel's cleats were still damp from the morning dew when Coach Marisol dragged a thick rope out of the equipment shed and dropped it across the center circle. "Tug-of-war," she announced. "Championship Saturday has one at halftime, and we are going to win it."

Devon, who lived upstairs from Samuel in the apartment building where their families were tenants, threw both fists in the air. "I've been waiting all season for this!"

They pulled in pairs first, then four against four, then all eight. Samuel gripped the rope in the eight-on-eight round and noticed something strange. When it had been just him against Devon, his arms burned and his legs shook. Now, with the whole team heaving together, his pull felt easier. Lazy, almost. He glanced down the line. Marco was definitely leaning back less than before. When Coach blew her whistle and called the pull "sloppy," Marco's face went pink.

That night Samuel couldn't let it go. He pulled a strand of spaghetti from his dinner and tugged it, thinking. He could infer something from what he'd seen: the more people on the rope, the smaller each person's pull seemed to get. But was that real, or was he imagining it? The only way to find out was a test.

At Tuesday practice he begged Coach Marisol for the spring scale she used for fitness testing. She hooked it to the rope and the fence post. Devon pulled alone and the scale read ninety pounds. Then four boys pulled together, and Samuel did the math in his notebook. Devon's share of the four-man pull was smaller than his solo pull. Same for Marco. Same for everyone. The pattern held.

"You sound like my grandfather," Coach said, laughing. "In 1913 Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller."

"Ringelmann," Samuel repeated, writing it down. "So what do we do about it?"

Coach rubbed her chin. "That, scientist, is your problem."

On Saturday, the stadium smelled like popcorn and cut grass, and the stands were louder than any game all season. At halftime, Samuel gathered his team in the end zone. "Every pull is your pull," he told them. "Nobody's hiding on this rope." He pointed at the opposing team's biggest puller, a tower of a kid. "He's not the rope. He's just one guy."

The whistle blew. Samuel planted his feet, kept his arms straight, and pulled as hard as if he were alone in his backyard. Down the line he heard Devon growling like a guard dog, and the rope came, inch by glorious inch, until the red flag crossed the chalk line. Devon tackled Samuel into the grass, and the whole team piled on, shouting, "Ringelmann!" at the sky.

Carter arrived at Deshawn's house with his backpack clanking, ready for history club, and found everyone arguing before he even got his shoes off. Three kids sat around the kitchen table with two photocopied pages in front of them, and the smell of burned popcorn hung in the air from an earlier disaster nobody would admit to.

"It says right here the British fired first," Priya said, tapping her page. "The colonist witness says so."

Deshawn shook his head. "My page is a British soldier's account, and he swears the colonists fired first. Same morning, April 1775, at Lexington. Somebody's lying."

Carter sat down and pulled both pages toward him. He read them twice, chewing the end of his pencil. Both accounts sounded certain. Both had details, the smell of gun smoke, the shape of the green, the shout of officers. If people on both sides each said the other side fired first, then either one witness lied, or both sides honestly remembered it differently. He wanted to know which, and he thought of a way to check.

"I want to replicate the argument," he said. "Kind of. Priya, you go stand by the sink. Deshawn, stand at the back door. Amelia, you're the shot. Slam the pantry door."

Amelia grinned and slammed it. "Who fired?" Carter asked. Priya pointed at the back door. Deshawn pointed at the sink. Neither had seen the pantry. They tried it again with different positions, and every time, each witness truly believed the other person's side had caused the bang.

"So that's it," Carter said slowly. "Nobody has to be lying." Historians still did not know who fired the first shot at Lexington, because the witnesses from each side each said the other side fired first, and maybe every one of them believed it. The kids sat quietly for a moment, letting that settle.

Deshawn's mom came in with a fresh bowl of popcorn, having noticed the earlier loss from the scorched smell drifting upstairs. "You kids want juice too?" She set down cups without waiting for an answer. Priya slid the biggest cup toward Carter, since he'd missed snack time entirely by reading twice.

"Next meeting," Deshawn said, "we find a case where the two sides actually agree. Something parallel to this one."

"Deal," said Carter, and reached for the popcorn.

Maya's dog, Biscuit, flattened himself under the coffee table the second the thunder cracked, and Peyton watched him shake. "He's scared," Maya said, not looking up from her phone. "It's happening right now, the storm. He's freaked out by the actual thunder."

Peyton nodded slowly. Maya had been quiet all afternoon, checking the weather app, then the soccer app, then the weather again. Her cleats sat by the door, already double-knotted, though the tryout was still four days away. "You keep doing that," Peyton said, pointing at the phone. "Is there thunder in there?"

"No. It's the tryout list. They posted the roster numbers and mine is eleven, which is fine, but what if they move me to defense, what if I trip in the first drill, what if Coach Reyes already decided." Maya set the phone face down, then picked it up again. Peyton thought about Biscuit under the table. He was shaking at the thunder that was actually booming outside. Maya was shaking at thunder that had not happened yet and might never happen at all. "So Biscuit is scared of the storm," Peyton said, testing the idea out loud, "and you're not scared, exactly, because nothing's happening right now. It's more like you're worried about what might happen Friday. My mom says that's anxiety. Fear is the reaction to a threat happening now, and anxiety is worry about a threat that might happen in the future."

Maya stopped scrolling. "So Biscuit has fear and I have anxiety."

"Basically."

"Great. The dog is more competent than me."

"He's hiding under a table," Peyton said. "You're sitting on a couch eating all my chips."

"That's my coping mechanism. Chips consume my stress." Maya held up the nearly empty bag as proof, and Peyton laughed and grabbed the last chip, calling a truce over the crumbs.

Maya stood, put the phone in a drawer, and closed it. "Okay. If it's about a might, not a happening, then I can practice instead of worrying. Want to go outside before the next rumble?"

They laced up their cleats on the back step. Maya had just struck the ball against the fence twice when the drawer, muffled, began to buzz.

Amelia spread her notebook across the library table and wrote "Five Reasons the Library Should Stay Open Until Eight" at the top of the page. Below it she made her outline: introduction, three reason paragraphs, conclusion. The librarian, Mr. Okafor, had told her class that a persuasive essay was like a court case, and each paragraph had to prove something. Amelia thought that sounded manageable until she sat down and realized she had exactly one fact, which was that some kids couldn't come to the library until after five because of the bus schedule.

Her friend Dev sat down across from her with a stack of books about frogs, because he was doing a report on animals that hibernate. "What's your essay about?" he asked.

"The library should stay open later," Amelia said. "Kids check out forty percent more books when it's open late."

Dev frowned. "Says who?"

"Says me. I made it up. It sounds convincing."

"That's not how it works." Dev turned a page. "If you put a number in there, people want to know where it came from. Like, if I write that wood frogs freeze solid all winter, I have to say the wildlife federation said that, or nobody believes me."

Amelia tapped her pencil. She looked over at the front desk, where Mr. Okafor was stamping returns, and got an idea. She wrote her opening paragraph on a fresh sheet, left out any sources, and walked it over to him. "Mr. Okafor, can you read this and tell me what you think?"

He read it and pointed at her number. "Forty percent more books. Says who?"

Exactly as predicted. Amelia grinned, went back to the table, and found the library's annual report in the reference section, which listed checkout totals by month and hour. The real number was smaller than her made-up one, but it came with a name attached: the report was published by the city library board. She wrote the sentence again with the real figure and added "according to the city library board's annual report," then took it back to the desk.

Mr. Okafor read it and nodded. "Now I can go look that up myself if I want to. That's a competent piece of arguing."

"But my first number was bigger," Amelia said.

"Bigger and useless. The expense of staying open late is real, so your argument has to be real too."

Dev raised his hand without being asked. "Point of order. I changed my mind about frogs. They don't all hibernate. Some just slow down and lurk under mud, being dramatic."

"That's not a point of order," said Amelia.

"It is now," said Dev, and he crossed out a whole paragraph with great satisfaction.

Raphael taped the cut list to the refrigerator, which his mother said was a strange thing to do with bad news. He had a reason, though. He wanted to look at it while he ate his cereal every morning until it stopped stinging, the way you keep touching a sore tooth.

His little sister Priya wandered in with her own agenda. "Is the kitchen table free tonight? I need it for my volcano."

"The volcano exploded already. Twice."

"It needs a rebuild. Mine has to be the most eloquent one in the class. Mrs. Teller gives extra credit for presentations that seem like real lava." Priya wanted that extra credit the way Raphael had wanted the team, so he shoved the cut list over and made room.

At school he found Dev, who had made the team, in the hallway by the gym. "Can I see the roster? The posted one with everybody's names?"

"You want to torture yourself?"

"Just curious."

Dev peeled the sheet off the cork board and handed it over. Raphael copied the birthdays into his notebook while sweat made the pages damp and he tried not to perspire onto the ink. Out of fifteen names, eleven had birthdays in the first half of the year. Dev himself was February. Four had the second half. Only one boy, a January kid, had been cut, and only two late-year kids had made it. Raphael was December. Youngest possible kid in the whole grade, by the calendar the school used for sorting players.

He showed Dev the notebook. "Look at the pattern."

"That's a coincidence," Dev said, and then, squinting, "maybe."

Raphael looked it up that night on the family computer, keyboard still gritty with Priya's volcano clay. There it was, plain as a bus schedule: studies of youth sports had found that players born early in the selection year were picked for teams more often than those born late.

"What's that called?" Priya asked, leaning over his shoulder like a small curious organism drawn to a light.

"The relative age effect," Raphael read aloud.

"Huh. So what are you going to do?"

"Try out again next year. And this year, I'm going to get so good they can't cut me no matter what month I was born in." He stood up, went to the garage, and pulled his basketball off the shelf.

Ellie split her garden into two square plots behind the barn, one for tomatoes and one for carrots, and wrote the plan on a popsicle stick. She would sprinkle the first plot lightly every single evening, because that felt like giving the plants a drink every day, and she would soak the second plot only twice a week, until the ground went dark and soft all the way down. Her little brother Owen had his own want: a stand at the end of the driveway by July, selling vegetables for money toward a new bike bell. "We have to classify what we grow," he announced, holding up a marker. "Tomatoes, fruit or vegetable? Customers will ask."

For three weeks both plots looked fine. Ellie hauled water from the hand pump, whose handle rose and fell like a piston while she counted out twenty slow strokes for the deep plot and five quick ones for the sprinkled plot. Owen stayed busy guarding the tomato side from the barn cat, a predatory orange thing that liked to flatten herself in the young rows and swat at leaves.

Then the hot week came. Five days of sun with no rain, and Ellie woke on the sixth morning to find the sprinkled plot drooping hard, leaves folded over like closed umbrellas, while the deep-watered plot stood green and almost cheerful beside it. She knelt and pressed her finger into each plot's soil. The sprinkled side was bone dry at the top. The deep side still held dampness down where her finger reached.

"Same sun," she said slowly. "Same everything. Except the water." She pulled up one wilted carrot seedling from the sprinkled plot, then dug carefully around one from the deep plot, and laid them side by side on the porch step. The wilted one's roots were short, huddled near the surface. The other one's roots ran down, long and pale, deeper than she expected.

Owen crouched beside her. "So light watering every day kept the roots up top," he said, "and deep watering once in a while made them grow down." He pointed at the dried crust of soil. "And the top dries out fastest, so up top is the worst place to be."

"Exactly," Ellie said. She grabbed the watering can and headed for the drooping plot. "New rule. We soak this one deep, twice a week, starting now."

Owen grabbed the second can and ran to catch up, marker still behind his ear. "My bell is going to be the loudest one on the street," he called, and poured.

The group chat pinged at 9:14, right while Zack was supposed to be asleep. It was Maya: "someone posted my old blog in the school forum. with screenshots. my OLD blog."
