Zack sat up in the dark, phone glowing under his blanket. "i thought you deleted it in fourth grade," he typed.

"i did. like, a hundred times. it's still THERE."

Three dots appeared, vanished, appeared again. Dev wrote, "deleted stuff can't just come back. unless somebody saved it."

Zack's stomach did a slow flip. Because he had a blog too, from back when he thought he was going to be a famous inventor, full of posts about his "unbreakable alloy spoon" project, which had actually snapped in half on day two. He had also, once, put up a photo of himself in front of his house. With the house number visible.

"hold on," he typed. He opened his laptop, keeping the screen tilted away from the door in case his dad checked on him. He searched his old blog's address, then tried something Maya had mentioned in the chat, something called the Wayback Machine. Since 1996, he read, the Internet Archive had been saving copies of public web pages, and anyone could look at old versions of many websites.

His heart was hammering by the time the page loaded. Slowly, line by line, his old blog rebuilt itself on the screen. There he was at nine years old, grinning in front of the house, number and all. There was his post about how the strength of his spoon would "fluctuate depending on the temperature of the soup." Maya commented on it. Total strangers could have commented on it. Total strangers could have read it, saved it, shared it.

He screenshotted nothing. He just sat there.

"Zack you still there?" Maya asked.

He typed with cold fingers: "found my blog too. the photo of my house is still up. and i found a page from my school's old site with the field trip schedule. anybody could have known where our whole grade was that day."

Dev wrote, "so deleting doesn't actually delete."

"not if it was ever public," Zack sent. He started a new list of things to fix, starting with telling his dad in the morning. Then Maya's name popped up at the top of the chat, and beside it, a stranger's account had just joined the group.

Evan had been building the same cardboard vessel at the park picnic table for three Saturdays, a sailboat with a mast he had cut so it stood perfectly perpendicular to the deck, and today Marcus was not sitting across from him. Marcus was all the way over by the duck pond, throwing pebbles, because yesterday Evan had told everyone in the cafeteria that Marcus still slept with a stuffed rabbit named Captain Fluff. Marcus had found out at lunch, and now here they were at opposite ends of the park on a Saturday morning.

Evan walked to the pond with the note he had written on notebook paper. He read it out loud instead of handing it over, because Marcus would not take anything from him. "Dear Marcus, I'm sorry if you were upset about what I said."

Marcus picked up another pebble and did not throw it. "That's a non-apology," he said. "You're sorry if I was upset. Like it's my fault for being upset."

Evan looked at the paper. He read the line again in his head. The "if" was the problem. He had written sorry about Marcus's feelings, not sorry about the thing he himself had said. He had said it out loud in the cafeteria on purpose, to get a laugh, and everyone had laughed, and Marcus had sat there with his tray.

"I have to do it over," Evan said. He went back to the picnic table, took out his pencil, and folded the old note into the boat's hull. He wrote a new one and walked back. "Dear Marcus. I'm sorry I told everyone about Captain Fluff. It was your private thing and I used it to make people laugh. That was wrong. I won't say anything about your stuff again. Do you want to finish the boat? I can't get the sail to stay up."

Marcus turned the pebble over in his hand. The wind came off the pond and smelled like mud and duckweed. "The sail keeps falling because the mast is too skinny for the hole," he said. "You need to wedge something in there. A rolled-up piece of paper."

"The old note," Evan said. He unfolded it, rolled it tight, and pushed it into the base of the mast while Marcus held the deck steady. The sail stood.

They carried the boat to the pond's edge and set it in the water. It heeled over, righted itself, and drifted out toward the ducks. "Still floats," Marcus said. "Even with a non-apology inside it."

At dinner Joseph pushed his lasagna around the plate and finally said it. "Grandpa, your fertilizer story doesn't prove anything." Grandpa set down his fork. Last summer he had told the story a dozen times: he'd sprinkled some blue powder on his tomato plant, and by August the plant had grown taller than the fence. "One plant, one summer, one story," Joseph said. "The company claims it works, and their claim is supposed to be backed by tested evidence. But how would we even test it ourselves?" His little sister, Mina, grinned around a mouthful of garlic bread, and his mother raised one eyebrow in a way that felt faintly sinister, like she already knew the answer and was waiting to see if he did.

The kitchen smelled of oregano and burnt cheese. Rain streaked the window, and the porch light refracted through the drops so that every bead glowed orange. Joseph stared at that glittering pattern while the problem turned over in his mind. He needed to know if the blue powder caused the growth, but a hundred things could make a plant tall: sun, water, luck. Then the idea arrived, so suddenly he knocked over his water glass.

"Two pots," he said, grabbing napkins while Mina shrieked about her poem notebook, the one with a stanza about tomatoes on the first page, which was now soaked. "Same soil, same seeds, same window, same water. Everything the same, except one pot gets the powder and one doesn't. Grandpa told me that's what scientists call the control group. It gets everything the test group gets except the thing being tested. So if the powdered pot grows taller, the difference has to come from the powder and nothing else."

Grandpa chuckled. "Six weeks, then. Winner picks the movie."

"Deal," Joseph said, and shook on it, blue powder already waiting in his pocket.

Rebecca sat at the kitchen counter with the family group chat open on her mom's phone, since her own was confiscated for the week. The chat had 23 unread messages, most of them from her little brother Marcus, who was campaigning to be allowed more screen time if he complied with every chore on the fridge list. Rebecca scrolled past all of it, looking for one thing: whether her mom had answered her private question from last night. She had typed it at eleven p.m., which she knew was risky. The question said, "Is it possible to forgive Priya but not want to be best friends again yet, or is that cheating?" Priya had blurted out Rebecca's secret in front of the whole lunch table on Tuesday, and the two of them had not spoken since.

Her mom's reply was waiting. "Forgiving means letting go of the resentment. Reconciling means rebuilding the relationship. They are two different things. You can do one without the other. Forgiving Priya does not have to mean the friendship goes back to exactly how it was." Rebecca read it three times. She had assumed forgiving someone meant pretending nothing happened, an all-or-nothing alloy of sorry and back to normal, fused together. The idea that the two could come apart felt strange, then possible, then like a door she could actually walk through.

She typed a reply with her thumbs while Marcus peered over her shoulder. "Can you text Priya's mom and ask if Priya can meet me at the park at four? Also Marcus gets his screen time, he did every chore, I checked." Marcus whooped and ran for the fridge list to prove it.

At the park, Priya was already on the swing, dragging her sneakers in the wood chips. "I'm sorry," Priya said before Rebecca even sat down. "I wasn't trying to be mean, it just came out." Rebecca took the swing beside her. "I forgive you. But I'm not ready for sleepovers yet. Is that allowed?" Priya thought about it, then pushed off with both feet. "Yeah. Race you to the fence."

Sofia heard the crash before she even reached the garage, which meant the trash cans were down again. Her little brother Marcus was already crouched behind the workbench, notebook in hand, watching through the window like a detective in a movie.

"It's the Hendersons' dog," Marcus whispered. "Every single trash day. That's my hypothesis." He said the word slowly, the way their science teacher said it, like it was something you could hold. "A testable guess. If I'm right, he'll do it again today."

"You've seen him do it?" Sofia asked.

"No, but the cans are knocked over every trash morning. Nine times now." Marcus flipped through his notebook, nine dates with a crooked checkmark beside each one. "Nine mornings, nine crashes. I'm going to win the science club bet. We took a ballot, and everyone voted that a raccoon was doing it. Everyone except me. If I catch the dog on camera, they have to vote again, and Best Hypothesis is mine."

Sofia pulled the old camcorder off the shelf and wiped the dust from its lens with her sleeve. Nine crashes sounded like proof, but something about it nagged at her. She remembered last summer, when her cousin Deja had insisted that every cat on the block hated water, and how smug she had looked right up until Sofia's cat Mister Pudding leapt straight into the wading pool. Deja had to confess the whole thing afterward, that she'd counted a dozen cats avoiding rain and thought that settled it. "A hundred white swans can't prove all swans are white," Deja had said, staring at the dripping cat, "but one black swan proves that wrong." Sofia hadn't fully understood it then. She was starting to.

"Nine mornings isn't proof," she told Marcus. "It just means the cans fall on trash days. The dog is a guess. So is the raccoon. So is anything until we see it happen."

They set the camcorder on the workbench, aimed at the cans, and waited. The garage smelled like oil and cut wood, and Marcus bounced his knee the whole time. At 6:40 the crash came, louder than usual, and they both lunged for the window.

A garbage truck rumbled past, its mechanical arm swinging wide, clipping the cans and sending them rolling across the driveway. Not a dog, not a raccoon, not anything with legs. Marcus stood frozen with his notebook hanging open, nine checkmarks suddenly meaning nothing at all.

"So I lost the bet," he said finally.

"You lost the bet," Sofia agreed, "but you won the science. Nobody else even tested theirs." She rewound the tape, and the truck swung its arm again on the little screen. Marcus watched it twice, then grabbed his pencil.

"I'm writing this down," he said. "New hypothesis. The arm's too long."

Jade crouched over an old picture frame in the backyard, arranging pebbles, bottle caps, and broken tiles into a mosaic for the neighborhood art contest. Her little brother Leo sat on the porch steps eating a pickle and offering advice nobody asked for.

"Put the big blue cap in the middle," he said. "Middle is best. Middle is the boss."

Jade tried it. The blue bottle cap went dead center, surrounded by a tidy ring of white pebbles, like a donut staring at her. She frowned. It looked like something from a plumbing catalogue, all neat and dull, not like the lagoon she'd imagined. She slid the cap left, then right, then almost center again. Still boring. Still a donut.

"Your art has the personality of a sock," Leo announced.

"Your face has the personality of a pickle." But he had a point, and she knew it. She flipped through her mom's old photography book on the grass, hunting for ideas, and stopped at a page with pictures marked up in pencil. Someone had drawn lines over the photographs, two straight lines one way and two perpendicular, cutting each picture into nine boxes like a tic-tac-toe board. The interesting subjects sat along those lines, or right where the lines crossed, never in the exact middle. The book called it the rule of thirds.

Jade grabbed a stick and drew the same grid in the dirt beside her frame, imagining the lines stretched across her mosaic. If the lines crossed in the four corners of the center square, then the blue cap belonged on one of those crossing points. She moved the cap up and to the left until it sat just off center, on a crossing, then rebuilt the pebbles around it so they swirled toward the cap instead of circling it like a fence.

She stood back and squinted. The whole thing suddenly had a direction, like water flowing somewhere. It wasn't a donut anymore. It was a lagoon.

"Whoa," said Leo, pickle paused halfway to his mouth. "It's looking at me sideways."

Jade took a photo on her mom's old phone to preserve the design in case a squirrel attacked, then carried the frame to the shade so the glue wouldn't dry too fast in the sun. Leo followed, dragging his pickle.

"Teach me the tic-tac-toe trick," he demanded.

"First, throw away that pickle. It smells like regret."

Leo sniffed it, shrugged, and took another bite.

The Hendersons' basement smelled like popcorn and damp coats, because the whole neighborhood had squeezed in to watch the championship game on their giant television. Carter had the best spot, right in front on the carpet, next to Mr. Henderson's humming generator, which kept the TV running whenever the storm outside knocked the power out. Rain tapped the high window, and the room felt humid with so many people cheering and groaning in one small space.

During a timeout, Carter's little sister Priya frowned at the screen. "Why do they even call it a basket? Nobody's carrying a basket. It's a net with a hole in the bottom."

Half the room started guessing at once. Uncle Ray said it was just an old word that stuck. Priya's friend Marta suggested it came from the shape. Their answers contradicted each other, so Carter knew at least some of them were wrong, and probably all of them. He wanted the real answer before the game ended, because Priya asked questions like a dog with a bone and would not let it go.

The clock showed eight minutes left in the second half. Carter went upstairs to the kitchen, where Mrs. Henderson kept a shelf of old books. He had seen a dusty blue one up there last summer, something about sports history. He found it wedged between a cookbook and a phone book, flipped through the thin pages, and there it was, with an old black-and-white photograph of men in a gymnasium.

"Listen," Carter said, sliding back down the stairs just as the third quarter buzzer sounded. "Basket was invented in December of 1891 by a man named James Naismith. He made it up at a YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts." Priya asked what the goals were, and Carter pointed at the picture. "Peach baskets. They nailed peach baskets up as the goals. That's why it's called a basket."

"Peach baskets," Priya repeated, satisfied, and settled back against the couch.

The lights flickered once, twice, and everyone held their breath, but the generator hummed steadily on and the screen stayed bright. With four seconds left, the home team's guard launched a shot from way outside. It dropped through the net without touching the rim, and the whole humid basement erupted. Carter stood up with the book still under his arm, grinning at the television.

"Somewhere," he told Priya over the shouting, "that went in a peach basket."

When Nora arrived at Priya's house, she nearly stuck out her hand for a shake, but Priya's grandmother pressed her palms together and nodded instead, so Nora copied her, palms together, and the grandmother smiled. Nora had brought a gift, a box of chocolates, and she handed it over with her left hand because her right was holding her coat. The grandmother took it, but her eyebrows did something small and strange, and she passed the box to her other hand before setting it down.

At dinner, the table was crowded with dishes Nora had never eaten before, rice and chicken and something spicy that made her nose run. She noticed something while reaching for the serving spoon. Priya, Priya's father, even little cousin Danial, all of them ate with their right hands only. Every time Danial's left hand crept toward the plate, his mother tapped the table beside it until he moved it back. Nora quietly revised her theory that the grandmother's eyebrows had been about the chocolates. It was about the hand.

She decided to test it. When the rice dish came around, she lifted it with her right hand and offered it to Priya's father, even though her reach felt awkward and elastic across the crowded table. He took it with his right hand too, and this time the eyebrows stayed calm.

"In Malaysia we use the right hand for eating and for giving and receiving things," Priya said, leaning close. "It's a sign of respect."

Nora kept her left hand in her lap after that. When the tea came, she received the cup with her right hand, and when she passed the bread, she used her right hand again, even when it meant setting down her spoon first. The grandmother watched her across the table, then ladled an extra spoonful of chicken onto Nora's plate and said something to Priya in a language Nora didn't understand.

"She says you eat like a proper Malaysian," Priya translated.

Nora grinned and picked up her spoon with her right hand.

At dinner Tyler pushed his peas around his plate while his little sister talked about Maya's bracelet stand at the fair. Maya had sold out on Saturday, at four dollars a bracelet, and now everyone wanted some.

"Everybody keeps asking her for more," Emma said, "but she's out of beads."

Tyler remembered the fair, the smell of kettle corn drifting past Maya's table, the way she'd stacked her bracelets in rows, brittle little shells of painted macaroni that clicked when you touched them. He'd watched a woman buy three at once without even asking the price. He'd wanted one himself, but four dollars was more than his allowance could stretch to after the settlement he'd made with his dad over the broken garage window, two weeks of chores for the repair.

"That's why nobody had them," Tyler said suddenly. "She didn't have very many, and everyone wanted one. So she could charge a lot."

"So?" Emma rolled her eyes.

"So watch what happens now." He grabbed a napkin and drew a table on it, the way he categorized things for science class, sellers down one side and prices across the top. "Maya made a pile of money at four dollars. If you could make bracelets, wouldn't you start?"

By Thursday he had his answer. Three new stands had popped up on his street alone. Mrs. Okafor had a folding table at the end of her driveway, and the twins from two doors down were stringing beads on their porch every afternoon.

"They're all three dollars," Emma reported that night, chewing a mouthful of spaghetti. "And Mrs. Okafor said she'd do two-fifty if you buy two."

Tyler set down his fork. High price, and now more sellers than he could count, all offering bracelets because four dollars had made it worth their while. He thought about the napkin chart, still folded in his pocket, and about waiting too long at the fair.

"So are you going to buy one?" Emma asked. "They're cheap now."

"Yeah," Tyler said, pushing back his chair. "Let's go before everybody in town opens a stand."

The gym at the Maple Street Community Center felt like the inside of a rain cloud. Leo dribbled down the court, and sweat rolled off his elbows before he even reached the foul line. "Come on, one more quarter!" Coach Rivera shouted, but half the Rockets were bent over with their hands on their knees, gasping like fish.

Leo had played in a tournament last month on a day that hit ninety-six degrees, and it had been brutal but somehow easier than this. Today the thermometer said eighty-eight, yet everyone was dragging. He mentioned it to Marcus during a water break. "Maybe we're just tired," Marcus said. "I hibernated all weekend playing video games. My legs are noodles." Leo shook his head. "Last game was hotter. This doesn't add up."

Then he noticed the window. The air outside was thick and hazy, and the glass had a film of moisture on it, even though nobody had touched it. He grabbed his water bottle, poured a little on his forearm, and blew on it. Almost nothing happened. The drop just sat there, shiny and stubborn, refusing to dry. In the drier tournament gym, his soaked jersey had dried stiff in twenty minutes. He tried an experiment on his other arm with a paper towel, fanning it. His damp arm felt cooler than the one with the plain water drop. "Marcus! Come feel my arm. Both of them."

Marcus pressed a finger to each forearm. "Whoa. That one's colder. Why?" Leo grinned. "Sweat's supposed to dry off us to cool us down, right? Today it just sits there and doesn't go anywhere." He jogged to the bench and told Coach. "So in humid weather we overheat more easily, even when it's not that hot out. Can we sub more often?" Coach squinted at him. "That's actually a credible theory. Fine. Rotating every four minutes."

The rotations worked. Fresh legs flooded the court every few minutes, and the Rockets clawed back from eight points down. With ten seconds left, Leo stole the ball at midcourt, drove past two defenders, and laid it up off the glass. The net didn't even ripple. "That," Marcus panted, throwing an arm around him, "is the sweatiest win of my whole life."

Declan had inherited his grandfather's heavy copper saucepan, and he intended to use it tonight to make caramel sauce for the vanilla ice cream waiting in Grandma's freezer. He had one problem: the last time he'd tried, at home, the sugar had gone from pale gold to black and bitter in what seemed like two seconds. Here at his grandparents' house, on a stove he didn't know, he had to figure out what he couldn't see directly, the exact moment the browning was done, before the pan told him by ruining it.

He set the pan over medium heat and poured in a cup of sugar, deciding to test a simple idea: if he watched the color change in tiny stages rather than waiting for one big change, he could catch the right moment. His little cousin Rosie leaned over the counter, chin in her hands, hair pulled back for what she called kitchen hygiene. "Is that the same browning as the crust on Grandpa's roast?" she asked, pointing at the pot where the sugar was just beginning to melt at the edges.

Declan stirred slowly and thought about it. The roast crust had needed the meat itself, not just heat, he was pretty sure. "No," he said. "This is caramelization. It's browning that happens when sugar alone is heated." Rosie frowned, so he added, "The roast is different. That's the Maillard reaction, and it also needs amino acids, from the meat. Sugar alone won't do it." He wasn't a hundred percent sure he had it right, but Rosie nodded like he was authentic, like a real chef, and turned back to the pot.

The sugar melted, then turned straw color, then amber. Declan pulled the pan off the heat at deep gold, exactly as his plan said, and whisked in cream while Rosie held the door of the freezer for the ice cream. But when Grandma dipped a spoon and tasted, she laughed. "Sweetheart, this is wonderful, but you know what your grandfather puts on his ice cream?" She reached into the pantry and held up a jar of store-bought butterscotch. "He's loyal to this. Has been since 1987."

Declan stared at his glossy caramel, then at the jar, then carried his sauce to the table anyway and spooned it over his own bowl. Grandpa took one bite of the butterscotch he always had, paused, and slid his bowl across the table. "Just once," he said. "Pour some of that on."

The phone had been dead since the last gas station, and Dad was still refusing to ask for directions. "Grandpa said the cabin is right on the lake, near a town called Eagle Point," he said, drumming the wheel. "I want to find it before dark. I promised him we'd fish at sunrise."

Bentley unfolded the big paper map across his knees, and it crinkled like an enormous candy wrapper. Across the top and down the side ran rows of numbers, and thin lines crossed the map into a grid. Next to Eagle Point he found a tiny pair of numbers in the index at the back: latitude 44 degrees and 12 minutes north, longitude 87 degrees and 30 minutes west. He stared at the word "minutes" for a long moment. "That can't be how long it takes to get there," he said. "It's not time." But then what was it?

He tested an idea. If the whole state sat between the 44 and 45 lines, and the town's number said 44 degrees and 12 minutes, then the 12 must be a way of measuring distance between the big lines, not minutes on a clock. He held the map up to the light and counted the small tick marks between the printed lines. There were sixty of them. So each degree had to be divided into sixty of these "minutes," and sure enough, some of the finer labels were broken down even further, into seconds. "Sixty seconds in a minute," he said slowly. "It's like the clock, but for space." Dad glanced over. "You figuring that out all by yourself?"

Bentley was secretly proud, and a little envious of kids who got to learn this in a classroom instead of in a hot car. He slid his finger along the 44 degree line, then up from the 87 degree line, and where his fingers crossed, there it was: a small dot labeled Eagle Point, tucked against a blue blot of lake. "Turn left at the next highway, then about twenty miles north," he announced. Dad raised his eyebrows. "That's your verdict?" "That's my verdict," Bentley said. "Unless you want to knock on a stranger's door and ask a random anonymous person in the middle of nowhere."

Dad laughed and took the left turn. The road climbed through pines, and Bentley tracked their progress with his finger the whole way, checking the line numbers at every crossroad. Then the trees broke open and the lake flashed silver in the late sun, with a small cabin at the near shore and a rowboat pulled up on the sand. Dad honked the horn twice, and Bentley folded the map into a neat square and held it up like a trophy as the gravel crunched under the tires. "Grandpa," Dad called through the open window, "we used a map, and my navigator got us here."

Emilia sat at the kitchen table with three ruined greeting cards in front of her. Each one had cracked along the fold, the thick card splitting into bumpy white lines that crossed her careful drawings of tulips. She was making a birthday card for her grandmother, and it had to be perfect, so she pressed a fourth card flat and folded it anyway, watching the paper splinter down the crease.

"There has to be a reason," she said to her cat, Biscuit, who was asleep on the chair beside her. She looked closely at the cracked cards. The folds were straight, but the surface was rough and broken, as if the card had been forced. She thought about the thin paper she folded into paper airplanes, which never cracked. Maybe the thick card was too stiff to bend cleanly on its own.

She tested a small piece of scrap card first. She took a blunt spoon from the kitchen drawer and drew it firmly along a ruler's edge, pressing a shallow line into the card. Then she folded along that line, and the card bent straight and clean, with no crack at all. She blinked at it, then tried a second scrap without the pressed line, and it split like the others. It was not luck. She had been negligent about one small step, and the small step was everything.

The next card transformed under her hands. She scored a line with the spoon before folding, and the spine of the card came out smooth and sharp. On the front she drew tulips, then a border of little stars. Biscuit woke up, yawned, and put one paw on the envelope, as if signing it too.

"You can deliver it with me," Emilia said. She slid the card inside, and the white paper whispered against the edges. On the envelope she wrote her grandmother's name and, underneath, in small letters, "Folded with a spoon."

Anna stood on Platform 4, gripping a sign she had made in marker: WELCOME GRANDPA JOE. The 3:15 from the city hissed in, and among the crowd she spotted his gray cap bobbing like a buoy. He waved with both hands. "One whole week," he announced, hugging her. "And I want to ride every train line this station has, even the slow one nobody likes." Anna grinned, but a worry buzzed at the back of her mind. Last year, when Grandma Rosa visited, Anna had meant to write down her stories and never got around to it. Grandma Rosa couldn't travel anymore, and those stories about her childhood felt like water slipping through fingers. She didn't want that to happen twice.

The week flew by. They rode the slow line to the harbor, and Grandpa Joe told her about the rat he had kept as a boy, a pet rodent named Whiskers who stole buttons. "Was that voluntary, keeping him, or did Whiskers just refuse to leave?" Anna asked, laughing. Grandpa Joe shrugged. "He moved in on his own. Like he chose me." On Friday, the last night, Anna studied him across the dinner table and tried to assess how many stories were still in there. Hundreds, maybe. How could she keep them?

Then she remembered the poster in the library window. A man had been recording his mother in a little booth. The poster had said the recordings go somewhere important, that people interview family members and, with permission, the recordings are saved at the Library of Congress. Anna had walked past it twice. Now she stopped walking. She grabbed her tablet.

"Grandpa, sit here and tell me about Whiskers again," she said, pressing record. "Why?" "There's a project called StoryCorps," she said. "People record interviews with their family, and with permission the recordings get saved at the Library of Congress. Like your stories could live there forever." Grandpa Joe went quiet. "Forever in a library," he murmured. "Then ask me anything, starting from the beginning." He leaned toward the microphone and said, "I was eight years old, and the button was missing from my coat."

The whole premise of the food bank, Dylan discovered, was not just giving food away but giving it away in the right order. He had enrolled as a volunteer that morning because his scout troop needed service hours, and Ms. Reyes had put him on the canned vegetable shelf. He worked fast, sliding the new donations from the big box right into the front of the shelf where his hand fit easiest. When he finished, the row looked full and neat, labels all facing out.

Ms. Reyes walked past, stopped, and frowned at his shelf. "Redo it, please. New cans go in back."

"But the front's the easy spot," Dylan said.

"The easy spot is for the old cans," she said. "First in, first out."

Dylan pulled the new cans out again and stared at the shelf, thinking. So whatever went in first had to come out first, which meant the old cans sat in front where the next volunteer would grab them. He tested it by checking the dates on a few labels. Sure enough, the cans already at the front expired sooner than the ones in his box. It was like a line at a water park: first person in line, first person down the slide. He slid the new cans behind the old ones, all the way to the back, and pushed the old cans forward until the dates ran in order.

By noon his arms ached, but the shelf had a system now, and he liked systems. When the afternoon crew came in, a girl named Priya started stacking a fresh box right into the front of his row. "Back," Dylan said, pointing. "Older stuff goes out first so less expires on the shelf."

"You figured that out yourself?" she asked.

"Sort of. I got it wrong first."

She laughed and carried her box around to the far side. "Race you on the soup aisle."

Edouard had been waiting for Grandpa's visit all summer, but by the second morning something felt wrong. At breakfast, Grandpa held the cereal box at arm's length and squinted at it like it was a distant bird. When Edouard showed him a comic from his favorite lush, tropical adventure series, Grandpa smiled and handed it back after one glance. "Nice cover," he said, which was a strange thing to say about a comic.

Edouard started watching. At the market café, Grandpa stretched the menu out so far he nearly knocked over the sugar bowl, and he ordered "whatever you're having" instead of reading the specials. In the guest bedroom, the book Grandpa claimed he was reading sat closed on the nightstand while he stared out the window. Edouard had a sinking feeling. Maybe Grandpa didn't actually like comics, or books, or him.

That night Edouard found a clue. Tucked into the suitcase in the guest room was a letter from Grandpa's neighbor back home, and the handwriting was enormous, the letters as big as his thumb. "Your eyes are getting worse," Edouard read, feeling like a spy. "Wear the glasses." There were no glasses anywhere in the room.

He remembered something from last summer, a flashback that rose up sharp and clear. Grandpa threading a fishing hook for him at the lake, holding the line far away and blinking, finally saying, "You do it, Edouard. Your eyes are younger than mine." Edouard had thought Grandpa was just being lazy that day. Now a new idea was forming, and it compressed everything he'd noticed into one tidy thought: Grandpa's eyes worked fine for far away, but not up close. He was hiding it because he didn't want to be a bother.

Edouard tested the idea the next morning. He wrote, in huge letters across a page, WOULD YOU LIKE TO GO TO THE BOOKSTORE? He held it up across the kitchen and watched. Grandpa read it instantly, and his whole face changed.

"Ah," Grandpa said quietly. "You've figured out my secret. After about age forty, the lens of the eye loses flexibility and cannot focus up close as well. It's called presbyopia. My reading glasses correct it, and I left them on the bus." He laughed at himself. "I was too proud to say so."

At the bookstore, Edouard picked out the comic he'd wanted to share and read it aloud in the café, doing all the voices while Grandpa leaned back, listening, easy and happy. When Edouard paused at a cliffhanger, Grandpa's hand shot out and turned the page, quick as a reflex.

"Keep going," Grandpa said. "I have to know if they escape the jungle."

The restaurant had one wall covered by a screen so big that Camille could see the goalkeeper's grass stains from across the room. Her whole family had pushed three tables together under it, along with Uncle Marco and his friend Rosa, because tonight was the final. Camille had ten dollars riding on the game against her cousin Benito, who wanted the other team so badly he had worn their jersey to dinner.

Between the pregame shows, the announcers ran a short piece about World Cup history, with old black-and-white film and a painting that portrayed a stadium packed with fans in flat, wide hats. A caption flashed by too fast for Camille to read. Uncle Marco leaned back and said, "Argentina won the first one, you know. That's why tonight matters so much to them."

"It was Uruguay," Rosa said. "My grandfather talked about it all the time. Nineteen thirty."

Uncle Marco shook his head. "Argentina. I'd bet money."

"You bet money on everything," said Camille's father, who drove a train and kept checking his phone in case the yard conductor called him in for an extra shift. He had already ordered a second basket of bread to make sure he stayed long enough to see the second half.

Camille wanted to settle the argument herself, because Uncle Marco would never give in to Rosa. She had seen the caption go by, but she had also noticed something else: the restaurant had a wall of old photographs near the restrooms, and one of them was from a stadium she recognized from the film, the same double-decked stands. She walked over and studied the small printed card beneath it. It said the first FIFA World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930, and that Uruguay won it, beating Argentina 4 to 2 in the final. She took a photo of the card with her phone, then came back and set it on the table in front of Uncle Marco.

He read it, snorted, and pulled out his wallet. "Fine. That's the equivalent of losing in the final. Worse, actually." He slapped a ten onto the table next to Camille's ten dollars and pushed both toward Rosa.

Rosa swept them up and said, "Four to two," just as the whistle blew and the screen went bright green.

Addison pressed her forehead against the airplane window and watched the clouds condense into gray towers below them. Their flight east to Rome had landed two days ago, and she still felt like her body was full of sand. She had fallen asleep at dinner, woken up at four in the morning, and dragged herself through the Colosseum while her little brother, Theo, bounced ahead of her taking pictures of every rock.

"Look at this one," Theo said now, holding up his camera in the Rome airport on their way home. He had one clear objective for the whole trip: get a photo of a pigeon sitting on something ancient. He already had pigeens on a statue, a pigeon on a wall, and, that morning, his prize, a pigeon on a broken column with the Colosseum in the background. "Best trip ever."

Addison couldn't argue, but something bothered her. On the flight out, she had been exhausted. Yet when they landed in Rome, Theo's eyes had gone wide and awake, and even her dad had said he felt strangely fine. It was the days after that had been terrible. On previous trips, flying home, everyone had seemed fine right away. She turned the thought over while they boarded.

Halfway across the Atlantic, she took out her notebook and made two columns. Trip out: flying east, awful afterward. Trip home: flying west. She looked at the columns. Could the direction itself matter? She decided to test it. "Theo," she whispered, "tomorrow, when we land, tell me how you feel. Really tell me."

"Fine, probably," he mumbled into his pillow.

They landed home at six in the evening. Theo ran through baggage claim chasing a plastic water bottle he was kicking like a soccer ball. Addison felt wide awake too, almost too awake, and at midnight she lay in her own bed staring at the ceiling. Her mother passed her door. "Can't sleep either," her mom said. "Funny, coming home is easier."

"It's because we flew west," Addison said. "Going east is the hard one."

Her mom paused in the doorway. "You know, I think you're right."

From down the hall, Theo's voice floated out into the dark. "Does Rome have pigeons at night?"

Cooper had never slept over at anyone's house before, and by eleven o'clock he was starting to worry that he wouldn't sleep at all. Dex's mom had already knocked twice. "Six a.m.," she'd said through the door. "The fishing boat leaves the dock at seven, asleep or not." Now the room was dark except for the glow of Dex's tablet, where they'd been watching video after video since nine.

At midnight Dex shut it off and they lay in their sleeping bags. Cooper stared at the ceiling. His body felt tired, but his brain wouldn't switch off, like a motor still running after the key was turned. Beside him, Dex rolled over for the tenth time.

"I can't fall asleep," Dex whispered. "Me neither," Cooper whispered back. He thought about it. They'd been lying in the dark for half an hour, so being in bed wasn't the problem. What else had they done? He tried to remember something his sister had said once, about light tricking your brain into thinking it's still daytime. It sounded plausible, but he wanted to test it before he trusted it.

"I hypothesize it was the tablet," Cooper said. "All that bright light, right up until we turned it off." Dex sat up. "What's the mechanism, though? How would light keep you awake?" "I don't know exactly. Something about the brain holding back a sleep hormone when it sees light, especially blue light, because it thinks it's daytime. So the hormone never builds up enough to knock us out."

Dex groaned. "Great. So we ruined sleepover night." "Or not," Cooper said. "If light held it back, maybe darkness lets it come back. We just have to stop giving our brains any light at all. No screen, no phone, nothing. Total black." He pulled his sleeping bag over his head like a tent. After a moment, Dex did the same, and the two of them lay there in the warm dark, breathing slowly.

From inside the bag, Dex's voice came muffled. "If this works, we're doing it at every sleepover." Cooper smiled in the darkness and closed his eyes.

Sophia heard the words "snow day" from the hallway and was out of bed before her alarm finished ringing. By nine she was dragging her red sled up Miller's Hill, where her friend Marcus was already stomping a path along the ridge. He pointed at a long sled with runners he'd borrowed from his cousin. "I'm breaking the hill record today," he said. "Cousin Tyler did the whole slope in twelve seconds. I timed him."

"First you have to help me with something," Sophia said. She had noticed it the day before, when she'd dug into the drift at the bottom of the hill. The deeper she'd gone, the less cold it felt. Today she wanted to test it properly, like the experiments they did in science, except this one was hers. They scooped and packed snow until they had a fort with walls as thick as Sophia was tall, and she hung a thermometer from a stick inside it. Then she tucked a second thermometer into a bush out in the open wind.

While they waited, Marcus scrutinized the snow around the fort, crouched low, frowning. "Look at this," he said. A thin, winding groove ran along the surface of the drift and vanished into it, like a tiny tunnel with a roof of snow. "Something's living under here." They followed the groove, careful not to cave it in, and Sophia remembered something from a winter documentary she'd watched in October, about how fresh snow is mostly trapped air, which makes it a good insulator, and how some small animals survive the whole winter in tunnels under the snow. "That's probably a vole," she said. "The snow is like a blanket over its hallways." Marcus said his grandfather had once shown them a moth larva curled under tree bark in January, and Sophia said that was the same idea: small things hiding in warm pockets while everything above them froze.

They ran back to check the thermometers, and Sophia could hardly keep still while she read them. Inside the fort it was several degrees warmer than out in the wind, and neither of them had done anything but pile up snow. "It works," she said. "It actually works." Then came the twist. From inside the grooved drift came a scrabbling sound, and a gray shape burst out of a hole near their feet, agile as a dart, streaking across the snow and diving into the next drift over. A vole, fat and quick, using its tunnels like a secret highway.

Marcus stood with his sled in both hands, watching the hole. "The snow fort is basically a giant vole tunnel," he said. "That's the best thing I've ever heard." He set the sled at the top of the hill and pointed down the slope. "Twelve seconds. Count them out loud." Sophia planted her boots at the bottom, cupped her hands around her mouth, and shouted, "Three, two, one, go!"

Harper flopped onto her bed with her tablet balanced on her knees and opened the group chat called "Stats Nerds Unite." Three names glowed at the top: Priya, Marcus, and Jonah. Marcus had posted first, with a photo of his baseball card binder spread across the garage floor.

"Settling an argument with my cousin," Marcus had written. "David Justice or Derek Jeter, nineteen ninety-five and ninety-six. I say Justice both years. My cousin says Jeter."

Harper pulled up the numbers on her laptop while Priya typed "getting my notebook." The garage door slammed somewhere behind Marcus's next message, a blurry photo of his cousin holding a card like it owed him money. Justice was ahead in ninety-five, Harper confirmed, and ahead again in ninety-six. Case closed. She typed it, dropped the phone, and went to find a snack, feeling pleased with herself.

When she came back with a granola bar, the chat had deteriorated into chaos. Priya had added the two seasons together, and somehow, in both years where Justice beat Jeter, Jeter's combined average for the two years was higher. "That's bizarre," Harper said out loud to nobody. Marcus typed it faster: "That's bizarre and impossible, someone typed something wrong." Jonah sent a single skeptical eyeball emoji.

Priya's next message read like a tiny letter, and Harper read it twice:

"Dear everyone who is wrong, I did the math three times. Justice wins each year. Jeter wins the two years put together. My brother says look at how many times each of them batted, then look again. That's all I'm saying. Signed, Priya."

Harper set down her granola bar. At-bats. She scrolled back to her laptop and stared at the columns she'd copied earlier, the ones she'd skipped past because only the averages had seemed to matter. One player had batted a whole lot more times in one of those seasons, and the other had batted barely at all in it. She didn't say why it worked. She just tested it, dragging her finger down the at-bat column, then up again, checking each number like she was counting steps in the dark.

"Okay," she typed. "Priya's right. Look at the at-bats."

"I'm making a treaty," Marcus wrote back. "Nobody in this chat declares a winner of anything ever again without checking everything, not just the famous number." Priya replied, "Seconded," and Jonah sent a handshake emoji.

Then a new name appeared at the bottom of the chat, one Harper had never seen before: Marcus's cousin, added somehow, asking if they could settle a basketball argument next.

Brielle stood in the wings of the music classroom, clutching her flute, and watched Marcus pace. He was two performers ahead of her, and his hands were shaking so hard that his sheet music rattled like a window in a storm.

"You okay?" she whispered.

"My voice is going to crack," Marcus said. He swallowed hard. "My mouth is so dry, and my heart is going like a million miles an hour." He held out one hand so she could see the tremble for herself.

Brielle had felt exactly the same thing at last month's audition, and it had nearly wrecked her. That afternoon she had gone home and scrutinized the notes she'd copied from a science magazine in the library, reading every line twice. The article said stage fright is the body's fight-or-flight response. Adrenaline, it explained, can cause a racing heart, a dry mouth, a shaky voice, and trembling hands. So her body wasn't breaking. It was doing what any organism does when it senses danger, even danger as harmless as forty kids with folding chairs. The weird part, the part she'd wondered about for days, was that her body couldn't actually tell the difference between a bear and a concert.

So she had tested an idea. At the audition, right before her turn, she had taken slow breaths and told herself, out loud in a tiny whisper, "Nothing here is attacking me. This is just a room." Her heart had still pounded, but her hands had gone steady enough to play.

She turned to Marcus now. "Try this," she said, and handed him her water bottle. "Sip. Then breathe with me, slow. And tell your body it's fight-or-flight stuff, that's all it is."

Marcus looked hesitant, but he sipped, and then they breathed together behind the curtain, in through the nose, out through the mouth, four slow times. Ms. Reyes called his name. He walked out, and Brielle watched his shoulders drop as he set his music on the stand.

His first note came out wobbly. His second one didn't. By the chorus he was singing full and clear, and when he finished, he grinned straight at the wings.

Then Ms. Reyes said, "Brielle, you're up."

Brielle walked to the front, lifted her flute, and whispered, "Just a room."

Sawyer refreshed the marketplace page for the third time that morning, and the Frost Dragon egg was still priced at four thousand gold. Last month it had been two thousand. He slumped in his chair, staring at the listing while his snow fox, Pip, curled up in the corner of the screen and began to hibernate, the way the game's pets always did when their owner ignored them too long.

Four thousand gold was impossible. He had been saving for weeks, selling bread from his bakery stall, because bread was a carbohydrate that every player's energy bar needed and it always sold. But at this rate, the dragon egg would stay out of reach forever. He scrolled through the listings and counted them. Only three eggs for sale in the whole market. Three weeks ago, when the price was two thousand, there had been nine.

He sat back. Fewer eggs, higher price. More bread, lower price, because bread was everywhere. Something invisible was pushing the numbers, like a hidden hand. He wanted to see if he was right, so he opened a notebook and started a chart: item, number of listings, price. Then his dad called from the hallway that they were driving to the hardware store.

At the gas station, while Dad filled the tank, a kid about Sawyer's age pointed at the sign. "Why did it go up since last week? It was cheaper." The station attendant, wiping his hands on a rag, shrugged. "Crude oil. The cost of crude oil is usually the biggest single part of the price of a gallon of gasoline, so when crude oil goes up, the pump price goes up too." The kid's dad nodded like this was ordinary news, and Sawyer stood there with his hand on the door of the car, thinking. A price could move because of something far away that you never saw. Crude oil for gasoline. Scarcity for dragon eggs. Maybe the same rule, wearing different clothes.

Back home, he tested his idea. He spent his gold on a cheap fertile soil seed instead of the egg, planted it in his garden plot, and waited three days while more players hatched dragon events. By Saturday, the marketplace showed eleven Frost Dragon eggs, and the price had slid to one thousand eight hundred. Sawyer bought one. In his notebook, under the chart, he wrote "scarce = up, plentiful = down" and drew an arrow. Then he set the egg beside the sleeping Pip, tapped it once, and whispered, "Okay, buddy, wake up. You're about to have company."

Grandma had been at the house since Monday, and by Wednesday Laurence had given up saying whole sentences to her at the park. She would shout across the picnic table by the duck pond, loud enough that a man walking his dog turned to look, and Grandma would still tilt her head and say, "What's that, dear? Speak up." Laurence couldn't understand it, because Grandma heard the ice cream truck's jingle from three blocks away, and she caught every word the deep-voiced park ranger said when he warned everyone about the geese. It was only Laurence's own voice that vanished.

Sitting on the bench, Laurence turned the puzzle over. Grandma had said her hearing was "mostly there, just blurry." Blurry sound. She thought about how the pond's shallow edge bent the light so the stones looked displaced, the way a straw in a glass seemed to refract into two pieces. Maybe sound could get blurry too, and maybe not all sound the same way. The ranger's low voice had come through fine. The ice cream truck, the wind in the reeds, the men playing chess, all low, all clear. Her own voice, and the shrieking little kids near the swings, all high, all lost. She felt a flicker of skepticism about her own idea, because it seemed too simple, but simple was worth testing.

She slid closer to Grandma and dropped her voice into the low register she used for reading the villain's part in class plays. "Grandma. The ducks stole my sandwich." She kept it quiet, quieter than a normal sentence, almost a mumble.

Grandma laughed out loud. "Both of them? Those fundamental criminals of the pond, always after the bread."

"You heard me?" Laurence said, still low. "I barely said it out loud."

"Loud enough, dear. It just wasn't all fuzzy." Grandma shook her head. "The doctor told me years ago, high-pitched sounds go first. I thought he meant bells and whistles. I didn't know my own granddaughter would count."

For the rest of the week, Laurence practiced her low voice until it felt like a coat she could put on. On Friday at the park, she leaned toward Grandma and rumbled, "The ice cream man is coming. My treat."

Grandma was already holding out her hand for coins.

On her third day at Millbrook Middle School, Scarlett got a seat by the window and a lab partner named Dee who kept a bag of gummy worms in her pencil case. "Emergency rations," Dee said solemnly. "Science is hungry work." Scarlett laughed for the first time in a week. After school she walked home to the new house, where the moving boxes still leaned against the walls like tired visitors.

Her mother had told her something at dinner, almost in passing. "I filed the permanent change of address with the Postal Service, so our First-Class Mail gets forwarded to this house for twelve months." Scarlett had chewed on that all evening. If mail could find her here, then Zoe's letters could too. But Zoe hadn't written yet, and Scarlett had no way to know whether the system actually worked or whether her letters would vanish somewhere between Ohio and here. She had a premise: if forwarding was real, a letter sent to the old address should come back to this one. All she needed was a test.

She wrote a note to herself, sealed it in an envelope, and addressed it to the old house in Dayton. "Dear Scarlett," it began, "if you are reading this, the mail is smarter than you thought." At the post office she asked the clerk to confirm it was First-Class Mail, because that mattered, and the clerk nodded and stamped it. Every afternoon for a week she checked the mailbox, finding only a pizza menu and something for her mother. "Be resilient," Dee told her at school. "Also, gummy worm? It helps."

On the ninth day the envelope appeared in the new mailbox, slightly bent, her own handwriting staring up at her. Scarlett whooped so loudly a neighbor's dog barked. That night she wrote Zoe a real letter, explaining the twelve months, telling her to write to the old address, and adding, "P.S. My new friend thinks mail is food for scientists. She is mostly wrong." She sealed it, and in the morning she ran the whole way to the post office, envelope flapping.

Jace had planted his tomato, pepper and squash seedlings on the first warm Saturday of April, certain that warm meant safe. "You're my tenants now," he told the little green rows, patting the soil around them, "and I'm the landlord who waters you." For two weeks they grew, and he thought the hard part was over.

Then the radio said thirty-four degrees tomorrow night, and Jace stood in the backyard frowning at the sky. Warm days had fooled him. He tried to remember what his grandfather had said last summer while picking peppers: "Can't put these out till after the last spring frost. Freezing kills them." Frost. That was the hidden thing, the cold that came at night when nobody was watching.

He wasn't sure the cold would really reach his plants, so he tested it. He covered every bed with old sheets and buckets, except one squash seedling that he left open on purpose, the far corner of the yard away from the house wall. If that one drooped by morning, he would know for certain it was the cold and not something else, like the neighbor's cat or too much water.

Morning came gray and glittering. Under the sheets the tomatoes stood stiff and fine, leaves untouched. The uncovered squash lay flat, its edges blackened and thin as wet paper. Jace knelt beside it, sorry he had needed proof at all. "That wasn't trivial," he said quietly. "That was your whole life." He decided to revise his plan completely: no more planting until frost season was truly over, and he would keep a journal by the window to track each cold snap.

He buried the squash by the fence, then heard the back gate. His little sister Mira stood holding her blanket. "Is it safe now?" she asked. Jace draped his biggest sheet over the pepper bed one more time and nodded. "Safe," he said. "Come on, let's count buds."

The nurse with the green scissors looked up from the cast cutter. "Ready to see your arm again?"

Lydia had spent six weeks thinking about almost nothing else. She'd broken her left wrist in an acute fall from the monkey bars, and ever since, she'd been running little experiments inside the plaster. Every night she'd squeezed her fist tight, then loosened it, trying to simulate the exercises her right arm got all day lifting her backpack, brushing her teeth, dealing cards. "Ready," she said, and held still while the cutter buzzed.

When the two halves of the cast came apart, Lydia stared. Her left arm lay there pale and thin, with a shadowy line where the wrist had healed. She put both arms side by side on the exam table, and the difference was so strange it felt like an anomaly, as if the bones themselves had shrunk. "That's not mine," she said. "That's like a stick."

"It happens," said the nurse, easing her thumb gently along the healed line. "Muscles kept still in a cast weaken and shrink. That's why the arm looks thinner when the cast comes off."

"So all my squeezing did nothing?"

"You kept the fingers moving, which matters. Give me a squeeze now."

Lydia wrapped her hand around the nurse's fingers and pressed. Her grip felt soft, like fruit gone mealy. She tried again, harder, and her arm trembled halfway through.

"I have a whole plan," she said, watching the thin wrist bend. "Squeeze a ball at breakfast, carry the milk jug at dinner, measure both arms every Sunday until they match."

"You'll get there faster than you think." The nurse wrote something on a card and handed it over. "For your mom. It lists the exercises."

Lydia folded the card and slid it into her pocket, then flexed her fingers open, closed, open again. "Deal me in next card game," she told her brother. "Left hand. I need the practice."

Zoe's grandmother had claimed the long stone ledge by the duck pond for her diyas, and she had brought forty of them, packed in a dented biscuit tin. The park was filling up with families for the Diwali celebration, and Zoe's job, assigned the moment they arrived, was to line the little clay lamps along the ledge before dark.

The problem appeared immediately. Her little brother Rohan, who Zoe had privately classified as a one-boy wrecking crew, kept walking the ledge like a balance beam, kicking diyas into the grass. She'd lined up twelve. Now there were nine standing and three in the pond, where a duck was inspecting one with genuine scientific interest.

Zoe crouched and thought. She couldn't watch Rohan and arrange lamps at the same time, and Mom was busy unfolding chairs near the pavilion. So she tested an idea. She moved the diyas from the top of the ledge to the ground beside it, leaving the flat surface empty. When Rohan came sprinting back for his next tightrope walk, he found a bare ledge, lost interest in about four seconds, and ran off toward the playground. It worked. The rule she'd guessed at, that her brother wanted the height and not the lamps, turned out to be true. It felt almost like a paradox: fewer diyas in the obvious place meant more diyas safe.

She was setting them back on the ledge when her grandmother returned with a box of matches and a thermos of chai. "Good, good," Grandma said, patting the row of small oil lamps. "Diyas, all ready for the five days of Diwali. Mr. Patel from the temple called me eccentric for bringing so many, but I told him, better too much light than too little."

"That's not eccentric," Zoe said. "That's just planning."

Grandma laughed so hard she nearly dropped the matches, then struck one and touched the flame to the first wick.

Maya heard the plows before she heard her mother, and by the time she reached the kitchen in her socks, the radio had already said the words she wanted: no school, roads closed, snow day. She ate her cereal fast, then pulled on her boots, her coat, and her grandmother's dark wool mittens, the black ones with the reindeer around the wrist.

The backyard had turned into a white plateau, flat and level from the fence to the swing set, unmarked except for one line of rabbit tracks. Snow was still falling, small flakes drifting sideways in the wind. Maya held out one mitten and let a flake land on the dark wool. She leaned close and counted the arms with her eyes. Six. She caught another. Six again, this one thin and starry. A third flake landed, melted too fast to count, and a fourth sat there long enough for her to be sure. Six.

She tried a pale gray mitten next, and the flakes vanished into it before she could see anything. That gave her an idea, and she tested it: dark wool, easy to see; light wool, impossible. So the mittens mattered. But something else bothered her too. Every single flake had six arms, not five, not eight, and she wanted to know whether that was luck or a rule. She stood in the falling snow for a long time, catching flake after flake on the black mitten, keeping a tally in her head. Twelve flakes with six arms. Thirteen. Fourteen, and then her fingers got too cold to hold still.

Inside, her little brother Theo was at the kitchen table drawing snowflakes on paper with a silver marker. Maya looked over his shoulder and frowned. "Yours have eight points," she said. Theo shrugged and kept drawing. "It's a snowflake. Snowflakes have points."

"Not like that," Maya said. "I counted real ones outside. Snowflakes almost always have six sides or six arms." She held up the dark mitten. "It works better on this one. Catch them on something dark." Theo hesitated, then slid off his chair and pulled on his own coat, the one with the broken zipper, inside out so it would close.

They stood together on the plateau of the yard, and Maya showed him how to hold the mitten flat and low, out of the wind. Theo caught a big feathery one and bent over it, lips moving as he counted. "Six," he announced. He caught another. "Six." A third flake landed square in the middle of the wool and held its shape while they both stared at it, every arm perfect. "Okay," Theo said, breathing out a slow cloud of steam. "Show me the marker that isn't toxic anymore, the one Mom put by the sink. I'm starting over with my drawing."

Muhammad held his candle like a torch and marched into the living room, where the whole family had gathered because the power had gone out for the whole street. "This is the third time this week," he announced, as if reporting news from a prestigious wire service. His older sister Layla groaned from the couch.

Ten minutes later, Muhammad crept to the kitchen and opened the refrigerator, letting its little bit of cold air spill over his face while he hunted for the yogurt. Layla caught him at it. "Again? You opened it five minutes ago!"

"I couldn't decide," Muhammad admitted. His conscience pinched him a little, because he knew she was right. Then Layla said something he had read on a fact sheet at school and never forgotten: "The USDA says a refrigerator keeps food safely cold for about four hours during a power cut, as long as the door stays closed." Muhammad stared at her, then at the fridge, doing the math. If the power had been out for one hour already, and he kept letting the cold out every five minutes, the four hours would shrink fast.

"So we get one opening," he said slowly. "One. We decide everything first, then open it once." He grabbed a pencil and wrote a note in the candlelight, which he read aloud with great ceremony: "Dear Fridge. Do not open. We are voting. Yogurt, grapes, or leftover rice. If you open this door before the family vote, you will retire from snack duty forever. Signed, Muhammad, Snack President." Layla laughed so hard she nearly dropped her candle.

They held the vote on the couch, everyone raising hands in the flickering light, grapes winning two to one. Then, together, they opened the fridge exactly once, grabbed the grapes, and shut it firmly. Muhammad taped his note to the door and saluted it. "Four hours," he whispered. "We can do this." Somewhere outside, a streetlight blinked back on, and the whole family booed, because now the vote had gone to waste.

Joseph had never walked so fast with a leash in his hand. Duke, the brown-and-white mutt from the shelter, trotted beside him with his ears up, and Joseph kept glancing down to make sure the dog was still there. "Two blocks to home," he told him, and Duke's tail swung like a piston pumping at top speed. A delivery truck rumbled past with its engine clattering, and Duke bolted, yanking the leash right out of Joseph's fingers.

Joseph tore after him, but the dog vanished behind the Hendersons' hedge and did not come out the other side. He ran his hands through the branches, ducked under, checked the drainage ditch. Nothing. He was about to presume the worst, that Duke was gone for good, when Mrs. Okafor called from her porch, "Your dog's in my garage! He knocked over my flowerpots and he's cowering behind the lawnmower." She added that he was harmless, not some venomous beast, though he was shaking like one.

Joseph knelt in the dim garage and coaxed Duke out with half the granola bar in his pocket. His hands were still trembling when Mrs. Okafor asked how the shelter would even know the dog was his. "That's the chip," Joseph said. "The microchip." He told her it was about the size of a grain of rice, and it held an ID number. A scanner read the number and pulled up the owner's contact details. That was how the shelter had found Duke's first family, and how, when they couldn't keep him, they had known to call Joseph's mom the moment a spot opened up.

Mrs. Okafor leaned close to Duke's shoulder. "A grain of rice? In there?" "Yep," Joseph said, clipping the leash back on, twice as tight this time. "They scanned him at the shelter and his whole file came up in minutes." He scratched Duke's ears and stood. "Come on, boy. Home's that way, and I'm not letting go again."

The camp bus smelled like granola bars and bug spray, and Carson had the window seat, which felt like winning something. Across the aisle, a boy named Dev held up his phone to illustrate the problem: a photo of his older cousin at Camp Windrow last summer, arms glowing an angry, luminous pink. "Put sunscreen on at seven in the morning," Dev said, "and by dinner he looked like a lobster. Explain that."

Carson leaned over the seat. He liked problems you couldn't see the answer to right away, the hidden kind. "Was he outside all day?"

"At the lake," Dev said. "From lunch till five. Swimming, mostly."

The bus rattled over a pothole, and Carson thought hard. Sunscreen went on once, but the sun kept going all afternoon. If the sunscreen washed off in the lake, or just wore off over hours, then one morning application couldn't last a whole day. That would explain the lobster photo without needing anything mysterious. "I think it's a schedule thing," Carson said. "You have to redo it. Like an algorithm. Apply, wait, apply again."

"How long is the wait?"

"That's the part I don't know," Carson admitted, which bothered him the whole rest of the ride. When they pulled into camp, a tall counselor with a whistle and a clipboard climbed aboard and announced that lake time started after lunch, cabins first. In the cabin, one boy named Marcus, who turned out to be that exact cousin from the photo, now a junior counselor himself, dug through his duffel and pulled out a battered tube of sunscreen. "Rule from the doctor," Marcus said, tossing it to the nearest bunk. "Reapply about every two hours outdoors, and right after swimming or heavy sweating. Learned that the hard way."

Carson felt the whole thing click into place like a puzzle snapping shut. Every two hours. Right after swimming. That was the missing line of the algorithm, and the lobster photo was the proof.

At the lake, Carson set a timer on Dev's phone and they swam until the whistle blew. When the buzzer went off, they clambered onto the dock, dripping, and slathered on another coat while the other campers stared. "What are you doing?" a girl asked.

"Following the two-hour rule," Carson said, holding out the tube. "Want in?"

The twist came at dinner. Dev's phone buzzed with a text from his mother, and his face fell. "It's my cousin. The other one. She's at a different camp." He turned the screen around: a photo of a girl, shoulders bright pink, holding up a sad thumbs-up. "She put it on this morning and forgot."

"Send her the rule," Carson said, already reaching for the phone. "Every two hours. Right after swimming. She can start tonight."

Dev typed it out, then looked up and grinned. "Camp doctor in training, huh?"

"Camp bus detective," Carson said, and hit send.

When Avery spotted the kitchen thermometer reading ten degrees Fahrenheit, she knew two things: school was cancelled, and the sledding hill would be perfect. She also noticed that the salt her dad had scattered on the front steps yesterday was just sitting there on top of the ice, doing absolutely nothing, like tiny white rocks on vacation.

"Weird," she said, crouching down. "Salt melts ice. It makes the water freeze at a colder temperature. So this should work." She flicked a few grains with her mitten. Nothing. She dashed inside and grabbed the outdoor thermometer, the one shaped like a duck, and pressed it against the porch rail. It settled at eleven degrees. Hmm. Her science notebook lay open on the hall table, and she read her own handwriting from a snowy experiment last winter: rock salt stops working well below about minus 10 degrees Celsius, which is 14 degrees Fahrenheit. Eleven was colder than fourteen. That was it. The salt wasn't broken; it was just too cold for salt to do its job.

To be sure, she drafted a quick message on a scrap of paper and taped it to the door for her little brother: EXPERIMENT IN PROGRESS. DO NOT STEP ON THE LEFT SIDE OF THE STEPS. SCIENCE THANKS YOU. Then she sprinkled fresh salt on the left steps only, drew a wobbly line down the middle with her boot, and marked the time in her notebook like a detective.

An hour later, after three runs down the hill on her saucer and one spectacular crash into a snowbank, she stomped back up the walk and inspected her crime scene. The right side of the steps, the untouched side, was solid ice under a thin layer of snow. The left side was bumpy and pocked, half-melted, with little tunnels where the salt had chewed through. She wrote it all down in what she called her intricate crime-scene formula: cold plus salt equals nothing, warmish plus salt equals slush. Her brother came out, read her note, and saluted her.

"Mad Scientist Avery," he said, "your steps are weird and slushy."

"That's called evidence," she said, and flicked a salt grain at him.

The line for the Solar Hours concert wrapped twice around the arena, and Addison had been in it since 6:40 a.m., which she considered a meticulous use of a Saturday. Her plan was simple: fifty-dollar tickets went on sale at ten, and she had fifty-two dollars, the extra two for a bottle of water. The problem was that everyone in line wanted the same thing, and there were only so many tickets. She could see the scarcity without being told; she just had to count the people ahead of her and hope the math worked out.

By 9:15 the man in the neon vest came down the line with a sign, and Addison read it twice. Front section tickets now eighty dollars, it said, because demand was heavy. Eighty dollars was more than fifty, and Addison watched the effect ripple through the line in front of her. A boy three spots ahead put his money back in his pocket and left. Two girls behind him studied the sign, argued in low voices, and left too. Addison held her fifty-two dollars and did not leave, because the regular seats were still fifty, and fewer people buying the expensive ones meant the line moved faster.

She tested her idea at the hot dog cart near the gate. All morning the cart sold lemonade for four dollars, and only a few people bought it, even though the day was hot enough to make the pavement shimmer. Then the vendor, wanting to empty his cart before the show, called out that lemonade was now two dollars. Half the line turned around. Kids who had walked past it twice came back, and the vendor ran out in fifteen minutes, his ice buckets scraped clean. Addison bought one, mostly for research, and drank it slowly in the shade.

Her brother Theo texted her a message while she waited for the doors: "Did you get tickets? Mom says scalpers are selling front row for 200 outside." Addison typed back: "Not buying. When the price went up to 80, half the line walked away. When lemonade dropped to 2, it sold out in 15 min." Theo replied with a single thumbs up, which she felt understated her achievement.

Inside, a girl with green streaks in her hair overheard Addison explaining the ticket math to a friend. "Oh, that's the law of demand," the girl said. "Price up, people buy less. Price down, they buy more."

Addison nodded as if she had known the name all along, and lifted her two-dollar lemonade in a small toast to the empty cart.

Hudson had exactly forty minutes to solve the last clue on the science center's field trip sheet, and the clue made no sense. It read: "Find the spotted guard who never rode." His pencil hovered over the blank line while his classmates stormed the gift shop like it was under siege, pressing against the glass until the clerk looked ready to call for backup.

Mr. Alvarez, the frugal chaperone who had handed out exactly one token per kid and not one more, tapped his watch. "Twenty minutes, then we regroup at the bus." Priya slid up beside Hudson, holding her own sheet with five of six blanks filled. "Guard who never rode," she said. "Armor hall? The knight exhibit?" She wanted the free pass to the robotics lab that came with a perfect sheet. Hudson wanted it too, but mostly he wanted to figure the thing out, because last month he'd skipped the puzzle table at his cousin's party and regretted it ever since. He wasn't skipping this one.

The halls branched three ways. Down one corridor, a prism display shot rainbows across the ceiling, and Priya paused to watch the light refract into separate colors. "Focus," Hudson said, though he almost didn't. Then he noticed the sign at the end of the corridor: Fire Safety Hall. "Guard," he said. "Like a guard dog."

Inside, an old hand-pumped engine sat behind a rope, and beside it hung a painting of a white dog covered in black spots. A younger kid from another school pointed at it. "Why is there a dog picture next to a firetruck?" His teacher shrugged and steered him toward the smoke detector display.

Hudson studied the wall instead. There was a faded photograph of the same kind of engine being pulled by a team of horses, and out in front of the horses, small and blurry, ran a spotted dog. Another photo showed the dog trotting alongside a horse like the two were old friends. Hudson felt something click, the way the prism had split one beam into colors you couldn't see before. The dog never rode. It ran. Ahead.

"It's a Dalmatian," he said, writing fast. "Dalmatians became firehouse dogs because they got along well with horses, and they ran ahead of the horse-drawn fire carriages, helping clear the way." Priya squinted at the photo, then at the painting, then copied his answer, which meant she'd gotten it from him, and they both knew it.

"So who gets the robotics pass?" she asked as the group gathered by the bus.

Hudson looked at the pass in the teacher's hand, then at Priya's stubborn, hopeful face. "Flip you for it," he said, and pulled a coin from his jacket pocket.

Wyatt crouched beside the camp stove, turning the sausages with a fork while his little sister Nora arranged the paper plates in a row and named them like prizes. She wanted to be the one who served dinner tonight, and she had told everyone at the lake that afternoon until Dad laughed and promised her the job. Wyatt had promised something too: the meal itself, fried sausage and toasted buns, all cooked by him without any help.

The oil in the pan popped once, twice, then flared. A ribbon of orange crawled across the surface and licked up the side, and suddenly half the pan was flickering. Wyatt's hand shot toward the water bottle by his knee, because water was what you threw on fire, and then he stopped. Two summers ago, at his uncle's cookout, he had watched a frying pan do exactly this, and his uncle had not reached for the hose. He had slid a lid over the flames instead, calm as anything, and the fire had gone out like someone had pinched its nose shut.

"Turn it off," Wyatt said out loud, to himself as much as to Nora, and he shut off the stove knob with a click. Then he grabbed the lid from the picnic table and slid it over the pan, angling it so the flames couldn't slip past the rim. The fire underneath fought for a second, then died. Nora peeked around his elbow.

"You didn't put water on it," she said.

"Never pour water on a grease fire," Wyatt said. "It has to be the lid."

He lifted the corner of the lid a minute later, checking. The sausages were browned, not burnt, and steam curled up in a thin white vapor that smelled like breakfast even though it was almost sunset. Dad came back from the woodpile with his arms full and stopped when he saw the lid.

"Little trouble?" Dad asked.

"A flare-up," Wyatt said. "I remembered Uncle Rob's pan. Lid on, heat off. Worked."

Dad set down the wood and looked at Wyatt for a moment, the way he did when a kid did something that wasn't kid-sized. "You want to elaborate on that plan for me?"

"You can't use water on burning oil. Water spreads it everywhere. But if you cut off the heat and cover it, the fire runs out of what it needs." Wyatt flipped the sausages onto a plate. "It's like the fire has rules. Once you know them, it's not scary, it's just probable. Flare-up, lid, done."

Nora lifted the plate high and marched it to the picnic table, announcing dinner to the trees. Wyatt followed with the toasted buns, and Dad said, "Same cook tomorrow?" and Wyatt was already planning pancakes.

Auntie Ru's car would pull into the driveway at six o'clock sharp, and Katherine still hadn't figured out what to do about the greeting. Her cousin Tama was coming all the way from New Zealand, and Mom had said, "He'll expect a hongi, so be ready." Ready for what? The word sat in Katherine's head like an opaque window she couldn't see through, and dinner was two hours away.

"Maybe it's a handshake," said her little brother Ben, who wanted nothing more than to be in charge of handing Tama his welcome gift, because handing people gifts meant being the center of attention for at least ten seconds. He had already claimed the job at breakfast. "Everybody does handshakes."

Katherine didn't think so. Mom had pressed her noses together in the air, twice, practicing in front of the hall mirror like a secret code. So it involved faces. Katherine tried it on Ben, leaning in forehead-first, and Ben dissolved into giggles and fell off the couch. Definitely faces, she decided, and probably not a kiss, because Mom never kissed anyone at the door except Grandpa.

At the table that night, which had been stretched with the good tablecloth and all three extra chairs, Katherine watched like a scientist. Tama arrived at 6:02 with a paper-wrapped parcel of chocolate fish for Grandma, and everyone murmured approval, because in this house you never arrived without something, whereas at her friend Priya's house you were scolded for bringing gifts, as if you doubted the host's generosity. Strange, Katherine thought. Same object, opposite meaning, like a coin with two faces.

Then it happened. Tama stood in front of her, tall and smiling, and leaned in. Katherine matched him.
