Their noses and foreheads touched, warm and brief, and stayed pressed together for one held breath. When they drew apart, Tama's eyes were bright, and Grandma made a small satisfied sound from her chair.

"What does it mean?" Katherine whispered as they sat down, because Ben was already unwrapping the chocolate fish without asking, elbows planted on the table, and Mom was clearing her throat at him in the family's universal signal for elbows off, which Tama noticed and seemed to file away like a rule for later.

"It's called a hongi," Tama said. "Sharing the breath of life."

Katherine looked at him across the breadbasket and wondered whether everyone he knew at home walked around carrying a piece of everyone else's breath inside them. "So we're kind of family now," she said.

"We were already," said Tama, and passed her the potatoes before Ben could reach them.

Noah burst through the kitchen door still wearing his boots, sending a spray of snow across the tiles. "It's a snow day! A real one!" He skidded to the counter and grabbed his mom's phone before she could say a word. On the weather app, the temperature read twenty-one degrees, but right below it sat a second number, and it made him frown. "It says it feels like nine degrees. Nine! How can it feel like nine when it's twenty-one?"

His little sister Marisol peered over his elbow, nose red from the yard. "Maybe your phone's broken," she said.

Noah scrolled, but the numbers stayed the same. Twenty-one. Feels like nine. He stomped back outside to test it himself, because that was what you did with a mystery. The air in the corner behind the shed, where the fence blocked the breeze, actually felt almost pleasant. He could stand there in his coat and think about the mountains of snow waiting for him. But the moment he stepped into the open middle of the yard, the wind found him, and the cold bit through his gloves like it had teeth.

"So it's the wind," he said out loud, marching between the two spots twice more to be sure. Behind the shed, comfortable. Open yard, freezing. Same sky, same snow, same twenty-one degrees. He cupped his hands around his mouth and shouted toward the house. "Marisol! Come feel this!"

She came, boots squeaking, and he walked her between the two spots like a tour guide. "Notice anything?"

"It's freezing out here and warm back there." She rubbed the tip of her ear, which had gone from pink to an angry red. "Wait. Is that why the phone has that other number? The wind one?"

"The wind chill," Noah said. "That's what it's called. The wind makes cold air feel colder." He pointed at the app, and Marisol's eyes went wide when she saw the gap between twenty-one and nine.

They got to work. Noah nominated the spot behind the shed as base camp for the day's operations, and Marisol seconded the motion instantly, since it was the only place where her ears stopped aching. From there they rolled the fattest snowball either of them had ever built, and by noon they had a snowman with a scarf, a bottle-cap nose, and two lumps of coal they'd traded a bag of pretzels for through the fence to the neighbor kid.

Noah patted the snowman's round belly. "We should nominate you for mayor," he said.

"His name is Lumpkin," Marisol announced, and stuck a stick arm straight up into the wind.

Livia slammed the gym doors open with her shoulder, basketball bouncing against her hip, because tonight was the night she was finally going to beat Marisol in sprints. The gymnasium smelled like floor wax and ambition, and the whole seventh-grade team was already stretching by the bleachers.

But Marisol looked terrible. She was the fastest player Livia had ever seen, the girl who trained every single day, even Sundays, even during a blizzard in February. Tonight, though, she jogged the warm-up lap like her shoes were full of sand, and Coach Delgado's stopwatch caught her at a time so slow that Marisol stared at it and then at the clock on the wall, as if the clock were lying.

"That can't be right," Marisol said. "I never take a day off."

That was exactly the problem, Livia realized, standing there spinning the ball on one finger. She had read a science article for health class about how muscles grow stronger during recovery after training, not during the workout itself, which meant rest days were actually part of getting better. Marisol was skipping that whole part. Livia had a theory, and theories needed testing.

"Bet you a fruit roll-up," Livia said, "that if you rest tomorrow, completely rest, couch-level rest, you'll be faster on Thursday."

Marisol squinted. "My cousin works at a sports corporation and he says champions train more, not less."

"Your cousin also said glitter would be permanent on your sneakers if you sealed it with hairspray, and it was gone by Tuesday."

Marisol laughed so hard she snorted, which made the whole team turn around, which made her snort again. "Fine. One day. One fruit roll-up."

Thursday night, the gym was loud with squeaking shoes. Marisol lined up, coiled like a spring, and when Coach blew the whistle she flew down the court so fast the stopwatch practically gave up. She turned to Livia, breathless and grinning.

"I owe you a fruit roll-up," she said, "and an apology to my legs."

Ivy wanted the Slate Pro tablet more than she wanted her next birthday, and the poster in the library hallway knew it. It showed five glowing checkmarks: SHARPEST SCREEN, FASTEST CHIP, MOST APPS, LIGHTEST BODY, COOLEST COLORS. Above the checkmarks, a famous singer named Rae Delgado grinned and said, "I never leave home without mine." At the bottom, tiny letters announced that the Tech Store two blocks away would close at 5:00. Ivy checked the clock above the librarian's desk. It was 4:20.

Her best friend Marcus was already at a table, doing homework he should have finished three days ago. "Look at this," Ivy said, spreading the poster flat in front of him. "Rae Delgado uses one. And five great features. Five, Marcus." She tapped each checkmark. "Everyone at school is getting one. Even Priya, and Priya still uses a flip phone."

Marcus squinted at the poster. "Rae Delgado also gets paid to smile at things. That's her whole job." He turned a homework page over. "And 'sharpest' and 'coolest' aren't really facts. They're just loaded words. It's like when my brother calls his sandwich 'legendary' so I'll trade him my chips."

"Okay, but the screen is sharper." Ivy paused. "Sharper than what, though?" She read the poster again, slower this time. Something felt off, like a puzzle with a piece missing. The ad listed everything the tablet was good at and nothing else. "It says lightest body. It doesn't say anything about the battery." That seemed strange to her, because the battery was the first thing her mom asked about any device. It seemed logical that an ad with five checkmarks would add a sixth for battery life if the battery were any good.

She marched to the computer catalog, typed "Slate Pro review," and found a magazine article. The tablet's battery lasted four hours. Four. Her cousin's ancient tablet lasted nine. "Marcus," she whispered. "They stacked the deck. Five great facts, and they left out the bad one." Marcus nodded. "My language arts teacher calls that card stacking. Showing only the facts that support your side, so the message seems stronger than it is." Ivy wrote it on her hand, because some facts deserve ink.

At 4:45 Marcus asked, "Are we still buying it? The store closes in fifteen minutes." Ivy looked at the poster, at Rae Delgado's grin, at the five checkmarks marching in a row like they had somewhere to be. "No. But we can walk past the store on the way home and look through the window. That's free." Marcus zipped his backpack. "Now that's a feature they should advertise."

The snow arrived overnight with no warning at all, so when Marcus woke up and saw the school parking lot buried, the day felt like a spontaneous gift. He suited up and hurried down Maple Street toward the hill behind Mr. Delgado's building, where his friend Theo was already packing snow onto a sled runner. Their favorite run started at the top, but a fallen branch had begun to obstruct the path halfway down, so they took turns steering around it, each pass a little faster than the last.

After an hour of climbing and crashing, Marcus pulled off one glove to shake the snow out and noticed something odd. His fingers were white and stinging, his ears had gone numb enough that he could pinch them without really feeling it, and the tip of his nose had that prickly, half-asleep feeling. Yet his chest and legs, under all those layers, were toasty. He tested the idea on the next run. He kept his gloved hands tucked under his arms, and sure enough his fingers warmed up while his ears stayed cold.

"Why do my hands hurt but my stomach doesn't?" Theo asked, rubbing his own red ears.

"I think fingers, toes, ears and the nose are the parts of the body most likely to get frostbite," Marcus said. "Everything else stays warm longer. My mom's landlord lost a toe that way one winter, so she's always going on about it."

Theo looked down at his boots. "Toes too?"

"Toes too. So we cover all four and we're good."

They dug spare hats and an extra pair of socks out of Marcus's garage, and Mrs. Delgado, watching from her window, waved them in for cocoa when their sled run ended in her hedge. Marcus pressed his warm mug against his cheek and felt his nose wake up, tingling.

"Same time after lunch?" Theo asked, already carrying the sled toward the hill.

The ferry to Owl Lake Campground took forty minutes, and Brielle's little brother Theo turned green ten minutes in. He sat hunched against the rail inside the cabin, staring at the floor, holding a paper bag.

"I'm going to throw up," Theo said.

"Look out the window," Brielle said.

"I did. It made it worse."

That was the strange part, Brielle thought. Watching the water had made him feel sicker, not better. She remembered the museum trip last spring, when the bus had jolted over potholes and she had felt fine the whole ride. What had she done differently? She had sat by the window, but not at the passing trees. She had watched the mountains, far away, which never seemed to move.

"Come on." She took Theo's sleeve and pulled him toward the deck door. He was impulsive about most things, ice cream, puddles, wasps, but moving took persuasion now.

The wind on deck was cold. Brielle steered him to the rail. "Don't watch the water. Watch the shoreline, way out there. The far end, where it doesn't move."

Theo gripped the rail and fixed his eyes on the distant line of pines. A swell rolled under the hull, and another. Slowly his shoulders came down from around his ears. The gray went out of his face.

"It works," he said. "Why?"

Brielle considered lying, then didn't. "I don't know exactly. Something about your eyes and your ears agreeing when you look at the horizon." She pointed anyway. "Keep watching. Dad said the campsite is near that second point."

Their father came out with two granola bars, ready to intervene with crackers and ginger candy, but Theo waved him off and kept his eyes on the far shore.

When the ferry bumped the dock, Theo was the first one down the ramp, running. "Race you to the car," he called.

Brielle jogged after him over the gravel, her knee cartilage aching from a fall off her bike the week before, but not enough to slow her down.

Theo stood in the kitchen with dirt on his shirt and two days until the science fair. On the counter sat four bean seedlings in paper cups, and beside them his project board, which currently said, in giant letters, MUSIC IS GOOD FOR PLANTS. His little sister Maya wandered in, eating a pickle.

"That's your whole project?" she said. "Good for plants how? Also, plants don't have ears, so, nice work."

"Thanks for the exceptional feedback," Theo said. He stared at the board. The trouble was, he couldn't prove music was good for plants, because he couldn't even say what would prove him wrong. He remembered his notebook from class and flipped it open. There it was, in his own handwriting: a useful hypothesis must be testable, meaning an experiment could show it is wrong. Below it, the form it usually takes: If... then...

"So make it testable," Maya said, peering over his arm.

"I'm getting there." He crossed out the giant letters and wrote: If I play music for two seedlings and keep two seedlings in silence, then the music plants will grow taller in one week. He pointed at it. "An experiment could show that's wrong. The quiet plants could win, or it could be a tie. Either way, I'd know something."

"That's less exciting than my idea," Maya said. "My idea is that pickles are good for plants."

"Please don't elaborate."

She elaborated anyway, describing a pickle-watering system, until he handed her a prism from the junk drawer and aimed her at the window. Sunlight split into a stripe of rainbow across her hands, and she went quiet at last.

The next morning Theo measured the cups. The music plants had grown a centimeter. So had the others. He wrote down every number, even the boring ones, then set his ruler beside the cups for tomorrow.

"Tie so far," Maya reported from the window, holding the prism up so a green spot of rainbow landed on the tallest seedling. "Your plants are all winning, basically."

Samantha balanced the mixing bowl on the picnic table and read her grandmother's recipe card again, the one taped inside the camper where the wind couldn't steal it. The card was really a letter Gran had sent last spring, ending with "Save me a slice." Samantha had promised she would, and tonight she intended to bake her first loaf over the campfire.

She remembered the bakery visit from last summer, how Gran had let her poke a squishy lump of dough that seemed to breathe. "It's not magic," Gran had said, winking. "Yeast makes bread rise by feeding on sugars and releasing carbon dioxide gas, which gets trapped in the dough as bubbles." Samantha had thought that was the strangest thing she'd ever heard, a fungus burping bread into existence.

She mixed flour, sugar, and the packet of yeast, then reached for the kettle. The water had been sitting on the camp stove while Dad ran the generator to charge the lantern, so it was good and hot. She stirred it in, kneaded the dough, and set the bowl near the fire in a sheltered spot, safe from any draft, because Gran's letter said cold air would slow the rising. Then she waited. The dough sat there, round and lazy, as lethargic as her little brother Theo after a swim.

"That's a bread rock," Theo announced twenty minutes later. "You're making bread rocks for dinner."

"It's still waking up," Samantha said, but her stomach twisted. She leaned close and studied the dough. No bubbles. No puff. Nothing. She thought about Gran's letter again, feeding on sugars, releasing gas. The yeast should have been eating and puffing like tiny balloon artists, and it was doing nothing at all. Something had gone wrong before the bowl ever got set down. She touched the side of the mixing bowl where she'd poured the water in. Warm. Very warm. Hot, actually, still hot enough that she pulled her fingers back. The yeast hadn't been sleeping. The yeast had been cooked.

Theo, who had declared the whole project doomed, suddenly changed his mind and became her assistant. "New plan," he said solemnly, holding the fresh packet like it was treasure. They mixed everything again, and this time Samantha tested the cooled water on her wrist, the way you test a bottle for a baby, warm but not hot. They set the bowl by the fire and watched.

Ten minutes later Theo grabbed her sleeve. "Look, look! It's a balloon!" The dough had swelled up round and dome-shaped, and when Samantha pressed one finger gently against it, the surface sprang back like something alive. She grinned and shaped it into a loaf. "Gran," she said, "is getting the biggest slice of all."

"Only if I don't eat it first," said Theo, already reaching for a stick to poke the fire.

Sofia stood in line outside the ticket kiosk in the west wing of the mall, third from the front, her fingers curled around the twenty dollars she had saved from dog walking. The kiosk sold tickets to the Bright Comet concert, and for one day only they were priced at ten dollars. Behind her, the line snaked past the pretzel stand, past the fountain where coins glinted under the water, and out toward the shoe store. She counted at least two hundred people.

At ten o'clock the metal shutter rattled up and the clerk began pulling tickets from a box. Sofia got hers, paper warm from the printer, and stepped aside to look at it. Behind her the box emptied fast. By the time the fiftieth person reached the counter, the clerk raised both hands and called out, "That's it, we're out." The rest of the line broke apart slowly, like ice melting. A girl near the fountain sat down on the rim and put her head in her hands.

"That's so unfair," said Malia, Sofia's neighbor, who had been two spots behind the shutter people. "Ten dollars, and they only had fifty tickets. Look at all these people." She swept her arm at the crowd still drifting, unwilling to leave. Sofia turned the ticket over in her hands. Half the people in that line had wanted a ticket and gotten nothing, because the price had been so low that everyone could afford one, and there weren't enough to go around. She remembered her brother once saying there was a word for that.

A man in a gray jacket moved along the edge of the crowd, speaking quietly. "Bright Comet, forty dollars, I've got two." Malia grabbed Sofia's sleeve. "That's the same ticket," she whispered. "Ten dollars at the kiosk, forty from him." Sofia watched a boy hand over the money and walk away holding the ticket like it was made of glass. Down the corridor, a cart selling phone cases sat stacked with hundreds of them, a sign reading five dollars, two for eight, and barely a customer stopping.

"My brother called it a shortage," Sofia said. "When the price stays low, more people want the thing than there are things to sell." She tested the logic in her head against what she had just watched: low price, long line, empty box. Then the phone case cart: plenty of cases, few buyers, price falling. It wasn't symmetrical, not exactly, but it fit both ways she looked at it.

Malia stared at the man in the gray jacket. "I was going to pay him forty," she said. "I had it in my pocket." She took out the bills, folded twice, and looked at them for a long moment. Then she put the money back in her pocket and straightened her shoulders. "Next time I'm getting here at seven," she said, "and I'm bringing a folding chair."

Megan sat cross-legged on her bed with her notebook open to a page titled "The Mystery." For months she had been collecting clues: the new shoes she needed in August, the two inches she had grown since spring, the way her mood could flip like a light switch for no reason she could see. Something invisible was running a schedule inside her, and she wanted to know the rules. Tonight her plan was a chart, because charts had helped her figure out her bean plants in science. Seeds germinate when the conditions line up, and she suspected her body worked the same way, on some hidden timetable she couldn't watch directly. Her hypothesis had germinated at Priya's house on Saturday, when Priya had flopped onto the rug and said, "My sister got her first period when she was ten. Ten! And she's still mad about it."

Megan had blinked. "My sister was fourteen. That's a huge difference."

"I know," Priya said. "I asked my mom, and she said a big CDC survey in the United States found the median age is about twelve, but with a wide normal range around it. So basically anywhere near that is normal."

Back in her bedroom now, Megan wrote TEN on a sticky note and FOURTEEN on another and stuck them on her wall, with TWELVE, MEDIAN in the middle. Median, she knew from math, meant the middle value, the one in the center when you lined everybody up. So ten and fourteen were both inside a wide range around twelve, like two houses on opposite ends of the same long street. That was her test: if the pattern held, then there was no single right age, and the flips and the new shoes and everything else were just the street she lived on. She texted Priya her theory, then pulled up the email Priya had sent that afternoon, because Priya had a project of her own going.

"Dear Megan," it read. "I'm making a poster for my cousin's birthday. She's turning thirteen soon and she's nervous she's 'late.' I want to tell her the survey thing but in a fun way, not a lecture. Can you draw me a timeline with shoes on it? You're better at drawing than me. Also my sister says hi. Your friend, Priya."

Megan grinned, and the grin felt contagious, like it spread all by itself to the pencil in her hand. She drew a long street with houses from ten to fourteen, put a big star on the middle of the block, and labeled each house with a different girl. Then she photographed it and hit send.

Two minutes later her phone buzzed: "PERFECT. My sister says she wants one for her wall too."

Megan taped her sticky notes in a neat row above her desk, stepped back, and nodded at her wall. "Wide normal range," she said out loud, and clicked off the lamp.

Emma had spread her poster across the picnic table at Grandma's backyard reunion, and that was the problem. For her social studies project she had made a bar graph of the origins of people in Brampton, Ontario, using numbers from a government website. She had checked her addition three times, and the totals still came to far more than one hundred percent. "That's impossible," she muttered, jabbing her pencil at the poster. "A town can't be more than all of itself."

Her cousin Priya leaned over her shoulder, holding a paper plate of samosas. "Maybe the website made a mistake," she said. "Or maybe you did."

"I despise this graph," Emma said, which wasn't true, but it felt true right then. Uncles and aunts drifted past the table, some carrying chairs, some arguing about whose turn it was at the badminton net. Grandma arrived last, drying her hands on a dish towel, and studied the poster the way she studied a chessboard.

"Uncle Ray!" Grandma called across the yard. "Come and settle something." Uncle Ray, whom everyone agreed was the most competent person in the family at anything involving numbers, worked at the town hall. He set down his lemonade and looked at Emma's graph for a long moment. Then he laughed, not at her, but the way people laugh when a puzzle suddenly makes sense. "That's the census," he said. "It's not wrong. Canada's census has let people report more than one ethnic or cultural origin since 1981, so the origin totals add up to more than the country's population."

Emma stared at him. "More than one," she repeated slowly. In her head she tested the idea against her own family, sitting right there in folding chairs. Grandma cooked pierogi every Christmas and told stories about monsoon seasons in Sri Lanka, where she'd taught school for ten years before emigrating. Priya called herself both Guyanese and Canadian and refused to pick. Auntie Joan's family had come from Scotland four generations back, and she still put tartan napkins on the table every reunion. If every one of them could tick more than one box, then of course the bars would stack up past one hundred percent. Nobody had counted twice by accident; everybody had counted all of themselves.

She grabbed a marker and wrote across the top of the poster: "Why the numbers are bigger than 100." Then she drew a small pie chart of her own family, one slice for each thing they claimed, the slices overlapping in the middle like a Venn diagram. "Priya, hold this corner down," she said, reaching for her pencil case. "I'm going to interview everybody before the potato salad runs out."

Brielle had planned the whole week before Grandpa's suitcase even reached the porch. She would show him the rope swing, the vegetable garden, and the dilapidated shed at the back fence where her old bike still leaned against a broken shelf. But on the second morning, the kitchen filled with smoke from toast nobody noticed, and Grandpa just sat at the table reading his newspaper while the slices turned black.

"Grandpa, the toast!" Brielle grabbed the fork and flipped them off the burner before the smoke alarm could intervene. She waved a towel at the ceiling and studied him. Last summer, he had smelled her burning marshmallow from across the entire yard. She tested him quietly, saying nothing about the cinnamon rolls she had hidden in the oven to surprise him at lunch. When she finally brought them out, warm and fragrant enough to make her own mouth water, he thanked her politely, as if she had handed him a paper napkin.

That afternoon she ran a careful experiment in the backyard. She set out five cups on the picnic table: vanilla, lemon, coffee, onion, and plain water. "Tell me what each one is," she said, and Grandpa, who loved games, agreed at once. He identified the coffee, slowly, and guessed wrong on everything else. The plain water he called "soap." Brielle sat back on the bench, thinking about her grandmother, who had always known it was raining before anyone else because she could smell it coming, and who had once found a gas leak that no one else had noticed. Maybe she, too, had stopped being able to smell near the end, and maybe everyone had mistaken it for not paying attention. Brielle wondered whether she should have visited more that year instead of choosing soccer camp.

That evening she typed her notes into the library computer and found a word waiting for her: presbyosmia. "The sense of smell naturally declines in old age," the screen said, "a change called presbyosmia." She read it twice, then printed it.

On the last day of his visit, Grandpa stood by the grill in the backyard while Brielle watched the hamburgers for him, flipping each one at exactly the right moment. He talked about his own grandfather's kitchen, and the bread that always seemed to come out of the oven a little too dark. "We teased him about it for years," he said, shaking his head. "Now I wonder."

"I'll be your nose while you're here," Brielle said, and handed him the spatula so he could do the honors himself.

Anthony raised his hand so fast his chair squeaked. "Mr. Ruiz, why does my voice do that croaky thing now?" It had happened that morning in the shower, mid-song, and again at lunch when he'd yelled for the basketball. Mr. Ruiz only grinned and said, "Ask the choir teacher. That's her frontier, not mine." Frontier, Anthony thought. Like his voice was wild, unclaimed land.

Flashback: last spring, in this same room, Anthony had sung the solo in the spring assembly without a single wobble. His voice had been light and steady, and his grandmother had recorded the whole thing on her phone. Now, three months into seventh grade, he had signed up to audition for the winter concert, and the audition was Friday. He wanted that solo more than he'd wanted anything since the new skate park opened.

So he ran an experiment. He borrowed a notebook and made a tally: every time his voice cracked, he wrote down the note he'd been trying to hit. In the shower he sang up a scale. Low notes: smooth. Middle notes: fine. High notes: crack, crack, crack. There was a distinct breaking zone, like a fence across his range. He tried warming up first, then drinking cold water, then not talking all day. Nothing moved the fence. Whatever was happening was happening on its own, invisibly, somewhere inside.

On Thursday he brought his notebook to choir practice and showed the tallies to Ms. Park. "It's the larynx," she said simply. "It grows during puberty, and the vocal folds inside it get longer and thicker, so the voice may crack while this happens." Anthony stared at his tally marks. Longer and thicker. It wasn't a fence at all; it was construction. His voice was being rebuilt, bigger.

That night he wrote a note and left it on the kitchen counter for his dad, who worked late.

Dad, I audition tomorrow. Don't be intimidated by any weird sounds from the music room, it's just my larynx renovating. Wish me luck. Anthony.

At the audition Friday, Anthony chose a lower song than the one he'd sung in spring. He reached the highest note of the new arrangement, felt a small tremor pass through like a truck on a distant road, and kept going. Ms. Park circled his name. "Solo," she said. "Second verse, low key."

Anthony punched the air so hard his pencil flew across the music room and rolled under the piano.

Brielle sat at the kitchen table with her left arm propped on a stack of cookbooks, the fresh white cast ending just below her elbow. The fall from the dilapidated porch railing had happened three days ago, and she was still turning over what Dr. Okafor had said. "The break missed the growth plate, which is the good news," the doctor had told them, and her mother had exhaled like she'd been holding her breath since the emergency room. Brielle hadn't asked why at the time, because asking felt like admitting she didn't understand something important about her own arm.

Her little brother Theo slid into the chair across from her, holding a jar of bean seeds he'd been trying to germinate on the windowsill all week. "When your cast comes off, we're playing catch," he announced. "Every day. I've been practicing my curveball so I can finally beat you." Theo had wanted to beat her at catch since spring, and now that she was benched, he kept repeating his plan like a promise.

"Growth plate," Brielle said slowly, watching him twist the jar lid. "That's what she called it. She said near the ends of long bones are growth plates made of cartilage, and that's where bones lengthen while you're still a kid." Theo wrinkled his nose. "Cartilage? Like your ears?" "Sort of, I think. So if a break goes through it, the bone might not grow right. Mine didn't, that's why it's good news."

She went to the hall closet and found the ball of twine. If her arm bone was still lengthening, like a bean seed swelling before it sprouted, she could catch it in the act. She looped the twine from her shoulder to her wrist on the right arm, cut it, and labeled the string with a marker: RIGHT, WEEK ONE. Then she did the same for the cast side, writing LEFT over the plaster instead.

"Do you actually think it's growing right now?" Theo asked, watching her tape both strings into her notebook.

"Seeds don't sprout while you stare at them either," Brielle said. "But the beans on the sill prove things happen slow." She closed the notebook and slid it to the end of the table, where they could both see it. "Six weeks. Then we measure again, and then, curveball or not, you're going down."

Theo grinned and set his jar beside it, fungus speckling the damp cotton inside. "Race you," he said. "Beans versus bone."

James stared at the jumbled tray of foam balls on his workbench and realized, not for the first time, that his whole plan might have been built on a wrong idea. In his garage, with the door half open to let in the afternoon light, he had promised his little sister Maya that he would build her a model of an atom by dinnertime. The trouble was that he had assumed every atom needed the same parts, like every sandwich needed the same two slices of bread.

He had learned this the hard way last summer, and the memory still made him wince. At the science museum he had confidently glued one big ball, one small ball, and a clump in the middle for the neutron, only to have a kid next to him squint at it and say, "That's not hydrogen." James had argued, in a vain attempt to protect his work, until the kid pointed at the chart on the wall. He had walked away without finishing the model, and he still wondered whether he should have just asked someone instead of insisting he was right.

Now he spread out the chart he had copied into his notebook and tested his idea with actual balls instead of glue. He pushed the pieces around on the bench like a puzzle. "Okay," he said to himself, "the most common kind of hydrogen atom has just one proton and one electron and no neutron at all." He set down one large red ball, then one tiny blue ball, and deliberately left the gray clump sitting alone in the tray. It looked unfinished. It looked almost like camouflage, a half-built thing pretending to be complete, but the chart said otherwise, and the chart had been right before.

Maya wandered in, sneakers squeaking on the concrete, and picked up the gray ball. "What's this lonely one for?"

"Nothing," James said. "That's the weird part. Hydrogen doesn't need it." She frowned at the two lonely balls on the wire, so he handed her the glue and the paint. "You do the electron. I'll hold the wire."

She dipped her brush in blue, and the small ball slowly turned from white to bright, spinning between her fingers.

Amelia stood on the porch of Kanya's house holding a box of oranges in both hands, exactly the way her mother had shown her. When Kanya's grandmother opened the door, the old woman pressed her palms together and bowed slightly. Amelia had no idea what to do with her hands, so she just nodded fast and hoped that counted.

Inside, everyone had left their shoes in a row by the door, so Amelia nudged her sneakers into line with the rest. She watched Kanya's little brother, Santi, who was six, dart under the dining table like a fish under a canopy of chairs and tablecloth. He popped out near Amelia and grinned up at her with a gap where his front tooth used to be. Without thinking, Amelia reached down to ruffle his hair.

"Wait," Kanya said, catching her wrist. "Don't touch his head. In Thailand the head is sacred, so touching someone's head, even to pat a child, can be seen as rude."

Amelia pulled her hand back. Santi didn't look offended, only curious, but she took Kanya seriously. She began testing her theory as the evening went on, watching closely. Kanya's father passed Santi a dish and never once patted him. When Santi fell off a chair, his mother checked his elbow, his knee, and carefully not his head. Nobody touched anybody's head at all.

At dinner, Amelia kept noticing more. The spoon went in the right hand, the fork in the left, and the fork pushed food onto the spoon. She copied Kanya move for move, and when she almost used the fork directly, she caught herself and switched.

"You're learning fast," Kanya said.

"That's because I'm extremely sophisticated," Amelia said, and immediately dropped a grain of rice on her shirt.

Santi laughed so hard he slid off his chair again. This time, when he stood up, Amelia bowed to him, palms together, just like the grandmother at the door. Santi bowed right back.

Parker scanned the field from the third deck, popcorn warm in his lap, and counted jerseys. His uncle had budgeted exactly enough cash for two hot dogs and one souvenir each, so Parker had chosen the popcorn to make his money last. He counted again, because the first count had to be wrong. "Maya, what numbers do you see out there?" he asked his cousin. She squinted through the railing. "Seventeen, thirty-one, six, nine, eleven." Parker checked the scoreboard roster. Every player had a number, and every number was there, except one. Nobody on either team wore 42. He wondered if 42 was bad luck, or against some rule nobody had told him.

Then the whole stadium went weird. The public address announcer said it was a special ceremony before the first pitch, and every single player on both teams jogged out wearing the same jersey, all with 42 on the back. "Why is everyone dressed the same?" Maya asked, tugging Parker's sleeve. "Did they lose their laundry?" Parker didn't laugh, because he was too busy thinking. Same number on every player, on every team, at the same time. That wasn't a coincidence. That looked like something people did on purpose, together, for one number.

The woman in the next seat, there with her grandson, leaned over. "You two look puzzled." She held up her grandson's tiny foam finger, which also had a 42 on it. Maya pointed at the field. "Why does everybody have that number?" The woman smiled. "In 1997, Major League Baseball retired Jackie Robinson's number 42 for every team. First time any professional athlete was honored that way." Parker whispered the words to himself so he would remember them. Retired, for every team. Not just one club, all of them. That was why he had never seen a 42 in any game he had watched on TV, not once. He had thought it was chance. It was the opposite of chance.

His uncle came back from the concession stand and handed Maya her hot dog before she even had to ask, because he always noticed who was waiting. Parker pointed at the field. "Uncle Theo, look. Every team in baseball gave up number 42 so one man could keep it forever." His uncle sat down slowly, looked at all those matching jerseys glowing under the lights, and put his cap over his heart. "Then let's stand up," he said. "All of us."

The snow came down all morning, and by ten o'clock the school district had given up and called a snow day. Charlie yelled so loudly that her upstairs neighbor banged on the ceiling, but she was already pulling on her boots. She texted her friend Maya, and they met at the little park on Maple Street, where the slide was frozen solid and Mrs. Park, who lived nearby, was grumbling that her landlord was negligent and still hadn't fixed the gate, so it hung crooked in the snow.

"We're building a snowman," Charlie announced. "A huge one. Three balls high." Maya knelt down and started packing, but the snow wouldn't cooperate. Every time she pressed a handful together, it sifted back apart like sugar. Charlie tried too, squeezing until her mittens ached. The ball just crumbled in her palms. "This snow is broken," Maya said, kicking at it. The powder flew up in a dry puff and drifted down again without sticking to anything.

Charlie scooped two handfuls and held them side by side, one from the shadow of the bench and one from the sunny patch near the swing set. The sunny one felt heavier, almost damp, and when she squeezed it, it held. "Feel this," she said, and Maya pressed it into a rough little ball. "Snow near freezing has some water in it," Charlie said, turning the ball over. "It's the dry stuff that falls apart." Maya looked around. Half the park sat in shade, where the snow stayed powdery and useless, and half of it was wide open to the morning sun.

"So we wait," Maya said. "It's not even noon yet." They climbed the frozen slide until their mittens froze, then took turns dragging each other on the crooked gate like a sled. Back at home, Charlie's mom made cocoa, and they watched the chocolate dissolve into the milk while the sun climbed higher.

By two o'clock they tested the shady snow again, and this time Charlie could feel the difference before she even squeezed it. The top layer packed, then the next, and the next. Their snowman stood three balls high before the shadows came back, with a stick arm waving at the swing set, and Charlie said, "Same park, same snow. We just had to wait for the sun to do its part."

Liam sat cross-legged on Marcus's bedroom floor with Marcus's phone, because his own phone had died on the bus and Marcus never minded sharing. He was supposed to be looking up cheat codes for Rocket Racers, but when he typed his own name into the search bar just to see what would happen, the first result made his stomach drop. It was a comment he had written two years ago, back when he was eight, under a video of a soccer match. "The goalie is so bad he has an infection of the hands," he had written, misspelling everything, and there it was now, next to his full name, glowing on the screen like it had been waiting for him.

"That's weird," Liam said. "I posted that on my old account. I deleted the whole account last year."

Marcus leaned over, chewing the last of his pretzels. "Try my name," he said. Liam typed it in, and a picture came up that Marcus's mom had posted publicly years ago, of Marcus in a bird costume for the school's migratory animals play. It had spread from one page to another, and now a stranger's blog had it, with a caption underneath that called him "this brave little flamingo."

"Search engines use crawlers," Marcus said, reading from the top of the results page. "Automated programs that copy and index public web pages." He pointed at the small gray text. "So if it's public, it can turn up in search results."

Liam tested it, because it seemed too strange to just believe. He posted a fake comment on a public video, using his first name and a made-up last name, then searched for it. At first nothing came up, but after Marcus made them both quesadillas and they came back with crumbs on their shirts, the comment appeared, sitting there in the results like a photograph pinned to a wall. He deleted the comment immediately, then thought about the flamingo picture, which had already been copied and would not go away just because Marcus asked.

"We should tell your mom about the picture," Liam said. "Before the whole school searches your name." Marcus nodded slowly, and Liam handed him the phone first, letting him decide whether to show her now or after dinner. Down in the kitchen, Marcus's mom was saturating the counter with soapy water, scrubbing a pot and humming. Marcus took a breath and held the screen out to her. "Mom, can you look at something?"

The waiting room clock ticked past 3:40, and Arianna's audition for the spring choir started at 4:15. She twisted a crumpled tissue in her lap, the third one since she'd sat down, each stained the same worrying shade of yellow-green.

"Look," she whispered to her dad, holding it up. "It's getting worse. What if I need antibiotics before I can sing?"

A boy across the aisle, maybe ten, leaned over his own pile of tissues. "Mine's green," he said, his voice brittle with worry. "Green means infection. My sister said so. I bet I need medicine today."

Arianna's name was called before she could answer. In the exam room, Dr. Patel listened to her lungs, looked in her throat, and said, "It's a virus. Rest, fluids, and you can sing tonight if your voice holds."

"But the mucus is yellow," Arianna said. "Practically green."

Dr. Patel smiled. "The color comes from your immune cells and an enzyme they release. Green or yellow doesn't tell us whether it's bacteria or a virus." She tapped the chart. "Your exam does, and this is viral."

Arianna folded the fact into her mind like a note she could pass along. On the way out, she stopped at the pharmacy counter to pick up tissues for the boy's mother, who was juggling a toddler and her purse.

"Hey," Arianna said to the boy, handing him the pack. "I asked the doctor about the green thing. It's just your immune cells and an enzyme they release. My doctor said the color alone can't tell you if it's bacteria or a virus. Mine's green too, and I don't need medicine."

The boy's shoulders dropped an inch. "Really? So I'm not super sick?"

"You're just full of germ fighters," Arianna said. "Same as me."

At 3:58 she and her dad raced for the car. In the parking lot she tested her voice on one soft scale, and the high note came out clean and clear, like a bell through an open window.

Evan had been waiting all week for the Sato family reunion at his aunt's house, mostly because of one thing: Aunt Mariko's ramen. He'd watched videos about it, and he'd even practiced with chopsticks at home using dry spaghetti, which his cat, Biscuit, kept stealing off the floor.

When he arrived, the greetings started immediately. On his mom's side, everyone hugged. On the Sato side, Aunt Mariko bowed slightly, so Evan bowed back, a little too deep, and nearly knocked over a lamp. Everyone laughed, and his cousin Kenji gave him two thumbs up. Kenji pressed a small wrapped box into Evan's hands. "For you. Don't open it yet, that part comes later," Kenji said. Evan clutched it like treasure. In his own house, gifts got ripped open on the spot, so waiting felt like holding a sneeze in.

Then came the ramen, steaming in huge bowls, and Evan's plan exploded. Everyone slurped. Aunt Mariko slurped. Grandpa Sato slurped so loudly it sounded like a drain unclogging. Evan froze with his chopsticks halfway up. At home, one tiny slurp meant a look from his grandmother that could diminish a person's appetite entirely. He glanced around the table, testing his idea: maybe here, the noise meant something good. He slurped one noodle, cautiously, like a scientist. Aunt Mariko beamed. "There it is!" she said. Kenji leaned over and whispered, "In Japan, slurping noodles like ramen and soba is acceptable at the table. It's not rude here." Evan slurped again, louder, and Grandpa Sato laughed and slurped back, like they were having a conversation in noodle language.

Between bites, Evan noticed his own bias had been the problem: he'd assumed one set of table manners was the only set. He also noticed Uncle Tadao served himself exactly one modest scoop of everything, frugal as ever, while Uncle Pete from Evan's side took enough for three people. Two families, one table, completely different rulebooks, and somehow it all worked.

Later, finally allowed to open his gift, Evan peeled the paper slowly and found a red ramen bowl with a dragon on it. "So you can practice at home," Kenji said. Evan held it up, grinned, and took his biggest slurp of the night, right out of the empty bowl.

Christopher sat on Marcus's floor with the phone box in his lap, because tomorrow was the big day and Marcus's dad had picked the phone up early so they could set it together. The plan had one catch, and Christopher had read it four times: two gigabytes of data a month, and that was all. He wanted to know what actually ate the data, since you couldn't watch it disappear.

"It's the videos," Marcus said. "Obviously."

"But Grandpa sends me videos of geese and they barely count," Christopher said. He remembered last fall, when Grandpa texted him a clip of a big migratory flock passing over the lake, and the data meter barely moved. That was the clue. So he borrowed Marcus's phone and ran a test: he played one video with the wifi off and wrote down the number, then played the same video on wifi and checked again. The wifi number stayed flat. It wasn't videos that used data. It was videos without wifi. The hidden rule showed itself, and Christopher felt like he'd pulled a curtain back.

"My dad says there's a poster at the store," Marcus said, pulling up a picture on his tablet. "It's supposed to depict the very first handheld cellular call ever made. Some Motorola engineer named Martin Cooper made it right on a New York street on April 3, 1973."

"Fifty years before phones like this," Christopher said, holding up the slim box. "Pocket phones are older than my parents."

Marcus read a message out loud that his sister had sent from the store: "Kid in front of me asked how long people have carried phones around. Manager said 1973. Kid said, 'That's it?' and everyone laughed."

Christopher texted his dad: I figured out the data. Wifi at home for videos. Regular stuff is fine anywhere. Dad sent back one word: "Deal."

Christopher slid the phone under his pillow like a buried treasure and set his alarm for tomorrow.

The tent smelled like pine and cold canvas when Lily unzipped her bag the first night in the park. She set her toothpaste, her sunscreen, and a half-eaten bag of trail mix in the corner by her sleeping pad, the way she did at home. Outside, her dad was hauling the cooler from the car to the metal bear locker by the picnic table, and her mom was being optimistic about the clouds breaking up before morning. Lily could hear the whole camp settling down, quiet except for a creek somewhere behind the trees.

At breakfast the next day, a ranger walked through the loop checking lockers. She stopped at their site and looked at the picnic table, then at the tent. "Everything with a scent needs to go in the locker overnight," she said. "In Yosemite and parks like it, anything scented counts as food. That includes toothpaste, sunscreen, and trash." Lily's dad thanked her, and the ranger moved on to the next campsite.

Lily sat with her granola bar halfway to her mouth and thought about that. Toothpaste counted as food? It was minty, not edible, at least not on purpose. She tried to imagine a bear caring about sunscreen. The rule seemed strange until she considered how a bear searches, not with its eyes but with its nose, and a nose did not sort things the way a grocery store did. If it smelled like something, it was something.

That evening she offered to transport the last load to the locker herself. She packed the toothpaste, the sunscreen, and the empty wrapper from her dad's sandwich, and she counted the items as she placed them inside, one by one, keeping her own little economy of scents, everything tallied, nothing left over. She zipped the tent empty and walked back under a sky going dark and blue.

"Did we get everything?" her mom called from the fire.

"Every single thing with a smell," Lily said. "The tent is clean."

Ella's little brother Theo banged his fork against his glass like a tiny judge with a gavel. "The bridge is flooded," he announced, holding up Mom's phone. "Tanya says the whole road to Grandma's is underwater. Look." The photo on the screen showed brown water swallowing a guardrail, waves distinct against the gray sky. Mom leaned in, her spoon of soup paused halfway to her mouth. She had promised to drive to Grandma's on Saturday to help her restock her freezer, and Grandma had been asking about the visit all week.

"Send it to me," Ella said, already pulling out her own phone under the table, which was allowed at dinner only for emergencies. Theo slid the phone across the tablecloth, nearly into the gravy boat. Ella remembered a day two summers ago when Theo had fallen off his bike and split his chin; he'd sat at this same table while Mom gently felt the curve of her own jaw and told him the hard part there was cartilage, and that his would heal. He trusted facts he could feel. But a flood photo was different. You couldn't feel where it came from.

"That's it," Ella said suddenly, standing up so fast her chair scraped. "A reverse image search can show where a photo appeared online before." She walked the photo into the search, fingers quick, while Theo hovered at her elbow. The results loaded, and there it was: the same guardrail, the same brown water, on a news site from years back. The photo was real, but it was old, being passed off as new. "Someone's recycling it," Ella said. "That doesn't mean today's flood is fake, but this picture isn't proof."

Mom exhaled and set down her spoon. "So I call the county road line in the morning instead of panicking tonight." She reached over and smoothed Theo's cowlick, which had been mimicking a rooster's comb all through dinner. Theo frowned at the screen, then brightened. "Wait. Can it find where that shark photo came from too? The one Marcus said was at the beach?"

Ella grinned and pulled up the shark.

Sadie pressed her nose close to the glass wall of the AgZone barn, where the science center kept three pigs beside its farm exhibits. It was the hottest day of the school year, and the field trip had already included a planetarium show and a room full of Tesla coils, but this was the part she had been waiting for. All three pigs lay in a shallow brown puddle, moving so little they looked like statues.

"They're just dirty," said Marcus, elbowing in beside her. "That's all pigs do. Roll in mud because they like being gross."

Sadie wasn't sure. She crouched down and watched. The smallest pig climbed out, trotted to the water trough, drank, then flopped back into the puddle on its side with a satisfied grunt. It did this twice more in ten minutes. The other two never left the shade of the barn roof, but their mud had dried pale and cracked on their backs, and one of them waddled over to the sprinkler line near the fence and stood in the spray. A pig that only wanted to be dirty wouldn't keep choosing water, Sadie thought. There was a rule underneath this, something the pigs knew and nobody had said out loud.

She found a small placard near the trough and read it twice, then walked back to Marcus with the whole pattern clear in her head.

"Pigs have very few working sweat glands," she said. "So they wallow in mud or water to cool off on hot days."

"So the mud is like their air conditioning," Marcus said slowly.

"Exactly. It's not about being dirty at all."

When the class gathered near the bus, their teacher asked someone to summarize the visit for the morning announcements. Sadie raised her hand and gave a quick report, ending with the pigs. On the ride home, Marcus looked out the window at the sun-baked fields and turned to her.

"Next hot day, I'm sitting near the sprinkler too," he said. "Right beside them."

Elliot set his fork down and stared at his sister Maya, who was grinning across the meatloaf like she had won something. "Bree made the team bulletin board," Maya said, sliding her phone across the table. "Perfect shooting percentage. One hundred percent. Coach printed it out and everything."

"That's amazing," Mom said from the stove, where the kitchen felt tranquil and warm, insulated from the cold rattling the window outside.

Elliot looked at the number. It glowed there, 100%, like it was made of gold. From his perspective, sitting at the far end of the table, it almost looked too clean. Last season flashed back to him, one rainy Saturday when he had gone to watch Maya's game. He remembered every girl taking shot after shot, misses raining down like the rain outside, and he remembered Bree on the bench the whole game except for one play near the end, when the ball happened to land in her hands.

"How many shots has Bree taken?" he asked.

Maya shrugged. "The board doesn't say."

"So you don't know if it's one out of one, or ten out of ten, or fifty out of fifty."

"It says one hundred percent. That's all that matters." Maya grabbed her phone back.

Elliot pushed his chair in and walked to the hallway where his sneakers sat. "Come on," he said. "The stats notebook is in the gym office. Coach lets us look at it."

They walked the six blocks in the dark, and Maya got quieter with every step, which Elliot took as a good sign. In the office, under the desk lamp, he flipped the notebook to Bree's row and ran his finger along it. Field goals attempted: one. Field goals made: one.

"One shot," Elliot said. "She took one shot the whole season."

Maya stared at the page. "She's going to kill me if I tell everyone."

"Tell her to keep shooting first," Elliot said, and closed the notebook.

Brielle sat in the big chair and read the chart on the far wall. The top letter, an E, looked like someone had dragged a thumb through wet paint. She held her book up close and the words smeared the same way, which was the whole reason she was here. It had to be the chart, she had told herself for months. It couldn't be her eyes, because eyes went blurry either near or far, not both. She was optimistic about that theory right up until the second row of letters turned to gray streaks.

The optometrist swung a metal device in front of her face and flipped lenses into it, one click at a time. "Better or worse?" Click. "Better or worse?" At the third flip the E snapped into shape, so sharp and black that Brielle sat up straight. Then the optometrist turned the lens a quarter turn in its frame, and the smear came back, sideways now, like the E had been stretched.

"Try turning it back," Brielle said. The optometrist raised an eyebrow but let her reach up and rotate the lens herself. Sharp. Turn it. Blurry. Sharp again. She did it twice more to be sure. The blur changed with the direction of the turn, which meant it wasn't random. "So it's not the chart and it's not the distance," she said slowly. "It's something about direction. My eye curves more one way than the other, so it smears everything, near or far."

"That's called astigmatism," the optometrist said. "Your cornea is shaped more like an egg than a sphere." She wrote numbers on a pad. "We'll fix it."

A week later Brielle put on her new glasses in the parking lot and stopped walking. The stop sign across the street had letters with edges, actual edges. She read a license plate, then her own hand, then the fine print on a parking meter, just because she could. Her little brother was tugging her sleeve toward the car, where their dad was checking a leaking tire valve, but she stood one more second, staring at a brick wall, counting bricks.

"Come on," her brother said. "You can look at bricks later."

Colton held the thermometer like a sword and pointed it at the chicken thighs sizzling on the grill. "Mom said chicken has to hit 165 degrees Fahrenheit in the thickest part before it's done. That's about 74 degrees Celsius, if you want the fancy version."

His little sister Nadia leaned over the picnic table, chin in her hands. "It looks done. It's all brown. Can we eat now? I want dinner before my show starts."

"Brown isn't the boss of chicken," Colton said. He poked the probe into the biggest thigh, right into the thickest part like Mom had shown him, and watched the numbers climb. 140. 148. The smell was making his stomach growl, and he was optimistic they'd eat within the minute. 151. Then it stopped.

"Stuck," he muttered. Why would it stop? He looked at the grill, and in the context of the flaming coals below, one side was practically a bonfire while the other side had gone gray and cool. He'd stacked all the coals on the left. The chicken over there was racing ahead while the right side lagged behind. He couldn't see heat, but the thermometer could, and it was telling him the truth: uneven fire, uneven dinner.

He slid the slow pieces toward the hot side, moved the fast ones away, and gave it another two minutes. Nadia groaned like a deflating balloon. "Your show will still exist," Colton said. "Raw chicken won't forgive us."

He tested the biggest thigh again. 167.

"Done!" He plated it triumphantly. "Sixty-five plus two for luck."

Nadia bit in, chewed, and paused. "Okay, this is actually amazing. You may cook forever."

Colton took a dramatic bow with the thermometer. "Every meal, madam. That'll be one remote control."

She slid the remote across the table. "Worth it."

Arianna stood in the dressing room with her violin tucked under her arm, watching the mirror shake whenever somebody slammed a locker. Tonight was the first school concert she had ever played in, and her hand kept sliding up the neck of the violin because her palm was sweating. Her friend Marcus, who played oboe, sat on the bench eating carrot sticks. "Those are nutritious," Arianna said, mostly to think about something other than the stage. "You're going to be the important one out there anyway."

"How do you figure?" Marcus asked.

"Every rehearsal, nobody plays a single note until you do. Then everyone tunes to that one tone, all at once. I've been watching for three weeks." She pulled the spine of her music binder straight so she could read her own notes, the ones she kept in the margins. "I want to test it tonight. If I tune to you before you play, and everyone else tunes to you after, we should sound exactly the same. If we don't, then I'm tuning to something else and I don't know what."

"What if it doesn't work?" Marcus asked.

"Then I find out why." She had looked it up in the library book about orchestras, and she could cite the page if anyone doubted her: orchestras tune to a concert A played by the oboe, because its pitch is steady and its penetrating sound is easy for everyone to hear. Nobody had explained it to her. She had noticed the waiting, asked the book, and matched the two together like puzzle pieces.

Backstage, the curtain went up and the lights hit the rows of chairs. Marcus stood, lifted his oboe, and played a single A that seemed to cut straight through the whole hall. Arianna set her fingers, tuned her A string to him, and heard the cellos and flutes settle around the same note like birds landing on one wire. When her turn came in the first piece, her entrance was clean, and her spine straightened up on its own.

After the last song, Marcus found her in the wings. "So it worked?"

"Perfect match," Arianna said, and held up her hand for a high five.

The funeral home smelled like carnations and old hymnals, and Ruby sat in the third pew twisting a tissue into a rope. Grandma June's casket sat near the altar covered in a spray of yellow roses, which would have made Grandma June snort, because she had always said roses were too showy and daisies were the only honest flower. Ruby's mother leaned over and whispered the worst possible sentence: "Pastor Dan wants you to say a few words up there. Just a little eulogy."

Ruby's stomach dropped through the pew and into the basement. She knew people gave speeches at funerals, but she had never heard the word before, and it sounded like a medical procedure. In the front row, her cousin Dex was drawing what appeared to be a shark in the margin of the program, and when Ruby slid next to him he showed her his sketch of "Grandma's spirit animal," a predatory shark wearing Grandma's reading glasses. Ruby laughed once, a small hiccup of a sound in the quiet church, and felt slightly braver for it.

"What's a eulogy?" she whispered. Dex shrugged, but the woman in the next pew, Aunt Fran, leaned in. "A speech praising the person who died," she said softly. "The word comes from Greek roots meaning to speak well of." Ruby turned that over. Praise. That meant one good thing, the best thing, spoken out loud in front of a hundred people whose eyes would all be on her. She started making a list in her head and then, one by one, had to abandon every memory that involved the dress Grandma sewed inside out, or the time she called the pizza place to complain about a pizza she had not ordered from them. Too funny, maybe. Or exactly funny enough.

The pianist finished playing, and Pastor Dan said her name. Ruby stood, walked the long carpet to the lectern, and discovered her legs worked fine, which felt like an anomaly because the rest of her was shaking like a wind chime in a storm. She looked out at the crowd, took a breath, and began.

"Grandma June believed daisies were the only honest flower," she said, "and she made the best grilled cheese in three counties, and she let me have the first tomato every summer even though technically it was her garden." She told about the tomato, how Grandma would hand it over warm from the sun and say, "Taste that and tell me the store sells anything close." Ruby could hear her voice saying it, clear as a bell.

When she finished and sat back down, Dex nudged her and held up the shark drawing, which he had labeled "Swimming Somewhere Warm." Ruby took it, folded it carefully, and put it in her pocket next to the tissue rope. Then she reached over and straightened one yellow rose in the spray, so it stood up straight instead of slumping. "You're still too showy," she whispered, "but you'll do."

The library meeting room smelled like old carpet and lemon cleaner, and folding chairs squeaked every time someone shifted. Rose sat in the front row with nine other spellers, her number pinned to her shirt, waiting for the librarian at the microphone to call her name. She had studied word lists all month, and she had sorted the words into groups in her notebook to make them easier to remember, deciding she could categorize them by language of origin, which helped her guess at letters she wasn't sure of.

The first rounds went quickly. A boy from her school got out on "buoyant." A sixth grader spelled "melancholy" with calm, slow certainty. Then the librarian said, "Rose, your word is 'chandelier.'"

Rose stepped up to the microphone. "Chandelier. C-H-A-N-D-E-L-I-E-R." She paused before the last syllable because something felt wrong, a small itch at the back of her mind. The judge was already reaching for the bell.

"Wait," Rose said. "Can I start over?"

The librarian glanced at the judge, who nodded. "You may start your word again," the librarian said, "but if you change any letters you've already said, that counts as a misspelling."

Rose stood very still. So she could say the whole word again, but she could not quietly fix a letter she had already spoken. If she said "C-H-A-N" again, it had to be "C-H-A-N." She tried to remember exactly what she had said the first time. C. H. A. N. D. E. L. Then it came to her: the ending was the trouble. She had been about to spell it like the end of "carrier," but the word came from French, and in her notebook French endings were the ones that liked an extra letter.

"Chandelier," she said again. "C-H-A-N-D-E-L-I-E-R. Chandelier."

"Correct," the librarian said, and Rose walked back to her seat with her hands still shaking a little.

In the next round the word was "vessel," which felt almost too easy after chandelier. "Vessel. V-E-S-S-E-L. Vessel." She got to watch the boy beside her go out on "genuine," and she felt bad for him, but she also noticed something: the words that knocked people out were ones where the spelling looked arbitrary, like the letters had been arranged by someone rolling dice.

Only Rose and the calm sixth grader, Priya, were left. The librarian looked at her card, then at the two girls, and said, "Rose, your word is 'privilege.'"

Rose stepped to the microphone. "Privilege. P-R-I-V-I..." She stopped. She had said the wrong vowel, and she knew it, and she knew that no matter how many times she started over, she could not take that "I" back.

"Privilege," she said. "P-R-I-V-I-L-E-G-E. Privilege."

The judge rang the bell, once, softly. Priya won the little plastic trophy, and afterward she came over and said, "You almost had it." Rose looked at the trophy, then at her own shoes, and said, "Same word next year."

Naomi had noticed it for a month without saying anything. Every day at lunch, her classmate Yusuf pushed his tray away untouched, and every afternoon he looked tired by last period. She had a theory, but theories about people were tricky, so she kept a list in her notebook: Monday, no pizza. Tuesday, no sandwich. Wednesday, he even skipped the chocolate pudding, which nobody skipped.

On Saturday morning her mother dropped her at the community hall with a plate of frosted cookies and one instruction. "The gift table closes at noon, so hand those in before the games start." The hall was already full. Streamers hung from the ceiling fans, and a line of aunties arranged platters of samosas and dates on a long table near the stage. Naomi recognized Yusuf near the front, wearing a white kurta she had never seen before, standing with his grandmother.

"You're here," he said. "This is Eid al-Fitr. It means Ramadan is over, the month when Muslims fast from dawn until sunset." He picked up a date and ate it, and Naomi watched him do it the way a scientist watches a test succeed. That explained the tray. That explained the tiredness. From her perspective, the whole month of school slid into place like a puzzle she had been holding upside down.

Then the problem arrived. Yusuf's little sister had entered the cookie-decorating contest, and the entry box shut at noon, but she was stuck at the back of a line for the bathroom. Naomi counted heads, counted minutes, and made a decision: she surrendered her own contest entry, slid her frosting tube and sprinkle jar across the table to the sister, and ran the plate of cookies to the gift table with the clock on the wall showing four minutes to twelve. Behind her, the judges called for last entries just as the girl's cookie landed in the box.

Afterward, sitting on folding chairs with paper plates balanced on their knees, Yusuf asked whether it had bothered her, guessing wrong for a month. "I thought maybe the cafeteria food was controversial at your house," Naomi said. He laughed so hard he nearly dropped his samosa. "You could have just asked." She pulled out her notebook, crossed out every line on the list, and wrote one word at the bottom: solved. Then she took a bite of his grandmother's biryani and asked for seconds.

The bean plant by the window had drooped overnight, and Alexis had ten minutes before the bell to figure out why. Her lab partner, Marcus, leaned over the pot and said, "That plant is ugly. It's the worst one in the room." Alexis frowned. "That doesn't help. I think somebody forgot to water it, and that's a claim we can actually test." Marcus shrugged. "It's my opinion. You can't prove an opinion wrong." Alexis stopped, spoonful of gravel for drainage in hand, because that sentence was exactly what her older brother had shouted at dinner last night before their mom made them both go to bed.

She scrutinize every part of the setup. The soil was dry and pulling away from the sides of the pot, so the plant had not been watered, that much was certain. But the control plant two tables over had also been skipped and it looked fine. So lack of water alone could not be the whole answer. Marcus tapped the window glass. "This one gets cooked by the sun all afternoon. That window is like a toaster." Alexis checked the blinds, which hung half open, and then felt the leaves. Warm, almost hot. Her reasoning went like this: dry soil plus hot leaves, versus dry soil and cool leaves across the room. The difference was the window.

"We water both plants the same amount," she said, pulling the blinds down on their side only, "and see which one perks up by tomorrow." Marcus wrote it on a sticky note and slapped it on the pot like a tiny flag. When Ms. Ortiz walked past, she raised an eyebrow at the flag, and Marcus pointed at Alexis. "Her experiment. I'm the official note writer. It comes with benefits." Ms. Ortiz moved on, but Alexis noticed she turned down the radiator near their table on her way, which had to mean something.

The classroom grew tranquil as the last students packed up. Alexis snapped a photo of the droopy plant so tomorrow they would have proof, not just a memory of it. On her way out she grabbed the watering can and topped off the control plant too, because fair tests deserved fair treatment. "Tomorrow," Marcus said at the door, holding it open for her, "we find out if I'm wrong." Alexis grinned. "You're wrong about the ugly part either way. That bean plant is my favorite one in the room, and nobody can test me on that."

Sebastian had ridden the number 14 bus every school day for two years, and he knew every ad by heart. There was the sneaker poster above the rear door, where the rapper Dash Malloy grinned down and said, "I never step on court without Zooms." There was the soda sign that shouted "Everyone's making the switch!" in letters so big they seemed to push the seats apart. And there was the one for Comet Bars, with the words "pure, honest, real chocolate" glowing like the bar itself was a hero. Sebastian barely saw them anymore, the way you stop hearing a clock.

What he did see was Marcus, three rows up, holding a Comet Bar. That was the problem. Sebastian was trying to get the whole grade to boycott Comet Bars because he had heard, over and over, that the company had dumped waste in Miller Creek. He leaned over the seats. "You're still eating those? They poisoned the creek." Marcus shrugged. A seventh grader near the window said, "Yeah, I heard that too." Two kids at the back chimed in, one after another, like popcorn. By the time the bus lurched around the library, five different people had said it out loud.

A girl named Priya, who was reading a science magazine, looked up. "Can I ask you something? Do you believe the creek thing because you saw proof, or because you've heard it five times?" Sebastian opened his mouth and nothing came out. Priya held up the magazine. "There's a study in here. In 1977, Lynn Hasher and her colleagues found that people rated statements as more likely to be true after seeing them repeated, whether or not they were true." She shrugged. "It just says that. Repetition. That's all it takes."

Sebastian decided to test it. At the next stop he said, loudly, "They're replacing the old trolley with one that has a real conductor in a striped vest." Two stops later he said it again. By the school, a boy he had never met told his friend, "Did you hear? The trolley's getting a conductor," and his friend nodded like it was settled fact. Sebastian felt his ears go hot. He had done the exact thing the Comet Bar ad did, the "pure, honest, real" thing, only faster. That afternoon he walked to Miller Creek himself. The water ran clear over the stones, and a man from the city was posting a notice about a leaking garage upstream, not a chocolate factory. On the ride home he tapped Marcus on the shoulder and held out the last of his own Comet Bar. "I got the creek story wrong," he said. "Split it with me?"

Emmett leaned over the kitchen table, where six paper airplanes lay in a row like tired birds. His best flight yesterday had gone seventeen feet, but he'd built it from the heavy poster paper Mom used for signs, and he'd also folded the wings up in a wide V instead of flat. Both changes at once. Now he couldn't tell which one had made it fly farther.

"If it was the paper, I'd want to know," he said to his sister Ruth, who was eating cereal at the counter. "Poster paper is heavy. Heavy could mean it glides better. Or the V wings. Or both. Or neither."

"So do it again and watch," Ruth said, not looking up.

"Watch what? I changed two things. Two." He flipped his notebook open and stared at his scribbled numbers. Flight three: twelve feet. Flight four: seventeen feet. He had no idea why.

Ruth came around the counter and tapped the notebook. "You know what Marcus did with his bean project? He changed the pot and the water at the same time, and the teacher said he couldn't tell which one mattered. She said you're supposed to change only one thing on purpose. That's called the independent variable."

"The one thing you change on purpose," Emmett repeated slowly. The words felt like a key in a lock.

He grabbed two sheets, one notebook paper and one poster paper, and folded them into exactly the same shape, flat wings, matching creases, careful match. Then he threw each one three times down the hallway, measuring with a tape measure and refusing to let Ruth announce the numbers until he'd written them down, because guessing first had become a mandatory rule in his notebook.

The poster paper beat the notebook paper every single throw.

"It was the paper," he said, grinning. Then he paused. "But what about the V wings?"

Ruth rolled her eyes. "Then change only that next."

He folded two fresh poster-paper planes, one flat and one in a wide V, and carried them to the hallway door.

Anais had packed her sleeping bag three times before her cousin Marisol's mom drove her across town to Priya's house. At Marisol's that afternoon, Marisol had been assertive about it: "Take the flashlight. Trust me." Anais had laughed, because Marisol's cousin had told her that at sleepovers, someone always tells a ghost story, and Marisol believed it like a rule of the universe.

Now it was eleven at night, and the rule had come true. Priya's older brother, Devon, had told a story about a figure that stood at the foot of the stairs and counted the steps out loud in the dark. Everyone knew he made it up. He even said so at the end. But when the last word finished, the room went quiet, and Anais noticed her own heart pounding hard and fast, and her breath coming quicker, like she'd run the block to the corner store. Priya's breathing was quick too. Anais could hear it.

Then a stair creaked, right outside the door.

Devon yelped and grabbed a pillow like a shield. Priya shrieked. The door pushed open and Biscuit, the family cat, strolled in, tail up, entirely unimpressed. Devon laughed so hard he fell off his mattress. "It's the cat! It's just the cat!"

Anais laughed too, but she was thinking. She tried to deduce what had made Devon jump, since he'd invented the story himself and knew every word was fake. She watched Priya put a hand on her own chest, still feeling it drum. "Yours too?" Anais whispered. Priya nodded. "And I knew it was made up," Priya said. "I watched him make half of it up on the spot."

So it didn't matter what you knew. Anais sat with that for a while, remembering Marisol's flashlight, which she had decided was silly and left on the dresser. It was in Marisol's room, a whole town away.

"Next time," she said, and clicked off the lamp.

"What?"

"Nothing," Anais said. Biscuit curled up on Devon's pillow and started to purr.

Rosalie's best friend Dexter swore that Zip Fuel made him run faster, and he had a witness: himself. "I drank one before the mile and shaved twelve seconds," he said at lunch, twice. Rosalie wanted to believe him, mostly because she had three dollars riding on it.

The problem was that Zip Fuel cost five dollars a bottle, which is why she found herself standing in aisle four of Ridgeway Pharmacy, staring at a shelf of vitamins, sugar-free mints, and a row of plain white bottles behind the counter. Her mother was at the drop-off window arguing with a pharmacist about an insurance settlement for a claim that had been denied twice. Rosalie drifted toward the counter, where a display of gel capsules labeled "Homeopathic Sleep Aid" sat next to a sign that said Non-Drowsy.

"Excuse me," she said to the pharmacist when he surfaced. "Do you sell pills that are just sugar? Like, nothing in them at all?"

He looked at her over his glasses. "We use those in trials sometimes. They're placebos." He set a small bottle on the counter. "Pharmacists can't sell you the real medicine without a prescription, but sugar is sugar."

Rosalie turned the bottle over in her hands and thought about Dexter. Twelve seconds. If the drink really worked, then a fake drink shouldn't work at all, and he'd run his normal time. If the fake drink did work, then maybe the running faster came from believing, not from the bottle. She could empty one of her dad's glass juice bottles, fill it with water, add two drops of orange food coloring, and tell Dexter it was Zip Fuel. He'd never tasted the real one; he'd chugged it cold at the track. To make the test fair, she'd have to exclude every other difference: same day, same weather, same time, same taunting from the eighth graders at the fence.

Her mother was still going with the settlement. "It's the third letter," she was saying. "The third. I'm immune to their apologies at this point."

Rosalie paid for the sugar pills with crumpled ones and a quarter she found in her jacket, then tucked the bottle into her backpack next to the empty juice bottle she'd brought from home. Monday after school, she handed Dexter the orange drink and watched him chug it at the start line, grimacing like a professional. He ran the mile in exactly his usual time, to the second, and spent the cooldown insisting his legs felt "incredibly springy."

"So," Rosalie said, holding up the empty bottle, "about those twelve seconds."

"Test it again," Dexter said. "One more lap. And this time I want the grape flavor."

Isaac spread the giant map of the Roman Empire across the living room floor, weighting one curling corner with a cereal bowl and the other with his sneaker.
