But on Friday afternoon, Dad carried the loose braided rug out of the guest room, rolled it under his arm, and headed for the garage.

"Why are you taking Grandma's rug?" Piper asked, following him. She liked that rug. It was blue and gold, and it smelled faintly of cinnamon.

"Falls are the leading cause of injury death for adults aged 65 and older," Dad said, setting the rug on a shelf. "In the whole United States. Mom told me that years ago, and I've never forgotten it."

Piper stood in the doorway, thinking. Grandma Ruth was sixty-eight. She hiked, and she could still do a cartwheel, though she claimed her knees filed complaints afterward. Still, the number Dad had said hung in Piper's mind like a question. She looked down the hallway: the rug gone, the floor bare, the bathroom door right there. Then she remembered the backyard. The stepping stones. Wobbly ones.

She ran outside and tested them, one at a time, pressing each with her sneaker like a doctor pressing a knee. The third stone rocked sideways with a squeak of gravel. That one, and the one by the fence, would tip under a foot that wasn't watching. She tried an experiment: she walked the path while carrying a tray of lemonade glasses, the way she'd carry it tomorrow, and nearly lost her balance when the third stone lurched. That settled it.

"Grandma's going to walk this path," Piper told Dad at dinner. "To see the lanterns. If a fall is the leading cause of injury death for people sixty-five and older, then a tipping stone is like a rug that fights back." Dad put down his fork. After dinner, the two of them knelt in the fading light with a bag of paver sand, tucking it under each stone, patting it firm, testing, adding more. The dirt smelled cool and mineral, and the sand gritted under Piper's knuckles.

Saturday arrived warm and buoyant, the paper lanterns bobbing on their strings as though they wanted to float away. Grandma Ruth came through the gate, hugged Piper long and hard, and then paused on the path. "These feel solid," she said, stepping carefully, heel to toe, heel to toe. "Someone nurtured this walkway."

"That was me," Piper said, holding out the lemonade. "And there's more. I have a whole list of things I'm checking before you go anywhere. The garage steps are next."

Grandma Ruth laughed and took her hand. "Then lead on, inspector. But first, show me how to make those lanterns."

Wyatt's new phone sat on his desk like it might ring at any moment, even though nobody knew the number yet. Mr. Ruiz had let the class keep their phones out for the morning lesson, and Wyatt kept sliding his closer whenever the teacher turned his back. Then the phone buzzed. A text from something called GalaxyGame Support read: "Your account will be deleted in 24 hours unless you verify your password. Reply now." Wyatt's stomach dropped. He had spent all summer building that account.

He typed his password halfway before he stopped. Something felt off. Mr. Ruiz had said that real companies never ask for your password in a message, and this was asking exactly that. Wyatt tried to diagnose the problem the way he would a broken controller: test one thing at a time. His idea was simple. If the message were real, the game's actual website would mention the deletion too. He opened the browser, logged into the official site, and found nothing but a banner announcing a new update. No warning. No deadline. Then he noticed the sender's address was a random jumble of letters, nothing like the company's name on the site.

"Mr. Ruiz," Wyatt said, raising his hand. "What's it called when someone pretends to be a company to trick you out of your password?" Mr. Ruiz nodded. "Phishing." Across the aisle, Priya leaned over. "You almost fell for that?" she asked. "On day one?" Wyatt admitted he had typed three letters of his password before stopping. Priya, who had told everyone last week that phones in class were a terrible idea, frowned at her own phone and then back at him. "Okay," she said, "maybe you're more responsible than I said." She held up her screen. "I got the same text this morning. I almost replied."

Together they showed Mr. Ruiz both messages, and he forwarded them to the front office so the school could warn other kids. Wyatt blocked the sender, then sent his mom a text of his own: "Got my first scam today. Did not give them my password. You're welcome." A minute later she replied, "Proudest I've been all year." Wyatt slid the phone into his backpack, where it stayed for the rest of class, buzzing once with her message still on the screen.

Layla sat cross-legged on her bed with her tablet balanced on her knees, staring at the team list in the lobby of Cloud Racers. Her best friend Marco had typed "Okay." into the chat after she suggested they team up for the tournament, and now he had gone quiet, which was strange, because Marco never went quiet. He usually typed so much that the chat window scrolled before anyone could read it.

"Did I do something?" she typed in the private message window, which was just for the two of them. In the public lobby, where forty strangers were arguing about track picks, she kept her messages short and neutral. That was the convention. Everyone said "gg" after races and "brb" for stepping away, and nobody used full sentences, because full sentences in a lobby felt like showing up to a pool party in a snowsuit.

Marco's reply took a full minute. "you sounded mad."

Layla squinted at the screen. "About what?"

"you wrote Okay. with the dot. like my mom when she's mad."

She scrolled up and checked. She had written "Okay." Marco's last three messages had no periods at all: "ok," "sure," "fine." She scrolled further, through weeks of their chats, and saw the pattern everywhere. When Marco was happy, no dots. When Marco was annoyed, dots appeared, like little period-shaped storm clouds. She had never noticed because a period was just a period, or so she had thought.

She tested it. In the private chat she sent two versions of the same word to herself, one with the dot and one without, and looked at them side by side. "Okay." did look mad. It looked like a door closing. The undotted "okay" looked like a shrug. She revised her next message carefully, deleting the period and typing "sorry i wasnt mad, just excited about the tournament," and sent it dot-free into the world.

"oh," Marco typed back. "ok good." Three seconds later: "my sister says theres a study, 2016, binghamton university, they found texts ending with a period seem less sincere than the same ones without." Layla raised an eyebrow at the screen, wondering if he had made that up and hoping she wasn't being gullible. "look it up," Marco added, as if reading her mind. Then a lobby notification flashed: the tournament countdown had started, and their team slot would go to someone else in ninety seconds.

"race you to sign up," she typed, no period, and hit enter before the lobby could fill.

Jace tied Grandma's apron around himself twice because it was built for a person with a lot more Grandma in her, and he flopped the ball of dough onto the floury counter. Tonight was his night to cook, and he had promised bread, real bread, the kind that came out of the oven crackling. He pushed the dough around for about forty seconds, decided that was plenty, and dropped it back into the bowl to rise.

An hour later he peered under the towel and frowned. The dough had puffed up, sure, but when he poked it, it tore instead of springing back. It looked like a sad, dense pillow. His little sister Nadia leaned over his elbow, sniffing.

"It smells like nothing," she reported. "Also, I want to braid it. I've been practicing on my hair, and I'm amazing now."

"You can braid it when it behaves," Jace said. He pulled off a small piece and stretched it gently. It ripped almost instantly, like wet paper. Something was missing, and it wasn't the flour or the water, because those were definitely in there. He had added water to flour, so whatever the water had done, it had already done it. The only step he had rushed was the pushing part.

He grabbed a fresh piece of dough and pushed and folded, pushed and folded, setting a timer for ten minutes because that was what Grandma's recipe card demanded in her cramped handwriting. Nadia chattered about her braiding plans, their dad wandered through in his tranquil Saturday mood and muttered something about the mortgage and the price of flour, and Jace kept going even when his arms complained. Around minute six something changed under his hands. The dough stopped ripping when he tugged it and started stretching, long and elastic, like it had opinions about being pulled and was winning.

"So that's it," he said. "The water makes something in there, and the pushing makes it stronger. The recipe card says the something is called gluten."

"Gluten," Nadia repeated solemnly, as if accepting a new member of the family. "Fine. It may be braided."

The second loaf rose tall and proud, and when Jace slashed the top it didn't collapse, it sighed. He slid it into the oven, and ten minutes later the kitchen smelled like the opposite of nothing. Nadia stood at the oven door with three slim ropes of dough already pinned to the counter.

"You have to let me braid it now," she said. "It's stretchy. I tested it. Gluten complies."

"Nobody says complies," Jace said, laughing, but he handed her a rope of dough anyway, and she got to work.

Sadie had been on the couch since Tuesday, buried under a quilt with a box of tissues, a mug of flat ginger ale, and a fever that came and went like a bad houseguest. Her throat felt like she had swallowed a handful of gravel. What she wanted most in the world, more than missed Halloween or the sixth-grade curriculum she was falling behind on, was for her headache to stop.

She remembered a flashback from when she was eight and had chickenpox, how she had scratched at the spots and her mother had carried her to the couch in this same living room, had even read her a chapter about kids who salvaged a shipwreck, and how a bottle of orange pills had sat on the shelf and nobody would give her one. Sadie had thought it was a punishment for scratching. Now, with her head pounding, she decided she was old enough to decide for herself. She got up, wrapped the quilt around her shoulders like a cape, and shuffled to the bathroom cabinet.

Aspirin. She tipped two white tablets into her palm and then paused, because taped inside the cabinet door was a note in her mother's handwriting: Not for Sadie during flu or chickenpox. Sadie stared at it. She was thirteen, not eight, and the flu was the flu, wasn't it? It seemed almost naive to think a couple of pills could hurt anyone. But her mother did not tape notes to doors for no reason. Sadie put the tablets back, carried the bottle to the living room, and waited by the window until the blue car pulled into the driveway.

"Mom," she said, holding it up. "Why is aspirin off-limits for me? I checked the label twice and there's nothing about age."

Her mother dropped her bag on the chair and took the bottle. "It's linked to something called Reye's syndrome," she said. "It's rare, but it's serious, and it affects the liver and the brain. Kids and teenagers shouldn't take aspirin during the flu or chickenpox." She set the bottle on the high shelf above the fridge, where it belonged. "There's ibuprofen in the cabinet, the small blue box. That one's fine."

Sadie took two blue tablets with a swallow of ginger ale and settled back under the quilt. Within an hour the pounding behind her eyes eased to a dull hum, and she salvaged the rest of the afternoon by reading the shipwreck chapter she never finished five years ago. When her mother checked on her before dinner, the bottle on the high shelf caught the last of the evening light, and Sadie raised her mug toward it like a toast.

Marcus held the box like it might go off, because in a way it would. Inside was his first phone, a birthday present from his parents, and he had carried it to Theo's house precisely so the whole thing could happen with a witness. Theo had gotten his own phone eight months ago and now moved through the world like a person who had signed some fundamental treaty with adulthood, which mostly meant he texted his mom from the kitchen to ask when dinner was.

"Open it already," Theo said, bouncing a tennis ball off the garage door.

Marcus peeled the tape slowly, remembering the last big thing he'd been trusted with, his grandfather's fishing knife, and how he'd lost it in the lake before summer ended. He decided this time he would be careful from minute one.

They set the phone up on Theo's porch, and Theo installed a flashlight app for him, "the most useful app ever invented," he said, holding it under his chin like a ghost. Then a box popped up on the screen. The flashlight app wanted permission to see Marcus's contacts. All of them.

"Why would a flashlight need my contacts?" Marcus asked. "It's a light. It shines."

Theo squinted at his own phone. "Mine asked for my microphone too. I just tapped yes. Everyone just taps yes."

Marcus did not tap yes. He sat back and tried to infer what was going on, the way his science teacher was always nagging them to do. A pattern was hiding under that little box, a rule about how phones worked. Maybe apps had to ask before they could use the camera, the microphone, or the contacts. And if they had to ask, maybe a no could happen whenever he wanted one, not just at the moment of asking.

"Where's settings?" he said, and hunted through the screens until he found a list of apps with little toggles next to them. Every app that had ever asked him anything was there, with its permissions listed like a confession. He flicked the flashlight app's contact permission off. The app kept shining. The light didn't care.

Theo leaned over his shoulder. "Wait. You can take it away later? I've been saying yes to everything since October." He scrolled his own settings and went pale. "This flashlight app has been listening to me. It has heard everything. It has heard me sing in the shower."

"You don't shower with your phone."

"It was near the bathroom."

Marcus laughed so hard he nearly dropped the new phone, then caught it, because minute one of careful was still going. He turned off Theo's microphone permission too, and they sat there in the porch light, two boys quietly rearranging the rules of their small digital kingdoms.

"My mom's going to say I should've thought of this months ago," Theo said, still scrolling. "She's going to be insufferable."

"Send her a text about it."

"I will." Theo grinned. "But not from the bathroom."

Lily felt fantastic after the first volleyball practice of the season. She had sprinted for every ball, done lunges across the whole gym floor, and jumped until the coach blew the whistle for water. On the walk home she was still buzzing, thinking that maybe this year she would finally make starting lineup instead of watching her chances dwindle as the roster got cut.

Two mornings later, she could barely climb the stairs to math class. Her thighs burned with every step, and when she lowered herself into her seat she made a sound like a deflating balloon. Her friend Priya leaned over. "You okay?"

"I don't get it," Lily whispered. "I was fine after practice. Great, even. And I didn't do anything yesterday. Why does it hurt now?"

Priya shrugged. "My arm was like that after my flu vaccine last month. Sore, but not until the next day, weirdly." She flexed her arm as if proving it.

Lily turned that over all through class. It didn't make sense that skipping a day would make things worse. Unless the soreness was on a delay, like mail that arrived late no matter what. She thought back to last season, when she'd sat out the first week with a sprained wrist and then gone to one hard practice; she'd felt fine that night and terrible two days after. She had blamed the cafeteria pizza at the time. Now she wondered.

At practice she tested her idea. She asked three teammates when they were soredest. Marisol said her shoulders ached worst the day after the spike drills, not the same evening. Jayla counted on her fingers and said it hit her hard around two days, then faded. Every answer landed somewhere between one and three days. Lily felt something click into place, a pattern she couldn't see but could map by asking.

The coach overheard them and paused her clipboard scribbling. "You girls discussing DOMS?" she asked.

"Is that what it's called?" Lily said. "Delayed onset muscle soreness?"

"That's the one." The coach went back to her lineup.

On the bench, tying her shoes, Lily weighed her next move. Last year she had quit soccer after one brutal week because the pain had seemed endless and she'd thought she was too weak for it. If she had known the soreness peaked and then faded, would she have stayed? She couldn't decide, and the question sat with her while the whistle shrieked and the team ran onto the court.

She had a plan, radical in its simplicity: schedule rest days right where the soreness would crest, then push hard again once it ebbed. Tonight she would ice her legs, stretch gently, and mark Thursday as her easy day. Lily stood, winced at her screaming thighs, and jogged toward the serve line anyway.

"You're limping!" Priya called.

"I know," Lily shouted back, and served the ball clean over the net.

Maria stood in Priya's bedroom with one shoe on and one shoe off, staring at the invitation on the desk. The dance started in ninety minutes, and there was still time to eliminate the whole plan, text Priya that she felt sick, and stay home. She had done it before, twice, and she knew exactly how it worked.

"Stop hovering," Priya said from the closet. "You're hovering like a small worried cloud."

"I can't dance. That's the problem. Everyone will see that I can't dance."

Priya held up two shirts, then dropped them both and pulled out her phone instead. "Watch this first." She tapped the screen and handed it over. On it, a white cockatoo with a yellow crest was bobbing its head and lifting its feet to a pop song, exactly on the beat.

"That's a bird," Maria said.

"He's called Snowball. Scientists studied him in 2009. Aniruddh Patel led the whole thing, and they showed that Snowball could really move in time to the music. And here's the part that got me." She took the phone back, tapped, and started the video again at a different speed. "Watch. They changed the tempo, and he adjusted. He kept matching it."

Maria watched the bird shift its rhythm, stomping a little faster, then a little slower, following along. Something in her chest loosened, like a knot someone had finally found the end of. "A cockatoo can do this," she said slowly. "A bird with a brain the size of a walnut can find the beat."

"Exactly."

"So a person can." Maria put on the other shoe. It felt like a decision, not a shoe.

At the dance, the gym had been turned into something almost unrecognizable, with paper streamers and a fog machine that made the far wall look faintly ominous until you realized it was just the fog machine. Maria stood near the punch bowl for two songs, and suspense built in her stomach like a soda shaken and not yet opened. Then the DJ put on the same song from the video, and without letting herself think, she started to bob.

She matched the beat. Then she matched it faster when the chorus came, then slower, and she thought of Snowball lifting his yellow crest feet one at a time, and she laughed out loud. Priya appeared beside her, doing a move that could only be described as interpretive flamingo.

"You're doing it!" Priya shouted over the music.

Maria lifted one foot, then the other, perfectly on tempo. "If the bird can adjust, so can I!"

A boy from her science class gave her a thumbs up, and the fog machine sighed another cloud across the gym floor.

The science lab chat was supposed to be for questions about the digestive system, so when Mr. Ortega posted "Reminder: intestine diagrams due Friday," Leah typed "Great, my favorite organ" and hit send before she thought about it. Three people replied with links about intestinal diseases. Marcus sent her a private message: "Are you okay? Do you actually have a stomach thing?" She stared at the screen. Her joke had traveled like a stone dropped in water, and every ripple had taken it literally.

She tried to clarify with a follow-up post: "I was joking, intestine diagrams are not actually my favorite." That only made it worse, because Priya asked why she would say that if she didn't mean it, and the whole chat scrolled on without her, arguing about whether Leah was being sarcastic or upset. Leah shut her laptop and watched Mr. Ortega sketch the small intestine on the whiteboard, feeling like the whole class had read a different sentence than the one she wrote.

That night she went looking for a way to fix it, and found something better. On a computer history site she read that on September 19, 1982, a computer scientist named Scott Fahlman had proposed the emoticon :-) on a Carnegie Mellon University message board, so readers could tell which posts were jokes. People typing to each other back then had the exact same problem she'd had, and somebody had invented a mark for it. She read the date twice. Her problem was older than her parents. Somewhere along the way she had thought of :-) as obsolete, a thing her aunt used, but clearly it had been doing its job since 1982.

The next morning she asked Marcus to meet her at the picnic table by the gym before first period. "I found out why my joke blew up," she said, and told him about Fahlman, the message board, the smiley meant to flag jokes. "So this afternoon I'm going to post one in the chat. An apology with a :-) at the end, and then a real joke with one too, so people can see the difference." Marcus turned his water bottle in his hands. "Or you could just say it was a joke in plain words." He had a point, and she sat with it for a second, remembering how her plain words had already failed once.

"Both," she decided. "Words first, smiley as backup." Fifth period, she typed her apology, added :-) and watched Priya reply with a laughing face instead of a question. Marcus leaned over from the next desk and typed, "Told you it was a joke," and Leah smiled at the little sideways grin sitting at the end of her sentence, still working after all these years.

Ryan had measured himself against the pantry door frame every Sunday since March, and in four weeks the pencil mark had climbed exactly one centimeter. One. His best friend Theo had shot up four centimeters over the summer and now looked like a lamppost wearing a hoodie. Ryan wanted numbers, proof, a plan, so when his mother scheduled his yearly checkup, he brought a notebook and a question he had written in capital letters: HOW MUCH GROWING IS LEFT?

The exam room smelled like hand sanitizer and bubblegum, the kind Dr. Patel kept in a jar by the sink. Ryan sat on the crinkly paper and heard it whisper every time he moved. When Dr. Patel came in, he skipped the small talk, which Ryan appreciated. "Before you listen to my heart," he said, "I need to know if I'm going to keep growing, and by how much, and when it stops."

Dr. Patel laughed, a short surprised sound, like Ryan had knocked on a door she didn't know was there. "That's a real question with a real answer," she said, "but not from a measuring tape. Bones don't tell their secrets from the outside." She turned to the computer and pulled up an X-ray of his left hand and wrist, taken last winter when he'd jammed a finger in basketball. "Look at the long bones. See those dark gaps near the ends?"

Ryan leaned in. The bones looked like pale sticks, and at each end there was a thin dark stripe, like a hairline crack. He perceived, suddenly, a pattern: every single long bone had the same stripe, always near the end, never in the middle. "Are those fractures?" he asked, half alarmed. "Do I have eleven broken bones?"

"Those are called growth plates," Dr. Patel said. "Bones grow longer at growth plates near their ends." She pointed at one stripe, then at the knobby end of a finger bone. "While they're open like this, you grow. Once these plates close after puberty, a person stops getting taller. They seal up, and that's it, the height you have is the height you keep."

Ryan did the math in his head, fast. He was twelve. His plates were wide open, stripes like little doors that hadn't shut yet. He still had time, maybe years of it. Then he looked at the X-ray again and noticed something that made him grin. "Wait," he said. "My fingers are getting longer too, right? So my hands will be proportional to the rest of me eventually?" Dr. Patel said yes, exactly, and Ryan wrote that down.

"So Theo isn't beating me forever," Ryan said. "He's just running the race early." Then, because it seemed scientific, he asked Dr. Patel to print a copy of the X-ray so he could tape it to the pantry door, right above the pencil marks. He wanted to watch those stripes the way his grandfather watched the beach, marking the slow erosion of the dunes year by year. As they left, he held the warm printout flat in both hands like something that might blow away, and said, "Next March, one centimeter is going to be three."

Alexander carried the cardboard box across the backyard with both hands, walking like someone balancing a full glass of water. Inside, under a flap of hay, sat a brown and white guinea pig named Biscuit, his first pet ever. His little sister Priya trotted beside him, already arguing that she should be allowed to hold Biscuit first because she had a special way of sitting very still.

"Biscuit is my obligation," Alexander told her, setting the box down by the new hutch under the maple tree. "That means I'm the one who takes care of him." Priya pouted, but she had her own plan. She wanted Biscuit to learn to eat from her hand so he would like her best, and she planned to sit by the hutch every single afternoon until it happened.

For the first week Alexander did what the pet store had said. He filled the bowl with dry pellets every morning and changed the water. The pellets smelled faintly sweet, like toast, and Biscuit crunched them happily enough. Then, on Saturday, Alexander noticed something odd. Biscuit was sitting in the corner of the hutch with his fur puffed up, and he didn't come to the front when Alexander rattled the bag. His eyes looked watery, and he had left his favorite tunnel untouched.

Alexander sat on the grass and thought. What had changed? Nothing, except the food, and the food had been exactly the same all week. He turned the pellet bag over and read the tiny print on the back, squinting in the sun. There it was: a line about added vitamin C. He went inside and searched on the family computer, and what he found made him sit up straight. "They can't make their own vitamin C, like humans, so they need it in their food every day," he read aloud to Priya, who had followed him in. Every day. The pellets had some in them, but Alexander remembered something else from the search, that the vitamin faded from stored feed over time, and their bag had been sitting on a shelf for who knew how long.

So he tested it. He cut a strip of red bell pepper, which the website said was packed with vitamin C, and brought it out to the hutch along with a slice of orange, wondering which one Biscuit would choose. The pepper smelled sharp and green in the cool morning air. Biscuit sniffed it, then snatched it and chewed so fast that crumbs of pepper flew onto the cedar shavings. He ignored the orange completely.

Alexander gave him fresh pepper every day after that, and within a week Biscuit's fur lay smooth again and he raced to the front of the hutch whenever Alexander's sneakers appeared on the grass. He wasn't just fine now; he seemed to thrive, popcorning straight up in the air when the food bowl rattled. Priya got her wish too, though not the way she expected. Biscuit decided the best place to eat his pepper strip was directly from her hand, and she sat by the maple tree every afternoon, giggling as his whiskers tickled her fingers. "He likes me best," she announced, and Biscuit, mouth full, made no argument.

Matthew spread his poster across the kitchen table and weighted the curling corners with the salt shaker and a mug. His assignment was a poster about the British monarchy, and he had drafted the design twice already, once in pencil and once in ink, but tonight he was adding paint: a crown, a castle, and a border of tiny red lions. He squeezed a blob of blue onto a paper plate and dipped his brush into his cup of water to thin it down for the sky. When the paint flowed smooth and pale across the paper, he felt like he might actually finish before ten o'clock.

Then he reached into his art bin for his good detail brush, the one with the fine point, and stopped. Every brush in the bin was stiff as a stick. He pressed the bristles against the table, and they didn't bend at all. Last Saturday he had painted at his friend Devon's studio, and afterward they had watched videos and eaten chips and somehow, in all of that, the brushes had never made it to the sink. They had sat overnight, then for five more days.

He held them under the faucet and scrubbed, but the dried paint stayed put, hard as plastic. While the wet paint on his poster could be thinned and washed away with water, this stuff had already dried, and the water just ran off it. His best brush was ruined, and the others looked nearly as bad. He remembered Devon saying, right before the videos, "Hang on, I gotta rinse mine." He had thought it was a fussy habit. Apparently it was more like a rule.

Matthew dug through the bin and found one old fat brush with soft bristles that he'd kept for spreading glue. It was almost obsolete for painting, but it would do for the sky and the castle walls. For the tiny lions, though, he had nothing fine enough. He sat back and stared at the poster, chewing the end of his pencil.

Then he got up, found the cardboard tube from a roll of paper towels, and cut a thin sliver off the end with scissors. He trimmed it into a point, dipped it in the red paint, and stamped lion after lion along the border. They came out looking like tiny enthusiastic potatoes, but from across the kitchen, his mom squinted and said, "Are those the royal beasts? Very nice."

"Those are my official brush substitutes," Matthew said. "The real brushes are currently in a monarchy of their own." He paused. "A kingdom of glue and ruin." He stamped one more potato lion, then carried his surviving brush straight to the sink and rinsed it under warm water until the bristles ran clean.

Rosalie pulled the laptop closer and typed her cousin Marcus's favorite player into the search bar, because the argument was still running from dinner and she intended to win it. "Told you," Marcus had said, pointing at the batting average on his phone. "Point two sixty. That's not a great hitter." Her grandpa had hummed at that, the way he did when he knew something, and Rosalie had spent the whole car ride home wondering what the hum meant.

The player page loaded, all numbers stacked in tidy columns. She scrolled past the average to the row of walks, and there it was: a lot of walks, more than half the hits. She clicked to another player, one with a higher average, and counted his walks too. Far fewer. She sat back. "Huh," she said to the empty kitchen, which felt less silly than saying it to nobody at all.

She texted Marcus: come over. He lived two streets away, and luckily his free evening happened to coincide with hers, because otherwise she'd have had to explain it all in messages and he never read long messages. He arrived still holding his phone, still sure of himself.

"Look," she said, spinning the laptop toward him. "Watch what I did." She pulled up both players side by side. "Count these. Hits, and then walks." Marcus counted, lips moving. "So?" he said. "A walk isn't a hit."

"A walk isn't a hit, but it's not nothing either," Rosalie said. "Here's the thing. A batting average is hits divided by official at-bats. And walks don't count as at-bats. So the number gives a batter no credit for walks. Your guy's average looks small because the walks are invisible."

Marcus leaned in, scrolling, checking. He found a third player with a fat average and only a handful of walks all season. "Okay," he admitted, "so the average is squashing everything down to one number and it drops stuff on the floor."

Rosalie thought about the settlement they'd made last summer, when Marcus had traded her his window seat on the trip to the lake in exchange for her last two pieces of licorice, and how she'd regretted it within an hour. Numbers could be like that too, she figured. You agreed to them because they looked simple, and then you found out what they left out. "So your player's underrated," she said. "You were right for the wrong reason."

"That still counts as right," Marcus said, and he pulled the laptop back toward himself, already typing the player's name into a new search. "Grandpa's going to be endangered when I tell him he started this." Rosalie laughed and slid her chair over next to him.

Justin slid the guitar case onto the table in Ms. Reyes's studio and popped the latches like he was opening treasure. One week of lessons, and he already knew three chords, though his fingertips knew something else entirely.

"I'm not quitting," he announced, "but I have to tell you, my fingers feel like I pressed them against a hot stove. Is my guitar broken? Maybe the strings are too tight."

Ms. Reyes set down her coffee. "Play me a G chord."

He pressed down. Even before he strummed, he winced. The tips of his left hand were pink and shiny, and yesterday they had stung through his pencil in math class. He strummed anyway, because quitting before the chord was not an option.

Ms. Reyes held out her own left hand, palm up. "Feel the fingertips."

They were hard, like small pebbles under the skin. "Whoa. What happened to your fingers?"

"Calluses," she said. "Want to know the funny part?"

Justin was already piecing it together, his mind turning on some hidden pivot, the way it did when a math problem suddenly swung from impossible to obvious. "You practice a lot, right? And I've practiced every day for a week, and my fingers are sore. So the soreness comes first, and then..." He stopped, ideas germinating faster than he could line them up. "Then the skin gets tougher, and it stops hurting?"

"Play a chord on my guitar and see how the strings feel."

He took her guitar and pressed a G. His sore fingers ached, but the strings felt different, lighter somehow. "Wait, is your guitar easier?"

"It's not the guitar," she said, grinning.

Justin sat back. If the pain was inevitable for every new player, then it wasn't a sign something was wrong. It was a sign something was starting. "So everybody who ever got good at this went through exactly this week?"

She nodded. He looked down at his pink fingertips and felt like he was holding tickets to something huge. "Then I'm keeping the schedule. Every single day."

For the rest of the lesson he hammered through chord changes, counting them like push-ups, and by the last one he laughed out loud at the sting.

"Same time next week?" Ms. Reyes asked.

"Same time next week," Justin said, and he pressed one fingertip to his thumb, testing it like a tiny promise.

Jaxon sat in the exam room drumming his fingers on his green cast, which ran from his knuckles to his elbow like a lopsided canoe. In forty-five minutes his soccer team picture was being taken at the field, and he wanted the cast off before the camera clicked. He had planned to dig his signature marker out of his backpack and excavate the little pebble his friend Marcus had wedged inside the plaster last week as a "fossil," but that plan died the moment the nurse said the doctor would remove the whole cast today.

"Can you hurry?" Jaxon asked. "The picture is at four."

Dr. Patel came in carrying something that looked like a small circular saw, and Jaxon's stomach dropped. He had seen his dad cut boards with a saw exactly like that, and boards did not grow back. He yanked his arm behind his back so fast he knocked a box of tissues off the counter.

"Whoa," Jaxon said. "That thing spins, doesn't it? I mean, saws spin."

The nurse, whose name tag said Ruth, held the saw where he could see it. "Want to feel the blade before we start? Go ahead. Touch it."

Jaxon touched it with one finger. Nothing. It felt like a butter knife left in a drawer. Then Ruth flicked it on, and the noise filled the room like an angry hornet, and she touched the flat of it to her own palm and slid it around. Her skin stayed skin.

Jaxon stared. The blade was vibrating, not spinning, wobbling back and forth so fast it blurred. In his head he ran it like a math problem: a spinning blade would dig into anything soft, but a blade that only jiggles back and forth could grind through hard plaster because plaster is stiff and brittle, while skin just rides along with the shaking. He remembered trying to cut a rope by pushing a knife straight into it, which was useless, versus sawing it back and forth, which worked. Maybe this was the opposite trick.

"So it cuts the hard cast but not my arm," Jaxon said slowly, "because the blade moves back and forth instead of spinning, and skin moves with it?"

"That's the idea," Ruth said.

"Then last month when Marcus said his cast removal almost cut him, he was just being dramatic."

"Extremely dramatic," Dr. Patel said, already lowering the saw.

The plaster split down the middle with a crack like a knuckle popping, and Jaxon flinched out of pure habit, then laughed at himself. His arm came out pale and skinny, like something excavated from an ancient tomb, and the pebble rolled loose onto the paper covering the exam table.

"Thirty minutes to picture time," Ruth said, checking the clock.

Jaxon washed the chalky dust off in the sink, flexing his arm like a rudder steering him toward the door. At the field he wedged himself into the back row just as the photographer raised her hand.

"Say soccer," the photographer called.

"Say saw," Jaxon whispered, and Marcus, standing next to him, snorted so hard the boy in front of him turned around.

The Cougars had lost seven road games in a row, and Vincent had started keeping notes in the back of his math binder about it. "We stink everywhere," said Marcus, dropping his bat bag on the bench, "but especially in other people's dugouts." Vincent flipped to a fresh page and wrote Saturday, HOME, then underlined it twice, because today the Cougars were finally playing at Maple Field, their own diamond, with their own ratty net behind home plate and their own crackly scoreboard.

First inning, Marcus robbed a line drive at shortstop. Third inning, their pitcher, Dev, struck out the side. By the fifth, the Cougars were up 4-1, and Vincent felt something weird bubbling up, a feeling he had almost forgotten existed while wearing this uniform. "We're good?" he asked the bench, like he was announcing a scientific discovery. "We're actually good?"

Then it hit him, standing there in the seventh inning with the tying run on second base. It wasn't luck. His notes proved it. Every single away game, ugly loss. Every home game this season, a win. Three straight at home now, if they held on. He turned to Coach Ruiz's nephew, Benny, who kept score and knew everything about baseball. "Benny. Is there a thing where teams win more at their own park?"

Benny didn't even look up from his scorebook. "Home advantage," he said. "Home teams win more than half their games on average. Across a lot of sports, not just baseball."

Vincent's jaw dropped. It was a rule. An invisible, actual rule of the universe, and he had found it with a binder and a bad season. He wanted to test it. If home advantage was real, then the other team's batter, this scary kid named Trevor who had already homered twice in away games against them, should be easier to handle right here. So Vincent, catching, called for a low curveball, a pitch Trevor had hammered on the road. Sure enough, Trevor's swing was late by a hair, and the ball popped up into the gray sky. Marcus caught it. Inning over.

"Your testimony as scorekeeper," Vincent said grandly in the handshake line, "will confirm my theory." Benny rolled his eyes. "It's a scoreboard, not a courtroom. We won 4-2." Marcus put an arm around both of them. "So all we have to do is never leave Maple Field again. I'll write a letter."

In the parking lot, Vincent flipped open his binder one more time and wrote home advantage, big and dark, then drew a box around it. His mom honked from the car. He shoved the binder in his bag, grabbed his bat, and sprinted across the diamond yelling, "Next home game, I'm testing whether it works twice!"

The X-ray screen glowed in the corner of the exam room, and Abigail leaned forward on the crinkly paper to study her own arm bones. Two weeks ago she had fallen off the monkey bars reaching for the far bar instead of taking the safe middle route, a choice she kept replaying. Dr. Patel tapped the image with her pen.

"See this line here? You had what's called a greenstick fracture."

"A greenstick what?" Abigail asked. She had assumed an arm was either broken or not broken, the way a stick is either snapped or whole, and a partly broken arm sounded like a partly flat tire.

Dr. Patel traced the bone with the pen. "The bone cracked on one side and bent on the other, like a young green branch. It happens mostly in children because our bones are more flexible." She smiled. "So your arm was bent and cracked, not snapped clean through."

Abigail frowned at the cast that now ran from her wrist to her elbow. She could not see the bone inside it, which bothered her. How was she supposed to believe in a crack she could not look at? After the appointment, in the parking lot, she salvaged an idea from the landscaping bin beside the clinic door: a thin, fresh sapling someone had pruned from the hedge. She took it home and, in the backyard, she pressed one end against the fence and pushed the other. The branch bent, and on the outside of the curve a pale line of split wood opened up, while the inside of the curve only wrinkled and folded. Cracked on one side, bent on the other. She pushed harder and it finally snapped, which made her stop and think about the monkey bars again, about how close she had come to the whole-bone version.

At school the next day, Marcus demanded to sign her cast, and while he drew a lopsided dragon he asked what had actually happened to her arm. "Greenstick fracture," she said. "The bone cracked on one side and bent on the other. Like bending a green branch instead of snapping a dry one. Kid bones do that because they're more flexible." Marcus looked at his own arm with sudden suspicion, as if his bones might be secretly soft too.

That night Abigail sat at the kitchen table turning the sapling over in her good hand, tracing the pale crack with her thumb. Her mom asked whether it had been worth it, that far bar. Abigail thought about the moment her hand had stretched, the air, the ground coming up molten-fast, and she still could not decide whether she regretted the reach itself or only the landing. She set the branch down next to her homework and picked up her pencil with her left hand. "Ask me again when the cast comes off," she said.

The morning of Grandpa Walt's funeral, Blake sat at the kitchen table with the newspaper open in front of him, pushing his eggs around the plate. Mom had said he could skip breakfast if he wanted, but he made himself take three bites anyway. At the bottom of the page he found a box with Grandpa's name at the top and a picture of him from years ago, back when his beard was still brown. Blake read it slowly, twice.

"It says here Grandpa was a sailor," he said. "On cargo ships. He never told me that."

Mom set down her coffee. "That's the obituary," she said. "It's a published notice that someone died, and it tells about their life. Family, work, what they loved."

Blake frowned at the paper. "But I saw him every summer for six years. He taught me checkers. He hated boats. He wouldn't even get in the paddle boat at the lake." It didn't make sense. Either the paper was wrong, or there was a whole part of Grandpa he had never seen, and that second possibility felt worse, like finding a hallway in a house you thought you knew.

He pushed the eggs away and decided he could not postpone figuring this out until after the funeral. He went to the pantry where Mom kept the old photo boxes, the ones Grandma had left behind, and dug through them while Mom dried dishes behind him. The first box was all babies and weddings. The second box was mostly blurry birthdays. Then, near the bottom, his fingers hit a stiff rectangle.

The photograph showed a man in a white uniform standing on a ship's deck, one hand on a railing, squinting into the sun. It was Grandpa. Young, skinny, and grinning like Blake had never seen him grin, not even when he won at checkers. Behind the photo, in pencil, someone had written: "Walt, first crossing, 1968."

"Mom," Blake called. "Come look at this."

She came over, wiped her hands on the towel, and when she saw the picture she sat down hard in the chair beside him. "I never saw this," she said quietly. "He never talked about it. Not once."

Blake turned the photo over, then back again. "Why wouldn't he talk about it?" he asked. "If I'd sailed across an ocean, I'd tell everybody. I'd tell the mailman."

Mom laughed a small, cracked laugh and put her hand on his shoulder. "Some people keep things," she said. "Maybe it hurt somewhere. Maybe he liked having one thing that was only his."

Blake had felt like despair was waiting for him all week, sitting in the corner of every room, but holding the photograph, something shifted instead. There was a version of Grandpa he had never met, and it wasn't a lie, it was a door. He slid the photo into the pocket of his dress pants, right over his heart, where it made a stiff little square against the fabric.

"Can I carry it into the church?" he asked.

"You carry it," Mom said, "all day."

The baby had been crying for eleven minutes, which Emilia knew because she was watching the clock on the microwave the way other people watched horror movies. Her cousin Priya had gone to a movie with her parents, and Priya's neighbor Mrs. Okafor had asked if one of them could watch eight-week-old Theo for the evening. Priya had a play rehearsal. Emilia, who was visiting for the week and had never babysat anything larger than a hamster, had said yes mostly to have something to do.

For the first hour it had gone fine. Theo had slept, and Emilia had explored Mrs. Okafor's apartment, which smelled like lavender and had a fridge magnet shaped like a saxophone. Then Theo woke up and began to cry, and nothing worked. She fed him. She changed him, which was an experience she would not describe to anyone, ever. She walked him in circles, sang to him, burped him twice. The crying continued at a volume that seemed to obstruct all rational thought, filling the room so completely that she couldn't hear herself deciding what to try next.

She was standing in the kitchen, bouncing Theo harder and harder on her shoulder, her arms aching, when she noticed the folder of notes Mrs. Okafor had left on the counter. Emergency numbers, feeding times, and a page headed IMPORTANT, which Emilia read while Theo screamed into her collarbone. Never shake him, it said. A baby's neck muscles are too weak to support his heavy head, and shaking can cause serious brain injury. If he cries and cries and you feel yourself getting frustrated, put him somewhere safe and step away for a minute. It's okay. Emilia stopped bouncing. Her arms had been doing something that felt, suddenly, like a bad idea from the future.

She carried Theo to his crib, set him down on his back, and walked to the far side of the room. He kept crying. She stood by the window, hands flat on the sill, and breathed until her shoulders came down from around her ears. It felt like breaking a treaty with herself, leaving him there, but the note had said it was okay, and the note knew more than she did. She texted Priya: "The baby has been screaming for 15 minutes. I put him in his crib and walked away like the note said. Is that normal or am I the worst babysitter in history?"

Priya's reply came fast: "totally normal. he does this. give it 5 min." Emilia watched the clock again, this time without dread. At minute four, Theo's cries slowed into hiccupy gulps. At minute five, the apartment went tranquil, all at once, like someone had lifted a lid off the room. She crept over and looked down. He was asleep, one fist against his cheek, red-faced and furious-looking even in defeat.

She sat on the floor beside the crib with the IMPORTANT page in her lap and read it again. Then she texted Priya one more line: "Tell Mrs. Okafor he slept from 8:40 to now, and I want hazard pay."

The lights died at 7:40, right in the middle of Colton's homework. He sat very still in his dark bedroom and waved a hand in front of his face. He could feel his fingers moving, but he could not see them at all. "Great," he said to nobody. "Blind and stuck on fractions."

In the living room his little sister Priya had already lit the emergency candle, and his dad was poking at the breaker panel by the door with his phone flashlight. "Nothing tripped," Dad reported. "Whole building must be out. Probably lost voltage on the whole block." Priya was busy drawing bees on construction paper by candlelight for a school poster. "Bees pollinate flowers," she announced. "That means they carry the powdery stuff around. My poster is going to be intricate. Like, super detailed." "Then you'll need more than one candle," Colton said, and she stuck her tongue out at him.

Colton went back for his phone and found the battery at four percent. He could not waste the flashlight, so he sat on the couch in the dark instead. That was when he noticed something strange. Ten minutes ago he could not even see his own hand. Now, when he waved it, he caught a pale blur against the darker blur of the wall. He turned toward the window, where a sliver of city glow leaked through the blinds, and slowly the coffee table appeared, then the edge of the armchair, then the intricate pattern of shadows the blinds threw across the floor.

"Okay, science experiment," he said out loud. "If I sit here even longer, can I see the whole room?" Priya scooted over to share the experiment, mostly because she wanted to be included. They sat side by side, not talking, staring into the dark while the minutes crawled by. The couch cushions grew clearer. The bookshelf separated itself from the wall. When Colton checked his phone, exactly half an hour had passed since the lights went out. He could make out the whole living room, soft and gray, like an old photograph. "Whoa," Priya whispered. "Our eyes are upgrading."

Colton remembered something his science teacher had mentioned once, about a pigment in the rod cells of the retina, and the word floated back to him. "It's called rhodopsin," he said. "It fades out when there's light, and in the dark your eyes rebuild it. Takes half an hour or more." He counted backward in his head and it matched, almost to the minute. "So the longer we sit here," Priya said slowly, "the better we see?" "That's the rule. Total darkness superpowers."

Then the lights snapped back on, blinding white, and both of them yelped and buried their faces in the couch pillows. From the doorway Dad laughed. "Congratulations, kids. Now your rhodopsin is toast." "Dad!" Priya shouted, eyes squeezed shut. "Turn it off, we weren't done with the experiment!"

Arthur had been waiting for the farm field trip since September, mostly because of the old farmhouse. The bus bumped up a dirt lane between fertile fields, past cows that barely looked up, and stopped at a red barn where a guide in a straw hat was already waving. Arthur's teacher, Ms. Okafor, counted heads twice, then said the magic words: "The farmhouse is a museum now. Everything inside is over a hundred and fifty years old."

Inside, the rooms smelled like dust and wood smoke. Arthur drifted toward a wide oak desk near the window, the kind with little drawers and a worn leather top. His hand was almost on the edge, fingers an inch from the wood, when a girl named Priya grabbed his sleeve.

"Don't touch that!"

"Why not?" Arthur pulled his arm back. "It's just a desk. It looks strong."

"It is strong," Priya said. "That's not the problem. Museums ask visitors not to touch objects because oils and salts from your skin build up over time, and they can stain or damage the surfaces."

Arthur frowned. Oils and salts? From skin? His hand looked perfectly clean. He turned it over and studied his palm like it might be hiding something. Could something invisible really hurt a desk that had survived a century and a half of farmers? A question formed in his mind, the kind he liked best: if the oils and salts built up over time, wouldn't there be proof somewhere?

He wandered the room with his hands jammed in his pockets, looking for evidence. He noticed the banister on the staircase first. The middle of each rail was darker than the ends, a smooth brown stripe exactly where a hand would slide. The doorknob on the pantry door gleamed like a polished coin, while the hinges above it stayed dull and gray. On the desk itself, he leaned close without touching and saw that the front edge, the part a person's arm would rest on, had a soft shine the rest of the wood didn't have.

"There," he said to Priya, pointing. "Look at the banister. It's darker in the middle, right where hands go. And the doorknob's all shiny. That's years and years of hands, isn't it? That's the buildup." He was starting to grin. One kid touching the desk once wouldn't matter, the way one raindrop wouldn't flood a field. But a thousand hands, ten thousand, every one leaving a little behind? That was different. The damage wasn't one moment; it was a pattern, and patterns left marks.

Priya peered at the banister and nodded slowly. "I never thought about it like that."

Arthur still felt a small sting of resentment about the rule, if he was honest. His fingers itched to feel that old wood, and it seemed unfair that a desk could sit there begging to be touched and nobody was allowed. But now he understood the motive behind the sign by the door, the one that said PLEASE DO NOT TOUCH in curly letters. It wasn't about him being clumsy or careless. It was about what he couldn't see sitting on his skin.

At the end of the tour, the guide let them touch one thing, a rough iron horseshoe from the blacksmith shed, and Arthur held it with both hands, running his thumb over the rust. Even this, he realized, would slowly change under a million thumbs.

"Next museum," he told Priya as they climbed back on the bus, "I'm bringing a magnifying glass. I bet I can find the shiny spots from the front row seat."

The bus dropped Leo's class at the nature reserve just as a fire truck rolled up beside the visitor center, a low brick building donated years ago by an affluent family whose name was carved over the door. "Smoke machine today," said Ms. Ruiz, checking her clipboard. "The firefighters set up a demonstration in the classroom wing, and everyone goes through it."

Inside, a firefighter named Captain Osei explained the drill. A haze machine would fill the room with harmless gray vapor, and each student had to cross from the door to the far window and back. Leo watched the first group go. Priya stood up halfway, coughed on the fake smoke, and had to start over. Most kids walked, heads bent, and bumped into desks they couldn't see. When Leo's turn came, he crouched at the door and paused. The smoke hung in a thick layer above him, and down near the carpet the air looked strangely clear, like the space under a floating blanket. Was the cool air actually down there, or did it just look that way? He had a theory, and a way to test it: he pulled his sweatshirt sleeve over his nose and stood up slowly, inch by inch, like a periscope rising. At knee height, nothing. At waist height, the sleeve went gray and his eyes stung. He dropped back down and crawled the rest of the way, fast and clean, without touching a single desk.

"Best time so far," Captain Osei announced, squinting at her stopwatch. "Anyone know why he kept so low?"

"Because the smoke and heat rise," Leo said, "so the cleaner, cooler air is near the floor. That's why you taught us to crawl low under smoke." He pointed up at the thick gray ceiling of vapor. "I checked, kind of. I stood up slowly to verify where the clean part ended. It's like an invisible line."

"That's some solid logic," the captain said, grinning. "Though next time, verify with your hand, not your face."

That evening Leo wrote a letter to his grandfather, who used to volunteer at a fire station.

Dear Grandpa, You'll like this. Today we crawled through fake smoke at the nature reserve and I found out the clean air hides at the bottom. Everyone else walked through the gray cloud like confused ghosts. Priya says hi. Did you ever crawl for real? Write back and tell me.

A week later the answer came, in shaky handwriting: "Twice, kiddie. Both times the floor saved me. Stay low."

Leo read it twice, then taped it above his desk, right where he could see it from his bed.

Ellie leaned against the humming ice freezer at Moe's Gas 'n Go, watching the thermometer on the pole creep past ninety. The air conditioner in Dad's truck had died on the drive to the lake, and this was the last stop before an hour of sweat. She had eleven dollars in her pocket, and the thing she wanted most in the world was a cold drink.

Then she saw the handwritten sign taped to the cooler door: ALL DRINKS $3.50 TODAY. Yesterday they had been two dollars. "Three fifty?" she said to Jayla, who had wandered over from the slushie machine. "Did Moe just decide to be mean?"

Jayla jabbed a thumb toward the pumps. Every single car was packed with beach gear, tubes, coolers, towels. The line at the register stretched past the beef jerky. "Half the town's driving to the lake today," Jayla said. "And the delivery truck didn't come this week. Moe's down to, like, four cases."

Ellie peeked into the cooler. Only the bottom shelf had anything left, and a man in flip-flops was already loading six bottles into his arms. She tested a quick idea in her head: if tons of people want a thing, and there isn't much of the thing, the price climbs. If nobody wants it, or it's piled everywhere, the price sinks. It was like the thermostat on the wall at home. The temperature didn't come from nowhere; something made it move.

Inside, two boys were arguing by the register. "Moe sets the price," one insisted. "It's his store. Sellers decide." The other shook his head. "No way. If we refused to pay it, he'd have to drop it. Buyers decide." They sounded ready to arm wrestle over it.

Ellie's dad was reading a battered paperback he kept in the door pocket, something called "Principles of Economics" by Alfred Marshall, from 1890. He thumbed to a page and held it up. "Listen to this. Marshall says supply and demand are like the two blades of a pair of scissors. It takes both to set a price."

"Both blades," Ellie repeated, and the argument in her head snapped shut like the cooler door. The boys were both right. Moe couldn't charge ten dollars or nobody would buy; the buyers couldn't force a dollar or there'd be nothing left to buy. Three fifty was where the two blades crossed.

Outside, a produce truck rumbled past with crates of watermelons strapped down tight, so many they were practically rolling off the sides. The farmer's handwritten board on its tailgate read: MELONS, 75 CENTS, TAKE AS MANY AS YOU WANT. Ellie grinned. She paid three fifty for one cold root beer, cherishing it like treasure, and spent two dollars on a fat melon that would feed the whole truck. The durable Styrofoam cooler in the bed would keep both cold till the lake. She climbed in, melon in her lap, and slammed the door.

"Drive fast, Dad," she said. "The lake is waiting."

Dinner was lasagna, the good kind with the crunchy edges, and Paige pushed hers around the plate in slow circles. Tomorrow morning she had to stand up in front of the whole class and read her poem out loud, and even thinking about it made her stomach feel like it was full of ice water. Her hands were clenched in her lap under the table.

"You're not eating," said her older brother Dex, who was home from soccer practice and working on his third helping.

"I have anxiety about the poem thing," Paige said. "That's what Mom called it last time. My chest gets all tight and my heart goes fast."

Across the table, six-year-old Theo waved his fork. "I'm a herbivore," he announced, stacking his zucchini slices into a tower. "I only eat plants. And garlic bread."

"That's not how it works, but fine," said Dad, breaking a piece of bread that had gone brittle in the oven. It crackled and showered crumbs across the tablecloth.

Dex set down his fork. "You know what my coach has me do before a penalty shot? Goalies and penalty takers, both. You breathe in, then let it out slow, like twice as long as the in breath. Long exhales." He demonstrated, puffing the air out so his cheeks went flat. "It's a coping skill. Whole team does it before a stressful moment, before we even walk on the pitch. It calms the body's stress response down. That's what he said."

"Does it actually work?" Paige asked.

"Try it and see. Can't hurt."

She was quiet for a moment. It seemed strange that breathing could change anything, since breathing was just a thing her body did anyway, like blinking. But there was a way to test an idea, and she knew it. You did it and watched what happened, the same way you'd check whether the toaster was broken or just unplugged. She took a slow breath through her nose, counted to four, then let it out through her mouth, long and thin, like she was fogging a window gently.

"Feeling any better?" Dex asked.

"My heart's not going as fast," Paige said, surprised. She did it again, and this time she paid attention on purpose. In, slow. Out, slower. The ice water in her stomach didn't vanish, but it turned into something more like cold tap water, which she could live with.

Later, in her room with the poem cards spread on the bed, she tried to replicate the exact same thing, in through the nose for four, out for six or seven. She did it three times before practicing the first line out loud to her poster of the solar system. Her voice came out steadier than she expected, and she said the second line to her reflection in the mirror, and then the third.

"Boundaries," she told Mars on the poster, holding up a hand. "You don't get to hear the ending until tomorrow."

At breakfast she set her fork down, breathed in slow, and let the breath out long, watching it fog a little against the cold window. Then she picked up her poem cards and walked out the door.

Rose had babysat exactly one other child in her life, and that child had been seven and mostly interested in Minecraft, so holding four-month-old Daisy felt like being handed an emperor who ruled by screaming. The Willises had left a note on the fridge, and Rose had skimmed it while Daisy gummed her fist in the bouncy chair. "Back to sleep," the note said. "Firm flat mattress. Nothing in the crib. No pillows, blankets or toys." At the time it had seemed strange to her, because every picture she had ever seen of a baby showed a nest of soft things.

By seven o'clock Daisy was rubbing her eyes and fussing in that windup way Rose was starting to recognize. She carried the baby upstairs to the nursery, where a crib stood bare in the corner, just a tight fitted sheet on the mattress. On the rocking chair, though, someone had folded a fluffy yellow blanket with bunnies on it, clearly meant for a baby, clearly meant for this room.

Rose reached for it. Then she stopped, because the note had been underlined twice, and Mrs. Willis did not seem like a person who underlined things twice for no reason. The blanket was soft and warm and exactly what she would have wanted if she were the size of a loaf of bread. But babies under one year sleep on their backs, on a firm, flat surface, with nothing soft around them. That was the whole point of the empty crib, she realized. It was not unfinished. It was deliberate.

So she tested her idea the way she tested things: carefully, one step at a time. She laid Daisy on her back in the center of the firm mattress. Daisy screamed. Rose almost grabbed the bunny blanket right then, but instead she set the bouncy chair beside the crib where Daisy could see her face, and patted the baby's chest lightly and hummed the only song she knew all the words to, which was the theme from a cartoon. After a minute Daisy's fists unclenched. After three minutes her eyes closed.

Rose sat in the rocking chair with the yellow blanket folded on her knees, not daring to move it anywhere near the crib. When the Willises came home at nine, Mrs. Willis peeked into the nursery and then looked at Rose for a long moment.

"She's flat on her back," Rose whispered. "Nothing in the crib. I almost used the blanket, but your note, the underlines."

Mrs. Willis let out a breath like she'd been holding it since the front door. "Most sitters don't even read it. That blanket was a gift, and honestly I can't wait until she's old enough to use it."

"It's really soft," Rose said, still holding it, and Mrs. Willis laughed quietly and told her she was the permanent sitter now, if she wanted the job.

"Every Saturday?" Rose asked.

"Every Saturday," said Mrs. Willis. "I'll emphasize it to all the other parents at the park, too. The one who reads the notes." Down the hall, Daisy slept on her back, breathing in small even whispers, the empty crib steady around her like a promise Rose intended to keep.

Jace noticed it at the fridge, where Marcus was standing with the door open without taking anything out. They had been friends since second grade, and Marcus never just stood at a fridge. He grabbed the juice, made a joke, kicked the door shut with his heel.

"You want a snack?" Jace asked.

"I'm not hungry." Marcus closed the fridge and sat down at the kitchen table. He pulled out his phone, then put it back. He picked up a pencil from the counter and tapped it against the wood, four taps, pause, four taps.

Jace sat across from him. Last week Marcus had skipped soccer practice, which he never did, and yesterday he had laughed at nothing Jace said, the fake kind of laugh that comes half a second too late. Jace had been building a theory in his head: something was wrong that Marcus wasn't saying out loud, and the pattern of small changes was the evidence.

In health class, their teacher had put up a poster and told them to read it themselves. Jace remembered the exact words because he'd copied them into his notebook for the quiz. Mental health includes a person's emotional, psychological and social well-being, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. He'd assumed it was quiz material, nothing more. But standing there now, he thought about the "social" part. If friendships counted inside mental health, then what happened between him and Marcus wasn't separate from how Marcus was doing overall. It was part of the same thing.

"Remember in fourth grade," Jace said, "when you got picked for the county math team and your dad called it the most prestigious thing that ever happened to our family?" Marcus's dad had framed the certificate and hung it over the toaster.

Marcus almost smiled. "He still points at it when he makes eggs."

"And then the team got cut because the county ran out of budget, and you were fine about it."

"I wasn't fine," Marcus said. He set the pencil down. "I told everyone I was fine."

Jace waited. In his theory, the missing money part mattered too, so he asked, "Is it your dad's shop?" Marcus's dad repaired bicycles, and the whole spring had been slow. Marcus looked up fast, surprised, then nodded.

"The revenue's been down for months. They might lose the lease. If we move, I change schools." His voice went thin on the last word. "I didn't want to say it out loud because it gets bigger when I say it."

"That's backwards," Jace said. "Stuff gets smaller when you say it. That's how it works with my mom and her stress thing. She calls her breathing exercises coping, and she says I can borrow them if I ever need to."

"My sister says I have anxiety," Marcus said. "She read about it."

"Maybe. You could talk to the counselor about it, and you could also just talk to me. I'm asking for that. Consider it a boundary: no more fake laughs, and no more standing at the fridge pretending you're hungry."

Marcus opened the fridge, took out the juice, and poured two glasses.

The group chat lit up at 7:02 p.m., right after dinner. Maya had posted a screenshot of an email from their teacher, and beneath it, eleven people were typing at once. Ella scrolled through the chaos: someone sent a string of exclamation points, someone else typed in ALL CAPS, and Priya dropped a single thumbs-up. "Guys," Ella typed slowly, "nobody can even tell what we're deciding."

The problem was real. Maya's birthday was in nine days, and she wanted to invite the whole class, all twenty-six kids, by email instead of paper invitations this year. But nobody had everyone's address. Some kids had never shared theirs, and Maya refused to ask people to send their emails to the whole group. "It's not fair to just hand out everybody's address to everybody," she wrote. "My mom says that's how spam lists start."

Ella stared at her phone. She thought about the email her soccer coach sent every fall, the one listing practices and field locations. When she'd hit reply once, the message had gone only to the coach, not to all the other parents, and she'd noticed the To line was strangely short. Somewhere in that memory, a word persisted in nagging at her: three letters, hiding in plain sight near the top of the email form. She opened her own account and started a new message, typing Maya's address in the To field, then looking carefully at the little links beside it. Cc. Bcc.

She clicked Bcc and typed in her own address, then sent a test message to Maya: "Look at the To and Bcc lines and tell me what you see." Two minutes later Maya replied, and then posted in the group chat: "ELLA. This is it." She pasted a screenshot. Ella typed the explanation she'd worked out: "BCC stands for 'blind carbon copy.' People you add in the Bcc field still get the message, but the other recipients can't see their addresses." Maya added, "So I can put everybody in Bcc and nobody's address gets shared with everyone."

The plan still had wrinkles. Maya's first attempt failed because she'd typed half the class into the regular To line by accident, and Priya gently pointed it out: "Same problem, different window. Try again." Maya tried again, and this time the test email arrived in Ella's inbox with a To line showing only Maya's own address. It was like mailing twenty-six sealed envelopes instead of one giant postcard.

The next evening, the invitations went out. Every kid in class got one, and when Dylan replied asking who else was invited, Maya could honestly say he'd have to wait and see. "The mystery is part of the party," she wrote, and Ella laughed out loud at her desk. Then a new message appeared, from Maya only to her: "Chronic overthinker saves the day again. You're getting the first slice of cake." Ella grinned and typed back, "Deal. But I want it in writing."

Victor had one job at Marcus's birthday sleepover: find out where the new kid, Aiden, was from, so they could put it on the team sheet for the international food day. He waited until they were all sprawled on the living room floor with pizza, because asking at the door would have been rude.

"So where are you from?" Victor asked, pencil ready.

Aiden pushed a pepperoni to the edge of his slice. "That's the problem. Singapore for three years, then Germany, then Brazil, and before all that, a place I barely remember. My parents say home is Ohio, but I've never lived there longer than a summer." He shrugged. "I always get stuck on that question. It's like asking a fish which puddle it owns."

The other kids offered guesses. Marcus said Ohio, because that's where Aiden's parents were from. Priya said Singapore, because that's where he'd lived longest. Aiden shook his head at every answer, and Victor noticed his shoulders creeping up toward his ears. The question itself seemed to obstruct the conversation, like a couch blocking a doorway: nobody could get past it to the actual kid sitting there.

Later, when the others had drifted toward the video games, Victor found Aiden alone at the bookshelf, looking at Marcus's mother's old sociology textbooks. Victor had an idea he wanted to test. His own dad had moved from one country to another before Victor was born, and Victor had once overheard a phrase at his aunt's house. "My aunt says there's a name for kids like you," he said. "Third culture kid. An American sociologist, Ruth Hill Useem, made it up back in the 1950s. For kids raised in a culture different from their parents' home culture."

Aiden turned around slowly. "Say the name again."

"Third culture kid."

Aiden said it back, once, then again, like he was trying on a coat that might actually fit. "So I'm not from nowhere. I'm from a third place, the one in between." He laughed, a real laugh this time. "It's a paradox, isn't it? The question made me feel like I had no answer, and the answer is that the in-between is the answer."

Victor wrote it down on the team sheet: Aiden, third culture kid, four countries. Priya read it over his shoulder and said they could make a dish from each place, a little buffet, and it would be the best table in the cafeteria, inevitable really, since no one else would have four flags.

Aiden grabbed the marker and drew a fifth flag with a question mark on it. "For the third culture," he said, and held it up for everyone to see.

Autumn had exactly one week to get her science fair project ready, and her only idea was to smear mud on a baking sheet and hope for the best. She sat on her grandmother's porch steps with her chin in her hands, staring at the garden hose coiled by the fence.

"What's the sighing about?" Grandma asked, setting down two glasses of lemonade even though Autumn hadn't asked for any, which was typical.

"I have to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years. Erosion and deposition. It's mandatory for the unit grade, and I can't picture it. A canyon is huge and slow, and I can't even see time." She took the lemonade anyway, because refusing Grandma's lemonade was like refusing a sunrise.

Grandma tipped her head toward the hill behind the garden, where a shallow gully ran down past the compost bin to the creek. "You see that ditch? Your grandfather filled it in twice. Twice. That gully beat him like an old adversary. Every hard rain carved it right back out."

Autumn walked up the slope and crouched at the edge of the groove. It was maybe a foot deep, with pebbles heaped at the bottom where the water had dropped them, and at its mouth, where it met the flat ground, a little fan of mud spread out like a tiny delta. The water had carried dirt away here and dumped it there, and it had done it all without her ever once watching it happen. She grinned, turned the hose on low, and aimed it at the top of the gully.

For an hour she experimented. A trickle barely moved anything, so she pinched the nozzle and made a torrent, and the gully deepened so fast she actually yelped. Then she watched the fan of mud at the bottom grow, layer after layer, and thought about the Colorado River doing that not for an hour but for millions of years. At school they'd read that the Grand Canyon is 277 miles long, 446 kilometers if you measured that way, and over a mile deep at its deepest point. She'd skipped past that number before. Now she stood at the bottom of the garden, looked up at where she'd started at the top of the hill, and tried to picture a mile of rock going down instead of up. Her brain stuttered. A mile was a whole mile, straight into the ground, and the river had done it one rainy afternoon at a time.

"Grandma, was Grandpa really mad about the gully?" she called.

"Mad enough to write it a letter," Grandma said. "I still have it somewhere."

Autumn laughed so hard she nearly dropped the hose, then got an idea so good she jogged back up the hill. She would build the whole project in a plastic storage bin, film the water cutting its channel overnight, and split the screen so the viewers could watch the canyon grow while she narrated in fast-forward. First, though, she washed out Grandma's gully-carved measuring cup, refilled both lemonade glasses, and carried them carefully back down the slope.

"Truce," she said, handing one over. "The gully and I are on the same team now."

The argument started three rows from the back of the bus, which was where most good arguments started. Marcus held up his phone with the district cross-country standings. "Torrance is number one," he said. "Riverview's girl is second. Torrance is obviously faster."

"Obviously by how much?" Ella asked.

Marcus looked at her the way people look when a question is more trouble than it's worth. "By first place. That's the whole point of first place."

Eella wanted the standings for a reason of her own. Her brother Cole ran for Torrance, and their dad had watched the state meet on TV last spring, where the silver medalist in the hundred meters lost by less than a blink. Cole had moped about it for a week, saying the guy was basically as fast as the winner. Their dad, who considered himself Cole's mentor in all things running, had disagreed at dinner every night since. Ella intended to settle it, because she was optimistic about her chances of winning an argument nobody had asked her to join.

She leaned over the seat. "Rankings don't tell you the gap. Torrance's girl could be ahead by a hundredth of a second or by a whole minute. First and second just tells you the order."

"You made that up," Marcus said.

"Then let's check." Coach Peters kept meet times on a clipboard that lived in the equipment shed, and Ella knew it came out of the shed every Thursday, when the equipment cart rolled onto the bus for away meets. Today was Thursday. When the cart rattled aboard at the next stop, she flipped the clipboard open on her knees while Marcus held the phone.

Torrance's top runner had run the two-mile in 11:42.06. Riverview's had run 11:42.07. One hundredth of a second. Marcus stared at the numbers, then at his phone, which said the same two names in the same order and nothing else.

"Okay," he said slowly, "but that's just those two."

She turned the page. Fifth place and sixth place in the standings were two kids from Farmington and Halloway. Their times were 12:10 and 13:05. Fifty-five seconds apart, and the ranking treated that gap exactly the same as the hundredth of a second, which was to say it didn't treat it at all.

Marcus wrote both pairs of numbers in the fog on the window with his finger, as if the glass might disagree too. The glass did not.
