When he turned to greet Aunt Rosa's father, the oldest person in the room, the bow went deep and slow, almost to the table's edge, and stayed there long enough for Daniel to count to four. There it was, a pattern: the deeper and longer the bow, the more respect it carried. The fifteen-degree one was pocket change; the deep one was a gold coin.

Daniel had a plan to test before dinner. He waited until Grandfather Ota settled into a chair by the window, then walked over, held out the candy with both hands the way Kenji's grandmother had offered her packages, and bowed. He bent as far as his balance allowed and held it, counting silently, one, two, three, four. When he straightened, the old man's eyes were bright. He said something to Kenji, who laughed.

"He says you bow like a resilient young reed," Kenji translated. "Also, sit with your palms up, not on the table like a hammer. Grandmother hates that."

Daniel looked down at his hands, already flat on the table, and flipped them over. "Like this?"

The pavilion at Riverside Park had been decorated since morning, and Gabriel arrived with his mother, his tía Rosa, and a plastic bag holding one sugar skull that had already lost an arm. A banner over the tables read "Día de los Muertos, November 1 and 2." His tía had explained in the car, more than once, that in Mexico these were the days for honoring family members who had died, and that families built altars in their homes for it. Gabriel mostly cared about one thing: he was supposed to add his grandfather's photo to the community altar today, and he had left the photo in the printer tray at home.

The altar stood at the end of the longest table. A girl from his class, Marisol, was arranging frames on it. "It's called an ofrenda," she said when he stood there too long without doing anything. "My great-grandfather goes here." She set down a photo of a man in a straw hat holding a radio.

Gabriel checked his mother's phone for the picture he wanted, the one of his grandfather laughing at a barbecue. The battery bar was red, then the screen went black. He borrowed Tía Rosa's phone, but the photo had never been sent to her. He had a copy only at home, and home was a twenty-minute walk.

While he decided what to do, he noticed something odd. The candles on the ofrenda kept going out. Marisol relit one, and it died again within a minute. An old man nearby blamed the candles themselves, saying they were cheap, but Gabriel crouched and watched. The flames all bent in the same direction, toward the lake. When a group of people walked past the open side of the pavilion, the flames accelerated sideways, flickered hard, and went out. It wasn't the candles. Wind was funneling between the two support posts on the north side, and the candles sat directly in that channel.

He tested it by holding a single candle near the posts, then behind the stacked pan de muerto at the center of the table. At the posts it guttered. Behind the bread, the flame stood still. He and Marisol moved the candleholders to the sheltered middle of the ofrenda, and none of them went out for the rest of the afternoon. The old man gave a small nod, as if he had suspected wind all along.

Then Gabriel ran home. He got the photo, ran back through the falling leaves, out of breath, and slid it into an empty frame Marisol had saved. He placed it beside her great-grandfather with the radio.

When his mother saw it, she said, "He would have liked being next to somebody who loved music that much."

Gabriel straightened the frame so his grandfather's grin faced the whole park.

Alexa sat in the back seat with her new orange cast propped on a pillow, staring at the place where the doctor had taped a copy of her X-ray to the folder in her lap. Mom pulled out of the parking lot and pointed the car toward home. "You did great in there," Mom said. "The nurse said most kids cry when they set a bone."

"I did cry," Alexa said. "Just before the medicine." She turned the X-ray toward the window light. Two pale stripes ran down her forearm, side by side, and only one of them had a dark crack in it, like a hairline in a windshield. She couldn't tell which stripe was which, and that bothered her more than the ache did.

In her mind she replayed the doctor's voice while he pointed at the film. "The forearm has two bones," he had said. "The radius, on the thumb side, and the ulna, on the little-finger side." Alexa laid her good hand flat on her knee and copied it with the cast arm, slow and careful, the way she was being meticulous about every movement now. The crack in the X-ray sat closer to the thumb stripe. So the broken one should be the radius. But her thumb side barely hurt. The worst ache ran down by her little finger instead, and that didn't fit.

"Mom, can we stop at the pool office?" she asked. "I have to enroll for the swim team before Friday, or the spot goes to the next kid on the list." Mom glanced in the mirror. "You heard the doctor. Six weeks, no swimming." "He said no swimming with the cast," Alexa said. "He didn't say anything about being on the team. Priya said they let injured kids do the dryland drills, the stretching and the running, until they're cleared." She had built her whole plan on that premise, and she knew Mom would try to poke a hole in it.

She tested her idea in the seat, wiggling first her thumb, then her little finger. The thumb moved almost freely. The little finger sent a thin wire of pain up the outside of her arm, and she hissed through her teeth. That settled it. The cracked stripe in the picture wasn't the radius at all, because the doctors had turned the film around when they handed it to her; the image was flipped, like a mirror. It was the ulna that was broken, the little-finger bone, which explained exactly where it hurt. "Two minutes at the office," she told Mom. "I'll sign the form left-handed."

Mom sighed and put on the blinker. "Two minutes. And don't you dare take that pen out of the cast pocket with your teeth." Alexa grinned, tucked the X-ray folder under her good arm, and reached for the door handle before the car had fully stopped.

Megan's bean plants stood in two rows on the science fair table, and the ones that had spent three weeks next to the speaker looked exactly as sorry as the ones that had grown in silence. She had wanted this project to work so badly. First prize was a summer camp scholarship, and without it the camp would be out of reach, an expense her family could not manage twice.

Priya leaned over the pots, frowning. "So music doesn't help plants grow?"

"That's not what I can say yet," Megan said, turning her notebook around. Her data table showed heights for both groups, nearly identical. "Mr. Okafor said our whole write-up is wrong because we never decided what no effect would look like. We just hoped the music plants would be taller."

Priya picked up the notebook and read the red comment at the top of the page. "Define your null hypothesis before you test it." She looked up. "What's that?"

"It's the statement that there's no relationship between the things you're studying," Megan said. "Music and growth, for us. The experiment doesn't prove music helps. It tries to reject that statement."

Priya set the notebook down slowly. "So if we'd written it down first, the null would say the two groups grow the same."

"And then our data would either knock it down or not," Megan said. She pointed at the rows of numbers. "Right now they're so close that I can't reject it. The plants grew the same either way." She felt her throat tighten and kept talking anyway. "But that's still a result. Judges want to see how you decide, not just whether you win."

They rebuilt the display board right there between the volcano and the homemade lava lamp. Megan wrote the null hypothesis across the top in careful block letters, then drew the height chart beneath it with both groups' bars nearly even. A boy from the next table wandered over, saw the board, and asked whether music had helped. "Not that I can show," Megan told him. "They look about equal, so the null stands."

When the judge stopped at their table, she asked Priya what they would change. Priya said, "We'd decide in advance what difference would signify a real effect, so we wouldn't just be hoping."

The judge nodded and made a mark on her clipboard. "Resilient beans, too," she said, tapping a pot. "They survived three weeks of my daughter's playlist."

Megan laughed, and straightened the tallest plant in the silent row. "Round two next year," she said. "Quieter music, bigger pots."

Eleanor had exactly one weekend to finish her science project on water quality, and she had just found the most bizarre website of her life. It showed photographs of a green, murky pond turning crystal clear in three days, all because of a special powder sold by a man named Dale. "One scoop a week and your water worries are over," Dale wrote beneath a picture of himself holding a jar. Eleanor leaned closer to the screen, her cat Pixel hopping onto the desk beside the keyboard. Her teacher had said every claim in the project needed a reliable source, and this one seemed too good to be true.

She typed "Dale's Clear Water Powder" into the search box and found something unexpected: a real science journal article about pond water, written by three researchers. On the first page, in small print, the article said it had been reviewed by two other experts before publication. Eleanor had never noticed a line like that before. She scrolled back to Dale's site and read every word, but nowhere did it say anyone had checked his work. It was just his own story, one person's experience with his own pond.

At dinner she told her older brother, Marcus, about the difference. "The journal article says experts looked at it before it got published," she said. "It's called peer review." Marcus nodded between bites of pasta. "So Dale's site is just him talking," he said. "Nobody checked anything." Eleanor pushed her noodles around her plate, thinking. The consequence of trusting Dale could be a bad grade, or worse, a project full of nonsense.

She wanted to document the difference properly, so she set up her own small test in the kitchen. She filled two identical jars with cloudy water from the fish tank filter, added a pinch of ordinary baking soda to one and nothing to the other, and labeled them with masking tape. Then she took photographs each morning and wrote down what she saw. By Sunday, both jars looked almost the same, which told her something real: a single scoop of anything was not a magic fix, and one person's glowing story proved nothing.

On Monday she turned in her project with both sources side by side, explaining which one had been examined by experts and which had not, and what her own jar test showed. Her teacher wrote "Excellent comparing" at the top in green pen. That afternoon, Eleanor opened her laptop and, out of curiosity, checked Dale's site one more time. There was a new comment at the bottom of the page, from someone named Ponds4Life: "Tried it for a month, my water's still green." Eleanor grinned and closed the lid.

Marcus had one job on Friday: bring a snack to share for the international foods lesson, and not embarrass himself in front of Wei's grandmother, who was visiting from Hong Kong and coming to watch. He had brought a box of grape juice and a bag of pretzels. It felt thin.

When Wei invited him over Thursday evening to practice, Marcus said yes mostly because Wei's building had the fastest elevator in town. They rode up together, and Marcus pressed the button for Wei's floor. That was when he noticed the panel. The buttons went one, two, three, five. He counted them twice, dragging his finger along the row to be sure.

"Your building doesn't have a four," he said. "That's not a mistake? Buildings don't just skip numbers."

Wei looked at the panel like he was meeting an old acquaintance. "My grandma says in Chinese, the word for four sounds like the word for death," he said. "So some buildings in East Asia skip the fourth floor." Then he shrugged, as if floors were only floors, and the doors opened.

Marcus tested the idea in his head on the way down. If the number were bad luck, it would be missing in other buildings too. In his own building, the fourth floor was right where it should be, home to Mrs. Okafor and her parrots. So it wasn't a law of nature. It was a custom, the way his own family hugged hello and Wei's family bowed slightly, palms together, which Wei had demonstrated that morning with the gravity of a chess move.

At the lesson, Wei's grandmother brought egg tarts in a tin, and Wei passed them out with both hands, which Marcus copied and nearly dropped doing. When he handed one back to say thank you for a second tart, she waved it off and pressed it toward him again, and it took him three tries to understand that refusing once was polite and accepting twice was the point. The whole class ended up eating with their hands or with chopsticks or, in Marcus's case, with a pretzel used as tongs, which even he had to admit was not thriving.

After school, Marcus walked home the long way, parallel to the creek, and thought about how his street had houses from a hundred years ago, one of the oldest settlements in town, and how nobody could see that just by looking. Customs were like that. Hidden floors in an elevator you hadn't ridden yet.

He stopped at the corner store and bought a box of mooncakes, which the label said were red bean. He would bring them Monday, with both hands.

"Mrs. Okafor is on four," he told his dad at dinner. "Of a building with no four in it."

His dad blinked twice. "I'm going to need you to start from the beginning."

Gabriella sat on the spinning stool at Bright Eyes Optical and swung her legs, waiting for her new glasses to be made. Her mother was filling out forms at the counter, which meant Gabriella had time to text her cousin Dev, who had just moved from London.

"How did your eye test go?" she typed.

"Perfect," Dev wrote back. "The doctor says I have 6/6 vision."

Gabriella stared at the screen. Six out of six? That sounded like a grade, and not a good one. If 20/20 was perfect, then 6/6 had to be way down the chart, like getting a six on a twenty-point quiz. She typed, "Only 6?? I'm getting glasses because my eyes are 20 something. Are you okay?" Dev replied with a row of laughing faces, which was no help at all.

Fine. She would investigate. Gabriella spun her stool toward the exam room, where the optometrist was hanging a new eye chart, and stood in the doorway with her chin lifted in a way her mother called her ambassador face, the one she used when about to ask for something. "Excuse me," she said. "If someone has 6/6 vision, is that terrible?"

The optometrist laughed. "Where's this someone from?"

"London. England. He just moved."

"That'll do it. Countries that use metres write normal vision as 6/6 instead of 20/20. Same eyes, different measurement."

Gabriella did the math in her head, sort of. So 6/6 was not a failing grade; it was perfect vision wearing a different coat. Dev hadn't been bragging badly or hiding a disaster. He'd been bragging correctly. She felt her cheeks go warm, then decided to be defiant about it and blame the eye drops. She marched back to the waiting area and typed, "You have perfect vision, you smug show-off."

"Naturally," Dev wrote. "Are those glasses emojis supposed to be you?"

Before she could answer, the technician called her name and handed over the new glasses, purple frames with tiny stars on the hinges. Gabriella slid them on, and the whole store sharpened like someone had finally focused a camera. She could read the tiny price stickers on the lens cleaner. She could see that the poster of an eye near the ceiling had eyelashes, which seemed like showing off.

She walked to the counter, where her mother was signing the last form. "Mom, guess what. Dev sees six out of six, which is the same as my twenty out of twenty, except his is in metres."

"His what is in metres?"

"His vision. His perfect, annoying vision." Gabriella pushed the glasses up her nose. "Also, I've decided to enroll in optometry school so I can put those little letter charts on people's walls."

Her mother paid, shaking her head. Gabriella waved at the optometrist on the way out. "Six out of six!" she announced to the whole parking lot.

At dinner, Charlotte's little brother slammed his fork down and pointed at her. "The poster at the community center is two faces," he insisted. "Two faces looking at each other. I saw it today."

"It is a vase," said her mother, ladling soup into bowls. "A white vase on a black background. I walk past it every Tuesday."

Charlotte stopped with her spoon halfway to her mouth. That was strange. Her mother and Dex had looked at the exact same poster, in the exact same hallway, and they had come home with completely different pictures in their heads. "Can you both see the other thing?" she asked. "Mom, can you see the faces? Dex, can you see the vase?"

Dex squinted at the ceiling as if the poster were painted up there. "Sort of? If I try really hard. But then the vase goes away."

"It's like a treaty," their mother said, smiling. "You can only have one at a time."

Charlotte pushed her bread around her plate, thinking. After dinner she found the community center's website and searched for the poster. There it was: black and white, and once she knew what to look for, she could make the white part pop out as a vase, or let the black part take over and become two faces in profile, nose to nose. It flipped. She made it flip again. But no matter how hard she tried, she could not hold both pictures at once, the way you could look at a picture of a dog and a cat together. It was vase, or it was faces. Never both.

Underneath the image she found a caption. "This is called a Rubin vase," she read aloud, and Dex leaned over her shoulder. It said the Rubin vase was introduced by a Danish psychologist named Edgar Rubin in 1915, and that it could be seen as either a vase or two faces, but not both at the same moment.

"So Mom was right," said Dex.

"So you were both right," said Charlotte. "That's the weird part." She was skeptical of one thing, though. Maybe it only worked because they expected it to. Tomorrow at school she would nominate the poster for show-and-tell, draw it big on paper, and ask her class to call out what they saw without any hints. If kids who had never heard of it still saw only one picture at a time, then it wasn't just her family being strange. It was something about how seeing itself worked, some hidden rule in the brain you couldn't watch directly, only test from the outside, like guessing what was inside a wrapped present by shaking it.

The next afternoon she stood at the whiteboard with her marker squeaking, filling in the black around the white vase shape. "First person to raise a hand," she said, capping the marker, "tell me what you see."

Eleanor pulled the tray of chicken out of the fridge and set it on the counter, right beside the cutting board she had just used to trim the raw meat. Outside the window the sky had turned an ominous gray, and rain streaked the glass, which meant her little brother would be trapped inside and cranky all evening. She had promised her parents a full dinner tonight, chicken and salad and rice, because Mom had to work late and Dad's bus ran slow on rainy days.

She rinsed the knife, dried it, and reached for the head of lettuce. Then she stopped, her hand hovering over the board. It looked clean enough, just a few faint streaks where the chicken had lain, but she remembered the health video from school and the word that had come with it. Something about invisible things traveling from one food to another. She couldn't see anything on the board, but that was exactly the problem. What you couldn't see could still be there.

"Cross-contamination," she said out loud, testing the word. Her brother, Sam, wandered in and stole a carrot from the bowl.

"Is that a band?"

"It's how bacteria spread from one food to another. Like from raw meat to stuff you eat raw, like salad." She slid the used board into the sink, ran hot water and soap over it, and pulled a clean board from the cabinet. She set the lettuce on the fresh plastic and started chopping, feeling a little smug about her own cleverness.

When Dad finally came in, shaking rain off his jacket, he found her arranging the salad and the chicken already browning in the pan. He peered over her shoulder at the two boards, one in the drying rack, one on the counter.

"Did you use separate boards for the chicken and the lettuce?" he asked.

"Of course," Eleanor said. "I'm not going to chop salad on the board that had raw chicken on it."

Dad smiled and began to elaborate on how proud he was, telling her about the time in college he'd made himself sick with a midnight sandwich, until Sam groaned and begged him to stop. While Dad set the table, the radio muttered about heavy precipitation moving in overnight, up to two inches, and possible flooding near the river.

"Great," Sam said. "Indoor recess forever."

"Then you're helping me make cookies tomorrow," Eleanor said. She tipped the salad into the good bowl, the one with the blue rim, and carried it to the table.

Justin stood in line at Hartley's Pharmacy behind his mom, breathing through his mouth because his nose was still packed solid. Two days ago he'd been flattened by the flu, shivering under three blankets and watching the ceiling fan spin. Now his fever was gone and he mostly felt like a deflated soccer ball instead of a popped one, which to him meant one thing: he was better.

The party was the problem. Devon's birthday started at two o'clock, and there would be pizza, a game tournament, and a dog named Biscuit who did tricks for carrot sticks. Justin had RSVP'd weeks ago, back when the flu was just a rumor in the seventh-grade hallway. He held the pharmacy's number card, number 17, and rehearsed his argument while the fluorescent lights buzzed overhead and the smell of hand sanitizer drifted from the counter.

"Prescription for Mara Ellis," the pharmacist called, and Justin's mom stepped up. That gave Justin an idea. While she signed the pickup slip, he leaned toward the pharmacist, a woman with silver hoops and glasses on a beaded chain, and asked his question like a scientist gathering data. "If somebody had the flu and their fever's gone on day two, are they done being contagious? Hypothetically."

She smiled at "hypothetically." "Nice try. According to the CDC, people with the flu are most contagious during the first three days of their illness. Day two means you're right in the middle of the danger zone, hypothetical or not."

Justin did the math in his head, and the math was terrible. He was on day two. Three days of maximum contagion meant tomorrow and part of Sunday too. He tested a loophole anyway. "What if I just don't cough on anyone? What if I stand by the window?"

"Viruses thrive in exactly the conditions you can't control," the pharmacist said, dropping the white paper bag into his mom's hands. "Kids at a party, sharing controllers, passing pizza."

Walking to the car, Justin tried one last angle with his mom. "Is a partial appearance feasible? Like, ten minutes?"

"You mean is it feasible for you to give Devon the flu for his birthday?" she said, unlocking the doors. "No."

So Justin built a backup plan. He video-called Devon at two o'clock, propped his phone against the cereal box, and played the tournament remotely, shouting instructions while Devon's little sister acted as his hands on the controller. He was losing badly and laughing about it when a knock came at his own door and his mom appeared with a plate. Pizza, she said, from a delivery that had mysteriously been ordered to the wrong address, which happened to be theirs.

"Devon says hi," she said, and behind her, faintly, through the phone, Biscuit the dog barked.

The clock above the whiteboard said twelve minutes left, and Maria still had no topic for the class discussion her grade depended on. Mr. Ruiz had given everyone until the end of the period to bring forward one real experiment and explain why it mattered. Around her, kids were scribbling last-minute notes about volcanoes and vinegar.

Then Marcus leaned across the aisle. "You were in the hallway yesterday when Devon and that seventh grader crashed, right? How fast were they going?"

"Fast," Maria said. "They smashed into each other. Twenty miles an hour, easy." She said it with certainty, and then a small cold feeling moved through her, because she realized she had only seen the last half second of it. The word smashed had come from her father, who had asked about the collision at breakfast. How fast were they going when they smashed into each other? That was what he'd said.

She raised her hand. "Mr. Ruiz, can I survey the class in the next ten minutes? For my experiment."

"Make it quick," he said, and shrugged as if he expected nothing.

Maria stood at the front with her notebook. Half the class had been in the hallway yesterday and half had only heard about it. She split them. To the window side she asked, "How fast were the two boys going when they hit each other?" To the door side she asked, "How fast were they going when they smashed into each other?" She kept her voice flat for both questions, like a scientist installing a sensor and walking away without touching it.

The door side shouted numbers at her. Twenty, twenty-five, one kid said thirty. The window side mumbled. Ten, maybe twelve. Nobody on that side went above fifteen. She wrote the two columns on the board, and the room went quiet in a way that felt almost sinister, everyone staring at the gap between them. Same collision, same boys, same tiled hallway. Two different sets of numbers.

"There was a real study," Marcus said suddenly, pulling out his phone. "My mom talks about it. 1974, Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer." He read slowly off the screen. "People who were asked how fast cars smashed into each other gave higher speed estimates than people asked about cars that hit."

"Say that again," Maria said, and he did. She checked her columns against it and her neck went hot. The direction matched. Her question, her one changed word, had pushed the numbers up, exactly as it had pushed her own memory up at breakfast.

Mr. Ruiz checked the clock. "Two minutes. So what's your topic, Maria?"

"People don't just remember things," she said. "The question itself gets into the memory. I know because my dad asked me if those boys smashed, and I was sure it was twenty miles an hour until five minutes ago." She tapped the board. "Same hallway. Same crash. The word did that."

Marcus looked at her column, then at his own door-side estimate, and raised his hand to lower his number.

The line outside the Riverside Pavilion stretched past the bakery and around the corner, and Raphael had been standing in it since six in the morning. Ahead of him, a man in a gray jacket moved down the queue, saying the same words to every group he passed. "Box office tickets, eighty apiece. Limited number. Cash only."

Raphael counted his money again. Fifty-two dollars, saved from mowing lawms all June. The box office price was supposed to be forty, but the sign taped to the window that morning had changed things: "Limited tickets available." When he'd bought tickets for this same band last year, the line had been short and the seats had sat empty in whole rows.

"Eighty," the man in gray said again, closer now. "Going fast."

Behind Raphael, two girls were whispering. "My mom did this with chips last month," one of them said. "Her favorite brand jumped to six dollars a bag, so she just bought the store brand instead. It does the same job, basically. She calls it a substitute." Her friend laughed. "Your mom and her economics." Raphael turned the word over in his mind. Substitute. A similar thing that does the same job.

He looked down the street. Three blocks away, a smaller theater had put up a banner that morning: a tribute band, same songs, same night, tickets fifteen dollars, and the sign under the window read "Plenty of seats available." The line there had only eleven people in it. As he watched, a boy from the concert queue peeled off and walked toward it. Then a couple followed. Then a family of four. It was contagious, the way the little line began to grow while the big one barely shrank.

Raphael's heart pounded. If he stayed, the man in gray might sell out before he reached the window, and he'd have nothing. If he left, he'd see the songs performed, but not the real band. He made himself wait ten more minutes, watching, testing his idea. The concert line stayed long and hungry. The tribute line kept growing. When the man in gray shouted "Last four tickets, eighty each," four hands shot up at the front, and that settled it.

He walked the three blocks, bought a ticket for fifteen, and still had thirty-seven dollars left. Ahead of him in the new line, the two girls from the concert queue had appeared, and the one who'd talked about chips grinned at him. "You switched too?"

"Substitute," Raphael said, holding up his ticket.

The doors opened, and the line surged forward.

The morning after Tuesday's practice, Simon's legs ached so much that walking down the bleacher steps felt like stepping onto two bricks. Marco, who caught for the team, climbed up beside him rubbing his shoulder.

"It's all that lactic acid," Marco said. "It builds up when we work hard."

Simon thought about that while they took infield drills. Practice had ended at five o'clock yesterday. His legs had felt fine at dinner, fine at bedtime, fine when he brushed his teeth this morning. The soreness had shown up today, more than a day later. If something was building up during practice, it seemed like it should hurt right after practice, not the next morning. He decided to run a test on himself. At the end of warmups he did ten full sprints from foul pole to foul pole, harder than he ever worked in a game, and then he waited.

An hour after the sprints, sitting in the dugout with his glove on his knee, he flexed his calves. Nothing hurt. He could feel his pulse in them, and they were warm, but the soreness was not there yet. The next morning it arrived, right on schedule, in both legs at once. It was the same pattern as Tuesday. Whatever was making his muscles sore, it was not still sitting in his legs from the exercise, because an hour after he stopped, everything felt normal. On Thursday he found Marco by the equipment shed, pumping up a flat football that someone had left in the bin. The pump handle squeaked with every stroke, and the ball grew round and firm with each push of air.

"Marco, I checked," Simon said. "I did sprints yesterday and felt fine an hour later. If lactic acid were the problem, it would have to stick around a whole day to make me sore this morning. It doesn't. It goes back to normal levels within about an hour after you exercise."

Marco stopped pumping and squinted at him. "Then what's making my shoulder hurt?"

"I don't know yet. But it isn't that."

Coach Alvarez walked past and told them practice was starting, and whether Marco's throw to second was late or on time, that was her call, though Marco muttered that the whole strike zone was subjective anyway, so why bother arguing. The football, fat with air now, sat on the bench forgotten. Simon picked it up, tossed it once in his hand, and handed it back to Marco.

"Hold onto this," he said. "We're testing your shoulder next."

The trumpet felt like a brick in Anthony's hands, and Mr. Ruiz had already called his name twice. "Measure sixteen, Anthony. From the top." The music classroom smelled like valve oil and old carpet, and the radiators radiated a dry heat that made his fingers stiff. Anthony lifted the horn, blew, and cracked the same high note he had cracked every Tuesday for three weeks.

Beside him, Priya slid her flute onto her lap and leaned over. "You practice, right?" she whispered. "Sunday night? Because you sound great for the first eight measures and then it all falls apart."

"Two hours," Anthony admitted. "Last night. The whole book." He had meant it as proof. Priya's eyebrows went up, and something about her face made him feel like he'd said the wrong thing even though he'd done more work than she had.

At lunch, Anthony sat with his sandwich untouched and thought it through like a math problem. Priya practiced every single day, he knew that, because she'd told the whole section once. Maybe twenty minutes a day. He did two hours in one night. Two hours was six times twenty minutes, so his total time was way more than hers, and yet she played the solo and he cracked notes. Same amount of practice should mean same result. Unless the total wasn't the thing that mattered. Unless the spreading out was the thing. He turned his milk carton around and around. There was only one way to find out.

He made a chart on the back of his science folder and ruled it into small boxes: fifteen minutes before school, ten at night, every day until the next Tuesday. He didn't tell Priya, in case it didn't work. His little sister, Rosa, pounded the piano keys while he practiced, so he started leaving a bag of pretzels on the bench for her, and she settled into playing her own made-up songs at a gentler volume, which helped them both.

The first few days felt slow. He kept missing the same leap in measure sixteen, and his grandfather's old trumpet, a dented brass alloy that had survived two wars and one fall down a staircase, seemed to laugh at him. But on Thursday something odd happened. He picked up the horn, cold, no warm-up except a few long tones, and his fingers found the fingering for the high note before his brain did. He hadn't drilled it harder. He had just... come back to it, again and again, letting each short session do a little work while he slept, ate, walked to school.

On Tuesday, Mr. Ruiz raised his baton. "Measure sixteen. Anthony." The room went quiet. Priya gave him a tiny nod across the stand. Anthony took a breath, thought of nothing at all, and let his fingers go where they had learned to go. The high note came out round and silver, and the kid on trombone, who had declared trumpets obsolete ever since the school bought the low brass section new instruments, said, "Whoa," into his slide.

After class Priya caught him at the door. "So what changed?"

Anthony held up his folder, the chart with its rows of small checkmarks. "Same twenty minutes every day," he said. "Not two hours the night before. Turns out that's the whole trick." Priya grabbed a marker from her pocket and said, "Draw me one."

The photo went up at 9:02 on a Tuesday night: Willow doing her weird victory dance after finishing her science project, socks half off, face scrunched like a raisin. She had meant to send it only to Priya, but her thumb hit the whole group chat instead. Eighteen people. She deleted it within ten minutes, heart hammering, and then sat very still in her dark bedroom, watching the chat scroll on about weekend plans as if nothing had happened. She let herself breathe. Gone meant gone, she decided, and went to sleep.

At lunch the next day, Priya slid her phone across the table. "Look at this." In a different group chat, one Willow wasn't even in, someone had posted the photo with the caption "found this gem." Beneath it, people she barely knew were typing laughing faces and the word "iconic." Willow's stomach dropped. She had deleted it. How could it be here, in a place she couldn't reach?

"I don't get it," she said. "I took it down."

Priya shrugged. "Deleting a post removes it from your page, but anyone who already took a screenshot still has it."

Willow stared at the screen. So that was the rule. It wasn't magic; it was a copy, sitting in someone's camera roll, free to travel anywhere. She scrolled up and found the name of the account that had posted it: a boy named Marcus from her math class. She barely knew him. But the photo hadn't appeared out of nowhere, and somebody had to have passed it along.

That night she ran a test, the way she would for a lab. She posted a harmless picture of her cat to the group chat, waited exactly ten minutes, deleted it, and then texted Priya: "Did you screenshot it before it vanished?" Priya sent back a screenshot, timestamp and all, plus a smug message about how the cat deserved a citation for cuteness. Willow laughed, but her mind was working. The copy survived deletion. That was the whole answer. She couldn't unsend the dance photo, and envying people whose embarrassing moments never surfaced wouldn't help either. What she could do was be objective about the situation, like her science teacher kept saying: state the facts, then act.

The next morning she walked straight to Marcus's table in the cafeteria. "You posted my photo in the other chat," she said, keeping her voice level. "I'm not mad, but I want to know who sent it to you, because I deleted it and it still got around." Marcus looked uncomfortable, then held up his phone. "It was Priya. She thought it was hilarious. She said you'd figure it out eventually." Willow turned around. Priya was standing behind her, grinning, phone raised, and Willow's cat was already on the screen.

Riley pressed three tomato seeds into the dark soil of her aunt's farm and patted them down like she was tucking them into bed. She had claimed the plot behind the barn on day one, and by June the seedlings were knee-high, and by July she had green marbles swelling on every branch. Her plan was simple and enormous: sell her tomatoes at the farm stand by the road, next to her aunt's jam and eggs.

The trouble started at the stand on Saturday. A man in a sun hat picked up one of Riley's ripe red tomatoes, weighed it in his palm, and said, "You've got these in the wrong bin, kid. Tomatoes are fruit. They belong with the peaches."

"They're vegetables," Riley said. "They go in the salad, not the fruit bowl."

"Fruit," the man insisted. "Seeds on the inside. That's a fruit."

Riley's cousin Marisol leaned over the cash box. "Then cucumbers are fruit too. And peppers. And pumpkins."

The man laughed. "Pumpkins? Now you're being ridiculous."

Riley wanted to win this. More than that, she wanted to be right, which she had learned was not always the same thing. That night she borrowed her aunt's laptop and typed one question: is a tomato a fruit or a vegetable. The answer made her sit up straight. Botanically, a tomato was a fruit, full stop. But in 1893, the US Supreme Court had ruled in a case called Nix v. Hedden that for import taxes, tomatoes counted as vegetables. She read it twice, then read it to Marisol over the phone.

"Nix v. Hedden," Marisol repeated slowly, like she was chewing it. "So the Court decided taxes, not lunch."

"So both of us were right," Riley said, "and both of us were wrong. Wait till Sun Hat Man hears this."

Sunday morning, Riley made two signs on cardboard, testing her idea before anyone could argue. One read FRUIT, SCIENTIFICALLY SPEAKING. The other read VEGETABLE, ACCORDING TO THE SUPREME COURT. She set them on either side of the tomato bin with an arrow pointing between them. Her aunt walked by, paused, and said, "Very sophisticated display. Now wash your hands, stand hygiene, customers are watching you handle their food."

The man in the sun hat came back for more tomatoes. He read the signs, read them again, and rubbed his jaw. "Huh. I was scientifically right."

"And I was legally right," Riley said. "The Court said they could enforce the tax that way. So the vegetable side wins for money, and the fruit side wins for science."

He bought two pounds and told two other customers on his way out, loudly, that he had lost an argument to an eleven-year-old and enjoyed it. By noon the tomato bin was empty, and Marisol was drawing a third sign that said SOLD OUT, SCIENTIFICALLY AND LEGALLY. Riley ran back to the garden to count what was still ripening on the vines.

"Ten more turning red," she called. "Tell everyone to come back next Saturday."

The bleachers in the gym were packed, and Victor sat on the folding chair on stage with his number pinned to his shirt, trying not to tap his foot. He had made it to the final three, and the word that had just knocked out the girl beside him was "colleague." Victor would have missed it too, two weeks ago. Back then he had been furious about words like "bite" and "knife," where the e sat at the end saying nothing at all, and he'd been ready to postpone the whole bee and quit.

Then he found a dusty book in the school library, a frugal little paperback with a cracked spine, and everything changed. He read that between about 1400 and 1700, English vowel sounds changed in the Great Vowel Shift, and it happened after spellings had started to become fixed. That was why the letters stopped matching the sounds. Victor tested it on a napkin at lunch, listing "bite," "mate," "hope," and realizing the pattern ran through half his list. The letters weren't broken; they were holding still while the sounds moved underneath them, like a fence on a shifting frontier. His friend Deja had leaned over his shoulder in the cafeteria and said, "The Great Vowel Shift? Never heard of it," and he'd shown her the book.

Now the judge said, "Victor, your word is 'misled.'" Victor's first instinct was M-I-S-L-E-D, because that was how it looked on the page. But he paused. Under the old pattern, that e would have made the i long, and nobody said "mizzled." The spelling was a trap from the same old shift, a fossil of how things used to sound. He thought it through again. "M, I, S, L, E, D." The judge nodded, and Victor let out a breath.

Two rounds later, only he and a tall kid named Rashad were left. Rashad got "biscuit" and spelled it cleanly. Then it was Victor again. "Your word is 'conscientious.'" Victor closed his eyes for a second. He used to think spelling was just memorizing nonsense, that some words were simply unfair. Now he saw each weird letter as a clue, something left behind by sound that had drifted away centuries before anyone alive was born. The c before the t, the tricky ious ending; he walked through it piece by piece.

"C-O-N-S-C-I-E-N-T-I-O-U-S." The gym went quiet while the judge checked the card, and then her voice rang out across the basketball court: "That is correct."

Rashad grinned and shook Victor's hand. "Rematch next year," he said. "But you have to tell me where you learned all that."

Camille counted her coins twice at the Saturday farmers' market, because the tomato seedlings had to go in the ground before the end of the weekend, and she only had six dollars. "How much for two?" she asked the man at the plant table.

"Three dollars, but I have to warn you," he said. "These are the same variety your mom bought last year, and hers didn't do well."

"My tomatoes got brown spots and fell over," Camille said. "All of them. In the back corner, by the fence."

The man rubbed his chin. "You plant tomatoes in that corner every year?"

"Every year. It's the sunniest spot. What else would I put there?" She waited, but he only shrugged and handed her the seedlings, so she paid and carried them home, frowning.

That evening, she sat on the porch steps and thought about her grandmother's farm, which she visited two summers ago. She remembered walking between the long rows while her grandmother pointed. "Tomatoes here this year, beans here, cabbage there," her grandmother had said. "Next summer, they orbit around, each row takes a turn somewhere new." Camille had thought it sounded tedious, all that moving and mapping. Now she wondered why her grandmother bothered.

On Sunday morning, Camille knocked on Mrs. Petrov's door, because Mrs. Petrov had the best garden on the street. "Can I ask you something?" Camille said. "If somebody plants tomatoes in the same corner every year, and they start getting sick, is it the corner's fault?"

Mrs. Petrov set down her watering can. "It could be. My father rotated crops, always, so the same plant family was never grown in the same spot year after year. He said it keeps the soil from making trouble." She tilted her head. "You know what family tomatoes are in?"

"No."

"Same family as peppers. Not the same as beans, or carrots, or lettuce."

Camille walked home fast, carrying the idea like a full bucket. She dug up the wilted tomato stems from the corner and dropped them in the compost pile, where the decomposers would break them down into dark, crumbly soil over the winter. Then she planted her new seedlings in the middle bed, where the beans had grown last summer. It wasn't the sunniest spot, but she could see it from her window, and she marked the corner with a stick.

All through June she measured the plants with a ruler and drew a map of the yard in her notebook. In the top corner she wrote "tomatoes, last year, sick." In the middle bed she wrote "tomatoes, this year," and every week the number of green dots on her sketch grew. On the last day of school, she counted fourteen little hard green tomatoes hanging from healthy stems.

She ran inside to get her brother. "Come look," she said. "And next spring, the tomatoes move again."

Luca carried four bean plants into the gymnasium, balancing the pots against his chest while his display board flapped in his other hand. Behind the folding table marked "Project 23," his heart was pounding. He had spent six weeks spraying three of the plants with different amounts of his homemade fertilizer, measuring their heights every single day, and his reputation as the kid who could actually finish what he started was on the line here.

The first judge, a woman with a clipboard, stopped at his table and tilted her head. "Interesting. Three plants, three fertilizer amounts. But which one would have grown like that anyway?" Luca opened his mouth and then closed it. He hadn't thought about that question at all. He looked at his data chart, the neat columns of numbers he was so proud of, and realized they showed nothing to compare against.

While the judge moved on, Luca sank onto a folding chair. His friend Priya leaned over from the next table, where her project on endangered wetland birds was spread out in a fan of photographs. "You look like your whole project just embarrassed you in public," she said. He explained the problem, and she squinted at his plants. "My cousin did a project like this. She kept one plant that got nothing new at all. Same sun, same water, just no fertilizer."

Luca stared at the fourth pot still sitting on his windowsill at home, the one he had grown but ignored because it got no treatment. "A control group," he said slowly. "It gets no change at all, so you can compare the tested plants against it." He grabbed his phone, texted his mom, and fifteen minutes later she walked in carrying the pot with a sheepish wave. Luca rearranged his table, putting the untreated plant right in the center, and added a new column to his chart in green marker: the heights of the plant that had grown on plain water alone.

When the judge came back around, Luca walked her through all four plants. "This one got no fertilizer," he said, tapping the center pot. "So the others are being compared against it, not just against each other." She made a note on her clipboard and gave him a small nod, the kind that meant something. Later, when Mr. Delgado announced the ribbon winners, Luca's name was third on the list for honorable mention. Priya squeezed his shoulder. "Next year," she said, "we start with the control group on day one." Luca grinned and slid the green marker back into his pocket.

Maeva stood in the kitchen with one sock on the tile and one bare foot in the air, frozen mid-step. The school dance was in three hours, and she had a problem with a name: Daniel Okafor. He'd asked her, she'd said yes, and then he'd texted, "Actually I don't know how to dance with a partner. Sorry." She'd stared at the phone so long her mom asked if the screen was broken.

"It's not broken," Maeva said. "It's just wrong."

Her little brother Theo, who had recently convinced Dad to install a basketball hoop over the garage door, was dribbling a ball against the refrigerator. "Dances are controversial anyway," he said. "Jayden says you have to hold a girl's hand and it's a hygiene hazard."

"You don't know anything."

"I know you're standing on one foot."

She put her foot down. Then she picked up her phone again, not for Daniel's text, but to search. Last summer at the community picnic she'd seen everybody from grandmas to six-year-olds doing the same steps in rows, and nobody had seemed paired up. She found a video from the picnic and watched it twice. Every person faced the same way, toward the picnic table with the lemonade. Every person repeated the same set of steps, over and over, a grapevine to the right, a clap, a stomp, a quarter turn. Nobody touched anybody. She tested her idea right there on the kitchen tile: she followed along, stumbled, tried again, and by the fourth repeat her feet knew the pattern without her watching.

"Whoa," Theo said. "What's that?"

"It's called a line dance," Maeva said. "A whole group does the same steps, facing the same direction, and you don't need a partner at all."

"Prove it."

She held out her hand for the ball, set it on the counter, and started the video from the beginning. "Just copy me." Theo knocked over a chair on the grapevine and laughed so hard he missed the clap, but on the second run he made it all the way to the quarter turn. On the third run they did it without the video, both facing the window, both stomping at the same moment.

At the dance, the gym was hot and loud and half the seventh grade stood along the wall like wallpaper. Daniel was there, arms crossed, alone. Maeva took a breath, walked over, and said, "You don't need a partner. You just need about four steps. Watch my feet."

The DJ started a song with a beat she knew. She stepped out onto the floor, faced the stage, and began.

"Like this?" Daniel said, two beats behind her.

"Just like that."

Elliot had exactly one week to figure out the difference between simple and compound interest before the fifth-grade math fair, and his poster board sat blank on his desk like a desolate white tundra. His want was simple enough: the prize was a real twenty-five-dollar savings bond, and his older sister Dana had won it two years ago. If a Reyes sibling won twice in a row, their grandfather promised to frame both certificates side by side in the hallway. Elliot wanted that wall.

The teacher, Ms. Okafor, had given them each a pretend bank account with one hundred dollars. "Simple interest pays on the principal only," she said, and left it at that, because the whole point of the fair was that they figure out the rest themselves. That was the dilemma: Elliot could calculate simple interest easily, five percent of one hundred dollars every year for five years, but compound interest did something strange on his calculator. Each year the interest payment grew a little, even though he added nothing.

He asked his friend Ruby, who was building a volcano and had her own problem, since her baking soda had run out and the fair was Friday. "Can I borrow your math brain for five minutes if I let you use my poster paint?" she said. Elliot agreed, but Ruby only shrugged at the numbers. "Mine stays the same every year. Yours goes up. That's all I've got."

The answer came in an unexpected place. Dana had written him a note and slipped it into his backpack, since she was away at a track meet and couldn't help him in person. "Dear genius-in-training," the note read, "Grandpa took me to the bank yesterday and I watched them post my interest. It grew from last year even though I deposited nothing, and the teller smiled and said compound interest is paid on the principal plus all the interest already earned, so the interest itself starts earning interest. Thought that might matter to you. Don't spend my paint. Dana." Elliot read it three times under his desk, then went back to his calculator with his heart drumming. One hundred dollars, five percent, five years. Simple gave him twenty-five dollars of interest. Compound gave him a little over twenty-seven, and the extra came from the interest earning its own interest, exactly as Dana's note said.

He raised his hand to clarify one thing with Ms. Okafor, only whether he could show both columns side by side, and she nodded. After school, Ruby knocked on his door holding a new box of baking soda her dad had bought, and a jar of glitter paint for him anyway. They worked at his kitchen table until dark, her volcano bubbling in the sink, his poster filling with two climbing bars, one straight and one curving slowly upward.

At the fair on Friday, the judge stood at Elliot's table for a long time, tracing the two lines with her finger. "Which one would you want?" she asked.

Elliot pointed at the curve. "That one. The interest gets paid interest too."

The seatbelt dug into Maya's chest in a way it never used to, and she kept tugging at it while Dad drove toward the mall. Everything about her felt slightly rearranged lately, like someone had moved the furniture inside her body overnight. She was thirteen now, and Priya's birthday pool party was on Saturday, and Maya had one thing on her mind that she couldn't say out loud: she hadn't gotten her period yet, and it seemed like everyone at school already had.

"Dad, can we swing by Priya's house on the way?" she asked. "Just for ten minutes?"

Dad checked the mirror. "Your brother has soccer at four. You're cutting it close."

"Ten minutes," Maya said. "I'll time it myself."

In the back seat, her little brother Leo groaned. He wanted to stop at the game store to trade in two old cartridges, and their errands were already piling up while the afternoon dwindled away. "You always get your stops," he complained. "I never get mine."

"Because your stops involve forty minutes of arguing with the guy at the counter," Dad said, but he turned onto Priya's street anyway, which made Leo slump against the window in defeat.

Priya dragged Maya up to her room, where the walls were covered with posters and her two older sisters' old trophies still sat on the shelf. "You look like you're on a mission," Priya said.

"I have a question, and you're the only person I can ask." Maya sat on the bed. "Your sisters. Did they get their periods at the same age?"

Priya blinked, then grinned. "That's your mission? No. Nina was twelve, almost exactly. Dia was fourteen. My mom said the same thing happened with her and her sister." She pulled a folded printout from a drawer, some school project. "There's this big CDC survey, it found the median age is about twelve. But Dia still counts as normal, because there's a really wide normal range around it."

Maya stared at the number. Twelve. She'd been doing quiet math for weeks, assuming there was a deadline she'd already missed. But a median wasn't a deadline, was it? It was just a middle. Half before, half after, all of it normal. Her logic had been wrong from the start, and the wrongness felt wonderful.

"So there's no single right age," she said slowly, testing the idea like a loose tooth. "There's just a middle and a spread."

"Exactly," Priya said. "Nina worried she was late at eleven. Dia worried she was weird at fourteen. Same family, same parents, totally different."

From downstairs, Dad honked twice. Maya hugged Priya fast, ran to the car, and buckled the rebellious belt without fighting it this time. Leo was still sulking about his game store.

"Hey, Leo," she said. "Want me to argue with the counter guy for you? I'm in the mood to win something."

He sat up straight. "You can try."

Kaylee sat on the crackly paper of the exam chair and stared at the chart across the room, where the third line had gone soft and blurry no matter how hard she squinted. The optometrist swung a heavy metal machine in front of her face and clicked lenses into it, one after another. "Better or worse?" she kept asking, and each time Kaylee answered, the world sharpened a little more. When the chair sank with a hiss, Kaylee glanced down and saw a small brass valve on the side, the kind that let air or fluid in and out. The optometrist must have noticed her looking, because she said, "Handy, right? I can lower it for kids and raise it back for adults."

In the frame room afterward, Kaylee tried on pair after pair while her mom watched from a stool by the window. Everything was too big, too round, or too much like something a grandmother would wear. Finally she found a thin wire pair with purple at the hinges, and the optician said they were titanium, durable enough to survive being dropped, which mattered, because Kaylee dropped things constantly.

"These are the ones," she said, turning her head in the little mirror. Then a thought hit her so hard she said it out loud. "Wait. What did people do before glasses existed? Like, in ancient times? Everyone who couldn't see just... couldn't read?"

The optician hummed and straightened a display of cases. "Well, glasses weren't actually that old an invention, if you think about it. The earliest eyeglasses were made in central Italy, around 1290."

"Thirteen ninety?" Kaylee said, gripping the mirror's edge.

"Twelve ninety. Central Italy."

Kaylee did the math, and the math made her dizzy. People had been writing things down for thousands of years before that, and for most of that time, anyone with eyes like hers would have had to hold a page practically against her nose, or give up entirely. She began to elaborate her theory out loud: that must be why some old paintings showed scholars holding books at arm's length, or squinting like she did at the whiteboard last Tuesday when she copied the homework wrong and got a zero she didn't deserve. That zero was the reason she was here. She'd spent a month blaming the teacher's handwriting before admitting the real cause was hiding behind her own eyeballs, invisible until she finally tested the idea by sitting in the front row and getting everything right.

"So for thousands of years," she said slowly, "everyone who needed glasses just didn't get any."

Her mom came over and rested a hand on her shoulder. "And now you do. That's something."

The optician slid the purple-hinged pair into a case and wrote the pickup date on a slip. "Next Thursday, after school."

Kaylee folded the slip into her pocket, right next to the crumpled zero she'd kept as evidence.

"Thursday," she said. "I'm going to see everything."

Jacob wanted the good table, the one by the window with the kettle and the plate of samosas, and the problem was that Table One had already claimed it. The community centre's heritage night had split into four tables for the games, and the split had been done by Mr. Okafor pulling names out of a cereal bowl, which felt fair and turned out not to be.

By seven thirty, Table Two, Jacob's table, was chanting "Two, two, two" at Pictionary. Table Three had a secret handshake nobody could have learned in two hours, because two hours was all that had existed of Table Three. Table Four had started calling Table One "the window hogs." Jacob had been dumped into Table Two between Priya, who was telling everyone about her grandmother's Diwali lamps with meticulous, loving detail, and a kid named Marcus who claimed his family invented barbecue, which Jacob doubted but let slide.

"We've known each other since six o'clock," Jacob said to Priya. "Why are we cheering like we're a tribe?"

"Because we're Table Two," she said, as if that explained anything.

It bothered him the way a loose tooth bothers you. He had read something once, in his sister's psychology book, about a man named Tajfel who ran experiments where people favoured members of their own group even when the groups had been assigned completely at random. Jacob had skipped past it at the time. Now he watched Marcus guard the felt-tip pens from Table Three like they were family heirlooms, and thought: that's us. We're the experiment. So he tested it. He stood on a chair and announced that the tables were random, that Mr. Okafor had drawn every name out of a bowl, that Table Two was not destiny.

It did not help. "So what," Marcus said. "We're still the best random table." Table Two applauded him. Jacob climbed down, the embarrassment warm in his ears, and considered the possibility that knowing about a thing does not switch it off.

But Priya had gone quiet, and when the samosa plate came out, she carried two over to the kids at Table One and asked what was in their dishes, and they turned out to be things their grandmothers made, with stories attached, and Jacob followed her. Mr. Okafor wandered by and tried to incorporate the moment into a speech about community, and Jacob said, "We're just eating, sir." The window table had room after all. Marcus arrived last, plate out, and said, "This doesn't make us friends."
"We're not tables," said Priya. "We're just hungry people near a window."
Marcus bit into a samosa. "Okay," he said. "That one's mine."

The trumpet wasn't working out, so Hailey switched to the flute, and now she had a new problem: reading music. She sat in the corner of the community center music room with a folded sheet of paper, glaring at the five lines and the fancy swirl at the start of every line. Her friend Marisol came over and dropped into the chair beside her.

"You look like the paper insulted you," Marisol said.

"I can find middle C. That's it. Then everything else is guessing." Hailey tapped the swirl. "And this thing just sits there like it's decoration."

Marisol leaned in. "My cousin plays piano. She calls that the G clef."

"The what?"

"G clef. That's the other name for it."

Hailey frowned at the symbol. A clef called G should mean something. She grabbed a pencil and copied the swirl onto her notebook, big and sloppy. Then she laid her flute sheet next to it and traced the curl slowly with her pencil tip, the way you'd trace a maze. The swirl looped around, dipped down, and curled back up, and where it curled it wrapped around the second line from the bottom. She checked her beginner book's note chart. The note on that line was G.

"No way," she whispered. The clef wasn't decoration. It was a marker, curling around the exact line where G lived, like a ring on a finger.

She tested it. G on the line, one space above was A, the line above that was B, and so on up the ladder. She played the little exercise from her book, and the notes came out in the right order for the first time. She played it again, faster, and grinned so wide her cheeks hurt.

Marisol pointed at the door. "Little kids are coming for vaccine day. The nurse is setting up in the big room, so we have ten more minutes before they kick us out."

"Ten minutes is plenty," Hailey said. "It's not trivial to me. This was the whole wall in my way."

A small boy in a dinosaur shirt peeked into the music room while waiting for his shot, looking scared. Marisol waved him over. Hailey held up her notebook, showed him the swirl, and traced the curl around the second line. "See the loop? It's holding one spot so you never get lost." The boy forgot to be nervous long enough to trace it with his own finger.

When the nurse called his name, he walked out taller, and Marisol hurried after him with his jacket. Hailey packed up her flute, but she tore the notebook page out first and pressed it flat inside her book, the page she knew she would cherish on every practice day to come.

"Same time Thursday?" Marisol called from the doorway.

"Bring your cousin's number," Hailey said, tucking the flute under her arm. "I have questions."

Alyssa carried the crate into the kitchen the way her mother had carried her when she was little, slow and careful, like the thing inside might break. Inside was a small brown dog with floppy ears, adopted that morning from the shelter, and Alyssa had already decided his name was Biscuit. She set the crate down, opened the door, and waited while he crept out and sniffed the baseboards, the table leg, her sneaker.

"You're home now," she told him.

Her friend Marisol came over after lunch to see him, carrying a bag of trail mix. They took Biscuit out to the backyard, where he chased a fallen leaf in circles until he tripped over his own feet. Marisol laughed so hard she had to sit down on the porch step. When Biscuit trotted over and put his chin on her knee, she reached into the bag.

"No, wait," Alyssa said, grabbing her wrist. Something was nagging at her, a memory she couldn't quite pin down. "Hold on. I read something."

"About trail mix?"

"About one thing in it. Give me a second." She closed her eyes and tried to interpret the fuzzy memory, the way you might squint at a smudged whiteboard. She had been in the waiting room at the shelter, flipping through a pamphlet while her mom filled out paperwork. There had been a list. She remembered the word "never."

The flashback came clear: fluorescent lights, a plastic chair digging into her back, a page with a box drawn around it. Grapes and raisins can cause kidney damage in dogs, the box had said, so they should never be given as treats. She had skimmed it then, thinking it was boring fine print. Now it felt like she'd read a warning label after already lighting the match.

"Raisins," she said out loud. "They're in trail mix. Grapes and raisins can cause kidney damage in dogs, so they should never be given as treats. That was in the pamphlet."

Marisol looked at the bag. "It's just raisins, not grapes."

"It said both. Grapes and raisins." Alyssa picked up the bag, walked it inside, and came back with a jar of peanut butter and a spoon instead. Biscuit licked the spoon clean and then tried to eat the spoon.

The rest of the afternoon Alyssa watched him closely, wondering how a thing as small as a raisin could matter so much, and how many other invisible rules were out there waiting. What else could hurt him that she hadn't read about yet? She made a list on the fridge: peanut butter, yes; raisins, no; grapes, no. Then she added a question mark, because there had to be more.

That night she looked up dogs and chocolate too, and the answer made her glad Marisol hadn't brought brownies. Biscuit curled up on her bedroom floor, mostly asleep but twitching, his paws moving like he was running somewhere. Dogs aren't nocturnal, she thought, so why was he awake? She wrote that down as her next question. Then Biscuit sighed, rolled over, and slept.

Lily sat cross-legged on Maya's bedroom floor with Maya's phone balanced on her knees, tapping through photos from Saturday. There was the one of Maya at the ice cream place, grinning with a double scoop. There was the one at the mall fountain. And there was the one Lily had taken of Maya outside Maya's own front door, because Maya had insisted the lighting was perfect.

"Send me the fountain one," Lily said, then stopped. "Wait. How many people can see these?"

"Just us. And my cousins. And probably the group chat." Maya flopped backward onto her pillow. "And that game I play, Frost Fox. It kind of posts stuff sometimes."

"Frost Fox posts your photos?"

"No, no. It posts where I am. Like, 'Maya unlocked the Glacier Zone at Maple Mall!' My aunt commented on it from two states away. She said, weren't you supposed to be at soccer?"

Lily scrolled to the game. A little map pin blinked beside a picture of a fox in a scarf, and next to the fox, Maya's last three locations were listed like trophies. Lily thought about the coyote that had wandered into their neighborhood last winter, how it had seemed to hibernate somewhere unseen all day and appear only at dusk, always knowing exactly which trash cans to visit. Someone had told her the coyote followed patterns, not luck. This felt like that, but backwards: the fox was following Maya.

"Can I check something?" Lily asked. She opened the phone's settings and hunted through screens until she found a list of apps with little arrows beside them. She recognized one arrow right away, because her dad had pointed at his own phone once and said, "That arrow means an app knows where you are." She tapped Frost Fox.

Three choices sat on the screen. Never. While using the app. Always.

"It's on Always," Lily said slowly. "That means it knew where you were even when you weren't playing."

Maya sat up so fast her ponytail whipped around. "You can pick?"

"You can pick for every app, one by one." Lily turned the phone so Maya could see. "My phone asks me the same thing. I always hit Always because I don't read the box. I just want the game to start."

"That's why Frost Fox knew I skipped soccer," Maya said, sounding both horrified and delighted. She jabbed the screen and switched the game to While Using. Then, defiant, she switched it to Never, just to watch the little map pin blink out.

Later, Lily texted her from home: did the fox die? Maya sent back a photo of Frost Fox wearing a blindfold, standing in an empty snowfield, with the caption "he asks where u at and I say none of ur business." Lily laughed out loud, then opened her own phone and went down her list of apps, one by one, arrow by arrow.

The last one, before bed, was a flashlight app. Always.

She stared at it. "You don't even know where I am," she told it, and pressed Never.

The train from upstate pulled into the dilapidated platform fifteen minutes late, and Grandpa Ray stepped down carrying one battered suitcase and a paper bag of maple candies. Vincent had been waiting for an hour, holding a sign he'd made that said WELCOME GRANDPA in marker. He waved it so hard the paper tore at the corner.

"I thought we'd lose you to that delay," Vincent said, grabbing the suitcase handle.

"Trains run when trains run," Grandpa said. "No use opposing it. Where's your mother's car?" On the way home, Vincent noticed Grandpa hadn't touched the water bottle Mom had packed, and he noticed it again at dinner, and again the next morning when the orange juice sat untouched beside Grandpa's plate.

On Tuesday they went to the park, and it was the hottest day of the week so far. Grandpa sat on a bench in the shade while Vincent did three trips across the monkey bars. When Vincent came back, dripping, Grandpa's face was flushed and his eyes looked heavy, but he said he was fine. Vincent fetched two waters from the fountain anyway and pressed one into his grandfather's hand. "You haven't had anything to drink since breakfast," he said. "I've been counting."

"I'd tell you if I were thirsty," Grandpa said, but he drank the whole bottle, and then a second one Vincent brought back. Ten minutes later he sat up straighter and said the bench felt cooler, which it didn't, because the sun hadn't moved. Vincent made an inference from that: something was off in Grandpa's own alarm system, not in the day itself. He called his mom at work and asked one careful question, and she said yes, the body's sense of thirst weakens with age, so older people can become dehydrated without ever feeling thirsty. Vincent hung up and made a decision on the spot.

For the rest of the week, he carried a water bottle everywhere and refilled Grandpa's glass at every meal without being asked, and he set a timer on his watch that buzzed every hour. Grandpa grumbled about being managed, but by Friday he was walking the whole loop around the pond without stopping, planning to teach Vincent chess that evening and to beat him, he claimed, in under twenty moves.

On Saturday morning, back at the same train station, Grandpa handed Vincent a fresh bottle of water before boarding. "For the walk home," he said. "You've got the habit now. Keep it." Then he stepped up onto the train, and Vincent stood holding the cold bottle until the last car disappeared around the curve.

Alexis had spent every summer at Abuela's house since she was six, and every summer the streets had felt like a map she carried in her head. This summer Abuela had moved to a new neighborhood, and the map was gone. On the first morning, Abuela handed her a canvas bag. "Take these to the donation bin on Calle Rosa," she said. "And take the phone. In case."

Alexis did not take the phone. She had spent the school year failing Spanish, and she had decided the class was useless, so she left the phone on the table to prove she could manage without it. She walked three blocks carrying the bag of clothes she was meant to donate, and then the streets stopped matching anything Abuela had told her. A man was sweeping in front of a shop with green awnings. She stopped, and the dilemma was simple: ask in English and get nowhere, or try the Spanish she had decided she didn't have.

"¿Dónde está Calle Rosa?" she said.

The man answered fast, too fast, and then slowed down. "Sí. La primera calle a la izquierda." He pointed with his broom, but the street split ahead into two left turns, and she could not tell which one he meant. She knew izquierda meant left, that much had stuck. But which left came first?

She tried the other half of what her teacher had drilled into them, the part she'd thought she'd never use: repeat it back. "¿La primera calle a la izquierda?"

"Sí," the man said. "La primera." He held up one finger.

Alexis looked at the split. One left turn was really just a driveway into a parking area. The other was an actual street with a sign. If the driveway didn't count as a street, then the real street was the first one, the one with the sign. She said "Gracias," walked on, and watched. The driveway went into a lot full of cars. It was not a street. The sign at the second left said Rosa.

The bin stood at the corner, next to a bakery. She pushed the clothes in, and the bakery door swung open behind her. It was the man with the broom, holding a paper bag. "You found it," he said in English. "First street on the left."

"You speak English?" Alexis said.

"All my life." He shrugged. "Your grandmother asked me to keep an eye out. She said you'd refuse the phone." He held up the bag. "Come, she ordered bread. And she says I make the best empanadas in the city, but that is subjective."

Alexis laughed and followed him down Rosa. On Monday, she decided, she would ask Abuela to speak only Spanish at breakfast. She took out her phrase list on the walk home and read it twice.

The group chat lit up at 4:02 on a Saturday: "Dude, why are you at GameStop? I thought you were broke." Brayden stared at his phone. He had told nobody he was going to the mall. He had left the house saying he was "going for a walk," which was technically true if you counted walking to the bus. He typed back, "how do u know where I am," and Marcus answered with a screenshot of a map. There was a little cartoon face on it, standing right on top of the GameStop dot at the Westfield mall. Brayden looked at the ceiling of the store, then at the exit, as if the answer might be floating somewhere between them.

"Bro, that's the Snap Map," Marcus wrote. "It shows your real-time location to your friends on a map." Brayden read it twice. Real-time. He thought about all the times he'd wandered around after school, killing time before his mom got home, and how somebody could have been watching a little cartoon version of him do it the whole while. Weird feeling, like discovering his shoes had been narrating his day out loud.

He decided to test it. It seemed like an inevitable part of figuring things out; you couldn't just panic, you had to run an experiment. His technique was simple: he would walk from GameSpot to the pretzel stand two stores down, and if the cartoon face moved too, then the map was tracking him right now, not showing some old, harmless record. He bought a pretzel he didn't even want, mostly for cover, and stood under the big yellow sign eating it with the concentration of a scientist. Marcus sent a new screenshot. The face was on the pretzel stand. "Enjoy your pretzel," he wrote, adding three crying-laughing faces.

Brayden nearly choked. "This is so creepy," he typed with one thumb, pretzel in the other hand. But another thought itched at him, the curious kind. If it knew where he was, who else could see it? Marcus was his friend, sure. But the settings had layers, he'd heard people mention "friends of friends" like it was nothing. Somewhere out there, maybe strangers were watching the little cartoon face eat its little cartoon pretzel. He wondered how many eyes a dot could collect before the dot's owner even noticed.

Back home, he dug into the app's settings until he found the map options and switched his sharing to Ghost Mode. Then he typed into the group chat, "ok new rule, if anyone knows where I am, it's because I told them." Marcus replied with a single face, the one wearing sunglasses, and a message: "Meet me at the arcade in ten?"

Brayden grabbed his jacket. "Bring quarters," he wrote back, and hit send.

The pitch counter app on Coach Alvarez's phone was still a prototype, a rough version his brother had built, and it glitched whenever someone's shadow crossed the screen. Brooklyn had volunteered to keep count on a clipboard instead, because she liked numbers better than surprises. She sat on the bench behind third base, marking every pitch Marcus threw, and by the fourth inning she had a funny feeling in her stomach. According to her sheet, Marcus had thrown sixty-one pitches. According to the coach's phone, he had thrown forty-four.

"Coach," she said quietly, jogging over between batters, "the app might be missing some. It freezes when it's sunny, and it was sunny all inning." She showed him her clipboard, where she had also noted which warmup tosses she had counted and which she had left out, so he could check her reasoning himself.

Coach Alvarez looked at the numbers, then at Marcus on the mound, then called time. He walked out, put a hand on the boy's shoulder, and led him back to the bench. "You're done for today, bud. You hit your pitch limit."

Marcus dropped his glove in the dust. "I don't even feel tired."

"That's not what the limit is about," Coach said. Brooklyn expected a lecture, but he just sat down next to Marcus and rubbed his own elbow like an old memory lived there.

Marcus stared at the dirt. "My cousin plays high school ball and throws a hundred pitches a game."

"That's because his bones finished growing," Marcus's older sister, Delia, called from the fence. She was a sophomore and had driven him to practice. "Yours haven't. You've still got growth plates, areas of growing cartilage near the ends of your bones. They're weaker than the bone around them, so young pitchers have limits on how much stress we can put on them." She shrugged. "I learned it in health class after I wrecked my shoulder swimming."

Brooklyn wrote that down too, in the margin, because it suddenly made everything make sense. The limits weren't about being tired. They were about something you couldn't see, working quietly inside a person's arm, and the pitch count was the only way to see it from the outside. She decided to test her idea. She flipped back through her sheets from the last three games and found that Marcus had also been participating in every throwing drill at every practice, on top of his games. When she showed him the tally, his face changed.

"Okay," he said. "Maybe I'll catch on drill days."

He picked up his glove, walked over to the cooler, and came back with two cups of water, handing one to Brooklyn before he sat down to watch the rest of the inning.
