Nora slid her vocabulary list across the desk and sighed. Fifteen word histories by Friday, and the definitions in the back of the book were so tedious that her eyes kept sliding off the page. The last word was "propaganda," and she almost skipped it, except that word had been bothering her all week. Marcus's posters for class president were everywhere, and something about them felt off, like a picture hung slightly crooked.

One poster said EVERYBODY'S CHOOSING MARCUS, with a long line of smiling kids drawn underneath it. Another called his opponent's ideas "dangerous" and "reckless," words that sounded exciting but meant nothing exactly. The biggest poster of all showed TJ, the eighth grader who could dunk, holding a thumbs-up: "TJ says Marcus is the real deal." Nora couldn't point to a single lie in any of them, and that was what made her uneasy. She flipped to the library's dictionary of word origins and ran her finger down the page.

There it was. The word came from a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622. Nora read the line twice, then copied it into her notebook. She raised her hand before she could talk herself out of it. "Mr. Reyes, I found where propaganda comes from. The Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622." A boy near the window snickered, and Nora felt her face go hot, but she kept going. "So it just meant spreading an idea around. It didn't start out as a bad word."

That night she tested a theory. If Marcus's posters worked by making people feel like everyone else had already decided, then a poster that pointed at the trick itself might break the spell. She made her own poster, plain and loud: "WHY DOES IT SAY EVERYBODY? ASK SOMEBODY." Underneath she drew a tiny panda chewing bamboo, with the caption "Pandas are herbivores. They eat facts, not hype." It was a strange joke, and she knew it, but she taped it up anyway, right between two of Marcus's.

By lunch, kids were standing in front of it. "What's a fact panda?" someone asked, and Nora said, "It only eats things that are actually true." Priya, who had been on the fence for a week, laughed and said, "Okay, that poster just got my vote for best poster. Marcus's are all sparkle and no sandwich." Marcus himself came down the hall, stopped, and read it twice. He peeled off his EVERYBODY'S CHOOSING MARCUS poster and looked at Nora over the top of it. "So what would a poster look like," he asked, "if I actually told people what I want to do?"

The pickup's air conditioner had given up somewhere outside Tucson, so George kept the window cracked and let the hot wind invade the car, ruffling the rainfall graphs he'd printed for his science project. His dad drove with two fingers on the wheel, and his little sister, Maya, had fallen asleep against a bag of trail mix.

"Ten inches of rain a year," George said to himself, looking at the bar graph for the Sonoran Desert. His pencil hovered over his notes. Back in September he had picked the rainforest for his project because it seemed easy, and he still wondered whether that had been a lazy choice. His teacher had called his last project "influential in all the wrong ways," which George had taken to mean that a poster with a hundred facts was somehow worse than a poster with ten.

He laid the two graphs side by side on his knees. The desert bars were stubby little bricks, barely ten inches stacked up across a whole year. The rainforest bars towered over them, taller than the page almost, month after month. Then he flipped to the third graph, the one that had confused him: a place called Antarctica, all white on the map, snow everywhere, temperatures below freezing half the year. Yet the bars were shorter even than Tucson's.

"There's no way that's a desert," George said out loud. Maya stirred. "It's snowing there right now, probably."

He decided to test it. His rule was simple: he would measure the total rainfall for each place, and if Antarctica came in under ten inches, the graph was calling it a desert whether he liked it or not. He added the bars with his pencil, carrying the ones, checking twice. Tucson: about eleven inches, just over. Antarctica: under ten. Under 250 millimeters, even. He looked at the temperature line and saw it drop below freezing while the rainfall stayed tiny.

"So it counts," he said. "A frozen desert."

Maya woke up long enough to say, "That's not a desert, that's a desert," pointing at the window, where saguaro cactuses stood along the roadside like green posts.

"Both are," George said, and showed her the graph.

They stopped at a pullout above a gray estuary, where the river met the sea and egrets stalked the mud. George got out, paper still in hand, and held both graphs up against the real desert, comparing. A raven landed on a rock nearby and screamed at him.

"Eleven inches," George told it, tapping the Tucson bar. "You're barely making it."

The drive to the coast had taken six hours, and Ethan had spent most of it reading the state park brochure he found in the glove box. His sister Maya said he was biased because he'd already decided the beach would be better than their trip to the mountains last summer. "You only like it because you found that sand dollar," she said. Ethan put the brochure in his back pocket anyway.

That evening a ranger named Ms. Okafor gathered everyone at the fire ring behind the dunes for a talk about national parks. "Whoever answers the final question wins a junior ranger badge," she announced. "The question comes in ten minutes, at sunset, so talk it over now." Ethan's dad immediately claimed he knew everything about parks. Maya said the first one was probably Yosemite. Dad shook his head and said the Grand Canyon, since it was the biggest.

Ethan didn't shout out a guess. Instead he thought about what he'd read in the brochure while the waves hissed in the dark behind them. There had been a whole paragraph about Yellowstone, and he was almost sure he'd seen a date there, and a president's name. It felt like remembering where he'd left his shoes: he couldn't see the page, but he could picture sitting on it. He tested the memory by saying it out loud under his breath. "March 1, 1872. Grant." It sounded like something he'd actually read, not something he'd invented.

The sun touched the water and Ms. Okafor held up her hand. "Final question. Yellowstone became the first national park in the United States on March 1, 1872, when which president signed it into law?" Dad whispered "Roosevelt." Maya whispered "Lincoln." Ethan raised his hand so fast he knocked over his cup of cocoa.

"Ulysses S. Grant," he said. Ms. Okafor smiled and pinned the badge to his jacket. Dad threw his hands up. "I was going to say Grant," he said. "You were going to say Roosevelt," said Maya. "I was collecting my thoughts," said Dad, and everyone laughed, even Ethan.

Walking back to the cabin, Maya poked the badge. "Fine, the beach trip is better than the mountains. For now." Ethan crouched by the tideline, where a dead crab was slowly starting to decompose among the kelp, and picked up a spiral shell. "Trade you," he said, holding it out. "Badge for shell." Maya snatched it and ran up the dunes shouting, "No take-backs!"

Tyler slid the meatballs across the table to his little cousin Ben before anyone asked, because Ben always wanted what was on the far plate. Their older sister Maren was home from college, and she was watching Ben stack the meatballs into a tower like she was counting them, a slow census of every meatball on the plate.

"Did you take Psych 101 this semester?" Mom asked her.

"Child development, actually," Maren said. "We just covered the Sally-Anne test. It was first used in 1985. Sally puts her marble in a basket and leaves. While she's gone, Anne moves the marble to a box. Then they ask the kid: where will Sally look for her marble?"

"Her basket," Ben said instantly, mouth full.

"Right," Maren said. "Kids from about age four usually say that. She'll look where she left it, not where it was moved while she was away." She grinned. "Ben just passed, sort of."

Tyler put down his fork. Ben was five, so that fit, but something about it bothered him. "Wait. He said basket because he heard the story. That doesn't prove anything."

"Prove what?" Maren said.

"That he understands Sally can believe something false. He might just be tracking where the marble started. That's a different rule."

Dad reached over and refilled Ben's milk without being asked, because Ben was reaching for it with meatball hands. "Sounds like somebody opposes his sister's whole field," he said.

"I'm not opposing it," Tyler said, though he kind of was. "I want to test it. For real."

"Go ahead, genius," Maren said.

Tyler waited until Ben was deep in the meatball tower. He took Ben's favorite green crayon, the one Ben had been drawing with all afternoon, and dropped it into his own cup, the durable blue plastic one that had survived three summers. Then he announced he was getting more bread and walked into the kitchen. Through the doorway he watched Maren quietly slide the crayon into Ben's backpack pocket.

When Tyler came back, he sat down and kept eating. Twenty minutes later, tower demolished, Ben started packing up his drawings. Tyler held his breath.

"Where my green crayon?" Ben scanned the table, then pointed straight at Tyler's blue cup. "Tyler take it."

Tyler's whole idea collapsed right there on the dinner table. He had expected Ben to hunt in the cup, the place the crayon had last been, and had built a little plan around proving Maren's class wrong, or at least proving his own theory right. Instead Ben had read the situation like a detective, tracking not the object but the cousin, and the cousin's history of borrowing things.

"You moved my plan," Tyler told Maren, but he was almost laughing.

"You lost your own test," she said. "Pass the bread."

Ben, meanwhile, had unzipped his backpack to grab his jacket and froze. "Hey. It's in here."

"Want the last meatball?" Tyler asked, sliding it onto Ben's plate. "You earned it, detective."

The lights went out while Alicia was watering her grandmother's tomato plants, and the porch swallowed itself into darkness so fast it felt like the evening had decided to accelerate. She stood in the backyard holding the dripping can, listening. No hum from the air conditioner. No glow from the kitchen window.

"Grandma?" she called, and heard shuffling inside. Her grandmother found her at the back door with a flashlight, its beam small and unimpressive next to the extravagant chandelier that hung, useless and dark, in the hallway. Grandma's cordless phone sat in its cradle on the counter, and when she picked it up and pressed talk, nothing happened. Not even static.

"Battery must be dead," Grandma said, tapping it against her palm.

Alicia took the phone and turned it over. "It's plugged into the wall," she said slowly. "The base is, anyway. If the power's out, maybe the phone isn't dead. Maybe the outlet is." Grandma raised an eyebrow, which was her way of saying go on. Alicia set the handset down and stood still, thinking. The phone needed the house's electricity. That part made sense. But something nagged at her, an old memory of phones with curly cords and no plugs at all. How had those ever worked? It seemed like a paradox, a thing with no power cord that still had power. Unless the power came from somewhere else.

"Grandma, did you ever have one of those wall phones? The kind with the cord?"

"Kitchen. Still there, behind the biscuit tin. I keep it because I hate throwing away anything that works."

Alicia pushed the tin aside and found it, a heavy cream-colored phone bolted to the wall with a cord coiled like a spring. No plug, no battery compartment. She lifted the receiver and held it to her ear, half expecting silence. Instead, a dial tone buzzed, steady and alive, as if the power cut had never happened. She nearly dropped it.

"Grandma! It works!" she shouted. "The line gets its power from the phone company, not from our house. That's why it still works."

"Well, I'll be," Grandma said, and then, because she was Grandma, "Call your mother before she worries."

Alicia dialed, and when her mother answered on the first ring, breathless and already reaching for her car keys, Alicia had to talk fast to keep her from driving over in the dark. "We're fine. We have flashlights, the stove is gas, and I found a phone that doesn't need electricity at all." Outside, a neighbor's generator roared to life, and somewhere down the block a dog barked at it. Alicia sat on the kitchen floor, the coiled cord stretching to reach her, and told her mother about the tomato plants she'd been watering when the world went dark. The dial tone hummed softly under her voice the whole time.

Gabriel had agreed to babysit the Hendersons' eight-month-old, Mia, mostly because the Hendersons' other kid, Ruthie, who was nine, had promised to do all the hard parts. So far the hard parts were real. Mia had dumped a bowl of oatmeal off her high chair tray twice, and now she was refusing the third bowl entirely, pressing her lips shut like a tiny dictator.

"She likes sweet things," Ruthie said, scraping oatmeal off the floor. "Mom puts honey in it sometimes. There's a jar right there."

Gababel reached for the jar on the counter. It was a fat glass bear, and the honey inside moved slow, like it had all day. He was about to twist the lid when Ruthie grabbed a paper off the fridge and held it up so fast it made a snapping sound. The paper said, in Mrs. Henderson's handwriting, NO HONEY FOR MIA. NO HONEY, NO EXCEPTIONS.

"She's nine months old," Ruthie said. "The rule is no honey until after twelve months. Mom says honey can have bacteria spores in it, and they can grow in a baby's gut and make her really sick. It's called infant botulism." She folded her arms, enjoying this. "It's a whole thing."

Gabriel set the bear down. His face went warm, and the embarrassment sat in his stomach like a swallowed rock, because he had almost done it, and because a nine-year-old had caught him. He tried to think of something a babysitter would say. "Good thing I was just, uh, checking the jar for cracks."

"Sure," said Ruthie, who did not believe him at all.

But Mia still wasn't eating, and Gabriel needed her to eat, because Mrs. Henderson came home in an hour and would ask. He looked at the list again. Under the honey warning, in smaller letters, it said Mia likes banana mashed in. So he peeled a banana, mashed it into the oatmeal with a fork, and offered the spoon. Mia considered him with deep suspicion, the way she might consider a large, clumsy stranger who had already dropped her snack twice. Then she inhaled the first bite so fast the spoon came back empty. She kicked both feet and banged the tray for more.

"See," Ruthie said. "Bananas aren't extinct yet."

"That's not what extinct means," Gabriel said.

"I know. I just like the word."

Gabriel fed her the rest of the bowl, one spoonful at a time, while the honey bear sat untouched by the sink, catching the afternoon light like it was proud of itself.

Tristan discovered the problem at seven o'clock on Tuesday morning, in the driveway, with the car still cold. He had been singing along with the radio, loudly, the way nobody could hear him, when the word "tonight" came out in two pieces. The "to" was high and normal, and the "night" dropped straight down into some gravelly cave he had never visited before. He tried it again. "Tonight." It cracked again, right in the middle, like a stick snapping.

In the car on the way to school, his sister Maya noticed him experimenting. "Why do you keep saying 'ahhh' like a dying robot?" she asked, buckling her seatbelt. Tristan ignored her, which was not easy, because the car was small and Maya was never indifferent to a chance to tease him. He was busy. He hummed a low note, then a high one, then the note in between where the break lived. It was like there were two voices inside him, an old one and a new one, and no bridge between them yet.

By Thursday he had begun to classify the evidence. Low notes worked fine. Talking worked fine, mostly. High notes were the problem, and the break always happened in the same narrow spot. Dad drove them to choir practice that evening, and Tristan spent the whole ride testing his newest idea: if he sang quietly enough, maybe the crack couldn't get enough air to happen. He whispered scales in the back seat. Maya put in her earbuds. "It still cracks," Tristan reported, half thrilled, half annoyed. "Just quieter."

At practice, Marcus got the solo in the new song, and Marcus sailed through the verse and then hit the big high note at the end, and his voice split exactly the way Tristan's had. Mr. Ruiz raised one hand. "Marcus's larynx is growing," he said, "so the vocal folds inside it are getting longer and thicker, and they may crack while that happens." Marcus turned red, but Tristan nearly fell off the riser. Folds. Longer and thicker. That was it. That was the hidden machine.

On the drive home, Tristan leaned forward between the front seats. "Dad, the vocal folds get longer and thicker, and that's why the voice drops. It's like a guitar string, kind of. Except inside." Dad glanced at him in the mirror. "A metaphor," Dad said. "Sure. Every guy in this car went through it." Maya pulled out one earbud. "Even Dad cracked?" "Ask your grandmother," Dad said. "I once scared the dog."

Tristan sat back. The car hummed along the dark road, and he hummed with it, low, in the new voice, the one with no cracks in it at all. He was already planning the choir solo for next year. "Marcus," he said to the window, "your solo is mine in October."

Georgia had measured her bean plants twice, and both times the numbers made her stomach drop. The six pots on the windowsill, the ones she had watered every morning with the special fertilizer her grandmother sent, had grown three inches in two weeks. That was the good part. The bad part was the question her friend Priya had asked at lunch: "Grown three inches compared to what?"

Now, in the kitchen, Georgia laid her science notebook on the counter and stared at her chart. Six plants, all fertilized, all tall. Beside the sink her little brother Theo was gluing popsicle sticks into what he claimed was an authentic Viking longship, though it looked more like a raft with ambitions. "You keep frowning at that notebook," he said. "Is it going to bite you?"

"Priya says my project doesn't prove anything. Maybe the beans would have grown three inches anyway." Georgia tapped her pencil against the page. Her instinct told her the fertilizer worked, but instinct wasn't allowed in the results section. "If I can't compare them to something, I can't tell."

Theo set down his glue. "Compare them to what, the Viking ship?"

"No. Beans." She went quiet, and then the idea landed all at once, so big she actually laughed. "More beans. I'll start six new pots, same soil, same window, same water, everything the same. The only difference is the fertilizer. That way, if the fertilized ones grow more, I know it's the fertilizer doing it, and not the window or the soil or dumb luck."

Theo's eyes lit up. "Can I be in charge of the new ones? I'll water them at the same time you water yours. We can coordinate it, like eight o'clock every morning before the bus." He was already pulling the bag of dried beans from the cupboard, the one Mom used for soup, and lining up six clean yogurt cups on the counter. He filled them with soil from the same bag Georgia had used, patting each one down twice, checking her old pots to match the depth.

"Careful," Georgia said. "The new ones get plain water only. Not one drop of the fertilizer, or it ruins everything." Theo nodded so seriously she believed him. He had wanted his own job for the project ever since she'd started it, and now he had one that actually mattered.

Two weeks later, they knelt side by side at the windowsill with the ruler between them. The fertilized plants had grown three and a half inches. Theo's plain-water beans, the ones nobody had fed anything special, had grown two. Georgia wrote the numbers down twice to be sure, then grinned at him. "Yours are the control group," she said. "The ones treated exactly like mine except for the fertilizer."

Theo straightened up like a soldier receiving a medal. "The control group," he repeated, tasting the words. "Can I put that on the label? In Viking letters?"

Sophie wanted to win the school science fair more than she wanted her braces off, and she had decided the way to do it was to settle, once and for all, which classroom surface had the most bacteria. Mr. Ruiz had given each table four agar plates, and Sophie's table got the pencil sharpener, the doorknob, the sink faucet, and the teacher's keyboard. "You can't see bacteria," said her lab partner, Marcus, peering at his plate. "So how do we know the shiny stuff isn't just soup?" Sophie pointed at the dots already blooming on the plate they had swabbed that morning. "We can't see them, but we can see what they do. That's the whole trick."

While they waited for colonies to grow, Marcus flipped through a magazine and held up a page. "Look at this ad. Germ-Away wipes change lives," he read. "Wow. Changes lives." Sophie squinted at it. "Fine, but how would you check that?" Marcus shrugged. "You'd have to find a bunch of lives, wipe them, and see." The table cracked up, and even Priya from the next table leaned over to see what was so funny.

Sophie couldn't stop thinking about it, though. She took out her notebook and wrote two columns. In one she put claims like "Germ-Away kills more bacteria than plain soap," which she underlined twice, because Mr. Ruiz had a bottle of each and a whole drawer of plates. You could swab, wipe, wait, count. In the other column she put "changes lives," and after a minute she also put her mother's favorite, "these vitamins make you feel unstoppable," because she could not imagine any plate, anywhere, that could ever prove that wrong. It was like an opinion wearing a lab coat.

"The kill-more-bacteria one is checkable," she told Marcus. "The changes-lives one gives us nothing to test. Not even in principle, whatever principle means." "It means it just can't be done," Marcus said, "even if you had a million plates and a robot." Priya nodded solemnly. "My brother wrote an algorithm that sorts true facts from false ones for his homework," she offered, "and even his algorithm chokes on stuff like that."

Sophie had to confess something then. "I was going to put 'Germ-Away is the best' on my poster, because it sounds strong." Marcus pretended to faint against the sink. "Be strong and checkable," Sophie added, writing it at the top of her column, right under the date.

The next morning the plates had turned into tiny, fertile gardens, gray and orange colonies crowding the pencil sharpener's plate worst of all, which made everybody groan and nobody surprised. Mr. Ruiz stopped at their table and looked a long time at the notebook with its two columns and the circled words "nothing to test." He tapped the page. "Whose is this?" Sophie raised her hand, braced for trouble. He wrote something in his binder instead. "Sofia," he said, "remind me to show you what Karl Popper did with this idea. You'll like him. He was even crankier than you."

Sophie grinned. "That's an opinion, Mr. Ruiz."

"Checkable," he said, and moved on to the next table.

Lily slid three dollars across the lunch table and watched Maya count out the last two bracelets from her shoebox. By Tuesday they were gone, and Maya had raised almost enough money to enroll in the Saturday art class she'd been talking about since September.

On Wednesday, four sixth graders walked into homeroom with sandwich bags full of woven bracelets, each one tagged with a price of three dollars. By Friday there were nine sellers, and the hallway outside the science room looked like a tiny market. Nobody was buying much, though, because everyone who wanted a bracelet already had one, or was now making them at home from leftover embroidery thread. Maya sat on the radiator, staring at her empty box and then at the crowded hallway. "Nobody wants mine anymore," she said, "and I still need eight dollars for art class."

Lily couldn't stop watching the sellers, wondering what had changed. Nothing about the bracelets themselves had changed. Was it just that there were so many now? She pulled out her notebook and did something systematic: a column for each seller, the price they asked, and how many bracelets they sold that day. A pattern jumped out by afternoon. The kids charging three dollars sold almost nothing. One boy who had dropped his price to one dollar had sold five. The same bracelets, the same hallway, different numbers. It was like the model wind turbine in Mr. Okafor's room, which spun faster or slower depending on something you couldn't see from across the room, the wind. Lily couldn't see a "price," but she could see what it did.

She shared the notebook with Maya. "When your bracelets were three dollars and there were only a few, everybody wanted them. Then the high price made selling seem worth it, so a bunch of people started making them. Now there are tons." Maya squinted at the columns. "So there's too many for the price they're asking." Lily nodded. "And that boy with the one-dollar sign sold out."

Monday morning, Maya taped a new sign to her shoebox: BRACELETS, ONE DOLLAR, PICK YOUR OWN COLORS. She let buyers choose thread from a box, since everyone else's were the same three patterns. By lunch she had sold eleven, and two of the three-dollar sellers had quietly crossed out their signs and written smaller numbers. After school Maya counted her crumpled bills on the bus, smoothed them flat, and grinned. "Nine to go." Lily looked out the window at the turbines spinning on the ridge past the soccer field, their long white arms turning at different speeds, and started a fresh page in her notebook.

The pharmacy smelled like soap and cough drops, and Kate stood by the shelf of shoe inserts while her mother picked up a prescription. In the basket under her arm sat a box of plasters, a comb, and the money she had saved for the display rack behind the counter. That was the problem: the pharmacy sold arch supports, but it did not sell what she actually needed, which was a reason her brother Tom's shoes had stopped fitting twice since September while his jeans still fit fine.

Kate turned the idea over while her mother talked to the pharmacist about antihistamines. Her premise was simple: if Tom's feet were growing, the rest of him should be growing too, at the same time. That was how she had always assumed growing worked, everything at once, like inflating a balloon. But the evidence did not fit. His trainers were pinching again, and his school trousers still hung the same as they had in autumn. She looked down the aisle as if the shelves could settle it.

She tested her idea on the pharmacist, a woman named Ruth with reading glasses pushed up into her hair. "If someone's feet got bigger twice this year but their legs didn't get longer at all," Kate asked, "would that mean the feet are broken?"

Ruth laughed. "No. Hands and feet usually grow first, before the arms and legs and the rest of the body catch up."

"So the legs will catch up," Kate said. "Later."

"That's the usual order," Ruth said, and rang up a packet of plasters for the woman behind them.

Kate stood there doing the sums. Two new pairs of shoes in one school year was a lot of money, and their family budget was not rich this winter; her mother had called it an impoverished month just last Tuesday, waving the electricity bill. So Kate made a decision she could defend. Instead of buying the sparkly display rack comb, she put her money toward Tom's next pair of shoes, and she wrote a note on the fridge: DO NOT BUY HIM JEANS YET.

When they got home, she found Tom in the hallway trying to jam his heel into the trainer he had outgrown a second time. "Save your trainers," she told him. "And don't ask for new jeans, because your legs are next."

Tom looked at her, then at his feet. "How do you know?"

Kate tapped his shoe with her own. "Your feet told me."

Sawyer refreshed the page for the eleventh time that afternoon. The sneakers he wanted, the white ones with the orange stripe, had been forty dollars two weeks ago. Now the lowest listing read seventy-five, and the little bar under the search filter said only three pairs remained. He had waited because he wanted to spend his lawn-mowing money on a concert ticket instead, and he was still not sure that had been the right call.

"Still checking those shoes?" his dad asked from the kitchen doorway. "Come on, we need gas."

At the station, the sign glowed in the fading light, each number luminous against the dark sky like something from a movie marquee. Sawyer noticed the price first because his dad groaned at it. "It was cheaper last week," his dad muttered, easing the nozzle into the tank.

A kid about Sawyer's age was standing by the next pump, squinting up at the sign. "Why'd it go up since Saturday?" the kid asked nobody in particular. "The gas is the same gas."

Sawyer found himself answering before he thought about it. "My uncle drives tankers, and he says crude oil is usually the biggest single part of what a gallon costs. Like, one chunk, bigger than any other chunk. So when crude gets more expensive, pump prices mostly go up too." He paused. "I think that's how it works, anyway."

The kid shrugged and wandered off, but Sawyer kept turning it over while the numbers climbed on the pump display. It was the same thing happening with his sneakers. Lots of people wanted them, hardly any pairs were left, and the price had shot up. When the warehouse restocked and there were hundreds of listings, the price would sink back down. He couldn't see the wanting or the scarcity itself, only the numbers moving, but the numbers were like footprints. Last month he had tested the idea by watching a different shoe, a pair everyone had said was finished, and he had watched the price fall for nine straight days until it hit nineteen dollars. His technique was simple: check morning and night, write the lowest price in a notebook, and never buy on the first day of a spike.

"Done," his dad said, hanging up the nozzle.

Back home, Sawyer opened his notebook to a clean page and wrote two columns, one labeled shoes and one left blank for now. Seventy-five dollars was too much, and he knew it. But restocks happened, and he could wait. He set an alarm for six in the morning, put the notebook by his pillow, and clicked the refresh button one more time. Two pairs left.

The restaurant smelled of ginger and scallions, and Claire's stomach growled before the waiter had even set down the menus. Mei's family owned the Golden Lantern, and tonight Mei's grandmother had insisted on cooking "something special," which turned out to be seven dishes that all seemed to revolve around one enormous pot of rice in the middle of the table. Claire wanted more than anything to make a good impression. Her plan was simple: eat everything, compliment everything, and not knock anything over.

The trouble started with the dumplings. They were slippery, and Claire needed both hands to fish one out of the shared platter. Without thinking, she planted her chopsticks straight up in her bowl of rice like two little flagpoles and reached across the table. The chatter around the table stopped. Mei's grandmother went very still, and her eyes flicked to the bowl and then quickly away, as if she had seen something she did not want to see.

"Nan, what's wrong?" Mei asked her grandmother in a low voice. Then Mei followed the old woman's gaze, and Claire watched her friend's face change from confusion to understanding. Mei leaned over and whispered, "Don't leave your chopsticks standing in the rice. It looks like incense offered to the dead." Claire pulled the chopsticks out so fast she nearly launched a grain of rice into the soy sauce. "Oh no. Oh no, I'm so sorry," she whispered back. Mei's grandmother said something in Chinese, and Mei laughed for the first time since the dumpling incident. "She says you have good reflexes. She once knocked over a whole teapot doing the same thing at her own grandmother's table."

Claire laid her chopsticks across the top of her bowl the way she saw everyone else do, resting them side by side like a pair of quiet birds. Then, because she wanted to be sure, she watched Mei's father closely through the next three courses. He never once left his chopsticks planted anywhere, not even when he answered his phone about some argument with the landlord over the leaking roof. Every time he needed a free hand, down the chopsticks went, flat beside the bowl. Claire tested her theory by pretending to need both hands for her napkin. Resting the chopsticks, she decided, was the safe pattern, the invisible rule that everyone at this table knew and she had just learned the hard way.

After dinner, Mei's grandmother pressed a small red envelope into Claire's hands. "For luck," Mei translated. "She likes you. She says anyone who apologizes that fast can come back anytime." At the door, Claire turned and held up the envelope with a grin. "Same time next month? I promise my chopsticks will lie down like well-trained puppies." Behind her, she heard Mei's grandmother laugh, a sound like small bells.

The list went up on the gym door at lunch, and Penelope was tenth in line to see it. The basketball coach had posted the rankings for Player of the Season, one number next to each name, and everyone crowded in to find out where they stood. Dexter, her best friend, pushed forward beside her, chewing the strap of his backpack the way he did when he was nervous. He wanted that award more than he wanted lunch, more than he wanted a snow day, and when he finally spotted his name, his shoulders dropped. He was fourteenth. Fourteenth out of fifteen, because the list counted only one thing, points scored, and Dexter hardly ever shot.

That night Penelope found a letter waiting on her desk, actual paper, folded in thirds. Her uncle had written it after their family dinner at the sports bar on Saturday, when she'd complained that the whole season had been squeezed onto one skinny list of numbers. Dear Penelope, it began. You asked a good question. Here's the story I promised. In 2003 a book came out, "Moneyball" by Michael Lewis. It described how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players. A low-budget team, competing against rich teams, because they found players everybody else ignored. He'd signed it with a doodle of a baseball. Penelope read it three times.

At school the next morning she sat in the cafeteria with her notebook and started writing. She had been at every game anyway, keeping score because Coach Ruiz made anyone on the bench supervise the clock. The tallying was tedious, all those little marks, but she had four games of them in her bag. If the Athletics could find hidden value in one statistic, maybe she could too. The question was what to count. Points were what everyone saw. But watching Dexter play, she'd noticed something nobody wrote down: every time he touched the ball, something good tended to happen for the team, even when he never scored.

So she tested it. For every player, she counted touches, and then the times a touch led to a basket, a foul drawn, or a possession kept alive. She called it "good things per touch." She worked through lunch, her pen moving down the columns while the cafeteria roared around her, Marcus and Priya arguing about whether the cafeteria's mystery meat came from a herbivore or a carnivore, which Priya insisted mattered, which Marcus insisted did not. By the time the bell rang, Penelope had one page of numbers and a hollow feeling in her stomach, because something strange was in them.

She didn't tell Dexter. Not yet. She needed the fifth game, the away game on Thursday, to be sure. She rode the bus with the team, notebook on her knees, and marked every touch while the crowd stomped the bleachers. The score stayed close the whole game, tied twice in the last two minutes, and Penelope barely breathed. Dexter got the ball with forty seconds left, everyone in the gym screaming shoot, and he whipped it sideways to Marcus, who was standing alone under the basket. Swish. Then Dexter stole the inbounds pass and got fouled, and made one of two free throws, and the game was over, won by a single point.

On the bus home, under the flickering dome light, Penelope finished her columns and counted the marks one last time, pressing hard with her pencil. She looked up and walked to the seat where Dexter sat with his headphones on, staring out the dark window.

She tapped his shoulder and held the notebook in front of his face, her finger under the final row.

"You're first," she said. "Nobody knows it yet."

The festival filled the park with tents and flags, and Edouard moved through the crowd with a folded card in his back pocket. His grandmother had pressed it into his hand that morning before he left, saying in their family's language, "This is for you, but read it at the lantern table, not before." Edouard understood every word she said. He had been answering her in that language since he was small, at Sunday dinners and on the phone every Thursday. But the card itself was written down, in looping script he could not read at all.

He found the lantern table near the fountain, where volunteers were handing out translucent paper shades for people to decorate and hang on the long strings overhead. Painting a message on a lantern before hanging it was the closing ritual of the festival, and his grandmother had done it every year since they arrived. Edouard unfolded the card, hoping that seeing the whole thing would somehow help. It didn't. The letters sat there like a fence he could walk beside but never get through. He spoke the language, and yet the writing was a stranger to him.

At the next table, a girl about his age was chatting easily with an elderly woman in a language Edouard recognized as the same one. Then the woman handed her a small note, and the girl's face went pink. "Halmoni, I can't read this," she admitted. "I can talk to you fine, but reading it is different." The older woman laughed kindly and read it aloud herself. Edouard drifted closer. "Same thing happens to me," he said. "I chat with my grandmother all the time, but I can't read a word she writes."

The girl, whose name was Naomi, nodded like she'd been waiting for someone to say it. "My cousin calls ours a heritage language," she said. "Because we speak it at home, but out here everyone uses the community's main language." She tapped the note. "So kids like us can speak it and still not read it." Edouard looked back at his card. It wasn't that he was bad at the language. It was that speaking it and reading it were two different skills, and only one of them had ever been needed at his house.

He had an idea. If the grandmother could read the note aloud, maybe he could test whether his ear could do the work his eyes couldn't. He asked Naomi's grandmother, politely, if she would read his card to him. She unfolded it, smiled at the looping script, and spoke the words slowly. As she read, Edouard followed along, and the sentence opened like a door: "Write your wish for the year on your lantern, in our language, any way you can."

His grandmother hadn't asked for perfect spelling. She'd only asked him to try. Edouard picked up a brush, dipped it in the deep blue paint, and, letter by careful letter, copying from the card in front of him, began to write.

The bus smelled like vinyl seats and peanut butter crackers, and Grace ran through her word list for the fourth time even though she knew every entry cold. In thirty minutes the regional spelling bee would start, and only the champion would go to nationals. Second place got a dictionary, which felt to Grace like getting a towel after swimming halfway across a pool. Across the aisle, Marcus leaned his head against the window and watched the fence posts go by.

"You look like you're going to be sick," Grace said.

"I might be," Marcus said. "If I come in second again. Last year I got out on 'rhubarb.' Do you know how it feels to lose to a vegetable?"

Grace opened her mouth to say she didn't care about his rhubarb, then closed it, because the truth was she had thought about little else all week except coming in second herself. She reached into her backpack and pulled out a folded note her older sister had left on her pillow that morning. She smoothed it out on her knee.

"If you get 'presume' in the bee, it's p-r-e-s-u-m-e," her sister had written, "because you presume you're right before you check. Don't presume. Ask for the definition every single time. Also eat something, you spelled better after breakfast at the last one. Love, Tessa." Grace smiled and passed the note across the aisle so Marcus could read it too.

At the bee, the rounds burned down from forty spellers to six, then to three, then to Grace and Marcus alone. He spelled "agile" without a hitch. She spelled "anomaly," asking for the definition first, exactly as the note said, and got it right. Round after round followed, and nobody missed. The pronouncer kept pulling fresh words from the box, and Grace noticed something she had never seen before: there was no rule for ending this. She remembered a fact her sister had mentioned once, and she raised her hand.

"Is it true that the 2019 Scripps National Spelling Bee ended with eight co-champions, because the spellers kept getting every word right?"

The pronouncer blinked. "That's correct."

"So if we both keep spelling everything right," Grace said, "there doesn't have to be a loser?"

The officials conferred in the corner, and Marcus caught Grace's eye across the microphone. He was grinning now, not green at all. Two rounds later, after Grace sailed through "moratorium" and Marcus handled "vitreous" without a stumble, the pronouncer lifted his hand.

"We are declaring two co-champions," he announced. "Both of you will advance to nationals."

Marcus held up his fist across the stage, and Grace ran over and bumped it with hers. In the back of the hall, her sister was already on her feet, waving the empty note envelope over her head like a flag.

Mya sat cross-legged on her bed with her phone six inches from her face, watching the group chat light up. The project was due Friday: make a page about where your family came from. Jordan had already typed three messages about presenting first because he wanted the class to remember his slide before anyone else's, and Priya had sent a photo of her grandmother's cookbook. Mya hadn't sent anything yet, because she had a problem. Her cousin Lena was visiting from abroad, and last night at dinner Lena had laughed so hard she nearly knocked over her water glass when everyone kept saying she'd flown in from Germany.

"It's Deutschland," Lena had said. "We never call it Germany. That's your word for us, not ours." Then she'd told Mya the names for the two kinds of words, and Mya had written them on the back of her math homework so she wouldn't forget.

She typed into the chat: "Hypothetical question. If we call a country one thing and the people there call it something else, which name should go on my poster?" Jordan answered fast: "Ours, obviously, it's for our class." Priya sent a shrug emoji. Mya tried a different approach, the way she'd test a rule in science: collect data. She messaged her uncle, her grandmother, and Lena's mother, asking each one what their family called the country in their own language.

The answers came in through the evening. Her grandmother wrote back a whole text about the village, and then added, "Here we say it our way, there they say it theirs, both are true names." Lena's mother sent one line: "Deutschland, always." Mya copied the messages into a document for her citation page, so her teacher could see where each name came from. She noticed a pattern: every family member used their own word, and not one of them used the English one, unless they were talking to someone outside.

"So which one wins?" Jordan asked, when she posted her draft. He still wanted his slide first and had moved on to arguing about presentation order, but Priya had gone quiet, and then sent: "Wait. My mom calls our family's country something different too. I just never thought about it. Can I put both on my page?"

Mya looked at Lena, who was leaning in the doorway in her borrowed sweatpants, reading over her shoulder. Lena tapped the screen where Mya had typed both names side by side, then the two labels underneath them. "A name a group uses for itself is called an endonym," Lena said, "and a name outsiders use is an exonym." Mya added the last line to her poster and hit send. Priya replied within a minute: "Doing it. Mine's going up first, Jordan."

"Fine," Jordan typed. "But I'm still going before the bell invades my free time."

Hannah crouched beside trail marker number four with her notebook, two pairs of tweezers, a set of chopsticks, and a paper cup full of seeds she had sorted by size on her bedroom floor. Her project was due Friday: she had to explain how beak shapes on the Galápagos finches had been shaped by natural selection, and she wanted to test it herself instead of just copying facts. Her plan was simple. The big tweezers were the big, crushing beaks. The skinny tweezers were the thin, probing beaks. The chopsticks were, in her opinion, just chopsticks, but she had run out of beak models.

"Are you eating bird food again?" her brother Marcus asked, hiking up behind her with a granola bar. Marcus wanted one thing on these walks, which was to spot a bird before Hannah did, because last month she had beaten him eleven to three and he had not recovered. "Because that's weird even for you."

"It's science." She dumped the large, hard seeds onto the flat rock beside the trail. "Big beaks first." She pinched the big tweezers, picked up a seed, and dropped it into the cup in four seconds. Then she tried the skinny tweezers on the same seeds, and the seed shot off the rock, rolled down the slope, and vanished into a patch of ferns. She recorded both times. When she switched to the tiny soft seeds in the crevice of the rock, the skinny tweezers were quick and nimble while the big ones fumbled like a civilian trying to do surgery with garden shears. The pattern was so clean it almost scared her. Where a food source was restricted to one kind of seed, one beak shape won, every time.

Then a small dark bird landed three feet away and started poking at the fallen seeds. "Blackbird," Marcus said instantly. "I win, that's my bird, point for me."

Hannah looked at it. Curved beak, striped chest, and now that she stared, not really blackbird-shaped at all. "I think it's a finch," she said slowly, and then felt her whole project tip sideways in her head. She had read a paragraph about Darwin and had skipped past a detail that suddenly seemed like the most important thing on the trail. She dug out her book and found the page. In 1837, an ornithologist named John Gould told Darwin that his Galápagos birds, which Darwin had taken for wrens or blackbirds, were actually a new group of closely related finches. Darwin hadn't recognized them either. The whole idea of beaks changing on different islands had come from a correction after the trip, from a scientist back in England who looked closer.

"Wait." Marcus leaned over her shoulder, chewing. "Darwin called them wrens? The evolution guy?" He started laughing so hard he had to sit on the rock. "Okay, fine, I change my vote, it's a finch. But I'm still claiming the point, because I saw it first."

"It's not a contest," Hannah said, already writing. The bird hopped closer, cracked a big seed with a quick sideways motion of its beak, and flew off into the sun.

Jake had one week to learn "Turkey in the Straw" on Grandpa's old fiddle before the family reunion, and so far he could play it exactly as well as he had on Monday, which was badly. He stood in the cluttered back room, rosin dust on his jeans, and played the whole tune through for the ninth time. Nine times, and the same spot still collapsed every single time, right where the notes jumped up quick in the middle of the song.

After dinner he found a worn notebook in the drawer under the sheet music. It had belonged to Grandma, who used to play the same fiddle. Inside, the pages weren't full of whole songs. Instead she had written the same four measures over and over, with little marks and circled notes, and in the margin: "Slow. Again. Slower." Why hadn't she just played her pieces from start to finish? He flipped through page after page and found the same strange pattern everywhere, small chunks with careful notes, almost nothing played all the way through.

He decided to test it. The next morning he ignored the beginning, which he could already play in his sleep, and played only the troublesome jumping section. He played it slowly, then a little faster, then slowly again whenever his fingers tangled. It felt odd, like rehearsing only one line of a joke. But by noon his left hand found the jumps without his eyes, and by evening the whole tune snapped together so smoothly that he played it twice just to hear it happen.

"Do you know what Grandma figured out?" he asked Grandpa at supper. "How you practice, working on your specific weak spots, matters more than just playing the whole piece a bunch of times. That's why she never wrote out full songs."

Grandpa chuckled into his potatoes. "Fifty years of playing and she was the most frugal woman I ever knew, too. Never wasted a single note, on the fiddle or anywhere else."

At the reunion, Jake stood on the porch steps and played the tune all the way through, and the jumping part in the middle, the old troublemaker, sailed by like it had never been hard at all. When he finished, his little cousin tugged his sleeve.

"That was good," she said, "but the best part was the fast part in the middle."

Jake grinned and leaned down to confide the secret. "That part? I played that one more than the rest of the song combined."

The letter arrived folded inside a seed packet, which was typical of Aunt Rosa. Dear Layla, it read. Congratulations on winning the community garden plot. My gift: corn, beans, and squash seeds, all mixed together on purpose. Plant them the way the old diagram in this envelope shows, and do not argue with me. Love, your aunt, who knows things. Layla held up the diagram. Three circles of dots, a mound in the middle, squash drawn all around like a green puddle. "Who plants three things in one hole?" she asked her friend Marcus, who was leaning on the fence eating a plum.

"That's not a hole, that's a traffic jam," Marcus said. Layla studied the diagram anyway, because her aunt's plans always had a secret inside them. She planted the corn kernels in a cluster at the center of each mound, exactly as the circles showed, and she saved the beans for later, which was the part that made no sense to her at first. Beans climbed things. Corn was a thing. Maybe that was the whole trick, and the squash puddle around the outside was doing something too, though she couldn't see what.

Two weeks later she had her first small fracture in the plan: a rabbit, or possibly Marcus's little brother, had flattened one mound entirely. Layla rebuilt it and wrapped the base of that mound with string, humming as she worked. "You're protecting it," Marcus said. "Trying to preserve the evidence," she said. "When it happens again, I want to know which criminal I'm dealing with." The string stayed untouched for three nights. The rabbit had simply lost interest, which Layla found slightly insulting.

When the corn stood knee-high, she pushed the bean seeds into the soil at its base, and only then did the pattern click. The beans sent out curling tendrils within days and grabbed the corn stalks like tiny green hands looking for a ladder. "They're using the corn as a trellis," Layla said, kneeling in the dirt. Marcus peered down at them. "The corn doesn't mind?" "Aunt Rosa calls it the Three Sisters method," Layla said. "The corn supports the climbing beans, and the squash leaves shade the soil. My aunt says people have planted it this way for centuries."

The part about the squash proved itself without any help from Layla. Her neighbor Mr. Okoye spent every Saturday hacking at weeds with a hoe, his plot bare between rows, while under Layla's sprawling squash leaves the ground stayed dark and nearly empty. She checked by lifting a leaf like a trapdoor, and there was nothing under it but shade. The beans grew so vigorous and heavy that by August the mounds looked like green tents, and the corn leaned together at the top as if huddling over a secret.

In September Aunt Rosa appeared at the garden gate, sunglasses pushed up in her hair. "Well?" she said. Layla handed her a basket: fat beans, golden corn, one squat squash with a dirty smiley face drawn on its skin. "The Three Sisters send their regards," Layla said. Aunt Rosa picked up the squash and studied the face. "Which sister is this one?" "The loud one," said Marcus, from the fence, still eating a plum.

The drive to the airport had been awful. Dad took the winding road along the ridge because it was faster, and Norah had spent the whole ride with her novel six inches from her face, which was why, by the time they reached the parking garage, she was green and sweaty and gripping the door handle. Her little brother Theo, who had stared out the window the entire way, bounced out of the car like nothing had happened.

"That's not fair," Norah said, leaning against the suitcase. "You ate three granola bars and you're fine."

"Motion sickness doesn't care about granola bars," Mom said, handing her a water bottle.

At the gate, while Theo played on the carpet with a toy plane, Norah sat very still and thought. She had been reading. Her eyes had been staring at a page, a page that never moves, so her eyes were telling her brain one thing. But the car had been curving and swaying up that road, and something in her inner ear, some balance thing, had been telling her brain the opposite. Her brain had gotten two conflicting stories about whether her body was moving, and she had felt sick. Theo had watched the trees and the guardrail whizzing past, so his eyes and his inner ear were saying the same thing. That had to be it. The idea was vague at first, like a word on the tip of her tongue, but the more she turned it over, the clearer it got.

"Okay," she said out loud. "Test one. On the plane, I read for ten minutes. Then I look out the window for ten minutes. Then I compare."

"Compare what?" Theo asked.

"Whether I feel like throwing up." Theo made a face and went back to his toy plane.

Boarding was the best part so far, the jet bridge humming, the flight attendant saying welcome aboard like she meant it. Norah claimed the window seat and pulled out her book before the plane even pushed back. Her plan to read might hinder her experiment a little, since the plane hadn't started moving yet, but she figured taxiing and takeoff counted.

Ten minutes after they leveled off, her stomach had that familiar wobbly feeling. She marked her page and pressed her forehead to the window. Clouds, a silver river, tiny squares of farmland scrolling past. Her stomach settled, slowly, like water going still.

She spun to Theo. "It works. When your eyes see the movement too, everything agrees, and you feel fine."

Theo held up his toy plane, flying it past her face. "Window seat next time," he said.

The sign outside Dell's Gas and Go had slushies for a dollar, and Lucy wanted one so badly she could already feel the brain freeze. Her little brother Marcus wanted one too, plus a bag of chips, plus a lottery scratcher he was not going to get. But between them they had exactly one dollar and forty cents, and Lucy's dollar was spoken for.

"Look at that line," Marcus said. Seven people were crowded at the slushie machine, and the sound of the motor grinding ice filled the whole store. The kid ahead of Lucy, Devon from her science class, filled his cup to the very brim, then filled a second cup for his mom.

When Lucy finally got her turn, the machine sputtered and went quiet. Dell came out from behind the register, tapped the tank, and shook his head. "Machine's out of syrup till my delivery Friday. That's the last of it."

"Great," Lucy said. "So no slushie at all."

Dell shrugged. "Unless somebody wants to pay for what's left in the cup tray. I'm charging three dollars a cup now."

Marcus gasped like she'd asked him to hand over a kidney. "Three dollars? That's robbery!"

But Lucy was watching, not listening to Marcus. Of the seven people in line, only Devon and one trucker actually paid three dollars. The other five put their cups back and drifted toward the soda cooler, grumbling. Lucy chewed her lip. Fewer buyers, higher price. She'd seen the flip side that morning at the farmers market, when the peach lady dropped her price at closing time and got mobbed.

"Hey, Devon," she said. "In social studies, isn't there a name for that? When the price goes up and people buy less?"

"The law of demand," Devon said. "When prices rise, people buy less. When they drop, people buy more."

"That's it." Lucy turned to Dell. "What if you tried one dollar a cup instead? I bet more people would buy what's left, and you'd clear it out before Friday."

"I don't need a jury of thirteen-year-olds running my store," Dell said, but he was rubbing his chin, and the stack of unsold cups wasn't getting smaller on its own. "One hour. Dollar a cup. If it works, you get the first one free."

It worked. Lucy stood by the door and counted, because she wanted her numbers to be consistent before she claimed anything. In forty minutes the tray was empty, and a man in a lawn-mower company truck bought the very last two cups at once. The one thing Lucy couldn't see, the invisible rule underneath the buying and the selling, had behaved exactly the way she predicted, and that felt better than the slushie.

Dell handed her a free cup, cherry red. Marcus held out his hand, eyes enormous.

"You were going to intervene on my behalf, right?" he said. "Because I'm your brother? Because family?"

Lucy sucked down a long, cold sip, considered him over the rim of the cup, and handed him exactly one third.

The lobby chat scrolled fast in bright blue text. DragonGrl99 had typed R U SERIOUS in all capitals, which Emilia had learned meant either excitement or fury, and a player named BeefWizard was typing what looked like a memoir, line after line about a match gone wrong. Emilia despised lobby chat on nights like this. Anyone could read it, anyone could jump in, and the tone flipped from joking to toxic in about four messages. She kept her own words short there: gg, ready, brb.

A private message popped up instead, quiet green text that only she could see. It was her cousin Sam, eleven years old and three states away. "I can't get in. It keeps asking for my birthday and then it says I can't make an account."

Emilia opened voice chat and invited him to a private room, because in the lobby everyone could hear you, but in a room only invited players could. "What did it say exactly?" she asked.

"It said I have to be thirteen. I put my real birthday and it kicked me out." Sam's voice went smaller. "Is it because they think eleven-year-olds are annoying?"

Emilia frowned at her screen. She thought about her own signup a few months ago. The same question, the same rule. Her friend Theo had grumbled about it too, and he had said something she half remembered. She typed to Sam, "Wait, don't make a new account yet. I'm going to test something."

She opened the signup page in another tab and filled it out with a fake name and a birthday that made her twelve. Sure enough, the page stopped and asked for a parent's email for permission. She closed the tab without submitting. "It's not about being annoying," she said. "Watch what happens when I say I'm twelve." She told him about the parent email screen.

"So they need a grown-up to say yes?"

"That's what it looks like." Emilia searched the rule on her phone and read the first line out loud. "It's a U.S. law from 1998. Sites have to get parental consent before they collect personal information from kids under thirteen. That's why they make you be thirteen."

Sam was quiet for a second. "So I just have to wait, or get Mom to sign?"

"Or get Mom to sign." In the lobby behind them, DragonGrl99 was typing in all capitals again. Emilia muted it.

"Fine," Sam said. "I'll go ask her right now. Stay in the room."

The game lobby glowed on Sofia's screen like a luminous fish tank, full of usernames drifting in and out. Her best friend Raj's tag, TurboPlumber42, popped up in the chat, and below it a message in bright orange: "SOS. Emergency. Meet me in party."

She clicked him into a private voice channel, which was the whole point of private, because in the public lobby anyone could read your business. "What's wrong with you?" she asked.

"I posted the video," Raj groaned. "The one of me singing the marshmallow song in my brother's shower cap. On my clan page. And then I deleted it. But people saw it, Sofia. Kwon saw it. He screenshotted the page before I took it down, and now everyone says the clan page is haunted because the video 'vanished.'" His voice dropped to a whisper. "Somebody named GhostLily left a comment saying she can still find it. How? I deleted it. It's gone. Deleted means gone, right?"

Sofia frowned at her screen. She thought about how her hamster could hibernate in one corner of his cage for days, invisible but absolutely still there, and how the pipes under her kitchen sink kept leaking even after her dad said he'd "fixed the plumbing." Things didn't always disappear just because you stopped looking at them. "Deleted from where?" she asked slowly. "The clan page is public, right?"

"Public. Anyone could see it."

"Then wait. My cousin showed me this thing once. Hang on." She opened a browser, typed the clan page's address, and then, remembering, went to a site her cousin had bookmarked. "The Wayback Machine has saved more than one trillion web pages, so something deleted from a public website can sometimes still be found," she recited, half to herself, half to Raj.

"Trillion? That's a number with, like, all the zeros."

"Shh. I'm being a detective." She pasted the clan page's address into the search bar and hit enter. A little calendar appeared, dotted with dates like spots on a ladybug. She clicked the most recent one, right before Raj's deletion. The old page loaded, and there it was: a post titled "MY GREATEST WORK," with Raj in a shower cap, mid-note, luminous with steam.

"It's back," Sofia said. "It never left, really. It was just hibernating."

Raj made a sound like a deflating balloon. Then he brightened, which was very like him. "Wait. This means I can see stuff other people deleted, too."

"That's not the lesson here, Raj."

He was already typing.

"Raj. Rude."

On the screen, TurboPlumber42's tag flashed once and went dark, like a fish ducking behind a rock.

Maelie pressed her ear against the metal trash can in her grandfather's garage workshop and tapped the side with a screwdriver. A dull thud answered her, nothing more. For three nights the strange scratching had come from somewhere in the garage, and every morning the traps she set stayed empty.

"You're going to catch it eventually," her cousin Theo said from the workbench, where he was lettering her science fair board in thick blue marker. He had steady hands, and she envied him that, because her own letters always slid downhill. The board needed a section labeled "Hypothesis" and she had asked him to leave space for it.

"Not eventually," Maelie said. "Tonight. I think I know what it is." She stood back and looked at the garage the way her grandfather had taught her, watching for the paths things took. The scratching happened only after dark, always near the back wall, always above the shelf where he kept his old maps of the river estuary, those curling charts of where the current met the sea. Nothing that scratched could be seen by day, so it had to be something hidden, something with a reason for coming out only at night. Her guess was that a mouse had found the bag of birdseed on the top shelf, but guesses were not enough for a science fair.

She looked up "hypothesis" in the dictionary on the workbench and frowned at what she found. "It comes from ancient Greek," she read slowly, "and it literally means 'putting or placing under.'"

"Under what?" Theo asked.

"That's all it says. Putting or placing under." She copied it onto an index card. A hypothesis, she decided, was like the board's foundation, the guess you placed under everything else, and the experiment stood on top of it. If the experiment collapsed, you had guessed wrong.

That evening she set two traps. One went beside the birdseed on the top shelf, where her mouse idea said it belonged. The other went under the trash can, in case the sound was traveling along the wall from somewhere lower and fooling her ears. Sound could do that, bounce and mislead. In the morning she found the top trap sprung, a seed hull beside it, and a gray whiskered shape gone, but the trail of hulls led up behind the maps and through a gap into the ceiling. Her guess had been placed in the right spot after all, and it had held.

At the fair, the judge paused at her board. "So your hypothesis was supported," she said.

Maelie touched the index card glued beneath the title. "It means putting or placing under," she said. "The Greek. I looked it up." She thought of her grandfather, who had wanted her to keep the workshop, and how she had almost said no; that choice still sat with her, not fully settled. The judge smiled and moved on, and Maelie straightened the card so it sat exactly under the words above it.

Brody sat on the flat wooden bench behind the baseball diamond, his right arm sweating inside its white cast. Six weeks, the doctor had said, and that was two weeks ago. Across the field, Coach Delgado was running drills, and Brody watched every throw like he could absorb it through his eyes.

His grandfather lowered himself onto the bench beside him with a grunt. Grandpa's left wrist wore a cast too, tan colored and dented at the thumb. "Ten weeks for me," Grandpa said, wiggling his fingers. "You'll beat me out of mine by a month, I'd wager."

Brody frowned. Same kind of break, he knew that much. He had been there in June when Grandpa tripped on the porch step, and three weeks later Brody had landed wrong diving for a line drive, and the x-rays had looked almost identical, side by side on the light board. Same bone, same crack, same doctor. So why ten weeks for Grandpa and six for him?

That was the question he turned over all through batting practice. It was plausible that the doctor just liked kids better, but that seemed weak. It was plausible that Grandpa's break was secretly worse, except the x-rays had matched. Brody liked explanations he could test.

So he tested one. At halftime of his sister's soccer game the next Saturday, he walked the sideline with a notebook and asked every person he could find who had ever broken a bone: how old were you, and how long was the cast on. Marcus, age twelve, five weeks. Marcus's mom, age thirty-eight, nine weeks. The referee had broken his ankle at forty-five and spent three months in a boot. By the end of the afternoon Brody had twelve names, and the pattern jumped right off the page. Every kid was out of a cast faster than every grown-up.

He showed the notebook to his grandfather on Sunday. Grandpa read it slowly, tapped the column of numbers, and laughed. "Young bones heal faster than old ones. Kids spend less time in a cast than adults with the same break." He shook his head. "Sixty-eight years old and learning it from a thirteen-year-old with a notebook."

The day Brody's cast came off, the nurse cut it away with a little buzzing saw and let the sunlight expose his pale, skinny arm to the air for the first time in a month. It looked strange, like it belonged to a younger kid. Outside, Grandpa was waiting in the truck with the window down and the ball bag already loaded.

"Think that arm still works?" Grandpa asked.

Brody rolled down the window the rest of the way, picked up a baseball from the seat, and fired it straight into his grandfather's glove.

The guest bedroom was the coldest room in the house, and Hazel knew it before she even opened the door. The floorboards chilled her bare feet, and the air smelled like dust and old lavender sachets from the closet. Her grandmother would sleep here for a whole week, starting tonight, and Hazel wanted everything to be perfect.

"You can have my quilt too," Hazel said, dragging the heavy blue bundle down the hall. "It's the warmest thing we own."

"That's kind of you, sweetheart." Grandma set her suitcase on the bed, moving with her usual careful steps. On the first night, Hazel checked on her before bed and found her tucked under both quilts, hands wrapped around a teacup she'd brought upstairs herself, her fingertips pale as paper. Grandma smiled and said the room was lovely. The radiator under the window was barely warm when Hazel pressed her palm against it.

She couldn't stop thinking about it the next morning. She remembered a school trip to the butterfly house two years ago, when the guide had explained that bees pollinate flowers by carrying pollen on their fuzzy legs, and how a small thing doing quiet work could keep something alive without anyone noticing. Her grandmother's cold hands felt like that, a small quiet signal of something bigger. So Hazel typed her question into the library computer, half sure she was being dramatic, and found what she needed in a paragraph she read three times: older adults face a greater risk of hypothermia than younger adults, a dangerous drop in body temperature, and they can get it even in a house that doesn't seem that cold, because they may not complain.

That afternoon she found her father arguing with her uncle on the phone about whether to replace the old furnace, a family controversy that had raged since Thanksgiving. Hazel waited until her father hung up, then showed him the paragraph on her screen.

"Hypothermia," she said. "That's what it's called. Grandma's room is freezing and she keeps saying it's fine."

Her father pressed his hand to the guest room radiator, the way Hazel had, and frowned. "You noticed something I missed," he said. "Let's fix it."

They carried up the space heater from the basement, and Hazel, who was small and agile, squeezed behind the dresser to plug it in where nobody else could reach. When Grandma came up after dinner, the room was toasty, and the smell of lavender had softened into something almost like a garden in July. Hazel watched her grandmother pull off the second quilt and settle in with just the sheet, her fingers pink again as she turned the pages of her novel.

"There was a drafty farm house where I raised your mother," Grandma said, patting the bed beside her. "I survived it, but I'm not sorry to skip that part this time." Hazel kicked off her slippers and climbed up next to her, tucking her cold toes under the warm edge of the blue quilt.

Mya's best friend Priya had been acting strange since Tuesday, and the only clue was a photo. It showed Priya's cat, Mr. Whiskers, sleeping on a windowsill, and Priya had sent it to the whole sixth-grade chat with the message "Guess where I am right now!" Everyone guessed the mall, the new pizza place, the library. Nobody guessed right, and Priya just replied with a smirking face and said "Nope, somewhere I shouldn't be."

That was the problem. Priya was supposed to be at her grandmother's house all week, recovering from the flu. Mya knew it because she had walked Priya's route home on Friday, carrying the homework packet like a good friend, and Priya's mom had said so at the door. So where was she, and why the secret?

At lunch on Thursday, Mya leaned over Devon's shoulder in the cafeteria. Devon was the kid everyone went to with phone problems, the one who could fix a cracked screen with tape and patience. "Can I see Priya's cat photo?" Mya asked. "Not the chat. The actual file." Devon raised an eyebrow but forwarded it, and Mya pressed and held the image until a menu appeared, then tapped the little "i" in a circle. A page of details filled the screen. Date, size, camera model. And then, lower down, a map.

The map had a single pin on it. Mya zoomed in, her heart going quick and light. The pin sat on a street she recognized, because she had walked it on Friday. It was Priya's own street, three houses down from where Mya had stood at the door. The photo hadn't just shown a cat. It had shown exactly where the cat was.

"It's called EXIF metadata," Devon said, peeking over. "My cousin learned about it after a whole controversy at her school. The phone writes the exact GPS coordinates of where the photo was taken into hidden data in the file." He shrugged. "Location services were on."

Mya stared at the pin. So Priya was home after all, hiding out for some reason, and now a whole chat of forty kids could technically see it too. She thought about how Mr. Whiskers would be resilient to this sort of thing, cats never worried about being found, but Priya was not a cat. Mya decided to invest her lunch period in figuring out the rest. She texted Priya directly: "You're on your own street. I saw the map. You okay?"

Three dots appeared. Then stopped. Then appeared again. The reply came before the bell: "Don't tell anyone. There's a fox den in my backyard and I've been filming the babies all week. My mom said no visitors till I'm better. Coming to show you at recess."

Adam had one job at the farmers' market: buy a jar of Mr. Ruiz's wildflower honey before it sold out. His grandmother's birthday was Saturday, and she'd said last month that his honey was the only thing she wanted. The problem was that everyone else's grandmother seemed to want it too, because Mr. Ruiz charged four dollars a jar when the other honey sellers charged nine.

By the time Adam reached the stall, the line stretched past the bread stand and curved around the corner. A woman near the front turned around and called back, "He's down to his last crate!" A groan rolled down the line like a wave. Adam stood on a crate to coordinate with his friend Priya, who was saving spots for each other whenever one of them needed to dash off, and waved to show her where he was. She held up two fingers. Twenty minutes from the front, maybe.

When Adam finally got there, a handwritten sign leaned against the empty crate: SOLD OUT, BACK NEXT WEEK. Next week was after the birthday. He stared at the sign, then at Mr. Ruiz, who was apologizing to person after person behind Adam. "Four dollars is my price," the man kept saying, shrugging. "I sell out by nine every week, and I hate turning folks away, but that's just what happens when more people want it than I've got." Adam walked back along the line, and it hit him: every single person still waiting wanted honey at four dollars. If it cost nine, like at the stall next door, half of them would probably walk away, and there would still be jars left. The gap between the crowd and the crates was the whole story.

"It's called a shortage," Priya said when he told her, still holding her tote bag. "My sister tried to get concert tickets last month. Cheap ones gone in four minutes, and hundreds of fans got nothing. She said that's the word for it, when the price is kept low and more people want the thing than there are things to sell." Adam looked back at Mr. Ruiz's empty crates, feeling the shape of the idea settle into place.

At the next stall, though, a farmer was practically hiding behind towers of zucchini. "Take a bag, take two," she told Adam, dropping the price from two dollars to one, then to fifty cents. Nobody wanted zucchini in August, not this much of it. Priya bought three and didn't even like zucchini. Adam bought a bag too, feeling a small flush of embarrassment for Mr. Ruiz and his stubborn four dollars, but also a plan forming.

"Could you do a trade?" he asked the woman. "My neighbor will trade you zucchini bread for honey. She does it every fall." The farmer thought, then nodded slowly. "Tell her to bring the bread Sunday. I've got jars." Adam texted his neighbor from the corner of the market, and she sent back a thumbs-up and three exclamation points. He walked home carrying zucchini for his grandmother's birthday bread, honey already promised, and Mr. Ruiz's empty crates still in his mind, waiting for next week.

Adam sat in his dad's car outside the gym, and his stomach did a slow flip, like a fish turning over in a bucket. His heart was hammering too, fast and loud, and he hadn't even opened the door yet. Beside him, his best friend Marcus was bouncing one knee against the glove box, which was his own kind of drumbeat.

"You look like you're going to throw up," Marcus said.

"I'm not. It's just that feeling. My stomach's doing backflips and my heart's racing like there's a generator inside my chest running at full speed." Adam stared through the windshield at the stream of kids heading for the doors, laughing, shoving each other, carrying glow sticks that had already been snapped and shook. "And it's weird, because I'm excited. I've been excited all week."

"Then why does your body act like it's an emergency?"

Adam thought about that. In science they'd done a unit on stress, and something clicked into place. "Okay, listen. When you're nervous, your body releases this stuff called adrenaline. It speeds up your heart, and it pulls blood away from your stomach." He tapped his own stomach. "That's the butterflies. That's all it is. Your stomach's just not getting the blood."

Marcus squinted at him. "You made that up."

"Ask Ms. Rivera Monday. But think about it. I'm nervous about the dance, so adrenaline kicks in, my heart goes fast, and my stomach flips because the blood got pulled somewhere else. Butterflies. It's not me actually being sick. It's a pattern, and once you know the pattern, you can outsmart it."

Marcus's knee was still going. "How do you outsmart butterflies?"

"That's the part I want to test." Adam reached for the door handle. "My theory is that if I just get in there and start moving, the nerves will burn off. Sitting still insulates them. Like keeping them warm and safe. Moving breaks them up."

"You sound like a health video," Marcus said, but he was grinning, and the grin was infectious, spreading to Adam even before they were out of the car. Marcus had his own mission tonight anyway: he'd promised the student council he'd get twenty kids to sign up for the spring talent show, and he'd brought a clipboard and three pens in his jacket pocket. He wanted to be the guy who made it happen.

They crossed the parking lot at almost a jog, weaving between cars still ticking as they cooled. At the doors, the music hit them like a wave, and Adam felt his heart give one more huge thump. He decided to treat it as the starting gun.
