"There was some controversy at school last month when Mr. Reyes said planes aren't really sealed like spaceships, and half the class didn't believe him. Conventional wisdom says the cabin is just like sea level, but it isn't, not exactly." He wrote out the plan in his careful block letters: one fresh sealed bag of chips in the backpack, one in the carry-on, checked at takeoff, mid-flight, and landing. If his idea was right, both bags would puff up hard somewhere over the ocean on the way home, then go soft again after they landed.

Their mom, who had been pretending to read her novel across the aisle, handed them a bag of peanuts without a word. Maya held it up. "Sealed at the factory," she said. "Want to save it for the flight home?" Theodore took it and tucked it into the front pocket of his backpack, right next to the notebook, and wrote one more line at the top of the page: Peanut bag, trial number one.

The lights went out at 8:40, right in the middle of Brooklyn's game, and the screen died to black. Her little brother Theo groaned from the couch. Their mom found the candles in the kitchen drawer, the ones shaped like pinecones that smelled like a fake forest, and set three of them on the coffee table. The flames leaned sideways whenever anyone walked past, throwing wobbly shadows up the wall.

"I was about to beat the whole level," Theo said.

"Beat it tomorrow." Brooklyn stared at the dark television. Then she remembered something her cousin Dev had told her last summer, after a storm knocked out power across his whole network of streets. He had lost his desktop computer that night. When the electricity came back on, he said, a surge of power had shot through the house and fried the machine. Emergency agencies told people to unplug their computers and other electronics during a power cut, because when the power returned, the surge could damage them.

"I didn't believe him at first," she said out loud, crouching behind the TV. "I thought he spilled juice on it and made up the surge thing." She pulled the console's plug from the wall and coiled the cord around her hand. Next she went to the desk in the corner and unplugged the desktop computer, then the router blinking dark on the shelf, then the microwave in the kitchen. Theo followed her with a candle, dripping wax onto a plate he carried like a waiter.

"What if the power comes back on while you're asleep?" he asked.

"That's the point. It can come back any time, and everything plugged in gets hit." She pointed at the lamp by the couch. "That one too, please."

The power stayed off until after 10. They played shadow puppets on the ceiling, and Theo made a shape he claimed was an authentic wolf, though it looked more like a rabbit with big ears. Brooklyn drew a map of the neighborhood in her notebook, trying to depict which streets might be dark, guessing it was just their block since the kitchen window showed lights glowing two houses down.

At 10:20 the ceiling fan spun once, the lamps blazed on, and the refrigerator started humming in the kitchen. The television screen stayed black and quiet, its plug lying on the floor where Brooklyn had left it. She smiled at it, then went around the room picking up her candles.

"Tomorrow, level twelve," Theo said. "Nobody fried."

"Nobody fried," Brooklyn said, and blew out the last pinecone.

The group chat lit up at 4:32 on a Tuesday. Marisol sent a screenshot of an old blog with a purple background and a clipart frog in the corner, followed by three crying-laughing emojis. "WAIT," she typed. "This is Dani's blog from third grade. It's still ONLINE."

Jonathan tapped the link. Sure enough, there was Dani's handwriting, scanned in, a whole page about her dream of owning forty-two hamsters. Below the frog, small gray letters said the page had been saved by something called the Wayback Machine. "What is that," he typed, "a time machine for frogs?"

"It's real," Dani answered, and he could tell from her short replies that she was not laughing. "Since 1996 the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages, and anyone can look at old versions of sites. My mom just showed me. That's how Marisol found it."

Marisol apologized right away, typing fast. Jonathan scrolled down the old page instead. Near the bottom, under a post about the class talent show, Dani had written her old address and a map to her house so friends could come to her birthday party. Forty-two hamsters, he thought, and one home address, sitting in an archive where anybody could read it.

He remembered his own post from last spring, the video of his dog Biscuit in the backyard, with the school name visible on his gym shirt in the background. He had deleted the video in June. He typed to the chat: "Meet me in the library computer lab tomorrow. I want to test something." Then, because it was Dani's page that started this, he added, "Bring that link. I want to see how far back it goes."

The next day, four of them crowded around one screen. They opened the archive and searched for Dani's blog. There it was, captured over and over, year after year, like a photo album nobody had asked for. Jonathan felt his stomach go quiet. "So deleting doesn't really delete," he said. "If a page was public, a copy might live there anyway." He tried to mimic the casual voice of someone who had known this all along, but nobody was fooled. Marisol put her hand on the back of his chair.

He pulled up his own deleted video account next, searching in a systematic way, page by page, checking dates. Not there. He let out a breath, then stopped himself, because Dani was still staring at her old address on the screen. He slid the keyboard toward her. "You could write to them," he said. "There's a contact page."

That night Dani sent the group a photo of the message she had submitted, asking politely if the page could be taken down. Two days later came her reply: "It's gone. And my new blog has hamsters, no frogs, and no addresses." Jonathan typed back, "Forty-two hamsters deserves a fresh page."

Gabrielle slid a folded paper across the dinner table, past the mashed potatoes, until it stopped against her brother Marcus's glass of milk. "Read the first line," she said.

Marcus picked it up with his fork hand. "'The city should paint a crosswalk at Fifth and Maple.'" He lowered the paper. "That's your opinion. The council gets a hundred of those a week."

"It's not just an opinion." Gabrielle pulled a crumpled notebook from her backpack and opened it to a page covered in tally marks. "I sat at that corner after school on Tuesday and Thursday. I counted eleven times when somebody almost got hit because there's no place to cross. Eleven near-misses in two days."

Their dad set down his serving spoon. "You counted near-misses? For how long?"

"Forty minutes each time." She tapped the tallies. "So when I say the city should paint a crosswalk, it's still my opinion, right? But an opinion with evidence behind it is more convincing than one with no reasons at all. Marcus's opinion is just words. Mine has eleven tallies."

Marcus frowned at the notebook. "Fine, it's more convincing than mine. But the council meeting is tomorrow at four. That's your deadline, right? You need signatures tonight."

"That's the problem." Gabrielle pushed her peas around her plate. "I thought I'd get spontaneous support, people just signing because it's obviously dangerous. But Mrs. Okafor next door said no. She wants proof. And I have proof, I just don't know if it's enough to sustain a whole argument, or if it's only a start."

"What else could you count?" her dad asked.

Gabrielle stared at the tally marks, then out the dark window toward the corner she couldn't see. She wondered whether more cars sped up on that stretch than on Oak Street, and whether you could even measure that without a radar gun. What about the number of kids who crossed there every day because the bus stop is on the wrong side? She flipped to a clean page and started writing questions faster than her handwriting could keep up.

"Slow down," Marcus said, watching her. "You have until four tomorrow, not four tonight."

"The bus comes at 7:10 tomorrow morning." Gabrielle was already standing, notebook in hand, chair scraping back. "If I'm there before school, I can count every kid who crosses. Then I'll have two kinds of proof."

She ran for the stairs, then stopped halfway and turned around. "Marcus, bring your watch. I need someone to time the forty minutes."

He sighed and drained his milk. "Fine. But you're carrying the clipboard."

Isabelle crouched in aisle four of Holloway's Garden Center, holding a carrot seed packet in one hand and a bean packet in the other. The packets felt papery and old, and the air smelled like wet soil and green tomato vines. She had one week before the county's junior grower contest, which required proof that a vegetable had been planted and sprouted by the entry deadline.

"Carrots by Saturday, huh?" said Marcus, balancing a bag of potting mix on his shoulder. "That's fast."

"The contest just needs them planted and sprouted," Isabelle said. "The rules permit sprouted seeds, not full plants. So they only have to poke up out of the dirt." She shook the carrot packet. Inside, the seeds rattled like sand. She tore the corner and shook one into her palm. It was flat and tiny, smaller than a comma in a book. Marcus opened the bean packet and tipped out a seed the size of his thumbnail, wrinkled and brown.

She frowned. Back in the spring she had planted beans in her grandmother's garden, dropping each one into a hole deep enough to bury a marble. The beans had come up in a week, fat and green. But her grandmother had also shown her a trick for carrots, barely scratching the soil surface and dusting the seeds over like pepper. "Carrots get a sprinkle," Gran had said, tapping the packet. "Beans get a real hole." Isabelle turned both seeds over in her palm and squinted at them.

"I think I see it," she said slowly. "A seed goes in about two to three times as deep as it is wide. Look. This bean is this big around." She held up her thumb and finger, spaced apart. "So it goes in about that deep, maybe a little more. And the carrot seed is barely anything, so it goes in barely anything at all. Almost on top." Marcus leaned in and compared the two seeds side by side, then nodded like something had clicked.

They bought both packets with Isabelle's birthday money and raced home before the rain. In the backyard, Marcus dug bean holes with two fingers while Isabelle pressed each bean in about twice its own width and patted the soil firm. For the carrots she scattered the seeds across the bed and sifted a whisper of dirt over them, no thicker than the seeds themselves. They watered gently so the tiny ones wouldn't wash away, and every evening afterward Isabelle patrolled the bed with a flashlight after dark, checking for slugs, which were nocturnal and always left slimy trails on the leaves by morning.

On the sixth day, the rain stopped long enough for sun. Isabelle knelt at the carrot bed and saw them: hundreds of hair-thin green threads, bent like tiny question marks, pushing out of the soil. The beans had already unfurled their first pair of leaves, fat and cheerful. She ran inside, grabbed the contest entry form, and wrote the date at the top. Then she carried her phone out to the garden, knelt down, and took a photo of the sprouts glistening in the morning light. "Look at you," she whispered. "Come on, carrots. Grow."

The bleachers smelled like hot dogs and cut grass, and Violet's whole family had claimed the middle rows for the championship game between the Riverside Rockets and the Northside Bears. Her uncle Marco was already hoarse from yelling, and the game had not even started. "The crowd wins games," he kept shouting, drumming his fists on the railing. "That's the whole point of home field!" Violet frowned. She wanted the Rockets to win, and she wanted to believe Uncle Marco, but something about his claim bugged her, like a math problem with a step missing.

She thought back to two winters ago, when she had watched football at her grandmother's apartment during the year of the empty stadiums. The TV had shown rows and rows of vacant seats, and the games had felt strange and quiet, like a forest with no birds. Grandma had read the season totals out loud from her newspaper at the time, and the numbers had stuck in Violet's head ever since. She pulled out her phone now and searched until she found the page again, just to be sure.

"Uncle Marco," she said, tugging his sleeve during a timeout. "You know the season when almost nobody was allowed in the stadiums? Home teams finished 127 wins, 128 losses, and one tie. There was basically no home advantage at all." Marco blinked at her. Her cousin Jayden leaned over. "Wait, so cheering does nothing?" Violet shrugged. "It did nothing that year, at least. Maybe it's something else about home field. Maybe it's the players, not us." Marco looked wounded, like she had told him his cooking was bad. "Fine, science girl," he said. "Test it. Next few plays, nobody cheers. Then everybody goes wild. See what happens."

Violet felt a little thrill. An experiment, right here in the bleachers. She asked the families around them, and even a man with a foam finger agreed to stay silent for the next three plays. The stadium went oddly quiet, and the Rockets gave up a sack. Then she raised both arms, and the whole section erupted. The next play, the Bears intercepted the ball anyway. Marco threw up his hands. "That proves nothing!" Jayden laughed. "You need way more plays than that. That's the point, isn't it? One moment can't tell you anything." Violet nodded. Three plays was noise, not a pattern.

So they kept going, quiet then loud, loud then quiet, marking each result in her notebook, and by the fourth quarter she had a messy little chart that proved absolutely nothing except that the Rockets were aggressive on defense no matter what the crowd did. When the final interception sealed the win, Marco swept her up in a hug anyway. "All right," he admitted. "Maybe the cheering is for us." Violet grinned and waved her notebook above her head like a trophy. "Best data I ever salvaged from a blowout," she said, and Jayden said, "Save me a seat for the rematch."

Kayla laced her sneakers at the kitchen table while her mom buttered toast, because today was her first day volunteering at the River Street Food Bank. "Remember when you were six," her mom said, "and you cried because we threw out the jack-o'-lantern?" Kayla laughed. She had wanted to keep it on the porch forever, and when it softened and collapsed, she had buried it under the maple tree with a popsicle-stick marker. She still couldn't stand seeing food thrown away, which was exactly why she had signed up to volunteer.

The food bank smelled like cardboard and oranges. A supervisor named Dara handed Kayla a box of donated groceries from Hartman's Market: lettuce with brown edges, apples with dents, peppers that had gone soft in spots. "Sort the good from the not good," Dara said. "Blemished is fine. Rotten is not."

Kayla worked down the row, but a question kept nagging her. These vegetables weren't rotten, they were just ugly or slightly old, and the store had gotten rid of them anyway. She counted the box quickly: forty-two items, and thirty-one were still perfectly good if you cut around the spots. That was more than half saved from the trash. She wondered how big that number would get if you counted every store, every kitchen, every school cafeteria in the whole country.

She found Dara stacking cans. "Do you know how much food in the whole United States just gets wasted, never eaten?" Dara smiled. "Actually, yes. The Department of Agriculture estimates between 30 and 40 percent of the U.S. food supply is wasted." Kayla stared. Out of every ten boxes like this one, three or four never fed anybody at all.

She wanted to test it. At home that afternoon, she pulled everything out of her own refrigerator and counted: sixty items. If the estimate held for her family too, somewhere between eighteen and twenty-four of them would end up in the garbage. She made a plan, writing it on the whiteboard by the fridge. Leftover rice became fried rice. Soft apples became applesauce. The half-onion went into soup. By the end of the week the trash can was nearly empty, and her little brother, Marcus, who usually complained about leftovers, asked for seconds of the applesauce and said it tasted better than the store kind, almost like something from the artisan bakery downtown, the way the whole house smelled like cinnamon.

At her next shift, Kayla told Dara about the experiment, and Dara gave her a new job: teaching the sorting table to keep slightly blemished fruit out of the discard bin. "You have a distinct talent for this," Dara said, handing her a permanent marker to label the rescue crate. Kayla wrote RESCUED on the side in big letters, then set a rescued apple on top, where everybody could see it.

Emmett slid the phone box across the kitchen table, but his mother held her palm over it. "Rules first," she said. The lamplight caught the syrup bottle and the folded newspaper, relics of a Saturday breakfast that had ended an hour ago.

"One hour on school nights," she said. "It charges in the kitchen at bedtime, not in your room." Emmett argued that everyone in seventh grade took their phones to bed, and she argued back that she wasn't everyone's mother, and that after the recession had chewed through their savings, a phone at all was a gift they'd had to be frugal to manage. That word landed on him like a wet towel. He stopped trying to justify keeping it upstairs and signed the paper she pushed toward him, a contract with his own shaky signature.

For five nights the phone sat in the kitchen drawer at bedtime, and for five nights Emmett fell asleep within minutes of his head hitting the pillow. He didn't notice anything, because there was nothing to notice. On Friday night his mother was out, and he crept downstairs, opened the drawer, and lay on the couch in the dark scrolling through videos until nearly midnight. When he finally climbed the stairs, his eyes felt like they'd been rinsed in cold soda, wide awake behind his lids. He lay in bed listening to the furnace tick, counting to five hundred, then starting over. His sister's slow breathing came through the wall. Two o'clock. Then almost three.

At breakfast he fell asleep sitting up, his cheek drifting toward the cold table. His sister poked his arm. "What did you do last night?" she asked, and he told her, defensive at first, then quieter, because a pattern was forming in his head like dots on graph paper. Dark room plus no phone equaled sleep. Dark room plus glowing screen equaled staring at the ceiling for hours. "It's the screen," he said slowly. "It only happens on screen nights."

"You want to know the word for what you messed up?" his sister said, chewing. "Melatonin. It's the hormone that makes you sleepy." She said their science teacher had explained that blue-enriched light from screens can reduce or delay melatonin being released in the evening, and Emmett had been bathing his eyes in it until midnight.

Saturday night he put the phone in the drawer himself, before anyone asked. He set his alarm the old way, on the clock radio shaped like a rocket, and lay in the dark listening to his own breathing slow down, the hallway light a thin gold line beneath his door. From downstairs, faintly, came the drawer sliding shut, his mother's hand, then nothing at all.

The lights went out at 7:42, and Eve knew the exact time because she had been watching the clock, counting the minutes until her cupcakes came out of the oven. The oven went dark too, along with the refrigerator, the hallway light, and the whole city block outside the window. Her little brother Theo crawled out from under the kitchen table with a flashlight and nominated himself Chief of Darkness, which meant he got to hold the flashlight and shine it wherever he wanted.

The real problem, as Eve saw it, was the freezer. Mom was stuck at work until ten, and the note on the counter said leftovers, chicken, peas, be careful. Eve stood in front of the closed freezer door and reasoned it out. Cold air sinks, she thought, so every time someone opened the door, the coldest air spilled out the bottom like water from a cracked glass. The rule she made up was simple: nobody opens the freezer, not even Chief of Darkness, not even to check. Theo agreed, mostly because Eve let him nominate the flashlight as an official member of their alliance against the blackout.

They ate crackers and cheese on the living room floor and watched the building across the street, where some apartments still glowed with candlelight. Theo asked questions about whether the ice cream would melt, and Eve said she didn't know yet, which was the honest answer. She put her hand flat on the freezer door now and then, as if she could feel through the porous old seal, but of course she couldn't. What was happening inside was invisible, and she hated that.

At 9:15 the lights came back, all at once, and the refrigerator hummed like it had never stopped. Mom arrived twenty minutes later with a phone in her hand and worry in her face. "How long was it off?" she asked, and Eve told her, an hour and a half. Mom bit her lip. "The chicken. If it's thawed, it has to go."

"Wait," Eve said, and pulled out the bag of chicken. It was still hard as a brick, with frost on the plastic. Then she took out the peas and opened the bag so Mom could see. Inside, among the loose green dots, tiny ice crystals glittered in the kitchen light.

"Look," Eve said. "Still ice crystals. I found it on the food safety site while the power was out, on my phone. Thawed food can be refrozen if it still has ice crystals, or if it's forty degrees Fahrenheit or below."

Mom felt the chicken with her fingers, then held the phone and read the whole line herself, including the part about four degrees Celsius. "Alliance of the freezer," she said, and held up her hand for a high five. Theo shined the flashlight on the peas one more time, like a soldier inspecting his troops, and slid the bag back onto the shelf.

Tyler sat on Marcus's bedroom floor with the phone glowing in his hands, scrolling up and down the same conversation for the third time. It was a thread with Jayla, started two days ago, and something about it had gone wrong, though he could not point to where.

"Read this," he said, holding the screen out to Marcus. The last message said Okay. That's fine. See you Monday.

Marcus squinted at it. The translucent curtain shifted in the window breeze, throwing pale light across the screen. "What am I looking at?"

"She's mad at me. I can feel it. But look at the words. They're fine."

"Then she's not mad."

"She didn't answer my last three texts for a whole day, and when she did answer, it had periods in it. Every sentence. Period, period, period." Tyler tapped the screen. "When she's normal, she writes like okay and lol see u. No periods anywhere."

Marcus leaned back against his bed and laughed. "You're mad because of punctuation."

"You don't get it. It's a different tone. It's like she's texting me from inside a glass box." Tyler remembered the fight they'd had last summer, the one he still wasn't sure he should have walked away from, and how she'd ended that argument with a single word and a period too. He had thought about that message more times than he wanted to admit.

Marcus pulled out his own phone and typed for a minute, then turned it around. On the screen was an article about a small 2016 study by researchers at Binghamton University. "It says messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the same messages without one," Marcus read. "They tested it. People actually judged the periods."

"So I'm not crazy."

"You're not crazy. You're just dramatic." Marcus dropped the phone on the carpet. "So what are you going to do, eliminate the periods and pretend nothing happened?"

Tyler stared at the message thread. His thumb hovered over the keyboard. He could send a joke, or he could send the question he'd been avoiding since June, the one about whether walking away had been the right call. A joke would smooth it over. A question might start something he couldn't stop, like an infection that spreads through a whole friendship before you notice the first symptom.

He typed: You sounded mad in that last text. Are we okay?

He read it twice, deleted the period at the end, and sent it before he could change his mind. The typing bubble appeared almost instantly.

Luke signed his name at the folding table outside the old hardware store, where the neighborhood cleanup had started at nine sharp. He wanted the volunteer hours for school, but he also wanted to matter, and a trash grabber seemed like a small way to matter. He worked the chain-link fence along the alley, pulling out a flattened soccer ball, a boot, and a strip of pink insulation that somebody had wedged between the fence posts, probably to block a gap. It crumbled in his hands and made him itch, so he dropped it in the bag fast.

By eleven, the pile of filled bags stood taller than he did. A woman in a green polo shirt backed a van up to the curb and started loading them, and Luke noticed the words on her shirt: Riverside Community Food Bank.

"You take the trash?" he asked.

"We take everything we can. The city drops the bags at the transfer station, and we compost the food scraps for the community garden." She held out her hand. "I'm Dana. You're the kid who did the whole fence line."

"Luke." He helped her lift the last bag, and then, because the van was still half empty, he asked what else went in it. She told him she was heading back to the food bank to shelve Saturday's delivery. "Sweet potatoes," she said. "A whole bin of them."

Luke frowned. "Where do sweet potatoes come from in October? Nobody around here grows them."

"Want to come see? We need hands tomorrow morning."

He rode along. The food bank occupied a low building with a loading dock and shelves that looked like a grocery store, except everything was free. Dana showed him where the canned goods went, then pointed to a bin of sweet potatoes with dirt still on them. "Saturday morning we go out to the Hartwell farm. You in?"

Luke said yes before he really thought about it. On the drive home that night, though, he turned the problem over. The bin had been full. Farmers sold their crops. Why would a farmer hand over perfectly good sweet potatoes to strangers? He was pessimistic about the whole thing, and he decided he would test it the only way he could: he would go, watch, and count.

Saturday morning the field was brown and stubbled. A machine had already gone through, and at first Luke saw nothing but dirt. Then he spotted one, half buried like a stone. Then three more within a step. The harvester couldn't get every potato, and the ones it missed were still good. He filled a bucket, then another.

Dana knelt beside him with her own bucket. "It's called gleaning," she said, "gathering what's left in the field after harvest."

"And it all goes to the food bank?" Luke asked.

"Every bit. Mr. Hartwell calls us when the machine's done, and we send volunteers out."

Luke counted his buckets. Eleven, by noon, and that was just him. The truck took them back, and at the food bank he helped Dana integrate the new sweet potatoes into the produce section, sliding them in beside the onions so the shelf looked full.

A woman came through the line with two kids and took a bag of them. Luke watched her put them in her cart, and then he grabbed one more bucket from the stack by the door and headed back to the truck.

Anna sat cross-legged on the worn rug in her grandmother's living room, a practice book open on her knees. In three weeks she would chant from the Torah for her bat mitzvah, and her portion looked back at her like a puzzle: Hebrew letters in neat columns, tiny vowel dots below them, and curling symbols stacked above and below like musical birds on wires.

"You have the ambition," her grandmother said, setting down two glasses of mint tea, "now you need the patience." Anna traced one of the little curls with her finger. "What are these marks, Savta? They weren't in the email Rabbi Feld sent." Her grandmother just smiled and said Anna would find out herself at Thursday rehearsal, which felt like being handed a wrapped box and told not to open it.

All week Anna tested an idea. She covered the vowel dots with a strip of paper and tried to read a verse cold. The letters sat there, silent and stubborn. When she uncovered the dots and chanted the melody from the marks above, the words flowed again. So the little birds carried the tune, she reasoned, and the dots carried the sounds. Both of them were her crutches. What would happen if she had to read without crutches? The question itched.

On Thursday, in the sanctuary that smelled of wax and old wood, Rabbi Feld unrolled the Torah scroll on the long desk. Anna leaned over it and her stomach dropped. No vowel dots. No curling birds. Nothing but bare letters marching in parallel columns, the same words she had practiced, stripped of every clue she'd leaned on. "Where did the marks go?" she whispered.

"They were never there," Rabbi Feld said. "The scroll is written without vowels or musical marks."

Anna stared at the bare letters. So that was why her practice book existed at all. She had assumed the book was a convenience, a softened copy for kids. Now she understood it was the opposite: the only place the tune lived. She had to carry the melody and the vowels in her head before she ever touched the scroll. Every night until the ceremony, she would be negotiating between her eyes, which wanted the dots, and her memory, which had to supply them.

She went back to her grandmother's house and tried again with the paper strip, covering the vowels, then covering the melody marks, then both, chanting louder each time. Her grandmother turned the pages of her own book in the corner chair, tapping her foot to Anna's rhythm.

On the third try, the whole verse came out whole and unaided, rising and falling in the right places. Anna lifted the strip of paper like a flag. "Did you hear that?" she said. "No marks. All me."

Aiden opened the group chat for the Science Olympiad team at 7:03 p.m. and found forty-one unread messages, which was never good. The facts, as far as he could piece together from the wall of text, were these: Marcus had left his weather station project at home, Priya had told Mr. Okafor that the missing data had been collected when it hadn't, and she'd done it because Marcus had covered for her little brother the week before when the brother got caught sneaking into the gym. Everyone agreed on all of it. Nobody agreed on anything else.

"she LIED to a teacher," Devon typed. "the rest of the team worked hard on real data and she faked ours. that's a fairness thing. rules apply to everyone or they apply to no one."

"she was paying back a debt," Zoe answered. "Marcus protected her brother. you don't drop people who helped you. that's loyalty, devon, look it up."

Aiden read it twice. That was the strange part. Devon and Zoe weren't fighting about what had happened. They were fighting about what it meant, using the exact same forty-one messages as evidence. He thought about how light bends through a prism and comes out in different directions depending on the glass, how the same beam refracts into colors that weren't visible before. Same light in, different light out. He had a hypothesis: the facts weren't the problem at all. He decided to test it.

He typed: "devon, name one fact you and zoe disagree about. an actual fact."

The chat went quiet for a full minute, which in this group was like a year. Then Devon wrote, "okay. none. she did it, marcus owed her, okafor believed her. we agree."

"so you agree on every single fact," Aiden typed, "and you still land on opposite sides."

"yes???" Zoe sent, followed by the confused emoji and then, "oh."

Aiden's mom knocked on his door and said something about the weather forecast, precipitation moving in overnight, did he have his rain jacket by the door. "Yeah, in a minute," he said, because something was happening in the chat. Devon had sent a screenshot of the team rulebook, and Zoe had sent a photo of the poster in the gym that said WE TAKE CARE OF OUR OWN, and they were now arguing about which document mattered more, which was, Aiden realized, the same argument wearing a new shirt.

He tried one more test. "imagine priya covered for someone who was NOT her friend. devon, would you be madder or less mad?"

"same," Devon said.

"same," Zoe said, "but because it would be pointless loyalty."

Aiden laughed out loud, alone in his room, at two people typing "same" about opposite feelings. He typed, "wait. you both just said priya values something different than you do. devon you value fairness. zoe you value loyalty. nobody's wrong about the facts. you're not even wrong about the values. you just have different ones."

There was a long pause. Then Marcus, silent for the entire fight, finally appeared.

"guys. I'm quitting the team either way. I don't want priya taking heat for me," he wrote. "also aiden you type like a documentary narrator but you're right."

Zoe sent, "we could split into two teams. one for fairness, one for loyalty."

Devon sent, "that's the dumbest idea I've ever heard. I love it."

Aiden looked at the rain starting against his window and went to get his jacket, and when he came back there was a new chat, created by Zoe, named Team Loyalty, and another one already created by Devon, named Team Fairness, and both of them had added him at the same time.

Elena stared at her phone in the kitchen, waiting for Priya to reply. Three days now, and nothing, not even the eye-roll emoji. They used to text forty times a day. Then Priya made the soccer team and Elena joined robotics, and somehow the replies got shorter and slower until they stopped coming at all. Elena typed "u up?" into their thread, deleted it, and opened the family group chat instead, because if she kept watching the empty thread she was going to throw her phone into the sink.

"Question for the group," she posted. "How do you fix a friendship that's already broken?" Her dad replied with a thumbs up and the words "have you tried apologizing," which was useless. Her grandmother sent a voice memo, and Elena played it while stirring her after-school snack. "In my day we wrote letters," Grandma said, "and I'll tell you, the friendships that lasted were the ones where we stayed similar. When Terez and I got different jobs, that was the end." Her cousin Marco, who was in college, replied next: "Actually there's real research on this. A 2015 study followed 573 friendships formed in seventh grade. Friends who were less alike were more likely to see the friendship end."

Elena sat with that. She and Priya had been practically the same person in seventh grade, both obsessed with the same dumb cartoon, both terrible at dodgeball. Now they were less alike. So maybe the silence wasn't because Priya was mad. Maybe it was just the pattern doing what patterns do. She thought of her uncle, who owned a building downtown, always saying a good tenant helped the whole place thrive, but a volatile one could ruin everything, and the landlord had to act fast either way. Elena decided to act. If being less alike was the problem, then the fix wasn't to apologize for nothing. The fix was to find something new they both still cared about.

She scrolled back through months of Priya's messages looking for it, hunting for a topic that had survived the teams and the clubs. There. Eleven months ago Priya had gone on for two full screens about a mural going up near the library, the artist, the colors, everything. Elena had barely answered at the time because she'd been cramming for a math test. She opened a news app, found out the artist was painting another one this Saturday, and typed: "the mural artist you liked is doing a new one by the library sat. want to go watch and judge it really loudly?"

The typing bubble appeared. It disappeared. It appeared again. Elena held her breath so hard she got dizzy.

"I thought you were mad at ME," Priya wrote. "I was mad at YOU," Elena sent back, then: "we're both idiots." The reply came fast: "obviously. saturday. I'll bring snacks, you bring the loud judging." Elena dropped the phone on the counter and did a small, embarrassing victory spin in the kitchen, and behind her the group chat lit up with her grandmother writing, "so did my advice work."

Dex slammed his backpack onto the bench and slid into his spot at the table before Mom had even set down the lasagna. "You guys hear about Ridgemont's point guard? Flunked his math class, so he's off the roster for the playoffs." He tore a piece of bread in half, grinning. "Their whole season is toast."

Nora's fork stopped halfway to her plate. If it was true, her school's team, who had lost to Ridgemont twice this year, might actually have a shot at the city title. "Who told you?"

"Marcus heard it from some kid at the arcade."

"That's like four people away from anyone who knows anything," Nora said, though a warm, satisfying feeling was already spreading through her chest. Of course the guy was failing. Ridgemont players were exactly the type.

Mom sprinkled parmesan on her pasta and said she'd believe it when she saw it, since her commute home ran past Ridgemont and there had been players shooting on the outdoor courts, same as always. Nora ignored that. She wanted the story to be true, so it felt true, like a sweater that already fit.

That night, in her room, she pulled up the league website on her laptop, telling herself it would take two minutes. The site posted eligibility lists every Friday. She scrolled, chewing the inside of her cheek, and found the current roster. The point guard's name was still there, plain as anything. Then she checked the stats page, where the league listed every player's scoring next to the median for the whole league. He was three points above the median and playing Friday night against her school. She sat back, the warm feeling gone, replaced by something colder. She had repeated the story at lunch today to two friends, confidently, and she hadn't checked a single thing. She'd just believed it because it fit what she already thought about Ridgemont. In science class there was a poster about exactly this, and now she said the phrase out loud to her dark ceiling: "Confirmation bias."

The next morning she caught Dex at the bus stop. "That thing about the point guard isn't true. He's on the roster, and he's playing Friday."

Dex squinted at her. "You actually looked it up? Man, don't be so gullible about Marcus."

"I was gullible," Nora said. "I believed it because I wanted it to be true. That's the whole trick of it." She pulled out her phone and showed him the eligibility list, then made him watch while she texted the two friends she'd told: not true, sorry, I checked the league site.

At dinner that night, Mom asked how the lasagna was, and Dex shrugged and said the point guard had dropped thirty points on their team, so thanks a lot, Nora. She laughed so hard she nearly knocked over her water glass. "Next time I'll hope for a better rumor," she said, and speared another piece of lasagna.

The vase had been on the windowsill since September, blue with a chipped rim, and on Monday morning it lay in pieces on the floor. Mrs. Alvarez stood over the shards with her coffee mug in one hand and said, "Nobody's in trouble. I just want to know what happened."

Abigail's mind was already running through the possibilities. Dylan said he'd seen Marcus back there before first bell, reaching toward the window. Marcus insisted he'd only been closing the blinds because the sun was in his eyes. Priya claimed she heard a thump while she was at her locker, which meant the vase fell before Dylan even walked in. And Rosa said flatly that the window had been open and the wind must have knocked it off, though the night before had been dead calm.

"I don't get it," Abigail whispered to Priya. "They can't all be true, but they all sound so sure."

That certainty bothered her the most. Last winter, when she had the flu, her father had put on an old movie to keep her company on the couch, Akira Kurosawa's 1950 film Rashomon. Four witnesses described one crime, a samurai's death, and every single account contradicted the others. Her father had let her watch the whole thing without saying a word, and when it ended she'd asked, "So which one lied?" He'd only shrugged. She'd spent three days thinking about it before she understood that the real answer might be that none of them were exactly lying, and none were exactly right.

She raised her hand. "Quick question for everyone who was in the room. What color was the vase?"

"Blue," said Rosa and Priya together.

"Green," said Dylan.

Marcus said, "White, I think. Sort of whitish."

Mrs. Alvarez emphasized each word as she repeated it. "The vase was blue." She set down her mug and pulled up the attendance screen. "Marcus, Dylan, you were both in the hallway by the water fountain. Priya, you were at your locker down the hall. Rosa, you came in first." She paused. "Rosa, did you touch the shelf?"

Rosa's chin came up. "I moved it two inches. The sun was going to crack it someday anyway. I didn't think it would just fall."

"Two inches toward the edge," Mrs. Alvarez said quietly.

Rosa stared at the shards, and Abigail realized something else, too: Rosa had opened the window to air out the room, then forgotten, and the wind she denied had come later, after the vase was already teetering. Two half-true stories stacked on top of each other, like the ones in her father's movie.

"You're not in trouble," Mrs. Alvarez said again, softer this time. "But next time, just tell me the whole thing."

Rosa knelt and began picking up the blue pieces one by one.

At dinner Jaxson slid his phone across the table before his mother could tell him to put it away. "Read this headline," he said. "Kids who eat oatmeal get better grades. It's all over the internet today."

His older sister Priya leaned over, noodles still twirling on her fork. "So we should eat oatmeal every morning? Lucky you, you already do."

"That's the thing." Jaxson set down his fork. He had eaten oatmeal almost every day since second grade, and his grades were fine, but plenty of kids in his class who ate sugary cereal had better grades than he did. Something about the headline itched at him. "I want to know how they know it's the oatmeal."

"Maybe they asked a bunch of kids what they eat and what their grades are," Priya said.

"Okay, but what else do oatmeal kids have in common?" Jaxson pushed his peas around his plate while he thought. The steam from the pot of rice fogged the kitchen window, and his father was ladling out seconds, but Jaxson barely noticed. He kept seeing the chart from the article, two lines rising together like teammates. He remembered something else with two rising lines he'd seen in a video last month. "Wait. Ice cream sales go up in summer, and sunburns go up in summer, but ice cream doesn't cause sunburns. Hot weather causes both."

"So what's the hot weather here?" his father asked, sitting back down.

Jaxson grabbed a napkin and drew two wobbly arrows pointing at the same box. He speculated out loud, throwing out ideas faster than he could test them. "Maybe oatmeal kids have parents who make breakfast, and parents who make breakfast also check homework, and that's the actual thing. Or oatmeal is cheap and fast, so maybe those families just have calmer mornings."

"That would be tedious to check," Priya said, "but you could try. Ask your class."

The next day Jaxson did an annoying but simple thing. Between classes he asked eleven kids two questions: what they ate for breakfast, and whether anyone at home helped them study. He tallied the answers in the back of his notebook during lunch, then again after school because he smudged the first page. The pattern surprised him. The breakfast foods were all over the place, cereal, oatmeal, leftover pizza, but the kids with the best grades almost all had someone checking in about school, whatever was on their plates.

At dinner he laid the notebook on the table between the rice pot and the salad. "The oatmeal might not be doing anything. Both things could be caused by something else." Priya tapped his chart of arrows and grinned.

"From your perspective, does that mean I can stop making oatmeal?" his mother asked.

"Keep the oatmeal," Jaxson said, spooning up another bite. "I just want the headline to say the true thing."

Kaitlyn crouched between the tomato rows with her notebook open on her knee, and the tomato on the healthy plant stared back at her like it knew something she didn't. Two rows, same seeds, same soil, planted the same afternoon in April. The left row stood tall and green. The right row drooped, its leaves curling under like old paper. Something invisible was at work, and she intended to find out what.

Her first guess was water. "It's a hypothesis," she told her little brother, Danny, when he wandered over with a popsicle. "A testable guess. I have one, and I'm going to test it."

"Sounds trivial to me," Danny said, working on the popsicle with great concentration. "They're plants. They droop. Big deal."

The bee numbers were down this year, everyone at the garden said so, the whole population in a recession, and Kaitlyn had already ruled out pollination, since the bees that did show up seemed happy to pollinate both rows equally. It wasn't the bees. She was almost sure it was the water, since the drooping row sat closer to the fence, where the sprinkler's arc might fall short.

So she tested it. She dragged a watering can down the droopy row every morning, a good soaking, and within a week the plants perked up. Case closed, she wrote in her notebook. Except they didn't stay perked. They sagged again, worse, and one of them turned yellow at the bottom. Kaitlyn stood there feeling like the notebook had lied to her.

Then she noticed the hose. Her mother had been rinsing the compost bin on the far side of the fence, and the runoff pooled near the drooping row every evening, standing in a low, sunken patch of ground. Kaitlyn's extra morning watering had landed on top of evening runoff, and the sick row was sitting in mud while the healthy row drained fine. Too much water, not too little. Her test had told her the wrong answer, and she wanted to know why. She looked at her notebook, then at the two rows, and saw it. In her test, the two rows had not been treated the same except for the water. The sick row also had the sunken ground, the afternoon shade from the fence, and the runoff. Everything was different, so the test had proved nothing at all.

She started over with two pots of the same seeds, same size, same soil from the same bag, set side by side on the flat part of the patio where the shade fell evenly. Same amount of water, measured to the line on a jar. Same spot, so the temperature stayed the same for both. Same timing, morning and morning, seven o'clock sharp, because that was the part Danny was in charge of, and Danny took the job suspiciously seriously for someone who called the whole project trivial. Two weeks later one pot stood green and the other, the one she'd doubled the water for, drooped in exactly the curling-paper way.

She wrote a single line at the bottom of the page and turned the notebook toward Danny. "Same amount, same temperature, same timing, everything the same except the one thing I'm testing," she read out loud. "And now the answer's actually the answer."

Danny licked the last of his popsicle off the stick. "So it was too much water all along?"

"It was too much water all along," Kaitlyn said, and closed the notebook with a snap.

Aurora had sixty-two dollars in her pocket and one hour before her mom picked her up at the food court, and she intended to spend both on the new Drift sneakers everyone at school was suddenly wearing. She had saved since March, skipping the fall festival and two movie nights, and last week she had even told her grandmother the money was for "plumbing repairs" on her locker, which still made her wince when she thought about it. She crossed the shiny tile floor toward the shoe store, past a kiosk where a sign shouted, "The hoodie EVERYONE is talking about!" Above it, a TV screen showed the rapper Zay Marlow holding up the same hoodie and saying it was the softest thing he'd ever worn. Aurora slowed down. She had almost bought that hoodie in September, until she saw the price.

Inside the shoe store, the Drifts glowed on a backlit wall like something holy. A banner read "LIMITED. LEGENDARY. LOVED BY MILLIONS." She turned a display box and found Zay Marlow's face on that too, grinning, with the words "Zay says: unstoppable." Last month she would have carried the box straight to the register. But something had changed after Saturday, when she was scrolling reviews for a phone case she wanted.

She'd been watching a girl named FoxiiBee raving about the case, calling it flawless, calling it life-changing, and Aurora had been one tap from buying when she noticed the tiny "#ad" in the caption. She'd looked it up, frowning at her phone in the kitchen, and learned that in the United States, the Federal Trade Commission requires influencers and celebrities to clearly disclose when they were paid or given free products to promote something. She'd scrolled back through three more of FoxiiBee's videos. Two had the tag. The video for the phone case did not, and neither did a blurry story that said "gifted!!" with no other marking.

Now, in the store, she asked a clerk with a silver nose ring, "Does Zay Marlow actually buy these shoes, or did Drift just send them to him?" The clerk laughed. "They send him a whole pallet. He's under contract. There's supposed to be a disclosure somewhere, you know, so it complies with the FTC rule. It's on their website, I think, in tiny print." Aurora picked up the box and studied the back, angling it so it sat perpendicular to the shelf edge, letting the light catch the fine print near the barcode. There it was, smaller than the size chart: "Compensated endorsement."

She stood there weighing the shoes in her hands. They were well made; she could feel that. Millions of people did love them, though that banner also told her exactly what the company wanted her to think. Maybe Zay liked them too. Maybe he'd have liked anything they paid him enough to like.

At the register, she set the box down and then, slowly, slid it back toward herself. "I'll take them," she said, "but I'm going to wear them because I like them, not because a rapper got a pallet." The clerk grinned and rang her up. As she walked out, she passed the hoodie kiosk again and shot the sign a look. "Everyone," she muttered, "except me."

Kaitlyn sat on the low wall by the swings with her right arm propped on her knee, the cast gone gray at the edges from two weeks of playground dust. Across the blacktop, the eighth graders were choosing teams for four square, and Marcus had already called her spot. She wanted that spot back. The trouble was that her arm was sealed away, and she could not see a single thing that was happening inside it.

She tried an experiment anyway. She pressed two fingers of her left hand along the cast, right where Dr. Okafor had drawn a small arrow on the fiberglass, marking the place the bone had snapped. Then she wiggled the fingers of her casted hand, slow, then fast, then slow again. They cooperated perfectly. She flexed her wrist as far as the stiff shell allowed. Not perfect, but close. That meant the tendons were fine, she reasoned, but it told her nothing about the bone itself, which was the part that actually had to heal. Something could be mending under there, or not, and no amount of wiggling would show it. She needed the follow-up appointment, and that was still three days away.

The appointment came on Thursday. In the exam room, the X-ray machine hummed, and then a new picture of her arm glowed on the light box beside the old one. Kaitlyn leaned in. On the first film, the bone ended in a clean, dark break, like a snapped pencil. On the new one, there was a fuzzy lump sitting right across the gap, a soft gray cloud where the sharp line used to be.

"See that?" Dr. Okafor said, tapping the lump with the end of a pen. "That's your callus."

"What's it made of?" Kaitlyn asked.

The doctor turned to her chart. "Cartilage and new bone," she said, writing something down. "It bridges the gap between the broken ends." Then she was out the door to the next patient, and Kaitlyn was left staring at the cloud. She had assumed healing would look like the bone knitting itself edge to edge, neat and invisible. Instead her body had built a lump first, a scaffold she could never have felt or seen from the outside. That was why her probing fingers had found nothing. The repair was happening in there anyway, steadily, whether she checked on it or not.

She thought about this on the walk to school the next morning. She had been treating healing like a negotiation, as if enough motivation and daily wiggling could speed it up. It was more like the four square rule nobody questioned: the ball must bounce once before you hit it. You could argue all you wanted, but the rule kept working the same way with or without you. Her arm, she decided, was probable to be ready by the tournament in two weeks, not because she wanted it, but because the callus said so.

At lunch, Marcus waved her over to the blacktop. "You're back! Want your corner?"

Kaitlyn bounced the ball once, then twice, testing her grip. "Actually," she said, "I reffed four square for two weeks with this arm. I know every dirty move you people make."

Marcus groaned. "That's exactly why we didn't want you reffing."

"Too late," Kaitlyn said, and planted herself at the center square with the ball under her good arm. "First serve. No doubles, no arguing, and Marcus, I saw that spin last Tuesday."

"The ref has a cast on," Marcus told the fourth square, "and she's still beating us."

"Whistle hand works fine," said Kaitlyn, and bounced the ball into his square so hard it spun twice before he touched it.

"Out!" she called, before it even landed.

Arthur sat on the living room floor with his laptop balanced on the coffee table, two news articles open side by side. His class project was due Monday, and he had promised his partner Nadia he would find two stories about the same event so they could compare them. He had picked the downtown march from last Saturday, the one his mom had driven past on her way to the store.

The first headline read, "Thousands Gather in Peaceful Protest for Cleaner Parks." The second read, "Rioters Disrupt Downtown, Businesses on Edge." Arthur scrolled down. Both articles described the same street, the same afternoon, the same crowd. Both mentioned a broken window at a bakery and a crowd estimate near four thousand. He read them again, then leaned back against the couch and stared at the ceiling fan.

He noticed something odd. When he read the first one, he pictured people holding signs, maybe singing. When he read the second, he pictured shouting and running, even though the article said almost the same things had happened. He tested it. He covered the headline on the first article with his hand and read only the body. Then he covered the second headline and did the same. The paragraphs underneath felt almost identical. The difference was the words on top.

"Protesters," he said out loud. "Rioters." He wrote both words in his notebook, then wrote "crowd of about four thousand" between them. If a word could make him picture two opposite scenes from the same facts, that was worth putting in the project. He could deduce that the writers had chosen those words on purpose, or at least that the words did work the facts alone didn't do. He underlined the pair twice.

Nadia came over at four, dropping her backpack by the door and flopping into the armchair. He turned the laptop toward her. "Read this one, then this one. Same day, same street." She read for a minute, frowning. "The second one makes me feel like it was dangerous," she said. "The first one makes it sound like a picnic."

"That's the thing," Arthur said. "They're loaded words." She raised an eyebrow, and he pointed at the screen. "Same crowd, but the word choice pushes you one way or the other." Nadia pulled out her phone and started typing notes.

"Wait," she said, "there's more. Look at this ad that keeps popping up before the video I need." On her screen, a basketball player Arthur recognized from the playoffs held up a sneaker and said everyone was wearing them this season. Arthur counted the tricks in his head. A famous athlete, a claim that everybody already had them, and the words " revolutionary" and "pathetic" in the on-screen text, describing the shoe and its rivals. "Athlete, bandwagon, loaded words," he said. "All three in fifteen seconds."

"It's like a simile that only goes one direction," Nadia said, tapping the screen. Arthur laughed, then opened a blank slide and typed the headline at the top. "Probable headline of our project," he said, reading it aloud: "How the Same Crowd Becomes Two Different Stories."

"The crowd was never two crowds," Nadia said, and hit save.

Paisley crouched between the tomato beds at the community garden, holding a slice of onion skin so thin she could almost see through it, like a scrap of cloudy glass. Mr. Ruiz had left the garden's old microscope on the picnic table before driving off to the hardware store, and Paisley wanted more than anything to see the cells before he came back. Her lab sheet had three empty blanks waiting for labels: cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus. She had never labeled anything under a microscope before, and she only had one shot at the prize for the summer science contest, a packet of heirloom seeds that everybody wanted.

Her friend Donte arrived on his bike, dropped it in the gravel, and peered over her shoulder. "My cousin said onion cells look like bricks in a wall," he said. "That's why they're easy to start on."

Paisley switched on the light and pressed her eye to the rubber eyepiece. The onion skin bloomed into view, a patchwork of little boxes, each one edged in a darker line. She drew a rectangle in her notebook and marked the outer edge. Cell wall. But where was the rest? Everything looked flat and faint, like a photograph underwater. "The nucleus should be a darker dot," she murmured. "Is it hiding, or is it just too small?"

"Maybe you need to turn it up higher," Donte said, squinting at the dial on the side. He spun the nosepiece until a longer lens clicked into place. "There. That one says forty."

Fifty times bigger sounded plenty to Paisley, but Donte shook his head. "It's the eyepiece times the objective," he said. "The top part says ten times, and this one says forty times, so it's four hundred times bigger, not fifty." Paisley lifted her head, checked the numbers stamped on both lenses herself, and did the multiplication on the corner of her page. Ten times forty was four hundred. Donte was right, and that meant her cells had been tiny ghosts before, too faint to hold a nucleus.

When she looked again, the patchwork sharpened. A pale dot floated near the center of one brick, and around it, just inside the dark wall, she could make out a thinner line hugging the edge like plastic wrap. Cell membrane. She labeled all three blanks, pressing hard enough to dent the paper, then taped the onion skin into her notebook to conserve it for the contest judges.

Donte leaned in for his turn, adjusted the fine focus with great care, and frowned. "Paisley. Are we sure these aren't the sinister ones?" He pointed at a cluster of cells near the edge of the skin, blotched and collapsed where her fingernail had squeezed too hard. "Looks like an infection got them." Paisley snatched back the notebook, but it was too late to salvage that corner. She grabbed the whole onion from the picnic table and started peeling off a fresh layer, layer after layer, saying, "Good thing onions have more skins than I have patience."

The quiz cards were taped beside the tanks, and whoever answered the most correctly by lunch would win a spot on the behind-the-scenes tour. Jack had his heart set on that tour, because the aquarium's newest harbor seal pup was being raised off display and only the tour group would get to see her. He was three for three until he reached the last card, near the jellyfish tank, where the question read: "True or false: every cow in a dairy barn has had a calf."

"False," Jack said immediately, and reached for the pencil.

"Wait," said Priya, who had been trailing him from tank to tank all morning. "Don't just pick something random. Think about it." She nodded toward the harbor seal pool, where a mother seal was nursing her pup. "See how she's making milk for the baby? My family used to board our horse next to a dairy farm, and I never once saw a cow being milked that didn't have a calf somewhere."

Jack frowned. He had been picturing the stereotypical dairy barn from television, rows of calm black-and-white cows giving milk all day, every day, forever. But if milk existed to feed a baby, then a cow would only have it after a calf was born. He tried to find a hole in the idea and couldn't. "So the answer is true," he said slowly. "Every single one of them." He erased his answer, changed it, and handed the card to the volunteer at the desk.

"Correct," the volunteer said, sorting the cards. "That's the one most people miss." Jack had been ready to resign himself to losing the tour, and now he was jumping like the sea otter two tanks over. Priya laughed and punched his shoulder, and the two of them followed the guide through a plain gray door marked Staff Only.

The guide led them down a corridor that smelled of fish and bleach, past freezers and hoses, and stopped at a low pool. The seal pup lay on the wet concrete beside her mother, blinking at them with round dark eyes. "She's growing fast," the guide said, "because her mom's making plenty of milk for her. Same as out at your farms, right?" Jack looked at Priya, and they both grinned. "Told you," she whispered. "Nobody makes milk without a baby." Jack leaned closer as the pup flopped toward the water, and the mother nudged her in with her nose.

Elena sat on the crinkly paper of the nurse's cot and squinted at the eye chart taped to the cabinet door. The top E was easy. The second line was a smear of gray. The third line might as well have been spilled ink.

"You failed the screening twice," Nurse Patel said. "The optometrist is already here for the sixth graders. Come on."

The optometrist's folding chair sat under the window, next to a rack of trial lenses. He flipped lenses in front of her eyes, one after another. "Read the line with the T."

"O, maybe D, then something with a tail."

"Better or worse?" He slid a new lens in.

"Better. The letters aren't smearing sideways anymore." Elena leaned forward. "Wait. Why did they smear? I thought you're either nearsighted or farsighted. My friend Marcus is nearsighted, and his stuff is blurry only far away. Mine's blurry everywhere."

"That's a different thing," the optometrist said. "It's called astigmatism."

"But what is it?" Elena asked, because Nurse Patel was no help and he kept flipping lenses.

He shrugged, already reaching for the next lens. "Your cornea, or maybe the lens inside the eye, is slightly egg-shaped. Curves more in one direction than the other. Blurs things at any distance."

Elena went still. An egg. She thought of the way light came through the porous curtain in her bedroom and stretched into ovals on the floor. If the curve was uneven, the light wouldn't land in one point. That would smear the letter sideways, near and far both, which was exactly what she'd been seeing since October, when the whiteboard turned to fog and she'd copied Marcus's notes out of desperation and felt a hot spike of resentment when he called her a cheater.

She had a theory to test. "Hold on. If it's egg-shaped, the blur should have a direction, right? The same direction everywhere?" She held up her hand and curled her fingers slightly, like a tunnel tilted one way. She looked at the chart through the gap. The letters stretched sideways. She tilted the gap the other way. They stretched the other way. "So a lens curved unevenly would smear the E left or right depending on which way the egg sits. Mine smears left. Every line, near and far."

The optometrist stopped flipping lenses and looked at her. "Try this one."

The third line snapped into focus. F, Z, B, D, 4. She read it clean to the bottom, and her eyes stung because she hadn't known letters had that many sharp edges.

Nurse Patel wrote something on a slip. "Glasses in a week."

"A week?" Elena said. "Can I at least keep the chart?"

On Saturday morning, Charlotte slid into her chair at the kitchen table and stared at the small white box beside her cereal. Her mother had left it there with a sticky note that read "After breakfast," which was the crueldest thing anyone had ever written, because how was a person supposed to eat with a phone box sitting eight inches from her elbow?

At the phone store, a kid named Theo was waiting too, dragging his dad toward the display cases. "I wonder how long people have even had phones in their pockets," Theo said, poking a demo model. "Like, did cave people text?" His dad sighed in a way that suggested this was not the first question of the day.

The saleswoman grinned. "The first call from a handheld cellular phone was made by Motorola engineer Martin Cooper on a New York street on April 3, 1973," she said, tapping the counter like she was announcing a sports score. Theo's jaw dropped. Charlotte filed that away, because it felt like the kind of fact that could win an argument someday, possibly against her little brother.

Back at the kitchen table, Charlotte set up the phone with the concentration of a scientist handling dangerous plumbing. One wrong move and something might leak, except instead of water it would be her entire screen time. Her mother watched over her shoulder. "Sixty minutes on school nights," she said. "I need you to reassure me that you can live with that."

"Mom," Charlotte said, holding the phone like a rare artifact, "in 1973, Martin Cooper made a phone call on a street in New York. One call. He was a Motorola engineer, and it was April third, and it was the first call ever from a handheld cellular phone. People back then survived with one call. I can survive sixty minutes." Her mother laughed so hard she had to sit down, which Charlotte took as a good sign.

But then came the test. Charlotte had an idea. If the phone was really hers to manage, she could prove it, so she set a timer, put the phone face down at the edge of the table, and read an entire chapter of her book while the clock ran out. When the timer buzzed, she switched the phone off herself, without being asked, and slid it into the drawer with the measuring cups. The kitchen went strangely tranquil, just the hum of the refrigerator and the last page turning.

Her mother peeked around the doorframe. "You turned it off. Voluntarily." Charlotte held up her book. "Tomorrow I'm going to call Theo and tell him the Cooper fact again, and also that I finished a whole chapter. He's going to be so jealous."

Emmett had one job at the mall: find a birthday gift for his grandmother while his mom picked up shoes at the other end. He had twenty dollars and forty minutes, and he was already wasting both at the phone repair kiosk, where his friend Rico worked weekends. His problem was simpler than it sounded. Grandmother had once mentioned a mug with a red fox painted on it, and Emmett could not remember where she had seen it. He pulled out his phone and typed his own name into the search box, on a hunch that he had once looked it up and saved the link.

The search results filled the screen, and near the top was something he did not expect: a comment he had written three years ago on the mall's public page, complaining about the arcade closing early on a Sunday. Anyone searching "Emmett" could read it, including strangers, and it even showed which mall location he had been at that day. He stared at it, then scrolled and found the same comment copied on a second site he had never visited.

"How is it on there twice?" he asked Rico, holding up the phone. "I only wrote it once."

Rico leaned over the counter. "Search engines use automated programs called crawlers to copy and index public web pages," he said, wiping a smudge off the screen. "So anything posted publicly can turn up in search results." He shrugged, like it was just weather. "Even old stuff. Even with your name on it."

Emmett tested the idea right there. He found the original comment on the mall's page, edited it to conceal his last name and the location tag, and then searched again an hour later, while eating a pretzel by the fountain. The old copy on the second site still sat there, unedited, because he had no way to reach it. His own fix worked only halfway, and he understood now that a public post was less like a note passed in class and more like something pinned to a board anyone could photograph. He typed a fresh comment under the mall's post, asking if anyone knew a shop that sold fox mugs, using only his first initial this time.

The reply came while he was standing outside the pet store, watching a small owl blink at him from behind the glass. The sign said it was nocturnal, which explained why it looked half asleep under the bright mall lights, while the monitor lizard beside it, according to the sign a carnivore, tracked every movement near its tank with wide-open eyes. Emmett's phone buzzed. A stranger named Doris had answered: try the kitchenware shop on level two, third store past the escalator. He walked toward the escalator, reading the message a second time, and said, "Thanks, Doris," out loud to nobody in particular.

The banner over the community centre doorway read Heritage Festival, and Bennett slipped past a cluster of kids to evade the line forming at the entrance table. His project board was due by four o'clock, and the caption still wasn't finished. He carried it under one arm, the glue drying in streaks, the last line blank except for a pencil mark where a word should go.

The problem was Mr. Okafor's note, folded into Bennett's pocket: "Check your wording before you submit." Bennett knew which wording. His caption read: "Drummer and throat singer, performances by an Inuit." He had copied the phrase from a library book, but something about it had started to nag at him on the bus, the way a pebble in a shoe does.

Inside, the hall smelled of fried plantains and cardamom. A woman in a printed headwrap was explaining a wall of photographs to two teenagers: "We call ourselves Igbo," she said, "not tribe, if you can manage it." Nearby, a Scottish pipe band tuned up with a sound like an argument between geese. Bennett walked the aisles, half listening, half rehearsing what he might ask a stranger.

At the northern tables, a man was arranging carvings of seals and a kayak paddler. A card beside the display said Inuit Artists Collective. Bennett stood there a moment, then made himself speak. "Excuse me. I'm doing a school project. Is it right to say a performer is an Inuit, or is there another word?"

The man set down a carving of a loon. "Inuit means 'the people,'" he said. "So it works for the group. One person is called an Inuk." He tapped the card. "That's why it says Artists, not one name. You wouldn't say an Inuit any more than you'd say a the-peoples."

Bennett wrote it on his palm in letters he could still read: one person, an Inuk. The man showed him how the word sat in Inuktitut, sounds Bennett tried and mangled, and the man laughed, not unkindly, and said the second try was better.

At four o'clock exactly, Bennett propped his board on the submission table at the back of the hall, where a judge with a clipboard was already moving down the row. He uncapped his pen and, in his most assertive handwriting, printed the new caption: "Drummer and throat singer, performances by an Inuk and by Inuit from across the north." The pipes started up behind him, swelling toward what had to be the climax of their set, and the judge paused at his board, clipboard steady, and read the last line twice.

"Nice fix," she said. "Half the entries get that wrong."

The power died with an abrupt click at half past eight, right in the middle of Ryder's game, and the whole house at Grandpa's went black except for the thin gray line of the window curtains. Ryder sat very still and listened. No furnace hum, no refrigerator drone, nothing. From downstairs, Grandpa's voice drifted up the stairs, calm as ever. "Well. Guess the county's having fun tonight. Candles are in the sideboard, third drawer."

Ryder felt his way down, bumping his hip on the banister, and found Grandpa already striking a match in the kitchen. The flame caught, and Grandpa set a stubby candle on the counter, then another on the table, converting the bright, familiar kitchen into something from an old photograph, all shadows and warm little pools of light. "You okay on your phone?" Grandpa asked. "Dead," Ryder said. "I forgot my charger." He'd been planning to charge it at home tomorrow. Now the screen was a dark black rectangle, useless as a brick, and something in his chest tightened at that.

Grandpa took a long flashlight from the mudroom shelf and nodded toward the back door. "Come on. When I was a kid, blackout nights were the best ones. Let's see if they still are." Outside, the whole street was dark, every porch light and window out, and the sky above them was not the sky Ryder knew. It was crowded. There were so many stars it looked almost messy, a spilled bag of salt, and across the middle of it ran a pale, hazy river of light he had never once seen from any city or suburb in his life.

"That's the Milky Way," Grandpa said quietly. "Haven't seen it from this yard since I don't know when." Ryder kept staring. He kept thinking there must be something wrong with his eyes, some smudge on his glasses, but no, it was real, and it was enormous, and it had apparently been hanging over his head his entire life without him ever knowing. Then he remembered where he'd seen something about this, a library book about the night sky he'd flipped through last month and mostly ignored. He'd skipped the paragraphs and read only the fact boxes. One of them had stuck anyway. "There was this atlas," he said slowly. "A world atlas of light pollution, from 2016. It estimated about eighty percent of North Americans can't see the Milky Way from where they live, because of artificial light." He checked Grandpa's face to see if he'd remembered it wrong, but Grandpa just nodded.

"Go get my laser pointer," Grandpa said. "Top drawer of my desk, the little silver one." Ryder fetched it, and Grandpa thumbed it on and traced a slow line up the black sky, pointing out Vega, then Deneb, then the whole glowing river itself, the green beam looking almost like it touched the stars. Ryder wanted to test something. If all that glow in the sky was really stars that the streetlights normally drowned out, then a single porch light coming back on should erase at least part of it. He stood squinting at the Milky Way, waiting for some house somewhere to flicker back to life so he could watch the stars vanish in real time. Nothing came on. The whole neighborhood stayed dark, and the sky stayed crowded, and the wait itself felt like its own strange gift.

The streetlights snapped back on all at once around ten, so sudden that Ryder flinched, and the Milky Way disappeared like breath wiped off glass. Only a dozen of the brightest stars survived. He hadn't even gotten to finish his test, but he'd seen enough: the stars had been there the whole time, waiting behind the porch lights and the glowing windows, and all it took to hide an entire galaxy was ordinary electricity. He'd spent the whole evening mad about his dead phone, and now, staring up at the washed-out sky he used to think was normal, he couldn't decide whether he wanted the power back or not.

"Same time next blackout?" Grandpa said, pocketing the laser pointer. Ryder watched the porch light buzz and steady itself, steady and bright and ruinous. "Yeah," he said. "But I'm bringing a blanket."

Luca stood at the canoe launch with his duffel at his feet, waiting for the camp van, and tried to look like a kid who had done this a hundred times. He had never been to summer camp. His cousin Diego had spent a month at one last summer and came home telling stories about a lake, a rope swing, and something he called the frontier, a stretch of woods at the edge of the property where the older campers got to hike. Luca wanted that more than anything, and he'd said so on the ride up, so many times that his mom laughed. Now he watched the driver load his bag beside seven others and climbed in anyway.

The first week was good, until Tuesday night, when cabin inspection turned into tick check. The counselor handed each boy a flashlight and told them to line up, and a kid named Marcus groaned loudly. "We didn't even hike today. Why bother?" He flopped onto his bunk and pulled his sleeping bag over his head like a tent.

Luca had been scratching behind his knee since the afternoon trail walk, and while Marcus complained, he thought about it. He hadn't hiked Monday either, but today they had cut through a field of tall grass to reach the swimming dock, off the trail, because it was faster. The itching had started after that. He couldn't see the back of his own knee, but the fact of the itching was data, like a footprint. He grabbed the kid next to him, a quiet boy named Owen. "Can you check behind my knee with the flashlight? We went through that tall grass by the dock."

Owen shined the light and went still. "There's something there. Small. Like a poppy seed with legs." Luca's stomach dropped, but he made himself think instead of panic. Marcus peeked out from his sleeping bag, suddenly interested. "Is that a blacklegged tick?" he asked. "My sister got one at her camp. She said they're also called deer ticks, and they can spread Lyme disease, so everybody had to check every night."

"Then check everybody," Luca said, pulling his pant leg down. "Especially anyone who was in that grass." Marcus sat up, all complaints gone, and helped Owen run the flashlights along ankles and hairlines and behind ears. They found two more ticks among the six boys who had taken the shortcut, and the counselor got them off properly and logged it, while Marcus explained to the next cabin over why the nightly check existed. "I take back what I said," he told them. "This is the most sophisticated reason to make us line up I've ever heard."

By Friday, the whole cabin had a system. Lights out, then flashlights on, then a rotation where each boy checked the boy behind him, faster every night, until it consumed barely five minutes. "Efficient," Owen said, with a small proud smile, and Marcus gave Luca a fist bump. On Sunday, the frontier hike opened for the older campers, and Luca's name was on the list.
