"We're short-handed on sorting today," she said, handing him a pair of gloves. The room smelled of cardboard and canned peaches.

His job was simple. Check each donated item, wipe it down, and put it on the right shelf: canned goods here, pasta there, cereal on the tall rack by the window. He liked the rhythm of it, and he started noticing patterns. Tuna cans lasted for years, judging by the dates. Pasta lasted a long time too. But cereal boxes had dates that were much closer, and half of them were already past.

Across the table, a woman named Rosa picked up a box of oat cereal, frowned, and dropped it into the discard bin. Tyler watched her do the same thing to the next box. Something about it bothered him. The boxes were sealed, undented, not even stale-smelling through the plastic inner bag. Why would perfectly good cereal get thrown away when the banged-up cans stayed?

"Those are only one day past the date," he said, fishing a box out of the bin. Rosa glanced at the printed date and shrugged. "Past is past," she said. "You don't want to give people expired food." Tyler turned the box over in his hands. The date didn't say "expired," though. It said "best if used by." He asked Rosa what she thought that meant. She hesitated. "That it goes bad after?"

That didn't sit right with him. Tyler went to the break room, borrowed the old laptop, and searched the phrase. The USDA's own words came up on the screen: a "best if used by" date shows when a food will be at its best quality; it is not a food-safety date. He read it twice, then carried the laptop back and set it in front of Rosa. She leaned in, squinting, then straightened up slowly. "Huh," she said. "So it's about taste, not about making anyone sick." "That's what it says," Tyler said. "So that cereal isn't dangerous. It's just maybe not at its peak anymore." He wondered out loud how many boxes had been tossed over the years for that exact reason, some hidden rule nobody had ever checked.

They tested the idea together, opening one dated box from the discard bin. The cereal snapped when Tyler bit a piece, crisp and plain, maybe a little less exciting than fresh. They sorted the rest back onto the shelf, and by noon the rack by the window was full again. The coordinator walked past and stopped, staring at the pile of reclaimed boxes. "Where did all this come from?" she asked. Tyler held up the oat cereal, one day past its date, and grinned. "Breakfast," he said.

Brayden lay on the couch with a box of tissues, a bowl of crackers, and three days of nothing but game shows. The flu had flattened him on Friday, right before his cousin Marcus's birthday party, which was tomorrow at noon. His mom had made a deal with him: if his fever stayed normal all morning, he could go. He wanted that more than anything, because Marcus had saved him the last slice of pizza every year since they were seven.

He was texting his friend Dev when a thought stopped his thumb mid-word. The sleepover. Dev had been there too, laughing and eating chips and winning every round of the racing game. Dev texted back that he was fine, but Brayden scrolled up in the group chat anyway. Saturday morning, two days ago, Dev had sent a single message: "ugh, think im getting the flu." Brayden stared at it, then counted on his fingers. Dev had been perfectly healthy at the sleepover on Friday night. Then, less than a full day later, he was sick.

Brayden sat up so fast the blanket slid to the floor. People with the flu could spread it starting about one day before they felt any symptoms. That meant Dev hadn't just caught it after the sleepover. He had probably been spreading it while they were all piled on the air mattress, sharing controllers and a bag of pretzels. Brayden's own fever had started Sunday, which was almost exactly one day after the sleepover. It lined up like a laser beam pointed straight at Friday night.

He had to test the idea. He messaged the other two boys from the sleepover. Ten minutes later, both had replied. Tyler: "fine so far." Owen: "my throat kinda hurts today." Owen had been the one who fell asleep with his head on Dev's shoulder during the movie. Brayden read the messages twice, letting the pattern digest. Two out of five boys sick within the same stretch of days, all of them exposed to the same person before that person knew he was sick.

Brayden walked to the kitchen where his mom was cutting fruit. "I figured out where I got it," he said. "Dev seemed totally fine at the sleepover, but you can spread the flu starting about one day before you even feel symptoms. So he was already contagious Friday night. Owen's getting sick too, and he was all over Dev." He took a breath. "So here's the thing. If I go to Marcus's party tomorrow, even with no fever, I might be doing the same thing Dev did."

His mom set down the knife and looked at him for a long moment. "That was an eloquent argument for a kid with a stuffy nose," she said. "Go call Marcus. Tell him the truth, and ask about that pizza."

Brayden dialed, and when Marcus picked up, he said, "I'm going to tell you something weird, and then I'm going to ask you a favor about pizza."

Zoe stood at the boards with the sign-up sheet in her mitten, waiting for Priya to finish her lap. Their winter tournament allowed each team one pick from outside its regular roster, and they had argued about that pick all the way to the rink. "It has to be Dana," Priya said, skating over in a spray of ice. "She scores every single game. Her average is two goals a game." Zoe frowned at the clipboard. "Morgan's average is two a game too. I wrote them both down." Priya snorted. "Then it's a tie, so pick Dana. Everyone ranks Dana higher."

"But that's what's bugging me," Zoe said. "If they're tied on average, why does everyone say Dana is better? Nobody can actually see who's better. We only see the games." Priya rolled her eyes, but Zoe had already flipped her notebook to a page of tiny numbers. She had gone through the league website the night before, eating a nutritious dinner of toast with peanut butter while she copied down every game log. "Look. Dana: two goals, two goals, two, one, three, two, two. Same every night." She tapped the second column. "Morgan: five goals, zero, six, zero, zero, one, two. Same average. But Morgan swings between great and terrible games, and an average hides how spread out the results are." She said it out loud and then checked her math again, because it seemed too strange to be true. Two players, same average, completely different players.

"So which one do we want?" Priya said. Zoe proposed a test instead of an argument. "Next scrimmage, we put Morgan on our line and watch. If the spread thing is real, we should see it." At Saturday's scrimmage Morgan scored four goals in the first period, and Priya threw her arms around Zoe at the bench. In the second period Morgan missed an open net twice and passed to nobody, and Priya groaned. "That was a humiliation," she muttered, pulling her helmet straight. "Mine too," Morgan said, embarrassed, sitting down between them. Zoe slid the water bottle over. "You're still averaging two a game," she said. "That's what my notebook says, and my notebook has never lied to me yet."

By the end of the third period, Morgan had scored twice more, and the swing had shown up exactly as the numbers promised. Zoe did not gloat. Instead she asked Morgan one question: "Tournament games are single elimination. One bad game and we're out. Do you want to be our pick, knowing that?" Morgan thought about it, chipped the ice off her skate blade, and said, "Pick Dana. She never stops at two. I'll take a regular spot if you have one, and I'll work on the zeroes." Zoe crossed off one name and wrote the other.

On the walk to the parking lot, Priya bumped her shoulder. "You solved it with a notebook and toast." Zoe laughed. "The toast was the nutritious part. The numbers did the rest." Inside the rink, the Zamboni began its slow loops, and the noise of the fans would not cease until every last scrap of ice was smooth. Priya pointed at the driver's booth, where a new standings sheet had just gone up, team averages printed in tidy rows. "Look at that," she said. "All those games, squished into one number." Zoe grinned and tucked her notebook under her arm. "Not for long," she said, and turned back toward the doors.

Felix sat at the kitchen table wrapped in a quilt that smelled like the linen closet, staring at a bowl of chicken soup he had no intention of eating. His fever had spiked overnight, and now every joint in his body ached like he had run a marathon in his sleep. His little sister, Poppy, kept orbiting the table with her thermometer, pretending she was a nurse on television.

"Mom thinks we should wait until Saturday to call Dr. Okafor," she reported, tucking the thermometer into her doll's armpit. "Dad thinks you're going to turn into a zombie by Friday."

"I heard that," Mom called from the stove. She stirred something and sighed. "His fever is 102, but it might break on its own. The office is always packed on Thursdays."

Felix pushed the soup an inch away, then pulled it back, then pushed it away again, like the bowl itself was making the decision. His brain felt like wet sand, but something was nagging at him, a memory from a pamphlet he had read in Dr. Okafor's waiting room back in September, mostly because the magazine rack had nothing but golf catalogs. He tried to reconstruct it. The pamphlet had said something about flu medicine, the kind you get with a prescription, and a deadline. Two days. The medicine worked best if you started it within two days after symptoms began.

He counted backward on his fingers, which took longer than it should have. "Mom. When did I start feeling bad?"

"Tuesday night, sweetie. You were shivering during dinner."

"So the clock started Tuesday." He held up two fingers. "Two days. That's my window. If we wait until Saturday, I miss it, and the medicine won't do much." He slid the soup toward her like a lawyer presenting evidence. "Calling today isn't arbitrary. It's the rule."

Mom tapped the spoon against the pot. Poppy whispered "zombie" in a spooky voice.

"You read that somewhere?" Mom asked.

"Waiting room pamphlet. Golf rack, remember."

She laughed, wiped her hands on the towel, and picked up her phone. While she was on hold, Felix took one bite of soup and, to his own surprise, kept going. When Mom hung up, she said the nurse agreed completely and they could come at three.

At the clinic, Dr. Okafor wrote the prescription and said, "Good timing. This antiviral works best when it's started within two days of your first symptoms, so you caught it just right."

"Did you hear that, Poppy?" Felix said weakly from the exam table. "Your almost-zombie brother caught it just right."

On the drive home, he leaned against the window and decided that being right was a kind of currency in their family, worth at least one extra hour of video games. He planned to spend it the moment his hands stopped aching.

Then Poppy leaned over from her booster seat and pressed the thermometer into his ear. It beeped. "Ninety-eight point six," she announced. "My medicine worked. That'll be five dollars."

The lights went out just as Nora was finishing her homework, and the whole house sank into a blue evening dimness. She found her way to the back door and stepped onto the porch, where her older brother Dev was already standing with a flashlight, shining it at the empty birdbath as if it might explain things. Their little brother Milo was in the kitchen, and Nora could hear the refrigerator door swing open, then shut, then open again.

"Milo, stop that," she called through the screen door. "You're letting the cold out."

"I want the yogurt," his voice drifted back. "I can't find it in the dark."

Nora went inside and held the flashlight while Milo rummaged, but the beam wobbled and he moved containers aside, and she felt the cool air spilling past her ankles like water from a cracked cup. She remembered a poster from the school cafeteria, the one she'd read while waiting in the pizza line: according to the USDA, a fridge keeps food safely cold for about four hours in a power cut, as long as the door stays closed. Four hours, if it stayed shut. Milo was spending those hours a few seconds at a time.

"We get one open," Dev said from the doorway, having apparently been thinking the same thing. "Everybody decide first, then we open it once, grab everything, and shut it for good."

Milo looked ready to argue, but then his lower lip trembled and he sat down on the cold tile. Nora crouched beside him and tried to console him, saying they'd have a yogurt picnic as soon as they planned it right, and after a moment he wiped his nose on his sleeve and agreed. They made their list on the porch by flashlight: yogurt, the leftover noodles, the milk, the cheese, the orange juice Milo pretended not to want. They stacked it all in a cooler from the garage, next to the porous old cinder block that their father used as a doorstop, and then they sat on the steps eating cold noodles with forks, listening to crickets.

The power came back at half past nine, humming through the porch light and glowing yellow against the dusk. Dev stood up, stretched, and opened the refrigerator to put things away, and every bulb inside blazed on cheerfully. Nora laughed so hard she nearly dropped her fork, because the fridge had come back to life precisely when they no longer needed to keep it closed.

"Four hours of careful planning," Dev said, "wasted on ten minutes."

"Get me the yogurt," Milo announced from the steps. "I've decided."

Ariana counted the steps from the cabin to the dock, because if she knew exactly how far the lake was, maybe it would stop feeling like the edge of a map. Camp Wanaset claimed to be the most prestigious canoe camp in the county, and the banners everywhere said so, and her older brother had spent two summers here winning the paddle trophy that sat in the lodge. Ariana had never been away from home before, and today was the day every new camper got in a canoe for the first time.

"New campers, you're with me," said Kaya, who was fourteen and the tutor for beginners, meaning she took them out on the water every morning. Kaya wanted that trophy more than anything, and she kept glancing at the older campers racing near the far shore. "We paddle after lunch. Nobody flips my group."

At the dock, a boy named Dex went first. He stepped onto the edge of the canoe instead of the middle, and the whole boat lurched sideways under him. He grabbed the gunwale, the canoe wobbled again, and Kaya hauled him back onto the dock before he went in. "You're not getting in like that," she said. Dex's face went red, and he muttered something about quitting, because he had told everyone at breakfast he would catch the biggest fish in the lake from a canoe, and now he couldn't even sit down in one.

Ariana watched the older campers next. Every single one of them stepped into the middle of the canoe, and kept low, knees bent, gear centered between them. Nobody had said anything about it. They just did it, like it was a rule written somewhere she hadn't been shown. She looked at Dex wobbling on the dock and made a quiet guess: the boats tipped when weight went onto the side, and stayed calm when weight sat low and centered in the middle.

"Me next," she said. She stepped straight into the middle of the canoe, crouched, and slid onto the seat. The boat barely moved. Dex stared at her.

"How'd you do that?"

"Watch." She nodded at the older campers. "They all get in the same way." Dex tried again, stepping into the middle, low and slow, and this time the canoe held steady under him. He gripped his paddle and grinned.

Later, they would transport their gear across the lake to the fishing spot, and the whole camp would see two first-timers paddling out flat and calm. For now Kaya pushed them off from the dock and jumped into her own boat, eyes already on the far shore.

"Race you to the reeds," Dex called, and dug his paddle in.

Katherine had exactly one class period to finish her shaded sphere for the art show, and her pencil was betraying her. The highlight kept turning gray no matter how lightly she touched the paper. Across the table, Marcus held up two pencils that looked identical, both yellow, both freshly sharpened. "Why does this one draw so dark and this one barely shows up?" he asked. "They're the same size. It's like one of them is lazy."

Katherine took both pencils and scribbled a quick swatch on scrap paper. One left a rich, velvety black; the other left a mark so faint it looked like a ghost of a pencil. She turned them near the window and noticed small letters on each one. The dark one said 4B. The pale one said 4H. "They're not the same kind," she said. "The letters are different." Marcus leaned over her shoulder, nearly knocking her eraser off the table, and she caught it before it rolled away.

"My grandpa has a whole coffee can of these at his house," Katherine said, turning the pencils over. "He told me once what the letters mean, but I forgot most of it." She remembered one part, though, a sentence he'd said while she sat at his kitchen table drawing horses: pencil cores aren't just one thing, they're graphite powder mixed with clay. She frowned at the pale pencil. "So if more clay makes a harder pencil that leaves lighter marks, then this 4H one must have more clay in it than the 4B."

"Test it," Marcus said, always ready for anything that sounded even slightly like science class. Katherine pressed down hard with the 4H, then feather-light with the 4B. Even under pressure, the hard pencil stayed pale, and even with the gentlest touch, the soft one smudged dark. "It's backwards from what you'd expect," she said. "The harder one gives you less." Marcus squinted at his own drawing. "So that's why my clouds look like storm clouds. I've been using the dark one for everything."

He looked so defeated that Katherine slid her 4H across the table to him. "Try this for the light parts. And press less with the dark one for the middle." She watched him shade a cloud so fluffy it looked ready to float off his page, and he grinned like he'd invented weather.

For her sphere's highlight, she finally understood what to do. Instead of pressing the dark pencil lighter and lighter, which only eroded the paper's tooth into a shiny smudge, she used the hard pencil with its faint, pale mark, letting the white of the page glow through at the very top. Her shading curved around the sphere now, giving it real perspective, the way Mr. Okafor kept saying, like it existed in actual space and not just flat on the desk. At the end of class he held up her sphere as an example, calling it "a thoroughly contemporary take on a classic exercise," which made Marcus whisper, "He just means it looks cool."

Katherine wrote 4H on the back of her scrap paper and tucked it in her pocket, next to two pencils she'd decided to keep forever. "Grandpa's going to be proud," she said. "That thing you figured out," Marcus said, gathering his cloud drawing, "can you teach it to my little sister? Her cat drawings look like they got caught in a rainstorm." Katherine laughed. "Bring her a 4H," she said, "and tell her the pale pencil is her best friend."

Mila had made Grandma Rosa's snickerdoodles three times this winter, and every batch came out the same: dry in the middle, puffy like little cakes instead of flat and chewy. She stood at the counter with the recipe card propped against the flour canister, reading it again. Her dad's voice drifted in from the hallway, where he was on the phone with her uncle about the wind turbine they were helping install at the school, and she half listened while she puzzled over the card. The recipe said two and a quarter cups of flour, the same as always. She hadn't changed anything.

Or maybe she had. She thought about how she measured. She dipped the measuring cup straight into the bag, the way she always had, and the flour came up in a dense block that she leveled with a knife. She remembered Grandma Rosa weighing her flour on the little silver scale instead, and how she used to transmit recipes by letter, with weights written beside the cups. Grandma had texted her the gram amounts last week: two hundred and seventy grams for two and a quarter cups. Mila had never bothered with them. Cups were faster.

She pulled the scale from the top shelf and set the bowl on it, pressing tare until the numbers cleared. Then she scooped a cup of flour the way she always did, packed and leveled, and poured it in. The scale read one hundred and sixty grams, not one hundred and twenty. She frowned and did the next cup. One hundred and fifty-five. She measured the last quarter cup and then checked the total: over three hundred and forty grams. Almost eighty grams more than the recipe meant. Eighty grams was like adding a whole extra half cup that nobody asked for.

"Whoa," her little brother Theo said, appearing at her elbow with his synthetic vanilla-spiked hot chocolate, which Mom had finally bought after the real vanilla bottle ran dry. "Why's the number so big?" Mila tapped the bag of flour. "Scooping straight from the bag packs it down, so a cup holds way more than the recipe wants. That's why they're coming out like little cakes." She dumped the flour back, spooned it gently into the cup, leveled it, and weighed again. One hundred and twenty-five grams. Closer. She did the rest the same way, watching the numbers climb toward two hundred and seventy exactly.

The dough felt different under her hands, softer and slacker, and it spread on the pan in fat rounds instead of sitting stiff. When the timer buzzed, the cookies came out golden with crackled tops, and when she broke one in half it pulled apart in strings. Theo took one before it was even cool. "These are the real ones," he said through a full mouth. Mila set two aside on the good plate and took out her phone to text Grandma Rosa a picture. She typed, "You were right, I weighed the flour," and pressed send. Then she ate the broken cookie standing up, right there beside the warm oven.

The casseroles kept arriving like a currency nobody had asked for, dish after dish stacking up on Grandma's old kitchen table, and Christopher hadn't touched a bite of any of them. It had been six days since Grandpa died, and in those six days Christopher had slept maybe two hours a night, maybe less. His legs felt hollow. He pushed a fork through the lasagna and watched the cheese go cold.

"You look terrible," his cousin Marcus said, cornering him by the punch bowl.

"Thanks."

"No, I mean it. Are you sick?" Marcus leaned closer. "If you're getting the flu the day before the funeral, my mom will lose her mind. She's already losing it."

That was the thing, the worry that had been circling him all week like a fly he couldn't swat. Because it wasn't just the sleeping. It was that food made his throat close. It was that his hands shook carrying the mail. He had started building a list in his head: mono, or something worse, something they'd catch too late, and he'd be in a hospital bed while everyone was already standing at a grave. Tomorrow. The funeral was tomorrow at ten, and he was supposed to read the card he'd written, and his body was falling apart on a schedule.

He tried an experiment that afternoon. He went into the den where his dad was sorting Grandpa's old photographs, and he said, straight out, "Dad, are you sleeping?"

His dad didn't look up. "Couple hours a night. Maybe."

"Are you eating?"

Dad finally turned. "Your aunt made me finish half a sandwich today. First real thing since Sunday." He squinted at Christopher. "Why?"

Christopher pulled a chair over. "My hands shake. My stomach's wrong. I thought maybe I was getting sick, but." He stopped. "You sleep two hours. You eat half a sandwich. And Aunt Terri looks the same way. And Marcus's mom was awake at three, I heard her in the kitchen."

Dad set down the photo he was holding, one of Grandpa holding a fish the size of a canoe paddle. "Grief doesn't just mess with your feelings," he said quietly. "It can get into your body too. Tiredness, sleep going bad, appetite going strange. It happens."

"So I'm not sick."

"You're not sick." Dad rubbed his eyes. "It's just grief, invading everything, the whole system."

Christopher sat with that. Then he asked about the second part of his test, the part that actually scared him. "Then how do I read the card tomorrow if I'm like this?"

"You eat something small tonight. You sleep as much as your body lets you. That's the fix. Not a radical one, just a boring one."

At the evening meal, in front of everybody, Christopher took a piece of bread and ate it slowly, bite by bite, while his aunts pretended not to watch. It went down. It stayed down. He went to bed at nine and lay in the dark listening to his grandmother's clock tick in the hallway, and he slept four whole hours, which felt like an ocean.

In the morning he put on the gray shirt his mom had laid out and found the card in his jacket pocket where he'd left it. At the funeral home, when the pastor nodded to him, Christopher stood up. His hands were steadier than they'd been all week. He unfolded the card, looked out at the folding chairs and the flowers and his father's tired face, and began, "My grandpa taught me to fish."

"Speak up, buddy," his dad called softly.

Christopher lifted his chin and said it again, louder, to the whole room.

The zamboni had just finished its slow lap, and the ice smelled like cold pennies and burnt rubber when Keira laced her skates at the boards. Day one of hockey tryouts, and forty girls were racing lines under the whir of the fans. Coach Reyes skated the perimeter to supervise each drill, whistle in her teeth, stopwatch in her glove.

Keira went all out. She sprinted the lengths, slammed through the checking drill, and won every board battle along the wall. By the end of practice her legs were trembling, but she felt great, and Marisol, her best friend and her rival for the last forward spot, felt great too. They compared notes in the locker room, dripping and laughing. "Tomorrow we do it all again," Marisol said, pulling her pads off. "I feel like a laser. Nothing's slowing me down."

Day two, Marisol hobbled in like a rusty robot. She gripped the rail in the lobby, wincing at each stair, and stared at her own legs as if they'd betrayed her overnight. "I was fine last night," she groaned. "I even did extra jumps in my driveway." Keira frowned. Her own thighs ached too, worse than yesterday, which was strange. If skating had hurt them, the hurt should have shown up right away, not a full day later, like a bill arriving in the mail. Her older brother had once complained he couldn't sit down for three days after his first squat workout, fine the first evening and destroyed on day two. Keira had filed it away as weird. Now she watched Marisol lower herself onto the bench and thought, this is the same thing.

She tested the idea on her own body. Her hamstrings, which she'd stretched gently that morning, ached but worked. Her quads, which she'd hammered, were stiff as boards. So the pain arrived late, somewhere between a day and three days after, and it picked whatever muscles had been pushed hardest. She said it out loud, grinning. "Delayed onset muscle soreness. My brother calls it DOMS." Marisol squinted. "So yesterday's practice is only hitting me now?" "Now through maybe three days from now," Keira said.

Then came the twist Keira hadn't planned. Coach Reyes split them into scrimmage lines and put Marisol on defense, not because she was slow but because her legs couldn't take forward sprinting today. Keira got Marisol's spot at wing, and she hated how she got it. Between periods she skated over. "You should have it when you're whole," she told her. "Coach, can we rerun this Friday?" Reyes raised an eyebrow, then nodded once.

Friday, both girls fresh-legged, raced the length of the ice side by side, sticks clattering, ice chips flying like glass. "Whatever happens," Marisol panted, "remind me never to do driveway jumps after day one again." Keira laughed and leaned into the turn.

The last chocolate chip cookie on the cafeteria table was about to cause a war. Rachel watched Danny wave two dollars over it while Priya held up three, and behind them a sixth grader was digging through a backpack with the focus of someone defusing a bomb.

"Sold to Priya for three dollars," said Marcus, who ran the bake sale table like a small corporation. He had one cash box, one price list, and no interest in fairness. Yesterday the same cookies had been fifty cents each, because yesterday there had been forty of them.

"That's not right," Danny said afterward, walking with Rachel down the hall. "The seller just picks whatever number he wants. Marcus decided three dollars."

"Priya decided three dollars," Rachel said. "She offered it. If nobody wanted cookies, Marcus would be giving them away by lunch."

They argued all the way to the library, where Rachel was supposed to be documenting sources for her social studies paper. Instead she typed "who sets prices" into the catalog, mostly to win the argument. One thin green book came up, and she pulled it off the shelf and sat on the floor between the stacks to read it.

"Listen to this," she called to Danny, who had followed her in. "Some economist, Alfred Marshall, wrote it in 1890 in his book 'Principles of Economics.' He said supply and demand are like the two blades of a pair of scissors. It takes both to set a price."

"So neither one alone does it," Danny said slowly.

"So we were both kind of right, which is the worst possible outcome." Rachel checked the page again to make sure she had the year right, because Danny was famous for claiming her sources were biased whenever they supported her side. 1890. The book said 1890. The scissors had been around a long time, cutting prices in half with two blades, and nobody at their lunch table had noticed.

The next morning Rachel brought a test. She baked a dozen cookies at home, with her mother supervising the oven part, and set them next to Marcus's table with a sign that said ONE DOLLAR. Marcus sneered at her amateur operation until fourth period, when his own cookies ran out and hers were the only ones left in the building. By lunch, kids were offering her two dollars, then two fifty, and one boy tried to reserve a cookie by paying in advance, which Rachel declined on the grounds that she was not a bank.

Then came the twist. At the end of lunch, Mr. Okafor, the vice principal, stopped at her table. Rachel braced for a lecture about unauthorized food sales. Instead he bought her last two cookies for three dollars and asked if she would be interested in running the snack table at the spring fundraiser, since last year's organizer had graduated.

"Fundraiser prices go up when it's a big crowd, right?" Rachel said, sliding him his change.

Mr. Okafor looked at her over the cookie. "Who have you been talking to?"

"A dead economist," Danny said, taking another dollar from a kid who had come back for seconds.

Colton sat on the crinkly paper of the exam table with his elbows on his knees, staring at the two dark half-moons under his arms. They had shown up halfway through morning announcements, and PJ Torres had announced them to half the hallway like it was breaking news. Now Dr. Marsh was tapping the screen, and Colton waited for his chance.

"Growing bodies sweat more," Dr. Marsh said. "It's normal." She handed him a sample card. "What matters is what you buy. Check the label."

That was it. No cure, no pill. In the waiting room, Mom flipped through a magazine while Colton's little brother narrated the fish tank, and Colton turned the sample card over and over. Whatever the doctor knew, she had left the actual answer for him to find.

The drugstore was two doors down. Colton stood in the deodorant aisle while his brother wandered toward the candy, and he read labels like his life depended on it, because tryouts were Thursday and the gym had no air conditioning. Two sticks sat side by side. One said antiperspirant, one said deodorant. He had always thought they were just two words for the same thing, but the fine print did not agree. The antiperspirant box said it reduces sweating by temporarily plugging sweat ducts. He read it twice, then turned to the other. That one never mentioned stopping sweat at all, only odor, reducing it or covering the smell.

"Those are opposites, basically," Colton said to his brother, who had drifted back with a pack of gum. "Antiperspirant stops the wet. Deodorant only handles the stink."

"So get the wet one," his brother said, already bored.

It was that simple, and it wasn't. Colton thought about PJ and the hallway jury that had laughed at his shirt. The antiperspirant stopped the actual sweating, which was the whole problem. The deodorant would just put perfume on top of it. His old stick, he realized, had been a deodorant all along, which explained a lot about the last month. Trying to fix it by layering on three swipes every morning had been reckless; it had done nothing but waste time.

He took the antiperspirant to the register with his own five dollars. Thursday afternoon, in the hot gym, he took his shot, ran the lines, raised his hand for the pass, and kept his arms up on purpose. Afterward, he pulled his shirt away from his body and looked. Dry. He walked past PJ on the way to the water fountain and lifted his arm to wipe his forehead.

"Nice tryout," PJ said.

Megan stared at the two jars on the back counter of Mr. Reyes's science classroom. One had held chicken soup sealed tight since Monday, and it still looked like soup. The other, covered only with loose foil, had turned cloudy and smelled like gym socks. Her science fair project was due in nine days, and all she had so far was one good jar and one gross one.

"Your problem is you're guessing," said Deshawn, who was building a volcano two tables over. "You can't just say germs floated in. Did you see them float in?"

That was the trouble. Nobody could see them float in. Megan wrote in her notebook: maybe the soup went bad because something in the air landed on it, not because the soup itself was rotten from the start. It was a guess, but a testable one. If she was right, then broth in a container where the air had to travel through a long, twisting path would stay clean, because the bad stuff in the air would not make it around the bends. If she was wrong, that broth would go bad just like the foil jar.

Mr. Reyes let her stay after class to look through his old science books, and there she found a drawing that made her sit up straight. Louis Pasteur boiled broth in flasks with long S-shaped necks, and the broth stayed free of microbes because dust and germs got trapped in the bend of the neck. She read the sentence three times. Someone had tested her exact idea a long time ago, and it had worked.

"It's like a trap," she told Deshawn the next morning, holding up a diagram she had copied. "The neck bends like a snake, and the germs get stuck in the bend. Sealed jar, swan-neck flask, both stay clean. Open jar goes disgusting."

"So your hypothesis was right," Deshawn said. "Somebody just proved it before you were born."

"That's not the point." Megan grabbed a marker and started sketching on her poster board. "The point is I can test it myself. I'll boil broth in three containers. One sealed, one with a bent tube for a neck, one open. If the bent one stays clean, my guess holds up. If it goes bad, I was wrong and I start over." She paused, marker in the air. "It won't go bad."

"Don't be reckless," Deshawn said. "Last time you promised the volcano wouldn't leak, and my protagonist ended up covered in baking soda."

"That was your volcano and your protagonist." Megan taped the diagram to the middle of her board and wrote her hypothesis across the top in careful block letters. She set the three containers on the windowsill where everyone in class could watch them, side by side, and slid a folded card in front of each one. On the third card she wrote a single question mark.

"Nine days," Deshawn said.

"Then we find out."

Brooke had promised the science fair committee a volcano, and now she regretted it, because everyone built volcanoes, and hers was going to look exactly like the one Marcus Reyes was building two lab tables away.

"You know why they erupt, right?" Marcus said, holding up his vinegar bottle like a trophy. "Baking soda plus vinegar. The baking soda is sodium bicarbonate, the vinegar is acetic acid, and together they make carbon dioxide gas. That's what pushes everything out. Everybody knows that."

"Everybody also builds the same cone out of papier-mâché," Brooke said. She looked down at her own cone, gray and lumpy, and decided she'd rather lose than present a third identical volcano. If the gas did the pushing, then the amount of gas ought to matter, which meant the amount of vinegar ought to matter, and nobody ever checked. She could test it. Three bottles, three different amounts, same baking soda each time, and a ruler taped to a wall behind the volcano to measure how high each eruption reached.

Mr. Okafor wandered past and did not offer help, which was his way of saying he trusted them, or possibly that he was being negligent about supervising the vinegar supply. Either way, Brooke got to work. The first trial, a small splash of vinegar, produced a sad burp that barely reached ten centimeters. The second, half a bottle, shot foam past the thirty-centimeter mark and splattered Marcus's notebook.

"Hey. That stuff hindered my data," Marcus said, wiping off his page.

"Then maybe you should collect some," Brooke said, and to her surprise, he came over. His project, it turned out, was just a volcano with red food coloring, no measurements at all, and the fair was in two days. He had an obligation to his partner too, which he had been ignoring.

They ran six trials together, trading the jobs of pouring and reading the ruler. More vinegar meant a taller eruption every single time, and the numbers lined up so neatly that Brooke wrote them twice to be sure. Marcus copied the last column into his notebook, then looked at his plain red cone the way you look at a sandwich next to a banquet.

"We're combining projects," he announced. "Your measurements, my cone. Mine has better paint."

Brooke considered arguing, but his cone did have better paint. "Fine," she said. "But I'm the one who says how much vinegar goes in the bottle."

"Deal," said Marcus, and handed her the ruler.

Mathis had been camped on the couch for three days, surrounded by crumpled tissues, a thermometer, and half a glass of orange juice he kept forgetting about. The flu was finally loosening its grip, but his nose still felt like a leaky faucet. His little sister Nadia wandered in, holding her toothbrush, and stood at the edge of his blanket nest.

"Why do you keep telling me to use soap?" she said. "I rinsed my hands with water just now. They're clean. See?" She held them out like evidence.

Mathis squinted at her from under the blanket. "Water just slides off the virus," he said. "Soap breaks apart the fatty outer layer that surrounds flu viruses. That's why washing with soap gets rid of them better than rinsing with water alone."

Nadia blinked. "The virus has a layer? Like a coat?"

"Kind of." He sat up, interested despite himself. "Think of it like grease on a pan. You can rinse a greasy pan forever and it stays greasy. Add soap and it comes apart." He paused. "At least, that's what I think happens. Let me check." He grabbed his phone from the armrest, typed with one thumb, and scrolled. "Huh. Yeah. That's the consensus. Every source says the same thing."

"So my hands are still covered in viruses?" Nadia stared at her palms like they'd betrayed her.

"Probably. I've been sneezing on every doorknob in this house for three days." Mathis pushed the blanket back. "Come on. Let's do an experiment."

In the kitchen, he found the olive oil and a dinner plate. He poured a thin puddle of oil onto the plate. "Pretend this oil is the fatty layer. Dip your finger in water and try to wipe it off." Nadia swiped at the oil. It smeared and stayed, a slick rainbow smear across the white plate.

"Now try with soap." She lathered her finger and dragged it through. The oil broke apart and lifted away, clinging to the foam in little beads. She did it again, and again, watching the plate go clean.

"So the virus just... falls apart?" she said.

"That's the idea. Its coat gets broken up." Mathis turned the plate under the tap, watching the last oily streaks vanish. It was strange to think about, all those invisible things on doorknobs and hands, held together by something so delicate. What else was floating around that nobody could see?

Nadia washed her hands at the sink, properly this time, humming while she scrubbed. Then she pointed at Mathis. "You should wash too. You're the one who's sick."

He held up his hands in surrender and headed for the bathroom. "Fine," he called over his shoulder. "But nobody touches my orange juice."

The notification buzzed at 9:47 p.m., and Noah picked up his phone to find the group chat already scrolling fast. "BIO PRESENTATIONS FRIDAY," Priya had typed in all caps, followed by Mr. Kessler's rubric screenshot. Under it, sixteen thumbs-up and one message from Tasha: "not gonna be there friday. doctor thing." Noah frowned. Tasha had a doctor thing for the last presentation too, and the one before that. He scrolled back through the chat history, and the pattern condensed into something he could actually see: every single time a presentation came up, Tasha vanished.

He typed, "u ok?" and then deleted it, because it felt like calling her out in front of everyone. Instead he sent a private message: "hey, you doing the bio slideshow? I can share mine if you want to compare notes." Three dots appeared, vanished, appeared again. "i'm skipping," she wrote. "my anxiety gets so bad before them i feel sick." Noah sat back against his pillow. He got nervous too, stomach flipping, heart loud, but he'd noticed something about his own stress that he couldn't leave alone. When he forced himself through a presentation, the next one felt a little smaller. When he ducked out of one, like the book report he'd faked a fever for in October, the fear afterward seemed to grow instead of shrink, like it was being fed.

He tested the idea out loud, typing slowly. "ok weird question. the ones you skip feel scarier the next time, right? like each one is worse than the last?" A long pause. Then: "yes?? how did u know." Noah's own coping trick was reading in the hallway for five minutes before class, or texting his brother a joke, anything to get his hands busy. "i think skipping gives you relief really fast," he wrote, "but then it makes the anxiety stronger later, because you never get to find out you could handle it." He stared at the sentence, hoping it didn't sound like a lecture from a health pamphlet. Tasha replied with a single shaking-face emoji, then: "friday is in 3 days. i can't."

"you don't have to do the whole thing," he typed. "do the first slide. one slide. i'll stand next to you." He suggested she set a boundary with Mr. Kessler, just tell him flat out she'd present last so she wasn't first up and panicked. The next morning Tasha showed him her slideshow, eight slides about axolotls, and admitted she'd been drafting it for two weeks without telling anyone. "so you already did the work," Noah said. "your brain just keeps saying run." She laughed a small, real laugh and said her mom kept an optimistic sticky note on the fridge that she'd started ignoring.

Friday came. Tasha went second to last, and she stood there with her note card shaking, and she read the first slide, and then the second, and after the axolotl regrowing limbs she looked up and saw Priya mouthing "whoa" in the front row. When she sat down she texted Noah from across the room: "that was awful and i did it anyway." He wrote back, "memoir title. 'awful and i did it anyway.' you're welcome." On the walk to lunch she caught up with him at the water fountain, still pale but grinning. "Next one," she said, "I'm going third."

The bean seeds on the windowsill had begun to germinate, tiny green hooks pushing out of the soil, but Samantha barely looked at them. She was still thinking about what she had said in the hallway that morning: that most students at their school walked to school. Marcus had laughed and called it a wild guess, and she had walked away with her ears burning.

Now Mr. Okafor was writing two words on the board: opinion and claim. He would not say much, only that the class would spend the period deciding which of the statements on his desk belonged in each column. Samantha slid her bean tray aside and leaned forward.

"Most students at our school walk to school," Mr. Okafor read aloud. "Opinion or claim?"

"Opinion," said Priya. "Nobody knows that."

"But you could find out," Samantha said, before she could stop herself. "You could ask everybody. Like a survey."

Marcus turned around in his seat. "Nobody has asked everybody."

"So?" Samantha's heart was beating fast. "It can still be checkable even if nobody has checked it yet. If we took a survey, we'd know."

The room went quiet. Mr. Okafor tapped the board. "Could we actually do that?"

"We could count," Priya said slowly. "At the doors, in the morning. Walkers, bus riders, car riders."

They planned it right there. On Tuesday, Samantha stood at the front doors with a clipboard, making a tally mark for every student who arrived on foot. Priya took the side doors and Marcus, who had volunteered before Samantha could ask him, took the gym entrance. By first bell Samantha's fingers were cold and her column of tally marks ran down the whole page.

They typed the numbers into the classroom database, which Mr. Okafor kept for experiments, and the bar chart appeared on the screen. Walkers were the tallest bar. Not by much, though, and the bus bar was close behind. Samantha stared at it, remembering how certain she had sounded in the hallway, how sure. She had been right, mostly, and somehow that felt less like winning than she had expected.

"Well?" Marcus said, leaning over her shoulder at the screen. "Were you right or not?"

"Close enough that it's probable I'd be right again next time," Samantha said. "But I'd have to count again to know for sure."

Marcus grinned and shook the clipboard at her. "Same time Thursday?"

The bus smelled like wet raincoats and old vinyl, and Cameron had the letter folded in his back pocket, which meant he'd read it eleven times since breakfast. Mr. Reyes had clipped it from the local paper and dropped it on Cameron's desk with a shrug, saying only, "Thought you'd want this, since you're at that park every Saturday." The letter said the new skate park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste, and Cameron's stomach had been clenched ever since.

He slid into the seat across from Dana, who was nursing a cold and sniffling into a tissue. "Don't breathe on me," she said. "My mom says this virus is going around the whole school." Cameron held his breath for three seconds out of politeness, then gave up. He unfolded the letter and smoothed it on his knee.

"Read this," he said. Dana read it. Behind them, Marcus leaned over the seat, because Marcus leaned over every seat on the bus, that was practically his job.

"Two million dollars," Marcus said. "That's a lie. My uncle works for the city. It was two million." Cameron frowned at the paper. If the number was right, then that part of the letter wasn't a lie at all. You could look it up. You could call the city office, or find the budget online, and the number would either be true or it wouldn't. Dana blew her nose and said, "So the letter's true, then?"

"No," Cameron said slowly. "Not all of it." He read the last words again. A waste. That was the part that had been buzzing in his head since breakfast like a fly against a window. His little sister had asked at dinner whether the park really was a waste, and their dad had said that was somebody's opinion, not a fact, but he'd said it fast and then gone back to his noodles, and Cameron hadn't gotten it until just now, on a bus that rattled over every pothole on Marsh Road.

"Here's the thing," he said, holding up the letter so both of them could see it. "The cost can be checked, but 'a waste' is an opinion." Dana squinted at him. "So?" Cameron tapped the paper. "So when Mr. Reyes asks us Monday about stuff like this, that's the whole trick. One sentence can have both in it. Like if I said the ocean, which covers most of Earth, is boring. The covering part you could check. The boring part is just me." Marcus drummed his fingers on the seat back. "So whoever wrote this could be right about the money and still be wrong about the park."

"Or right about the park and lying about the money," Dana said, and sneezed into her tissue.

The bus groaned around the corner by the field where the last endangered cranes nested each spring, and Cameron folded the letter along its old creases. He was already planning what he'd write back to the paper, something that started with the number and ended with Saturday morning, his board under his arm, the whole park loud with wheels and nobody complaining. "First thing Monday," he told them, "I'm asking Mr. Reyes if we can print both."

Kate sat cross-legged in the desk chair, the house quiet except for the hum of the old computer and the smell of her mother's soup drifting up the stairs. On the screen was a half-written email: an invitation to her thirteenth birthday party, addressed to nobody yet. She had typed all twenty-six names from her class list into a text file, but when she tried pasting them into the To field, she stopped. Last year Marcus had sent a party invite to everyone, and every single address had shown up right there at the top, where anybody could copy them. Kate's dad called it a "chain of everybody knowing everybody's business," and he treated careful email habits like something hereditary, passed down from his own mother, who had always double-locked the front door.

She scrolled through the compose window and noticed a small link that said BCC, next to a link that said CC. CC she knew; her English teacher had used it once when forwarding a reminder about citations for their research papers, and both classes had been able to see each other's addresses. BCC was a mystery. She clicked it, and a new empty field opened below the To line.

Kate reasoned it out the way she reasoned out anything: she tested it. She put her own address in the To field, put her grandmother's address in the BCC field, and wrote "testing, ignore this" in the body. Then she walked to the kitchen, logged in on her mother's laptop, and opened the message that had arrived there. Her own address appeared in the To line. Her grandmother's address appeared in the BCC line, because Mom's laptop was logged in as Grandma sometimes. But when Kate checked the copy that arrived at her own address, there was no BCC line at all, and Grandma's address was nowhere in it.

"BCC," said her brother Dev from the doorway, reading over her shoulder with a cracker in his hand. "Blind carbon copy. The people you put there get the message, but the other recipients can't see their addresses."

"That's what I thought," Kate said, though she hadn't, not for sure. She went back upstairs, past the soup smell and the settling creaks of the evening house, and pasted all twenty-six names into the BCC field. In the To field she typed only her own address, so the email would still look like a proper invitation and not like a message sent to nobody. She added the party details, the time, the request to bring a swimsuit, and a line about the one rule that would govern the whole afternoon: no presents, just food and the pool. Then she pressed send and listened to the little whoosh the old computer made, like a breath let out.

Within a minute, replies began to arrive. Priya wrote "I'M COMING" in all capitals, which Kate knew meant excitement and not shouting, since Priya always wrote that way when she was happy. Leo replied with a single thumbs-up emoji. Kate closed the laptop lid halfway, leaving it open a crack the way she always did, and went down to set the table before her mother called her.

Brayden balanced the mixing bowl on the picnic table and checked the recipe again, though he had memorized it by now. Mom's birthday biscuits, the ones his grandfather used to make, and Brayden had promised the whole family a batch at tonight's backyard dinner. The garden behind him was lush after a week of rain, and the grill already smelled like charcoal, but the biscuits were his job alone.

He reached for the tin marked baking powder and tilted it. Empty. A few grains sifted out and that was all. The nearest store was a twenty-minute bike ride, and the potatoes needed watching on the grill, so riding away wasn't really an option. He stood there with the tin in his hand, feeling the old resentment from last summer rise up, the time he'd quit halfway through Grandpa's recipe book and Grandpa had quietly finished it himself. This year Brayden wanted to preserve that recipe, not lose it, and quitting twice felt like the same failure twice.

In the cupboard by the back door he found a box of baking soda and thought, close enough. He stirred it in, cut the dough, and set the tray on the grill's side shelf where the heat was gentle. Ten minutes later he lifted the lid and stared. The biscuits had gone flat and faintly bitter, nothing like the tall golden ones in the photo.

He sat down on the step and turned it over. The pancake batter Grandpa made used buttermilk, sour and tangy, and it always rose high. These biscuits used plain milk. Soda went in where buttermilk went in. Powder went in where nothing sour went in. Brayden stood up slowly. The box of baking soda needed something acidic in the batter to do its work. He grabbed his phone and read the label on a baking powder tin in a photo: it already contained both baking soda and a dry acid, which was why a recipe didn't need anything acidic for the batter to rise.

"Then I'll add the acid myself," he said out loud. He found lemon juice in the fridge, mixed a fresh batch with plain milk, soda, and a careful spoonful of juice, and slid the tray back onto the warm shelf. His little sister wandered over and peeked under the foil.

"Smell like Grandpa's," she said.

"Better," Brayden said, and lifted the lid on eight tall, golden biscuits.

Chase had one goal for the field trip to the Harlow Living History Farm: get through the day without his group's egg basket ending up on the ground. So far, so good. The morning had revolved around chores, and Mrs. Teller had assigned him, Priya, and Milo to the chicken coop, where a dozen hens strutted around like they owned the county.

"Collect the eggs, handle them gently, and bring them to the kitchen porch," the guide had said. Milo immediately dropped his clipboard, which did not inspire confidence.

Chase crouched in the straw, sliding his hand under a speckled hen who squawked at him like he was a parasite who had come to drink her blood. "Easy," he muttered. "I'm not even hungry." Priya snickered behind him, and the first egg went into the basket without incident. By the fourth, Chase felt like a professional.

Milo, holding two eggs up to the light like precious gems, suddenly frowned. "Hey. There's no rooster anywhere. I've been watching. Zero roosters. So if we keep these eggs somewhere warm, will they hatch?"

Chase considered the question while a hen pecked at his shoelace. No rooster, that was true. He tried to picture it: twenty eggs under a heat lamp, and one morning, twenty chicks. Something about it felt wrong, like a vending machine with nothing stocked inside. "I don't think so," he said slowly. "My grandma's neighbor has hens and no rooster, and she sells the eggs as eating eggs. If they hatched, she'd basically be running a chick factory for free."

"So what's the difference?" Milo demanded. "Eggs are eggs."

"Maybe not." Chase looked around the coop again, checking rafters, checking the yard through the wire. The hens were the whole population. An idea formed, simple enough to test. "Every chicken we've seen today came out of an egg. If these eggs could hatch on their own, the farm wouldn't need to buy chicks ever, right? But the guide said they order chicks in the spring."

Priya gasped. "She did! I wrote it down. I write everything down." She flipped her notebook open to a page with the words CHICKS ARRIVE, APRIL underlined twice.

Milo looked personally betrayed by biology. "So without a rooster, the eggs can't hatch into chicks at all?"

"That's my theory," Chase said. "Hens lay them either way. Rooster or no rooster, you still get eggs. But no rooster, no chicks. Ever."

They carried the basket to the kitchen porch, where the guide was demonstrating an old butter churn, its wooden lid so clouded and opaque with age that nobody could see inside. Milo set the eggs down with exaggerated ceremony, like a funeral.

"Good work," the guide said. "Those go to the frying pan tomorrow. We'll have a demonstration about breakfast in the 1800s."

Milo opened his mouth, closed it, and finally said, "So if I had kept one in my hoodie, nothing would ever happen. No matter what."

"Nothing," Chase confirmed, "except you'd smell like egg."

Priya raised her hand anyway, notebook at the ready. "One question. If hens lay eggs no matter what, then what exactly does the rooster do all day?"

From somewhere beyond the barn came a sound that was definitely not a cow.

The train swayed through pine hills, and Elena's little sister Dory kept her fist closed tight on the seat between them. Their family trip was almost over, and Dory had been quiet since they left the park, which was not like her at all.

"Let me see it," Elena said. Dory tried to evade her eyes, staring out the window instead, but slowly she opened her fingers. In her palm sat a chunk of rose quartz, streaked with pink, about the size of a plum.

"Isn't it gorgeous? I found it right by the waterfall. The waterfall was the climax of the whole trip, and this is like a souvenir of it." Dory cupped her other hand over the stone. "It's mine now."

An affluent-looking man across the aisle glanced over the top of his newspaper, and Elena lowered her voice. Something was nagging at her, a memory she couldn't quite see. At the visitor center there had been a display, and the ranger had said the words on it out loud, but Elena had been too busy looking at the wolf skull to pay attention. She thought back. The words had come in a list, she was almost sure, and the list had been long enough to fill a whole poster. She dug through her backpack, pushing aside granola bar wrappers until her fingers found a folded paper: a brochure she had grabbed because it had a picture of a marmot on the front.

She unfolded it on the tray table. There it was, exactly as she remembered, a list of seven principles under the heading Leave No Trace. She read down the numbered lines. Plan ahead and prepare. Travel and camp on durable surfaces. Dispose of waste properly, which explained the ziplock bag of orange peels their dad had carried out. Then the fourth line: leave what you find.

"Seven of them," Elena said, tapping the page. "And number four says leave what you find. That rock belongs there, Dory. If everybody took one, there wouldn't be any left."

Dory's chin wobbled. "But I want to remember the waterfall."

"You can remember it another way. Remember the junior ranger badge you wanted so bad?" Elena leaned closer. "A ranger's job is following these rules. If you take the rock, you can't really call yourself one."

Dory stared at the stone for a long moment, then at the brochure. "Fine," she whispered. "But I'm drawing it first. Every single stripe." She pulled her sketchbook from under the seat and flattened it against the window, and Elena handed her a pencil.

Elliot's little sister had been coughing for three nights, and his mother had sent him to the pharmacy on Marsh Street with twenty dollars and one instruction: bring back something that actually worked. He stood in the cold-and-flu aisle between two boxes. The first box, bright orange, had a photograph of a smiling man and the words "I felt better in one day!" printed across the top. The second box, plain white, said "Tested in a study of 420 adults." Elliot turned both boxes over in his hands. Forty-two dollars, though. Way over budget. There was a third option, a store brand for eight dollars with no photograph and no study, just a list of ingredients.

A man in a rain jacket was standing beside him, holding a tube of sunscreen. "Get the orange one," the man said. "That stuff saved me in February. One dose and I was a new person."

"Thanks," Elliot said, but he didn't reach for the orange box. One person. One February. He put the eight-dollar store brand in his basket anyway, because it had the same ingredients as the white one, which he'd checked twice, letter by letter.

At the counter, he counted his money and found he could also afford the sunscreen, which his mother had asked for if there was anything left. The pharmacist, a woman with reading glasses on a chain, rang it up. "Good timing on this," she said. "We ran out all week. Our supplier tested it on volunteers who live right near the equator, where the sun is strongest. They couldn't keep it on the shelf down there."

Elliot looked at the tube. "How many volunteers?"

"About three hundred, the label says." She turned the tube so he could see the small print. "Big studies like that, they're more reliable than one person swearing by something. With enough people, the flukes just even out."

"That's what I was thinking," Elliot said, and he meant it, though he hadn't been able to articulate it that clearly in the aisle. He thought of the man in the rain jacket, one person, one February. He thought of the smiling face on the orange box. Then he thought of 420 adults, all coughing, all taking the same white pills, most of them getting better. Maybe some of them hadn't. But with that many people, the ones who would have recovered anyway and the ones who never improved wouldn't be able to hide the truth. His own idea felt more robust suddenly, less like a guess.

He was almost out the door when he noticed a shelf of cough drops with a sign: "Voted Best by Our Customers." Underneath, in smaller letters, it said "Based on a survey of 350 shoppers." Three hundred fifty people. He imagined his three friends from science class voting on something, all agreeing, and how that could still be wrong. This was different. He picked up a bag of the honey-lemon drops and added them to his basket.

At home, his sister took the syrup without complaint, and the drops turned out to be the real prize. She held one up and studied it like a tiny amber stone.

"Where'd you get these?" she asked.

"The pharmacy," Elliot said. "A lot of people picked them."

Isaac sat in the back seat with his knees pressed against the driver's seat in front of him, which had never happened before this summer. Last year his legs had fit the car the way they always had. Now, on the drive to his grandmother's house, he kept shifting because his sneakers jammed into the seat pocket, and when he pulled his knee up to sit cross-legged, his shorts rode up and he saw them: thin lines, pale pink, running sideways across the skin above his knee like tiny scratches that had never bled.

"Stop wiggling," his sister Maya said beside him. She was eleven and had claimed the window seat, an argument Isaac had lost that morning and was still evaluating. Maybe he should have let her have the middle instead. Three hours of a wedged elbow was worse than forty minutes of no window.

"What are those?" Maya asked, pointing at his knee. "Is that a rash?"

"It's not a rash." Isaac bent closer. He turned his leg toward the light from the window. The lines were on both knees, he discovered, almost exactly matched, and he had not fallen, not scraped anything, not even gone through the blackberry bushes behind the gym. So they had come from inside somehow. He thought about his cousin Theo, who was fifteen and had lines kind of like these on his shoulders, and about how Theo had shot up four inches in a single season of basketball. Isaac had grown two shoe sizes since spring. Maybe that was it. Maybe when you grew too fast, the skin got left behind, like a note arriving after you'd already moved.

"I have them too," Maya said suddenly, in a smaller voice. She tugged her waistband down a half inch at her hip. "Right there. I thought something was wrong with me. I've been hiding them at the pool."

Isaac studied hers. Hers were fainter than his, thin pale streaks. "Those are stretch marks," he said. "From growing fast." He remembered then, on his own thigh, marks from two years ago when he'd had his first big growth spurt. He pulled up his shorts to check. You could barely find them now, just ghost-smudges in the light. "Look, my old ones mostly went away. They fade."

Maya inspected his leg, then hers, comparing. In the front seat their dad reached over and tapped the thermostat down two degrees because the sun had shifted onto his arm. "Everything okay back there?" he asked.

"Fine," Maya said, and pulled her waistband back up. "Isaac, tell me again about the fading part when we stop. Slowly. I want to remember it at the pool on Monday."

Christopher sat two rows behind Marcus and refused to look at him, which was hard, because Mr. Delgado had just asked the class to nominate a partner for the history project. Marcus raised his hand and pointed at Priya. He did not even glance back.

At lunch Christopher didn't sit with him, and at afternoon study hall he wrote in his notebook: Marcus picked Priya, so Marcus is done with me. But the sentence bothered him. Priya had the best notes in the class, and Marcus needed a good grade to stay on the basketball team. Maybe Marcus hadn't picked her over him at all. Maybe he had just picked a good partner. Christopher couldn't see inside Marcus's head, but he could test one idea. He wrote a second line: If I tell him what I think happened, and repeat back what he says, I'll know if he's mad or just busy.

In English the next morning, their teacher mentioned that the term "active listening" was introduced by the psychologists Carl Rogers and Richard Farson in 1957. It means trying to understand the speaker's point of view, Christopher thought, often by repeating their meaning back in your own words. He copied the sentence down, then circled it twice.

He caught Marcus by the lockers after the last bell. "You could've asked me to be your partner," Christopher said. "I was going to, but you skipped lunch on Tuesday and I thought you were avoiding me, so I panicked," Marcus said. "So you felt I was already dumping you as a friend," Christopher said, repeating the meaning back. Marcus's shoulders dropped about two inches. "Yeah. Exactly that."

Christopher had been sure Marcus had chosen Priya because Priya was cooler, or because their friendship was somehow over, and now he could feel that certainty cracking apart. It was strange how a thing he couldn't see, the reason behind one raised hand, could look so dark from two rows back and so ordinary up close. "Mr. Delgado says we can have groups of three," Marcus said. "Priya's cool with it. We're doing descendants of local founders, and apparently one of them had a controversial past, some land dispute thing." "I'm in," Christopher said. "But I pick where we work. My house. Your mom's dog ate my homework once." Marcus laughed and shoved his locker shut. "Deal," he said, and they walked out together into the cold.

Emilie spread the poster board across two folding tables at the family reunion, her markers lined up like tools. Her friend Priya's sign-language club needed a banner for the school fair, and Emilie had promised it for Monday. Across the top, in fat blue letters, she had written: PRIDE IN deaf CULTURE. Her cousin Marco leaned over her shoulder, arms crossed, frowning at the small d.

"You got that wrong," he signed, his hands quick and sharp. His mother, Aunt Rena, translated from the lawn chair beside the table. "He says the D should be capital."

"Since when does deaf get a capital letter?" Emilie signed back, slowly, because her signing was still clunky. Marco snorted and wandered off toward the volleyball game, leaving her with the poster and the problem.

She remembered the club's first meeting in September, how Priya had stood at the whiteboard and said her grandmother was deaf and that the club would learn her language. Nobody had mentioned capitals then. Emilie had assumed deaf was like tall or tired, just a description. But Marco had grown up with two Deaf parents. If he was fussy about one letter, the letter meant something, though she could not see what. The rule was invisible; she needed someone to show her where it lived.

She found Marco's mother by the dessert table, filling a plate with lemon bars. "Aunt Rena, why does Marco care about the capital D?"

"Because of something from 1972," Aunt Rena said. "A linguist, James Woodward, proposed writing Deaf with a capital D for the community and culture of sign-language users, and lowercase deaf for the hearing condition itself." She tapped the plate. "Two different things, one spelling apart."

Emilie turned that over while Aunt Rena went back for a second lemon bar. Capital D for the people, the language, the belonging. Small d for the ears. Priya's club was about people and language, so it was Deaf. Marco wasn't being picky; he was being exact, the way Grandpa was exact about calling himself an artisan instead of a hobbyist woodworker, because the word carried who he was.

Back at the table, Emilie tested the rule on every line of the poster. Deaf culture, capital. When the club text mentioned Priya's grandmother losing her hearing, that part was deaf, lowercase, the condition. She filled in the big D with red marker, pressing hard, then held the poster up across the yard so Marco could see it.

He jogged over, studied it, and gave her a slow thumbs-up. "Better," he signed. Then he pointed at her blank bottom margin and grinned. "Now make it beautiful."

"Give me those yellow markers," Emilie said. "And somebody keep Uncle Vic away from the table. Last year he signed my name on my own birthday banner and I was gullible enough to hang it up."

Marco laughed, a sound like two hands clapping, and tossed her the yellow.

The gym smelled like popcorn and floor wax, and Felix had his phone out before the buzzer even started the game. His best friend Dara leaned over from the next bleacher.

"You're checking baseball stats at a basketball game?"

"It matters," Felix said. "My dad says Justice was better than Jeter in the nineties. My uncle says Jeter. I'm settling it." He tapped through the seasons, one by one, and felt his stomach drop a little. In 1995, David Justice had the higher batting average. In 1996, David Justice had the higher batting average again. He scrolled back up to check, then down again, calibrating his eyes to the columns the way he'd line up a free throw. Same result both years.

"Justice," he announced. "Twice. Case closed."

Dara snatched the phone. "Then add them together. Two seasons, one winner." She found the combined numbers and went quiet. Then she turned the screen toward him, and Felix read it twice, but the numbers did not change their minds. Jeter's two-year average was higher.

"That's broken," Felix said. "He lost both years. How does he win the whole thing?" Down on the court, the home team was committing foul after foul, and the crowd groaned with each whistle. Felix barely heard it. He tried adding the averages himself, then multiplying, then starting over, and nothing came out the way the screen said. He passed the phone along the row to his older sister, Priya, who was home from college and only came to games when she wanted the nachos.

"Look at this," he said. "Justice beats Jeter in ninety-five, Justice beats Jeter in ninety-six, and then combined, Jeter's on top."

Priya squinted at it, shrugged, and handed it back. "Numbers are weird," she said, and went back to the nachos. That was the cost of asking Priya anything.

The buzzer sounded for halftime with the home team down by twelve. Felix kept scrolling while the cheerleaders tumbled across the floor. The whole game was numbers too, he realized. Field goal percentage, rankings, that "significant scoring drought" the announcer kept mentioning, as if four empty minutes could be squeezed into one tidy phrase. All those shots, all those misses, pressed into a single figure, like a cliff slowly worn down to one smooth number. Erosion, his science teacher would call it.

The twist came in the fourth quarter, when Dara nudged him, grinning, holding the phone. "I found it. It's a famous thing. Justice, Jeter, all of it."

"Does it say why?"

"Doesn't matter," Dara said. "Your dad and your uncle were both right."

The home team lost by two on a last-second shot that rimmed out. On the walk to the parking lot, Felix texted his dad one line: "Everybody won." The reply came back before he reached the car: "That's not an answer."

Charlotte slid into her chair just as her mother set down the pasta bowl with a clunk. Her mother had been on the phone all afternoon with the corporation's office in another city, and now she was stirring parmesan into the pot like it had personally offended her.

"You okay, Mom?" Charlotte's little brother Theo asked with his mouth full. He had been building an intricate fortress out of breadstick sticks, and their mother's mood was clearly messing with his architecture plans.

"I'm fine," their mother said, in the voice that meant the opposite. "The merger means half our team might migrate to the Chicago office next spring. I found out an hour ago. My anxiety has been through the roof since."

Charlotte watched her mother's hands, noticed the way she kept checking her phone even though it was silent. She remembered what Zoe had told her at lunch, after Zoe had failed her math quiz. "My counselor says coping means the ways you handle stress or hard feelings," Zoe had said, counting on her fingers. "Healthy coping is stuff like exercise, getting enough sleep, and talking with someone you trust. I used to just stay up scrolling, which is the bad kind." Charlotte had rolled her eyes at the time. Now she wondered.

She decided to test it. "Mom, remember when you made us walk the loop at the park after Grandpa's funeral, and you said moving helps you think?" she asked. "Want to go after dinner? Theo can come."

"I have emails," her mother said.

"Zoe says talking to someone you trust counts as coping too," Charlotte said. "So we could walk and you could talk. That's two healthy ones at once."

Theo looked up from his fortress, which had collapsed during the phone-checking. "I want to come. I'll rebuild the walls outside with sticks."

Their father raised his eyebrows at their mother. "The emails will still be there at nine," he said.

They walked the loop while the sky went orange. Theo collected sticks for a new fortress and their mother talked, haltingly at first, about boundaries she should have set months ago, about saying no to the extra projects that had swallowed her whole spring. By the second lap her shoulders had dropped an inch, though Charlotte noticed she still checked her phone twice at the corner where the signal came back.

At bedtime, Charlotte found her mother on the porch with her laptop, working anyway, because the merger was still happening and a walk could not change that. But she had also left her office chair pushed back from the desk, pointed toward the door, and a sticky note stuck to the screen that said "9:00, park?" Tomorrow the anxiety would be back, Charlotte knew. Still, she texted Zoe: "It worked on my mom. Mostly." Zoe sent back a running emoji and the words "sleep counts too." Charlotte put her phone in the drawer, where it buzzed once, twice, and then went quiet.

Rosalie spread her supplies across the picnic table: a stack of square paper, a magnifying lens she used for examining folds, and a bottle of water that was already going warm in the afternoon sun. The library origami club was meeting on Saturday, and she had promised to bring a paper crane that actually stood up. Three cranes lay in the grass, each one slumping over like it had given up.

Her neighbor Marcus climbed over the fence, the way he always did, and picked up one of the failed birds. "Still the same problem," he said, turning it toward the light. "The neck folds are too loose."

"I know that," Rosalie said. "What I don't know is why they keep coming out loose when I do exactly what the diagram says." She flattened the third crane and studied the creases through her lens. Each fold looked sharp on top, but when she held the paper up, she could see faint ghost lines underneath, running the wrong direction. Those hidden creases had been pressed into the paper during her earlier failed attempts. The problem was not in the fold she was making now; it was in the folds she had made before.

She tried to paraphrase the idea for Marcus. "So it's like the paper remembers." He shrugged, so she grabbed a fresh square. "Watch. No practice creases, no reusing paper." She folded slowly, and this time the crane's neck stood stiff and straight, its head pointing at the sky.

Marcus sat down on the bench. "Hey, at the club meeting, Priya said the word origami means something different. She claims it just means folding."

"It's both parts," Rosalie said. "Origami comes from 'ori', meaning to fold, and 'kami', meaning paper."

Marcus frowned. "Then Priya's only got half of it."

"You can tell her Saturday," Rosalie said. "Bring a crane so she knows you actually fold." He borrowed a square of paper and tried to copy her steps, but his bird turned out crooked, and after a minute of pressing and pressing at the wing he gave up and dropped it in the grass.

"That was a vain effort," he admitted, and Rosalie laughed. She lined up her one good crane on the table where the sun caught it, and set a fresh square beside it for tomorrow.

The minivan smelled like sunscreen and French fries, and Ariana was pretending not to sniff her own gym shirt when her little brother, Milo, leaned over from the back seat. "You smell like the boys' locker room," he announced, delighted with himself.

"Rude," Ariana said, but she cranked the window down anyway. She had showered after gym. She had even put on the deodorant she'd bought last month, the one with the intricate swirl design on the stick that had fooled her into thinking it was fancy. So why could she still smell herself? She turned the question over while Mom navigated traffic toward Grandma's house.

Then she remembered Thanksgiving, when her cousin Dez had been home from college. Some kid at the adult table had asked why his deodorant suddenly mattered, and Dez had laughed and said, "Fresh sweat has almost no smell. Body odor comes when bacteria on your skin break down sweat from the armpit glands, and those glands don't kick in until puberty." Ariana had been half listening then, busy with pie.
