Now the words snapped into place like a puzzle she'd finally found the edge of. That was why she'd never needed deodorant before this year. It wasn't that she'd gotten lazy. Her whole armpit situation had been rewritten.

She had a hypothesis, and a hypothesis needed a test. "Milo," she said, spinning around in her seatbelt, "smell my wrist." Mom said, "Eyes forward, please," but Milo was already grabbing her arm and taking a huge sniff. "Nothing," he reported. "Soap, I guess." "Exactly!" Ariana said. "My wrists sweat, but no smell. So it's not sweat itself." She was so excited she nearly bounced off the seat. "It's the armpit glands. Puberty ones. Bacteria eat their sweat and that's the smell. I'm basically running an experiment right now."

"You're basically being weird," Milo said, but he was grinning, already sniffing his own wrist like a detective. Mom muttered something about science happening in the car instead of at the dinner table, and Ariana pulled out her phone to text Dez: "Your armpit speech just solved my whole afternoon." She paused before sending, already anticipating the next problem. If bacteria were the culprit, was her deodorant even the right kind? Maybe she needed the antibacterial one, the one with the ingredient list long as a polymer chain, which was the only thing she'd retained from science class this week. "Next stop, the drugstore," she said to the windshield. Mom sighed. "We're going to Grandma's." "Then after Grandma's. This is important, Mom. This is a matter of reputation." Milo snickered. "Reputation of what, Stinky?" Ariana flicked his cap sideways and grinned at the road ahead.

Easton lay on his bed with three crumpled tissues on the blanket and his tablet propped against a pillow. His cold was almost gone, but his mother had made him stay home one more day, and he had spent most of that day wondering about one thing. Two weeks ago his sister Priya had a cold, and he had caught it from her. Last winter he had caught a different one from his friend Marcus. His flu shot had protected him against the flu every year, so why was there no shot like that for colds?

He typed his question into the search bar. The first answer made him sit up straight against the pillows. More than 200 different viruses could cause the common cold. He read the number twice, then said it out loud to the empty room. Two hundred. And the page said rhinoviruses are the most frequent cause, which meant some little family of viruses he had never heard of was responsible for more of his sniffles than anything else.

Priya appeared in the doorway holding two mugs of tea. "Mom said to bring you this. Why do you look like you solved a mystery?"

"Because I kind of did," Easton said. "I always blamed you for my colds. But you can't make a vaccine that covers two hundred different viruses the way the flu shot covers the flu. That's why nobody's ever given us one." He turned the tablet toward her. "Rhinoviruses. That's what usually gets us."

Priya set the mugs down and climbed onto the end of his bed. "Okay, but here's my problem. I want to stop catching your colds, since you clearly can't stop catching mine." She pulled a marker from her pocket, the special gold one she had been saving for a school poster, and drew a line down the middle of a tissue. "Sick side and healthy side."

Easton tested her idea against what he had just read. "That works for us, but it doesn't work for the world," he said. "We could hide from each other forever and still get colds, because there are so many different viruses out there. Any one of them could be the one that gets you next." Priya frowned at her golden line, clearly wanting a better answer than that.

"Then we do both," she decided. "Tissue rule in this house, and you wash your hands before you touch my mug." She traded him her tea for the tablet and started reading, and after a minute she looked up with an exceptional grin, the kind she saved for good ideas. "I'm going to tell my class this on Monday. Two hundred viruses, and rhinoviruses win. I'll sound like a health diplomat negotiating peace between us."

"Just don't cough on my poster markers," Easton said, and she threw a clean tissue at him, and it landed right on the sick side of the line.

Jaxson sat cross-legged on Devin's bedroom floor with his phone balanced on one knee, watching the group chat scroll. Devin's little sister thumped down the hallway outside, and somewhere below them the kitchen TV murmured through the floor. The chat was for planning Saturday at the skate park, but nobody had answered Jaxson's last three messages. He had written "anyone going early?" an hour ago, and it sat there like a coin dropped in an empty well.

Then Marcus posted, "I can come at ten." Right after, Priya posted, "me too, bringing my new board." Jaxson's question had never existed to them. He stared at his screen and thought about it. It wasn't that they disliked him. It was something quieter, something about how a small gray bubble among thirty others just vanished. He needed his message to have weight without being annoying, and he wasn't sure those were even different things yet.

He typed "WHERE ARE YOU GUYS MEETING" and hit send before he could second-guess himself. For three seconds nothing happened. Then Priya replied, "why are you yelling?" Marcus sent a single wide-eyed emoji. Jaxson's ears went hot. Yelling? He hadn't shouted a word out loud. But sitting there on Devin's floor, hearing how loud those capital letters looked against Priya's calm lowercase reply, he could see what she meant. In here, on the screen, caps were a raised voice, even in a silent room.

"It's like you walked into a library and hollered," Devin said, peering over from his bed. Jaxson had to digest that for a moment. The same words could be quiet or loud depending only on their shape. It was a small paradox: he had used the biggest letters to be noticed, and the bigness itself was what made him look wrong. "Sorry," he typed, all lowercase. "ten works for me too. I'll bring the extra bearings."

"finally someone has bearings," Priya answered, and Marcus sent a row of thumbs-up. Jaxson noticed the pattern then. Priya used lowercase even when she was excited. Marcus never used periods unless he was serious. The chat had rules nobody had posted, and he had been reading them wrong this whole time, like standing too close to people without knowing it.

He put the phone face-down on the carpet and listened to the TV muttering below, Devin's sister's footsteps, the radiator ticking. The morning was still going to be awkward maybe. But it was a solvable kind of awkward. He picked the phone back up and typed slowly, in ordinary small letters, "want me to come early and help set the ramp?" Priya's reply came fast: "yes please." Jaxson grinned at the screen and said, "Marcus owes me a soda for the bearings."

The community center gym smelled like floor wax and old popcorn, and Victor liked it best on Tuesdays, when the whole basketball season still stretched out ahead of him. This Tuesday, though, Coach Reyes had something different planned. She dragged a thick rope out of the equipment closet and told them to try tug-of-war before shooting drills, just for fun, just to see. Victor was picked for the six-person side, and even though their team weighed more than the five-person side, they lost. Twice.

"That's strange," Coach Reyes said, coiling the rope. "You all look like you're easing off out there." She didn't say it in a mean way, but Victor felt his ears go hot, because it was true. When he pulled with five others, he couldn't tell if he was pulling hard or hardly at all.

That night he typed tug of war pulling less with more people into the library computer, mostly to prove it wasn't his imagination. He found it right away. "In 1913 Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller," he read. So a bigger team didn't automatically pull harder. Each person's average pull shrank. He wrote it on a scrap of paper and folded it into his sock drawer, then thought better of it and put it in his gym bag instead. The tournament was Saturday, and Coach Reyes had announced that tug-of-war would open it, one pull against the Riverside team to start the day.

At Thursday practice, Victor asked to try something. "Let's pull one at a time," he said. "Watch the rope move each time, so everybody knows what their own pull looks like." Marisol went first, and the rope jerked a clear arm's length. Then Devon, then Victor, each one marked with a sneaker on the floor. After that, when all six pulled together, Victor counted under his breath, one two pull, one two pull, and the rope moved farther than it had on Tuesday.

"It's like the whole center," Marisol said, wiping her hands on her shorts. "My mom calls it an ecosystem. Basketball, the garden club, us. Everything works when everybody does their part." Devon, who had spent Tuesday sulking that the rope game was pointless and that they'd lost because of Marisol, nudged her shoulder. "Okay, I take it back. You were pulling fine. I just couldn't see it."

Saturday morning came gray and cool, and the permanent trophy case gleamed by the front doors, waiting for a new plaque with the winner's name. Riverside's team was bigger, eight to their six, and their captain grinned like the win was already his. The whistle blew. Victor gripped the rough rope, found the rhythm in his head, and heard five teammates breathing in time beside him. The red flag in the rope's center slid, steady as anything, across the painted line.

Hazel stood in her grandmother's crowded living room holding a wrapped box of almond cookies and trying to remember the plan. Her French cousins were arriving any minute, and her grandmother had said the meal would be on the table at six o'clock sharp, which gave Hazel exactly one hour to figure out the kissing thing before she embarrassed herself in front of everyone.

The trouble had started at the airport that morning. Aunt Céline had swept in and kissed Hazel's cheeks twice, left then right, while Uncle Marc had given her three kisses, which meant Hazel had to tilt her head an extra time and nearly bonbed noses with him. Then Coco, who was thirteen like Hazel, had kissed her twice again. Hazel smiled through all of it, but inside she was thinking hard. Her aunt and uncle were from the same family, so why didn't they match?

The doorbell rang, and the room turned turbulent with relatives hugging, untying scarves, and passing gifts. Coco's little brother Théo came in shaking rain off his jacket like a dog, and their grandmother handed out presents, insisting that the smallest children open theirs first, which was different from Hazel's house, where everyone waited and tore in at once. Hazel put her cookies on the gift table, then edged toward Coco in the kitchen, where a pot of mussels was steaming and someone was pulling the black hulls off bread slices that had gone soggy in the rain.

"Can I ask you something?" Hazel said. "At the airport, your mom kissed me two times, but your uncle did three. Did I do it wrong?"

Coco laughed, not meanly. "You did fine. It's called la bise," she said. "The number of kisses depends on where you live in France. My mom's from a place where it's two. Uncle Marc grew up somewhere it's three."

Hazel felt like a code had cracked open. It wasn't about her, or about being polite or rude; it was a pattern, like area codes. She wanted to test it. When Grand-mère Lucie arrived early, before the others, Hazel watched carefully. Two kisses. "You're from the same region as Aunt Céline," Hazel said, and Grand-mère Lucie beamed and kissed her twice more, right there on the spot.

By the time everyone sat down at six, with elbows off the table because in this house hands rested beside the plate, Hazel had counted kisses from four more relatives and gotten every single one right. Uncle Marc leaned over during the salad course and said, "You have conquered the bise, Hazel. Better than my own son." Théo, mid-mussels, protested loudly, and the whole table dissolved into laughter while Hazel ducked her head, grinning, and passed the bread.

The highway signs said sixty more miles to the coast, and Luca's little brother Nico had already asked "are we there yet" four times, which had to be some kind of record. Their dad drummed the steering wheel. Their mom read the map out loud even though the GPS was talking too, because she didn't trust it. She said it was biased toward highways.

Luca watched the pine trees flick past the window and thought about last summer, the same beach, the same cramped car. That was the trip when he'd made his big mistake. He'd been in the water when he felt the ocean start to pull, a steady tug out toward the deep, and he'd rebelled against it, swimming straight back toward the sand with everything he had. The harder he fought, the farther out he went, until his arms burned and his dad had to splash in and drag him back. The lifeguard on duty had scolded him gently afterward, and Luca had nodded without really listening, too embarrassed.

"What's that sign say again?" Nico asked now, digging through the photos on Mom's phone. He'd found one from the beach boardwalk, a yellow warning sign with a picture of a swimmer and an arrow.

"Rip current," Luca said. "It's the thing that got me last year."

"What do you do if the water pulls you out? Like, for real?"

Luca was quiet for a second. He'd thought about it all winter, replaying that afternoon, wondering what he should have done instead of panicking. He'd even tested an idea in the pool at school, swimming along the lane line sideways instead of turning against the current the teacher made with the paddle. It was slower, and it felt wrong, like giving up, but it worked. "You don't swim straight back at the beach," he said. "That's what I did, and it just kept pulling. You swim parallel to the beach instead, along the shoreline. The current's narrow, so you get out of it that way, and then you can come in."

"You're sure? You tried it?"

"Sort of. And the lifeguard said the same thing after Dad pulled me out. I just didn't want to hear it back then." Luca shrugged. "Tomorrow you can watch me do it right. If there's even a current."

"There better be," Nico said, "or I'm pushing you in."

Hunter sat on the low wall by the basketball courts, his right arm wrapped in a bright orange cast that everyone had already signed twice. Three weeks ago he had been racing Devon across the wet blacktop, slipped, and thrown his hands out in front of him the way anybody does. His left palm had skidded harmlessly. His right wrist had taken everything, and now the radius, the bone on the thumb side of his forearm, was knitting itself back together in a sleeve of fiberglass.

The doctor had told him something that kept circling back in his head. "Of all the broken bones we see in kids," she had said, scanning his x-ray, "a fracture of the radius near the wrist is the most common. Almost always from landing on an outstretched hand, like you did." Hunter had nodded then, but now he was watching the playground with new eyes, because Devon was about to test his theory.

"You're going to eat it on that patch," Hunter called. Devon was on his board, rolling toward the spot where the drainage grates made the pavement buckle. The new kid, Marcus, had an opaque monopoly on the good ramp by the fence, hogging it since lunch began, so everyone else had to make do with the broken ground.

"Watch me stick it," Devon said, and of course he didn't. The board shot sideways and Devon went down with both arms flung forward, palms slapping the blacktop. He bounced right up, shaking out his wrists, grinning.

"See?" Hunter said, hopping off the wall. "Everybody catches themselves the same way. Hands out. That's the pattern." He had started allocating his lunch periods to this, standing by the courts with a notebook, tallying every fall he witnessed. Twelve falls so far, twelve outstretched hands, four kids rubbing their wrists afterward. Two of them had ended up in the emergency room like him, one with a swollen wrist and a story identical to his own.

"So what do we do about it?" Devon asked. "Fall on our faces?"

"That's the problem," Hunter admitted. "You can't not put your hands out. It just happens." He looked down at his cast, at the signatures blurred where his thumb rubbed against it, and for the first time the orange didn't seem like a badge from a cool crash. It seemed like the tuition for a lesson he could never quite teach anyone, because the body never listens in the moment.

Devon picked up his board. "Race you to the wall," he said, and took off running.

Hunter ran after him, one-armed and slower, and lost.

Sebastian had been waiting for this watch party since Tuesday, and now that everyone was crowded into the living room, he could hardly sit still. Chips bowls covered the coffee table, his uncle had claimed the good armchair, and the pregame show blared while his cousins argued about which team would win. Only Grandpa Ray sat quietly near the window, polishing his glasses, and Sebastian noticed he was smiling like he knew a secret.

"You should have seen the very first one," Grandpa Ray announced during a commercial. "I remember it like yesterday. The Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs thirty-five to ten."

Sebastian frowned. Grandpa told great stories, but he also claimed he'd once shaken hands with a president, which nobody in the family believed. The first Super Bowl sounded ancient, older than Dad even. "Wait," Sebastian said, grabbing his tablet. "When was it?"

"January fifteenth, 1967," Grandpa said without hesitating.

Sebastian typed fast. The kickoff show returned on TV, everyone shouting, but he ignored it. If the date checked out, maybe the rest did too. His cousin Dana leaned over his shoulder. "What are you doing? You're missing the highlight reel!"

"Fact-checking Grandpa. He says he remembers the first Super Bowl."

Dana snorted. "Nobody remembers that. He probably made it up, like the president thing."

The search results loaded, and Sebastian froze. January 15, 1967. Green Bay Packers, Kansas City Chiefs, 35 to 10. Every number matched, exactly, with no wobble. He checked a second site, then a third, because a single page could be wrong. Dana kept tapping his arm, saying he should resign himself to the fact that Grandpa exaggerated, that the old man's stories were just an extravagant metaphor for a life he wished he'd lived. Sebastian shook her off.

"Grandpa," he said, standing up in front of the TV, which earned him a groan from his uncle. "It's all true. Every bit."

Grandpa Ray put on his glasses and grinned wider than Sebastian had ever seen. "Told you. And the president thing?" He paused dramatically. "That one's not true." The whole living room erupted, Dana laughing loudest, and she admitted she'd completely changed her mind about Grandpa's stories. She dropped onto the couch beside him and demanded he start from the beginning.

Just then the whistle blew, the game kicked off, and Grandpa leaned forward, pointing at the screen. "Now watch this next play. I've got a feeling about it."

Austin slid into his chair just as his mom set down the spaghetti, and his phone buzzed against his leg before he even picked up his fork. It was the group chat. Someone had posted a screenshot of the photo he'd put on his page last night, the one of him asleep at his desk with his mouth open and a pencil stuck in his hair. He had deleted it after only ten minutes. Now here it was again, with a row of laughing emojis underneath.

"That's the third time your phone has buzzed since you sat down," his dad said, twirling noodles onto his fork. "Rule of the table, buddy."

"I know, I know." Austin put the phone face down, but his mind kept snagging on the problem like a sleeve on a nail. He had deleted the photo. He'd watched it disappear from his page himself. So how was it sitting in the chat, crisp and complete, as if it had never left? He took a bite and barely tasted it.

"Earth to Austin," his sister Maya said, waving a garlic bread stick at him. "The jury has decided you're being weird."

"The jury?" he said.

"Maya's class did a mock trial today," his mom explained, sprinkling parmesan. "She's very proud of her guilty verdict."

Austin pushed his plate forward a half inch, thinking. His sister would probably be the perfect person to ask, because she took screenshots constantly. "Maya, when you screenshot something, where does the picture actually go? Like, whose is it?"

She shrugged. "Mine. It's in my photos. It's just a copy I made." She bit the end off the bread stick. "Why? What did you post?"

Heat crawled up his neck. "Nothing. Hypothetically, if somebody deleted something from their page, could it still exist somewhere?"

"Sure," Maya said, like it was the most obvious thing in the world. "Deleting it takes it off your page. Anybody who already took a screenshot or saved a copy still has it."

Austin sat back. The steam from the spaghetti drifted past his face, and somewhere in his head, gears turned over. So the photo had never really vanished. It had just moved, quietly, into other people's phones, like coins slipping between couch cushions. Where else might it be? He started a mental checklist and decided to be systematic about it. Three people had probably been on their phones right after he posted. Ben, for sure, because Ben had liked it. Priya, maybe. And that kid Dylan from science class, whose name he wasn't even sure how to interpret half the time, since Dylan never said anything in words, only in screenshots and stickers.

"Okay, one more buzz and the phone goes in the drawer," his dad said, eyeing him.

Austin finished his water and asked to be excused. In his room, he opened the chat and typed, not mad, just curious: "who sent that, and did you save it?" Ben answered first with a single word: "saved." Then Priya: "me too, sorry lol."

Austin looked at his own empty page, then at the three copies of his sleeping face glowing in three other phones somewhere out in the world. He took out a notebook and wrote at the top, "Who has it?" Under that he started his list.

The sneeze plague hit Kayla's town the same week the oak trees turned lush with pollen, and by Thursday her little brother Marcus was miserable. Their mom clicked onto CareMarket, the online site where neighbors sold extra medicine, and typed in "allergy tablets." Kayla leaned over her shoulder and stared at the screen. The same box that cost six dollars last month was listed for eighteen, then twenty-two, then thirty, each new seller's price higher than the one that preceded it.

"Nobody's going to pay that," Kayla said.

Three of the boxes sold while they watched. A fourth sold in the minute it took Mom to enter their payment information for the one at thirty-one dollars.

That night Kayla sat at her own laptop, where she sold beaded keychains on the same site. Her llama keychains used to go for eight dollars, but lately three other kids had started making llamas too, and the whole page was flooded with them. She dropped her price to five, and hers finally sold. She scrolled back to the allergy listings and frowned. On her page, more sellers meant lower prices. On the medicine page, more buyers meant higher prices. Same website, opposite direction.

She tried an experiment. She listed two llama keychains at nine dollars each, higher than anyone else. Neither sold for two days. She lowered them to four and both sold before breakfast. So people could walk away from keychains. She looked at the medicine page again. The price had climbed to thirty-five, and the little "sold" tags kept appearing anyway.

She messaged her friend Desmond, whose dad was a pharmacist. "Why do people keep buying allergy pills even when the price doubles?" she typed.

"Because they have to," he wrote back. "Dad calls that inelastic demand. Necessities, like essential medicines, barely change how much people buy when the price changes."

Kayla read it twice, then copied it into her notebook under a heading: RULES OF THE MARKET. Rule one: plenty of something, price falls. Rule two: everyone wants something scarce, price rises. Rule three: if people can't do without it, the price can climb and they'll still buy.

The next morning she checked CareMarket before school. The pollen count was even higher, and a new listing had appeared at forty dollars. She watched a buyer snap it up in eleven seconds.

"Forty dollars," Marcus croaked from the couch, wiping his red eyes.

"Next year," Kayla said, "we're buying in March."

Mathis slid into the back seat and pulled the folded paper out of his jacket before his mom had even started the engine. "I got my prescription," he announced. "But there's something bizarre on it. It says minus two point zero zero."

"Minus?" His little sister Lena leaned over from her booster seat, craning to see. "Like you got a negative score on your eyes?"

That was exactly what Mathis had assumed at first, and it had rattled him all through the waiting room. A negative number sounded like failing. He studied the paper again as the car pulled out of the parking lot. At the top it said the prescription measured lens strength in diopters. Below that, next to the word for his right eye, sat the dash and the numbers: -2.00.

"Two diopters," he said slowly. "Not a grade. The minus has to mean something else."

"So what does it mean?" Lena asked.

"I'm testing it." He flipped the paper over, where the optometrist had scribbled a note comparing his lenses with his dad's old pair. His dad was farsighted, and next to his numbers there was no dash at all, there was a plus sign. Mathis traced it with his finger. "Dad's is plus. Mine is minus. They're opposites."

"Opposite how?"

"I can see stuff up close but far away is blurry. Dad's the other way around. So minus goes with mine, nearsighted, and plus goes with his." He grinned. It felt like cracking a code. "The sign isn't good or bad. It's a direction."

His mom glanced in the mirror. "So you're not failing?"

"I'm minus two. That's all it is." He said it out loud twice more, trying the words on. Minus two diopters. It sounded almost official.

At the next red light, Lena dug through the glove compartment and came up with their dad's old sunglasses case. "These could be a candidate," she said, holding them up. "Try Dad's plus ones."

Mathis put them on. The world outside the windshield went soft and wrong, the stoplight smeared into a red smear. He laughed and yanked them off. "Nope. Minus for me, plus for Dad. Confirmed."

"When do your real glasses come in?" his mom asked as the light turned green.

"Thursday." He pressed the paper flat against his knee. "Thursday, I'm finally going to read the scoreboard at away games."

Lena bounced in her seat. "Two diopters of scoreboard."

Anna wanted the limited-edition hoodie from the mall's skate shop, and she wanted it before her brother Marcus bought the last one, which was why she was half jogging past the fountain with her phone out, snapping a photo of the store window to post to her friends. "First one here," she typed, and added the location tag, because why not.

The comment came in before she reached the door. Not from Marcus, not from Priya, but from an account with no picture and a username she didn't recognize. Seen you at the fountain. Red jacket. Anna stopped walking. She looked around the crowd near the pretzel stand. Plenty of people, none of them looking at her, which somehow made it worse.

She found Priya at the phone kiosk, where Priya was comparing screen protectors. "This account knows I'm here," Anna said, holding up the phone. "Never seen it before in my life." Priya read the comment twice. "Okay, don't panic. Marcus would say this is toxic, but let's just test it." She tapped through Anna's settings like she'd done it a hundred times, which she had, for her mom last weekend. "Every app on here lets you choose whether it can use your location. Always, only while you're using it, or never."

"So?"

"So look at your game." Priya turned the screen around. The game Anna played every day, the one where you catch creatures that appear on a map of your own neighborhood, had its location set to always. Not only while you're using it. Always. Anna stared at it. "It's been on even when I'm not playing." She thought about the trail that would leave: school, home, the mall, the fountain, every Saturday for months, stored somewhere she couldn't see it and shared with who knew who. She set the switch to never, then posted a new photo of a completely different window, on the far side of the mall, with the location tag for the food court.

Then they sat on the bench by the fountain and watched her phone. The stranger account went quiet. No comment, nothing, for ten whole minutes. Priya demonstrated the answer by posting her own picture of the same far-off window, and still nothing arrived. Anna blocked the account, bought her hoodie, and texted Marcus: store's sold out, too slow. As they walked out past the fountain, Priya nodded at the crowd and said, "Tomorrow we're checking every app on your phone."

The big screen at Rosa's Pizza Palace showed the stadium seconds before kickoff, and Theodore had claimed the best seat in the house, the one dead center with an unobstructed view. Around the long table sat his parents, his little sister, and his cousin Matteo, who had flown in that very morning from Italy and had strong opinions about everything, including which toppings counted as credible pizza and which were crimes against dough.

On the screen, the whole stadium suddenly rose in a rolling line, section by section, thousands of arms flung up like a wave crossing an ocean. Theodore shot to his feet and hollered, "Do the wave!" His sister stood up, then his dad, and soon half the restaurant was bouncing up and down like popcorn in a hot vessel. Matteo just laughed and shook his head.

"You call it the wave," Matteo said. "We call it the Mexican wave."

"You're making that up," Theodore said. "It's just the wave. Everybody calls it the wave." Matteo shrugged in that infuriating way of his and went back to his slice. Theodore could not let this go. It felt like being told the sky was called something else in another country, which, now that he thought about it, was exactly the kind of thing that might be true. He decided to test it. He pulled out the family tablet in the corner by the arcade games and searched, half expecting Matteo to have invented the phrase as a joke, because Matteo's jokes thrived on Theodore believing them.

The search results loaded, and Theodore read them twice. The wave had become known worldwide at the 1986 FIFA World Cup in Mexico, and that was exactly why so many English speakers outside North America called it the Mexican wave. Matteo had not made it up. Theodore walked back to the table slowly, the way a detective delivers bad news.

"I owe you a meatball," Theodore said, sliding half of one onto Matteo's plate. "The Mexican wave is a real thing. It got famous at the World Cup in Mexico, and people outside North America actually call it that." Matteo grinned and raised his soda like a trophy. On the screen, the crowd did another wave, and this time Theodore stood up first, shouting, "Mexican wave, everybody! We're doing it the international way!" His little sister stood up so fast she knocked over the parmesan shaker, and Matteo caught it one-handed without even looking away from the goal.

Eli slid his thumb across the new phone's screen for the tenth time, and for the tenth time the glass answered him with a small, satisfying glow. The phone had cost him two years of birthday money and a summer of mowing lawns, and his mother had made him sit at the kitchen table and sign a paper about screen time before she would hand it over. "You budget your minutes," she had said. "The phone doesn't get to do it for you." He had signed it while the smell of her burnt toast still hung in the air.

By afternoon he had downloaded his favorite game, and by dinnertime a text arrived. YOUR ACCOUNT WILL BE DELETED IN 24 HOURS UNLESS YOU VERIFY YOUR PASSWORD. The message claimed to be from the game's official support team. Eli's stomach tightened. He had spent four hundred hours building that account. He tapped the link, and a login page appeared, gray and plain, asking for his password. He typed the first letter, then stopped. The real game company already had his password. Why would they need him to send it to them?

He tested his idea. He opened the game itself, from the icon, not the link. It loaded fine. No warning banner, no deletion notice, nothing in his inbox. Then he checked the sender of the text. The number had a strange stretch of digits, and the web address in the link, when he looked closely, had an extra letter jammed into the company's name, like a bad photocopy. The salt shaker sat cold under his fingertips as he read it twice.

"Mom," he called. She came in wiping her hands on a dish towel. He showed her the message. "It says verify or be deleted."

"That's phishing," she said. "Somebody pretending to be a company you trust, trying to get your password."

He deleted the text, blocked the number, and reported the message from inside the game's own help menu, which had a button for exactly this. His heart was still beating fast, but the beat had shifted into something steadier. He had almost handed over the keys to four hundred hours of work because a gray page looked official in the right context. He set the phone face-down on the table.

"So how was your first day with it?" his mother asked, sliding a plate toward him.

Eli picked up his fork. "Somebody tried to rob me before dinner."

She laughed. He didn't. He turned the phone back over and moved the phishing report into a folder he named, out loud, "Evidence."

Emily had been sitting at the kitchen table for twenty minutes, trying to write her social studies essay with her left hand, because her right arm was wrapped in a bright green cast from wrist to elbow. The essay was about tariffs, and she had managed one sentence: "A tariff is a tax on goods that come from another country." Her pencil grip was clumsy, and the words on the page looked like they had been written during an earthquake.

Then the itch started. It began as a small tickle under the cast, right near her wrist, and grew into a fire. Emily squirmed. She shook her arm. She pressed her palm against the cast and pushed, which did nothing at all. Her eyes drifted to the plastic ruler lying beside her essay, thin and flat and perfect.

She was sliding the ruler toward the edge of the cast when her little brother Theo walked in, eating a granola bar. "Mom said dinner's in ten minutes," he said. Then he saw the ruler. "Are you going to scratch with that? Mom told me the doctor said not to. She said doctors warn against sliding objects like pencils or sticks into a cast, because they can scrape the skin and damage the cast's lining."

Emily froze with the ruler halfway to her wrist. "Great. Now what do I do?"

"You could bang on it," Theo offered, and he rapped his knuckles on the hard green surface. The vibration traveled down, and for one second the itch faded. Emily grabbed a wooden spoon from the counter and tapped the cast gently, once, twice, like a woodpecker. It worked, a little, but the itch always crept back.

"We need a real plan," she said. She thought about the cool pack of frozen peas in the freezer. Cold might travel through the cast where scratching couldn't. Theo fetched the peas and held them against the itchy spot while Emily kept tapping. Between the cold and the tapping, the fire dulled to a small ember.

"That's the most eloquent solution to an itch I've ever seen," Theo said, mouth full of granola.

"It's not eloquent, it's desperate," Emily said, but she was smiling. "You should advocate for the peas method at school. You could make posters."

"Poster number one: The Ruler Is Not Your Friend."

Emily laughed so hard the peas slipped, and Theo lunged to catch them before they hit the floor.

Chase stood in the Kellers' kitchen with a baby on his hip and a note on the counter that read, "Back by nine. Sophie naps at seven." Mrs. Keller had barely reached the front walk before Sophie started screaming. It was a full, red-faced scream, the kind that made Chase's ears ring, and it did not stop.

"Okay, okay," he said, bouncing her the way he had seen his mother do. Sophie screamed louder. He checked her diaper, which was fine. He offered the bottle from the fridge, and she knocked it away with one small furious hand. Through the window he watched Mr. and Mrs. Keller stroll down the sidewalk, completely unaware, and something in his chest went cold. What if something was actually wrong? What if he had to call them back five minutes into his first babysitting job?

Then he remembered his sister talking about her psychology class. "Crying when a parent leaves is called separation anxiety," she had said. "It's a normal stage of development. It usually starts in the second half of a baby's first year." Sophie was eight months old, and this afternoon Sophie had waved bye-bye to a spoon, which meant she was old enough to know exactly who had just walked out the door.

So the screaming had a hidden cause, and it was not a broken anything. Chase looked around the kitchen for a distraction. He restricted himself to three rules: nothing sharp, nothing small enough to swallow, nothing from the top cabinets. That left the wooden spoons and the pot drawer.

He set Sophie on the floor, crouched down, and slid the drawer open slowly. The metal pots caught the light. He banged a spoon against a saucepan once. Sophie's scream broke in the middle, like a dropped plate. He banged again, a little rhythm this time. Sophie stared, then grabbed a spoon with both fists and smacked the pot herself. Within two minutes she was laughing so hard she hiccuped.

When the Kellers came back at nine, they found their living room arranged like a drum set and Sophie asleep in Chase's arms, one spoon still in her fist. "She cried the whole time, didn't she?" Mrs. Keller asked, wincing. "Only at the start," Chase said. "Turns out she's basically the ambassador of pot music." Mr. Keller laughed and paid him, and at the door Mrs. Keller said, "Same time next Friday?" Chase grinned. "I'll bring my own spoon."

Jade sat in the exam room with her right arm propped on the paper-covered table, the fiberglass cast scratchy against her chin. Six weeks ago she had broken her radius falling off the garage roof while installing a birdhouse with her dad, and today, finally, the doctor would cut the cast off. In the waiting room she had seen a boy about her age leave with his arm out of a sling, and something about it had bothered her. His newly freed arm hung thinner than the other one, the skin pale, like a stick taped to his shoulder. She kept turning the image over in her mind, and by the time the nurse called her name, she had a guess: an arm that stays completely still for weeks loses something.

"So you think you can keep the muscles working from inside the cast?" her little brother Theo asked from the corner chair. He wanted her home by three, because he had plans for the two of them to build a model volcano before dinner, and every extra minute in this office felt like a stolen one.

"That's the idea," Jade said. "I've been squeezing this." She dug a stress ball out of her jacket pocket with her left hand, the one that had done everything for six weeks, and pressed it into her casted palm. Her fingers curled around it, faint and effortful, like they were moving through syrup. "Ten squeezes, four times a day, since week two. If stillness makes an arm shrink, then some movement should keep it from shrinking so much." She had no way to see inside the cast, which was the frustrating part. She could only measure the results today.

The saw whined, the shell split, and the two halves came away. Jade stared at her right arm and her stomach dropped. It was noticeably thinner than her left, the wrist narrow, the muscle of her forearm soft and small where the other one was round and firm. Her experiment had not saved it. "It's so skinny," she said, holding both arms side by side. "Why is it so much smaller?"

The doctor paused on his way out. "Muscles kept still in a cast weaken and shrink," he said. "That's normal." Then he was gone, and Jade turned back to her arm, flexing it, watching a small tremor run through it.

"Theo, grab my notebook," she said. She wanted to write this down while it was fresh: date, arm measurements, squeeze counts. Physical therapy would start next week, and the therapist had warned her that progress would hit a plateau at some point, where the arm would stop improving for a while no matter what she did. She intended to be ready with data, a whole coherent record from cast to recovery. Theo dug the notebook from her backpack and slapped it onto the table.

"Volcano at three," he said. "Deal?"

"Deal," Jade said, and wrote the first number down.

George set the two bean pots side by side on the picnic table, then moved them apart again, because side by side meant the taller one would shade the shorter one, and he wasn't testing shade. His question was simpler: did the plant food he'd bought with three weeks of allowance actually make beans grow faster? Pot A got the food. Pot B got plain water. Everything else, he'd promised himself, would stay exactly the same.

For nine days it worked. Pot A pulled ahead, and George measured both stems every morning with a ruler he kept in his back pocket. Fourteen centimeters versus nine. He wrote the numbers in his lab notebook and tried not to grin, because a real scientist, he figured, would be more like an artisan with data, careful and unhurried, immune to showing off.

Then his little sister Nadia came outside with a popsicle and stopped by the table.

"Why is this one all leaning?"

George looked. Pot B, the plain-water pot, leaned hard toward the fence, its leaves angled sideways like they were trying to escape. Pot A stood straight. He walked around the table twice. Both pots had the same soil from the same bag, the same amount of water from the same cup, the same kind of seeds from the same packet. So why would one lean?

He got down on his knees and scrutinized the yard from pot level, the way a bug would see it. From there he could see it plainly: the picnic table sat half under the big maple, and Pot B was in the shade of the trunk for most of the afternoon, while Pot A caught the window-side sun. Sunlight came from one direction, so Pot B had been bending toward the bright strip along the fence.

He stood up fast. His whole experiment was broken. The fourteen-versus-nine comparison meant nothing, because the pots hadn't been treated the same. One sat in the sun and one didn't, so the difference in the plants could be sun or food or both mixed together, and he couldn't tell which. He pressed his palms flat on the table.

"What?" Nadia said, licking her popsicle.

"Everything was supposed to be the same except the food. That's the whole point. If anything else is different, I can't say the food did anything."

"So make them the same."

He moved both pots to the open middle of the yard, where neither one got shade and neither one leaned anywhere, and turned them so the leaves that had bent all faced the fence. Then he found a scrap of paper and wrote in his notebook: START OVER, DAY 1. FAIR TEST MEANS ONLY ONE THING CHANGES.

The science fair was in eleven days. Not much time, but enough, if nothing else moved. He poured the measured water into each pot, marked the levels with tape, and carried his ruler inside.

"Can I have the plant food for my Venus flytrap?" Nadia asked.

"No." He shut the screen door. "You'll confuse my variables."

The lights went out just as Autumn was reaching for the last slice of pizza, and the whole farmhouse dropped into blackness so complete she couldn't see her own hand. "Grandma!" she called, already grinning, because a power cut at their dilapidated old house felt like the start of an adventure, not a disaster.

She heard her grandmother's chair scrape in the dark, then the sound of a drawer opening. "I'll get the candles," Grandma said. "There's a box on the pantry shelf."

"Wait, don't!" Autumn shot up from the table, arms out in front of her like a sleepwalker, bumping the doorframe before she found the hallway wall. She counted doorways in her head, the way she'd memorized them on a boring afternoon last summer, and felt her way into the kitchen. "We're not using candles. Where are the flashlights?"

"The candles are right here, dear. I've used candles in outages since before your mother was born."

Autumn found the drawer by touch, pulled it open, and her fingers closed around the rubber grip of the big flashlight. She clicked it on and the kitchen blazed back into existence, and she felt absurdly proud, as if she'd personally restored electricity. "In fire safety we learned that safety agencies recommend flashlights rather than candles during a power cut," she said, holding it up like a trophy. "A candle can easily start a fire in a dark house."

Grandma paused with the matchbox in her hand. Outside, the wind threw a gust against the shutters, the tail end of the week's storms that had soaked the fields until the ditches ran like little rivers. "Well," Grandma said slowly. She looked at the candle stub, then at the flashlight, and set the matchbox back in the drawer. "I suppose the house has stood two hundred years. I'd like to preserve it a bit longer."

"So it's flashlights?" Autumn was already digging for the second one, the small one with the crank handle that her grandpa kept for camping trips.

"It's flashlights," Grandma agreed, and she laughed. "Look at me, changing my mind at my age."

They carried the lights out to the porch and sat on the swing, watching the stars come out over the dark valley, brighter than Autumn had ever seen them without the porch light washed out. The pizza got cold inside, but Autumn didn't care. She cranked the little flashlight and aimed its beam at the barn roof, then traced it along the fence line toward the road. Somewhere out there the power crews were working, and the lights would come back eventually, but for now the whole dark world belonged to them.

"Want to see how far the beam reaches?" Autumn asked, standing up on the porch rail.

The living room was so crowded that Christopher ended up on the floor with his back against the couch, wedged between his cousin Marisol's knees and the coffee table. On the screen, the game was tied with two minutes left, and Uncle Ray kept standing up whenever his team scored, which blocked the diagonal view from the armchair where Grandpa sat. During a timeout, a commercial for sneakers came on, and Marisol said, "Wait. Why do they even call it a basket? Nobody's shooting into a basket. It's a hoop with a net."

"Because it used to be a real basket," Christopher said. "A peach basket."

"You made that up," Marisol said, and Uncle Ray laughed from the kitchen doorway, which Christopher took as a signal that the whole room was about to humiliate him if he didn't produce proof. He had read it somewhere, in Grandpa's old sports almanac, but he couldn't remember where the book was now. While everyone argued about whether the referee had missed a foul, Christopher crawled along the floor to the shelf under the window, where the almanac lived between a dictionary and a stack of TV guides. He found the entry under basketball and ran his finger down the page.

"James Naismith invented basketball in December 1891 at a YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts," he read, "using peach baskets as the goals. Peach baskets. That's why it's called basketball. They didn't cut holes in the bottom at first, so somebody had to climb up and get the ball out every time somebody scored."

Marisol leaned over his shoulder to see the page herself. "Huh," she said. "You weren't making it up." Uncle Ray came back in with chips and said, "That's actually true. They used peach baskets." Christopher felt himself grinning, but then the game came back on and Grandpa stood up fast, and the almanac slid off Christopher's lap onto the carpet, page down, spine bent.

Grandpa's team lost by one point on a shot at the buzzer, a long diagonal runner that banked in off the backboard. Grandpa sat down slowly and didn't say anything for a while. Marisol picked up the almanac and smoothed the bent page with her thumb, and Uncle Ray turned the TV off, which felt strange after all that noise. "Next timeout," Marisol said quietly, "tell me the one about why it's called a foul." Christopher shrugged and looked at Grandpa's face, decided against talking for a minute, and passed his grandfather the last chip from the bowl between them.

"December 1891," Grandpa said at last, shaking his head. "Peach baskets. And my team still can't make a free throw."

Riley had one goal on Saturday morning: get the library's quiet study room before Marcus did, because Marcus hogged it every weekend. He was halfway across the lobby when he heard voices near the computers, sharp and worried.

"It's the creek," said a girl from his class, Priya, pointing at her screen. "My mom just shared this. Breaking news, it says. The flood is coming tomorrow." A dozen people stood behind her, staring at a photo of brown water swallowing a parking lot. A boy added, "My aunt's packing her car right now. Everybody's saying evacuate."

Riley leaned in. The picture looked terrifying, and everybody's aunts were panicking, but something snagged in his mind. The photo had a strange flatness to it, and he noticed a car in it that looked like a model nobody drove anymore. He couldn't say exactly what was wrong, only that it felt old. That was just his opinion, he realized, the way he felt about roller coasters or cafeteria pizza. But whether the photo was really from yesterday was different. That was a thing somebody could actually check.

"Can I try something?" he asked Priya. He sat down, right-clicked the picture, and saved it. "My cousin showed me this trick last summer," he said, typing. "A reverse image search can show where a photo appeared online before." The screen filled with rows of results. Priya leaned so close her braid brushed his shoulder. There it was: the same parking lot, the same brown water, on a news site from years ago. The photo had been passed off as new, but it wasn't. It was an old picture, recycled.

"It's not tomorrow," Riley said, and Priya grabbed her phone to call her mom. Around them, people started forwarding the results instead of the photo. The boy with the packing aunt sat down slowly, looking relieved and a little embarrassed. Riley brought him a cup of water from the fountain without being asked, because the kid's hands were shaking.

Then Ms. Adeyemi, the librarian, hurried over, saying the dilemma she faced was whether to post a correction on the community board when the flood rumor felt imminent. Priya held up the search results. "You don't have to take our word for it. Look." Ms. Adeyemi studied the screen, nodded, and said she would need to get the post authorized by the head librarian first, but she would do it within the hour.

By noon the study room was full, so Riley and Marcus ended up sharing the big table by the window. Marcus slid a paper over. "You're the photo detective now, huh?" he said. "Okay. Then tell me if this one's real," and he pointed at a picture of a shark swimming down Main Street.

Mia boarded the school bus on Monday clutching a flyer that read "Bus Radio Coming Friday," with nothing else printed on it but a cartoon speaker and a music note. She had heard rumors all week. Devon, three rows back, swore the school was installing a radio that would play only jazz, because his older brother had said so. Priya insisted it would play pop, because obviously everyone liked pop best. By the time the bus lurched away from the curb, the two of them were arguing so loudly the driver turned up her own dashboard radio to drown them out.

"It's a fact that it'll be pop," Priya said, arms crossed. "Ask literally anyone. Pop is the best."

"That's not a fact," Mia said, turning around in her seat. "That's an opinion. It's just what you like. An opinion is a belief or a feeling, so no evidence can prove it true or false."

Priya rolled her eyes. "Fine, then it's a fact that it'll be jazz, like Devon says."

Devon leaned into the aisle, smug. "My brother heard it from a janitor."

Mia frowned. That part might actually be checkable. A claim like "the radio will play jazz" wasn't a taste; it was a statement about the world that evidence could confirm or knock down. She just needed evidence. The flyer had no contact name, so at lunch she asked the office secretary, who said the radio had been approved by the principal, but she didn't know what it would play. The secretary pointed Mia toward the main office, where a notice on the wall was taped above the mailboxes, half of them labeled with teacher names, the wall around them otherwise sparse and bare. The notice was a permission form, and at the bottom it said the radio system had to be authorized by the district before installation.

That single word, authorized, sent Mia straight to the district website during study hall. She found a monthly facilities report, scanned it until her eyes burned, and finally found the entry: the radio would play one station, chosen by a vote of the bus drivers. The drivers had voted the previous Thursday. The winning station was listed at the bottom of the report, and when Mia read it, she laughed out loud in the middle of the silent library.

On Friday, everyone waited. Priya had already announced the radio would prove her right. Devon had a bet going with a kid from his math class. The bus pulled out, the driver reached over, and the speakers crackled to life with a weather report. Then traffic. Then, at last, music: classical violin, soft and slow.

"Classical?" Devon shouted. "Nobody voted for classical!"

"Wait," Priya said slowly, staring at the driver's head. "Who voted?"

The driver glanced in her mirror and smiled. "Me and my colleagues," she said, turning the volume up.

The cast had been on for eleven days, and Vincent still caught himself reaching for the ball with his left arm before he remembered. He sat on the bleachers at the edge of the soccer field, watching his teammates run drills, while Coach Marsh called out the date that mattered to everybody: tryouts for the travel squad were in three weeks, on the last Saturday of the month. If Vincent's arm was not out of the cast by then, he would spend the whole winter on the rec team, and everyone knew the rec team was mostly a commerce in orange slices and lost games.

He had gone up for a header two Saturdays ago, an aggressive challenge he had not needed, and come down with his forearm under him. At the hospital, the doctor had studied the X-ray and then said something Vincent could not stop turning over. "Good news. The break missed the growth plate." Vincent had asked why that was good news, and the doctor had explained that near the ends of long bones there are growth plates made of cartilage, where bones lengthen during childhood, and a break through a growth plate can affect how the bone grows. Vincent had nodded, but later, in the car, a cold thought arrived: his left arm was already a little shorter than his right, according to the measurements his gym teacher took every fall. Both arms had growth plates. If one stopped growing, would they end up different forever?

Nobody could see inside his arm. That was the part that bothered him. The bone could be healing crooked, or the plate could be quietly damaged after all, and he would not know until the follow-up X-ray, which was scheduled for Friday, one day before tryouts. So he tested what he could test. Each night he pressed a pencil against the skin at his elbow and his wrist, marking the distance between the marks with a ruler, writing the numbers in his notebook like a scientist watching for movement. Tuesday the distance was 24.1 centimeters. Thursday, 24.1. Sunday, 24.2, or maybe his ruler had slipped.

On Friday his mother drove him to the clinic, and Vincent brought the notebook, in case the numbers could disclose something the machine could not. In the exam room, the technician took new films, and then Dr. Okafor clipped them to the light box and leaned in.

"There it is," she said, tapping the pale band near the end of the bone. "Growth plate. Open and healthy."

"So it's still growing," Vincent said.

"It's still growing," she said, and started unrolling the casting saw.

Vincent stared at the plate of cartilage, invisible under his skin his whole life until now, quietly doing its work. He thought about the header, about whether he would go up like that again. Maybe, he decided. Maybe exactly like that.

"When can I play?" he asked.

Dr. Okafor smiled. "Ask me that question at the end of the appointment, and bring your notebook."

Austin had played in hotter games than this one. That was the part he couldn't get past. Last July, in a tournament two towns over, the thermometer on the snack shed read ninety-six, and he'd pitched five innings and felt fine. Today the field clock said eighty-eight, and by the third inning he felt like somebody had wrung him out like a rag.

"You're dragging," Marcus said at the fence between innings. He tossed Austin the water bottle. "You accuse me of dogging it every time I strike out, so I'm allowed to say it."

"I'm not dogging it." Austin drank, but the water didn't fix anything. His jersey was soaked through, clinging to his back like a second skin. The sweat just sat there. It didn't dry.

Their opponents were from Fairview, an affluent town with a fancy shaded dugout and matching coolers. Those kids looked fresh. Austin's whole team looked boiled. Devon had already gone to one knee in right field, and even Coach Reyes, who never admitted anything, kept squinting at his players like something about the math was wrong.

Between the fourth and fifth inning, Austin stood by the fence and turned the problem over. It was cooler today than that tournament. Same length of game, roughly the same effort. So why did today feel worse? He kept coming back to his shirt. That day in July, his shirt had been stiff with salt by the second inning, because the sweat had dried. Today nothing dried. The towels on the bench stayed wet. His batting glove stayed wet. His logic told him the difference wasn't the heat. It was the air. The air was already soaked, and it wouldn't take the sweat off his skin.

He grabbed the dugout's damp rag and hung it on the chain-link in the sun. Then he took the dry paper towels from the first aid kit and hung one beside it, after dunking it in his water bottle. Five minutes later, the dry air hadn't come and both towels hung there, dripping and useless, like two little flags of confirmation.

"Fifth inning!" the umpire called.

Austin jogged out to the mound and did the only thing he could think of. He dumped the cooler's ice water over his head, and when Coach shouted at him for wasting it, he waved the empty jug. "It works better out of me than in me," he said. "Trust me on this one. The sweat can't dry in this air, so I've got to get cool some other way."

The twist came after the game. Fairview's shortstop, the freshest kid on the field, collapsed in the handshake line, and Austin was the only one who wasn't surprised. He ran for the ice water first.

Ryder sat on the crinkly paper of the exam table, swinging his feet, waiting for the doctor to come back with his chart. This was his third cold since school started in September, and he had a theory about that. His theory was that something was wrong with him. Nobody else in his class kept getting sick like this. Devonte had caught one cold, back in October, and had talked about it for a week like he'd climbed a mountain.

When Dr. Patel had checked his ears and throat, Ryder had asked the question straight out. "Is my immune system broken? Because this is my third cold since fall." Dr. Patel had said, "Hold that thought," and stepped out to pull his file, which was not the answer Ryder wanted.

While he waited, he looked around the room. There was a poster about washing hands, a diagram of an ear, and a rack of pamphlets by the sink. He slid off the table to verify his count in case he was remembering it wrong. September, the sneezy one. November, the coughing one. Now this one, in February, with the sore throat and the fever his mom had made him stay home for. Three. It was definitely three.

Then a pamphlet caught his eye, a CDC one about colds in kids. He picked it up and read the middle paragraph twice, because the first time he thought he'd misread it. Adults average two to three colds a year, the pamphlet said, and children often catch even more than that. Ryder stood there holding the paper. Three colds in five months wasn't proof of anything broken. Three colds since fall was just... being twelve.

He heard footsteps and climbed back onto the table, keeping the pamphlet in his hand.

"So," Dr. Patel said, coming in with the folder open. "Third cold since fall, and you want to know if your immune system is broken. Here's the thing." He paused. "Actually, you go first. You've got a look on your face."

Ryder held up the pamphlet. "I already figured it out. Adults average two to three colds a year, and kids catch even more. So I'm basically normal." He hesitated. "I thought I was a walking science experiment."

Dr. Patel laughed. "I was going to tell you exactly that. You beat me to it."

"Mom's going to say I'm dramatic," Ryder said. "She has this whole anecdote about how I cried over a splinter when I was five, and she tells it every time I say anything hurts."

"Then here's your homework," Dr. Patel said, tearing a corner off the pamphlet and writing on it. "Show her this number. Three colds is right on schedule." He handed Ryder the scrap of paper, and Ryder folded it carefully and put it in his pocket with his library card, which was where he kept things that mattered.

Emile was sprawled on Denzell's bedroom floor with his phone propped against a stack of comics, waiting for the game to load, when Denzell's little sister Nadia appeared in the doorway holding the family tablet like it had bitten her. "It keeps asking my birthday," she said. "Every time I try to make an account, it asks, and then it says I can't." She was eleven, and she wanted to join the app where everybody in her grade supposedly already was.

Denzell didn't even look up from his controller. "Just put a different year, dummy." Emile watched Nadia's face go stubborn, which he knew from experience was worse than crying. He picked up the tablet mostly to make her stop hovering, typed twelve in the birthday box, and got the same rejection. Then, out of curiosity, he tried thirteen. The screen blinked and moved on, asking for her name and a username. So there was a line, and the line was a number.

He frowned at it. Why thirteen? Not sixteen, not eighteen. He typed the question into his phone and read, scrolling while Nadia bounced on her toes. "Okay," he said slowly. "It's a law. The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998. It says websites need parental consent before they collect personal information from kids under thirteen." He looked up. "So most sites just make you be thirteen instead of dealing with all that." Nadia squinted. "Then why didn't they just say that?" Emile had no answer, because the app had said nothing at all, just rejected her over and over like she'd failed a test she never got to study for.

"You could ask Mom to consent," Denzell said, finally setting down the controller, "if you actually advocate for yourself instead of whining." He made it sound easy, but Emile had heard their mom on the phone with the school, brisk and impatient, and he could picture the consequence already: a whole evening of questions, rules, and maybe a no. Nadia took the tablet back, holding it perpendicular to the light to check her reflection in the dark screen, considering what she might look like with an account.

She sat down on the edge of Denzell's bed with the tablet on her knees, and Emile could see the cursor blinking in the birthday field, waiting. "If I change the year," she said quietly, "nobody ever checks, right?" Emile thought about the line at thirteen, invisible until you crossed it, and about how fast you could cross it with two taps of a thumb.

The game finished loading behind him. Denzell said, "Emile, we starting or what?" Emile picked up his phone but kept his eyes on Nadia's fingers hovering over the numbers.

Sadie had been squinting at menus, at her phone, at the whiteboard for months, and today, finally, the optician's shop in the corner of the mall was going to fix it. She pushed through the glass door with her little brother Marcus trailing behind, already begging to look at the sunglasses rack even though it was November.

"You get one turn through the machine that puffs air in your eyes," she told him, "and then you sit still."

Marcus had his own ambition for the afternoon: he wanted the orange frames with tiny lightning bolts on the hinges, even though his vision was perfect. He'd been talking about them since they walked past the shop two weeks ago, planning exactly how he'd convince Mom they were "a personality statement."

The technician, a woman with silver rings on every finger, ran Sadie through the exam. When it was done, she tapped her screen. "You're farsighted. Light focuses behind the retina in your eyes, so anything close up comes in blurry. The good news is convex lenses will pull it right back where it belongs."

"Convex," Sadie repeated, testing the word. The technician nodded and pulled a tray of lenses out of a drawer, and Sadie leaned in like they were treasure.

While the frames were being fitted, Sadie spotted Priya from science class by the mirror wall, trying on sunglasses even though she wore her regular glasses pushed up on her head. Priya's ambition was simpler and bigger than Marcus's: she wanted to look like a movie star by the time the school dance rolled around, and she'd decided the right frames were step one.

"Try yours on," Priya said. "Look, mine make my eyes look tiny." She slid her glasses down and stared at Sadie in the mirror. It was true. Behind Priya's lenses her eyes shrank to dark little buttons.

Sadie put her new pair on and turned to the mirror, and then she actually laughed out loud. Her eyes looked enormous, wide and startled, like a cartoon character. "Mine go the other way. My eyes got huge and yours got tiny."

"That's so weird," Priya said, poking at her own lenses. "Why would they do opposite things?"

Sadie turned the idea over. Her lenses were convex, bulging out in the middle; the technician had said so. She held Priya's glasses up beside hers and squinted along the edges. Priya's were thinner in the middle, curving inward instead. She lined both pairs up on the counter and peered through Priya's lens at a price tag across the store; the tag actually looked smaller.

"Okay, I think I've got it," Sadie said, talking fast now. "My eyes focus the light too far back, behind where it's supposed to land, so close stuff is blurry. My glasses bend the light the opposite way with those fat convex lenses, and they make everything behind them look bigger, including my eyeballs. Yours must do the flip side of that." She slid her glasses on and off, watching her eyes balloon and shrink in the mirror, doing the experiment three more times just to be sure.

Priya grinned. "So we cancel each other out. We should stand together in photos."

Marcus appeared at the counter, orange frames already on his face, radiating pure confidence. "These," he announced. "These are the ones."

Sadie looked at her own reflection one more time, at the enormous, delighted eyes behind the convex lenses, and turned to the register with her wallet already out. "Two pairs," she said. "The glasses, and whatever my brother is wearing, before he loses his mind."

Eleanor stood at the edge of the festival lawn, where the food stalls gave way to a long table draped in blue cloth. Behind the table, a Torah scroll lay open on a wooden stand, its letters small and crowded, and a woman named Rabbi Ora was letting visitors look but not touch. Eleanor's bat mitzvah was in three weeks, and she still could not get through her portion without stumbling at the same verse. She had come here to petition the rabbi for extra practice, though she had rehearsed the asking all morning and now the words felt too big for her mouth.

"My reading keeps breaking in the same place," she finally said. "I thought maybe the scroll itself would help. Seeing it instead of the photocopy."

Rabbi Ora slid the scroll along the stand so the tricky verse faced Eleanor. "Read it here, out loud. The whole festival will hear you, so you might as well practice being nervous."

Eleanor began, and her voice wobbled exactly where it always did. She leaned closer, squinting at the tight rows of letters, and her finger drifted toward the parchment to hold her place.

"Use this instead." Rabbi Ora pressed a slim silver pointer into her hand, shaped like a small hand with one long finger. "It's called a yad."

"What does that mean?"

"Hand. The scroll doesn't get touched, so the reader follows the words with the yad instead of a finger."

Eleanor fit the silver finger beneath the line she was reading, and something unexpected happened. The verses she had been sure she hated, the ones she had grumbled about for a month, went smoothly, because she stopped losing her place. She had been biased against the whole passage, blaming the words themselves, when the real problem was that her eyes kept sliding off the line. Now the pointer held them still. She finished the verse, then the next one, and the crowd noise around the table seemed to fold itself away.

"That was it," she said, almost laughing. "That was the whole problem."

"It usually is," Rabbi Ora said. "Though you'll have to carry the melody alone at your ceremony. No excuses about photocopies then."

Eleanor looked down at the yad lying light in her palm, silver warming to her skin, and thought of the morning she would stand in front of everyone with this same scroll, her grandmother's congregation watching from the third row where her grandmother used to sit. She would get the words right now. That was the gain. The cost she understood only partly: some doors, once opened, showed you exactly how much you still owed.

She handed back the pointer and touched the silver one last time, right at the tip of its long finger.

The visitor center at the Marsh Hollow Nature Reserve used to be Chicago's Engine Company 21, an old brick fire station with a symmetrical front and a square tower where the hoses once dried. Aiden noticed the brass pole first, running from the second floor straight down to the main room, polished bright and roped off with a velvet cord. "Who puts a slide in a fire station?" he asked.

"Nobody slides on it," said Priya, who had been reading the plaque by the door and clearly wanted to be the first one with the answer, because Ranger Dana had promised that whoever solved the pole riddle would get to release the rescued red-tailed hawk this afternoon. "It's for, like, decorations."

Ranger Dana gathered the class beside the pole. "Here's the riddle," she said. "Fire stations had these poles instead of just taking the stairs. Why? Take ten minutes, look around, and tell me your best guess. I'll only accept a full answer: the city, the year, and what actually happened." She handed out clipboards, because they were also supposed to sketch seeds that had begun to germinate in the greenhouse trays. Aiden could not have cared less about seeds right now.

He climbed the stairs to the second floor and counted: fourteen steps, a landing, then fourteen more. Then he stood at the top of the pole and stared down. The pole was one straight drop. The stairs zigzagged. He borrowed Maya's stopwatch and asked Marcus to time him doing stairs at a dead run: nine seconds, and he nearly flattened a display case of antique helmets doing it. Then he leaned over the pole and dropped his clipboard strap down it. It hit the floor in barely a breath. Straight down beat zigzag. That was the whole idea. The pole wasn't for fun; it was for speed. He found the date scratched into the brass collar at the base: 1878. Engine Company 21, Chicago, 1878. Somewhere back then, one firefighter had gone down the pole and beaten everybody else down the stairs, and after that, poles spread everywhere.

Priya got there first anyway, breathless, and said, "Because poles look cool and impress people!" Ranger Dana winced. "Partial diagnosis, but no." Aiden raised his hand and said, "Chicago's Engine Company 21 put in the first fire pole in 1878, after a firefighter slid down a pole faster than the others could take the stairs."

Ranger Dana unclipped the velvet cord, and a hour later Aiden stood in the open field behind the station with a leather glove on his arm and the hawk gripping it, wild-eyed and ready. "Go on," he whispered, and lifted his wrist toward the sky.

The phone buzzed against Antoine's math homework at 7:42 on Tuesday night. In the group chat, Dominique had posted a screenshot of the rec league stats page with the caption, "Guess who's the best shooter on the team." Her name sat at the top of the list at 100 percent. Antoine squinted at the tiny numbers beside it: one for one.

He remembered the game it came from, back in November, when Dominique had grabbed a loose ball near the free-throw line and tossed up a lucky shot at the buzzer. The gym had gone wild, and Coach had even let her elaborate on the play at the next practice, describing how she'd "seen the whole court." Antoine had been on the bench with a sprained wrist, watching from the sideline with a bag of ice taped on. One shot, he thought. One shot all season, and it went in.

Down the chat, Kayla, who took most of the team's shots, was getting annoyed. "I make nine out of twenty every game," she typed, "and I'm ranked below her?" Someone else wrote, "Stats don't lie." Antoine didn't answer right away. He opened the league page himself and started counting. Kayla's line said 45 percent. He did the math on paper: she had taken eighty shots and made thirty-six. Dominique had taken one and made one. A perfect percentage built on a single attempt. It felt naive to trust the number without looking at how many tries were behind it.

He typed carefully, because he didn't want to ruin Dominique's fun, only make the ranking fair. "One for one is 100 percent, but it's one shot," he wrote. "Kayla's is out of eighty. Shouldn't the list count how many attempts too?" Then he added, "Also whoever runs that site should know the ball covers are polymer anyway, so they clearly like numbers and materials, they can handle one more column." Kayla sent a row of laughing emojis. Dominique typed three dots, then stopped, then typed again. "Okay that's fair," she said. "Ask the league to add attempts."

Antoine emailed the league office that night, and by Thursday the stats page had a new column. Dominique was no longer first, but she didn't seem upset; at Friday's practice she told Kayla, "Feed me the ball, I'm due for shot number two."

The after-school Heritage Club met in the library on Tuesdays, and Kaitlyn had joined for one reason: she wanted a real answer about her own last name, Novak, which nobody at school could pronounce right. Today's ritual was the display table, where every member put out one object that stood for their family. Kaitlyn had brought a postcard her great-grandmother sent from Budapest in 1949, signed "Novak Anna," and she had written below it, "Great-grandma Anna Novak, who made a mistake signing this." She felt proud of the label until Dani, whose grandfather was Hungarian too, stopped in front of it and frowned.

"That's not a mistake," Dani said. He pulled a card out of his backpack, a birthday card his grandfather had signed for his mother: "Kovacs Peter" in careful blue ink. "My grandpa signs everything backwards like that. Mom says he does it on purpose."

Kaitlyn looked from the card to her postcard and felt something shift. If two people did the same thing, it probably was not a mistake at all. Maybe it was a pattern, and patterns meant a rule was hiding underneath it. She needed more evidence, so she went to find Min, who had brought a calligraphy scroll with her Korean name on it, "Kim Jiwoo," family name first, the way Min always wrote it. Kaitlyn set the card, the postcard, and the scroll side by side on the table.

"Dani's grandfather signs his family name first," she said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "My great-grandmother did the same thing. And your name is written that way too. Min, is that just a Korean thing, or could Hungarian work like that?"

"Korean, Japanese, Chinese, and Hungarian," Min said, pointing at the three objects in a row. "Same order in all of them. Family name first."

"So in Hungarian, a person's family name is written before the given name," Kaitlyn said, and as she said it, the whole table of objects rearranged itself in her mind. Her great-grandmother had not been confused. She had been following the custom of her own language, the same order used across the world in Chinese, Japanese and Korean names. Kaitlyn crossed out her label, and the smudge where "mistake" had been did not quite diminish her relief. It made it heavier, somehow.

"That's actually a legitimate reason to fix the sign," said Mr. Okafor from across the room, where he was stapling the banner for Friday's heritage night. Kaitlyn rewrote it: "Novak Anna, my great-grandmother, who wrote her name the Hungarian way." Then she sat back and looked at the corrected card, and a small ache settled in beside the satisfaction. She had solved the puzzle, but the woman who wrote that postcard was gone, and would never know that a great-granddaughter in a library had finally understood her.

"Friday night, you're reading this out loud," Dani said, tapping the postcard. "Both of us. Our grandfathers would like that."

Kaitlyn slid the postcard to the center of the table, next to Min's scroll, and left it there.

Beatrice set the catapult on the kitchen table, loaded a marshmallow, and pulled the release arm. The marshmallow sailed across the room, bounced off the refrigerator, and landed in the fruit bowl.

"That's forty-two inches," said her little brother Oscar, holding the tape measure at arm's length like it might explode. "Can I have the marshmallow?"

"It touched the floor near the bowl. No." Beatrice wrote 42 on her data sheet under Trial 1, then frowned at it. Forty-two was great. Forty-two would probably win the science fair, or at least beat Dwight Yang's volcano, which had won for three years straight mostly because it glowed in the dark.

She reset the arm and launched again. This time the marshmallow went eleven inches and rolled off the table into Oscar's shoe.

"You wrote eleven," Oscar said, reading over her shoulder. "That's terrible. You should erase it and keep the forty-two."
