Quinn had thought the same thing six weeks ago, before Dr. Patel had turned the saw on and pressed it straight against her own palm to show her. The blade didn't spin at all. It vibrated, buzzing back and forth so fast it looked blurry, and that was how it cut through the hard plaster without cutting the skin underneath. Rosa had let Quinn touch the flat of it, and it had only tickled, like a phone buzzing against her hand.

"It spins," the boy said again, louder now, yanking his arm away from his mother.

Quinn pulled the crumpled pad from her backpack, the one she'd used for notes all month since she couldn't talk in class with her arm propped up. She wrote slowly, because writing was the one skill that would contract to nothing the moment the cast came off and she went back to typing.

The note said: "Ask her to put it on her hand first. Watch. It doesn't spin. It wiggles so fast it cuts the hard stuff but not your skin. I touched it."

She leaned over and held it out. The boy read it twice. When Rosa picked up the saw again, he lifted his chin like someone deciding to be braver than he felt. "Put it on your hand first," he said. "Please."

Rosa grinned and did exactly that, pressing the humming blade flat against her own palm, then letting the boy press his finger against it, quick, like testing a stove that turned out to be cold. He laughed one surprised syllable, and after that he sat perfectly still while the cast came off in curling strips.

Quinn's turn came next. The saw buzzed, the plaster split, and there was her arm, thin and strange and hers. She flexed her fingers and they obeyed, stiff but willing. On the counter lay a note her best friend Priya had slipped into her backpack that morning, and she read it while Rosa finished: "Sad you're better. Nobody else lets me draw on their cast. Coming Saturday? Bring markers anyway."

Quinn smiled, then didn't. Six weeks of signatures and jokes and a tiny dragon on her wrist, all of it about to go into the trash, and only Priya had thought that was worth mourning. She folded the note and put it in her pocket.

Rosa carried the broken cast toward the bin.

"Wait," Quinn said. "Can I keep it? Just for a while."

Rosa paused, then handed it back, plaster dust and all.

Felix's grandfather had died on Tuesday night, room 414, with the TV still murmuring a weather report nobody was watching. Felix had been in the waiting room, doing his homework on fungi for science class, which felt wrong and then, strangely, like the only thing holding him together. His grandfather, a retired biology teacher, had taught him that mushrooms were decomposers, the quiet clean-up crew of the forest. "Nothing wasted," he used to say, tapping the page with two careful fingers.

The funeral was Thursday. Afterward, relatives streamed through Felix's house for what his mother kept calling shiva. He finally asked his cousin Ruth what the word meant. "Shiva is Hebrew for seven," she said, ladling soup. "It's seven days of mourning after the burial, and visitors come to comfort the family." Seven days, Felix thought. A deadline, like the fungi unit test at school.

The problem was that Felix couldn't make himself say anything to anyone. Guests hugged him and told stories, and he nodded like a broken gate. He decided to test an idea: if he couldn't articulate his sadness, maybe he could just be present, standing in the room, listening, the way visitors were apparently supposed to comfort them anyway. So on day five he parked himself beside his great-aunt Miriam, who told a story about Grandpa accidentally setting his own beard on fire at Hanukkah, 1979. Felix laughed so hard that soup nearly came out of his nose, and then, because laughing and crying turned out to run on the same wire, he ended up doing both at once. Great-aunt Miriam patted his knee as if this were perfectly normal, which, in that living room, it was.

His meticulous plan for the eulogy he'd never given, three drafted pages folded in his desk drawer at home, began to feel less necessary. On day six, Mr. Okafor from the hospital, the nurse who had let Felix sneak Grandpa extra pudding, knocked on the door holding a paper bag. "He told me you were studying decomposers," Mr. Okafor said. Inside was a field guide to fungi, with a sticky note in Grandpa's cramped handwriting: For the kid who asks why about everything.

Day seven arrived too fast. Felix sat on the porch steps with Ruth as the last visitors' cars pulled away, the house suddenly quiet in a way that had teeth. Seven days hadn't fixed anything; the deadline just ran out and the sadness kept going. But he opened the field guide to a bracket fungus and read aloud the description of how it slowly turns a dead log into soil for new seedlings, and Ruth leaned her head on his shoulder and said, "He would have made that a whole lesson." "Two lessons," Felix said. "Minimum."

Audrey pressed her pencil against the sketchbook, shading the wing of a paper hummingbird, while her cousin Marcus sat as far from her pencil case as the art room stools allowed. Marcus was nine and had refused to pick up a pencil all morning. "I'm not touching those," he said, pointing. "Chewing on them gives you lead poisoning. Tyrell said so."

"Tyrell also said the cafeteria hamsters are robots," Audrey said. But she wondered. Could a pencil really poison you? Kids chewed pencils constantly, and none of them glowed green or anything. She turned her pencil over and read the side of it, where the words had started to wear away. "Graphite, clay, polymer," she murmured. The barrel was wood, the yellow coating was some kind of polymer paint, and the gray core was graphite. No lead anywhere on the label. So why did everyone call it lead?

She flipped open the classroom dictionary, the big one that lived next to the glue sticks. Under "lead," she found a note that made her laugh out loud. Early writers had mistaken graphite for a kind of lead ore, and the wrong name had stuck ever since. So the stuff inside a pencil had never contained the metal lead at all. It was like calling a hot dog a dog, except this mistake was five hundred years old.

"I need proof," Audrey said. Marcus wanted proof too, though his real want was to draw the dragons he kept folded in his back pocket. "Tell you what. Draw one dragon, and if you're not poisoned in an hour, you owe me nothing. If you are, I'll take the blame."

Marcus eyed the pencil the way you'd eye a strange dog. "What's the gray stuff called, really?"

"Graphite," Audrey said. "A mineral. Not the metal lead."

He took the pencil and drew. He drew fast at first, ready to drop it, then slower, then not thinking about it at all. By the end of class he had filled two pages with dragons, and Audrey's hummingbird sat finished on the drying rack beside them. Mr. Okafor paused at Marcus's work and turned it toward the light.

"Nice crosshatching," he said. "Who taught you that?"

"Nobody," Marcus said. "I was trying to conceal where the wings attach because I couldn't make them look right."

"Keep it," said Mr. Okafor. "That's style."

Marcus walked out waving his pages, and Audrey realized the twist only as she packed up: Tyrell had been half right. The name really was lead. The metal wasn't in the pencil, but the mistake was in the word, hiding there the whole time. She snapped her pencil case shut and ran to catch Marcus at the door. "Hey," she called. "Does Tyrell know the hamsters?"

Sarah stood at the door of the church hall clutching a loaf of banana bread wrapped in a tea towel, wondering if she had made a mistake. Her mother had said never visit anyone's house without food, but Sarah had never been to Aunty Wiki's church before, and she did not know which rules traveled and which ones stayed home. At her own church people shook hands and said good morning. Here, the elders pressed their noses and foreheads together, one after another, and Sarah could not see any pattern to who did it and who didn't.

The new student, Tama, arrived beside her, jet-lagged and blinking. He had moved from Samoa two weeks ago, and Mrs. Pale had paired them for the welcome lunch. "Do I bow?" he whispered. "Shake hands? I don't want to be rude."

"That makes two of us," Sarah said.

They watched Aunty Wiki greet an elderly man, noses and foreheads touching, unhurried, like it was the most natural thing in the world. Sarah noticed that everyone who came through the door got the same greeting, young and old, strangers and family. Her idea formed quickly: maybe it was not about who you were. Maybe it was about arriving. She decided to test it by walking in exactly when Tama did, so whatever happened to him would happen to her too.

"Kia ora, you two," Aunty Wiki said, folding them toward her. Tama looked sideways at Sarah, panic accelerating across his face. She gave the smallest nod, and they both leaned in. Aunty Wiki's nose touched Sarah's nose, warm and brief, and then her forehead, and then the same for Tama.

"What is it called?" Tama asked afterward, rubbing his nose. "Back home we kiss the cheek."

"The hongi," Aunty Wiki said. "Sharing the breath of life."

Sarah felt something loosen in her chest, an infectious kind of calm that spread to Tama too, because he grinned and said, "Then you and I have officially shared breath, so you have to sit with me at lunch."

At the long tables, Sarah watched before she ate, the way her grandmother had taught her at dim sum. Here nobody reached across; the food was passed, and the elders were served first, always. When the roast vegetables came around, Tama piled his plate, then noticed everyone else taking a little and passing on. "Am I a herbivore now?" he whispered, holding up a stack of kumara. "Is that the rule?"

"I think the rule is take less, more often," Sarah said. She slid the basket of banana bread down the table, and it traveled all the way to the far end and came back empty, which her mother would have called a good sign.

Aunty Wiki caught her eye and raised an eyebrow. Sarah raised her tea towel in reply, like a flag.

The cemetery gate had a sensor that beeped when someone walked through, and it beeped now for Autumn and her mother and the urn of white flowers they had recruited Aunt Rosa to help arrange. Grandma Pearl's grave was halfway up the hill, the stone still new enough to look like it did not belong yet, standing perpendicular to the slope the way the crew had set it.

Autumn set the urn down and stood with her hands in her pockets. One week ago she had gone to the movies with Priya, four days after the funeral, and she had laughed so hard at some scene about a raccoon in a mailbox that she'd cried. Then she'd stopped, right there in the dark theater, because it felt wrong. Grandma Pearl was in the ground and Autumn was laughing at a raccoon. She hadn't told anyone, not even Priya, who had noticed anyway and asked if she was okay.

"Turn it toward the road," her mother said, tilting the urn so the flowers faced downhill. "That's how she'd want it. Showing off."

"She never showed off," Autumn said.

"She showed off quietly." Her mother knelt and pulled a weed from the base of the stone, then sat back on her heels. "You've been quiet too. Quieter than you think I notice."

Autumn picked at the label on the urn. She could ask now or carry it another week, and she'd already carried it for seven days, and it hadn't gotten lighter. "At the movies I laughed," she said. "Like, a lot. It was three days after the funeral and I laughed until I cried." She stared at the grass. "I keep thinking I did something wrong."

Her mother didn't answer right away. She brushed dirt from her knees and looked at the stone, at PEARL ALVAREZ, 1947 to this year, and Autumn braced herself for a correction.

"Remember when I took that psychology class at the community college, the year you were in fourth grade?" her mother said. "There was a researcher named Margaret Stroebe and another one named Henk Schut. In 1999 they described grieving people as moving back and forth between focusing on the loss and getting on with daily life. They called it the dual process model."

"Dual process model," Autumn repeated. Back and forth. Loss, then daily life, then loss again.

"So laughing at a raccoon is part of it?"

"That's the getting-on-with-daily-life part, yes. And being sad here is the other part. You're allowed to do both. You're supposed to do both."

Autumn thought about testing it, the way she'd test an idea in science class. Yesterday she'd made herself look at Grandma's mug on the shelf and had to sit down from the ache of it. Today she'd hummed along with the radio without noticing until the song was over. Back, then forth. Maybe the guilt was just her misreading the data.

A wind came up the hill and bent the white flowers toward the road, showing off for nobody, and Autumn squatted to turn the urn a little more, just to be sure.

"There," she said. "That's better."

The lights went out at 7:40, right in the middle of Nicholas's homework. He sat still and listened. No wind outside, no crash, no siren. The whole street was dark, every window on the block, so the problem was somewhere upstream, a line or a substation he would never see. His mother found the candle box in the hall closet and set two on the coffee table.

"Dinner's a loss," she said. "The oven's electric."

"I'll make sandwiches," Nicholas said. He held his hand in front of his face and could barely make out his fingers. The candlelight reached about a foot and then quit. He walked to the kitchen with one hand on the wall, found the bread by touch, and came back with a plate.

His little sister Marta accused him of taking the last of the peanut butter, which was true, so he gave her his second sandwich and didn't argue. They ate on the couch. Marta wanted to play a board game, but by candle flame the board was just a blur of shadows, and the pieces kept getting mixed up.

"It's not fair," Marta said. "Owls can hunt in the dark. Why can't we?"

"We're not nocturnal," Nicholas said. "But wait." He had noticed something while carrying the sandwiches. Twenty minutes ago he had to feel his way along the wall. Now, from the couch, he could see the outline of the armchair, the shape of the bookshelf, the dark rectangle of the doorway to the hall. He hadn't lit another candle. Nothing had changed except time.

He set his phone timer and told Marta to watch the room, not the candle. "Tell me what you can see," he said every few minutes. At first she said nothing, just the couch. Then the lamp. Then the lamp and the window. He remembered a line from a library book about deep-sea divers and dark caves, something about the eyes building back a pigment in the rod cells. "It's called rhodopsin," he said. "It takes half an hour or more to come back. That's the mechanism, I think. Your eyes get more sensitive the longer you sit in the dark."

By the time the timer hit thirty minutes, Marta could count the game pieces on the table without leaning over them. They set up the board, moved their pieces by the gray light, and didn't knock anything over. Somewhere outside, a truck rumbled past, and the street stayed dark, but in the living room Marta moved her piece to the final square and said, "Checkmate."

Nathan stood at the edge of his aunt's backyard holding a wrapped box and trying to work out where to put his shoes. Everyone else had left theirs in a heap by the back door, even though they were outdoors, so he kicked his off too and carried the box up the steps. The party was for his cousin's engagement to a woman named Kanya, whose whole family had flown in from Thailand, and Nathan had been told exactly one thing by his mother on the drive over: do not embarrass us.

The greetings were the first puzzle. Kanya's parents did not shake hands the way his uncles did. They pressed their palms together at the chest and bowed slightly, and Nathan copied it, feeling clumsy, and saw Kanya's father smile like the awkwardness itself was fine. Then his grandfather came over and clasped Nathan's shoulder in the big two-handed grip their family used, and Nathan realized that different people in the same backyard were greeting him in entirely different systems, and both systems were correct.

The gift was the second puzzle. His box held a fantasy novel, his favorite genre, chosen because Kanya's little brother Sun, who was nine, had spent the whole week reading on the porch steps. Nathan handed it over the way he would to anyone, but he noticed that Kanya's mother received gifts with both hands and a small dip of her head, and that Sun did not tear the wrapping open at once. He turned the package over and set it aside to open later, which made Nathan feel like a guest in a country he was standing inside already.

Lunch was long and shared, dishes moving in circles. Nathan watched which spoon took food from which bowl, how people served the person beside them before themselves, and how his own loud slurping made Kanya's grandmother glance over, once, without a word. He ceased slurping and took smaller portions, and the grandmother put an extra piece of chicken on his plate, which he decided, being pessimistic by nature, to interpret as forgiveness rather than a test.

The problem came after lunch. His little cousin Mia, who was six and loved Sun already, reached up on tiptoe to ruffle his hair the way she ruffled everyone's hair. Nathan grabbed her wrist before he thought about why.

"Wait," he said.

Mia blinked at him. Sun looked at the hand in Nathan's grip and then at Nathan's face. Nathan let go of Mia's wrist slowly. "In Thailand the head is sacred," Sun said, plainly, like he was naming a street. "So touching someone's head, even to pat a kid, can be seen as rude." Nathan thought back over the afternoon, the greetings, the both hands, the small bows, and saw the pattern running underneath all of it, like a water pipe hidden in a wall.

Mia pressed her palms together and bowed to Sun instead, so solemn that Sun laughed and bowed back even lower. Then she bowed to Nathan too, and Kanya's father, watching from his chair, raised one hand and patted the empty air above Mia's head, touching nothing at all.

The diner smelled like bacon and burnt coffee, and George had never been less interested in food in his life. His dad slid into the booth across from him, cheerful as a game show host, while George's little sister Priya attacked a stack of pancakes like they owed her money.

"Eat something, buddy," Dad said. "We've got four more hours of driving, and the hotel only holds the room until ten."

"That's what I keep telling him," Priya said through a mouthful of syrup. "Ten o'clock. Deadline. Tick tock."

George put his forehead on the cool formica table. It was nine in the morning back home, which meant his body believed it was six, and his body had opinions about six. The weird part was the trip out. Two weeks ago they had flown west to California, and he'd felt fine, practically bionic. They'd landed, retrieved their suitcases from the carousel, and gone straight to the beach. He hadn't been tired at all.

"You were up until two in the morning," Priya reminded him helpfully. "I heard you talking to your shoes."

"One conversation," George said into the table.

He lifted his head and started working the problem like a math sheet, because that was what he did when he felt terrible. Out west, fine. Back east, wrecked. Same kid, same plane, same crummy airline pretzels. The only thing that had changed was the direction. He pulled the paper placemat toward him and drew two arrows, one pointing left, one pointing right. Under the left one he wrote FINE, SUPERHERO, HANDSOME. Under the right one he wrote ZOMBIE.

Priya leaned over. "What's that?"

"Evidence," George said. "Going west, I felt great. Coming home east, I'm a puddle. It's not random. It's a pattern." He tapped the arrows. "I think jet lag is just harder going east than going west."

"That's your testimony?" Priya raised her hand like she was swearing in. "State your name for the record."

"George. Also a zombie."

She giggled, then paused with her fork in the air. "Wait. That's actually a thing? It's not just you being dramatic?"

"It's a thing. I tested it. There were two flights, and I was the experiment." He'd been meticulous about it, in a sleepy way. On the flight out, even the crossing of three time zones hadn't knocked him down. On the flight back, one day home and he was awake at three in the morning, staring at the ceiling, listening to Priya snore.

Dad had been watching the whole performance over his coffee. "So what you're telling me is that next summer we fly west again."

"Forever," George said. "We just keep flying west for the rest of our lives. It's science."

The waitress came by with a plate of hash browns nobody remembered ordering. "Heard the word zombie from three tables away," she said. "These fix most things."

George looked at the hash browns. His stomach considered the offer. Slowly, suspiciously, he picked up a fork.

"Better hurry," Priya said, pointing at the clock. "Nine forty."

George took a bite, then another, and felt something almost like being a person again. "Okay," he said. "New plan. We get to the hotel by ten, I nap like a normal scientist, and tomorrow we take the longest way possible to school. Westward."

"Deal," said Dad, dropping a twenty on the table. "Everybody in the car. Zombie first."

Priya grabbed the placemat with the arrows and folded it into her pocket. "I'm keeping this for the record."

"Objection," said George, and followed her out the door.

Piper sat on the low wall at the edge of the skate park, her left arm in a bright green cast, watching her friend Dara drop into the bowl. Two weeks ago that had been her. She remembered the exact moment her board slipped out from under her on the coping, the way she'd put her arm down to catch herself, and the sound that was not really a crack. More of a bend. Like a stick that doesn't quite snap.

At the hospital, the doctor had looked at the X-ray and said the words that had been circling in Piper's head ever since. "Good news. It's a greenstick fracture, so it's partly broken." Piper had stared at the ghostly image of her own bone and asked, "Partly? How can a break be partly?" The doctor pointed to a line that stopped halfway across, like a crack in a sidewalk that runs out of steam.

Now she couldn't stop thinking about it. She'd asked her little brother to bring her a green branch from the backyard, and yesterday, while nobody was watching, she'd pressed her thumb against it. The bark split on one side only, and the branch bowed away on the other, still connected. That was her bone. That was why kids got this kind of break, the doctor had said, because their bones are more flexible than adults'. Older bones snap clean, like dry kindling. Younger ones bend first and crack on just the one side.

"You're doing the branch thing again," Dara said, rolling up beside her with a clatter. She nodded at the twig in Piper's right hand.

"Watch," Piper said. She bent it slowly, splitting the bark a little more. "One side cracks, the other side bends. I keep wondering if my arm would've snapped all the way through if I'd fallen harder. Or if I was, like, eighty."

Dara laughed, then went quiet, spinning her board under one foot. "I always thought a broken bone was a broken bone. Like, all the way or nothing." She frowned at the branch. "So your arm's not really broken?"

"It is," Piper said. "It's just broken on one side and bent on the other." She set the twig down carefully, the way you'd set down evidence. "I'm going to invest my whole recovery in figuring out how it heals. Does the bent side pull the cracked side back straight? Or does the crack fill in first?"

"That's a lot of thinking for a kid with a cast," Dara said, but she was squinting at the branch now too.

Piper traced a line down the middle of the twig with her finger. "This is like the equator of the branch. One half splits, one half holds. If I taped the split side, could the bendy side still flex?" She looked up at the bowl, where sunlight made a bright curve of the concrete. "Next week I get the short cast, the one that lets my elbow move. Doctor says skating again in a month might be feasible if the X-ray looks right."

Dara kicked her board up into her hand. "Race you to the vending machine, then."

Piper was already off the wall, green cast swinging, running on legs that worked just fine.

Georgia set up her easel by the window of the dilapidated community art studio, where the paint-spattered sink dripped and one fluorescent tube flickered. She was painting a sunset over the lake for the studio's fundraiser show. Anything that sold would count toward the studio's revenue for the year, and Ms. Ruiz had said they needed at least four hundred dollars to fix the window in the ceramics room. Georgia wanted her painting to be the one that sold.

She laid in the sky with broad strokes of orange, then began adding the red band above the horizon where the sun sat. Under her brush, the red and orange melted together and turned a dull, muddy brown. She frowned, scraped the area with a palette knife, and tried again with fresh paint. The second band turned brown too, worse than the first. The third attempt looked like gray mud. Her lake was still blue and clean, but the sky looked ruined.

Across the table, Marcus was mixing greens for a forest scene. "What's wrong with your sunset?" he asked. "It looks like dirt."

"I keep adding red and it keeps going brown," Georgia said. She looked at his palette, where his green paint sat next to a tube of red he had used for a barn door. On the studio wall there was an old color wheel chart, its plastic film peeling. She walked over and traced her finger from the red wedge straight across the circle to the wedge opposite it. Green sat there. Then she looked back at the lake in her painting, which she had underpainted with green before adding the blue water on top. Some of that green was showing through where her strokes were thin, right where the red bands turned muddy.

"Complementary colors," Marcus said, squinting at the chart. "That's what they're called. They sit opposite each other on the wheel, like red and green."

Georgia went back to her easel and ran a quick test. On a scrap of canvas she dabbed pure red, then touched green into half of it. The dab turned the same dull brown as her sky. Then she painted a swatch of red over an opaque layer of white, with no green underneath, and it stayed bright. She let out a breath. It wasn't her paint or her brush. It was the green showing up from underneath, mixing into the red as she blended.

She covered the lake area with two thick coats of white gesso, waited for it to dry while she cleaned her brushes in the dripping sink, and then painted the red band fresh over the white. This time it burned clean and bright against the orange. She layered the colors up toward a deep violet, and the whole sky glowed the way it did over the water in September. Marcus came over and stood beside her, brush in hand.

"That one's going to sell first," he said.

Georgia signed her name small in the corner, then flipped the painting around to face the window, sunset light falling across wet paint.

The sign-up sheet at the community center said the Wolves were a brand-new team, and by the second practice Jaxon understood exactly what that meant. Nobody passed to anybody. Marcus, who had told everyone at school he would be captain someday, called for the ball on every possession even when two defenders were draped over him. By the third week, things had begun to deteriorate, with shouting matches in the layup line and one kid, Deshawn, quitting before the first game. After practice Jaxon sat in the center's reading room, pretending to work on his math homework, while the coach's caterpillar tank sat on the windowsill, one fat larva hanging from a twig in its slow way of becoming something else. He pulled a dusty psychology book off the shelf mostly to have something to do, and found a chapter about groups.

A psychologist named Bruce Tuckman had proposed in 1965 that groups go through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing. Jaxon read the sentence twice. Forming, when everyone is new and polite. Storming, when the arguing starts. He thought about last Tuesday, when Marcus and Ravi had gone nose to nose over who should take the last shot in a scrimmage, and Coach Odum had to blow the whistle four times. Maybe the Wolves were not broken. Maybe they were just in the middle of a list.

He remembered the first practice now, back in that warm gym that smelled like floor wax. Everyone had stood in a loose circle, saying "nice pass" and "my bad" in quiet voices, nobody wanting to step on toes. That was forming, he realized, and it had lasted exactly one week before the storm rolled in.

So he tested it. He made a chart in the back of his notebook, a row for each practice, and he marked down the arguments in one column and the assists in another. He said nothing to anyone, because "the team is storming" did not sound like a legitimate excuse for a bad practice, and he figured the guys would laugh at him. The pattern held anyway. Week one, three arguments, two assists. Week three, seven arguments, zero assists. Week five, two arguments, nine assists, and Marcus drove the lane and kicked it out to Ravi for a corner shot without either of them yelling.

Before the game on Saturday, Jaxon finally showed Marcus the chart in the locker room. "A psychologist named Bruce Tuckman said groups go through stages called forming, storming, norming and performing," Jaxon said. "I think we're in the norming one."

Marcus studied the page for a long moment, jaw tight. "So I don't have to call for the ball every time?"

"You can still call for it sometimes," Jaxon said.

Marcus grinned and slapped the notebook shut. "Fine. But after the game, we talk about me being captain."

They ran out through the double doors into the noise of the gym, sneakers squeaking on the bright floor, and the caterpillar on the windowsill hung motionless in its chrysalis, waiting for its wings.

The lobby filled fast, and Aaron watched the names stack up like seats in a bus. Some players typed in ALL CAPS, some dropped six emojis per sentence, and one kid named PixelFox mimicked the admin's formal greeting style, "Welcome, competitors," copying it word for word until half the room was saying it. Aaron knew the rules of this place: public chat was loud, jokes were subjective, and nothing you typed there belonged to you anymore.

His friend Dex was running late, as always. Their team of five needed a jumper, someone to switch sides and fill the last slot, and the match locked in eight minutes. Aaron opened a private window to their smaller chat, the one just for the team, and typed, "Is Dex coming or should I grab Reena?" Then he made a mistake. In a second private window, meant for only one person, he typed something sharper: "Honestly, Dex has been dead weight all season. We carry him every game."

The countdown hit six minutes when a screenshot appeared in the public lobby chat. It was his message, word for word, his username cropped but his orange avatar icon still visible in the corner. Somebody had pasted it for everyone. The public room, which had been chaotic and silly, went quiet in the way a cafeteria goes quiet when a tray hits the floor. Then the messages came fast: "ooooh," "who sent that," "Aaron is that you?"

He stared at the screenshot and worked backward through what he knew. He had sent it to exactly one person, in a private chat. That meant the screenshot had to come from that person, or from someone looking at their screen, because a private message only stayed private if the person who received it kept it that way. It could be screenshotted and shared by anyone who got it. The only name in that window was Tic. Tic, who had been friendly all week, Tic, who had asked him yesterday what he "really thought" about the team.

Four minutes. Aaron opened a window to Dex and typed fast, a short message on the screen between the countdown numbers: "You'll probably see something about you in lobby chat. It was my worst sentence, not my real opinion. You held the bridge in the semifinal alone. I'm sorry." Then he turned to the public chat, took the sting at his own expense, and typed where everyone could see it: "That was mine. I said it, it was cruel, and I regret it. Dex, the jumper slot is yours if you want it."

Two minutes. PixelFox, still copying people, typed "I'm sorry, Dex," and then everyone was typing it. The lobby door chimed, and Dex's name slid into the last slot on the team list. No message came from Dex, not in public, not in private, not for the whole countdown. Then the loading screen swallowed the lobby, and the match began.

Florence sat in the third row of the empty auditorium with her borrowed trumpet on her lap, staring at the three valves like they were keeping a secret from her. Seven notes she could get without pressing anything, but three little buttons made dozens. It didn't add up. Three buttons ought to make three notes, maybe four if you counted no buttons at all.

She had come in early before community band practice because her bedroom was too small for loud mistakes, and the auditorium swallowed them politely. She lifted the horn and played an open note, listening. Then she pressed the middle valve alone and blew. The note dropped, lower than before. She let it go, and the note climbed back up. She tried the first valve alone. Lower again, but by a different amount.

"So the buttons don't just pick notes," she said out loud, because the empty seats didn't mind. "They change the tubing." She slid the trumpet out of its case and turned it over in the light from the stage. The piping coiled and looped like a brass maze, and she followed one loop with her finger until she lost it behind another. She couldn't see inside, which was exactly the problem. Something invisible was doing all the work.

She tested it, one idea at a time. She hummed an open note, then pressed the second valve and hummed the note she'd heard. Pressing the valve made the note lower, every single time, never higher. Then she pressed all three at once, and the sound came out so low and wobbly that she laughed and the laugh turned into a squeak. The more tubing she used, the farther the sound slid down, as if the air had to walk a longer hallway before it was allowed out.

"Every valve opens an extra loop of tubing," she said to the trumpet. "So the air column gets longer, and the note gets lower." She tried combinations, writing them on her music folder: none, two, one, one and two. She was halfway through her list when footsteps echoed behind her, and Mr. Alvarez's nephew Theo, who played tuba, dropped into the seat beside her.

"That's my aunt's old horn," he said, leaning over. "The valve caps on the loops are sticking. Watch the third one." He pointed at a small cap on a coiled loop near the middle of the tubing, and when Florence pressed the third valve, she saw it: that cap barely moved, the loop only half engaged. That was why her three-valve notes had sounded sour all week. She polished the cap with her sleeve, spun it a quarter turn the way Theo mimed, and pressed the valve again. The note came out round and full and low.

Florence raised the trumpet and ran her new combinations up and down, one clean note after another, while Theo kept time on the armrest with his palm.

Brooke had been at Dana's kitchen table for an hour, and the history project was due Monday, which gave them one weekend. They were supposed to build a small database of World War II propaganda posters, tag each one, and write about which posters had been most influential in selling war bonds. Dana had nominated Brooke to present it in front of the class, and Brooke had said yes before her stomach could catch up. Now the cursor blinked on an empty screen while Dana went to get snacks.

Through the doorway, Brooke could hear Dana's mother on the phone in the living room, saying something about a doctor's appointment on Tuesday. When Dana came back with a bowl of pretzels, her hands were shaking slightly and she set the bowl down harder than she meant to, scattering salt across the table. "Sorry," Dana said. "The poster with the pointing uncle, is that ours to write up?"

"You did that one already," Brooke said slowly. She watched Dana pick up the same index card she had just filed, read it, and file it again in the wrong slot. That was the third time. Dana wasn't being lazy; something else was going on, something Brooke couldn't see directly. She remembered Dana leaving the cafeteria early all week, and the field trip Dana had skipped in October, and the way Dana's mother had just mentioned a doctor.

Brooke tried an idea out, careful as stepping on ice. "Is Monday freaking you out?" Dana's shoulders went up around her ears. "The presenting part," Dana said. "I stress about that stuff. Everybody does. But mine doesn't stop. It's like a fire alarm that goes off when there's no fire." She rubbed the salt granules between her fingers, and the scratchy sound filled the quiet kitchen. "I finally told my mom, and Tuesday I'm seeing a doctor about it. My cousin did the same thing. Hers was bad enough and lasted long enough that it got in the way of school and everything, so the doctor said it was an anxiety disorder, not just regular nerves. And it's treatable. She's way better now."

"So it's not just you being weird," Brooke said. Dana almost smiled. "No. There's a name for it and stuff that helps. I've been trying my own coping stuff, like breathing exercises, but my mom says the doctor can do more." She glanced toward the living room, then straightened the scattered cards. "Also, I have to say this. You can't text me at midnight anymore about homework. I lie awake staring at my phone. I need some boundaries, even with you."

"Deal," Brooke said. "No texts after ten." Then she slid the pointer card across the table. "I'll present the database part if you take the posters. Fair?" Dana thought about it, tapping the card against the edge of the table, and finally nodded. "Fair." She picked up her pen, and the fire alarm in her head, wherever it was, stayed quiet enough to let her write the first line.

Emilia stood on the porch of the Tanaka house holding a wrapped box of maple candy from her grandmother, and she could not decide whether to take off her shoes before the door opened. At home nobody cared about shoes. Here, in the entryway, six pairs of sandals sat in a neat line, so she lined hers up too, smallest to largest like at the shoe store, and hoped that was right.

Inside, everyone stood to greet her, even Grandmother Tanaka, who rose slowly from her cushion with a hand on the table. Emilia's own family waved from couches and shouted hellos across rooms. She bowed the way her friend Kenta had shown her in the school hallway, a small dip, and Grandmother Tanaka bowed back even lower, which made Emilia wonder if she had done it wrong. Kenta's mother took the candy with both hands, not one, and said thank you twice, once in English and once in Japanese, and set the box on the shelf unopened. At Emilia's house gifts were torn open immediately so everyone could admire them, so she decided they must be saving the box for later, like dessert.

The real trouble began with the ramen. Bowls of steaming broth and noodles appeared, and Emilia picked up her chopsticks carefully, the way she had practiced with two pencils on her desk at home. Then the slurping started. Grandfather Tanaka slurped. Kenta slurped. Even quiet little Suki, who was only seven, drew her noodles in with a sound like a small wave. Emilia froze with her chopsticks halfway to her mouth. At her own table her father gave one look to anyone who made noise while eating, and her grandmother's memoir of growing up on a farm had a whole chapter about manners, including a line she had read aloud at Thanksgiving: "A quiet table is a polite table." Emilia had always believed that. Now she was not so sure.

She decided to verify it, quietly, like a science experiment. She waited until Grandfather slurped again, and she watched every face around the table. Nobody frowned. Nobody glanced at him. Kenta's mother refilled his tea and smiled. If slurping were rude here, Emilia reasoned, someone would react, the way her father's eyebrows reacted at home. Then she tried the smallest test she could manage: one noodle, drawn in quickly. It made a gentle sound, and Grandmother Tanaka nodded at her and said, "Good, good," and slid the plate of egg closer to her side.

"Better flavor when it's loud," Kenta whispered, leaning toward her. "That's how we do ramen. And soba too." Emilia slurped again, longer this time, and the noodles actually did taste better, hot and quick instead of cooled and slow.

When the bowls were empty, Suki climbed into Emilia's lap and asked whether America still had volcanoes that were extinct. Emilia said most of them were, but a few were only sleeping, and Suki found that so funny she laughed until she hiccupped. Grandmother Tanaka pointed at Emilia's bowl, then at the teapot, and raised her eyebrows. Emilia held out her cup with both hands, the way the candy had been accepted, and watched the tea pour.

Sara set two cereal boxes on the kitchen table, then slid them behind the bread maker where nobody could see the labels. Her science fair project was due Friday, and she had one evening left to prove her idea. "Marcus," she called, "I need you in here. Bring your honest face."

Her brother wandered in with a granola bar hanging out of his mouth. Sara took it away from him. "You're a participant now. No snacks before the test." She poured the name-brand flakes into a bowl marked A and the store-brand flakes into a bowl marked B, then shuffled the boxes deeper behind the bread maker so even she could forget which bowl was which. She copied a code onto a folded slip of paper, taped it shut, and set a heavy mug on top of it.

"What's the mug for?" Marcus asked, dropping into a chair.

"So I can't peek. It's a blind test. You don't know which sample is which, so what you expect can't sway your answers." She slid the bowls toward him with a glass of water between them. "Taste A. Swish. Tell me what you think. Then B. No guessing which is the fancy one."

Marcus chewed slowly, like the flakes might lie to him. "A is crispier," he said. "B tastes a little like the box."

Sara wrote it down. That was the answer she had predicted, and it bothered her. She had guessed her brother would pick A because he always begged for the name-brand stuff, the kind with the artisan bakery logo on the front that made everything sound handmade and expensive. If he couldn't tell the boxes apart and still picked A, maybe his tongue actually knew something. She made him repeat the test with fresh pours, swapping the bowls' positions. Again he chose A.

Then Dad wandered through and Sara made him sit down too. He tasted both, tapped the table, and pointed at B. "That one's better. Toastier."

Sara sat back. Two tasters, opposite answers, and no boxes in sight. She unfolded the slip under the mug and stared at the code. Bowl A was the store brand. Marcus had picked the cheap cereal twice, without knowing it, and praised it. Dad had picked the expensive one. Her prediction had been wrong in the most interesting way possible: people's expectations couldn't sway their answers because people didn't know which sample was which, so the answers were all over the place. Taste, not labels, was doing the talking.

She wrote "Trial Three" at the top of a fresh data sheet and looked up at her father. "Dad, there's water in the glass for a reason. You have to do it again."

The food court smelled like fryer grease and cinnamon pretzels, and Oliver had exactly forty minutes before his mom picked him up. He set his tray down across from Priya, who was already scrolling on her phone. "I need your help," he said. "Last night my dad mentioned a blog he wrote before I was born, about his pizza shop. He thinks it's gone forever. I want to find it."

Priya locked her phone. "Websites die, Oliver. When a page gets deleted, where would it even go?"

"That's what I want to figure out." He pulled a napkin toward him and wrote the blog's old address from memory: pizzaoliver.blogspot. His dad had repeated it twice at dinner, laughing about the cheesy header photo. "If it's deleted, there's nothing to load. But something has to hold old pages somewhere, or nobody could ever prove what a site used to say." He had tried the address on the mall's free Wi-Fi kiosk already and gotten a dead link. So the next candidate had to be somewhere that kept copies, if such a place existed at all.

Priya leaned over the napkin. "Type the address into the Wayback Machine," she said. "It's this thing my brother uses to win arguments. He pulls up a store's website from ten years ago to show the price was lower." She typed it in, and a timeline appeared, dotted with little marks going back years. One mark sat all the way at the far end. She tapped it. The screen filled in with his dad's old blog, header photo and all, the whole page exactly as it had looked decades ago.

"Who keeps that?" Oliver asked, scrolling through posts about flour deliveries and a broken oven. The page even had a photo of the shop with the old sign, back when it was near the fountain, three stores down from where they were sitting. Priya shrugged. "Some place called the Internet Archive. It's been saving copies of public web pages since 1996. Anyone can look." Oliver read that line off the bottom of the screen, then looked up sharply. "Wait. Anyone. So if my dad posted a photo of the shop's old location, strangers can still see it. That means people can find out where a place was, years later, from stuff they thought was gone."

They tested it. Priya pulled up her own old dance-studio page in the archive and found a post from three years ago with the studio's address and a photo of her in the recital lobby, which she had completely forgotten publishing. She went quiet, then deleted nothing, because you couldn't delete it anyway; she just screenshotted it to show her mom. Oliver screenshotted his dad's blog too. Then he pocketed the phone, dumped their trays, and walked toward the fountain to find the spot where the old sign used to hang, holding the picture up next to the real wall. "Right there," he said. "Behind that toxic-green smoothie stand."

Jordan had read the text forty times since Friday. "Meet me at the gate at 7," Marisol had written, "my little brother's tagging along, hope that's ok." Then a second message: "don't laugh, he's obsessed with you ever since you taught him that card trick." Jordan had typed and deleted six replies before sending a thumbs up, which now seemed like the lamest response in history.

He stood by the gate with two hot chocolates and one dollar left in his pocket, watching the crowd funnel past the ticket lady whose whole job seemed to be enforcing the no-outside-drinks rule. When Marisol appeared, waving, with a nine-year-old in a puffy coat trailing behind her, Jordan felt as exposed as the away team's kicker, standing alone on the field with everyone watching. His face went hot, and he knew without a mirror exactly how red he looked, because his cheeks felt like they were radiating heat into the cold October air.

"Dominic, you remember Jordan," Marisol said.

"The card trick guy!" Dominic shouted. "Do it again."

Jordan tried the trick. His hands were shaking and he fumbled the double lift, and Marisol laughed, which made him grin, which made his face burn even worse. He turned toward the fence and pretended to study the scoreboard.

"It's blushing," said Dominic, with the authority of a kid who had recently done a report on it. "My science teacher says blushing is when blood vessels in your face widen and more blood flows near the skin."

"Okay, emperor of embarrassing facts," Marisol said, poking her brother, whose coat had a gold collar like the team's penguin mascot, the Emperor.

Jordan half listened, but something snagged in his brain. Widen. More blood near the skin. If widening made red, maybe narrowing made less red. He couldn't see his own vessels, couldn't see blood moving anywhere, but he could test the idea. He pressed the cold hot chocolate cup against each cheek, one, then the other, like a man applying aftershave.

"What are you doing?" Marisol asked.

"Nothing," he said. "Cold cup."

By the third quarter, Dominic had abandoned them for the concession stand and Marisol scooted close on the cold bleacher. "You don't have to hide when you blush, you know," she said quietly. "It's kind of the best thing about you."

Jordan didn't believe her, but he put the cup down anyway, letting his cheeks do whatever they wanted, even when she laughed at his terrible joke about the referee. Then Dominic came sprinting back with a foam finger and a problem: he'd spent their bus money on it. Marisol dug through her pockets and found nothing, and Jordan found one dollar and a lot of silence.

They walked the two miles home in the dark, all three of them, taking turns wearing the foam finger. Marisol held his hand somewhere around the fourth block, and somewhere around the sixth, Dominic snatched the last of the hot chocolate without asking. Jordan let him keep it.

The line for the langar hall stretched past the glass doors, and Maya could hear the dhol already thumping inside the cultural center. She had one job today, which was to keep her seven-year-old cousin Harjit from wandering off, and one wish, which was to trade jobs with anyone. Her older cousin Simran got to carry the orange flag at the front of the Vaisakhi procession this afternoon, and Maya envied her so much it made her jaw tight.

"Stay by me," she told Harjit, gripping his sleeve. Behind them, the parking lot was filling with cars and a small knot of geese traced overhead, the first of the migratory birds heading north, though nobody else seemed to notice but her.

"Maya, why is everyone so happy today?" Harjit asked. "Is it because of the food?"

She opened her mouth and realized she didn't have a good answer. It was a harvest thing, she thought. New year, spring, like the poster in the lobby with the wheat on it. "Something like that," she said, and hated saying it, because Harjit repeated everything and would announce her guess to the whole hall.

At the door, Uncle Kirpal was handing out small paper flags. Harjit tugged his kurta. "Uncle, why does this day matter?"

Uncle Kirpal smiled, but he was busy, and his answer came in pieces as he passed out flags. "Vaisakhi. The year 1699." He handed a flag to a boy. "Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru." Another flag. "He founded the Khalsa at Anandpur." Then he was swallowed by the crowd.

Maya stood still, holding the pieces together in her head like a puzzle she hadn't known was a puzzle. So it wasn't mainly the wheat. It was that. She bent down to Harjit's level, because if he was going to repeat her words all afternoon, they should be right ones. "It's about something that started a long time ago," she said. "In 1699, Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur. That's what we're celebrating."

Harjit nodded slowly, the way he did when he was filing something away. Then he raised his paper flag and marched toward the dhol, and Maya followed, her hand hovering an inch from his collar.

In the hall she found her mother arranging trays and made her offer, a quick negotiation: she would serve food for the whole afternoon if, next Vaisakhi, her name went on the list for the flag. Her mother squinted at her, then at Harjit, who was already telling a stranger, "1699," with enormous confidence.

"Deal," her mother said, and handed her a tray. "Start with that table by the window."

Easton slid the box across the kitchen table until it bumped his milk glass, because if he was going to open it, he wanted to do it slowly enough to remember. Inside was his first phone, dark blue, with a case his mom said was durable enough to survive being dropped off a roof. He turned it on while his little sister Priya leaned her elbows on the table and breathed directly on his shoulder.

"Screen time rules," his mom said, sliding the charger across like a business deal. "Homework first, phone in the kitchen at nine. And you have to let me enroll you in the family safety thing tonight." She said it lightly, but she watched his face while she said it, and he nodded because he meant it.

The first thing he wanted was a flashlight app, since his room's ceiling light flickered like it was trying to quit. He found one with a cartoon bulb icon, tapped Install, and stopped. A box had come up. The app wanted permission to use his camera, his microphone, and all of his contacts. Easton frowned at it. "Why would a flashlight need to hear me?" he asked the kitchen.

"To hear if you're scared of the dark," Priya said solemnly.

He didn't tap Allow. Instead he hunted through Settings, tapping into Apps, then Permissions, because his cousin Malik had once said something Easton only half remembered, something about controlling what apps could touch. What he found surprised him: a list. Camera. Microphone. Contacts. Little toggles beside each one, all off. He tested it. He granted the flashlight permission to the camera, then took it away again with one tap, and the toggle went dark. So apps had to ask first, and he could take the permission back later, anytime, right there in the settings.

He tried two more apps to be sure. A drawing app asked for nothing. A free game asked for contacts, microphone, camera, and something about his location. He denied everything, and the game still worked. "Interesting," he said.

"What's interesting?" his mom asked, coming back with two mugs, setting the cocoa one in front of Priya first.

"The flashlight wanted my contacts. Why does a flashlight need to know Priya's friend Gabby's phone number?"

His mom laughed into her mug. "Maybe the bulb wants pen pals." Then she put her hand briefly on his shoulder, the way she did when he did something right without being told. "Take the permission away, then. You know how now."

He did, one tap, and the flashlight turned on anyway, a clean white beam across the table that made Priya's cocoa steam glow like a tiny ghost.

"It works without asking for anything else," Easton said. "So all that asking was just an illusion, like the app was being polite when it was really just being nosy."

"Like Malcolm at recess," Priya said, and both of them cracked up, because Malcolm asked everyone's business and called it journalism.

At nine that night, the phone went in the kitchen drawer, screen glowing through the gap one last time before it slept.

Piper counted the seats before she counted the faces, because the desks told her something the people wouldn't. Twenty-six desks, twenty-five filled, one empty beside a girl with a green binder full of guitar tabs. She took it. The girl glanced over, then back at the board.

"You're new," the girl said when the teacher turned to write.

"Piper."

"Marisol."

That was all until lunch, when Marisol set her tray down across from Piper without asking. Piper had planned to eat alone and text her old friends in Millbrook, but the phone stayed in her pocket. They talked about the guitar tabs, then about a teacher who assigned homework on Fridays. Thirty-one minutes, Piper figured, maybe thirty-five with the walk to the table.

That night she looked up what she half remembered from a magazine in the dentist's office. There it was: a 2018 study by Jeffrey Hall of the University of Kansas found it takes about 50 hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend. She read it twice. Fifty hours. She did the math on the back of her science homework. Lunch was about half an hour. At one lunch a day, a hundred days, more than the whole school year. That couldn't be right for everybody. Her best friend Dana had taken a single disastrous summer of soccer camp to become inseparable, but that was hours a day, every day. It added up faster than Piper had ever thought about.

So she ran a test. She wrote 35 on a sticky note and stuck it inside her binder. Every lunch, every group project, every walk to the bus loop, she added the minutes. Thursday brought a surprise: Marisol sat with her at lunch and then again in study hall, and Piper caught her sneaking a look at the sticky note.

"What's the number for?"

"Hours. Sort of." Piper flattened the note on the desk. "There was this study, 2018, Jeffrey Hall, University of Kansas. It takes about fifty hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend. I'm keeping track."

Marisol frowned at it. "That's weird and also not wrong."

"You think it's wrong?"

"I think it's slow." She tapped the number. "My grandmother says friendship isn't an antibiotic, one dose and done. You have to take the whole course."

Piper laughed, the first real one in two weeks. "My mom says I inherited my stubbornness from my grandfather. The rebellious gene, she calls it."

"Good," Marisol said. "Then don't wait for the study to hit fifty." She pulled out her phone. "Saturday. My cousin's band plays at the community center. It's three hours and it's loud and you'll hate half of it."

Piper looked at the sticky note, then wrote +180 under the 35.

"Pick me up at six," she said.

Jaxson had signed up for the talent showcase because Mr. Ferro left the sign-up sheet on the auditorium door for two weeks, which felt almost like a dare. Now he stood backstage with the school's borrowed guitar, and the sixth string sounded wrong. Not slightly wrong. Totally, embarrassingly wrong, like a bear groaning while everyone else was singing.

The showcase started in twenty minutes. He had learned three chords over a month of lunchtime practice in the empty auditorium, and his whole song depended on that string sounding right. He sat on the edge of the stage, turned the tuning peg, and the note sank even lower. He turned it again, the same direction, and the note dropped again, deep and fuzzy.

He stopped with his hand still on the peg. Okay, he thought. Something was happening here that he could not see. The string was doing something when he turned the peg, and turning it that way made the sound go lower, every single time. So the direction mattered, and whatever invisible thing made the note was being changed by it. He turned the peg the other way, slowly, and the note climbed, rising tighter and brighter until it passed the right pitch and kept going. He backed off a hair. The string settled into a clear, steady tone, and when he pressed his chord, the whole thing rang instead of groaning.

"Is that the trick?" a voice asked. Priya from homeroom was crouched by the curtain rail, holding a violin case that hindered her view of the stage. She had signed up too, and her hands had been shaking since third period, though she kept her face neutral about it.

"It's a pattern," Jaxson said. "The tighter you make the string, the faster it vibrates, so the note goes higher. Loosen it and the vibration slows down and the pitch drops." He plucked the string, tightened it a touch, and plucked again so she could hear the rise. "I loosened it wrong twice before I figured out which way the peg even went."

Priya set down her case and tried it on her violin's E string, turning her peg a sliver, listening, turning back. Her note steadied, and her shoulders came down an inch. She looked at Jaxson like he'd handed her something. "Play it for me?" she said. "The song. I want to hear it while nobody's out there yet."

He glanced at the half-empty rows of seats, then at the little label on the guitar's headstock that read steel and bronze alloy strings. Fine strings, he decided, even if they took figuring out. He set his fingers on the first chord, and Priya settled into the front row, tapping her violin bow softly against her knee to give him a beat.

The Coleman stove hissed on the picnic table while Thomas poured a cup of sugar into the heavy pot his dad always called the dynasty pot, because it had survived three generations of family camping trips. Tonight it was his turn to make dessert, and he had decided on caramel, the real kind, made from nothing but sugar and heat.

His little sister Maya leaned over his shoulder as the sugar began to melt. "It's turning brown," she said. "Is that the same browning as the crust on the roast? Dad's roast got all brown this afternoon too."

Thomas stirred slowly and thought about it. The roast had browned in the fire, and the sugar was browning on the stove, but something felt different about the two. The roast was meat, and meat was not just one thing. The pot held sugar alone, nothing else. He remembered a page from a science book at the school library, something about browning reactions having names depending on what was in the pot.

"I don't think they're the same," he said. "The browning in this pot is called caramelization, because it happens when sugar alone is heated. The crust on the roast is a different reaction, the Maillard reaction, and that one also needs amino acids." Maya wrinkled her nose at the word, and he shrugged. "Meat has amino acids. Sugar doesn't. That's the difference."

"Prove it," Maya said, which was her favorite thing to say lately.

He couldn't exactly prove what was happening inside the pot, since browning was invisible work, molecules changing where no one could watch. But he could test the rule. He spooned a tiny pile of plain sugar onto a piece of foil and set it near the fire, then set a small piece of the roast beside it. Both browned, but he already knew that would happen, so it proved nothing. The real test was the other direction: he took a spoonful of his caramel, which contained no amino acids at all, and mixed a pinch of baking soda into part of it to see whether the browning would cease or keep going when he moved the pot off the heat. The color held. Sugar alone could do this. It didn't need anything from meat.

The caramel finished at exactly the right moment, amber and glossy, and Thomas poured it over sliced apples in the dented metal bowl. His dad came back from the wash station and took the first bite, his eyebrows going up in a way that made Maya laugh. "Endangered species, this dessert," Dad said, going back for seconds. "It won't survive the night." Thomas dished out the last of it before his sister could beat him to it.

The spaghetti steam fogged Hailey's glasses as Dad launched into the ad again. "It said half the town's water has poison in it. Half, Hailey. You're drinking it right now." He tapped her water glass with his fork, twice, like a tiny judge banging a gavel.

"That sounds off," Hailey said. She twirled noodles, listening to her little brother slurp beside her. "A commercial can say whatever it wants. That's not the same as it being true." Mom stirred her sauce and said ads were allowed to have opinions, the same way Grandma was allowed to think cats were better than dogs. Hailey put her fork down. "But a cat being better is an opinion. Nobody can look it up. Water having poison in it is different. Somebody could actually test that."

"So test it," Dad said, scooping more garlic bread. "Go ahead, refute the nice television."

She pulled out her phone, thumbs already moving. Grandma sniffed at phones at the table, but Grandma wasn't here tonight, and Dad had literally challenged her. She typed the exact words from the ad, the ones about water in a town. A result popped up fast, from a site she'd never used before, called PolitiFact. It had checked the claim, and it had a whole page for it. At the top was a little meter graphic, half-full of orange, labeled with the site's rating scale, which it called the Truth-O-Meter. This claim sat between True and False, in a zone marked Half True. Down at the bottom of the scale, past False, was a rating that made Hailey snort so hard her milk nearly came back up. "Pants on Fire."

"What?" Dad leaned over, garlic bread frozen halfway to his mouth.

"Their scale goes from True down to Pants on Fire. Like, the worst rating. This one's Half True. The site started in 2007, it says. And it rates claims, not people." She scrolled, the screen's glow bluish against the red sauce. "So the ad took something real, a few old wells that got flagged, and stretched it to sound like the whole town."

Dad chewed for a while. The kitchen clock ticked, and her brother's fork scraped his plate in slow circles. "So they didn't exactly lie," he said finally.

"They took a small true thing and made it sound huge. That's not an opinion like 'this sauce is spicy.' That's a claim with a number in it, and the number doesn't hold up. You can't check 'spicy.' You can check 'half.'"

Mom set down her ladle. "So what you're saying is, I should get a prescription for skepticism."

Hailey laughed, then stopped, because she was rereading the page. The claim had come from a political ad, and the politician was the same man whose campaign office had just called their house twice this week. The name on the screen matched the name Mom kept grumbling about.

"Mom," Hailey said slowly, turning the phone toward her. "This is the guy you were going to vote for."

Mom peered at the screen, then at Hailey, then at the little orange meter.

Aria had never volunteered anywhere before, and the food bank took up half the library's basement, past the biography shelves and a door marked Staff Only. Her job was simple: match donation slips to boxes. By ten o'clock, the slips said there should be eleven boxes of canned vegetables, and she could only find nine.

"You lost two boxes?" Marcus worked the folding table beside her, stacking peanut butter faster than anyone. He was fourteen and wanted the supervisor to notice him so he could move up to the delivery van. "Just recount. Somebody always miscounts."

Aria counted again. Nine boxes. She checked the slips twice. Eleven written in blue ink, signed by Mr. Okafor, who had left for the bank run an hour ago. The missing boxes had existed on paper and then, somehow, evaporated between the loading dock and the basement. Nobody had taken anything out through the front, because the front was the library's circulation desk, and Priya at the desk hadn't seen a cart go by.

In the break room, while she rechecked the clipboard, Aria stopped at a framed page on the wall. The first food bank, it read, was St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, started in 1967 by John van Hengel. She read it twice. The words stuck with her on the walk back down, mostly because of one word: bank. A bank kept things safe and tracked them. This place tracked things with slips. If the slips were right, the boxes were somewhere, because boxes didn't just stop existing.

She tested it. If two boxes had come down on the cart, they were somewhere between the dock and the shelves. The elevator only stopped on two floors. On the main floor, past the fiction section, she found a leaning tower of boxes tucked behind the large-print mysteries, next to an eccentric old book cart with one square wheel. A man in a gray cardigan was reading the top box's label with great leisure, like he had all morning, which he apparently did.

"Those are for the food bank," Aria said.

"I know," the man said. "I volunteer Tuesdays. I set them here so I could shelve them after my shift." He blinked. "That was yesterday."

They carried the boxes down together. When she stacked them, the count came to eleven, and she showed Marcus the slip and the shelf.

"All right," Marcus said. "You were right, it wasn't a miscount." He looked at the elevator, then at her clipboard. "Next time stuff goes missing, we search the floors first. Tell Mr. Okafor it was your system."

Mr. Okafor came back from the van run, glanced at the slip, then at the full shelf, and raised an eyebrow at Aria.

"Eleven for eleven," she said.

Madison set the mashed potatoes down hard enough to rattle the salt shaker. Her little brother Theo had ruined her whole afternoon, and now she had to sit through dinner pretending everything was fine.

"Pass the green beans," Theo said, mouth already full.

"After what you did today? You told everyone in class the Eiffel Tower is in Berlin."

Dad looked up from his plate. Mom stopped cutting her chicken.

"It's my opinion," Theo said. "You can't argue with somebody's opinion. That's what Mr. Randall says. Respect the opinion."

Madison gripped her fork. She had replayed the moment all through last period, her face hot while kids snickered. She wanted to prove him wrong, but she wasn't sure how to fight a word like opinion. It seemed like a shield you could hide anything behind. She pushed a bean around her plate, thinking so hard she barely tasted her food.

"But it's not an opinion," she said slowly, testing the idea out loud the way she'd test a loose tooth. "Pineapple pizza tasting good is an opinion. Nobody can check that. But the Eiffel Tower being in Berlin, that's something you can look up. You can find the tower, find the city, and see they don't match." She pointed her fork at him. "It's still a claim even though it's wrong. It's just a wrong claim."

"That's a hard shot," Dad said, half smiling.

Theo slumped. "So my report is a wrong claim?"

"Your whole poster," Madison said. She remembered the glitter he had used, three evenings of it, and felt a small sting under her victory. He had been proud of that poster.

Mom cleared her throat. "Well, since we're being careful with facts, we need to talk about the science curriculum money. The school board wants to cut the wetland field trips to conserve funds." She and Dad started trading worried numbers, and Madison let their voices wash past her while she watched Theo. He was quietly moving his beans into a pile, not eating them.

Later, while Mom loaded the dishwasher, Madison found Theo's crumpled poster in the trash can by the back door. The Eiffel Tower stood in silver glitter above the word BERLIN, and along the border he had drawn a flock of migratory birds flying south, because his teacher had said every city poster needed one real fact about the place. He had gotten that part right, at least. She smoothed the paper against her knee, thinking she might help him fix the tower part tomorrow, if he'd let her.

She carried the poster upstairs and taped it above his desk, glitter flaking onto the carpet. When Theo came in and saw it, he stood in the doorway for a long moment.

"Paris," he said finally. "It's in Paris."

The gym had flooded on Tuesday, so Coach Ruiz held the basketball tryouts in Alex's backyard, which meant Alex couldn't be late even if he tried. He stood at the fence in his sneakers, watching nine other kids dribble around the folding chairs Coach Ruiz had set up as cones.

"You're lucky," said Marcus, jogging over. Marcus lived two streets down and had walked over eating a bagel, which he was still finishing. "Tryout at your own house. Home-court advantage."

"You can't have home-court advantage on grass," Alex said.

Marcus shrugged and sat on the porch steps to watch the others, saving his legs, as he put it. He wanted to see who his competition was before wasting any energy. Alex had done something like that once, at last year's tryout, sitting out the warm-up to study the other kids, and then running his sprints like his shoes were full of wet sand. He still didn't know exactly what had gone wrong, and it bothered him the way a loose tooth bothers you.

So the night before, he'd run an experiment. His sister Priya had timed him on her phone while he sprinted the length of the backyard cold, and he'd done it in a time neither of them wrote down because it was too depressing. Then he'd tried a gradual warm-up, easy jogging and moving stretches, the kind where you walk and reach and swing your legs rather than hold a stretch still, until he could feel his heart working faster and his legs warmed through. After that, the same sprint was nearly a full second faster. Same boy, same grass, same shoes. The only thing that had changed was the warm-up. Priya had made him do it twice more to be sure, which he suspected was mostly because she enjoyed bossing him around, but the numbers held.

"Line up," Coach Ruiz called. "Shuttle runs first, then layups."

Marcus stayed on the porch steps, observing. Alex started the light jog around the chairs, then the moving stretches, keeping it easy, nothing dramatic. He could feel it happen again: his heart rate climbing, his legs going warm.

"You're going to be tired before we even start," Marcus said from the steps.

"I'm warming up," Alex said. "Light jogging, moving stretches. Gets the heart rate up and the muscles warm."

"That sounds like extra work."

It did sound like extra work, which was maybe the point. When the whistle blew, Alex ran the shuttle like the grass owed him something. His legs answered on the first step instead of the fifth. Marcus, meanwhile, went from sitting to sprinting with nothing in between, and by the third shuttle he was moving like a different, slower boy, one whose shoes were, presumably, full of wet sand. He kept glancing at his own legs with an expression approaching despair.

At the layup station, Marcus missed his first four, all of them short, clanging off the front of the rim. On the fifth he banked it in and raised both arms as if he'd solved something.

"Tired already?" Coach Ruiz asked him.

"Unlucky rims," said Marcus. "Homemade."

Coach Ruiz looked at the portable hoop, then at Marcus, and wrote something on his clipboard that was probably not "unlucky rims."

At the end, Coach Ruiz read the list of names for the travel team. Alex made it, third from the top. Marcus did not make it, and stood by the porch steps staring at the grass like it might apologize.

"I had a bad day," Marcus said.

Alex picked up the folding chairs and started stacking them. "Come over tomorrow. We'll warm up first."

"Warm up," Marcus said, as if the word tasted like the bagel had probably tasted. "Fine. But only because your rims are weird."

Avery knelt in the dirt beside the tomato plants and counted the wilted leaves again, even though she already knew the answer was seven. Something was stealing water from the bed near the fence, and the thief was invisible. The soaker hose ran the whole length of the garden, but the far end had gone dry, and only the tomatoes on the north side drooped. "It's a reasonable guess," she said to the dog, who panted at her hopefully. "If I say the hose is blocked somewhere in the middle, and I cut the water on and feel along the line, the guess either works or it doesn't."

Her little brother, Marcus, wandered out with a popsicle, which began to irritate her immediately, because he had a way of leaning over her shoulder and dripping. "Miss Kaylee at the science centre says the hose thing is called a hypothesis," he said, as if this settled something.

"You didn't even go to the science centre."

"I did. On the field trip. The guide asked if evolution was real and Thomas said it's 'just a theory,' and the guide said no, a theory is not a guess, it's an explanation that's been tested over and over, and it's been supported every time. A hypothesis is the idea still being tested. Thomas got so red." Marcus licked his popsicle with enormous satisfaction.

Avery turned that over while she ran her fingers along the hose, one knuckle of rubber at a time. Her blocked-hose idea was still just a hypothesis until the test came back. If she found a kink, the test would support it. If the hose ran clear all the way to the end, the idea would be overturned, and she would need a different explanation entirely, maybe a root crushing the pipe under the fence. She kept pressing forward, wetter and wetter, and just past the basil she felt a hard, folded lump where the hose had doubled back under a stone.

She moved the stone and straightened the kink, and by the time the popsicle stick was dry, water had reached the far end and darkened the whole strip of soil. The climax came at sunset, when the seven wilted tomatoes lifted their leaves like hands unclenching. "So my guess was supported," Avery said. "I tested it once. I'd have to test it a lot more before it turned into anything like a theory."

"Like a tomato theory," Marcus said.

"Sure," she said, and wrote "hose hypothesis, day one" on a plant tag with a stub of pencil, then pressed it into the mud beside the fence.

Grace watched the class group chat blow up during lunch. Someone named DragonRider42, who had to be Marcus because he never shut up about dragons, had typed "SURE. WHATEVER." at Priya after she suggested a meeting time for the history project. Priya had replied with three sad faces and then gone silent. Now half the chat thought Marcus was furious, and the other half thought Priya was overreacting, and Mrs. Okafor had already posted "We will discuss this tomorrow."

The problem was that nobody could tell what anyone meant. Grace scrolled back through the messages. Marcus used all caps for everything, even "GOOD MORNING." Priya used exclamation points the way some people waved. And a kid named Devon had typed just "k" an hour ago, which somehow made the whole thread feel desolate, like a hallway after the last bell. Same chat, same words, but each person carried a different tone into it, and the tone vanished the moment they hit send. That was the hidden thing Grace wanted to catch.

She hypothesized that the trouble wasn't the people. It was the missing signals. In person, Marcus said "sure, whatever" in a joking drawl and Priya laughed. Online, the drawl disappeared, leaving only the skeleton of the words. If she could prove that, then the fix wasn't apologies. The fix was rules that put the signals back.

After school she found Marcus at his locker and read his own message out loud in his exact joking voice. "Sure. Whatever." He grinned. "That's how I meant it. I say everything like that." Then she read it flat and cold, the way Priya must have heard it, and his grin faded. "Oh," he said. "That sounds terrible."

That night Grace searched whether anyone had ever bothered to write down official online manners, because it seemed like the kind of problem adults would have noticed decades ago. They had. One of the first written guides to online manners was called the Netiquette Guidelines, published in 1995 as a document called RFC 1855. She sat back. That was older than her parents' marriage. People had been fighting about all caps since before she was born.

The next morning she got to Mrs. Okafor first. "Can I set the rules for the chat?" she asked. "There's a real thing to base it on. One of the first written guides to online manners was published in 1995, a document called RFC 1855." Mrs. Okafor raised an eyebrow. "You looked that up?" "Last night. It has a principle I like. Assume the reader can't hear your voice, so don't send anything your face wouldn't survive."

Marcus posted an apology before homeroom, in normal lowercase, and Priya answered with a thumbs-up and "thanks!" with the exclamation point, which Grace now knew was Priya's wave. At the end of the period Grace added one line to the pinned rules: if you mean it as a joke, say so out loud someday, where people can hear you smile.

She clicked the pin, and the little gray flag appeared beside the rules.
