He knew it had flopped, even though nobody said anything mean. They just sat there, polite and quiet, while he read. "It's a good genre," his friend Marcus had said afterward, "it just sounded, I don't know, bumpy." Tyler wanted this time to be different.

The trouble was, when he read the pages silently, they looked fine to him. Every sentence seemed okay. His grandmother drifted past with a watering can, pausing to sprinkle her African violets on the windowsill. "Still working on the mystery?" she asked. "I nurture those violets for a year before they bloom, you know. Some things take time." Tyler nodded without really hearing. He read the opening again in his head and still couldn't find the bump.

Then he tried something. He read the first paragraph out loud, alone in the kitchen. "The old dark spooky house loomed darkly on the dark hill." His own tongue tripped over it like a shoelace. He tried the next line. "Tom walked up the path. Tom opened the door. Tom went inside." Reading it silently, he'd never noticed how every sentence marched the same length, like boots on pavement. Out loud, he actually stumbled, and stumbling made him hear it.

"Grandma, can I read you something?" he called. She set down the watering can, sat across from him, and listened. He read the whole first page aloud, and every time his voice caught, he marked the spot with the red pen. When he finished, she tapped one sentence. "Right there you slowed down," she said. "The one about the very big enormous shadow. I got lost in the extra words." She had a want of her own, too. "Read me the ending," she said. "I've been dying to know who took the painting." Tyler covered the last page with his hand. "You have to wait like everyone else, Grandma."

He cut the weak adjectives first, the very big enormous shadow becoming just the enormous shadow, the old dark spooky house becoming the crooked house on the hill. Then he broke up the march of same-sized sentences, letting some run long and complex while others stopped abrupt, like a door slamming. Reading aloud, he could hear the difference now, the rhythm shifting when Tom crept through the halls instead of walking, walking, walking.

At the writing club on Thursday, Marcus leaned forward during the part with the hidden painting. When Tyler finished the last line, a short one, the room stayed silent for a second and then everyone started talking at once. "That was so much better," Marcus said. "What'd you change?" Tyler shrugged and clicked his pen. "I made myself trip over it first."

Owen arrived at Grandma Ruthie's house on Friday afternoon with a bag of gummy worms and a plan. Last month at his friend Danny's house, all the phones had gone into a drawer right when the sky turned orange, and nobody would tell him why. They only said one word, "Shabbat," and Danny's mom had smiled like it was an inside joke Owen wasn't part of. Owen wanted in on the joke.

Grandma Ruthie was lighting candles in the kitchen, humming. "Stay for Shabbat dinner," she said. "Sunset's at seven tonight."

"Grandma," Owen said, being very diligent about his investigation, "if I wanted to know exactly when Shabbat starts, would it be, like, seven o'clock exactly? Or when it looks dark?"

"It begins at sunset on Friday," she said, "and it ends tomorrow, after nightfall on Saturday." Then she shooed him out of the kitchen because the soup was boiling over, which Owen thought was dramatic but fair.

He hypothesized that Shabbat must follow the sky instead of the clock, since sunset moved around all year. He decided to test it. At 6:58 he stood in the backyard like a diligent little astronomer, watching the horizon. At 7:01, when the sun finally slipped behind the Hendersons' roof, he heard the front door open and his grandpa called out the blessing, loud enough for the whole block.

"So it's the sun, not the clock," Owen announced at dinner, waving his fork. "The sky is the boss."

"The sky is the boss," Grandpa agreed solemnly, "which means the sky is responsible for this soup being cold by the time we sat down."

"The soup is not my fault," said the sky's employee, Grandma Ruthie.

After dinner they sang a song Owen half knew, and when he accidentally knocked his water glass into Grandpa's lap, nobody checked a single phone. Grandpa just mopped his pants with a napkin and said, "At Danny's house, did they do this part too?"

"This part?" Owen asked.

Grandpa leaned close. "The part where the kid ruins my pants."

"Every week," Owen said. "It's called tradition."

Anthony slumped in front of the library computer, staring at the assignment sheet. Create one strong password, it said, and explain in writing why the same password should never be used on two different websites. He knew how to make one that was hard to guess. What he could not figure out was the second part. If his password was strong, why did it matter where else he had typed it? Nobody could see it floating around out there, could they? He wanted to hand in something he actually believed, not just a sentence copied from the board.

He pulled up his grandfather's email address next to him, because Grandpa typed the same password, "Butterscotch7," for everything, and Anthony had been nagging him about it for weeks. He remembered a website his cousin had mentioned at Thanksgiving. "It's called Have I Been Pwned," she had said, and he typed it in now, his science worksheet on decomposers, half finished beside the keyboard, curling under his elbow. The site loaded. It said a security researcher named Troy Hunt had launched it in December 2013, and that it let people check whether their email address had appeared in a known data breach. A breach. Anthony chewed his pencil. That meant a company somewhere had gotten robbed of its whole list of usernames and passwords.

He typed in Grandpa's address and hit search. His stomach dropped. The address had shown up in an old breach, from some shopping site Grandpa barely remembered joining. Anthony tested his idea quickly: the same password reused everywhere meant one break-in could unlock them all, like one key for every door in the neighborhood. That was the pattern he could not see before, and now he could see it plain as a bruise.

He typed his paragraph fast, then grabbed his worksheet and hurried to find Marcus at the lunch table. "My grandpa's email is in a real breach," he said. "I'm going to show him after school." Marcus looked up from his sandwich. "Does he even know what that word means?" Anthony grinned and slung his backpack over his shoulder. "He's about to find out."

Aurora spread her poster board across the archive table and frowned at it. Her class assignment was a calendar of ancient Egypt, and she had drawn four neat seasons, spring, summer, autumn, winter, because that was what a year had. Her best friend Milo leaned over from the next table, where he was squashing a paper pyramid flat for the third time.

"Mine keeps collapsing," Milo said. "Ancient Egyptians were geniuses. I can't even make one out of cardstock."

Aurora flipped through a folder of copied papyrus records and stopped at a page listing festival months. She counted on her finger. Then she counted again. "Milo. This only has three seasons. Three. Not four." The library lights hummed above them while she traced the strange words with her pencil. One section repeated a word, Akhet, over months that mentioned high water everywhere. Another, Peret, appeared beside drawings of green shoots. The last one, Shemu, matched pictures of sickles and stacked grain. She turned the page slowly, feeling the paper's dry edge, and the pattern almost snapped into place.

"It's the river," she said. "The Nile. Their year follows the water." She grabbed a blank sheet and drew a wide blue curve down the middle. "Look. Akhet, the flood. Then Peret, the growing season. Then Shemu, the harvest." Milo set down his flattened pyramid and stared.

"So they didn't have winter at all? No snow days?" He looked genuinely wounded.

"They had flood days, probably worse." Aurora laughed. She began to incorporate the three seasons into her calendar, splitting the poster into three bright bands with the Nile curving through all of them. She had almost been biased toward four seasons just because that was what she had always known, and that was exactly why the Egyptians hadn't counted that way. Their whole farming year depended on the river, not the sky.

Milo taped a lopsided pyramid onto the corner of her poster. "There. Factor in a pyramid and it's perfect."

Scarlett held the violin under her chin and plucked the A string, and the note wobbled like a fence post about to fall over. Mr. Herrera had gone down the hall to fetch coffee, leaving the class to practice, and he had played one clear A on the piano before he left. "That's your reference note," he had said. "Match it." That was all. No instructions, no diagram.

The problem was that Scarlett had no idea which way to turn the peg. She remembered last summer at her grandpa's house, when her cousin Marco had tried to tune the old guitar in the den. Marco had cranked a peg with great confidence, and the note had sunk lower and lower, like a whale diving. Grandpa had laughed and said, "Other way, kiddo. Tightening a string raises its pitch. Loosening it lowers it." Marco had turned back the other way and the note climbed up out of the whale depths. Scarlett, watching from the couch, had thought it looked like magic. Now she realized it was more like a rule.

She plucked the string again, then hummed the piano's A in her memory. Her string sat below it, saggy and sour. If her string was too low, then the peg must be too loose. She turned it a tiny bit, plucked, and listened. Still low. Another small turn, and the note rose to meet the one in her head, close enough that the wobble between them slowed like a spinning coin settling.

"Whoa," said Priya from the next stand. Priya wanted first chair more than anything and had been eavesdropping with her whole body. "How did you do that without a tuner?" Scarlett offered the violin over. "String's too low, tighten. Too high, loosen. Want to try your D?" Priya grabbed it, turned the peg the wrong way, and the note dropped so fast they both winced. "Okay," Priya said, wincing. "Whale. I heard the whale."

Scarlett took the violin back and eased the peg forward, and the D climbed up pure and bright, and somewhere down the hall she heard Mr. Herrera's footsteps returning.

Samantha's flight to Grandma's was delayed, which meant two hours in Terminal B with nothing but her brother Theo, who wanted nothing in the world except a giant cinnamon roll from the bakery by Gate 14. "One roll," Theo said, staring through the glass like the pastry might flourish right off the shelf and into his hands. "One roll, and I'll be the happiest organism in this entire airport."

"Everything in this airport is an organism except the planes and the luggage," Samantha said, but she was barely listening. She had Grandma's postcard out, the one that said FIND ME, along with the numbers Grandma always scribbled at the bottom: 40, then a little N, then 105, then a little W. In the gift shop Samantha had found a desk globe the size of a grapefruit, and she spun it slowly, tracing the lines with her finger.

The lines running up and over the top of the globe were the ones she needed. She noticed something odd: down near the equator they sat far apart, like fence posts, but near the top they crowded together until they all touched at one point, like the spokes of an umbrella squished to nothing. "Grandma's 105," she said, turning the globe, "is a skinny slice here near the top but a fat slice down there." Theo leaned over her shoulder, still hoping. She set the globe on the window ledge and laid the postcard flat against the glass, using the horizon outside like a giant map. "One degree is about 111 kilometers wide at the equator," she announced, jabbing the globe's middle. "Near the poles it shrinks to zero, because the lines all meet there. Zero! That's smaller than your cinnamon roll."

"That is the smallest thing I've ever heard of," Theo said solemnly. She marked 40 N and 105 W with her finger, right on Denver, then held the globe up next to the departure board. "Grandma's city. Found her." Theo clapped once, then pointed at the bakery. "Now find me that roll." Samantha laughed, spun the globe one last time, and grabbed her backpack. "Okay, navigator first, roll second."

The math club room smelled like pencil shavings and the orange juice Marcus had spilled near the protractor box. Ms. Ruiz had written "y = 2x + 1" on the board and told everyone to graph it before the bell, but Julia could perceive only five minutes left on the clock, and she had plotted exactly one point, at (1, 3).

"Two-step equations, then the graph," Marcus groaned beside her. He had six points on his grid and a cramping hand.

Julia worked her second point fast. If x was 2, then y = 2 times 2 plus 1, which was 5. She plotted (2, 5) and stared at the two dots, wishing she could perceive the whole line hiding inside the equation the way you can hear a whole song from two notes. "That's not enough," she muttered. "I need more points."

"Actually," said Priya from across the table, leaning over her own grid, "try putting your ruler through your two points and drawing. I did it last week." Julia laid her ruler down, and it touched both dots with no wiggle room, so she drew one clean line to the edge of the grid. Then she tested it. She picked x = 4, solved y = 2 times 4 plus 1, got 9, and checked the grid. Her line ran straight through (4, 9). She tried x = 0 next, and the line passed through (0, 1) too, right where the y-axis met it.

"It works!" Julia said. "The graph is always a straight line, so two correct points are enough to draw the whole thing with a ruler." Ms. Ruiz, walking past, tapped Julia's paper and smiled. "Nice work. That's the real thing, not a shortcut."

Marcus copied her method, and Priya gave Julia a thumbs up. Julia wrote "line of y = 2x + 1" in her notebook, and when the bell rang, she carefully tore out the grid and folded it into her pocket.

Rebecca had read the bylaw three times on the bus, and it still said the same tedious thing: no wheeled vehicles of any kind on the paths of Hollow Creek Park. Her skate ramp petition had forty-one signatures, and tonight she was going to read them out loud at the town hall meeting.

In the lobby, Mr. Alvarez was pacing with a stack of papers under his arm. He wanted streetlights for the community garden, where his tomatoes kept getting trampled after dark. "You go first, kiddo," he said, holding the door. "Youth before vegetables."

But when they reached the clerk's table at the back of the chamber, the woman behind it shook her head. "Are you registered to speak? Delegations have to sign up with the clerk's office before the meeting." She tapped the schedule in front of her, and Rebecca saw that every speaking slot already had a name printed neatly beside it. Mr. Alvarez exhaled so hard his mustache fluttered.

"Before," Rebecca repeated. Not at the door, not in line. Before. That was why the list looked so orderly, she realized; it wasn't luck or favors. There was a rule underneath, invisible until you bumped into it, like a glass door. "So if I come back for the next meeting, I need to register first with your office? That's how a delegation gets on this list?"

"That's exactly how," the clerk said, and pulled a small card from a drawer. "Next meeting's the fifteenth. You can register with me now, if you like."

Rebecca filled out the card in her best handwriting, then slid a second blank card across the table toward Mr. Alvarez. He blinked at it, then at her, and took his pen out of his shirt pocket.

"For the tomatoes," he said.

"For the tomatoes," Rebecca agreed, and they sat down in the front row to watch how it was done.

Nolan set the recipe card on the counter and read it twice before touching anything, because last time he had tried this, he'd added the salt twice and the muffins had made his little sister Bree gag dramatically at the breakfast table. Today was different. Mom had promised that if he could bake a batch from start to finish, following every step without calling her into the kitchen, the muffins were officially his recipe. Bree wanted one in her lunchbox tomorrow, and she had already picked out which muffin liner she liked best, the one with tiny green frogs on it, so the pressure was real.

He turned the dial to three seventy-five to preheat the oven, mixed the dry ingredients, and then cracked the eggs. One tiny piece of shell went in, and he fished it out with another piece of shell, which somehow worked better than the spoon. When he added the wet ingredients to the dry and stirred, the batter puffed up slightly, like it was breathing. Nolan frowned at it. Batter wasn't supposed to do that, was it? He glanced at the recipe again and noticed a line he'd skimmed past: the batter could rest for a few minutes before going into the oven. That seemed backwards to him. If the batter was already bubbling, letting it sit should make the bubbles disappear, like a forgotten glass of soda.

He remembered a school unit where they'd read that double-acting baking powder releases gas twice, once when it gets wet in the batter and again when it is heated in the oven. He had thought it was boring then, just words on a worksheet, but now he stared at the puffed batter and a whole chain of ideas clicked together. The bubbles he could see were only the first round. The second round had to come from the heat of the oven, so letting the batter wait a few minutes wouldn't ruin anything, because the oven would start a fresh burst of rising. He decided to test it. He filled five muffin cups right away, set the timer for five minutes, and filled the other five cups after the timer buzzed, keeping the two groups on opposite ends of the pan like a tiny experiment.

"Are they done yet?" Bree asked, drifting in barefoot and hovering near the oven, where the smell had started to leak out warm and sweet. "Because I already picked my frog liner, and I'm not sharing it with anyone."

"They need eighteen minutes," Nolan said, watching through the oven door as all the muffins rose, the early ones and the late ones both climbing into rounded golden tops. He couldn't see inside the batter, but he could see the proof, the ones that had waited rose just as proudly as the ones that hadn't. Maybe even a hair taller. He wrote both results on the back of the recipe card, because a good narrator of his own experiment, he decided, should record what actually happened rather than what he expected.

When the muffins came out, Bree claimed the tallest one for her frog liner and pronounced it "actually legendary." Nolan bit into his own and tasted blueberry and lemon and the small, private satisfaction of having figured something out by himself. His grandpa would have been proud; there was a frail old photo of him in his bakery apron on the fridge, and Nolan had started this whole project because he wanted to bake like that someday, not from a box, but for real. He licked a smear of batter off his thumb and slid the recipe card into the drawer next to Grandpa's old wooden spoon.

"Same time next month?" Bree asked, already reaching for a second muffin. "I vote chocolate chip."

Emily slid her French workbook across the library table until it bumped the dictionary, which was the size of a brick and just as heavy. On the page in front of her, the assignment stared back: describe your family and pets in full sentences, and read it aloud to a partner on Friday. Friday was two days away. She had written four sentences already, and she was almost sure two of them were wrong.

"J'ai une soeur," she read under her breath. "Elle s'appelle Katie." That part felt solid. The trouble started with her sentences about the dog, and with one word she had copied off the board so fast that her handwriting had turned it into a smudge. She copied it again, carefully, onto the corner of a napkin: avoir. She didn't know what it meant. The board had been erased before she finished writing, and Madame Rossi had already left for the day.

Across the library, Marcus was building a tower out of encyclopedias, which the librarian pretended not to see. Emily knew Marcus took French too, and Marcus was, in her private opinion, reckless about checking his work. He'd once turned in a whole paragraph about his "horse mother." She carried the napkin over anyway.

"Do you know this word?" she asked. "Avoir?"

"Sure," Marcus said, not looking up. "It's how you say stuff. Watch, I'll do my age." He straightened up and recited, proud and loud enough that the librarian glanced over. "Je suis onze ans. I am eleven."

Emily was already shaking her head. She had found the pattern, and the pattern was the thing you couldn't see on the page. "That's wrong. You used être, to be. But look." She flipped her workbook to the family page and pointed at the model sentence Madame Rossi had printed at the top, the one Emily had skipped and then gone back to: "J'ai douze ans." Twelve. Her own age. "It says j'ai, not je suis. And you know what j'ai is, because we say j'ai un chien all the time."

Marcus frowned at the sentence. "So it says I have twelve years? That's weird."

"It means 'I am twelve,'" Emily said, tapping the page, "but word for word it says 'I have twelve years.' You have your years, like you have a dog. Or an organism," she added, because the science poster on the wall behind him said organisms have traits, and her brain had made the leap before she could stop it.

Marcus tested it out loud, slower now, watching her face for the verdict. "J'ai onze ans." She nodded, and he grinned and wrote it on his arm, which she chose not to comment on.

She went back to her table and fixed her dog sentence the same way, using avoir for everything her family owned: a sister, a mother, a father, and one enormous brown dog named Biscuit who shed on everything. The pile of sentences that had looked wrong an hour ago had not diminished at all, but now every one of them sat quietly on the page, behaving.

On Friday, Madame Rossi listened to Marcus first. He took a breath and said, "J'ai onze ans," and Madame Rossi's eyebrows went up, just a little, before she wrote a small check in her book. Emily watched from her seat, holding her own paper, and mouthed one word across the room.

Isabella slid her notebook across the library table and counted on her fingers for the third time. Seven paragraphs. Mr. Ruiz had said the essay contest entries were due at the end of writing club, forty minutes from now, and her draft was seven paragraphs long.

"You look like you lost a shoe," said Devon, dropping into the chair beside her. He had a reputation for finishing assignments early, which annoyed everyone, including Isabella.

"I wrote too much. I don't know what to cut." She flipped the pages. "I'm trying to convince the city council to build a skate park, and I put in a paragraph about ramps, one about safety, one about cost, one about a park in another town, one about weather, and I don't even know what this one is."

Devon leaned over. "It's about pigeons."

"It was going to be about litter. It got away from me." She laughed, then stopped laughing. "Mr. Ruiz said something at the last meeting. About the shape of a persuasive essay. I was doodling a dragon and didn't write it down."

"A dragon," Devon said. "Right when he was explaining the most important thing of the whole year. Very spontaneous of you."

"You're not helping." But she was already thinking, staring at her seven paragraphs like they were a puzzle with pieces hiding underneath. Five, he had said. She was almost sure he had said five. If the essay had five paragraphs, and the first one had to introduce the whole argument and the last one had to wrap it up, that left three in the middle. She counted again. Intro, then three body paragraphs, then a conclusion. Five. Her seven meant two extras.

"Okay," she said. "I can delegate. One body paragraph to ramps and safety together, one to cost, one to the other town's park. The weather paragraph goes. The pigeon paragraph really, really goes."

Devon held out his hand. "Give me the pigeons. I'll read it to Marisol so she can laugh too."

Marisol, across the table, waved a purple pen. "I'll trade you. I'll check your conclusion if you check my commas. My essay is four paragraphs and I can't figure out why it feels wrong."

"You probably squished your conclusion into your last body paragraph," Isabella said. "Happened to me last month."

Isabella crossed out, rewrote, and handed pages to Devon as she finished them. With twelve minutes left, she numbered her paragraphs: one, two, three, four, five. She slid the entry into the contest envelope and licked it shut.

"Pigeons," she said, dropping the crumpled page into the recycling bin.

Logan had one hour before his social studies presentation, and the only thing he knew about pyramids was that they were pointy. He spread his notes across the library table and glared at them, as if staring hard enough might make the facts crawl onto the paper by themselves.

"Your hair is going to catch fire if you think that hard," said Priya, dropping into the chair across from him with her own stack of books.

"Very funny. Why did they build those giant things? And why did they farm where they farmed? Mr. Osei wants reasons, not just 'the pyramids were big.'" Logan flipped a page and stopped. A picture showed fields right beside a river, dark stripes of soil against pale sand. He remembered his grandmother's garden boxes at home, the one with the darkest dirt, where her tomatoes grew so fat they looked smug. The sandy box, the one by the fence, grew only sad little stalks that a parasite had chewed to lace.

He grabbed a pencil and drew the Nile on his notes, then the flood rising, then the flood going down. "Okay, watch this. The flood goes down, and it leaves mud on the fields. Dark mud. Dark soil grows the best plants, like Grandma's tomatoes. So that's why their farms were there." He slid the drawing to Priya.

She studied it, tapping the pencil against her chin. "I read that they had a name for it," she said. "They called their land Kemet, the black land."

"That's my reason! They named their whole country after the good dirt." Logan copied it in his neatest handwriting, feeling optimistic for the first time all week. He decided to monitor the clock on the wall so he wouldn't run out of time, and by the time the bell rang, his note cards were stacked and ready.

In class, he held up his drawing of the smug tomato. "If you want to understand Egypt," he said, "start with the mud."

Jaxon slid the Monopoly box under the table with his foot, hoping Marcus wouldn't bring it up again before the tacos were served. Marcus had come over straight from school, and everything had gone fine until he landed on Free Parking and reached for a pile of money that wasn't there. "Where's the pot?" he had demanded, and Jaxon had said, "What pot?" and after ten minutes of arguing they had flipped the board onto the carpet and stomped downstairs.

At dinner, Jaxon's grandmother noticed that Marcus was pushing his lettuce around his plate instead of eating it. "You look like a boy who lost his favorite marble," she said, and passed him the bowl of rice before he even asked. Jaxon watched his friend shrug and decided he couldn't let the whole evening end like that.

"It's my fault," Jaxon said. "We had a fight over the game."

"Over a board game?" his father said.

"Marcus thinks when you land on Free Parking you collect all this money. We never do that." Jaxon stopped, because he had just noticed something. In every argument they'd had, they hadn't been disagreeing about what was fair. They'd been disagreeing about what the rule even was. It was like two people arguing about the weather when one of them was looking out a window on the other side of the house. His grandmother's face conveyed nothing but patience while he worked it through. He wanted to test the idea before he said it out loud.

Jaxon knelt under the table, dug out the box, and pulled the rulebook from the lid. He flipped through it while his father cleared the plates and his grandmother cut Marcus a second taco without being asked. The book said nothing about collecting money on Free Parking. Nothing at all. Free Parking was just a free space. "See, it's not in here," Jaxon said. "It's a house rule. We never used it, so I thought it was made up. But your family plays it at your house, so you thought it was real."

Marcus leaned over the book, reading the paragraph twice. "So it's not official? Huh." He looked almost relieved. "Then we weren't both being jerks. We just learned different rules."

"That was the whole problem," Jaxon said. "Not that either of us cheated." He could see it clearly now, the pattern behind the fight. Nobody at the table was immune to that kind of mess, either; his father admitted that his brothers used to flip the table every Christmas over the same argument, a contradiction between their two houses that lasted for years because nobody ever checked the rulebook.

"So here's a fair way to do it," Jaxon said. "We play the official rules, because those are the ones in the box and nobody has to take anybody's word for anything. But if we both agree on a change before we start, we can do that too." He held out his hand. "Deal?"

Marcus shook it, grabbed the last tortilla, and was already carrying the board back upstairs. "Railroads," he called over his shoulder. "I'm buying every railroad, and this time you can't stop me."

Aubrey sat on the back step with her poster board and a pencil that had been sharpened down to a stub. The assignment was due Monday: draw a food chain, starting with the sun, ending with a top predator, and be ready to explain what happens if one link disappears. She had the sun. After that, nothing.

She sketched the clover patch near the fence, then the rabbits that showed up every evening to nibble it. Then she stopped. Something had been visiting the yard at night, something that left a pile of gray fur by the compost bin and knocked over the low-voltage garden lights. She had never seen it. She drew a blank circle at the top of the chain and labeled it with a question mark, because she could not put an animal she had never met into her homework.

While she waited, she turned over an old log to study the pill bugs, tiny decomposers breaking down the dead wood into dark soil, soil that fed the clover. She wrote that on a scrap paper. Then her little brother Marcus stomped out with a granola bar. "What are you doing?" he asked.

"Sorting who eats what," Aubrey said. "The rabbits eat the clover, so they're eating only producers. Animals that eat only producers are called primary consumers." She tapped her pencil. "The thing that eats the rabbits would be a secondary consumer."

"A thing eats rabbits?"

"That's what I'm trying to find out."

The light dimmed. The clover rustled once, then twice. Aubrey held her breath as a red shape stepped out of the shadow of the fence, low and quick, ears pricked toward the rabbit trail. She did not move. She did not even blink. She just slid the poster closer and wrote one word inside the blank circle: fox.

Marcus whispered, "Erase the rabbits and see what happens."

"Then the fox goes hungry," Aubrey whispered back, "and the clover takes over the whole yard."

The fox's amber eyes turned toward the steps.

Ms. Rivera's science cabinet was notorious for eating equipment, so Lauren had to negotiate with Marcus for the last working lamp while he was still untangling its cord. "You can have it Tuesday," Marcus said. "I need it now," Lauren said, holding up a Styrofoam ball. "I'm proving my cousin wrong before he texts me again."

Last night her cousins had argued over video call until Grandma told them to hush. "The Moon's getting bigger this week," Dante had insisted. "It's shrinking," Priya had shot back. "It looked fatter yesterday." Lauren had said "I don't know" at the time, and it had bugged her ever since, like a pebble in her shoe.

She set the lamp in the middle of the darkened science room and stuck the ball onto a ruler, a quick adaptation of a proper orbit model, since the stand for it had gone missing sometime around the Ice Age. Priya's friend Zoe held the lamp steady while Lauren walked the ball in a slow circle. From where they stood, only half the ball ever caught the light, but the lit slice they could see changed as it went around.

"There," Zoe said, when the ball neared the far side of its circle. "From here it looks like a little fingernail."

Lauren walked the ball onward and the bright part grew, night by night, position by position, until it was nearly full. "Waxing," she said out loud. "That's the word for when the lit part grows. So Dante was right, this week the Moon is waxing." Then she kept walking the circle, and the lit part began to shrink, sliver by sliver. "And waning is the opposite. Priya will be right in two weeks. They're both right, just at different times."

She grabbed her phone and typed fast: come over Saturday, bring Dante, I have a lamp and a ball and you're both going to lose the argument.

Penelope stood on her toes at the Mandarin booth at the cultural festival, breathing in the smell of fried dumplings and jasmine tea. Her grandmother had promised her a red paper lantern if she could introduce the whole family in Mandarin, and Penelope wanted that lantern more than she wanted the dumplings, which was saying a lot. She had practiced all week. "Wǒ yǒu māma, bàba, mèimei," she said to the smiling volunteer, feeling proud. Then she pointed at the photo on her phone. "Wǒ yǒu yī māo."

A woman beside the volunteer laughed, but not in a mean way. It was her grandmother's friend from the tai chi group, and she held up one finger. "Not yī māo," she said. "Yì zhī māo. Mandarin needs a little word between the number and the noun. For animals, that word is zhī."

Penelope stared at her phone, where her cat Mango was yawning in the picture. A little word? It was like discovering a hidden step in a dance everyone else already knew. She tried it out. "Yì zhī māo." The word zhī sat there between the number and the cat, and suddenly she heard it everywhere, in her memory of her grandmother counting dumplings, in the vendor calling out three skewers, a little word hopping along in every single sentence. She grabbed her notebook and transformed her messy practice page into a chart: numbers on one side, nouns on the other, zhī marching between them for every animal she could think of.

Then came the twist. Her grandmother arrived, hugged her, and asked her to prove it. Penelope took a deep breath and pointed at Mango's photo. "Wǒ yǒu yì zhī māo. Tā hěn pàng." Everyone laughed, including her grandmother, because Mango really was fat. Her grandmother handed her the red lantern, and its paper crinkled warm and smooth against Penelope's fingers.

"Wǒ yǒu yì zhī māo," Penelope repeated to the cat photo, "and wǒ yǒu yí ge hěn hǎo de wài pó." Her grandmother tapped the lantern. "Good try," she said. "That one's a different little word."

Evelyn pressed her badge against the glass case marked Fungus Lights, where ghostly mushrooms glowed faint green, and wished her circuit at the workbench glowed at all. She had a battery, a switch, a bulb and three wires, plus a worksheet with one question: Why does the bulb light? Her partner Marisol had wandered off to the prism wall, where the afternoon sun refracted through the triangles and threw rainbow stripes across the floor, so Evelyn was alone with the parts that refused to work.

She clipped the wires, snapped the switch closed, and got nothing. She flipped the switch open, then closed again, slower this time, watching the little metal arm touch its contact. Nothing. The problem had to be somewhere she couldn't see, inside the flow itself, and that was the maddening part. She checked the battery, positive to positive. She tightened every clip until her thumbs ached. Then she held the last wire against the bulb's side with her finger instead of the clip, and the bulb blazed on so suddenly she gasped.

The clip was bad. The connection, not the battery, had been the hidden trouble all along. When Marisol came back trailing rainbow light on her sleeves, Evelyn was already drawing on the worksheet. "Look, we need two bulbs for the next part," Marisol said. "If one breaks, everything goes dark, right? Like last time at school." Evelyn hesitated, then remembered the case at the entrance, the two glowing mushroom patches that stayed bright even though the sign said one patch had gone out. She sketched fast, splitting the wires so each bulb had its own path back to the battery instead of sharing one.

"A parallel circuit," Marisol read off the sign above the next bench, grinning.

They unscrewed one bulb to test it. The other bulb kept burning, steady and bright.

"Told you," Evelyn said, and switched them both off and on again, just to watch.

The marble hallway of the courthouse smelled like floor polish, and Joshua's note cards were sweating in his hand. His class was holding a mock committee hearing in a real courtroom, and each student had to explain how a bill becomes a law. Joshua's problem was smaller and stranger: the handout from their teacher kept calling the school-safety proposal "the School Safety Bill" in one paragraph and "the School Safety Act" in another. Same proposal, two different names, and nobody seemed to think that was weird.

"Maybe it's a typo," whispered Priya as they waited outside the courtroom doors.

Joshua didn't think so. The pattern was too tidy. Every time the handout mentioned the proposal being introduced, debated, or voted on, it said bill. Every time it mentioned the thing after the final vote, it said Act. He tested the idea in the margin, writing a small B next to the early mentions and a small A next to the later ones. The letters split perfectly at the moment of passage. The name changed when the proposal crossed the finish line.

When his turn came, Judge Marquez, an influential volunteer who ran these hearings every spring, asked him to walk the class through the stages. Joshua decomposed the process on the whiteboard, step by step: introduction, committee, debate, votes in both chambers. Then he stopped at the last box he had drawn.

"This is where it confused me," he said, tapping the marker against the board. "It's called a bill until it passes all its stages. Once it passes, it's not a bill anymore. It's an Act."

"So it's like a caterpillar and a butterfly," Priya called out. "Same creature, different name depending on the stage."

Judge Marquez smiled and turned to the class. "Mr. Speaker, I move we vote on the amendment." Every hand went up, and the gavel came down with a crack that made even the bailiff jump.

John pressed his back against the cool plaster wall of Ms. Prieto's studio and sang his part of the round for the ninth time. The song was "The Emperor's New Melody," a silly tune Ms. Prieto had written herself, and the whole choir would perform it in two-part harmony at the spring concert. That was the problem. Every time Marisol started the high part, John's low part slid right up after it like a lost dog following the wrong owner.

"You did it again," Marisol said, lowering her sheet music. "You're singing my note."

"I am not." John scrutinized the page as if the answer might be hiding between the staff lines. "I'm singing a G. It says G."

They tried it again, and again John's voice climbed, and Marisol laughed so hard she snorted, which made him laugh too, and Ms. Prieto tapped her tuning fork on the edge of the piano.

"Lessons are over in ten minutes," she said, "and this harmony is becoming controversial. Half the parents will text me if it sounds like a car alarm." She settled onto the piano bench with her coffee. "Figure it out, you two."

John hummed his G. Then, out of pure stubbornness, he hummed Marisol's note, the one that kept stealing his voice. He hummed them one after the other, back and forth, and squinted at the piano keys like they owed him money. Something itched at him. The two notes didn't clash at all. They sounded like the same note, just one tall and one short, like the same kid standing on a chair.

"Play a G," he told Ms. Prieto, "and then the next G up." She did, and John grinned. "Marisol. We're both singing G. Yours is just higher. Same note, different heights." She tested it against the piano, and her eyebrows went up.

"So when I follow you," John said, talking it through with his hands, "I'm not really leaving my part. I'm climbing up to your height, because my ear thinks the same note should sound the same. But it doesn't have to." He remembered a diagram from a book in the library, wavy lines rising and doubling. "That high one vibrates twice as fast as mine. Exactly twice. That's why they match."

Ms. Prieto set her coffee down slowly. "Nobody taught you that today."

"The library did."

They sang it one more time. John kept his G low and steady, and when Marisol's high G floated in above it, his voice held firm, locked to the floor like a good anchor. The two notes stacked together, warm and shivery, and Ms. Prieto didn't say anything at all, just closed the piano lid with a soft click.

"Encore," whispered Marisol, and started them off again.

Grandpa's truck engine knocked on the drive up, a sound like a piston tapping out a complaint, and it stopped only when they reached the campsite beside Miller Lake. Lily climbed out and unfolded the old atlas he kept under the seat. Last summer she had left it out in the rain, and the corners were still rippled and soft. She was glad he had never thrown it away.

"I need to know where we are," she said. "Exactly." Her parents were hiking the ridge on the far side of the lake, and they had promised to call at noon with their position. Grandpa's phone had no bars. If the call somehow came through on the radio instead, the ranger would want coordinates, not the name of a lake that appeared on half the maps in the county.

The atlas had thin curved lines drawn across it, numbered along the edges. She found a word printed beside the horizontal ones. "They're called parallels," she said slowly, "because they never meet." Her eyes followed two of them across the whole country, side by side, and sure enough, they never crossed. The vertical lines had a name too: meridians. So a place had two numbers, one from each kind of line. She put her finger on the campsite, read sideways to the edge, then up. "Forty-four degrees north, seventy-one west." It felt like holding something solid.

She remembered the rainy afternoon when she'd ruined the atlas, and how she had hidden it under the seat instead of telling him. She could apologize now, or she could keep turning pages and hope he never noticed the water stains. She kept turning pages.

At noon the radio crackled, and her father's voice came through, giving numbers. Lily checked them against the ridge on her map and traced the meridian up from the bottom edge with one finger until it crossed the right parallel. "They're three miles northeast," she told Grandpa, and marked the spot with a pencil stub, pressing hard enough to imply that this crossing, at least, was permanent.

The score was stuck at one. Oliver leaned closer to Maya's basement computer, where a little conductor sprite in a blue hat was supposed to award a point every time the player's train caught a falling coin, and the score had gone up exactly once, on the very first coin, and never again.

"You need a loop," Maya said, spinning her desk chair around. "Right now your script runs one time and quits, like it's clocking out." She popped the cap off a marker and drew a circle on the whiteboard her dad kept down there. "Everything inside this circle happens over and over until you say stop."

Oliver dragged a "repeat until" block out of the purple Control drawer and snapped it around his coin script. He tested it, and the coin fell, and fell, and kept falling straight off the bottom of the screen forever. "Okay, that's a problem," he admitted, laughing. The loop worked, but nothing told the coin to go back to the top and try again. He added an "if then" block: if the coin touched the conductor's net, add one to score, then move the coin back up. If it missed and hit the floor, back up anyway, no point. He clicked the green flag and held his breath.

One. Two. Three. The score climbed every single catch. Oliver pumped both fists and nearly knocked over Maya's stack of library books. "Four! Maya, it's working, it's actually keeping score!" He wanted to integrate a timer next, and maybe a level where the coins fell faster, and he started stacking blocks so fast the program looked like a rainbow had exploded.

Footsteps came down the basement stairs. It was Maya's grandpa, carrying a plate of crackers. He set it down and peered at the screen over their shoulders, his eyebrows climbing. "You two are writing a computer program? Where's all the code? The walls of numbers and letters, like in the movies?"

"There aren't any," Oliver said. "You just snap blocks together, like LEGO." He dragged a block out, snapped it back in, and the whole script glowed blue for a second.

Grandpa shook his head slowly, delighted and confused at the same time. "Who thought of that?"

"It's called Scratch," Maya said. "It came out of the MIT Media Lab, back in 2007."

"Blocks that code," Grandpa said, mostly to himself. "My whole career in the signal corps, and now an eleven-year-old builds a game by clicking pieces together." He tapped the edge of the monitor. "Is that laptop of yours durable? Because you're going to be at this for a while."

"He's not getting it back until I beat his high score," Maya said.

Oliver cracked his knuckles, moved the "when green flag clicked" hat block to the top, and grinned at the screen. "Ready, conductor?"

Grandpa's computer room smelled like dust and old records. Simon sat at the desk with his game open in Scratch, frowning at the cat sprite. The problem was the score. Every time the cat touched a flying beetle, the score went up by one, but sometimes it jumped by three or four in a single second. He wanted it to count fairly.

Grandpa came in carrying a cardboard box and set it on the floor. On the screen, the score climbed from 5 to 9 in one blink.

"That's fast," Grandpa said.

"I think it's counting the beetle twice, maybe three times," Simon said. He could not see it happen, because it happened in a fraction of a second, so he had to guess at the cause. "The cat and the beetle are still touching when the loop runs again."

He tested a simple idea. He dragged the beetle away the instant the score changed, using a block that moved the beetle to a random spot the moment the cat touched it. He pressed the green flag and played. This time the score climbed one number at a time. The if-then block was doing its job, and the loop only counted once per catch.

Grandpa lifted a black disc out of the box and held it up. "You know why they call that program Scratch? DJ scratching. A DJ moves a record back and forth on a turntable to remix sounds."

Simon looked at the record, then at the sound blocks in his game. He added a pop sound to the beetle, then a chirp to the cat, and made the score change remix them so every tenth point played both together, like a little song cutting in and out.

"It's like being the emperor of my own arcade," Simon said, "except the beetles keep escaping."

"They sound predatory, those beetles," Grandpa said, and slid the record back into its sleeve.

Simon changed the beetles to look like hunting wasps, wrapped the record sleeve in a towel to insulate it from the dusty shelf, and pressed the green flag again. The score ticked up, the chirp cut in, and Grandpa leaned closer to the screen.

Florence stood at the festival's German booth with a tablet in her hands and a poster behind her that said "Beschreibe deine Familie," describe your family. Her task was to write five sentences about her family and pets in German, then read them aloud at the microphone in an hour. She typed her first sentence carefully: "Ich habe einen hund und eine katze." The tablet's spell-checker immediately underlined two words in red, "hund" and "katze," even though she had checked them in the dictionary twice. Why would it flag words she knew were right?

She despised being wrong in public, so she looked for a pattern. She scrolled through the German phrases on the booth's display: "Meine Familie ist groß. Mein Vater hat ein Auto. Wir wohnen in einem Haus." Hund, Katze, Auto, Haus, Vater, Familie. Every single one of those words started with a capital letter, even when it sat in the middle of a sentence. English only did that for names and sentence starters. Was there something about German where every noun began with a capital letter, no matter where it appeared? If that were true, the spell-checker wasn't saying her words were misspelled. It was saying they were lowercased.

Florence decided to test it. She typed "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze," capitalizing both animals, and the red underlines vanished. She tried it again with "Meine Mutter hat zwei Katzen," and nothing was flagged. The pattern held. She laughed at the irony of it: the checker had looked like her enemy when it had actually been teaching her something.

She wrote out all five sentences, watching the screen like it was a transparent window into the language's rules, and every noun got its capital. At the microphone, she read, "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze. Meine Schwester hat zwei Kaninchen." The volunteer grinned and said, "Perfekt!"

Noah had spent forty minutes looking for the Moon the night before, and he hadn't found it anywhere. "Maybe it vanished," his little sister had said, and even though he knew that was silly, he couldn't say why. So when Ms. Ruiz set a lamp in the middle of the science room and announced that today they would illustrate the Moon's phases, Noah sat up fast.

She darkened the windows, switched on the lamp, and told them the lamp was the Sun. Each pair got a styrofoam ball on a stick. "Earth is your head," she said. "Walk your Moon around it and watch what happens." Noah partnered with Priya, who held her ball up like a lollipop and spun in a circle just to make people laugh.

Noah kept his ball slow and steady. Halfway around, he stopped. From where he stood, the ball was between his head and the lamp, and the lit side of the ball faced completely away from him. His side looked dark, like nothing at all. He turned his head carefully. If he was Earth, he realized, he would be staring at the unlit half of the Moon straight on. "Priya," he whispered, "come look from my spot."

Priya squinted into the dark half of the ball. "It's invisible," she said. "Like it vanished."

"That's what happened last night," Noah said. His mind was racing through it. At new moon, the Moon lies roughly between Earth and the Sun, so its lit side faces away from us, and it looks dark. He hadn't lost the Moon. It had been out there, dark, hidden in the Sun's general direction, which was also why he couldn't see it well after sunset. "I thought something was wrong with the sky. It wasn't an anomaly. It was supposed to happen."

"You mean new moon?" Priya asked.

"That's the one." Noah walked his ball a quarter turn farther, and a thin bright crescent curled into view along its edge. Then a half. He kept circling, and the lit part kept growing, until the whole face near the lamp side glowed round and white. Priya copied him, calling out each shape: crescent, half, full. When Noah reached the dark spot between Earth and Sun again, he made his ball pause there on purpose, the way you'd check a math answer by redoing it.

Ms. Ruiz walked past their table and watched the dark ball pass through the space between Noah's head and the lamp. "Nice pacing," she said, and moved on.

At lunch, Priya leaned across the table. "So last night it was somewhere near new moon?"

"Roughly between us and the Sun, dark side toward us," Noah said, tearing his bread in half to demonstrate, one piece bright under the window, one shadowed in his palm. "Tonight I'm going to find it anyway. There's a thin one coming in a couple of days, low in the west after sunset."

Priya pointed at the shadowed piece of bread in his hand. "Show me that crescent part one more time."

Alexandra spread her fraction cards across the table in the math club room and frowned at them. Her problem was simple and urgent: the club's bake sale was Saturday, and she had promised to bring exactly one cup of granola, but her grandmother's recipe called for a half cup of oats and a third cup of seeds, and she could not figure out whether that made a whole cup or not. Half plus third. She wrote "1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5" on her paper, because two and five were the numbers she had.

Across the table, Marcus was stacking his cards into a tower, which was what he did when he wanted to look busy without actually solving anything. He had a reputation for finishing worksheets first, but today he kept glancing at Alexandra's paper. "That's wrong," he said finally. "It has to be more than a half, and two fifths is less than a half."

Alexandra looked at her answer. He was right, and she had not even noticed. She flipped her cards over so the shaded pie drawings faced up: a circle cut in two, a circle cut in three. "You can't count these together," she said slowly. "The pieces aren't the same size." Last summer at her grandmother's house she had learned the same thing with real measuring cups, pouring a half cup of flour and then a third cup and watching the bowl, because her grandmother's old cups had no markings and she had to guess whether she'd reached one cup. She had guessed wrong that day, and the cookies had spread flat as pancakes.

She pulled out a fresh card and drew a rectangle, then divided it into six thin columns, darkening three of them, then two more. Sixths. Both the half and the third could live on the same rectangle. Three sixths plus two sixths made five sixths. "The denominator names the size of the pieces," she said, mostly to herself, and Marcus leaned over so far his card tower toppled.

"Wait, do it again with fourths and eighths," he said, grabbing a pencil, because if she had found a trick that worked, he wanted to be the one who used it fastest. Alexandra drew another rectangle and slid the pencil across the table to him.

Sara's grandmother had a habit that made no sense to her: twice a month, she refused rice. Not once, not on random Tuesdays, but twice, and never when Sara expected it. One night Grandma would pass the rice pot to Sara's dad and eat only fruit and milk, laughing while everyone else had seconds. "Are you on some secret diet?" Sara asked once. Grandma only smiled and said her stomach was resting, like a student on a school holiday.

So Sara turned detective. She dismantled the kitchen calendar from its hook and carried it to her room, where she circled every day Grandma had skipped rice, according to her mom's memory and her own notes from the last two months. The circles didn't land on weekdays, which would have been too easy. They didn't land on the same dates either. Six circles sat there like footprints with no trail, and Sara glared at them while chewing her pencil.

Then Mom mentioned, almost by accident, that the family followed the moon's calendar for festivals, not the square one on the wall. Sara looked up the lunar month and found it split in two halves. She counted forward from the new moon and the full moon, and both times her pencil landed on the same number. Eleven. Every single circle. She counted twice more, because she didn't trust herself, and then she ran downstairs yelling, "It's the eleventh day! Both halves! Mom, it's the eleventh day every time!"

Mom laughed so hard she had to sit down. "That day is called Ekadashi," she said. "Your grandmother keeps it for Vishnu. No grains, no beans."

"Grains and beans," Sara repeated, writing it on her hand so she wouldn't forget. Then she made a decision, quickly, because Grandma was coming to visit tomorrow and Sara wanted to surprise her. She would keep the day too, at least until dinner.

The next morning Sara hid the toaster from herself, which mostly meant putting a chair in front of it. By lunch she was hungry enough to consider eating the chair. Her little brother, home with a cold and a spoonful of antibiotic, offered her his crackers out of pure mischief. "Those are grains," she said grandly, and pushed them back.

When Grandma arrived, Sara set the table with fruit and milk at her own place and waited. Grandma looked at the plate, then at Sara, and raised one eyebrow. "Eleventh day," Sara said. "Ekadashi. Grains and beans, gone."

Grandma sat down slowly and pressed her hand over her heart. "You counted?"

"I counted."

Then Grandma picked up a banana, sliced it in half, and set the bigger piece on Sara's plate.

The third dryer rumbled to life just as Mya's mother handed her a ten dollar bill and a short list written on the back of a dryer sheet. "Milk, and nothing from the candy rack," her mother said, already turning back to the laundry baskets. "You know the way. Corner store, two blocks, left on Pine." Mya stood there for a second, holding the bill like it might chirp. Last summer she had been allowed only as far as the mailbox. Now she was being sent out into the world with money and a mission.

Walking the two blocks took less stamina than she'd expected, though her legs felt hesitant at the corner of Pine, where she had to wait for a car that turned out to be going much slower than it looked. She remembered the time she'd begged to go to the store with her older cousin and been told no, and how she'd cried about it for an hour. She winced a little at the memory. Maybe being kept home hadn't been an insult. Maybe it had just been a door that opened late.

The store smelled like cardboard and oranges. In the dairy cooler she found the milk and then stopped, because there were choices. One two-litre carton for $3.49, or one-litre cartons for $1.89 each. Her list said "2 litres," so two small ones would do it. She reached for the small cartons, then paused. Beneath the big price stickers, in smaller print, there were more numbers: $1.74 per litre on the big carton, $1.89 per litre on the small. She leaned closer, checking that she was reading it right.

"Unit price," said the man behind the counter, without looking up from his crossword. "It's printed right there." Mya nodded slowly. So the big carton was cheaper per litre, which meant she'd save fifteen cents a litre if she bought it. She did the math on her fingers: $3.49 versus $3.78. Twenty-nine cents. Twenty-nine cents was a piece of gum, roughly.

But then she checked the shelf one row down, where the chocolate milk sat, and noticed something that made her frown. The big carton of chocolate milk said $2.15 per litre, and the small one said $2.10 per litre. The bigger carton was more per litre, not less. So bigger wasn't always cheaper. The rule she'd just discovered had a hole in it, and somehow that made the whole thing more interesting, not less. She had to look at the numbers every single time.

She carried the big white carton to the counter. The total came to $3.71 with tax, and the man counted her change into her palm: six dollars and twenty-nine cents. She counted it again on the walk back, one coin at a time, and it matched. At the laundromat door she held up the carton like a trophy.

"I got the big one," she said. "It was cheaper per litre." Her mother raised an eyebrow at the change, counted it, and smiled. "Next time," she said, "check whether the orange juice follows the same rule."

The zucchini on the table gleamed like little green submarines, and Alexis intended to turn three of them into muffins before lunch. Her grandmother had emailed the recipe from Arizona, and the first line said: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees. Alexis's family's oven, however, had been bought in Lisbon, and its dial only went by Celsius, which was like being handed directions in a language she'd studied for exactly one week.

"What does 350 even mean?" her little brother Theo asked, peering over her shoulder at the phone. "Three hundred fifty what? Dragons?"

"Degrees, obviously." But obvious it was not. The dial climbed from 100 to 250, and nowhere did it say 350, so somewhere between the recipe and the oven, the numbers had to be hiding a rule. Last summer, Alexis remembered, she had tried to bake cookies at the highest number on the dial because it seemed logical that hotter meant faster. The cookies had come out like charcoal coasters, and her grandmother had laughed so hard she'd had to sit down. Alexis did not want a repeat of the Great Charcoal Incident.

She set the zucchini on the cutting board and tried to classify the problem in her head. Same recipe, different numbers, so the two systems had to be measuring the same heat with different names, like a cat named Gato. The question was the ratio, and ratios could be hunted. "We're going to the farmers' market," she announced. "The bread stall. Bakers know ovens."

At the market, Mrs. Almeida was arranging loaves in diagonal rows across her table, tilting each one so the slashes in the crust caught the morning light. Alexis explained her dilemma, holding up the phone like evidence in a trial.

"Ah, the American recipes," Mrs. Almeida said, wiping flour off her hands. "Three hundred fifty degrees Fahrenheit is about one hundred seventy-five to one hundred eighty Celsius. My daughter-in-law bakes from those websites all the time."

Alexis did the arithmetic twice, because a wrong oven setting was how monarchies fell, and she was not going to lose her muffin empire the same way. She dialled to 175 and waited while the oven ticked and hummed its way up to temperature. She grated the zucchini, cracked the eggs, and folded the batter with the patience of someone who had once produced charcoal and learned from it.

The muffins rose into golden domes, and Theo grabbed one before it had even left the pan. "Ow. Ow. Worth it," he said around a mouthful, and Alexis slid the rest onto a cooling rack, diagonal like Mrs. Almeida's loaves, because presentation mattered.

"Two minutes?" Harrison said, bouncing a tennis ball off the garage wall. "You can't say anything important in two minutes."

His sister Maya looked up from her phone. "Mr. Reyes assigned you a two-minute speech. That's the assignment. Opening hook, three points, closing."

"Two minutes is nothing. That's like the time it takes to microwave a burrito."

Maya grinned, which meant she knew something he didn't. "The Gettysburg Address. Abraham Lincoln, November 19, 1863. It was about 272 words long, and it took roughly two minutes to deliver. That speech is famous, and it was shorter than your book report."

Harrison caught the ball and stared at her. Two minutes. Two hundred seventy-two words. That meant the rule wasn't "say less," it was "say only what counts." Every extra word would exclude a better one, the way his mom removed junk from the garage to make room for the ping-pong table. If Lincoln could do it, so could he.

He grabbed his notebook and wrote fast. Hook: a question about why nobody remembers the two-hour speech that came before Lincoln's. Three points, each one sentence. Closing: the burrito line, because if his classmates were going to remember anything, it would be that.

"You're actually excited," Maya said. "Weird."

"It's like a puzzle. I get exactly 272 words and I have to make every single one matter."

He rehearsed in the kitchen while she timed him. First run: two minutes forty. He cut words until his throat hurt. Second run: one minute fifty-five. Close enough. He added back "roughly," just to be exact.

The morning of the speech, Harrison stood in front of the class with his palms sweating and his heart hammering, and watched heads actually lift when he opened with the question about the forgotten two-hour speaker.

After class, Mr. Reyes stopped him at the door. "Where did you learn that about Lincoln?"

"My sister. She's kind of infectious that way." Harrison grinned. "Ask her about the income tax speech she has to give next week. It's three minutes, and she's furious about the extra one."

Parker stood in the Build-an-Atom room of the science museum, holding a tray of marbles, pompoms, and Styrofoam balls, and glaring at the instruction card like it had insulted his sneakers. The card said: construct a model of an atom with protons, neutrons, and electrons in the right places. Right places? Nobody had ever shown him an atom. They were sneaky like that.

He started cramming. Red marbles for protons, gray marbles for neutrons, all smooshed into a fat Styrofoam ball, with blue pompoms stuck on the outside like sprinkles. It looked like a donut that had given up on life. Beside him, a girl named Ruby was doing the exact same thing, packing her foam ball solid with beads and humming, completely confident.

"You're making yours solid too?" Parker asked.

"Obviously," Ruby said. "Stuff is stuff. Solid stuff is solid."

Something itched in Parker's brain. He flashed back to last summer, when his grandfather had taken him to this same museum and they'd stood in front of a big display with a glowing gold sheet in the middle. His grandfather had read the plaque out loud, slowly, the way he read everything. The gold foil experiment, run by Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden under Ernest Rutherford. They fired alpha particles at gold foil, and most of the alpha particles passed straight through. The plaque's last line had said it plainly: an atom is mostly empty space.

Mostly empty. Parker looked at his jam-packed foam ball and felt his ears go warm. If atoms were mostly empty space, then his model was like drawing a crowded swimming pool to represent a desert.

"Wait," he said. "We're doing it wrong. Rutherford proved atoms are mostly empty space. Geiger and Marsden shot alpha particles at gold foil, and most of them passed straight through."

Ruby squinted at him, clearly deciding whether he was biased in favor of his own cleverness. "Passed through gold? Gold is metal. Metal stops my teeth."

"The experiment says it, not me," Parker said. He pulled the marbles back out of his ball, which made a sad, squeaky sound, and clumped the protons and neutrons into one tight knot in the center. Then he hung electrons far out on wire loops, alone in all that nothing. The model suddenly looked like a tiny solar system floating in a lot of lonely dark.

Ruby poked a finger through the empty space around her own bead ball. "Huh," she said. "My hand is basically not touching anything. Somewhere in there. Sort of."

A museum volunteer strolled by, announced that the model jury would vote on favorite atoms at three o'clock, and warned that she would strictly enforce the no-gluing-your-fingers rule, since last week had been a disaster. Parker and Ruby looked at each other.

"Want to fuse our leftover beads into a giant electron?" Parker asked, holding up the shiniest one.

Ruby grabbed the wire. "Only if I get to make it wobble."

Elena spread her poster board on the picnic table and weighed the corners with four smooth stones from the garden path. Her assignment was due Monday: draw a food chain, starting with the sun, ending with a top predator, and explain what would happen if one link disappeared. She had chosen the pond in her own backyard because she could watch it instead of guessing.

She began with what she could see. Sunlight fed the algae and the pondweed, so she drew the sun with long yellow rays touching a green smear of plants. Then came the snails, rasping quietly on the stones at the edge. Then the mallard duck that paddled across the water every afternoon, and at the top, the fox she had spotted once at dusk, slipping along the fence line. Sun, plants, snails, duck, fox. She wrote the arrows carefully and sat back, pleased with how neat it looked.

Her little brother Theo came out with a cup of crackers and leaned over her shoulder. "Why's the duck eating snails?" he asked. "I saw him munching the weeds this morning. Right over there." Elena started to say he was wrong, then stopped. She had seen that too, hadn't she? The duck tipping forward, tail in the air, tearing at the pondweed. She got her binoculars from the porch and settled onto the grass to watch. For twenty minutes she kept her eyes on the water. The duck ate pondweed. Then it gulped something small from a rock, and when Elena checked the spot, the rock was empty of the snail that had been there before.

"So he eats both," she said slowly. Her beautiful chain had a duck with two arrows coming in, from plants and from snails. And the snails, she realized, ate the algae, which was different from the pondweed. That meant there wasn't just one chain. There were chains that crossed. She grabbed a fresh board and started again, letting arrows branch and tangle until the whole page looked like a net. "It's a food web," she told Theo, holding it up. "Most animals eat more than one kind of food, so the chains get linked together." Theo nodded, mouth full, and pointed at the fox. "What about him?"

Elena thought about her teacher's question, the one about losing a link. She covered the snail with her thumb. The duck still had the plants, so the duck would be fine, and so would the fox. But cover the plants instead and the snails would go hungry too, because they needed the algae, and then the duck would lose both meals at once. One missing thing could shake several chains. She drew a big red X experimentally across the plants, then wiped it away.

"Why do you keep erasing and drawing it again?" Theo asked, shivering a little in the shade. Elena draped the old blanket from the porch swing around his shoulders and handed him the last of her crackers, since he'd finished his. "Because my motivation was to make it neat," she said, "but the pond isn't neat. The pond is messy and connected, and I kind of cherish that now." Theo chewed, watching the duck glide past the reeds, and Elena bent back over her tangled, crossing, truthful arrows.

The wall map in Delgado Travel was bigger than the one at school, and Oliver stood in front of it with his notebook open and his pencil going nowhere. His teacher had asked for the exact location of one city, given in latitude and longitude, and Oliver had picked London mostly because it sounded easy. Now he was staring at the thin curved lines covering the ocean like a net, and he could not figure out where zero was supposed to start.

"Looking for something specific, or just hiding from your mom?" asked Mrs. Delgado, coming out from behind her desk with a stack of brochures. She was small and quick, and today she kept glancing at a poster of the Thames that had been hanging crooked for a month. Her boss had promised that whoever sold the most London packages this spring would get the window display, and Mrs. Delgado wanted that window badly.

"I need London's coordinates," Oliver said. "But I don't get longitude. Latitude goes up and down from the equator, that part's fine. Longitude goes sideways, but sideways from where?" He tapped the map. "There's no middle ocean line to count from. It's like the equator just vanished."

Mrs. Delgado set down her brochures. "Tell you what. Help me fix this poster and straighten the globe stand, and you can use the big magnifier from the desk drawer. Half my customers my age complain the numbers are too small." The globe was old and a little frail, its stand cracked, and when Oliver steadied it with one hand while she tightened a screw, he noticed the zero line of longitude ran right through a notch in England, just past a city called Greenwich. He had assumed the zero line would pass through Washington, D.C., because that was where the big international conference of 1884 had met to settle it. He had read that on a homework sheet and built his whole notebook page around counting east and west from Washington. Clearly that idea was wrong, and he had just tested it against the actual globe.

"So the conference was in Washington," he said slowly, following the line with his finger, "but the zero isn't. It's here, at Greenwich." He leaned closer to the map and found the Royal Observatory marked with a tiny dot right on the line. "The prime meridian," he read off the legend, and wrote the words down. London, then, was close to zero degrees longitude, and about fifty-one degrees north of the equator. He checked it twice, counting on his fingers along the printed lines.

"You know, my husband stood on that line at Greenwich," Mrs. Delgado said, smoothing the Thames poster until it hung straight. "Feet in two halves of the world at once. He said it felt like nothing, which somehow made it better." She held out a London brochure. "For your project. And tell your teacher we said come see us when your class picks a destination."

Oliver folded the brochure into his notebook, next to the numbers. Fifty-one degrees north, zero degrees longitude, a dot on a line drawn through a observatory by a conference an ocean away from it. He looked up at the crooked spot where the poster had been and saw it hanging level now, the river running bright across it.

"One foot on each side," he said. "Next time I'm in London, I'm doing that."

Mrs. Delgado laughed and pinned the brochure up in the window.

Zoe had agreed to keep Shabbat with her grandmother from Friday sundown until Saturday night, which meant no phone, no screens, no writing, for a whole day and part of another. She figured she could integrate one quiet afternoon into her life without much trouble, but by Saturday at four she was pacing the kitchen while her grandmother sliced apples for a cake nobody needed.

"Sit," her grandmother said. "The day ends when the sky says so, not when you do."

"How does the sky say so?" Zoe asked.

"Three stars. When you can see three stars, we say Havdalah. Havdalah means separation. It separates Shabbat from the rest of the week." Her grandmother slid the knife into the drawer. "Your mother and her brothers used to race to the window, all three of them, fighting over who counted first."

Zoe went to the front window anyway, mostly because the kitchen smelled like cinnamon and she had nothing else to do. Her cousin Theo, who was seven and lived next door, was already pressed against the glass. "I see one," he announced. "It's a star."

"It's a plane," Zoe said. "It's moving." She watched it slide sideways and blink out of sight, and she thought about that. If she counted moving lights, she'd end the day too early, and it wouldn't count. The rule, whatever principle was behind it, needed actual stars, and stars held still. So she made a plan: she would watch until each light had stayed put for a whole slow count of ten before she called it a star.

While they waited, Theo dug a folded paper out of the drawer under the phone, an old wooden thing Zoe had never seen anyone use. "Grandma said don't open it till after," he said, "but I can look at the outside." The paper was translucent where it had worn thin, and through it Zoe could make out the shape of handwriting on the other side. Her grandmother's, but older, with the letters pushed hard into the page. It was addressed to her mother, dated the summer her mother turned twelve. Zoe put it back in the drawer, unopened, because a promise was a promise even when nobody watched.

The sky went from gray to deep blue, and Theo bounced on the windowsill. Zoe counted her slow tens at each point of light. One star. Ten. Two stars. Ten. Then a third, small and steady above the neighbor's chimney. "Three," she said, and Theo yelled it toward the kitchen, and her grandmother came in with a braided candle, a small dish of spices, and a cup of wine.

But as her grandmother lit the candle, Zoe leaned close to the glass and checked her third star one more time. It had drifted. An airplane after all, creeping east. "Wait," she said. "That one's moving. I only have two."

Her grandmother cupped her hand around the flame. "So we wait," she said, and stood there in the doorway, patient as furniture. Zoe realized she had been hoping to catch her grandmother out, to prove the whole day was just rules somebody made up, and instead she had just caught a plane. A few minutes later a true star appeared beside the other two, holding its place through her count of ten, and this time she was sure.

They said Havdalah over the flame, and Theo tipped the cup so the wine ran out onto the dish, and Zoe smelled the spices and watched her grandmother's face flicker in the candlelight. Afterward she opened the drawer. The letter, it turned out, was one her mother had written to her grandmother that long-ago summer, saved and returned to the house by mail years later, asking to come home from camp because she missed Shabbat. Zoe read it twice, then texted her mother a photo of the window and the three dark patches of sky where the stars had been.

The rain drove everyone into the craft cabin, and Payton's cabin had claimed the only table with the Monopoly box before Cabin 4 even finished tramping inside. Marcus from Cabin 4 wanted to play too, and after some arguing they agreed he could join, but only if he was the top hat, because nobody else wanted the top hat.

By the third lap around the board, trouble started. Marcus landed on Marvin Gardens and shook his head. "Too expensive. I'm saving for the railroads." He slid his token forward, but Payton put her hand flat on the board. "Wait. Nobody owns it. What happens now?" Devon shrugged. "Nothing happens. He skipped it." Payton frowned. She had a feeling, the same feeling she got in math class when an answer was too easy, that something hidden was going on, a rule nobody had ever read. She dug into the box and pulled out the folded rule sheet.

"There," she said, running her finger down the tiny print. "The official Monopoly rules say that if a player lands on an unowned property and chooses not to buy it, the bank auctions it to the players." Marcus groaned. "So I don't get to just pass it by?" "Nobody gets to just pass it by," Payton said, already sliding her chair forward. "Let's simulate it. Devon, you're the bank. Auction it off." Devon cleared his throat like a fancy auctioneer, which was so terrible it made everybody laugh, and Marvin Gardens went to Payton for a hundred and ten dollars because she was the only one who had read the whole rule.

Marcus bounced back fast, though. "Fine, but you're all being warned. I'm going to be the most versatile player this camp has ever seen. Railroads, utilities, whatever it takes." Nia pointed at his neat row of nothing. "Right now you're more like an herbivore. You only nibble the safe stuff." Marcus threw a plastic hotel at her, missed, and hit the top hat off the board. "Auction that," he said.

Violet sat at her mother's desk on a Saturday, using the office computer because their laptop at home had died. She needed to find out why her science teacher had made the class debate one question all period: if a company pays to look like a normal search result, is that fair? On Monday each student had to bring one piece of evidence. Violet typed in "are ads fair" and got a page full of links about sneakers.
