She tried again. "search results ads." Still mostly shopping pages. Her friend Dee had once told her that searching was like aiming a slingshot; sloppy words, sloppy hit. So Violet narrowed it. "search engine paid results rules." That worked. One link went to a government page, and she clicked it.

The page talked about the Federal Trade Commission. In 2013, the FTC had told search engines that paid results must be clearly distinguishable from natural results, or they risk deceiving users. Violet read the sentence twice. Natural results, she realized, meant the ones the computer found on its own, and paid ones sat in the same list looking identical unless you caught the little label. She remembered a moment from Tuesday, a quick flashback that arrived whole: she had searched "best free math help," clicked the first blue link, and landed on a site that wanted her credit card for a "free trial." She had shut the page and blamed herself for not reading carefully. Maybe she hadn't been careless. Maybe the link had been dressed up to fool her.

Now she had a test. She opened a search page and typed "cheap headphones." The top three entries looked like ordinary results, but a small gray box in the corner of each one said "Ad." The fourth entry had no box at all. She tried "homework help," then "dog food," and counted each time. The boxes were small, but once she knew the rule, she could see the pattern everywhere, like suddenly noticing that the first three ducks in every flock wore collars.

She thought about her mother's lawyer talk, the way an amendment to a contract had to be spelled out so nobody was misled, and how a thick folder of papers could insulate a client from a bad deal only if every line was plain. Search results should work the same way, Violet decided, and the FTC seemed to agree with her mother.

Her mother came by with two granola bars and glanced at the screen. "Find your evidence?"

"Yep," Violet said. She highlighted the sentence and hit print. The printer started up with an abrupt clunk, and the page slid out warm into her hand.

Jaxon stood in front of the Japan booth at the spring cultural festival, holding a paper card with his speech written on it. In ten minutes he had to introduce his family in Japanese, on the little stage under the luminous paper lanterns, and he still could not get through one sentence without messing it up. His partner for the booth, a girl named Mei who was hanging ceramic tea cups on a rack, kept glancing over at him.

"Ready?" she asked.

"Kore wa haha desu," Jaxon began, pointing at the photo of his mother taped to his poster. "Okaasan wa sensei desu. My mom is a teacher." Then he pointed at a drawing of his dog. "Inu wa..." He flipped his card over. "Inu wa totemo oishii desu."

Mei nearly dropped a cup. "Your dog is very delicious?"

"That's not what I wrote! I meant totemo isogashii, very busy. He's a busy dog." Jaxon laughed, but then his stomach tightened, because Mei was still looking at him strangely.

"You said okaasan," she said. "For your own mom, you say haha. Okaasan is for somebody else's mother, like mine."

Jaxon stared at his card. So that was why the girl in the practice video had switched words halfway through. He had thought she just messed up. There were two sets of family words, and he had been using them backwards. He grabbed a pencil, crossed out okaasan, and wrote haha above it. Then, to test it, he pointed at Mei and tried, "Anata no okaasan?"

"Hai," Mei said, grinning. "My okaasan is right over there, selling rice balls. She refuses to retire, so she works the festival every year."

When the booth announcer called his name, Jaxon walked to the stage. The lanterns glowed above him, and near the back an old fisherman was carving a wooden vessel, turning it slowly in his hands. Jaxon took a breath. "Kore wa haha desu. Haha wa sensei desu. Watashi no inu wa totemo isogashii desu." The audience clapped, and Mei gave him two thumbs up.

"Totemo oishii!" someone shouted from the back.

"Not delicious," Jaxon said into the microphone. "Busy."

The speech was due on Friday, and by Wednesday Kaitlyn had written exactly one sentence. Ms. Reyes had drawn the shape of it on the board: a hook, three points, a closing, two minutes, no more. Kaitlyn's hook was "Has anyone here ever held a live octopus?" which was a lie, since nobody had, including her. She crumpled it up and started over.

The real problem was her hands. Every time she stood up in class, even to read a paragraph from social studies, her fingers buzzed like a phone on silent. In the bathroom before last period, she watched them shake in the mirror and made a decision: she would test whether the shaking had a pattern, like weather. If it only happened in front of the whole class, then the class itself was the cause, and something could be done about that.

She started small. At lunch she stood at the end of the table and gave her opening line to five friends. Her hands went quiet. Then Priya, who was next on the list for Friday, put down her sandwich and held out her own fingers, which were trembling over the tray. "It's called glossophobia," Priya said. "Fear of public speaking. My cousin told me it's one of the most commonly reported fears there is."

"You mean everybody's hands do this?" Kaitlyn said.

"Like a club," Priya said. "A huge, terrible club."

Kaitlyn felt the idea turn in her head, the way a rudder turns a slow boat. If half the room was secretly shaking, then shaking wasn't a personal failure; it was just the water everyone was sailing in. So on Friday she stood up, held her note card in both hands so the paper would hide the buzzing, and opened with the octopus question anyway. Nobody had held an octopus, and she said so, and the class laughed with her instead of at her. She sailed through her three points, closed with the octopus line turned upside down, and sat down as the timer beeped at exactly two minutes. Behind her, Priya walked to the front, gripped her note card, and began.

Mathis crouched between the tomato rows with his sketchbook balanced on his knees, trying to draw a food chain that started with the sun. His science teacher had said the chain had to run all the way to a top predator, and Ms. Okafor had promised the best poster would hang at the community garden's fall festival. Mathis wanted that spot on the fence more than he had wanted anything since the school talent show, where his magic act had flopped in a truly spectacular way.

He drew the sun with rays that radiate outward, then an arrow to the tomato leaves, then a fat green caterpillar chewing a leaf, then a songbird, and then, at the end, a hawk perched on a branch. His pencil hovered. Was a hawk really the end? Something about it bothered him.

That was when Priya from Plot 12 stomped over, dragging her watering can. "You put an owl at the top of my chain, and my cousin says owls get eaten by hawks, so hawks are the top, not owls."

"Not always," Mathis said. He flipped to a fresh page. "Let's test it. If the hawk is the last one, then nothing eats the hawk. Nothing." He drew a box after the hawk and left it empty. "My grandpa calls the last animal in a chain the apex predator. As an adult, nothing hunts it. It's at the end with no predators of its own."

Priya frowned at the empty box. "So an owl can be one too, if nothing eats the owl where it lives."

"Right. It depends on the chain." Mathis drew two chains side by side, hawk at the end of one, owl at the end of the other. Then he had another idea, and this one felt bigger. He crossed out the caterpillar in his first chain, hard enough to tear the page a little.

"Hey," Priya said. "Now your songbird has nothing."

"Exactly. Watch." He drew the songbird thin and hungry, then drew the hawk's box smaller, then put a big question mark after it. "You pull one link, and everything after it gets squeezed."

Priya grabbed her own pencil. "The garden fence. If we spray the caterpillars, the birds go, and then..." She trailed off, drawing arrows.

They worked until the sun dropped behind the apartments on Maple Street, the ones Mr. Ruiz was always worrying about losing to the bank because he couldn't pay his mortgage. Mathis taped both posters to the fence side by side and stepped back.

"Two top predators," Priya said, "one fence."

Ms. Okafor walked over with her thumbtacks already in her hand.

Mathis turned the oven dial until the needle crept up to the number the recipe card demanded, three seventy-five, and then stood there feeling foolish, because preheating meant waiting with nothing to do. He wanted these blueberry muffins to be perfect. His sister Camille had laughed when he announced he would bake from start to finish with no help, and that laugh had been quietly thwarting him all morning, pushing him to make everything flawless.

He measured the flour, cracked the eggs, and folded the wet into the dry. The batter looked lumpy, though, speckled and uneven, and lumpy felt wrong. Last summer he remembered watching Grandpa whisk pancake batter until it poured like silk, and those pancakes had been the best he ever tasted. So Mathis kept stirring. He stirred until every lump surrendered and the batter gleamed smooth as frosting, then spooned it into the paper cups and slid the tray into the hot oven.

Twenty minutes later he pulled them out, golden and dome-topped, and broke one open while it still steamed. It was chewy in a way muffins should never be, and when he looked closer, long tunnels ran through the inside like wormholes. "What happened?" Camille asked, leaning over his shoulder. Mathis frowned at the crumb, turning the halves in the light.

"The recipe said stir just until combined," he said slowly. "I thought smooth was better. But the tunnels..." He'd read a warning on the back of the flour bag once, a line about gluten, and it surfaced now like a bubble. "Stirring too much makes gluten. Gluten makes them tough, and it leaves these tunnels." Camille raised an eyebrow, but he was already reaching for the bowl again.

There was enough batter left for six more. This time he counted his strokes and stopped while the batter still looked shaggy and lumpy, which felt naive but right. He scraped it into the cups, and while the second batch rose in the oven, he thought about how the first tray had taught him something no perfectly mixed bowl ever could. When the timer rang, he split a warm muffin open. No tunnels. Crumbly, tender, exactly what a muffin should be.

"Told you I'd do it," he said, and handed Camille the biggest one.

Grandpa dealt the cards and said, "We play according to Hoyle in this house." Payton's cousin Dex slapped his hand down on the table before anyone had even picked up their cards. "Last time we played Spoons, you grabbed my spoon," he said. "That's why I lost." Payton felt the old resentment rising, the kind that could ruin a whole dinner if she let it. She was about to shout back when she stopped and thought about Grandpa's word.

"Hoyle?" she asked instead. "Who's that? Some guy who makes up rules?" Grandpa smiled around a mouthful of potatoes. "Edmond Hoyle. His book from 1742 set down the rules of the card game whist. That's where the phrase comes from." Payton turned that over in her mind while Mom passed the green beans. So "according to Hoyle" just meant following the rules exactly, written down somewhere so nobody could argue about what they were. That was interesting, because right now she and Dex were about to argue about rules that had never been written down at all.

She laid her cards face down and looked at Dex. "Here's the problem. We've been playing Spoons two different ways, and neither of us ever said which way is the real one. You think grabbing is allowed if it's your spoon. I think you have to touch your own nose first." Dex frowned, but he didn't yell, which felt like a small miracle. "So whoever makes up the rule first wins forever," he said. "That's why I grabbed fast."

"No," Payton said. "Here's my idea. We test it. We write down one rule tonight, both agree on it, and we follow it exactly, like Hoyle. If it turns out bad, we change it before the next game, both of us together." She found a napkin and a pen from the junk drawer, and at the table, between the mashed potatoes and the rolls, they wrote: "You must touch your nose before taking a spoon." Dex read it twice, then nodded and shook her hand across the bread basket.

Grandpa cleared his throat. "You know," he said, "plenty of family fights have gone extinct the same way." Payton picked up her cards and grinned at Dex. "Deal me in. Nose first, spoon second."

The waiting room smelled like mint and old magazines, and Landon was trying to read one upside down when his voice cracked right in the middle of a sentence.

"I'm twelve, not two," he had told his mom that morning, but now, telling the hygienist "I have a cavity on my left side," the word "side" came out in two pieces, a squeak and then a boom, like a door slamming on a mouse. His face went hot. At school last week his voice had cracked during his presentation on how bees pollinate apple trees, and he'd wondered about it ever since.

In the chair, he stared at the poster of a kid's growth chart, arrows pointing everywhere. Bigger feet. Broader shoulders. Then Dr. Kim leaned him back and said, "Say ahh," and Landon felt something in his throat he'd never noticed, a firm shelf that hummed when his voice went low.

"That's your larynx," Dr. Kim said. "Yours is growing, and so are your vocal cords, getting longer and thicker. That's why your voice is getting deeper."

Longer and thicker. Landon's brain lit up like the exam light above him. That was the pattern. His cousin Marcus was fifteen, and when Marcus talked it was like a tuba. Landon himself was more of a squeaky recorder. And the changes weren't just on the chart where you could see them. Some were hidden, like the sweat smell he'd noticed in gym class after his deodorant ran out and he'd kept using the empty stick for three days at the expense of his friendships, apparently, because Bruno had changed seats.

After the appointment, Landon marched to the pharmacy next door and bought deodorant with his own money, a significant purchase, two whole weeks of allowance. He also bought a little notebook. On the first page he wrote: VOICE, FEET, SMELL, ALL CHANGING. NOT A ROBOT GLITCH.

That night he pressed two fingers under Marcus's chin and made him talk, then did the same to himself in the mirror. The humming felt slower, lower, bigger.

"One day I'll sound like a tuba," he told his reflection. "A tuba that showers every day."

Olivia counted the coins twice on the garage workbench, where Dad had set up a pretend store out of an old cardboard box. Three dollars and forty cents for the milk, so out of the five dollar bill Mom gave her, she should get one dollar and sixty cents back. She had to distinguish the quarters from the dimes by feel, because Dad kept turning the porch light off to make it harder. "Sixty cents, a dollar sixty," she said, and Dad slid the coins across the bench like a real cashier.

Mom's note was folded in Olivia's pocket, and she read it again at the end of the driveway. You can do this. Go straight to Mr. Patel's, buy one gallon of milk, come straight home. Love, Mom. It was the first time she'd ever gone alone, and the walk felt longer without anyone talking beside her. At the store Mr. Patel counted her change out loud, dollar sixty, and Olivia checked every coin before she put it in the bag with the cold gallon.

Halfway home, Zoe yelled from her porch. Olivia had been hoping for something spontaneous like this, an unexpected swim in Zoe's sprinkler, and she almost dropped the bag on Zoe's front step and ran. Then she stopped. It was over ninety degrees today, which meant over thirty-two Celsius, and last week she'd read a sign at the store that she hadn't been able to stop thinking about. Perishable food like milk should not sit out for more than two hours, and in heat above thirty-two Celsius, only one hour. She'd tested the rule in her head on the walk, counting the minutes, and now it mattered.

"We can't leave the milk out here," Olivia said. "It's way too hot. Can I put it in your fridge?" Zoe's mother said of course, and the girls carried it to the kitchen, then ran back outside and through the sprinkler until Olivia's shirt was soaked. When she finally walked in her own door, milk cold, change correct, Mom just looked at the clock and the receipt and then hugged her, wet shirt and all.

"Sixty seconds to spare," Olivia said, holding up the coins.

Payton was measuring flour for Saturday's batch of snickerdoodles when her phone buzzed and buzzed and buzzed again. Maya was texting from her own kitchen two streets over, and the messages came fast: "I can't breathe right." "Tryouts Monday." "What if I freeze in front of everyone?" Payton set down the measuring cup, typed "just calm down, it's fine!!" and hit send, already looking forward to Maya saying thanks and then to the smell of cinnamon filling the kitchen.

The reply came back in three seconds: "WOW thanks. SO helpful. Nobody gets it." Payton stared at the screen. The flour dust on her fingers suddenly felt heavy. She had helped, hadn't she? She reread her own message and frowned. "Calm down" was what you said. It was what everybody said. Maya's next text arrived before she could think of anything better: "Forget it."

Payton paced between the counter and the stove, thinking hard. When her little brother cried about a nightmare, telling him to stop never worked either. What worked was sitting next to him and letting him tell the whole scary dream, start to finish. Maybe worry worked the same way. She tested the idea, typing slowly: "That came out wrong. Tell me what you're scared of. I'm listening for real." She added, "You don't have to make it short or summarize it. Send everything."

Maya sent eleven messages. Payton read every one, then answered each worry like it deserved a real reply: yes, freezing in front of the whole team would feel awful; yes, the new coach was intimidating; no, one bad tryout would not erase three years of practice. When Maya finally wrote "okay. that actually helped," Payton pumped her fist in the air and did a quick spin right there on the kitchen tile. She had been about to tell Maya that skipping tryouts seemed like the safe move, but she caught herself. That was her own bias talking, wanting to fix things fast. Listening had worked better, and listening was something she could do again anytime, no recipe required.

One text from Maya still glowed on the screen: "still scared tho." Payton thought about Mrs. Okafor, the counselor who kept a jar of fidget toys on her desk, and typed: "Tell Mrs. Okafor Monday morning. She's the right person for the big stuff. I'll walk with you." The oven timer dinged. Maya answered with a single word: "Deal." Payton slid the cookie sheet in and grinned at the warm orange light behind the glass.

Brayden sat at the spare desk in his mom's office, staring at the setup screen for her new work laptop. "I can't reuse the one from home," Mom said, shaking her head. "If somebody guesses it there, they could get in here too. One password, everything gone." She handed him a sticky note with the office rules on it and went to her meeting. Brayden frowned at rule number four: create a strong password. His old one, dragon77, suddenly looked as flimsy as a paper towel.

He remembered last summer at his cousin Priya's house, when her account for a game had gotten broken into. "Somebody logged in from another country," she had said, "and they consumed all my gold buying dumb hats." Brayden had thought it was magic at the time. Now he wondered: how did a stranger even get her password? Probably because she used the same short one everywhere, so whoever stole it once could walk into everything else, like a key that opens every door on the street. That was the hidden pattern, invisible but real, and it made his stomach feel weird.

He scrolled through the company's tips page and found an old webcomic from 2011 taped to the bottom of the article, an xkcd comic, the caption said. In it, a stick figure compared a short jumbled password to a passphrase of several random words, and gave the example "correct horse battery staple." Brayden read it three times. Several random words were long enough to be hard to guess yet easy to remember? He glanced around the cubicles, half expecting a trap. "Correct horse battery staple," he whispered, and started to giggle. He could already picture it: a very precise horse standing next to a car battery and a staple. He would remember that forever.

But did it actually work? He decided to test it the only way he could think of. He opened the password checker tool the office provided, typed dragon77, and watched the bar flash red like a fire alarm. Then he typed seven-purple-burrito-tuba. Long enough to be hard to guess, easy for him to remember, and nothing like Mom's other passwords. The bar stretched green, elastic and satisfying, all the way across the screen. He did a small fist pump under the desk.

When Mom came back, he showed her the comic and the green bar, then his notebook page titled PASSWORD ANALYSIS, with three doodled horses. "Correct horse battery staple," she read, and burst out laughing. "That's ridiculous." "That's the point," Brayden said. "Ridiculous is memorable. Try making up your own." She chewed her lip, looked out the window at the parking garage, and started typing. "Wobbly raccoon elevator taco," she announced.

The trail smelled like wet leaves, and Rebecca had Mr. Okafor's folded poster jammed in her backpack like a crime she was trying to hide. Marisol's poster. Every arrow on it pointed the wrong way, so the grass appeared to be eating the rabbit, and the rabbit appeared to be eating the hawk, which Rebecca thought would be an interesting hawk but probably not a real one.

"Check this," she said, catching up to Marisol at the creek crossing. She flattened the poster on a boulder and jabbed a finger at the first arrow. "Which way is it supposed to point?"

"From the grass to the rabbit," Marisol said. "Obviously. Grass, then rabbit, then hawk."

"Right, but the arrow itself. Your arrow points from the rabbit to the grass." A dragonfly whirred past, and Rebecca watched it snatch something small out of the air. "I think the arrow goes the other way. From the thing that gets eaten to the thing that eats it. That's the direction the energy flows."

Marisol squinted. "So grass to rabbit to hawk."

"Grass gets its energy from the sun, the rabbit eats the grass, the hawk eats the rabbit. Each arrow shows the energy moving up the chain. Your version makes it look like every organism is being eaten by the plant." Rebecca flipped her pencil around and sketched it in the dirt, arrows small and neat. She was not a chronic poster-ruiner like Marisol, whose projects had suffered a long history of glue incidents, but even she could see this was fixable.

"Then erase and flip all eleven," Marisol said with a groan.

"You only have nine."

Marisol counted, twice, and got nine both times. Rebecca handed her the pencil and watched her flip each arrow, one by one, until the chain finally made sense. At the top, Marisol paused over the hawk.

"What if there's no hawk?" she asked.

Rebecca looked down the trail, where the grass grew thick and rabbits-shaped holes had been chewed into it. "Then a lot more rabbit."

Marisol drew a small arrow in the margin and wrote "sun" next to it. "Poor sun," she said. "Everything eats it and nobody says thanks."

Zachary's mother worked the counter at First Savings on Saturdays, and he was allowed to sit in the back with a stack of brochures as long as he stayed out of the way. He was folding a brochure into a paper airplane when the edge of the paper sliced across his thumb, thin and quick, and a bead of red welled up like a tiny button. He blinked at it. How could something as floppy as paper do that? It was like being beaten up by a cloud.

"Paper cut," said Ms. Alvarez, the teller on window two, without even looking up. She slid a white first-aid box across the floor to him with her foot. "Corner of the paper. It's all edge, no face."

Zachary opened the box and found gauze, tape, three sizes of bandage, and a brown bottle labeled hydrogen peroxide. He knew that bottle. It fizzed white and bubbly on cuts, like a science experiment, and he'd always assumed the fizz meant it was working. He unscrewed the cap, but a laminated card was tucked under the bandages, and he paused to read it. Clean the wound with mild soap and water, the card said. Do not clean a cut with hydrogen peroxide or iodine, because both can irritate the wound. He read the line twice. "Huh," he said out loud. "The fizzing stuff is the wrong stuff."

"You learn something new every day," Ms. Alvarez said. A man at her window was arguing about a fee, so she lowered her voice. "My nephew soaked a scrape in peroxide last month. It stayed angry-looking for two weeks."

So Zachary tested it, in his own small way. He washed the cut under the break-room tap with soap and water, pressed the edges together, and peeled a bandage from its wrapper. He angled it so the pad covered the cut exactly, then smoothed the sticky wings down. The whole thing took less than a minute, and nothing fizzed at all. He tried to replicate the wrap on his other thumb with a second bandage, just to practice, and laughed when he got it crooked. "That one's for my left hand," he announced. "Left hand, crooked standard."

The card had one more part, a short list, and he read it under his breath: if the wound is deep, has ragged edges, or won't stop bleeding, see a doctor. His cut was shallow and clean-edged, and it had already stopped. He held his thumb up to the light like a jeweler inspecting a gem. "You pass," he told it.

On the way out, he passed a poster about mosquitoes, left over from some summer campaign, with the word parasite printed in bold across a cartoon bug. "Hey," he said to Ms. Alvarez, tapping the poster, "which is worse, a parasite, or a paper cut from a savings brochure?" She counted out twenties for her customer and kept a straight face. "At work, kid, everything's toxic to morale." Zachary grinned, pocketed two bandages for his backpack, and pushed through the heavy glass door with his uninjured hand.

Connor had promised to bring something homemade to the school bake sale, and not just anything: the winners of the bake sale contest got their photo in the town paper, which everyone agreed was the most prestigious honor a sixth grader could earn without playing a sport. So on Saturday morning he stood at the counter with a recipe card, a bag of flour, and the feeling that he was about to find out whether he could actually do this alone. First instruction: preheat the oven to 375 degrees. He twisted the dial, watched the little orange light blink on, and wondered how the oven knew when it was hot enough. It had to have some kind of sensor inside, he decided, because the light didn't just click on and off at random.

He read the recipe twice before touching anything, the way his grandmother had told him to. Blueberry muffins: mix the dry, mix the wet, fold together without overbeating, fill the cups. When he got to the line that said "fold in blueberries," he paused. Fold wasn't a word he associated with baking. He tried it with a spatula, turning the batter over gently like he was tucking the berries into bed, and noticed how the streaks of purple slowly spiraled through the yellow. Maybe that was the point, he thought. Maybe stirring hard made the whole thing turn gray.

The batter went into the paper cups, the tray went toward the oven, and that was when his friend Maya walked in through the back door, home early from her sister's soccer game. "Smells good already and nothing's even baked," she said, hoisting herself onto a stool. "Also, is that a nut recipe? My allergy says I can only watch if there are no walnuts involved." Connor checked the card and showed her: blueberries only. Maya relaxed and stole a berry from the bowl.

When the timer finally buzzed, Connor grabbed the oven mitt from its hook beside the sink, where it had been hanging all morning. What he didn't know was that when he'd rinsed the berry bowl earlier, water had splashed up onto the counter and soaked one corner of that same mitt. He pulled it on, reached for the oven door, and Maya shot off the stool so fast it scraped the floor.

"Stop! It's wet!" She pointed at the dark patch on the cloth. "Water in the cloth carries heat fast, way faster than the dry part, and it can turn to steam. You could get burned right through the mitt." Connor stared at his hand, then at the oven door with its heat shimmering faintly above it. He tried to picture it: heat leaping through the damp weave while steam hissed up against his palm, all in the second it took to lift a tray. Slowly he peeled the mitt off, dried his hands and the counter with a dish towel, and swapped it for the dry one from the drawer.

The muffins came out golden, domed, and steaming gently in the morning light. Maya leaned over one, breathing in. "So," she said, "when we win that contest, do we split the credit sixty-forty, or do I get a whole muffin for saving your hand?" Connor laughed and slid the tray onto the wire rack. "You get first pick," he said.

Alyssa sat in the third row of the town hall with her notebook open on her knees. The fluorescent lights buzzed overhead, and someone had propped the side door open to let in the evening air. She had come for one reason: the newspaper had printed two different versions of a bill about a new bridge, and she wanted to know which one would become law.

She raised her hand during the question period. "The paper showed the House version and the Senate version, and the words aren't the same. Which one wins?"

A man in a green jacket stood up near the front. "Neither one wins yet. A bill has to pass both the House of Representatives and the Senate in identical form before it goes to the president."

"Identical," Alyssa repeated, writing the word down. "So if they're different, nothing happens?"

"They have to agree on one exact text," the man said. "That's the rule."

Alyssa looked at her notes. In the House version, the bridge money went into a category called transportation. In the Senate version, it sat in a category called infrastructure. The sentences weren't just rearranged; they said different things. She raised her hand again.

"So the Senate can't just paraphrase the House bill and vote on that?"

"Correct," the man said, and a few people laughed.

After the meeting, Alyssa found her father by the coffee table under the luminous EXIT sign. She flipped her notebook to the page where she had copied both versions, then drew a box around the words that matched.

"They matched here and here," she said, tapping the page. "At first I thought the longer version was the real one. But it doesn't work like that. Nobody's version is real until both houses pass the same words."

"Which words do you think they'll pick?" her father asked.

Alyssa capped her pen. "I'm going to write to our senator and find out."

Aurora spread her materials across the kitchen table: six red beads for protons, a box of gray ones for neutrons, and a spool of thin wire for the electron rings. The science fair was tomorrow morning, and her model of a carbon atom still looked like a pile of beads waiting for permission to become something.

Her friend Marisol arrived at four with her own bag, shaking rain off her jacket. "I built mine last night," she said, pulling out a finished atom. Six red beads sat clustered in the middle with eight gray ones around them, and six small blue beads hung on wire rings above.

Aurora counted the gray beads in Marisol's model, then counted her own. Hers had six. "You made yours wrong," she said. "Carbon has six protons, so it should have six neutrons. That's why it's carbon."

Marisol frowned and turned her atom over in her hands. "My brother read me the numbers off a website last night. Six protons, eight neutrons. It said carbon."

"That can't be right. Then they'd be different atoms."

They sat with the disagreement while rain streaked the window and the kitchen smelled of the tomato sauce simmering on the stove. Aurora picked up one gray bead and rolled it between her fingers. If Marisol's model was wrong, then two sources disagreed, which had never happened to them before. If Marisol's model was right, then something about atoms was stranger than the worksheet had let on.

"Let's test it," Aurora said. She pulled up the school science website on her mom's old laptop and typed in "carbon." The page loaded slowly, then a line appeared: carbon-12, with 6 protons and 6 neutrons, and carbon-14, with 6 protons and 8 neutrons. Aurora read it twice. "Both are carbon," she said. "They just have different numbers of neutrons. They're called isotopes."

Marisol leaned over her shoulder. "So mine is carbon-14 and yours is carbon-12?"

"I guess so." Aurora sat back. "We were both right. We were just making different versions."

"We can't both take an atom to the fair that doesn't match," Marisol said, glancing at the clock. It was already five, and Aurora's mom would be calling them for dinner soon. The verdict came from Aurora, who pointed at the stack of poster board in the corner. "We incorporate both. One big poster, two atoms side by side, carbon-12 and carbon-14. Then nobody has to be wrong."

They worked until the sauce had gone thick and lush on the stove and the light outside turned from gray to blue. Aurora glued the beads into two neat centers, six red in each, six gray in one and eight in the other. Marisol bent the wire rings and hung the blue electrons at careful even distances. When they set the finished poster against the wall, the two atoms stood together like brothers from the same family.

Aurora's mom came in with two plates and stopped to look. "Which one is the real carbon?" she asked.

"Both," Aurora said, and turned the poster so the light from the lamp fell across the two small glittering centers.

Emma's rough draft looked like five separate islands, and Mrs. Okafor had written one word in the margin: "Choppy." The essay was due tomorrow, and Emma wanted a B or better because the top three essays in the class would be read aloud at the school assembly. She sat at the corner table by the window, where afternoon light came through the tall glass and laid a long prism of color across the wood.

She read her paragraphs out loud in a whisper. "Dogs need exercise. Dogs help people relax. Dogs teach responsibility." Each sentence stood alone like a kid standing alone at a dance. Her friend Priya slid into the chair across from her with her own draft. "Mine got the same word," Priya said. "Choppy."

Emma stared at the prism on the table and turned her pencil over. She remembered a poster in the computer lab: a bridge between two cliffs. She flipped to the back of her binder, where she had copied phrases from a list on the board weeks ago. First. However. Furthermore. Therefore. "Transition words," she said slowly. "Maybe that's what the poster meant."

She tested it on her first paragraph. "Dogs need exercise. Furthermore, dogs help people relax." Then she tried the next pair. "However, some people think cats are easier." It was like watching stepping stones appear across a stream. Priya leaned over and read the new version. "It reads like one essay instead of five little ones," she said. "The words show how the ideas connect." Priya had said all morning that her own draft was hopeless and she would just turn it in as it was. Now she borrowed Emma's list and began adding words to her own sentences, crossing out, rewriting.

The two of them read the finished drafts aloud to each other in low voices. Emma's essay moved from her introduction, through her three reasons, and landed in a conclusion that began "Therefore, dogs make the best pets for families." The librarian glanced over and smiled at their whispers. Emma slid the draft into her folder and closed it. "Read yours again," Priya said. "The last part. Out loud this time."

Scarlett had spent all of Tuesday's canoe class proving she was competent with a paddle, so on Wednesday the counselor, Ren, put her in charge of the new girl, Priya, who wanted more than anything to win Friday's talent show with her poem. Priya practiced constantly, whispering lines to herself by the lake. But at lunch Scarlett noticed something odd. Priya's chest rose and fell fast, like she'd run the trail, even though they'd been sitting still for ten minutes, and when Scarlett pressed two fingers to Priya's wrist during a hand game, the pulse thumped quick as a rabbit's.

"Your heart's going crazy," Scarlett said. "Are you sick?"

"No." Priya stared at her sandwich. "It happens whenever I think about reading the poem out loud. My body acts like it's in actual danger. Why would it do that when nothing's even happening?"

Scarlett didn't know, and she didn't want to guess. She'd learned at school that guessing could create a bias, where you decide the answer first and only notice facts that fit it. So she tested her idea instead. She had Priya read the poem to just her, alone behind the boathouse. Priya's breathing still went fast and her heart still pounded, even though there was nothing dangerous anywhere, only frogs and dragonflies. Then they hid behind the mess hall and watched a raccoon, and Priya's heart slowed to normal. Whatever was speeding her up was tied to the poem, not to any real threat.

That night Scarlett looked it up in the camp's one tattered encyclopedia. She found Priya at breakfast, sliding the book across the table.

"It has a name," Scarlett said. "It's called fight-or-flight. Anxiety triggers it, and it releases adrenaline, which speeds up your heart and breathing even when there's no real danger."

"So my body's not broken?"

"It's just loud." Scarlett grinned. "But Ren reads poems at every campfire. If anyone knows how to handle a pounding heart before a show, it's her. Want to ask?"

Priya closed the book, stood up, and marched straight across the mess hall toward Ren's table.

Hazel's science teacher had posted a challenge on the board: bring one mystery item from your kitchen, and the class would vote, physical change or chemical change. The winner got to dismantle the old toaster oven in the lab, taking it apart screw by screw, which was the only prize anyone cared about. Hazel wanted that toaster more than she'd wanted anything at school since October. But her item had to fool people, and she didn't have one yet.

On Sunday she slept over at Priya's house, and Priya's one wish was to cook breakfast entirely by herself, no help, because her older brother always claimed she couldn't. Priya cracked an egg into the pan and watched the clear white turn solid and white. "It's like a magic trick," she said, sliding it onto the plate. Hazel stared at it, fork paused in the air. When the egg cooled, she poked it, waiting for it to go clear again the way ice went back to water. It didn't. She nudged it. Still white, still solid.

"It won't go back," Hazel said slowly. "Ice melts back. This doesn't."

"So it's broken?" Priya said, worried her breakfast was ruined.

"No, it's..." Hazel turned it over with the fork. "It's like when Dad left the bike out in the rain and it rusted. That never un-rusted either."

In class on Monday, Hazel set the cold fried egg on the front table and said nothing. Kids voted physical change, six to four. Then she held up the phone video Priya had taken, the clear white going solid and white in the pan, and the shot of the cooled egg, unchanged. "Frying an egg is a chemical change," she said. "The heat permanently changes the proteins in the egg white, so it turns solid and white, and it stays that way." The six voters groaned. Marcus, who had brought a squished marshmallow, muttered that stretching was obviously physical and this was rigged. The toaster oven sat on the back counter, and the teacher handed Hazel the screwdriver set.

Later, in the hall, Priya texted her brother a photo of the screwdriver in Hazel's hand with one line: "Told you I could cook."

Gabriella flopped onto the kitchen floor with the big atlas, the one with the coffee ring on Peru. With the recession tightening everything, Dad had said no trips this year, not even to Aunt Rosa's two states over. So Gabriella had made a deal with herself: if she could not go anywhere, she would learn to find every place on the map.

She already knew the trick for latitude and longitude, the crisscross of thin lines with numbers along the edges. You matched the horizontal number with the vertical one, and where they crossed, there was your city. Her problem was the opposite. She wanted to work backward, to name a city from its numbers alone, because Dad had promised a dollar for every capital she could locate without peeking at the labels.

She picked a hard one on purpose. The horizontal line, the latitude, read almost zero, and just a hair south of the equator line itself. She ran her finger along that line, past Africa, across the Atlantic, over the bumps of the Andes in South America. It was ironic, she thought, that a city sitting almost exactly on the equator, where the sun was straight overhead, should be famous for cool mountain air. Her finger stopped on a dot in Ecuador. She checked the edge numbers again, then persisted, sliding her fingertip sideways to the longitude line, tracing it down until both numbers crossed in one place. Quito. The capital of Ecuador.

She stood up so fast the atlas pages flapped. "Dad! Quito, Ecuador. It's less than a quarter of a degree south of the equator, so its latitude is almost zero."

He came in drying a plate, looked at the atlas, looked at her, and pulled a crumpled dollar from his pocket. "Prove it."

Gabriella laid the ruler along the equator line and tapped the dot beside it. "See for yourself. Almost zero."

Amelia's grandmother sang alto in the church choir for forty years, and on Saturday mornings the whole house smelled like toast and sounded like scales. Amelia wanted the solo in the spring concert, but the choir director had made it plain: no solo for anyone who could not hold a part in two-part harmony. Amelia could sing the melody fine. The moment a second voice came in, hers slid away from it like water finding a drain.

"Try it with me," her grandmother said at the piano. She played two notes at once, then sang the lower one. Amelia was supposed to sing the upper one and keep it there. On the first try, she drifted down within four beats. On the second try, she drifted faster.

After lunch Amelia went looking for the reason. It felt strange that the problem was invisible; nobody could point at the spot where the mistake lived. In the bookshelf by the sewing room she found a thin book about singing with a diagram inside. The diagram showed the larynx from above, and inside it two thin strips labeled vocal folds. The caption said they vibrate as air passes between them. Amelia put her fingers lightly on the front of her throat and hummed. Something buzzed under her skin. She hummed higher and felt the buzz change.

"So when I go for the high note," she said, turning the page, "I've been squeezing everything."

"Grandpa squeezed like that at my cousin's wedding," her grandmother said from the doorway. "Strained for a high note and it cracked in half. Two vocal folds in there, that's all, and he was strangling them."

Amelia tested it right there. She sang the high note once while tightening her whole throat the way she usually did, and it came out thin and sharp. Then she took a breath low in her chest and thought about letting the two folds tighten just enough, without her jaw and neck trying to contribute. The note came out round and steady, and it was easier. She sang it three more times to make sure it wasn't luck.

The real test was the harmony. Her grandmother sat on the piano bench and sang the alto line of "Down to the River," and Amelia took the soprano part. When the two lines crossed in the third phrase, Amelia felt the old pull, the want to sink toward her grandmother's note. She kept her breath low and her throat loose, and the pull passed under her like a current under a boat that didn't sink. They finished the verse and the room went quiet.

"How long before the concert?" Amelia asked.

"Six weeks."

Amelia set the book on the piano, open to the diagram. "Then I'll practice every morning." Her grandmother started the verse again, and Amelia came in on the high part.

Maya sat in the waiting room of the animal clinic with her rabbit carrier on her lap and her science folder open on her knees. Tomorrow she had to draw a plant cell and an animal cell side by side, and she could not remember which parts belonged only to the plant one. Her little brother Theo had told her the floppy lettuce seedlings on the classroom windowsill had something to do with it, but he had not explained how, which was annoying, because Theo rarely explained anything.

Dr. Patel came out to weigh Biscuit the rabbit, and Maya noticed something taped by the scale: a poster of a dog cell, labeled in careful letters. "Dr. Patel, is that a real animal cell?" she asked. "It's a drawing of one," Dr. Patel said, holding Biscuit gently. "Under the microscope it looks like a fried egg, sort of. No box around it." Maya wrote in her folder: no box around it. Theo had said something about a box. She stared at her plant-cell drawing and put a thick line around the outside, then wrote a question mark next to it.

While Biscuit was being checked, Maya found a letter folded into her folder from her teacher, which she had forgotten to give her mother. "Dear families," she read silently, "our lettuce seedlings drooped over the weekend, so we will observe them before and after watering. Students should be ready to justify their answers in class on Friday." Maya frowned. Before and after watering. Something changed inside the seedlings when they were watered, and it had to do with the box, and with the blob in the middle of every plant cell drawing she had ever seen.

She texted Theo from the corner by the fish tank. "What's the blob in the middle of a plant cell called?" He wrote back fast, which surprised her. "Central vacuole. It's like a water balloon. When it's full it presses outward against the cell wall. Cell walls are the box. Only plants have them." Maya read it twice. A water balloon pressing outward against a box. If the balloon emptied, the pressing would stop, and the whole leaf would go floppy. She looked at the droopy seedling Theo had stuck in a plastic cup on the counter near the rabbits, waiting to be brought back to school. "Can I test something?" she asked Dr. Patel, and carried the cup to the sink.

She watered the seedling and set it on the windowsill, then drew her two cells one more time: the animal cell with no box and no big balloon, the plant cell with both, arrow drawn from the balloon pushing outward. An hour later, when Biscuit was ready to go home, the seedling's leaves had lifted off the cup rim and stood up in a row. Maya wrote "temporary" under her first droopy sketch, because the floppiness had not lasted, and then, thinking of the giant poster in the waiting room that said THIS CLINIC CURES EVERYTHING, she laughed and labeled it in her head as propaganda.

On Friday she stood at the front of the room with her drawing. "Only plants have cell walls," she said, tapping the box she had outlined. "And a central vacuole, like a water balloon. When it's full of water it presses outward against the wall, and when it loses water the plant wilts." Her teacher smiled, and Maya held up the cup with the standing-up seedling, the proof in her hand.

Carter sat on the floor of Marcus's kitchen with a laptop and a bag of pretzels, trying to make an account for a game. "Password rejected," the screen said, for the fourth time.

"Just type your dog's name and some numbers," Marcus said, reaching for the pretzels.

"Rusty12 got leaked last year when that game site got hacked. I got sixteen spam emails about lawn gnomes after that." Carter winced at the memory, mostly the lawn gnomes. He had used Rusty12 everywhere, so everywhere had a hole in it. That was the part he was still figuring out: one password was like one key for the whole neighborhood. Lose the key and everybody's garage is open.

Marcus's mom came in carrying a box of old keyboards. "Marcus, is this motion sensor still in one piece, or is it obsolete like the rest of this junk?"

"It works," Marcus said. She set it on the counter and sighed at her phone. "My office makes us pick a new password every single month. By now I just do Winter1, Winter2, Winter3."

Carter looked up. "My cousin said there's a government thing, NIST, and their rule is that systems should not make people change passwords on a schedule. Only when there's evidence a password got stolen."

"Then my office is doing the opposite of the rule," Marcus's mom said.

"Wait," Carter said, and pulled up the NIST page on the laptop. He read it twice, then typed a new password into the game: four random words strung together, nothing like Rusty12, nothing like anything else he used. The screen flashed "Account created."

"Congratulations," Marcus said. "Now write it down before you forget it like your gym locker combo."

"I don't forget combos. I forget whether I already used them." Carter copied the password onto a sticky note and slapped it against the laptop lid. "New rule. Every key gets its own door."

Peyton slid into her seat in the computer lab just as Mr. Ruiz said the magic words: today they each got an account on the school's coding site. The only catch was a password screen, glowing and waiting. Her best friend Dex leaned over from the next computer.

"Easy," he whispered, typing fast. "I always use monkey. Six letters. It's plenty long."

Peyton frowned at her own empty box. Six letters sounded like a lot, but something about it bothered her. "Wait," she said. "You always use it? Like on other sites too?" Dex shrugged. "It's one word. Why remember twenty words when one works everywhere?" Peyton couldn't classify what felt wrong about that, whether it was a small worry or a big one, so she decided to test it. She opened the class activity sheet and read the part about guessing. It said crackers try every possible password, letter by letter, until one fits. Then she found a sentence that stopped her cold: using only lowercase letters, every extra character makes 26 times as many possibilities to guess.

"Twenty-six times," she said out loud. "For one letter." She grabbed scrap paper and started multiplying. Six letters was 26 times 26, six times over. When she added a seventh letter, the number she got was twenty-six times bigger than the six-letter number. It grew so fast her pencil couldn't keep up. "Dex, your password is twenty-six times easier to guess than one that's just one letter longer."

Dex squinted at her paper. "That seems like a contradiction. Adding one tiny letter can't matter that much."

"Look at the numbers," Peyton said, spinning the paper toward him. Then a second thought hit her, and this one felt worse. "Also, if a cracker gets your password on one site, and you use it everywhere, they get it everywhere. That would be toxic for your whole account list. One leak, everything gone." Dex's shoulders slumped like a balloon losing air.

"So I need a different password for every site?" he groaned. Peyton was already typing, experimenting on her own screen. She tried mixing uppercase, numbers, and a symbol, watching the little strength meter climb from red to green, wondering how much bigger the possibilities got with each new kind of character. She made one for the coding site, one she'd never used anywhere else, and wrote a hint in her notebook instead of the password itself. Dex deleted "monkey" and hunched over his keyboard, muttering letters and numbers to himself. At the front of the room, Mr. Ruiz called out, "Five minutes to log in." Peyton hit enter, and the screen bloomed open into a page full of blinking code.

"Made it," she said, and held up her hand for a high five.

Ariana sat cross-legged on the kitchen floor with her notebook open to a page titled "My Family, in Mandarin." Her assignment was to record a video describing her family in full sentences, and she had most of it ready: her mom, her dad, the cat, the goldfish. The trouble was her twin brother, Marco, who was currently trying to submerge his entire arm in the fish tank so he could rearrange the plastic castle.

"Stop drowning our fish," she said, then froze with her pen in the air. Her teacher's list said Mandarin had a word for older brother, gēge, and a different word for younger brother, dìdi. Marco was her twin, born ten minutes after her. Did ten minutes count?

She wrote to her language partner, Mei, who lived three streets over and always answered fast. The message said: "Quick question. My brother is my twin. I was born ten minutes before him. Is he my dìdi or my gēge? This is urgent and also my grade." While she waited, she watched Marco nudge the castle toward the bubbler and felt a small flicker of resentment, because the video was due tomorrow and he wasn't even helping.

Mei's reply popped up in two minutes. "Ten minutes counts! If he was born after you, he's your dìdi. My cousin is a twin too, and she calls her brother dìdi even though they celebrate on the same birthday."

Marco leaned over her shoulder to read it. "That's ridiculous," he said, looking skeptical. "Ten minutes? We're basically the same age. I'm not your little brother."

"So it's official," Ariana said, grinning. She pressed record on her phone. "Wǒ yǒu yí gè dìdi. He was born ten minutes after me, which makes him forever younger, and I have one older sister zero times, because I'm the oldest." She said it slowly, carefully, and Marco covered his ears with both hands.

"That's not fair," he protested. "Ten minutes is nothing."

"It's ten minutes forever," Ariana said. "Every single day, you wake up ten minutes younger than me."

Marco glared at the goldfish as if the fish had invented the rule. Then his shoulders dropped and he sighed. "Fine. I'm the dìdi. But in the video, can you at least say I'm taller?"

Ariana checked. He was, by almost two inches. "Wǒ de dìdi hěn gāo," she said, which meant her little brother was very tall, and Marco allowed that this was acceptable. She finished the last sentence about the cat, hit stop, and sent the video to her teacher before anyone could change their mind.

Marco stuck one finger back into the tank, adjusting the castle one final degree to the left.

Owen had one class period to finish his outline before the drafting began, and his topic kept sliding around on the page like a wet bar of soap. He wanted to argue that the school should plant a garden behind the gym. He had a thesis, mostly, and three points: gardens teach science, gardens improve lunches, and gardens make the courtyard nicer. The teacher, Ms. Ruiz, had said the outline had to list each main point with its evidence underneath, and Owen had written the words but not much under them.

That afternoon he stopped at his grandfather's house, because Grandpa had promised him tomato seedlings if the project ever got approved. Grandpa was at the kitchen table with a napkin covered in pencil marks. "Writing my letter to the county," he said. "Trying to save the community pool." Owen leaned over. The napkin had a one-sentence claim at the top and three points below it, and under two of the points were little notes: numbers of swimmers, a quote from a lifeguard, a fact about pool repairs. Under the third point, the words summer monsoon storms flood the parking lot, there was nothing at all. Just blank napkin.

"You've got a hole," Owen said, tapping it.

"Exactly why I do this on a napkin first," Grandpa said. "The outline shows me the weak point before I spend an afternoon writing paragraphs around it." He frowned at the empty space. "That one might be true, but I can't prove it, so out it goes." He crossed it off and wrote a replacement, then added a note about swim team fees. Owen stared at his own notebook, where point three, gardens make the courtyard nicer, sat with no evidence under it either.

At school the next morning, Ms. Ruiz walked the rows to distribute a rubric for the drafting stage. When she reached Owen, he showed her his paper. "I cut my third point," he said. "It was just an opinion with nothing under it. I swapped in a new one, that garden food gets used in the cafeteria, and I have a note from the cafeteria manager." The note was short, in blue pen on the back of a menu: "Owen, we would happily serve school-grown vegetables. Last year we used forty pounds of local carrots. Mrs. Dale." He had gotten it Tuesday, after a ten-minute visit to the kitchen.

Ms. Ruiz read the note twice and checked his outline. "Strongest one in the class so far," she said. "You found the gap before it cost you a whole draft."

Owen sat back down and began his first paragraph, the one about science, which had three pieces of evidence lined up beneath it like seedlings in a row. Outside the window, clouds were stacking up over the roof of the gym, dark and heavy, and rain felt imminent. He wrote faster, thinking that if the garden ever went in back there, it would drink up every storm that came.

"Forty pounds of carrots," he muttered, and underlined his thesis.

Between rounds at the debate tournament, the coaches announced a surprise improv workshop in the cafeteria. Nathaniel signed up because his partner, Priya, had the flu and he had nothing to do for two hours except reread his note cards about highway tolls. Improv sounded easy. You just made things up, and he made things up all the time.

The workshop leader, a tall high school volunteer, paired him with a girl named Ruthie from another school and told them to build a scene together, one line each. Ruthie went first. "We're on a boat," she said, grabbing an invisible wheel.

Nathaniel panicked. A boat made no sense to him, so he said, "We're not on a boat. We're in the cafeteria."

The audience of waiting debaters went quiet. Ruthie's arms dropped to her sides. Nobody laughed, and the volunteer called out, "That's called blocking," in the same flat voice he used for taking attendance. Nathaniel's ears burned. He sat down and watched the next pair.

A boy named Marcus started a scene with "This is my dog, Biscuit," and his partner said, "No, that's not my dog," and again the scene just stopped, like a car rolling to a dead stop at the bottom of a hill. Twice in a row. Nathaniel chewed his pen and thought about it. The problem wasn't that the offers were silly. It was that each one got knocked down. He couldn't see why a scene died, exactly, because a scene isn't a thing you can watch breathe, but he could see the pattern: every time someone said no, the energy in the room dropped.

He had a hypothesis. What if you had to say yes to whatever your partner offered, and then add something new? He whispered the idea to Ruthie, who shrugged and said, "Fine, one more try."

The volunteer called them up again. "We're on a boat," Ruthie said, hands on the invisible wheel.

"Yes," Nathaniel said, "and I've never steered anything with a snack bar before." He pointed at an imaginary counter stacked with chips. Ruthie grabbed the idea instantly. "Yes, and the snack bar is where we hide from the captain, because he's a goose." The cafeteria crowd actually laughed, a real laugh that rolled forward instead of dying. They went back and forth for a whole minute, the boat growing a goose captain, a treasure chest full of bus passes, a storm made of confetti.

Afterward Marcus walked over, looking defiant, arms crossed like he expected to be teased. "How'd you do that?" he asked. "I kept going blank up there."

Nathaniel almost explained the whole theory, but instead he said, "Let's try a scene. You start."

Marcus straightened up. "We're the last two kids in the school library," he said, "and the books are floating."

"Yes," said Nathaniel, "and the first one floating is the one I never returned in third grade." He reached up on tiptoe for it.

Elizabeth pulled the tarp off her grandfather's workbench and coughed at the dust that rose into the shaft of light from the garage door. She was hunting for a measuring tape, but what she found instead was a poster tube rolling out from a shallow recession in the wall behind the bench, a square gap lined with old plywood where the bricks had never been laid. The tube's cap popped off, and a paper scroll slithered out across the concrete.

It was a periodic table, brittle and yellowed, with handwriting in the margins. Number 31 had no name at all, just a blank box with a question mark. So did number 32. Elizabeth frowned. Her science test was Friday, and she had just learned that the atomic number told you the number of protons, so carbon, number 6, had six protons, and gold, number 79, had seventy-nine. But a box with no name and no symbol gave her nothing to count.

Her friend Marcus came through the side door carrying two sodas, and the cans hissed when he cracked them. "What's that smell?" he asked.

"Old paper. Look at this. Somebody made a table with holes in it." She traced her finger along row four, stopping at the empty square. "Thirty-one protons are sitting in there somewhere, and the poster just skips it."

Marcus leaned in, close enough that she could hear him breathing. "Maybe the guy who printed it messed up."

Elizabeth didn't answer right away. The garage was quiet except for a wasp tapping against the window. She stared at the question mark in the box, and an idea began to form, acute and sharp, like a splinter working its way to the surface. A mistake would be crooked, sloppy. This blank was neat. It was waiting. Whoever had drawn it seemed to imply, by leaving it empty, that something belonged there but had not shown up yet.

She dug through the cardboard boxes stacked under the window, where her grandfather kept his geology magazines, and found one from decades back with a feature on metals. She flipped pages fast, then slowed, because there it was: gallium, atomic number 31, discovered years after the old table was drawn. She held the magazine up beside the poster so Marcus could see both. The blank square and the glossy photograph lined up exactly.

"It wasn't a mistake," she said. "Mendeleev left gaps in his table for elements that hadn't been discovered yet, and later discoveries such as gallium filled them." She tapped the box. "He saved my square a seat."

Marcus set down his soda. "So the question mark means he was right before anybody could check?"

"He was right before anybody could even see it." Elizabeth copied the number 31 onto her palm in ballpoint ink, then looked at the second blank square and grinned. "Now let's find out who moved into box thirty-two."

She flipped the page.

Nicolas had a problem shaped like a shoebox full of crumpled papers. For three weeks he had been counting how many books kids at his school checked out from the little free library he ran, and he had written the numbers on receipts, napkins, and once on the sole of his sneaker. His friend Priya had told him that if he put the numbers into a spreadsheet, the computer could add them and draw a chart for him. So on Saturday morning he carried the shoebox to the public library, sat down at a computer by the window, and opened the program.

The blank grid of cells stared back at him, hundreds of little rectangles waiting to be filled. He typed his categories in one column: comics, mysteries, sports, animal facts. Then he typed the counts next to each one. He remembered the day an entire second-grade class had descended on the animal facts shelf, and he smiled as he typed the number 41. A librarian walked past, and he asked her how to make the machine total a column. She showed him a formula with a word like SUM and said, "Click the empty cell below your numbers, then type that." When he pressed Enter, the total appeared instantly: 117 books. It felt like a magic trick, except it was completely logical. The computer was just doing what he would have done with a pencil, only faster and without smudges.

Next came the chart. He highlighted his two columns, found the button with tiny colored bars, and clicked. A chart popped onto the screen, and Nicolas leaned back. Then he frowned. The comics bar stretched sideways, running along the bottom of the picture like a worm, and every other bar lay flat too. Mysteries, sports, even the giant animal facts bar lay there pointing right. It looked like the whole chart had been knocked over. Maybe the computer was broken. Maybe he had pressed something wrong. He tried clicking again, and a second sideways chart appeared beside the first.

Priya arrived twenty minutes later with a snack and found him squinting at a screen with two horizontal charts on it. "Why are they sideways?" she asked, which was exactly the question he had been asking himself. "I don't know," Nicolas admitted. "The bars go left to right instead of up and down." He clicked through the menu again, reading the names of the chart types, and there he saw it. One option was labeled column chart. Column, like a column in a building, standing upright. He highlighted his data and chose that one instead. The new chart snapped into place with the bars reaching straight up, animal facts towering over everything else.

"So that first one was just the wrong kind?" Priya said, chewing. Nicolas nodded slowly, then tested it to be sure. He built the other chart again on purpose and watched the bars lie down flat again. "A bar chart has horizontal bars," he said, "and a column chart has vertical bars. They both compare amounts across categories. They're just different shapes." He dragged the column chart front and center, and the two sideways ones to the trash, though he salvaged one small piece of the wreck by printing it, because the flat version was actually easier to read the long labels on. He pinned both printouts side by side and studied them, wondering which one a second grader would understand faster.

He thought of Mr. Delgado's science classroom, back in fourth grade, where they had drawn pictures of a pond organism called a paramecium, and Mr. Delgado had made them draw it twice, once under low power and once under high power, so they could see how the same thing could look different depending on how you looked. This felt like that. Same numbers, same idea, two different pictures.

Nicolas saved the file twice, once on the computer and once to his flash drive, and slid the shoebox of crumpled papers into the recycling bin on his way to the printer. "Monday I show the principal," he told Priya. "And this time the bars go up."

Felix sat in the back of the school library with a photocopy of a diary page in front of him and a pencil that had gone blunt twenty minutes ago. His assignment was to use one primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s, and the page he had drawn from the box was written by a settler named Amos Teague. The trouble was the page Felix wanted, the one about the trail, only said that the family had crossed a river in the rain and buried a cow. It never said why they had left their old home at all.

He flipped back two pages and read slower this time. "The bank took the farm in October," Amos had written. "Father says Ohio is finished for us. We will go where the land is cheap and the soil is black." Felix copied the line onto his notepad and then stopped. Why would a family with a farm pick up and risk a river crossing that killed their cow? Losing the farm had to be the reason, but he wanted to check before he built his whole paragraph on it.

He carried the page to the shelf where the history books stood and pulled the one covering the early 1800s. The index sent him to a short entry about the Panic of 1837, which, the book said, caused a long economic depression in the United States. Many ruined farmers later headed west looking for cheap, fertile land. Felix read the entry twice. Amos's family had lost their farm, and the country had been in a depression, and other ruined farmers had done exactly what the Teagues did.

At lunch he tested his idea on Dana, who sat across from him picking the crusts off her sandwich. "Say you read a diary where a family loses their farm and then goes west on a dangerous trail," he said. "Would you believe the lost farm was the cause, or would you think they just wanted adventure?" Dana considered it. "If a lot of other farmers did the same thing after the Panic of 1837," she said, "then it's not adventure. It's the pattern." Felix nodded. One diary line was a clue; a hundred families doing the same thing was proof.

In class the next day, Felix read his paragraph aloud. He quoted Amos on the bank taking the farm, then explained that the Panic of 1837 had caused a long economic depression in the United States, and many ruined farmers later headed west looking for cheap, fertile land. Mr. Ruiz asked how he had connected the diary to the bigger event, and Felix held up the book and the photocopy side by side. "I looked for what happened to everybody, not just to him," he said. "The diary tells you one family. The pattern tells you why." Mr. Ruiz wrote something on his clipboard, and Felix sat down, sliding the photocopy back into its folder with the pencil mark still circling the line about the bank.

Mackenzie had one goal at the mall: convince her dad that a phone upgrade made sense before eighth grade started. She had her argument ready, complete with a coherent list of reasons she'd rehearsed in the car. But on the way to the phone store, they passed a bank kiosk with a banner that said TEEN SAVINGS, START TODAY, and her little sister Priya stopped dead.

"I want to open one," Priya announced. "Alyssa's in that category, kids with accounts, and she says they're basically rich."

"They're not rich," Mackenzie said, but she was already eyeing the display table, where a sample statement lay pinned under plastic. The table had a five-year plan sheet, and a rep was inviting anyone who wanted to participate in a quick demonstration. Mackenzie raised her hand before her dad could steer them onward.

The rep slid over a mock statement for something called simple interest. Mackenzie scanned the column of yearly interest payments and frowned. "Wait. This is wrong, isn't it? Year one is twelve dollars, year two is twelve dollars, all five years are twelve dollars. Shouldn't it grow?"

"That's what simple interest does," the rep said. "It's paid only on the original deposit."

"That's called the principal," Priya read off the sheet, tapping the word with her finger. "The original amount deposited."

Mackenzie grabbed the second sheet, the one marked compound, and laid them side by side. "Okay, so on this one, year one is twelve dollars, but year two is more. Twelve dollars and something." She checked the third year, then the fourth. "It keeps climbing. So the simple one adds the same dollar amount every single year, like a flat staircase, and this one is more like a ramp." She pulled out her phone and totaled both columns. Simple interest gave sixty dollars over five years. Compound gave more, and the gap widened every year.

"I changed my mind about the phone," she said suddenly. "Sort of. If I put my four hundred dollars of birthday money in the compound one instead, by the time I actually need a new phone, the interest does part of the work for me." Her dad raised an eyebrow, and she held up the sheet like evidence. "Look at year five. It's not a huge difference, but it's free."

"Can I get one too?" Priya asked. "I have thirty-one dollars."

"You can get anything you want with thirty-one dollars," the rep said, laughing, and slid a starter form across the table.

Priya snatched the pen and started printing her name, letter by careful letter, while Mackenzie filled in her own form and circled the word compound at the top twice, hard enough to dent the page.

Sebastian's sister Priya stood in the middle of the living room with her arms crossed, staring at the carpet like it owed her money. "I froze again," she said. "Third time today. Monday I have to improvise a scene in front of the whole drama class, with a partner I've never even met."

"You? Freeze?" Sebastian set down his book. Priya performed constantly, narrating their mom's cooking like a nature documentary, dramatizing every scraped knee. Freezing made no sense, so something hidden had to be causing it. He needed to see it happen.

"Okay, do one with me. I'll be your partner."

"Fine. You start something and I'll join in." She cleared her throat and shook out her hands.

Sebastian had no idea what improv partners actually did, so he just said, "Hi, I need help." Priya opened her mouth, then closed it. Her eyes darted around like she was searching for the right answer and finding none.

"See?" she whispered.

He chewed on that. The problem wasn't her imagination, because she had plenty. The problem was that "I need help" gave her nothing to be. What if the first line had to nominate a role for the other person, the way a costume did? He tried again, changing one thing.

"Doctor, my arm hurts," he said, holding his elbow. "You're the only one at this clinic."

Priya snapped upright. "Sit down, sit down, this looks serious. Nurse, bring the x-rays!" She was suddenly brisk and bossy, stethoscope made of a jump rope, and for two whole minutes they ran a hospital where Sebastian's arm had been crushed by a falling turbine blade, which he invented on the spot, and Priya declared the clinic "impoverished, with no anesthesia but plenty of spirit." They were both laughing by the end.

"It's like you handed me a costume," Priya said, catching her breath. "At drama camp they called it endowing. Giving your partner a role through what you say. I forgot."

"So Monday, if your partner just stands there being vague, you fix it."

"By endowing them first. 'Captain, we've cleared the asteroid field.'" She spun in a circle, pretending to dodge asteroids. "Or, 'Professor, the volcano's about to blow.'" Then she stopped and pointed at him. "You're my brother and also my hero. Now hold still, Doctor, this turbine accident won't survive without you."

Cameron wanted his street to look real, the way the one in his head did, with buildings leaning in like they were listening to each other. Instead his drawing looked flat, like buildings pasted onto cardboard. Ms. Ruiz had pinned a print of an old fresco above the supply shelf, and Cameron kept glancing at it while his pencil stalled.

A girl about his age, Dana, was standing in front of the print with her finger hovering over the glass. "Watch," she said. "The ceiling lines, the floor lines, they all run to one spot." She dragged her finger along each edge of the painted vault, and every one, ceiling and floor and side arches, aimed at the same small point directly beneath the cross. "It's Masaccio's Holy Trinity, from Florence," she said. "Painted around 1427. My aunt says it's one of the earliest paintings built on a single vanishing point."

"A vanishing point," Cameron repeated. The words felt like a spell name. He looked back at his flat street and devised a plan on the spot: he would become a scavenger of lines, hunting every edge in his drawing the way Dana had hunted the fresco's, and dragging them all to one mark.

He started with a hypothetical street where he already knew the answer, one straight road, two rows of buildings, one point dead ahead. He tapped a dot in the center of the page, then drew a roofline from the top corner of a building straight to the dot. It looked wrong until he added the ground line slanting to the same spot, and suddenly the building leaned back in space like it had weight and a shadow. The road itself was just two lines running together, but now it ran somewhere.

"Every edge obeys the dot," Cameron said, half to Dana, half to his pencil. He imagined the dot as a tiny magnet buried in the road, pulling every brick and windowsill toward it, and him too, if he stood on the paper. Windowsills slanted up toward it from below; roofs slanted down to it from above. The street began to breathe.

He drew a lamppost near the front and made it tall, then a matching one far down the street, small, its top aimed at the same invisible mark. Dana leaned over his shoulder. "It's like standing inside it," she said. Cameron put his finger at the vanishing point and pressed down, like he was holding the whole street in place.

Nathaniel stared at the assignment sheet on the kitchen table. "Explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years," he read aloud. "Presentation Thursday." His problem was simple and enormous: how could he show something that took millions of years when he had four days? He couldn't exactly demolish the backyard with a river. He needed a way to make time itself smaller.

His little sister Priya wandered in, eating toast. "What's a canyon doing on your homework?" she asked. He told her, and she shrugged. "You need a river, obviously." That gave him an idea. He grabbed the garden hose, a plastic bin, and the big bag of play sand from the garage, and dumped it all on the patio in a sloping pile. If a real river could carve rock over millions of years, maybe a trickle of water could carve sand in an afternoon. It was worth testing.

He packed the sand into a smooth slope, dug a small pond at the bottom and filled it with water, then turned the hose to a trickle at the top. At first nothing happened except dark wet patches spreading. Then the water found a path and began to run, and within minutes it had cut a channel as deep as his thumb. He cheered so loudly that Priya came back out. When the channel collapsed and the flow split into two directions, he faced a dilemma: dam one side, or let the river choose? Priya voted to let it choose. "Be impartial," she said. "It's your river's decision."

So he let it run, and something strange happened where the water reached the pond. The current slowed, and all the sand it had been carrying sank right there, building a spreading fan of new land that pushed out into the water like a small triangle. Nathaniel crouched at the pond's edge. Every grain the river had torn from the slope upstream was being dropped downstream, and the fan kept growing, grain by grain. "I've seen a picture of this," he said slowly. "It's called a delta." Priya leaned over and patted the wet little triangle. "Ours is better than the picture."

Thursday came, and Nathaniel carried the whole bin to school with a spray bottle to keep the river alive. During his presentation, he ran the water and let his classmates watch the delta grow while he described the canyon millions of years wide and the river patient enough to carve it. When it was over, Priya was waiting at the classroom door, since Mom had brought her along. "So?" she asked. "Did our river behave?"

Nathaniel held up the bin, delta still dripping. "It built land out of nothing," he said. "Want to see it do it twice?"
