Amos wrote about river crossings and sore feet and President's mood swings, but nowhere did she find anything about how the Native American nations whose lands the trail crossed saw the same events. She checked the last page, then the first, feeling like she'd dropped her ice cream cone on the sidewalk. "A primary source shows one person's view," she said slowly. "Amos's view. Nobody else's."

"That's a problem for your essay," Marcus said cheerfully, because it wasn't his essay. Eleanor stuck her tongue out at him. Then she had an idea, and she tested it the way you test whether a pudding cup is actually sealed: with a push. If Amos couldn't tell the other side, maybe a different primary source could. She marched to the computer, typed in the names of the nations along the trail route, and started hunting for interviews, oral histories, anything recorded from their side.

Twenty minutes later she was scribbling notes so fast her pen squeaked. She found an oral history, passed down and later written down, describing the same rivers Amos had forded, and it didn't just disagree with his diary, it flat-out contradicted it. Amos wrote "empty land"; the oral history described busy trade routes, villages, and wagon ruts cutting straight through planting grounds. Same events, two windows, facing different directions.

Mr. Alvarez stopped at their table on his way past. "Finding everything you need, Eleanor?"

"Better than that," she said. "I found two windows." She held up her notes and Amos's diary side by side. "Guess which ox doesn't show up in the second one."

Camille stood in the wings of the community theatre, listening to the wooden floor creak under the feet of the advanced improv troupe. She had one week to learn what they made look easy. The spring showcase was open to everyone, and her partner, Theo, had already signed them up.

Their first practice went badly. Theo walked onto the empty stage, mimed pulling a heavy rope, and said, "Careful, this anchor is slipping." Camille froze. "There's no rope," she said. "We're just standing on a stage." The room went quiet, and Theo's arms dropped to his sides. Someone in the front row actually laughed, but not in a good way.

Ms. Rojas, the troupe's oldest member and unofficial mentor, gave Camille a ride home that night. She didn't lecture. She only said, "What you did back there has a name. Blocking." Then she turned up the radio and let Camille think.

Camille remembered the troupe's last showcase, weeks before she'd joined. Two boys had done a scene where one said, "Your dog is chewing my shoe," and the other answered, "No, that's not my dog." The audience had gone quiet right there, and the scene had stumbled to a stop, like a car rolling into a ditch. At the time Camille thought the second boy had just been unfunny. Now she wondered if there was a rule underneath it. Rejecting your partner's offer, or even ignoring it, seemed to stop the scene from moving forward. And maybe the opposite was true too. If she accepted every offer and added something of her own, the scene might build instead of die.

The next practice, she decided to test it. Theo started a scene by sitting on an invisible chair and announcing, "Grandma, the spaceship landed in our cabbage patch." Instead of denying him, Camille hobbled over as a grandmother, squinting at the window. "Then get my vacuum cleaner, sweetheart. I've always wanted to fight aliens with it." Theo's whole face changed. He grabbed the imaginary vacuum, and suddenly they were blasting cabbage thieves into orbit while the new kids in the audience laughed for real.

They ran it again, and again, and Camille noticed something. Every time Theo offered something, no matter how strange, and she said yes and added more, the scene grew richer. Every time either of them hesitated, it went flat, an impoverished little skit about nothing. "You changed your mind about me," Theo said at the end of practice, still holding the invisible vacuum. "Last week you looked at me like I was crazy."

"I thought you were breaking the rules," Camille admitted. "Turns out you were making them."

At the showcase, Theo turned to her on stage, held out an empty hand, and said, "Ready? The anchor's slipping." Camille gripped the rope.

Jace pressed his pencil so hard against the paper that the vanishing point turned into a small gray bruise. All his lines were supposed to meet there, and most of them did, but the street on his page still looked like it was falling sideways into a ditch. Mr. Okonkwo had said only one thing all period: "One point. Everything runs to it." That was it. No rescue mission, no demonstration on Jace's paper. Art class had quietly become Jace's most difficult subject, which was annoying, because he had signed up for it thinking it would be an easy A.

"Switch seats with me," said Priya, sliding her drawing across the table. Her street looked like a real street. Buildings on both sides, curb, sidewalk seams, all of it rushing toward a tidy dot.

"Why? Yours works."

"Because I want to draw the window side, and you've got the window seat." She pointed across the room, where their friend Dario was already set up at the tall table by the glass, looking down at the parking lot. "He's doing the street from up there. I'm doing it from down here. Same street, different height."

Jace looked at her drawing, then at his own, and felt the familiar itch of a mystery. Her horizon, the line where the vanishing point sat, was low on the page, barely above the car roofs she'd sketched in. His own horizon sat near the top. He had put it there because the top of the page seemed like a reasonable spot for a line, which, he now suspected, was a completely arbitrary decision.

Last semester flashed back to him, sharp and embarrassing. He'd argued with Dario for a full ten minutes about whether their comic panels were the same size, holding a ruler like a sword, only to discover he'd been measuring from the wrong edge the whole time. Dario had never let it go. "Measure twice, Jace," he said every time they split a pizza. Jace had made an adversary out of a ruler that day, and the ruler had won. He wasn't going to do that again with a horizon line.

He carried his paper to the window and crouched down, then stood on his toes, then crouched again, watching where the far end of the parking lot seemed to touch the sky. Down low, everything towered over him; up high, he was looking down on the hoods of cars. Back at his seat, he erased his high horizon and redrew it low, near the bottom, then recalibrated every line so they ran toward the relocated dot. He slowed down, checking each one against the edge of the ruler twice before committing.

The street changed under his pencil. The buildings rose like cliffs. The doors loomed. It looked less like a map now and more like standing at the bottom of the block on a summer afternoon, when he was eight and the ice cream truck's music came around the corner and everything seemed taller than him. Whether he'd liked being small like that, or had just gotten used to it, he honestly couldn't decide, and the drawing wasn't going to answer for him.

"Whoa," said Priya, leaning over. "Yours looks like a kid drew it."

"Thanks," Jace said, and then, hearing it, "I mean, thanks."

"Come here," Dario called from the window, waving his paper. His horizon sat high on the page, and his street lay below it like something spread out on a table, roofs visible, cars small and distant. He held it up against the glass, comparing. "Same street," he said slowly, "totally different view. That's wild."

"That's the whole point," Priya said. "Yours looks like the window drew it."

Jace set his drawing beside Dario's on the sill and stepped back to look at both. "Mine's from the curb," he said. "Kid height. Yours is from upstairs." He tapped the low horizon, then the high one. "I want to try one in the middle next."

Dario grinned and slid his ruler across the sill. "Measure twice," he said.

Harrison had exactly one free period before the code club demo, and he was spending it in the computer lab staring at a program that refused to behave. His prime checker worked for 7, it worked for 13, it even worked for 100, which was satisfyingly not prime. But the moment he typed 0, the screen announced that 0 was prime, which felt like being told his shoe was a bird.

"Try negative five," said Priya from the next computer, leaning over with the confidence of someone who had already broken her own program six times. "If it says that's prime too, I'm going to laugh."

He typed it. IS PRIME, said the screen.

"That's not even a little bit prime," Priya said. "My little brother knows that, and he thinks cartilage is a type of cheese."

Harrison scrolled through his code. The loop started at 2 and checked every possible divisor up to the number. For 0, it never found anything to reject it with, so the program fell through to the "prime" message. Same for 1. Same for every negative number he could throw at it. The loop started at 2, and there was simply nothing below that doing any work. He dragged his fingers through his hair. "So the loop can't catch them. They just slip past."

"Then catch them before the loop," Priya said, as if it were obvious, and stole his chair's spare cushion.

He typed a check at the top of the program: if the number was below 2, print NOT PRIME, then stop right there and never even start the divisor loop. It felt almost too simple. He saved the file twice, because his flash drive was old but durable, having survived a full year at the bottom of his backpack next to a leaking water bottle and a bag of gravel, or what had once been pretzels.

He typed 0. NOT PRIME. He typed 1. NOT PRIME. He typed negative 5, negative 12, and, feeling reckless, negative 900. NOT PRIME, every time, in neat gray letters.

"Okay, that's actually kind of beautiful," Priya admitted.

At the demo that afternoon, Mr. Alvarez asked for a volunteer number, and Marcus, who had once told Harrison that programming was for people who hated sunlight, called out "zero" with a grin. Harrison typed it in. NOT PRIME. Marcus's grin folded in on itself like a compromised sandwich.

"Fine," Marcus said. "Do negative four million."

Harrison's fingers were already moving.

Arthur had one goal at the science museum: beat the new exhibit before his sister Bea did. The exhibit was a giant touch-screen periodic table built into a wall shaped like a plateau of glowing squares, and a sign above it read, "Find the simplest element on the table. Win bragging rights."

"Simplest," Bea read out loud. "That's got to be gold, because it's the prettiest."

"That's not what simplest means," Arthur said, but he wasn't sure what it did mean. He started in the bottom rows, poking at squares. Uranium, number 92. Lead, 82. Everything down here had huge numbers in the corners, and the numbers felt like clues, though clues to what he couldn't say yet.

"Give up?" Bea teased after five minutes. "Want me to document your failure with a photo?"

"Push the wrong square again and I'll document yours." He worked his way up the wall, row by row, watching the numbers shrink: 20, then 11, then 6. It was like walking down a mountain, and the top of the mountain had to be the smallest number of all. He climbed to the top row and looked at the far left corner, and there it was, the very first square, sitting alone like a kid at the front of the class. Hydrogen. The number in its corner was 1.

"Every hydrogen atom has exactly one proton," the screen announced when he tapped it. "Atomic number 1 means one proton. That's what makes it the simplest element." Confetti exploded across the display, and Arthur did a small victory spin that he would later deny.

Bea peered at the square. "One proton? That's barely an atom. That's an atom with one sock."

"And it's still beating you." He tapped carbon next, number 6, and read its protons off the corner. Six. Then oxygen, 8. The rule held all the way down, and he began racing through squares, calling out numbers like a game show host.

A museum guide wandered past and smiled at the confetti. "You two found hydrogen, I see. First one today."

"Top left corner," Arthur said, pointing. "One proton. It was hiding in plain sight the whole time."

"Ironic," Bea said, "that the answer was the easiest thing to find, and we both made it hard." She grabbed his sleeve and dragged him toward the next room. "Come on, genius, the dinosaurs aren't going to defeat themselves."

Muhammad's social studies teacher had given every seventh grader the same assignment: go somewhere public, find one right listed in the country's constitution, and explain it in your own words to a real person. That was why Muhammad was standing outside the gymnasium of Lincoln Elementary on a Tuesday morning in November, holding his notebook like a shield.

The gym had been turned into a polling station. Folding tables stretched in rows, and machines at the far wall emitted a soft, steady beep whenever someone finished voting. A long line of adults snaked past the drinking fountains, everybody stamping their feet against the cold that leaked in whenever the doors opened. Muhammad's plan was simple. He would ask a poll worker to let him read the copy of the Constitution the library kept on display, pick a right, and explain it to his grandfather, who was somewhere in that line.

He found the display case first, right beside the "Vote Here" sign. The pages behind the glass were open to the amendments. He read down the list, mouthing the words, until one line made him stop. The Fifth Amendment. He knew that phrase. His older cousin watched a police show every Sunday, and the suspects on it were always saying, "I plead the Fifth," right before the dramatic music played. Muhammad had never known what it actually meant.

He copied the line into his notebook, letter by letter. Then he walked back toward the line to find his grandfather, and that was when he saw the problem. A man at the second table was arguing with a poll worker, his voice rising. "You can't make me tell you who I voted for," the man was saying. "I don't have to answer that."

Muhammad slowed down. He stood near the drinking fountain, pretending to fill his water bottle, though it was already full. The poll worker, a woman with silver braids, kept her voice low. "Sir, nobody's asking who you voted for. We only need your name for the check-in list." The man frowned, repeated his refusal, and the woman wrote something on a slip of paper and handed it to him. He took it and moved along, still grumbling.

Muhammad's heart was beating fast, though he couldn't have said why. Something clicked. He looked at the line in his notebook: no person can be forced, in a criminal case, to be a witness against themselves. The man at the table had borrowed the idea, maybe from a TV show, and Muhammad suddenly understood both what the man had meant and what he had gotten wrong. It was about criminal cases. Being a witness against yourself.

His grandfather was third from the front now, so Muhammad had maybe two minutes. He practiced under his breath, crossing out his first attempt, which sounded like he'd swallowed a textbook. His second try was plainer.

"Abu," he said when his grandfather reached the table, "I figured out my assignment." He held up the notebook. "The Fifth Amendment says no person can be forced, in a criminal case, to be a witness against themselves. Like, if someone got arrested, they don't have to answer questions that would get them in trouble."

His grandfather read the notebook page, then looked at him for a long moment. "That's an eloquent way to put it," he said. "Now tell me why that fellow at the table was wrong."

Muhammad glanced back toward the second table, where the silver-braided worker was already helping the next voter. The man with the slip of paper stood by the machines, hesitating, the paper crumpled slightly in his fist.

"I think," Muhammad said slowly, "he thought it meant he never had to answer anything. But it's only criminal cases."

His grandfather nodded toward the voting machines. "Go ask her," he said. "The worker. Ask what the paper says."

Muhammad looked at the paper in the man's hand, then at the worker's calm face, and started walking over.

Michael sat cross-legged on the rug in Dev's basement, balancing the laptop on a stack of old board games. The screen glowed in the dim room, and somewhere behind the water heater a fan hummed steadily. He had typed a heading, "Dev's Comics Reviews," in big letters at the top of his very first web page, and now the words sat stubbornly against the left edge.

"I want it in the middle," Michael said. "Exactly the middle."

"Then you need CSS," said Dev, who was sprawled on the couch with a comic open on his chest, only half watching. "Add a style. There's a thing called text-align."

Michael tried it, typing text-align: center into the style for his heading, and hit refresh. The words slid to the middle of the page, right where he wanted them. That should have been the end of it, but a question snagged him. The middle of what? Before, the letters had hugged the left side, so how did the page know how far to move them? He stared at the heading and tried to imagine invisible measurements underneath it.

"Wait," he said slowly. "When it was left-aligned, the text only took up this much space." He held his thumb and finger a few inches apart. "But to find the middle, something has to know the whole width. The letters aren't that wide."

Dev set his comic down. "Try an experiment. You're the scientist type anyway."

Michael retrieved a small notebook from his backpack and wrote the word MIDDLE, then an approximate sketch of the page with the heading drawn in. He had an idea. If the heading itself stretched all the way across, then centering the text would land it in the middle of the page. If the heading were only as wide as its words, the text would sit off to one side. He gave the heading a temporary background color, a garish green, and refreshed again.

The green bar ran from the left edge of the page to the right edge, the whole width, with the centered words floating in the middle of it. Michael laughed out loud. "It's a block element. It stretches across the full width of its container. That's why the text lands in the middle of the page when I center it." Dev leaned over the couch arm to look, nodded once, and went back to his comic.

Michael removed the green background and saved the file. The heading sat clean and centered, exactly where he had wanted it, and beneath it he began typing the first line of Dev's first review. "Start with issue number one," Dev said without looking up. Michael's fingers were already moving.

Blake stared at the screen in Dev's basement, where the words "Enter a number:" blinked at him like a challenge. The program was supposed to say whether a number was prime, and it was supposed to say it correctly, which was the part currently failing.

"Nine is not prime," Dev said, reading the output. "Your program says it is."

"That's impossible. It only divides by two." Blake leaned closer to the laptop, as if the bug might crawl out where he could see it. Bugs were like that, he thought. You couldn't watch one work. You could only see the mess it left behind, like footprints in snow, and work backward.

"So follow the footprints," Dev said, sounding way too pleased with himself. He pulled a marker and a sheet of paper out of a drawer full of markers, paper, and one very old granola bar. "Write the numbers one to fifty. We'll check every answer by hand."

Blake copied the grid while Dev typed another test. "Twenty-five," Dev called. The program declared it prime. Five times five, Blake thought. Twenty-five was definitely not prime, so the program was wrong in a way it hadn't been wrong for nine, and the hidden cause had to be the same one, just hiding better.

"Your program's like a consumer that trusts the label and never checks the box," Dev said.

"It's not a consumer, it's obstinate," Blake said. "I told it to divide by everything up to the number, and it just... isn't." He squinted at the loop. There. The range stopped one step too early. He fixed it, ran it again, and twenty-five came back not prime. "Ha!"

"Now we check the whole grid," Dev said, and started crossing out numbers. He circled two, then crossed out four, six, eight, every second number. Then he circled three and crossed out its multiples in turn. Then five, then seven. What remained, uncrossed, were the primes.

"Wait," Blake said, scanning the paper. "Eleven, thirteen, seventeen. My program says those are prime too. Every single one matches."

"Know what this is called?" Dev said, holding up the paper. "The Sieve of Eratosthenes. Some ancient Greek method."

"So my laptop and a guy with no electricity agree," Blake said. "Two thousand years apart."

Dev grinned and slid the granola bar across the table in tribute. Blake pocketed it, typed "one hundred and seven" into the program, and the word "prime" popped onto the screen.

Jackson stared at his blank page and wished his characters would just shut up, except they weren't talking at all. His rough draft was all summary: Maya went to the lake, then Maya found the boat, then Maya got scared. Mr. Ruiz had circled three paragraphs and written "Where is the dialogue? Where is your climax?" in aggressive red ink that made the paper look like it had been in a fight.

Across the table, Priya flipped her worksheet over and sketched a jagged line climbing upward. "Mine looks like a mountain," she said. "The climax is the peak." She tapped the top of her drawing. "It's called Freytag's pyramid. My cousin told me about it. It comes from a guy named Gustav Freytag who wrote a book on drama in 1863." She drew the line falling down the other side. "The plot rises to the climax at the peak, then falls after."

Jackson borrowed her pencil and drew his own mountain under Priya's, because hers left room. "So my story's been flat." He plotted dots along the slope. "Maya hears a noise at the bottom. Then she sees the boat. Then the boat drifts loose with her little brother on it, and that's the peak." He tested the idea by rereading his draft. Every event sat on the low ground, bunched together. That was why the story felt like a list instead of a climb.

He started rewriting at the lake itself. "What are you doing out here?" Maya called. Her brother's voice came back thin over the water: "Getting the rope off the propeller." Jackson remembered the rules from the board, quotation marks around the words, comma before the tag, new paragraph whenever the speaker changed. He messed it up twice and fixed it, and Priya leaned over.

"Your dialogue does the rising now," she said. "Every line makes it worse for Maya. That's the climb." She pointed at his peak. "You could nominate the brother to shout something scary right there. Like the motor starting by itself." Jackson laughed and wrote it: "It's going, Maya, it's going, I can't reach the key!" The fall came fast after that, Maya swimming, the rope, the shallow water, the two of them coughing on the bank.

Mr. Ruiz walked the rows and stopped at their table. He read Jackson's page, then the mountain on the back of Priya's worksheet, and his eyebrows went up. "You made an inference from a drawing," he said. "Not bad." He set a sticky note beside Jackson's climax: Read aloud to the class? Jackson looked at Priya, who gave him a thumbs up, and he wrote one word under the note: Yes.

Every night before the canoe trip, Alyssa's stomach felt tight and upset, and on Tuesday she could not fall asleep until the raccoons outside the cabin were already raiding the marshmallow bag. She assumed the bug was going around camp. But when she thought about it, the stomachaches had started the exact day Ms. Ruiz posted the sign-up sheet for the canoe trip, and they seemed to orbit that sheet the way the moths orbited the porch light. That was a pattern. Patterns meant something.

On Wednesday night the stomachache came back, along with sweaty palms, and by Thursday she had a headache too, right behind her eyes. Three symptoms. Her bunkmate Dree leaned down from the top bunk and said, "You look like a ghost that lost its sheet."

"I feel like a ghost that lost its whole laundry," Alyssa said. She held up her hands. "Look. Sweaty palms. Again."

Dree climbed down and sat on the edge of the lower bunk. "My cousin used to get stomachaches every Sunday night," she said. "And a pharmacist asked her mom if something big happened at school on Mondays. It turned out it was stress. Stress can show up in the body like that. Headaches, a tight or upset stomach, sweaty palms, trouble falling asleep. She had basically the whole menu."

Alyssa lay back and stared at the ceiling. She was not sick. She was stressed, and her body was reporting it like a walkie-talkie. But that raised a question she could actually test. If stress was causing the trouble falling asleep, maybe she could do something about it. The next afternoon she found Ms. Ruiz, who had told everyone on day one that she was there as their mentor, not their boss. "Can I ask you something that isn't about canoes?" Alyssa said. "How do you calm down before something scary?"

Ms. Ruiz laughed. "Slow breathing. In for four, out for six. I do it before I drive over that narrow bridge to town, and I used to be aggressive about honking at anyone who slowed me down on it."

That night, Alyssa tried the breathing in her bunk. In for four, out for six, while her brain insisted the canoe would tip and the lake was full of imaginary sharks. She also made a routine: same order every night, teeth, bag packed for morning, flashlight off at exactly nine. On Friday she fell asleep before the raccoons even clocked in. On Saturday her stomach was quiet and her hands were dry, and she paddled the whole lake without tipping, although Dree splashed her once with an aggressive backstroke on purpose.

"See?" Dree shouted from the other canoe. "No stomachache!"

"No menu!" Alyssa shouted back, and dipped her paddle into the cold green water.

Claire slid Hamlet across the study table until the book stopped against the lamp, its edges worn soft by a hundred hands before hers. The assignment was due Monday: paraphrase Act Three, Scene One into modern English, and Mrs. Okafor had written one word in red at the top of the instruction sheet, "soliloquy," underlined twice. Claire was fairly sure she was the only one in ninth grade who didn't know what it meant, and she wasn't about to ask Devon, who had already told half the cafeteria that she'd spelled "rhythm" wrong on the last quiz.

The library hummed around her, quiet but not silent: the heater ticking, a cart of returns squeaking somewhere behind biography, the smell of old paper and lemon floor cleaner. She read the first line again. "To be, or not to be, that is the question." Easy enough. She wrote, "Should I keep living, or should I not." Then the speeches turned strange. Hamlet wasn't talking to anyone. No Horatio, no Ophelia, nobody. He just stood there spilling everything, thinking out loud about death and sleep and dreams, and the more she read, the more it felt like eavesdropping through a wall.

She flipped back through the scene, checking each speech. When Claudius spoke, Rosencrantz answered him. When Polonius lectured Ophelia, she at least stood there listening. But Hamlet's long speeches had no listener at all, and that was the pattern, the same shape repeating. She grabbed a pencil and drew a small X beside every speech where the character was alone, talking to nobody but the room. Four X marks. Then she flipped ahead to the scene where Claudius prays, and found another X there too, a king alone, confessing a murder to the empty air.

Her pencil went still. Claudius wasn't confessing to anyone in the play. He was confessing to her, to whoever sat in the dark beyond the stage. That was the trick of it, and she felt the whole structure click into place like a combination lock. The word itself must mean this, a private speech poured out on purpose so the audience hears the secret. She underlined "soliloquy" in her notebook and wrote beside it, "alone on stage, thoughts aloud, audience eavesdrops." Then she began the paraphrase again, slower this time, because now the words had a direction, like a letter addressed to her seat in the theater.

At the next table, Mr. Ferris from the front desk was reshelving parliament debates from the history section, thick blue volumes that smelled of dust. "How's the Bard treating you?" he asked, peering over.

"Better now," Claire said. "He's telling me secrets."

She read Hamlet's line once more, wanting her version to preserve that private, overheard feeling rather than flatten it. The heater ticked. Down the aisle, the book cart squeaked and stopped. She wrote, "The real question is whether to keep going at all, and whether it's braver to put up with everything or to end it," then crossed out "everything" and wrote "the whole mess," because that was how a boy alone at midnight would actually say it. Somewhere behind biography, a page turned, soft as a held breath.

The rain began just after they finished pitching the tent, and Penelope spread her two printed satellite images across the picnic table under the tarp, weighting the corners with pinecones. The picture on the left showed Asia in January. The one on the right showed the same continent in July. Her best friend Rumela crouched beside her, arms crossed against the drizzle, waiting.

"Your mom really farms rice back there?" Rumela asked, and Penelope nodded. Last summer, during the video call, her grandmother had stood in a flooded paddy field and held the phone low so Penelope could see the water catching the sky. That field needed the rain, her grandmother had said, or the rice would not grow, and Penelope had promised to understand it properly before the family visited next year.

"I keep getting it wrong in practice," Penelope said. "My presentation just says rains come, then rice grows. That's not an explanation. That's a weather report with a plant stuck on the end." She tapped the January image. "Look here. There's a band of clouds around the middle of the Earth, near the equator. It's like a belt." She ran her finger along the bright white streak crossing the ocean below India. Then she moved her hand to the July image and stopped. The belt had moved. It sat farther north, draped over South Asia itself, right where her grandmother's fields were.

Rumela leaned in, rain dripping off the tarp between them. "So in January the band is down here," she said, pointing at the equator, "and in July it's up over India. What's it called?"

"The Intertropical Convergence Zone," Penelope said. "It's a rainy band of rising air." She stood very still, because the pieces were lining up in her head the way knots line up before they come undone. The band shifted north in the northern summer. The band was rainy. When it shifted over South Asia, the rains came with it. That was the monsoon, arriving because the band had moved, not out of nowhere. "That's why the rains come when they come," she said slowly. "The whole thing follows the band."

She grabbed a pencil and, on the back of a permission slip, drew a rough map with a cloud stripe, then sketched the same map again with the stripe pushed upward, the two drawings side by side and almost symmetrical. "I can show these on the projector and let everyone watch it move," she said. "Nobody has to take my word for it. They can see it themselves." She thought of her grandmother standing in the flooded field, the crop rising out of water that had traveled halfway up a continent. "If I mess this up in class, I can't exactly retire from being half-Indian," she said, and Rumela laughed. "The protagonist of this presentation is the cloud band anyway. I'm just the narrator."

The rain drummed harder on the tarp. Penelope slid both images into a plastic sleeve, zipped it into her pack, and said, "Rice and rain. One follows the other. Grandmother, you're getting a good report this time."

Elliot stood in the synagogue library with his reading packet in one hand and a pencil in the other, staring at the same Hebrew line for the fourth time. In two weeks he would chant his bar mitzvah portion in front of everyone, and so far he had memorized exactly one and a half verses out of nine.

"You look like a boy who lost his shoes," said Mr. Adler, who shelved books on Tuesdays. He was not the rabbi, just a man who liked quiet and order.

"I keep saying it and it disappears," Elliot said. "I'll get a line perfect, then the next one contradicts it in my head. Same words, different order, and my brain picks the wrong one every time."

Mr. Adler tapped the packet. "My grandmother used the method of loci," he said. "Ask your mother what it means. Or figure it out yourself, which is better." Then he wheeled his cart away, which was how he ended most conversations.

That night, Elliot sprawled on his grandmother's living room rug while she knitted in her chair. He told her the problem: nine verses, all tangled, a contradiction between every other pair of lines in his memory. She set down her needles.

"Try my house," she said. "Walk through it in your mind. You know every corner."

So he did. First verse went at the front door, where the mezuzah sat at a tilt nobody fixed. Second verse in the hallway with the mirror. Third on the kitchen table, next to the bowl of walnuts. Fourth in the pantry, fifth on the basement stairs, sixth by the washing machine, seventh in the sewing room, eighth under her humming ceiling fan, ninth at the back door with its sticky handle. He placed each line in its spot and said it there, out loud, until the words seemed to belong to the walnuts and the mirror and the stairs.

The next morning he tested it. He closed his eyes and walked the route in his mind: door, mezuzah, hallway, mirror, kitchen, walnuts. Each verse rose up out of its place, in order, whole. He walked the route three times without a single slip, and when his grandmother shuffled in with tea, he recited all nine verses standing in her actual kitchen, grinning like the fan above him had made him buoyant.

On the bimah two weeks later, Elliot closed his eyes for half a second, saw a tilted mezuzah, and began. His voice held steady through the pantry and the sewing room and the sticky back door, and when he finished, Mr. Adler nodded once from the third row. After the service, Elliot's little sister tugged his sleeve.

"How did you remember all that?"

"Meet me at Grandma's," he said. "I'll give you the tour."

Grandpa's kitchen smelled like coffee and toast, and the kettle was sending thin curls of vapor toward the ceiling when Madison opened her laptop. Grandma slid a plate of biscuits beside her and said, "The principal wants my survey numbers by seven tonight, sweetpea. Two hundred kids answered, and I can't make heads or tails of the list." Madison had promised she could do it. She had watched one video about pivot tables last night, twice, and she figured that was enough.

She dragged the Grade column into the rows area, then dragged Answers into values, and the spreadsheet snapped everything into tidy counts: sixth grade, seventh grade, eighth grade. And then a fourth row she had not asked for. "Grandma, is there a fourth grade at your school?" Grandma leaned over her shoulder, squinting. "There is not." The extra row sat there in gray letters, labeled "(blank)", with eleven kids in it.

Madison tapped the table with her pen. A hidden cause, she thought, like a draft you can't see moving the curtains. She could infer what it meant, or she could test it. She went back to the raw list and sorted the Grade column, scrolling until the empty cells clustered together at the bottom. Eleven of them. Eleven rows where somebody had answered the survey question but left the grade box untouched. Eleven kids who skipped it. The counts matched exactly. She sat back so fast the chair squeaked.

"Those eleven didn't write their grade down," she said. "So the table gives them their own group, "(blank)"". Grandma laughed and patted the table like it had done her a favor. "Skippers. Every school has them." She copied the numbers onto a lined pad for her meeting, and her handwriting was quick and sure, the way it used to be before the tremor came.

The clock over the stove said six forty when Madison added the totals to Grandma's notes, checked them twice, and emailed everything to the principal. Grandma hugged her, then stood a moment at the window with the pad still in her hand, and Madison saw her mouth the numbers silently, rehearsing, the way she did now to keep hold of things. There had been a time Grandma would have presented without notes at all, without needing anybody.

"You'll come with me Thursday?" Grandma asked. "You can fix it if the laptop fusses." Madison said yes, even though Thursday was the night of the recital she'd been practicing for since September. The kitchen light hummed. Grandma poured the last of the coffee, and the steam rose off the cup and vanished before it reached the ceiling.

The basement smelled like old carpet and grape soda, and Marisol's older brother had covered one wall with posters of eccentric inventors, Tesla chief among them, glaring down over the desk where two laptops sat. Asher pulled his chair closer and cracked his knuckles.

"Okay," Marisol said. "You write it. I'm not touching the keyboard." She slid a napkin across the desk. On it, in her cramped handwriting, was the plan: ask for a number, then try dividing it by everything smaller, and print whether it was prime. Asher had exactly one reason to be here. On Friday, a kid in math class had bet him a candy bar that he couldn't explain how a computer decided such a thing, and Asher, tired of nodding along while other people understood the world, had said he could learn by Monday.

He typed while Marisol peeled electrical tape off a science-fair motor in the corner, wrapping the bare spots to insulate the wires so it wouldn't spark again. He could hear the tape ripping in little strips. The heater in the basement clanked, and somewhere behind the wall a copper conductor hummed with whatever electricity a house carried around inside it.

His first version ran. He typed 9, and the program filled the whole screen with "not prime," the same two words fifty times, scrolling and scrolling like something possessed. Asher sat back. "It works," he said, "sort of. But why so many?" He read his own loop out loud, tracing it with his finger. The answer rose up slow, the way a shape appears in fog. The loop kept going after it already knew. Every single smaller number got its own announcement. "The loop doesn't know it's done," he said. Marisol leaned over, chewing the end of a pen.

"So tell it," she said.

He wasn't sure how, so he texted his cousin, who was away at camp: MY PRIME CHECKER PRINTS NOT PRIME A MILLION TIMES HELP. The reply came as a single sentence, and Asher read it twice. "A break statement stops a loop immediately," he said aloud. Marisol wrote it on the napkin, right under the plan, and underlined "immediately" twice. So the checker could quit as soon as it found a single divisor. One divisor, one answer, done.

Asher indented a new line, typed the word, and ran it again. He entered 9 and the screen printed "not prime" exactly once, then went still and waited. He entered 7. Prime. He entered 51, feeling sneaky, and the program said "not prime" without flinching. Marisol pumped her fist and slid the candy-bar wager napkin across the desk so he could draft his reply to the kid from math class. Asher cracked his knuckles again and started typing.

"Wait," Marisol said, pointing at the screen. "What about the number one?"

Edouard balanced his notebook on his knees as the bus rattled toward the science center. Every Thursday, the six members of the Inventors Club met on the long ride to their workshop, and today was the first time he would run the meeting himself. He had typed an agenda the night before: tinker at the old item first, then vote on the new project, then assign jobs. His friend Sam leaned over the seat and read it upside down.

"An agenda," Sam said. "Very official."

"It's so everyone gets a chance to speak," Edouard said. "Even quiet people like Priya."

The meeting started well. Priya reported that the club had finally managed to acquire the small motor they needed, which meant the robot arm could actually be built. Then Marcus raised his hand, which was good, except that what he said had nothing to do with the robot arm. He wanted to build a cat feeder out of the old cereal dispenser. The whole bus seat erupted into an argument about whether cats would even use it.

"Back to item two," Edouard said. "The vote on the new project."

They got thirty seconds of voting before Yasmin remembered a component she had seen at the hobby shop, a wheel that glowed in the dark, and suddenly everyone was debating glow-in-the-dark wheels. Every time Edouard dragged them back, another idea burst loose like a leak in a boat. He noticed a pattern: it was never the quiet members who derailed things. Priya had spoken exactly once. The loud voices were the chronic ones, speaking over and over, and the good ideas that pulled them off track were almost always the loud ones too.

So Edouard tested a simple idea. Instead of shutting Marcus and Yasmin down, which just made them louder, he wrote their ideas down in a list at the back of his notebook. Marcus's cat feeder. Yasmin's glowing wheels.

"What's that part of the agenda?" Sam asked.

"It's called a parking lot," Edouard said. "A list where the meeting leader writes down off-topic ideas so they can be discussed later, instead of derailing the current item."

Marcus squinted at it, then sat back, satisfied that his idea was safely stored somewhere. Yasmin stopped talking, because she could see her wheels sitting on the page, waiting for her. The bus went quiet in a strange new way, and in that quiet, Priya raised her hand.

"I think the cat feeder could be the next project," she said. "But the robot arm is due Friday. If we finish the arm first, Marcus's feeder could use the leftover motor mounts."

Nobody interrupted her. Marcus actually wrote that down.

At the workshop, the vote took four minutes, and the club finished the robot arm with time left to sketch the feeder. On the ride home, Priya tapped Edouard's notebook.

"Your parking lot," she said. "Can I run the meeting next week?"

The sunflower seeds in Addison's cup were the only thing she had managed to grow all summer, and even those had just begun to germinate, tiny pale hooks pushing out of the soil on the camp's nature shelf. She checked them every morning before breakfast, mostly to avoid the table where Dex Turner sat. For the third day in a row, Dex had dumped Noah's tray supplies into the mud, called him "Shrimp Boy," and laughed while his two friends laughed with him. Noah was smaller than everyone, and he never said anything back. Addison kept deciding it wasn't her business, and every night the decision sat in her chest like a stone.

On Thursday she watched Marcus and Ben argue over a paddle by the canoe dock. They shouted, shoved each other once, and then Marcus said, "Fine, take it," and they were laughing again by lunch. That was when the pieces started fitting together in Addison's head. One argument, between two boys who were basically equal, ended on its own. What happened to Noah was different. It happened again and again, and it was always three against one.

"So it's not the same thing at all," she said to Noah at the craft table, keeping her voice low.

"Not the same as what?" Noah asked, weaving a lanyard with frail, careful fingers.

"Marcus and Ben fighting. That's just a one-time thing between equals. What those guys do to you is repeated, and they've got all the power because there's three of them and one of you." She picked up a strand of plastic lace. "My cousin told me researchers actually define it that way. If it's repeated and there's an imbalance of power, it's bullying."

Noah's hands stopped moving. "I thought it was just joking," he said quietly.

"That's what he wants you to think," Addison said. She felt the guilt of three silent mornings rise up, and she made herself a promise about it. "Here's my idea. We don't fight him. We just make sure you're never alone, and we tell Counselor Rivera exactly what happened, with dates. Repeated things leave a pattern, and patterns are easy to prove."

On Friday, Dex reached for Noah's water bottle at the archery range, and Addison stepped into his path. "You've done something to him every single day this week," she said, loud enough that the group turned. "Counselor Rivera has the whole list." Dex's two friends looked at their shoes. Dex shoved his hands in his pockets and walked off toward the target shed, alone.

Noah shot an arrow that landed near the center of the target. Then he turned to Addison and asked, "Did the sunflower seeds sprout this morning?"

Grayson slid his copy of "The Lottery" to the center of the table and tapped the first paragraph, where he had folded the corner of the page. "Read the opening again," he said. "Out loud. Trust me."

Priya, who ran the book club and had the only working thermos in the room, raised an eyebrow but picked up her own copy. "The morning of June 27th was clear and sunny, with the fresh warmth of a full-summer day; the flowers were blossoming profusely and the grass was richly green." She kept going. "Bobby Martin had already stuffed his pockets full of stones, and the other boys soon followed his example, selecting the smoothest and roundest stones."

"Stop there," Grayson said. "Yesterday I skipped right past that. Stones seemed like, I don't know, kids being kids on a nice morning." He had read the whole story that night in one sitting, and when he reached the last page he had gone back to the beginning because something about it bothered him. "But the story was in The New Yorker back in 1948, and it ends the way it ends. The stones are sitting right there in the first paragraph."

The folding table wobbled as Dev leaned forward. "So it's like a hint?"

"It's called foreshadowing," Grayson said. "The writer plants something early that points at what happens later." He felt a little shaky saying it, since until this morning he had called it "the stone thing" in his notes. "When I reread that paragraph after finishing the story, the stones weren't harmless anymore. They were the ending, hidden in plain sight on page one."

Priya set down her thermos, which she guarded like a sacred vessel, and looked almost proud, which made Grayson remember the meeting two months ago when he had shown up without reading the book and sat there barren of anything to say while everyone else argued for an hour. He had decided that night to nurture a new habit: read everything twice, once for what happens and once for how it was built.

"Okay," Dev said, flipping pages. "So what else is a hint? The black box? That's got to mean something too. The name, the color, all of it."

"That's symbolism," Priya said slowly. "When an object stands for something bigger than itself." She frowned at her page. "Although what exactly it stands for, I'm not sure I want to say out loud yet."

Grayson pulled his chair closer and grabbed a pencil. "Then let's make a list. Every object, every detail, and we mark which ones feel like hints and which ones feel like symbols. Nobody leaves until we've argued about all of them."

Priya refilled the thermos cup and slid it across the table to him. "You want the last of the tea before we start? Because once I get going on that box, there won't be any left."

"Dude, I'm going to find the biggest prime number ever," Henry announced, dropping his backpack next to Marcus's basement couch. "And then they'll name it after me."

Marcus spun around in his desk chair, laptop open, a bag of chips between his knees. "You can't. Also, we're supposed to be writing your Python program today, remember? The prime checker? For extra credit?"

"That's exactly the plan." Henry pulled out his notebook, already covered in numbers. "The program tests if a number is prime. So I test bigger and bigger numbers until I find one so big nobody's ever tested it. Boom. Henry's Prime." He cracked his knuckles like he was about to lift something heavy.

Marcus chewed a chip and watched his friend open the laptop. The basement smelled like popcorn and old carpet, and the ceiling fan clicked in its slow, chronic way, a sound Marcus's dad kept promising to fix and never did. Henry typed fast, tongue between his teeth.

"I'm asking for a number," he explained, "and then the program checks if anything divides into it. If nothing does, it's prime."

"Okay, but you have to tell it how to check," Marcus said, leaning over. "It's not just going to know."

That was the part that provoked Henry into actually thinking instead of just typing. A number either had divisors or it didn't, but the computer couldn't see that. It had to try dividing, one number at a time, like feeling around a dark room. He wrote a loop, dividing by two, then three, then four, and if any division came out even, the number failed. If the loop survived all the way through, it was prime.

"Try nine," Marcus said.

Henry typed nine and hit enter. NOT PRIME, the screen said.

"Try eleven."

PRIME.

Henry whooped so loud Marcus's dog barked upstairs. They tested a hundred, then a thousand and nine, then six thousand fifty-three, which turned out to be prime, and Henry wrote it on his arm with a pen because his notebook was across the room and that seemed too far to walk.

Then he typed a number with twelve digits. The cursor blinked. The fan clicked. The screen just sat there, thinking, and Henry's heart started thumping like the program was a racehorse he'd bet on. Finally: PRIME.

"Okay, that's a big one," Marcus said. "Is it the biggest?"

Henry started typing a bigger one, then a way bigger one, digits spilling across the line like a runaway train. Somewhere in the middle of all this, Marcus's older sister came down to do laundry, saw the screen, and laughed.

"You know there's no biggest prime, right?"

"There has to be," Henry said. "There's a biggest everything."

"Not primes." She shoved clothes into the washer. "Euclid proved it. Around 300 BC. He wrote it in this book, the Elements. Infinitely many primes. They just never stop."

Henry stared at her, then at his screen, where his giant number sat with PRIME glowing under it. He felt a strange dip, like missing the last step on a staircase. No Henry's Prime. No naming ceremony. His whole plan had a hole in it the size of forever.

He sat back down anyway. His twelve-digit prime was still up there, still real, still his, even if it wasn't the last one. "Fine," he said. "Then I'll find a bigger one than anyone at school has ever seen."

"That's the spirit," Marcus said, and Henry's fingers were already back on the keys.

"Give me a number with twenty digits."

Camille stood in the langar hall after morning services, a photocopied page of Gurmukhi trembling in her hand. Her grandmother had promised the whole family would come from Brampton in three weeks, and by then Camille had to know Japji Sahib by heart, every line, without the paper. She had recited it four times that morning and stumbled at the same spot every time, where the sounds doubled back on themselves like a path that loops.

Outside, her little brother Arjan flew his drone over the parking lot, its propeller catching the sun. Through the window she watched him modify the angle of the landing skids with tape, adjusting after each rough touchdown, and she thought about how he never fixed the crash, only what came after it. She had been trying to fix her mistake the same way, repeating the broken line louder, as if volume could glue the words together.

"You're grinding your teeth," said Simran, sinking onto the bench across from her. Simran was seventeen and had gone through her own ceremony last spring, though she never talked about it much. Camille wanted to ask why she'd done it so young, but that question felt like opening someone's lunchbox.

"Why does it have to be this prayer?" Camille asked instead. "Why not something shorter?" She was thinking of a conversation she wasn't supposed to have overheard, her uncle saying fourteen was too young to choose the Amrit Sanchar path, her mother saying nothing at all.

Simran turned her steel bracelet slowly around her wrist. "It's recited at the ceremony itself," she said. "The Khalsa initiation. Amrit Sanchar. You'll hear it on the day, standing right there." She said it plainly, the way you'd say the bus comes at eight, and Camille felt the ground shift a little. The prayer wasn't just a test to pass and forget. It would be in the room with her, in the moment itself, and everyone who had taken that step before her had carried the same words in their mouths.

That night Camille tried something different. Instead of attacking the broken line, she went back two lines before it and recited forward slowly, like walking a hill from the bottom instead of being dropped on the ridge. On the fourth try the difficult phrase arrived on its own, riding the rhythm of what came before it, and she understood that the mistake had never been in the line at all. It was in the approach, hidden further back, invisible until she tested it.

She called Simran, who picked up on the second ring. "I got through the whole thing," Camille said. "Twice." Through the phone came the sound of dishes being set down. "Twice," Simran repeated. "Then tomorrow you do it three times, out loud, standing up." Camille laughed, set the phone on her desk on speaker, and began again from the first line.

Lillian sat at the kitchen table trying to look casual, which was hard with a page of notes in her lap labeled "PLAN." Across from her, eight-year-old Theo was cutting his grilled cheese into perfectly symmetrical triangles and announcing that he was an herbivore this week, "except for cheese, and also turkey on Saturdays."

"I need to practice something on you," she said. "Pretend you're Dylan Reyes."

"Theo Reyes," he said, mouth full. "That's my name now."

"Fine. Theo Reyes. Yesterday in the cafeteria, Marcus tripped carrying his tray, and Dylan laughed and called him Plates, because the tray went flying, and everyone started chanting it. Today it happened again. Tomorrow I want to do something, but if I yell at Dylan, I'll just provoke him in front of everybody and it'll get worse for Marcus. So I'm testing a different move."

Theo pushed a cheese triangle toward her as a fee. "Go ahead."

Lillian took a breath. "Hey Marcus, come sit with us, there's room." She said it flat, then tried it again, warmer, like an afterthought, like it wasn't a rescue at all. Theo chewed and considered. "The second one," he said. "The first one sounded like you felt sorry for him. Marcus hates that. He bit me at daycare once for that exact reason."

Lillian wrote "casual. warm. not sorry-sounding" on the page. Then she slid her science binder across the table and pulled out a worksheet Theo was supposed to be finishing, because Mom had put him in her charge until six. At the top of his reading sheet was a boxed fact for a question about playgrounds: In 2001, a study of school playgrounds found that when a classmate stepped in to stop bullying, the bullying stopped in more than half of the cases.

She read it twice. "Theo. Kids stepping in actually works? More than half the time?"

"That's what the box says. I have to write if it surprises me." He frowned. "It does surprise me, because Marcus is huge."

"Shhh. You're being Marcus's conscience now." Lillian tapped the worksheet with her pen. She had been assuming that stepping in meant a showdown, a speech, a confrontation that would only feed Dylan an audience. But the study didn't say the classmate fought anybody. Maybe most kids stepped in the way you'd step in anywhere: sideways, ordinary, like it was nothing. An extra tray carried. A seat offered. A chant left unjoined until it died of quiet.

The kitchen smelled like toasted butter and the lemon cleaner Mom had used on the counters, and outside somebody's sprinkler ticked against the fence in a steady rhythm, and Lillian typed a message to the group chat with one thumb while Theo watched over her shoulder like it was television.

"Marcus. Lunch tomorrow, our table, me and Priya and Sam. Bring the tray, we like the drama."

She hovered over send. Too jokey? No, jokey was right, jokey was the casual warm voice, jokey made it not a rescue. She sent it. Three dots appeared, and she held her breath through an entire symmetrical bite of Theo's cheese.

"ok," Marcus wrote. Then, "nobody's ever asked before."

Theo solemnly closed the worksheet. "Write that it surprised me," he said.

Lydia had one hundred ninety dollars in her sock drawer and a snowboard in the mall's sporting goods window with a tag that said $549. The tag also said FINANCING AVAILABLE, in smaller letters, which Lydia suspected was the retail equivalent of a trapdoor. She had five years until she finished school and, according to the poster by the mall fountain, the new credit union kiosk was offering savings accounts at five percent. She got in line behind a man arguing about a late fee.

The teller, whose name tag said DARA, asked if Lydia needed help. Lydia slid the snowboard brochure across the counter and said she wanted to know what five percent would do to one hundred ninety dollars over five years. "Simple or compound?" Dara asked, and Lydia said, "The one that's better," because that seemed like the obvious answer. Dara handed her a calculator and said, "Compounded once a year, the balance after n years is P times 1 plus r, to the power n." Then she got pulled away by the man with the late fee, which Lydia decided was fine, since she had her own brain and a power key.

She typed 190, then multiplied by 1.05, then hit the power key with a 5, trying not to feel optimistic before she saw the number. The screen said 242.35. She stared at it. Five percent of 190 was 9.50, and five years of that was 47.50, which would make 237.50, not 242.35. She did the simple version again on paper to be sure, and it still said 237.50. The compound version was 4.85 more, which was not a fortune but was, notably, more, and it had come from nowhere she could see. She tried three years: 219.73 compound versus 218.50 simple. The gap grew every time she added a year, like something quietly accumulating behind a wall.

The man with the late fee had positioned himself to obstruct the whole kiosk, waving a statement at Dara, so Lydia worked at the end of the counter. She ran the numbers again with P as 300, just to see if the pattern belonged to her 190 dollars or to the rule itself. It belonged to the rule. Compound won by more, the longer she left it alone.

"Find out what you needed?" Dara asked, finally escaping.

"Five years of compound gets me to 242," Lydia said. "Simple gets me 237.50." She looked at the brochure. The snowboard would still cost 549. "So my actual plan is birthday money plus a summer job."

"Mathematical," Dara said, "and realistic."

Lydia folded the brochure into her back pocket and headed for the food court, already doing the arithmetic on wages and time.

Juliette slid her notebook across the cafe table so Marta could see it, then wished she hadn't, because Marta's eyebrows went up in a way that promised ridicule before she'd read a single line. The writing club had claimed the corner booth again, four mugs and one shared lemon pound cake between them, and tomorrow every member had to turn in a one-page essay with a real argument in it.

"My thesis is that homework makes students tired," Marta announced, tapping her pen. "Done. Now I just need three points."

"Everyone knows homework makes you tired," said Dev, without looking up from his laptop.

"Exactly. It's true." Marta spread her hands, triumphant.

Juliette looked down at her own page, where she'd written and crossed out the same sentence three times: School starts too early for teenagers. Her hand ached and her eyes had that gritty fatigue that came from staring at one line for forty minutes. Something about Marta's thesis was bothering her, and she couldn't name it yet.

"Play it out," she said slowly, testing the idea the way she'd test a wobbly table, by pressing on it. "Imagine a hypothetical reader. You say homework makes students tired. Who says no? Who argues back?"

"Nobody," Marta said. "Because it's obvious."

"So what's your essay for? You're just telling people something they already agree with." Juliette felt the thought click into place. "A thesis has to be a claim a reasonable person could disagree with. If it's just a plain fact nobody would dispute, there's nothing to argue. Nothing for your three points to do."

Dev finally looked up. "Then what's a good one?"

Marta chewed her cake and stared at the window. "Homework should be banned entirely," she tried.

Juliette laughed. "Okay, that one, plenty of people would fight you on that."

Marta rewrote her thesis at the top of a fresh page, and Dev started typing fast, and the club felt like a club again, everyone building at once. Juliette turned back to her own paper. School starts too early, she wrote, then crossed it out and kept going: School should start later even if it means sports practice ends in the dark. Her grandmother would say it was a waste of a Saturday afternoon, arguing on paper about school hours when she could be outside.

That night her mother read the thesis over her shoulder and frowned. "Later starts? Then I'd have to drive you in the dark instead of the light. I'd argue with that."

Juliette grinned and underlined the sentence twice.

"Good," her mother said, handing the page back. "You realize your father disagrees completely, though. He loves early starts."

Juliette sat very still. The one reasonable person guaranteed to be at her breakfast table every morning for the next four years was now her essay's perfect audience, and he was also the last person on earth she wanted to win against.

Samantha's mother worked Saturdays at the Sunrise Travel Agency, so Samantha sat in the back with the globe, doing her science homework. Her assignment sheet said: compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs. Mrs. Alvarez had printed two graphs, one for Cairo and one for Manaus, and Samantha was supposed to write a paragraph explaining what the numbers showed. The problem was that the numbers made no sense to her. Both places were hot. Manaus got over two hundred millimeters of rain in some months. Cairo got nearly zero, all year. Same sun, same planet, and one place was a swamp and the other was sand.

She spun the globe to look for a pattern, because the paragraph was due Monday and she refused to write something random just to fill the page. The Sahara. She put her finger on it. Then the Arabian Desert, then the Kalahari, then the Australian deserts, then the Atacama. She grabbed a sticky note and marked each one, then stepped back. They were not scattered. They lined up in two bands, one north of the equator and one south of it, like belts around the planet. She measured with a ruler against the globe's stand. Roughly thirty degrees north for the Sahara, and the Kalahari sat about thirty degrees south.

"So the deserts aren't random," she said. "They're all about thirty degrees from the equator. North or south."

Her mother looked up from a brochure. "The customer who comes in at noon is booking a trip to Egypt. Ask him. He's a geography professor."

When Professor Okafor arrived, Samantha had taped her graphs to the counter beside the globe with its sticky notes. She showed him Cairo's rainfall line, flat near the bottom, next to Manaus's line, jagged and towering. "These are both hot," she said. "But the rainfall is opposite. And the deserts all line up in two belts near thirty degrees. Is that the foundation of it? Is that why Cairo's line is flat?"

He leaned over the globe, tapped the Sahara, then traced south across the equator to the Kalahari. "Many of the world's hot deserts lie near thirty degrees north or south of the equator," he said. "That's where sinking air warms up and dries out."

"Where the air dries out." Samantha wrote it fast, then crossed out her old draft. "So the flat line isn't a mistake in the data. The belt is the cause." She laid the ruler across the globe again, checking the Arabian Desert against the thirty-degree mark, and slid the sticky note two millimeters to line it up exactly.

Nevaeh had sold exactly four tubs of cookie dough for the robotics club fundraiser, and the club needed to know the total by Friday. Mr. Ruiz's spreadsheet assignment was due the same day, so she decided to combine the two problems into one. She opened her laptop in the media center, typed the four names into column A, and put the dollar amounts into column B: 12, 8, 15, and 10.

"Now the formula," said Marcus, sliding into the chair beside her. He was already done with his chart and kept leaning over. "You type equals, SUM, then the range in parentheses."

"I know," Nevaeh said, though she didn't. She typed =SUM(B2:B5) the way he had said it, and pressed Enter. The cell filled with 45. That matched her own addition, which she had done on paper first, because she trusted paper.

She highlighted the four amounts and clicked the chart button. Four bars appeared, and the tallest one belonged to Priya, who had sold the 15 dollars' worth. Nevaeh dragged the chart next to the numbers and sat back. It looked finished, almost authentic, like something a real club treasurer would send out.

Then Priya herself walked by the table on her way to the printer. "That says I did fifteen," she said, pointing at the chart. "It was nineteen. Devon wrote it down wrong." Nevaeh checked her order form. Priya was right. She braced herself to redo everything, the sum and probably the chart too, the way she would have on paper. But first she changed the 15 to a 19 in cell B4, just to see.

The total became 49. Nobody had typed the formula again. The total had become 49 all by itself, and the tall bar grew taller while she watched. Nevaeh stared at the screen, then typed 15 back in, and the total dropped to 45 again. She changed it to 19 once more and left it there. "It fixes itself," she said. "The SUM watches the whole range."

"So you don't have to redo the math," Marcus said.

"Which is the whole irony of me doing it on paper first," Nevaeh said. She saved the file, attached it to an email for the club president, and wrote in the subject line: Total is 49, and it will still be right if someone finds another typo. Then she printed a copy for Mr. Ruiz, and the chart came out of the printer with Priya's bar reaching nearly to the top of the page.

Lucas had thirty minutes before his uncle's restaurant opened, and three things to finish at once: rice, curry, and a stack of chapatis. His uncle had left him alone in the kitchen on purpose, saying only, "Everything arrives at the table together, or nothing works." Last summer Lucas had let the rice go soft while he wrestled with the dough, and every dish had come out late and wrong. He had thought about that night all year, and he still wasn't sure whether giving up that shift had been smart or cowardly.

He started the rice first because it took longest, measuring the water the way his grandmother had shown him in her cramped flat, where the noise of the city never stopped. Then he chopped onions for the curry, keeping one ear on the bubbling pot behind him. The curry needed twenty minutes of simmering, he decided, and the chapatis only a minute or two each, so the flatbread would have to wait near the end. He wrote the order on a scrap of receipt paper, a small systematic plan: rice, curry, then bread.

His friend Dev pushed through the swinging door to drop off a delivery box and stopped dead. On the pan in front of Lucas, a flat circle of dough had suddenly ballooned, round and golden like a tiny moon. "It's alive," Dev said. "How does it do that?"

"Water in the dough turns into steam," Lucas said. "That's what puffs it up." He had learned it by accident. His first chapatis had come out flat and stiff, and he had stood there wondering what he'd missed. Then he remembered his grandmother flicking drops of water onto the dough before pressing it flat, and he had tested it, one dry circle, one wet one. The dry one stayed flat. The wet one rose.

"So you add more water and it puffs bigger?" Dev asked.

"I tried that. It just gets soggy." Lucas flipped the puffed chapati onto the wire rack and started the next one, glancing at the rice, then at the curry, checking his watch. "There's no monopoly on the answer. You have to test it."

The rice finished resting just as the curry thickened, and Lucas slid the last chapati onto the plate beside them, everything hot at the same moment. His uncle came through the door, looked at the three dishes, and said nothing, which Lucas took as the highest praise the man had ever given. Dev leaned against the counter, arms crossed. "Fine," he said, "but tomorrow I'm making one."

Leo's essay was due Monday morning, and by Saturday afternoon he had one paragraph, which his teacher had already crossed out because it said "heaven is where you go after you die, probably." The assignment was to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death, and Grandpa, who was Christian, had taken him to a burial at church last month, so that half was easy. The other half was the problem, until the phone rang.

"Anil's father passed this morning," Grandpa said, setting down the receiver. "The ceremony is at four. Come along, and keep your eyes open. And put on a shirt with a collar."

The Rao family lived three doors down, and their yard was full of neighbors by the time Leo and Grandpa arrived. At the far end, on a bed of wood, lay Mr. Rao's father, covered in flowers. Anil, who ran the corner store and knew Leo by name because of the ice cream budget, stood beside it, steady and quiet. His uncle touched Leo's shoulder and spoke near his ear. "We cremate our dead. The body goes back to the five elements."

Leo's hand went to his pocket, where he had a folded page of notes for the essay. Five elements. He wrote it later on the back of a bulletin from Grandpa's church, squeezed between two folding chairs: body returned to five elements. At church, the casket had gone into the ground, and the pastor had talked about resurrection and a permanent home with God. Two very different pictures, and his essay could finally stand up on both legs.

Then Anil walked him to the back fence, where a small mound of fresh earth lay under the guava tree, ringed with marigolds. "My son," Anil said. "He was six. We didn't cremate him." Leo didn't ask why, but Anil went on anyway, his voice even. "Young children we bury. Some holy people too." He knelt and set a flower on the mound. "Different, even inside one faith. Your essay will say that, I hope."

"It will now," Leo said.

That night Grandpa read the draft at the kitchen table, tapping the page with one finger. "You wrote that Anil's ice cream revenue dropped this month. What's that got to do with anything?"

"Context," Leo said, and Grandpa laughed so hard he had to put down his coffee.

On Monday Leo handed it in, and on Wednesday the teacher read one line out loud to the class: "Maybe no one can see past death directly, so every faith builds its own bridge." After school, Grandpa was waiting by the gate with the car already running.

"Ice cream," Grandpa said. "Anil's buying."

The gym smelled like floor wax and coffee, because the gym was a polling station today and Aria's civics class had been sent to run a student vote beside the real one. Her job was the Charter table. She had to get a voter to read one right from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and explain it in their own words, then write the explanation on a card for the class wall. Her teacher wanted ten cards by lunch. She had two.

The cards she had were thin. One man had read "everyone has the right to life, liberty and security of the person" and written "be safe," which was not going to pass. Aria stared at the photocopied Charter pages taped to the table and noticed something she had skipped before. Beside section 15, the equality rights, someone had written a date: 1985. Every other section said 1982.

"Grandma," she called across the table, where her grandmother stood in line for the real ballot. "Come here a second."

Grandma waved at the returning officer and stepped over, still holding her voter card. "Make it quick, they'll call my name."

Aria pointed at the page. "Why does this one say 1985? The rest say 1982."

Grandma squinted. "Section 15?"

"Equality rights. Equal protection and equal benefit of the law, without discrimination."

"Ah." Grandma tapped the number with one finger. "That one came into force in 1985. Three years after the rest."

"Three years? Why would a right be late?"

"Governments needed time to update their laws. All the old laws had to be changed to match it."

Aria wrote that down, fast, because the line was moving and a poll worker was already calling "next voter." Grandma squeezed her shoulder and went to get her ballot, and Aria sat with the fact turning in her head like a coin. Three years. The right existed on paper but waited, on purpose, so everything else could catch up.

She tested the idea out loud on the next student voter, a boy from her math class wearing a candidate's campaign button that had saturated overnight with rain, the blue ink bleeding into the white. "Pick a section," she said. "Any one."

He shrugged and jabbed at random. Section 15.

"Okay. Read it. Then tell me what it means, your words, not the book's."

He read it twice, lips moving. "It means the law can't treat you worse because of, like, who you are. And everybody gets the same protection from it."

"Good. Now the weird part." She showed him the dates. "This one started in 1985, three years after the rest. The other rights came in 1982. They gave the governments time to update their laws first."

He frowned at the page. "So they knew the laws were unfair, and they left them unfair for three more years?"

"That's not what it says."

"Feels like it, though."

Aria didn't answer. She took his card, looked at his plain words beside the delayed date, and pinned both to the class wall, where the equality card hung apart from the conventional row of 1982 sections, alone at the end of the line.

"Pins are in the cup," the boy said, and slid them across to her.

Brayden tapped his pencil against the rainfall graph for the Sonoran Desert, then against the one for the Amazon rainforest, and felt his stomach drop. Mr. Okafor had promised that whoever made the best comparison poster would get to present it at the seventh-grade science assembly, and Brayden wanted that spot more than he had wanted anything since he made the travel team. The problem was that every poster in the room looked the same so far: a cactus, some trees, two graphs, done. His wasn't going to be done. His was going to be right.

"Your rainforest line just sits there," said Priya, leaning over from the next desk. "Did you plot it wrong?"

"No, look." Brayden traced the temperature graph for the Amazon with his finger. The line hardly moved all year. The desert line, though, swung up in the summer and plunged in the winter like a roller coaster he would never be brave enough to ride. "The desert changes month to month way more. That's the whole comparison. Hot place that varies, hot place that doesn't." He wrote that on his poster and felt pretty good about it for almost ten minutes.

At lunch, his little sister Elena texted him a photo of her duffel bag, half packed, because she was leaving Friday on a school trip to Ecuador. Guess what, it said, we're going to a rainforest reserve. Then: what do I pack? Brayden typed back shorts obviously, it's hot every month, and hit send. He was the science poster kid. He knew things. Somewhere outside the cafeteria window, a kid was running a vigorous lap around the track, and Brayden watched him without really seeing him, because something was itching at the back of his mind.

That night he pulled up the climate data again, and this time he didn't skip past the second sheet, the one labeled hourly readings. The desert graph he'd memorized showed month to month. This sheet showed something else: day by day. And the rainforest's daily line jumped high at noon and sank low at midnight, over and over, a sawtooth. He grabbed a ruler and measured. The wiggle between day and night in the rainforest was bigger than the flat little yearly change on his poster. He sat back so fast his chair squeaked. He texted Elena before he could talk himself out of it. Bring a sweater. For nights. Trust me.

The next morning he rebuilt the poster around it. He found a photo of a rainforest rodent, some agouti-looking thing, curled against a leaf, and captioned it warm days, cold nights, and he made the sawtooth line the biggest thing on the page so nobody could miss it. Priya read it twice. "I thought rainforests were just hot," she said slowly. "So did I," Brayden said. "I told my sister not to bring a sweater. I was wrong." Saying it out loud felt like stepping on a scale in front of the whole class, but Priya just nodded and said, "That's the best poster in here."

Friday after school, Elena's first photo from the reserve came through: her, grinning in the dark, wrapped in a sweatshirt with the hood up, a caption underneath that said you were right, I'm freezing. Brayden laughed out loud in the kitchen, then screenshotted it and printed it in color for the corner of his poster, right beside the sawtooth line. Then he slid the poster into his backpack, carefully, flat against his books, so it wouldn't bend before the assembly.

Jordan sat cross-legged on the damp-smelling carpet of Marcus's basement, laptop warm on his knees, while the dehumidifier hummed in the corner like a sleepy robot. On the screen was his very first web page, and it was a disaster. Every single word, the heading and all three paragraphs about his dog Biscuit, had transformed into one enormous bold line that stretched past the edge of the screen. Marcus leaned over his shoulder, chewing a pretzel.

"I didn't type it like that," Jordan said. "I typed h1 in brackets before the heading, just like the tutorial."

"Then type it again and watch," Marcus said, flicking a pretzel salt off the trackpad.

Jordan retyped it, slower this time, and the page still looked like a giant had shouted across it. He sat back and stared. The computer was doing something invisible to him, something he couldn't see, and it had to have a rule behind it. Last summer, he remembered, the city pool had turned green overnight and nobody could figure out why until the lifeguard tested the water and found the chemical balance was off. Invisible cause, visible mess. He had liked that day, in a strange way. He scrolled up and down his code, looking for his own invisible cause.
